# THE STATES
# GENERAL
### OF THE
## UNITED
## NETHERLANDS,

To all those who shall see or hear these presents read, greetings. *Be it known*, that we have consented, agreed, and granted privilege, as we do consent, agree, and grant privilege by these presents to *Pieter Mortier*, Bookseller residing in Amsterdam, his heirs or those acquiring his rights, for the term of the fifteen next ensuing and consecutive years, to the exclusion of all others, within these united Provinces, Lands, Cities, and Members thereof, to be permitted to print, have printed, publish, and sell the Histories and Art-Prints of the Old and New Testaments <term>Art-Prints</term> <note>Original: "Konst-Prenten." This refers to the high-quality engravings that were the primary selling point of Mortier's Bible.</note>, counting from *the day that the aforementioned work shall be fully printed*, in all sorts of Languages and Formats, even in abridged or shortened versions of the Histories and of the Prints; forbidding any and all Residents of the aforementioned United Netherlands, Lands, Cities, and Members thereof, and specifically all Illustrators, Engravers, Printers, and Booksellers, to imitate or copy the aforementioned Plates or the Histories of the Old and New Testaments within the aforementioned term of fifteen years; to reprint or have reprinted, publish, or sell them, in whole or in part, in large or small format, in whatever language or languages, or under whatever pretext or cover it might be, directly or indirectly, whether under the appearance of reduction, improvement, or change of name or title, of whatever nature it might be, or to bring, trade, publish, or sell such reprints made elsewhere into these United Netherlands, Lands, Cities, and Members thereof, upon pain of forfeiture of the reprinted, imported, traded, or sold copies, and additionally a sum of one hundred and fifty guilders <term>guilder</term> <note>The Dutch "gulden" was the standard currency; 150 guilders was a significant fine, roughly equivalent to several months' wages for a skilled craftsman in 1700.</note>, to be applied as follows: one third part for the benefit of the Officer who shall make the seizure <note>Original: "Calange." This refers to the legal prosecution or challenge of the copyright infringement.</note>, the second third part for the benefit of the Poor, and the remaining third part for the benefit of the aforementioned *Pieter Mortier*, his heirs or those acquiring his rights; provided nonetheless that the same *Pieter Mortier* shall be bound to request and also to obtain the attachment <note>A formal endorsement or local permit required to make the federal privilege valid in specific provinces.</note> of this our Grant from those Province or Provinces where he shall wish to have the aforementioned Prints printed, offered for sale, and sold. Done at the Assembly of the High-Mentioned States General, in The Hague on the 22nd of May, Seventeen Hundred.

H. J. ROELINCK. <note>original: "vt." An abbreviation for "vidit" (seen) or "vidit ut" (seen as presiding), indicating the presiding official of the assembly.</note>

## THE STATES
### OF
# HOLLAND
### AND
## WEST FRIESLAND

Be it known: That it has been shown to us by *Pieter Mortier*, Bookseller, residing in *Amsterdam*, how he, the Petitioner <note>Original: "Suppliant." A formal term for someone submitting a request or petition to a governing body.</note>, having labored for about seven years on Art-Prints of the *Histories of the Old and New Testaments*, and for that purpose invited learned Men, Theologians, and Ministers of the Reformed Church to arrange the stories without any cause for offense and to depict the same according to truth and character; he, the Petitioner, with very great cost, effort, and labor, through the foremost artistic Painters, the best Master Draughtsmen and Engravers, has brought the work so far that never have Art-Prints belonging to Biblical Histories come to light so correct, curious, and magnificent. For the execution of which work he, the Petitioner, having had to hazard and spend very significant sums of money, and currently intending to publish the Histories of the Old and New Testaments, enriched with more than four hundred Print-depictions, cut in copper, he, the Petitioner, was concerned that possibly some profit-seeking people, by reprinting the same work, would come to grossly damage and disadvantage him, the Petitioner, and he, the Petitioner, would thus see himself deprived of the fruits of his labor and costs spent in the execution of the mentioned work. Therefore he, the Petitioner, turns to us, humbly praying and requesting that it be our gracious pleasure to grant him, the Petitioner, his Heirs, and those acquiring his Rights, a special <term>Octroy and Privilege</term> <note>Original: "Octroy en Privilegie." In this era, "copyright" did not exist as a general law; publishers had to apply for a specific government grant (an octroy) to protect a single work from being copied by others.</note>, to be permitted to print, have printed, publish, and sell the same work alone, and to the exclusion of all others, within our Lands of *Holland and West Friesland*, during the term of the fifteen next ensuing Years (counting from the day that the aforementioned work shall be fully printed), in all kinds of formats and languages, even in an abridged or shortened version of the Histories and Prints, with a prohibition to all *Draughtsmen, Engravers, Plate-printers, Book-printers, and Booksellers*, as well as to all and every person, whoever it might be, to reprint, remake, or copy the aforementioned Plates or Histories of the Old and New Testaments, or have them reprinted, published, or sold, in whole or in part, in large or small format, in whatever language or languages, or under whatever pretext and cover it might be, directly or indirectly, whether under the appearance of addition, improvement, or change of Name or Title, of whatever nature it might be, or having been כך reprinted elsewhere, to bring, trade, publish, or sell them within our Lands of *Holland and West Friesland*, all upon forfeiture of the reprinted, remade, imported, traded, or sold Copies, as well as such further fine and penalty as is usually decreed in similar cases against the Transgressors of our Octroys and Privileges, for the prevention of the Petitioner's damage. **SO IT IS**, that we, having considered the matter and request aforementioned, and being inclined to the prayer of the Petitioner out of our certain knowledge, sovereign power, and authority, have consented, agreed, and granted privilege to the aforementioned Petitioner, his Heirs, and those acquiring his rights, and do consent, agree, and grant him privilege by these presents, so that during the term of fifteen next ensuing and consecutive Years he may make, print, publish, and sell the aforementioned Art-Prints and Histories of the Old and New Testaments, which the aforementioned Petitioner currently has in hand, and no further, within our aforementioned Lands alone. Prohibiting therefore all and everyone from reprinting the aforementioned Art-Prints and Histories of the Old and New Testaments in whole or in part, or bringing, publishing, or selling those reprinted elsewhere within our same Lands, upon forfeiture of all the reprinted, imported, or sold Copies, and to forfeit a fine of three hundred guilders in addition, to be applied one third part for the Officer <note>Original: "Officier." The local legal official or prosecutor who enforced the seizure.</note> who shall make the claim, one third part for the Poor of the place where the case shall occur, and the remaining third part for the Petitioner; all on the understanding that we, wishing only to favor the Petitioner with this our Octroy for the prevention of his damage through the reprinting of the aforementioned Art-Prints, do not in any part intend thereby to authorize or avow the contents thereof, and much less to give the same any greater credit, standing, or reputation under our protection and defense, but the Petitioner, in case anything improper should be included therein, shall be held to answer for all the same at his own charge; to that end expressly desiring that if he wishes to place this our Octroy before the same Art-Prints, he shall not be permitted to make any abbreviated or contracted mention thereof, but shall be bound to print or have printed the same Octroy in its entirety, and without any omission; and that he shall be bound to bring a Copy of the aforementioned Art-Prints, bound and in good condition, to the Library of our University at *Leiden*, and to provide proper proof thereof; all upon pain of losing the effect thereof. And to the end that the Petitioner may enjoy this our Consent and Octroy as is proper, we charge all and everyone whom it may concern, that they allow the Petitioner to enjoy and use the contents of these presents quietly, peacefully, and completely, ceasing all hindrance to the contrary. Done in the Hague, under our great Seal, which we have caused to be hung here, on the 1st of April, in the Year of our Lord and Savior seventeen hundred.

->A. HEINSIUS. <note>original: "vt." - an abbreviation for "vidit," meaning "seen" or "authorized."</note><-

# PREFACE.

One can never impress the understanding of the Sacred Histories <note>original: "heylige Hiſtoriën." This refers to the narratives found within the Bible.</note> too deeply upon people, nor present them too often in various forms—provided they are sketched sincerely and according to the original account—to lead them toward reading them. It is through this reading that one can perceive the greatness of God’s works, the wonders of His Providence <note>original: "Voorzienigheyd." The protective care of God or nature as a spiritual power.</note>, and the depths of His mercy and wisdom for the salvation of mankind. It is through this that one finds the greatest examples of all kinds of virtues that have ever been seen on earth. In short, it is through this reading that the Saints are instructed, and that man learns to know the root of his own corruption, the vanity of human affairs, and the infinite happiness which God in His mercy has prepared as a reward for godliness. Furthermore, there has never been any reading so highly recommended by the Church Fathers <note>original: "Oudvaders." Refers to the influential early Christian theologians whose writings established the intellectual foundations of the faith.</note> as that of Holy Scripture. Their writings are full of praises for this Divine Book, and of the utility that lies in reading and well ruminating <note>original: "herkaauwen." Literally "re-chewing"; a common metaphor for deep, meditative study of scripture.</note> upon the same, for those who with humble—

But two things generally make people negligent regarding this reading; one is the length of the divine Scriptures, which, being all joined together, comprise such a book that the laziness of man’s spirit cannot easily adapt to it, especially when that laziness is accompanied by a scattering of thoughts, which is the usual result of the many occupations of most people: the other is the great variety of histories told in the Scripture, which often seem to cut off the thread of the History, especially in the books of the Old Testament <note>original: "Ouden Testaments"</note>. Certainly, if one understands it well, herein consists the ornament and the wealth of the divine Books, and it is that which should be a motive to read them more, and with greater attention. But then one would have to have people who are made differently than those with whom the world is full. Naturally, the mind does not like to keep itself long attentive to things that proceed from such an authority to which it ought to remain subject; and the heart finds itself under the strict rules of godliness, which it meets everywhere in Scripture, all too much in a state of confinement, to take pleasure in such a constraint, and not to escape from it as soon as it can. One cannot deny that these are the unfortunate dispositions in which the largest part of people find themselves—yes, in which we would all be—if God had not enlightened the minds of those for whom He specifically gave His writings, and touched their hearts. These are they whom the Apostle Paul <note>original: "Apostel Paulus"</note> calls *spiritual people* <note>original: "geestelyke menschen"; those who are spiritually minded or led by the Spirit</note>, who [have] the gift

# PREFACE.

[enlightened] to have a sense of the excellence of God's Word <note>original: "Góds Woord"</note>, and to distinguish the truths presented to us therein from all other readings and all the sciences with which worldly people occupy themselves, and with which they flatter the vanity <note>original: "ydelheyd"; a common 17th-century term for the fleeting or empty nature of worldly pursuits</note> of their minds. It is these to whom God, as that same Apostle says, has given *enlightened eyes of the understanding, to know what is the hope of his calling, and what the riches of the glory of his inheritance.* <note>A reference to the New Testament book of Ephesians 1:18.</note> Everything is bland and tasteless for a soul that begins to gain some taste for this; with Saint Paul, they regard all else as nothing, and view it as smoke in comparison to the knowledge of all these things.

If our lives were much longer than they are, and less troubled, we could devote a part of them—which perhaps would not be entirely lost—to various types of scholarly exercises, and make many occupations for ourselves, each according to how his nature and temperament inclined him; but since we have so little time to live as we do, and since of that little time given us to live, the two extremes—namely, childhood and old age—are hardly illuminated by the light of Reason <note>original: "Reden"</note>; just like the two poles of the world <note>original: "aſpunten der waereld"; literally "axle-points," referring to the North and South Poles</note>, which are hardly ever shone upon by the rays of the Sun; can one then prevent the mind too much from scattering itself, or bring it back too often to the only thing necessary, namely the knowledge of God and the practice in His Word? One is seized with heartache upon seeing in what manner most people spend the best of their lives; they take a thousand paths by which their spirit and heart, yearning for vanity, are exhausted. Someone involved in trade <note>original: "koophandel"</note> keeps his thoughts busy only with enriching himself, and, swept away by an earthly interest,

<note>edge of his salvation, yet</note> he almost forgets that he is a Christian, and hardly allows his gaze to fall upon the Book wherein the only interests worthy of his diligence and zeal are sealed. Another sacrifices all his time to his ambition <note>original: "staatzucht"; literally 'state-lust' or political craving</note>; he entangles himself in a thousand difficulties to surpass his rival, and when he has climbed so high that he finds himself only a few steps lower than the Throne, he feels to some extent the weight of the scepter and the crown without having the glory of them; his offices overwhelm him, and his mind is distracted by such a multitude of different matters that he does not have a single free moment to gather his thoughts and fix them on the contemplation of God's Word. What a high flight one sees clever intellects and great spirits take towards human wisdom, so that they toil night and day leafing through profane <note>original: "ongewyde"; meaning non-sacred or secular</note> writers, with no other aim than to know how the Greeks and Romans spoke more than two or three thousand years ago? And how they sweat over the difficulty they encounter regarding some word, or over some ancient customs that no one has anything to do with nowadays? One should not, however, entirely reject that kind of literary study; one must only take care not to lose oneself in it. They are excursions into rarely traveled lands to fetch from there what may serve our use; but one must return as soon as possible to make Holy Scripture one's principal study.

Could one wish enough that the world were not so filled, as it is becoming, with so many useless books, often ruinous to faith and good morals; with books that, under the charm of something new, [offer] to the curious...

Since God has, so to speak, portrayed Himself with His adorable perfections in this divine Book, the knowledge thereof is inexhaustible; and the more one tries to search into it, the more one perceives from afar its ornaments and riches. A certain Pagan Orator <note>This refers to Longinus, a Greek teacher of rhetoric, who in his treatise "On the Sublime" famously praised the literary power of the Book of Genesis.</note>, of an accurate judgment regarding the fine refinements of Eloquence, reading in Moses the history of Creation, found such a loftiness in the manner in which that divine Historian relates that God made the world, that he could not grow weary of marveling at that word, which is like the soul of that great History: *GOD SAID*, *Let there be light; and there was light.* But it is not from a single perspective—properly to satisfy the curiosity of the mind, or to fill oneself with learning—that one must read the Scripture; it is, to tell the truth, like that mystical tree, whose *leaves are for the healing of the nations* <note>original: "geneezinge der Heydenen"; a reference to Revelation 22:2</note>; its words and its idioms have their beauty and their power: but it is to the matters hidden beneath those words and beneath those idioms that one must go: everything there is great, everything there is divine.

Plato, Aristotle, Zeno, and a thousand others before them in Egypt and Assyria, and just as many or even more after them in Greece and Italy—all those great Spirits did nothing but crawl whenever they wished to raise themselves to the origin of the world, and not one of them was ever able to climb so high. One feels ashamed when reading their books, or what the Writers of their time have written regarding their sentiments; one feels ashamed, I say, to see such wandering and disorder in the human spirit: they are nothing but childishness and idle figments of the imagination <note>original: "ydele herſenſchimmen"; literally "empty phantoms of the brain," meaning groundless fantasies.</note>. The world must necessarily have had a beginning, and it cannot have had it except from a Being which itself never had one; and this eternal Being, who must have been infinitely wise and powerful to make the world, how could He have made it but through an act of supreme authority and absolute power, without any limitation—an authority which needs to do nothing other than to will and to command? This, now, is properly the idea that Moses has given us of the creation: *God said*, and the deed was done.

The particular History of the origin of Mankind was also one of those things, the knowledge of which was hidden from all the Sages and Scholars of the world. Moses has torn the veil from it, and in revealing the matter to us, he has presented to our eyes a collection of many wonders and several great mysteries, united into one. The flood <note>original: "zondvloed"; the Great Deluge of Noah's time.</note> which God sent upon the earth to destroy the humans, whom He had made masters of it, gives us such a great idea of God’s holiness, that one cannot take notice of it without giving honor to His Justice, which could not tolerate that

### THE
# TRANSLATOR
### TO THE
# READER.

Among all the **translations** <term>translations: rendered from "vertaalingen"; the act of turning text from one language into another, in this case likely from a scholarly Latin or French source into the Dutch vernacular</term>, brought to light by my pen, there has never been one which I have undertaken and brought to completion with greater pleasure and zeal than this one, and that for two reasons; the first, that the subject matter of this work is taken from the **Bible**, or the **Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments**; the other, that the description of this **History** <note>original: "Historie"; here referring to the chronological narrative of biblical events rather than "history" in the modern secular sense.</note> has been so excellently executed by the **highly learned Author**, that I doubt whether anyone could be found who could have put this on paper with greater dignity and luster, within such a narrow scope as the circumstances here required: for if one looks at the clarity, everything that appears somewhat obscure is explained and enlightened; and if one keeps an eye on the content, the virtues contained within the histories are pointed out and shown in a powerful and instructive manner, the vices painted in their true colors to deter from evil, the sacred furnishings of the **Tabernacle** <term>Tabernacle: from the Dutch "Tabernakel"; the portable earthly dwelling place of God used by the Israelites during the Exodus, described in great detail in the book of Exodus.</term>

and the Temple presented with meaningful and fitting explanations, the reverence for the Divine Majesty and its works instilled with emphasis everywhere, and in a word, everything that is in any way remarkable is presented in a charming manner; not with lowly and insipid words, but with lofty expressions, with compelling language, and where the matter requires it, with high-sounding phrases. To what extent this style has been followed in this translation is left to the judgment of the Lovers of our **Dutch language** <term>Dutch language: translated from "Nederduytsche spraake"; at the time, "Nederduytsch" was the standard term for the Dutch language, distinguishing it from "Hoogduytsch" or German.</term>; indeed, I have striven to deviate as little from the footsteps of my predecessor <note>The "predecessor" refers to the original author whose work Séwel is translating.</note> as the nature of our mother tongue could allow. ### THE
# BOOKSELLER
### TO THE
# R E A D E R .

There are no books which the people of our profession ought to print with more pleasure than those which concern the instruction of mankind in God’s Word. It was to fulfill this duty, and to follow my own inclination, that I resolved some years ago to publish a complete History of the Bible, with copper plates and prints, in which the most important stories related in the Holy History were presented to the eyes of the Reader. All the world knows how much such pictorial representations, when well made, clarify the understanding of the matters one reads, and how powerfully they assist the memory in retaining the most remarkable deeds. 

But all the world also knows well that it is very difficult to find engravers <term>Engravers: from the Dutch "Plaatsnyders," literally "plate-cutters," who etched images into copper for printing.</term> who are fully capable of giving their work that elegance of proportion, that posture and stance, and those fine and soft lines which add all the charm and ornament to such images—without which they tire the eye and are shoved into a corner of the house or left lying about in shops. To prevent such a fate from befalling the work I was undertaking, I diligently sought out the most capable and renowned masters, both in the arts of drawing and painting and in engraving, whom I could find; and I have spared no expense to pay for their labor and to encourage them to make the work as perfect and refined as possible. 

As a result, it will be easy for connoisseurs to perceive how accurately they have observed the light and dark <note>The publisher is referring to "chiaroscuro," the use of strong contrasts between light and dark to give the illusion of volume.</note>, the sunlight, moonlight, candle and torchlight, indoor lighting, shadows, dawns, cloudy skies, storms, perspectives, proportions, and generally everything that can give refinement and vividness of color to images of that nature. 

Just as I have gone to great expense to have the copper plates worked on with all conceivable accuracy for several years, so too have I applied every possible diligence to have the History printed on beautiful paper and with a new typeface, which I had specially cast for this purpose. This History was composed in French by Mr. David Martin <note>David Martin (1639–1721) was a prominent French Protestant theologian; his "History of the Bible" became a standard text for illustrated Bibles in the 18th century.</note> based on these pictorial representations, and I have sought to deliver this edition as beautiful as one could desire. I have also published this same work in two large Folios <term>Folio: the largest standard book format, made by folding a full sheet of paper only once to create two leaves (four pages).</term>, featuring much larger prints, type, paper, and volume, and even generally better and more extensively prepared; of which the Lovers of books <note>original: "Liefhebbers"; in this period, it referred to collectors or connoisseurs.</note> can obtain copies as long as they last. I shall now also publish a smaller work, which will be a short explanation of some of the most important Histories of the Bible, with French and Dutch <note>original: "Duytze"; in the 18th century, "Duytsch" was commonly used for the Dutch language as well as German.</note> verses, intended for the edifying use of children; hoping that all will be pleasing to the world.

## The Creation of the World.

### Genesis Chapter I. verses 1, 2, 3. etc.

<margin>The Year of the World 1, and before J. Christus 4004.</margin> <note>This date follows the "Ussher chronology," a 17th-century calculation that was once standard in English and Dutch Bibles.</note>
Neither great scholarly training nor a deep penetrating intellect is required to understand that the World had a beginning; one can easily be convinced of its novelty by observing the origins of all the arts, which serve as the support and binding of human society. But to go back to its first origin, and to know in what manner such a rare masterpiece was made, is something that entirely exceeds the powers of human ingenuity. God alone could have created the world, and God alone could show us the manner in which He created it. He immediately made, as Moses His Prophet tells us, an immeasurable matter, which He brought forth out of nothing, solely from the fruitfulness of His infinite power; and out of this still unformed matter, He drew all those various products of which the Universe is composed. He spent six days on this work, which He could have made in a moment, if His power were not always regulated by His will, and His will always directed by His wisdom. On the first day He made the light, which of all material beings is the purest, and most closely resembles the Divine nature; which made an ancient philosopher <note>Likely a reference to Plato or the Hermetic tradition, which often equated the Deity with light.</note> say that if he had to give a body to the Deity, he would have assigned light to it. God did so with such greatness and majesty, that at His mere word the light was brought forth: *Let there be light*, He said, and there was light. On the second day He created the Heaven, and that vast expanse of the air, which is between

<column-break/>

the Heaven and the Earth. On the third day He made a separation between the Earth and the Sea; and the Earth, which until that time had been mixed with the water and tangled beneath it, received on that day, through the blessing of its Creator, a rich fertility, which immediately caused plants, trees, flowers, and fruits to emerge from its womb. On the fourth day God created the Sun, the Moon, and all the Stars of the firmament. The fifth day was spent on the production of birds and fish, and God granted to both a power to multiply, above everything noticed in all other animals. Finally, the sixth day appeared, on which the earth, by God’s command, brought forth animals of infinitely differing kinds. God said,

> Let the Earth bring forth living souls <note>original: "leevendige zielen"; in this context, it refers to living creatures or "nephesh."</note> according to their kind;

and God, Moses adds, made the wild beasts of the earth according to their kind, to teach us that His commands are only powerful when He Himself works in His creatures that which He commands them.

Until that moment there was nothing on the earth but inanimate beings and animals devoid of reason, unable to know the beauty of the Universe, or to wonder at the mighty hand that wrought all these marvels. God then proceeded with the creation and formed man; He made him from the dust of the earth, and He poured into that dust a spiritual and intelligent soul, which is like a ray of the Divine nature. He imprinted in that soul the seal of holiness and righteousness, and through that glorious impression, man became the **image of God**. By this, God distinguished man from all the rest of the animals and made him worthy to rule over them: He Himself declared this to him and appointed him as a Lord and lawful possessor of all the fruits of the earth, and of all the animals which the Air, the Sea, and the Earth had brought forth.

<vocab>**Creation** (Schepping), **Genesis**, **God** (Gód), **Universe** (Heelal), **Moses**, **World** (Waereld), **Philosopher** (Filosoof), **creatures** (schepfelen), **image of God** (beeld Góds)</vocab>

<summary>This page describes the biblical account of the first six days of Creation, emphasizing that while human reason can grasp that the world had a beginning, only Divine revelation can explain its origins. It culminates in the creation of humanity as the "image of God," gifted with reason and dominion over the earth.</summary>
<keywords>Creation, Genesis, Six Days, Image of God, Adam, Moses, Light, Universe</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the narrative of the Creation from the previous page, specifically concluding the sixth day and addressing the theological question of why angels were not explicitly mentioned in the Genesis account. It then transitions into the description of the Garden of Eden and the four rivers.</meta>

HISTORY of the O. TESTAMENT.

brought. Thus the creation of the Universe was completed, and so the sixth day ended.

One will perhaps be astonished that Moses, in this entire narrative, makes no mention of the Angels, who are nonetheless no less God’s creatures than all the others of which he has spoken; since everything that exists, and which is not God Himself, must necessarily be God’s work. But Moses sufficiently suggested their creation in these first words: *In the beginning God created the Heaven and the Earth*; which saying, in its totality, includes everything that is in Heaven and on Earth; and according to the opinion of some theologians, when he says in the second chapter: *Thus were*

<column-break/>

*completed the Heaven and the Earth, and all their host*, in the language of Holy Scripture it is not only the stars that are called the *heavenly host*, but also the *Angels*. Furthermore, it appears from the brief manner in which Moses speaks of Heaven—of which he says nothing but in two words—that he wished to set powerful limits to curiosity, and that his primary purpose was to show us our own origin, so that he might begin from there the History of the Church, which he pursues throughout this entire book and in the following ones.

### *Adam is placed in the earthly Paradise.*

#### Genesis Chapter II. verse 1. etc.

<margin>4004 years before J.C.</margin> <note>This date refers to the Ussher chronology, a 17th-century calculation that placed the date of creation at 4004 BC.</note>
When God had created the animals, He left them to their own guidance, and let them wander in the fields and woods, according as each was driven by its natural inclination: but concerning man, God wanted to choose a dwelling place for him Himself, which had all the allurements and charms that Nature—rendered magnificent by the beauties it had received from the hand of the Creator—could offer to this King of the World. Moses gives this place, which was destined by God as a dwelling for innocent man, the name of the *Garden of Eden*, which means a *Garden or orchard of delights*. It was a vast region, situated in the loveliest quarter of the world, and planted, says the Holy Scripture, with every tree desirable to the sight and good for food. *The tree of Life, and the tree of Knowledge of good and*

<column-break/>

*evil* are distinguished from all the others; they were planted in the middle of Paradise, and placed as if opposite one another, so that man could better cast his sight upon them, and make such observations upon them as those magnificent and profound names, which God had given to those trees, deserved.

Four great rivers watered the Garden of Eden; the *Tigris*, in Holy Scripture called *Hiddekel*, flowed from one side, and the *Euphrates* from the other; these subsequently having joined their waters at the place where the famous city of Babel was built shortly after the flood, flowed through the middle of that vast field to which Moses gives the name of the *Garden of Eden*, where, dividing again into two branches, they formed those two other rivers which Moses calls *Pison* and *Gihon*, and which caused their waters to flow through a portion of Paradise.

In this delightful place it was that God placed man, so that he should taste all the innocent pleasures that were in accordance with his physical and animal nature, as long as his soul, at the sight of all those objects, [applied itself] to the contemplation 
<meta>The catchword "van" (of) indicates the next page begins with the continuation of "contemplation of..."</meta>

Adam received the command, when he entered the Garden of Eden, to cultivate it. Not that the earth—which was not yet soiled by sin, and which felt itself permeated by that abundant fertility which God had poured out upon it during creation—would not have brought forth, of its own accord and without labor or agriculture, all kinds of plants and fruits for the benefit of man, whom God had appointed as its Lord, and whom Heaven beheld with great pleasure and affection; but God desired from man that zeal and diligence regarding agriculture, so that it might serve in some way as a counterweight to that self-love <note>original: "eygenliefde"</note> with which he might have been flattered, had he seen all of Nature busy in his service as if by itself. At the same time, God confirmed the gift He had made to him of the fruits of the earth, and placed it in his power to eat of everything that in his judgment was the most choice and delicious in Paradise; yes, He did not even exclude from this the *Tree of Life* <note>original: "Boom des Leevens"</note>, which, possibly through a supernatural power, could have maintained man’s body in that happy condition which God

<column-break/>

Himself had formed within it; or which at least (which is also quite as probable) would have served man as an assurance and pledge that neither death, nor old age and decay, would ever have approached him, so long as he maintained his innocence. It was only the fruit of a single tree that God did not allow Adam to eat; this tree was named *the Tree of the knowledge of good and evil* <note>original: "de Boom der kennisse des goeds en des quaads"</note>; not that this fruit, by some natural power, gave knowledge; but because God, having forbidden it under penalty of death, intended that man, by looking upon that fruit, would learn the good that lay in obeying God, and the evil that lay in disobedience toward Him. God's prohibition contained in itself no severity at all: on the contrary, we should note here that a God who had made man master of everything, and who had reserved nothing for Himself but the fruit of one tree alone—just like a mighty King who gave all his cities and provinces to someone, without keeping for himself anything other than a small coin as an acknowledgment of his supremacy—undoubtedly deserved an absolute love and reverence.

## *Adam gives names to all the animals, and God creates the Woman from one of his ribs.*

### Genesis Chapter II. verses 19. 20.

After God had placed man in the earthly Paradise, He caused all the animals to come before him, so that he might give to each a name that suited it according to its nature. It must truly have been a very pleasant spectacle for man to see that the

<column-break/>

beasts of the field arrived from all sides, and the birds settled themselves close to him. A secret command from the Creator of all things, which those animals obeyed without knowing it, caused them all to assemble in one place. It was a kind of homage which they came to perform for man, as their Lord and Master; and consequently, it sprang from the supreme authority which God had given him over them, that he gave them such names as he pleased. Since Adam's understanding was not yet darkened by sin, he knew, at the mere sight of all those different kinds of animals, that which a long experience has since taught us regarding nature

One still finds many of these in the Hebrew language, which was the tongue that Adam used, from which one can judge how well the names he gave to the animals fit each of their kinds. Thus, in that language, the ox bears a name that signifies the steadfastness with which that animal treads; the stork is called by a name that expresses the affection which, according to the accounts of Naturalists, the young of that species show to their mother. <note>The Hebrew word for stork is *chasidah*, which shares a root with the word for "kindness" or "piety."</note> The ostrich, on the other hand, is signified by a name that expresses the hardness which it displays toward its young, since it takes no care for them but exposes them to all kinds of accidents, according to what Job remarks concerning this in the 39th chapter of his book. But nothing expresses that deep knowledge which Adam had of the animals—giving them names according to their innate nature—better than the account which Moses gives of it: *When the Lord God, he says, had made out of the earth every beast of the field, and every bird of the air, he brought them to Adam to see what he would call them; and whatever Adam called every living soul, that was its name:* for from this it clearly appears that Adam had such a certain and extensive knowledge of all things that he could not be mistaken in them.

Until now, man was alone and had no companion of his own kind, as did all the other animals that had appeared before him. God then made one for him, so that he might share his happiness and joy with her, and that they

<column-break/>

might together show to their Creator the duties that are due to Him. He did not wish to form her from the dust of the earth, as He had formed the man, but He took her from the man himself, so that the woman, being a part of the man—namely, flesh of his flesh and bone of his bones, as the Holy Scripture says—there might be a mutual and tender affection between them. God then caused a deep sleep to come over Adam, which, holding all his senses bound and clouded, took from him the knowledge of what He was about to do. Thereupon God took from him one of his ribs and closed the flesh again so tightly that no scar nor any defect remained. It was easy for that wise and Almighty hand, which had made man from the clay of the earth, to take a rib from the man without thereby doing any harm to his perfection. From that rib, God made a woman for him, and Adam, having awakened, perceived through a divine revelation that she had been taken from his flesh and bone: therefore he received her from the hand of God, who offered her to him as a companion who would be his other self, with whom he must remain closely united forever. In all this, God had some very secret and profound purposes, which the Apostle Paul makes known to us in the fifth chapter of his Epistle to the Ephesians; from which we learn to worship the ways of God with a respectful silence when we cannot grasp them due to their height and depth.

...retained a guilty soul, after he and his Angels—who were of a spiritual nature—had miserably fallen from their first holiness and were banished from Heaven forever, he forged a plot to lead man into mutiny. He immediately judged that to better carry out his design, he should approach the Woman directly; whether because he believed she had less knowledge of God's prohibition than her husband (to whom God had given the command), or because he, being shrewd and discerning, knew she was more susceptible to outside impressions than Adam, who was the Head. He then had to take on a visible form to speak with Eve; for this, the human form would have been the most suitable, but that deception would have been too easily discovered, because the Woman well knew there was no one in the whole world of their kind except herself and her husband. He then took a Serpent, an animal by nature cunning and crafty, and which in that first time of man’s innocence had nothing about it that one needed to shun or fear approaching, as it did after the sin. To the tongue of this animal, the Devil gave such a bending and movement, which it did not have by nature, by which he made it able to speak, giving it at once thoughts and reasoning. It is highly strange that Eve did not conceive any mistrust of this trick, since it is not natural for a beast to speak: but she, being filled with wonder at God's works and not daring—against what her eyes saw and her ears heard—to conclude that there was no one but man who had received the use of speech from the Creator, had no evil suspicion of the Serpent, and even less of the Devil, whose nature and crimes she likely did not yet know. The Serpent then approached the Woman, and pretending to take an interest in her affairs, he skillfully gave her to understand that it pained him to see that God had forbidden her from eating such a rare and choice fruit as that of the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and

<column-break/>

Evil. It is true, said Eve, God has given us that prohibition on pain of death; but he has given us all the other fruits that grow in Paradise. "That is but a threat," said the Serpent, "which he will not carry out. God has not made you so excellent only to kill you for the fruit of one tree; he only wants to prevent you from becoming wiser, and that through that wide extent of knowledge which you still lack, you do not become like Gods." This conversation was suited to flatter the human heart, which is by nature inquisitive; and the uncommon beauty of the forbidden fruit, which perhaps seemed even more beautiful because of the prohibition, helped not a little to awaken desires in the heart of the woman which she should have fended off. Curiosity was thereupon stirred up, the desire for the forbidden fruit ignited, and the understanding being enchanted by delusions, the heart failed, and the hand plucked the fruit which she was forbidden to touch. Eve ate of it, and satisfied her lust in defiance of her duty. She did even more: Adam as yet had no part in her crime, so she sought to involve him in it as well; and to all misfortune, this design succeeded; Adam let himself be talked over by his wife, he received from her hand the deadly fruit which she had eaten, and he ate of it as well as she. Moses has kept the name of that fruit secret from us, and since reasons of deep wisdom moved him to do so, it is also wisdom for us not to wish to know it, and to make no useless efforts to discover it. Through that disobedience which Adam and Eve committed, sin entered the world, and through sin, death: and that fruit, which Eve believed would be an inexhaustible fountain of knowledge, has been—by a righteous judgment of God—the cause of all our errors, and has overwhelmed Mankind with the thickest darkness of ignorance and blindness, which can be dispelled only by the supernatural Light of Grace.

### The punishment of Adam and Eve and their expulsion from Paradise.
### Genesis Chapter III. verses 16–23.

---

<margin>4004 years before J.C. <note>original: "J.C." refers to Jesus Christ. This date reflects the traditional Ussher chronology of the Bible common in the 17th and 18th centuries.</note></margin>
The first effect which the fruit of the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil produced in Adam and Eve, after they had eaten of it, was the knowledge of the crime involved in being disobedient to God. The Scripture says that their eyes were opened, to signify that they then openly saw the filthiness of their mistake, from which—at the time they committed it—lust, pride, and various other passions together had turned their sight away. They then felt the arrow that the Devil had shot into their soul; and the deadly poison of sin penetrating to the innermost part of their conscience, as the juice of the forbidden fruit spread through their veins, they felt themselves pinched by a cruel remorse that left them no rest. Upon hearing the rustling of a wind that rose in the Garden, they fled before their Judge, whose voice they thought they heard, and whom they feared they would find everywhere. They ran from

In that moment, He declared His decree: the Serpent, which had served as a tool for the Devil, was doomed to eat dust and to grovel in the dirt; and the Devil was doomed to be eventually defeated and cast to the earth by a Son <note>This refers to the "Protoevangelium," the first messianic prophecy in the Bible, interpreted by Christians as the future victory of Jesus over Satan.</note> who was to be born of this woman whom he had deceived. The man was made subject to the necessity of cultivating the earth—upon which a curse had descended due to his rebellion—with toil and in the sweat of his face; and that earth would often produce nothing for all his trouble but thistles and thorns. To the woman, God foretold that she would bring no children into the world except with deadly pains, and He commanded that she should stand under the dominion of her husband. In short, they were both doomed to death, and Adam heard that terrible sentence which was pronounced against him and his wife: *You are dust, and to dust you shall return.* It is true, the execution did not immediately follow the sentence; God, who had not permitted the fall of man except to create from that first crime the material for exercising His mercy in the redemption of the human race, allowed those criminals to live until the time appointed in His eternal Council, so that they might bring children into the world and the earth might be populated with people. Meanwhile, Adam and Eve were driven out of the Garden of Eden, being unworthy to dwell in such a delightful place; and so that these rebels—who, at a time when nothing was lacking for their happiness, had the audacity to lay hands on the forbidden fruit—should not show similar recklessness by trying to return to the Paradise from which they saw themselves banished after their state had become so miserable, God had the same guarded by Angels. These Angels, armed with flaming swords, deprived man of all hope of ever approaching the Garden of Eden again. What he now

<column-break/>

found most difficult of all, and what inflamed his desires, was a tree that was the glory and wealth of Paradise: namely, the *Tree of Life*. He sighed only for the fruit of this tree, imagining that if he could eat of it, he would not die. This was an error and a delusion with which Adam occupied his mind in that extremity to which he saw himself brought, when his soul was besieged from all sides. But the fruit of the Tree of Life had no virtue or power except for the innocent man; and once Death had gained an entrance into the heart of man along with sin, there is nothing more in Nature powerful enough to drive it out and give life back to a sinner. It was not, then, strictly in the fruit of that Tree, but in the innocence of man, that life resided. It served only as a symbol, containing a mystery, that this famous tree bore the name of the Tree of Life; because it was the sign of the covenant and the pledge of life, which God would have preserved eternally in man if he had always remained holy. But man sinned, and through his sin he lost at once the right to life and to the sign of the covenant of life. Adam did not immediately make these observations, which the agitation of his spirit and the terror of his conscience prevented him from making; and it was to show how much that man—who had imagined he would be ignorant of nothing when he had eaten of the fruit of the Tree of Knowledge—had, on the contrary, become dull and foolish by eating that fruit, that God said: *Behold, the man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil: now, therefore, let him not stretch out his hand and take also from the Tree of Life, and eat, and live forever.* <note>The author interprets God's words here as divine irony or a rhetorical way to highlight Adam's self-deception, rather than a literal fear that Adam could achieve immortality while in a state of sin.</note> For these words served only to signify the deceit with which Adam misled himself after the fall, and in no way reflected what God Himself thought about those matters.

## The Offering of Cain and Abel.
### Genesis Chapter IV. verses 3, 4, 5.

<margin>The year of the world 130. Before J.C. 3874.</margin>
The first child that Adam and Eve brought into the world was born with all the inclinations of a sinner. Vice passed from father to son along with nature itself, and it is a law that has never allowed any exception in the course of centuries, nor ever will: namely, that from a sinful father, sinful children are born. However, Eve did not look so far ahead at once; instead, enraptured with joy because she saw what she had never seen before—namely, that a human creature was born—she cried out in the first ecstasies of her wonder and joy: *I have gotten a man from the LORD*, and to that end, she gave her child the name *Cain*, which means an *acquisition* <note>The Hebrew name *Qayin* is traditionally linked to the verb *qanah*, meaning "to get" or "to acquire."</note>. Some even doubt whether she did not mean to say that she had obtained *the man of the Lord*, namely, that son of blessing and promise who would take vengeance on behalf of the Woman, and at the same time on behalf of all humanity, for the deception of the Serpent, and crush that enemy's head <note>This refers to the "Protoevangelium" mentioned on the previous page—the promise that the offspring of the woman would defeat evil.</note>. Her words could bear that meaning, and it is quite probable that a mother, as distressed as Eve was because she had brought death into the world through her crime, would draw such great hope for her comfort from this first son whom God had given her. After him *Abel* was born, whose name—which means the *instability* and *vanity* of a thing, or *mourning* and *sadness* <note>The Hebrew name *Hevel* (Abel) literally translates to "vapor" or "breath," suggesting something fleeting.</note>—could be regarded as an effect of the remorse Adam and Eve constantly felt for falling from their original state, or as an omen of

<column-break/>

the short life of this second son, whose death would one day be so painful to them. Cain devoted all his diligence and labor to agriculture, and Abel was a shepherd. But if their occupations were different, their inclinations were even more so. Cain was proud and haughty, loving nothing but himself and considering himself alone worthy of Heaven's favors. Abel, on the other hand, was gentle and humble, sighing under the weaknesses of Nature and finding his highest pleasure in godliness. Nevertheless, Cain had this in common with Abel: that he, like his brother, made a profession of religion. For Impiety and godlessness, in a time so close to the Creation, had not yet dared to raise their heads from the abyss and show themselves in the world. Cain showed submission to God with the fruits of the land, and Abel offered Him the firstborn of his flock—namely, the finest and fattest that his sheepfold produced. On a certain day when they solemnly made their offerings to God, God declared Himself for Abel and testified through a clear and glorious sign that He favorably accepted his offering. Moses does not tell us what kind of sign God gave; but his silence suggests enough that it was the same as that which God used in the time of that Prophet, and in following centuries, on similar occasions. It was a fire that descended from Heaven upon the offering and consumed the entire sacrifice; for God declared through that symbol that the offering, which in Scripture is called the *Food of God* <note>original: "Spyze Gods"</note>, was pleasing to Him—just as food we enjoy eating is to our taste, so that we leave nothing of it. It was not the sacrifice itself that pleased God and made Him favorable; for in the fiftieth Psalm He Himself declares the following regarding this:

## The Murder of Abel.
### Genesis Chapter IV. verses 8, 9.

<column-break/>

<margin>The same year.</margin>
The offering of Cain did not have the same outcome as that of Abel, for God did not look upon it. It was not that the material of which it consisted was not good in itself, for it was the first fruits of the products of the land; and God, who later demanded the same from His people Israel as an acknowledgment of the gift He had made them of the land of Canaan, would not have refused them at a time when He had placed man in possession of the entire earth, if there had been nothing else wrong. But God, who always looks more at the heart than at the offering, did not find in Cain's heart the required dispositions to make his gifts acceptable. Faith had to be present, for *without faith it is impossible to please God*; and Cain had no faith. Being devoid of this heavenly virtue, he also lacked all others, and in their place were nothing but false virtues or actual vices. Thus, instead of humbling himself when he saw his gifts despised, and appeasing God through his tears and prayers, he complained about it as

<column-break/>

if it were some injustice; he became angry with Abel, who had been set above him, and envy began to extinguish in him that tender friendship which Nature inspires toward a brother, but of which he had never been very sensitive, because the wicked never bear a perfect love for godly people. He took a resolution to remove from his sight forever that brother whose happiness had become his torment, and whose honor had become his shame. To prevent such a wicked and horrific design, God—seeing Cain completely dismayed and troubled—had even taken care to comfort him, by assuring him that his offerings would be accepted in the future as well as Abel's, provided that he, like his brother, had good inclinations and did nothing but what was fair and just. *Why are you angry?* the Lord said to him, *and why has your countenance fallen? Is there not, if you do well, an uplifting? Will your offering not then be accepted?* <note>A translation of Genesis 4:6-7. The "uplifting" refers to the acceptance of the sacrifice or the lifting of Cain's downcast face.</note> This should have been enough to awaken joy in a good heart; but Cain did not value the honor of making himself pleasing to God and seeing his offerings well-received so highly. He wanted to be wicked while his brother was righteous. If he could have avenged himself on God, he would not have been too good for it.

To commit this horrific murder more freely, he lured his brother out into the field: Abel went there with his integrity, and Cain with his treacherous heart. That which deception had begun was completed by madness; Cain fell upon his brother and struck him dead. The earth, which daily hides so much innocent blood, could not keep this blood hidden: God saw it and immediately took the vengeance to heart. He asked Cain where his brother was: *I do not know*, answered this villain, whose hands were still stained with the blood they had shed; and adding boldness and godlessness to the murder, he said, *Am I my brother's keeper?* But God convicted and cursed him. Upon hearing this sentence, terror crept into his breast; despair was pictured on his face; everywhere it seemed to him that he saw his brother's blood; he fled without knowing from whom he fled, or where he went, and a thousand times he would have succumbed under the agitation and the terrors that assaulted him, had not the same Justice that pursued him left him alive, to give in his person to future ages a venerable monument 

<column-break/>

of the interest it took in the avenging of innocent blood. Moses says that the *LORD set a mark upon Cain, so that anyone who found him in the future, when the earth would begin to be populated, would not kill him.* Curiosity has long sought, and still seeks, what that mark might have been, and almost all the world has believed that it was a letter <note>Historically, some traditions suggested the Hebrew letter 'Vav' or 'Yod' was marked on his forehead.</note> that appeared on Cain's face, and a constant trembling that showed in his whole body. But that is adhering too much to the literal letter; humans put visible marks on everything they desire not to be mixed with other things; the Hebrew painted the posts of his house door with the blood of the Passover lamb; and Rahab marked her house with the scarlet cord: but although God in His Scriptures speaks to us as a human, to accommodate Himself to our ways, He nevertheless acts as God, and not as a human; and His mark in any matter is His will and His decree regarding that matter; and this decree is unshakeable, and never fails to be executed. Such in Ezekiel was the letter *thau* <note>original: "thau" (the Hebrew letter Tav). In Ezekiel 9:4, this mark was placed on the foreheads of the righteous to protect them.</note>, or the mark set on the foreheads of the Israelites whom God wished to preserve in the slaughter He had carried out in Jerusalem; and such also was the mark He set on Cain, namely the decree to prevent, through His Providence, anyone from killing him.

Adam lived then nine hundred and thirty years: it was long in comparison to us, whose days pass by like a *shadow*, and whose 

<column-break/>

We do not find that God ever extended human life longer, even in those first ages, when His wisdom allowed men to live long so that they might populate the world and, through long experience, invent necessary arts for the common good; and also so that, in a time when writing was not yet in use, and when the memory of the most remarkable events was preserved only through tradition <note>oral transmission from generation to generation</note>, the fathers, during a long series of generations, could tell the history of the first origin of Mankind, and alongside that, the history of the world, to their children and grandchildren. Adam still lived two hundred years after the birth of Methuselah, and Methuselah six hundred years after that of Noah, and up to the year of the Flood; which made the tradition of that time so certain and easy, that it was preserved entirely in its integrity, and with all its circumstances, within those households.

...flourish. If his example had not possessed enough power to suppress the godlessness in the descendants of Cain and to breathe the fear of God into them, it at least ought to have strengthened the others in their holy course and instilled in them a new zeal for Heaven. But the evil inclination of the heart gained the upper hand over the good examples of Enoch, and over the wise caution which the godly Enos had long before exercised to prevent his tribe from mingling with that of Cain. *The sons of God*, says Moses, *took them wives, and went in unto the daughters of men.* These "Sons of God" were the descendants of Seth, whom God regarded as His own household, and upon whom He poured out His Spirit of grace and holiness; men, it is true, like others, and children of Adam just as they were; but who nevertheless bore the image of God—which the others no longer possessed—and who, as the Apostle Peter says, had become *partakers of the divine nature* in righteousness and holiness, which are its most brilliant rays. The people with whom the sons of God now allied themselves were of Cain’s lineage, entirely of flesh and earth, merely human as one sprung from Adam, without anything spiritual or divine. The beauty of the daughters of men seized the eyes of the children of Seth and wounded their hearts; so that they desired them in marriage and, listening to nothing but their passions, took them as wives. It was then that the two lineages, which divided all of mankind and had remained separated for more than twelve centuries, began to intermingle and confuse one another. Then, for the first time, were seen those monstrous marriages where light, so to speak, entered into a kinship with darkness, virtue with vice, and faith with unbelief—an offensive example seen all too often since in Solomon, and in the Jews of the Babylonian captivity, and still seen all too often daily. Just as the children of God could not ally themselves with the daughters of men—disregarding the honor of being God’s chosen people and His precious, select jewel—without exposing their religion to almost inevitable danger, so God 

<column-break/>

was greatly provoked thereby and decided to take vengeance for it. "It has gone too far," He says, "I shall no longer share my spirit with such fleshly men, who make so little of my covenant; it is necessary that I hand them over to my justice, and that they all be destroyed. Yet I still wish to give them some time to reconsider; I grant them one hundred and twenty years; and if, after such a long delay, I still find them in disorder, I shall remove them from the earth and root out their name from under heaven." This is essentially the meaning and content of the complaint that God makes regarding this in the sixth chapter of Genesis. And Moses adds another expression that makes us sufficiently understand how violently and sharply it grieved God to see His people thus degenerate from the godliness of their fathers and mingle with the impure lineage of the cursed Cain. *It repented the Lord*, he says, *that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him at his heart.* The ingratitude of man must truly have been great, and his vices hideous, for it to trouble a God who is so good and so patient to have brought forth a creature on the earth which appeared before His eyes as nothing other than a terrible monster. To speak the truth, this language of Moses is entirely figurative <note>original: "verbloemd," meaning veiled or metaphorical</note>; for strictly speaking, God never experiences repentance or torment; evil can never go so far as to cause Him pain; and insofar as He is always blessed in Himself, nothing can disturb His joy. As He is also infinitely wise, He can never be mistaken in what He does; and as nothing happens that He has not foreseen (for the present and the future stand equally before His eyes), He can never have repentance for what He has made. But on such occasions, and many others like them, we ought always to remember that the Scripture speaks to humans, and that the Holy Spirit, to accommodate Himself to our understanding, uses our ways of speaking so that we might trace His meaning and attribute nothing to God that is unbecoming of Him. Thus, God's wrath is His justice; and His repentance for having made man was the decree He made to destroy all of mankind through a general deluge.

### Noah builds the Ark to protect himself from the flood
#### Genesis Chap. VI. verses 14–22.

<margin>* The year of the world 1536. Of Noah’s age 480. Before J.C. 2468.</margin>
That which a certain Prophet has said of God—that when He has caused grief, He will also have compassion, or, that at the very time He is angry, He is also mindful to have mercy—was proven true in a wonderful way when He made the decree to root out the people on the earth. He looked upon Noah and his entire household with a favorable eye and did not wish him to be involved in the general destruction of mankind. Noah was a holy man, a worthy follower of the virtues of Enoch his great-grandfather, and walked, like him, with God. But his godliness did not limit itself to himself and his own conduct; it

<column-break/>

also took an interest in that of others. This righteous man, seeing the lawlessness that was committed daily, grieved over it as if over his own sins; and with all the fervor and steadfastness which a zeal for God's glory breathes into a holy soul, Noah rebuked the vices and labored for the conversion of sinners. For this reason, the Apostle Peter calls him the *Preacher of righteousness*, and the Apostle Paul proclaims the praise of his faith in the eleventh chapter of the Epistle to the Hebrews. With such uncommon qualities, it could not be otherwise than that he must be pleasing to God; and God—who, as Abraham said, is not inclined to *destroy the righteous with the wicked*—could not allow such a pious life to be extinguished in the waters of the flood. To protect him from it, God commanded him to build an Ark, and provided him with a design for it Himself.

One cannot see from the description which Moses has left us that it had the shape of our ships; it had no masts, sails, nor rudder; nor was it the hand of man that was to steer it. Through such reasonings and light-hearted conversations, the people of that time hardened themselves in their unrepentance and continued in their sinning. Noah had to endure their stinging remarks for one hundred and twenty years, and defend himself against the temptations with which an abyss of unbelief and mistrust—natural to all men—constantly assaulted his faith. But just as his patience endured the mockery of the sinners, so his faith achieved victory over the temptations of his own heart, and has thus earned being presented as an example to all the ages of the Church.

Noah had received a command from God to take a male and a female of every kind of animal, whether they fly in the air or walk upon the earth, without even excluding the creeping creatures that swarm in the dust, so that the species might be preserved and might multiply after the flood just as they had before. And regarding the clean <term>clean: animals considered ritually pure for food or sacrifice under later Jewish law</term> animals, of which the Law of Moses later gave a precise and detailed list, Noah was commanded to take seven pairs of each kind, so that he might be able to make various offerings from them. One sees from this how ancient the distinction between clean and unclean animals is: just as one kind is by nature no cleaner or more unclean than another—at least regarding that sort of uncleanness which involves something moral and affects the soul of man—and since only a command or a prohibition from God could have made such a distinction, God must necessarily have noted this from the beginning of the world and commanded it Himself in the offerings, since it was primarily for the purpose of the offerings that this distinction was made. All the care and diligence that Noah could have applied to gather so many different kinds of animals together would have been insufficient to carry out the command he had received in every part; but God relieved him of that trouble. Just as He had previously led all the animals before Adam, so that he might give them their names, so now for the second time He caused those same animals to come before Noah, so that he

<column-break/>

Some came, gliding on their wings, to present themselves before Noah, and without being startled by the presence of a human, they humbled themselves under the hand that reached out to take them. Others came walking or running, according to whether Nature had given them light or heavy feet; and those to whom she had not been so generous came only slowly, and with much difficulty, crawling along. Noah received them all and placed them in the Ark. Upon entering, they all abandoned their shy, or wild, or fierce nature which they had before, and which they took up again after their departure: yet it was not so much the partitions that Noah had made in the Ark that brought about peace and harmony there, as it was the internal change which God, through a special direction of His Providence, brought about in those animals. After them, Noah's three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth, with their wives, and Noah with his spouse—in all eight persons, who were the only ones in the world whom God wished to protect from the waters of the flood—went into the Ark. It was in the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, and the sixteen hundred and fifty-sixth after the creation of the world, in the second month—which is considered to correspond in part with our Slaughter-month <note>Slagtmaand: the traditional Dutch name for November, when livestock were typically slaughtered for winter</note>—on the seventeenth day of that month, that all the animals, and with them Noah and his household, finished going into the Ark. After that, the Ark was closed; and God, having nothing more to wait for to carry out His threats, delayed no longer in sending the Flood over the earth.

# The Form or Shape of Noah’s Ark.

### Genesis Chapter VI. verses 15. 16.

PEople have much difficulty understanding how Noah could have placed all the species of animals, and all the necessary provisions to keep them alive for an entire year, within the Ark. But to clear away the primary difficulties that one might raise in this regard, one need only observe the size of the Ark and its internal arrangement. The Ark was three hundred cubits <note>original: 'ellen', a unit of measurement based on the length of the forearm</note> long, fifty wide, and had thirty in height, from which Noah made three stories, giving to each more or fewer cubits according to the use for which it was intended. The first of these three stories was designed to receive the four-footed beasts; but because these are very different in shape, and also in size—indeed, even in nature, whereby for the most part they cannot get along with one another—God commanded Noah that he should partition the space into stalls, so that he could put animals of one and the same kind in each stall. It was not necessary for Moses to show us exactly how that Holy Patriarch went to work in that regard to follow the plan which God had given him: one can easily understand that God guided his hand in that whole work, and that He imprinted in him all the understanding and insight necessary to complete the same. The number of species of four-footed animals that are substantially different does not extend nearly so wide as one might imagine. Possibly there are only very few that have escaped the diligent investigation which many persons at various times in all parts of the known world have made of them; yet one counts in total no

<column-break/>

more than about one hundred and thirty species <note>The author reflects 17th/18th-century natural history; modern science identifies thousands of mammal species</note>; and even assuming there were a third more—which, after all the effort expended and costs incurred to know and identify them all, one can hardly imagine—there was still space enough in a span of three hundred cubits long and fifty wide for more stalls than were needed, and to give to each stall as much space as was required according to the size of the beasts that had to be placed there. If one has but a little knowledge of Geometry <term>Geometry: original 'Landmeetkunde', literally land-measuring or surveying</term> and reflects upon it with some attention, one can easily make that calculation. Each stall must have had its grates, whether small or large, through which to let the filth of the animals fall to the bottom floor; and because they had to be arranged in such a way that Noah and his sons could walk to bring the necessary fodder and water to the beasts confined therein, one can easily imagine that they were all made in a row, and that there were many aisles throughout the length and breadth of the Ark through which Noah and his sons could go in all directions. In the illustration seen here, many species of four-footed beasts are shown, which were placed in the lowest story; and by placing this sketch before one’s eyes, the intent is only to assist the reader’s understanding in forming a reasonable idea for themselves of how the matter could have been, without claiming that Noah would have strictly kept to the plan given in this print. But just as it would be reckless to positively assert a matter that is so uncertain, so it would also not be very reasonable to deny that it could have been so.

## The Flood.

### Genesis Chapter VII. verses 11---24.

<margin>
The year of the world 1656. Before J.C. <note>Before Jesus Christ</note> 2348.
</margin>

No sooner had Noah entered the Ark, than the air grew dark, the sky became overcast with clouds, the rain poured down in abundance, the sea overflowed its shores, the rivers swelled out of their beds and flowed over the fields, the smallest brooks became great floods, and the waters that roll through the hollows and openings of the earth—and, as if through so many veins, moisten this enormous body—came forth by new paths to join those of the heavens, the rivers, and the sea; and the earth was submerged. Scripture says, with its usual loftiness and majesty when it speaks of God’s judgments, that the fountains, or the dikes, of the great abyss were broken up, and the floodgates of heaven were opened. By the one, it represents the inundation of the sea, which—no longer restrained by the respect it bears for the marks that the finger of its Creator had imprinted upon its shores, nor by the prohibition given to it not to drive the swelling of its water-waves any further—

<column-break/>

rose up entirely enraged from the depths of its whirlpools, and with a terrifying noise and an unruly rage, came running from all sides to carry out the vengeance of a provoked God, who makes the winds His Angels and the waves His servants. And by these floodgates of heaven being opened, Moses <note>The traditional author of Genesis</note> depicts for us somewhat that region of the air where the clouds gather, like a suspended sea, whose waters God allowed to burst loose from all sides, so that they crashed down upon the earth with plunging and overwhelming floods. This terrible spectacle lasted forty days and forty nights without ceasing. Bewilderment and terror spread everywhere with the waters of the flood: then everyone thought, but all too late, of Noah's prophecies, and each attempted to save his life. But where can one flee from God's presence? His piercing eyes sought the criminals even in the most remote deserts and on the thick tops of the highest trees; indeed, no sooner had these wretched people found a hiding place than the water reached them: they immediately ran to another, but with just as little luck as they had run to the first; often the water surprised them on the way, or when they had wasted all their strength with running,

The waters rose to the highest peaks of the mountains, indeed, they swelled **fifteen cubits** <note>original: 'ellen'; an 'el' was a traditional Dutch unit of measurement, but in the context of the Bible, it refers to the 'cubit,' approximately the length of a forearm</note> higher: the Ark alone, tossing upon the waters and burdened with the **precious pledge** <note>This refers to the remnant of humanity and animal life entrusted to Noah's care</note> committed to it, was neither submerged nor damaged by those pitiless waves, which turned the earth into a second **chaos** <note>original: 'baijerd'; a term for a confused mass or the primordial state of the world before creation</note>. The intellect of men, which wishes to know everything and find the cause of all things, examines from where such a massive flood could have come; and being unable to conceive that the sea and the clouds could have provided such a great quantity of water, it is tempted to believe that the Deluge was not universal, and that God did not send it except over the lands inhabited by men, because it was only the men whom He wished to punish. But the words of Moses are too explicit to be thus invalidated. *The waters*, he says, *prevailed exceedingly upon the earth; so that ALL the high mountains that are under the*

<column-break/>

*WHOLE heaven were covered.* Reason is shocked by this account, but faith finds nothing difficult in it; it remains assured that God can do all that He wills, and that His Word says nothing but what is true. Even in secular histories, the difficulties one finds in understanding how various events described there could have happened are not always a sufficient reason to call them into doubt; even though one knows that the men who wrote those histories are subject to being deceived and to deceiving others. Why then should Reason refuse such an equal, or even greater, reverence to a book dictated by the Holy Spirit, solely on the pretext of difficulties found in a history recounted therein? Moses did not wish to instruct us in the natural causes of the Deluge as a **philosopher** <note>In this historical context, 'philosopher' refers to what we would now call a 'natural scientist'</note>, but as a believer: and we must humbly remain still where he himself remained still; especially because he has told us elsewhere—to instill in us a reverence even for the silence of Scripture—that *the secret things belong to the Lord, and those that are revealed belong to the children of men.* <note>A reference to Deuteronomy 29:29</note>
