# HISTORY of the O. TESTAMENT. 13

them, and He gives them to them as food and nourishment, just as He did the plants and fruits of the earth. He does even more; He enters into a firm covenant with Noah and his sons, through which He assures them of His protection and blessing. He wills that the wondrous Bow, which is formed in the clouds by the rays of the sun, shall be to them a glorious sign and an irrevocable pledge of His promise: that never again, throughout the entire course of the ages, shall He send a flood upon the earth. It was unnecessary for God to give any other assurance of His promises than the promises themselves; because He, being the supreme Truth, finds it as essential to fulfill everything He promises as it is essential for Him to be God. But humans are accustomed to demanding a confirmation from one another of the words they give; sometimes they wish them to be accompanied by oaths, and sometimes by pledges and tokens. God accommodates Himself to our ways; on certain occasions, He adds an oath to His word to give more weight to what He says, if possible, and to further assure us of it, according to the observation of a certain Apostle <note>A reference to Hebrews 6:17, where God confirms His promise with an oath.</note>; and on other occasions, He gives us pledges as an assurance that He will carry out His promises. Such are the Sacraments in the Covenant of Grace <term>Covenant of Grace: The theological concept of God's redemptive relationship with humanity through mercy.</term>, and such was the Rainbow in the covenant made with Noah. A Rainbow is a phenomenon entirely natural; it is a pure effect of the mixing of the sun’s rays with the outer edges of a cloud that is not very thick or heavily laden with water; as such, it was consequently nothing new to Noah, for he might have often seen such phenomena before the flood. But God, as He does in all signs of a covenant, adding grace to nature, made it a sign of His covenant; and for that reason, He calls it His Bow which He had placed in the clouds: *My Bow*,

<column-break/>

He says, *I have set in the clouds: and it shall be for a sign of the Covenant between me and the earth. And it shall come to pass, when I bring clouds over the earth, that the Bow shall be seen in the clouds. Then I will remember my covenant, which is between me and you: and the waters shall no more become a flood to destroy all flesh.* But if the Rainbow, in its own and proper arrangement, was not only a sign that God would send no more floods, but also presupposed that God was reconciled toward men—having a natural relation to the Covenant of Grace—then the Rainbow could also be applied to that. And that is why, in the Book of Revelation, God is depicted sitting on a throne surrounded by a Rainbow, to signify through that symbol His reconciliation with men and the unchangeableness of the Covenant of Grace, which shall never be revoked. God declared Himself thus through the Prophet Isaiah, speaking to His Church: *With everlasting kindness will I have mercy on thee: for this is as the waters of Noah unto me, for as I have sworn that the waters of Noah should no more go over the earth; so have I sworn that I would not be wroth with thee, nor rebuke thee.* Noah saw all this in the Bow which God showed him in the clouds; and filled with comfort when he saw that God would never again destroy the earth by a flood, the Faith which animated his heart—and which *is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen*—made him cast his gaze upon the Covenant of Grace, and assured him of the eternity of peace which we have with God through our Lord Jesus Christ; since he, according to the testimony given to him by an Apostle, *became heir of the righteousness which is by faith.*

### The Drunkenness of Noah, and the Cursing of Ham.
#### Genesis Chapter IX. verses 20—25.

Although the waters of the flood had covered the earth for many months and entirely changed its surface, God did not allow it to lose its fertility completely, nor that any species of trees and plants that had existed before the flood should perish entirely. The earth then began to recover gradually, and Noah began to cultivate it anew. From the half-decayed roots, plants shot up here and there that were thought to have perished; and the new sprouts, which came forth in places where trees had previously stood, daily restored to the earth some of its former ornaments. Since God had not entirely withdrawn His blessing from the earth, the trees still felt in their sap and core that ancient power which made them bring forth fruit, each according to its kind: and the plants also brought forth their first flowers and bore their seeds. Noah thus saw with joy that Nature was being renewed as if from itself; and in order to nurture such beautiful beginnings through his diligence and industry,

<column-break/>

he gathered the most useful seeds it produced, with which he sowed the lands that had lain fallow for so long, whereupon they returned the same to him in abundance. He did likewise with the trees whose fruits were worthy of his care and effort, and finding several shoots of a grapevine growing far and wide from one another, he collected them and planted vineyards from them. The delicious fruits they bore him once gave him the idea to press them, so as to extract the liquid enclosed in the grapes: but he drank more of it than moderation allowed. Having no distrust of a drink he did not yet know—whose sweetness was pleasant to the taste, and whose power gladdened the heart and renewed its alertness—he, who was already weakened by age and adversity, and possibly at that time also fatigued by labor, was overcome by the allurements of the wine; so that its vapors rose to his head, and his understanding was clouded thereby. In that state, he no longer knew himself, indeed, he knew not what he did; he stretched himself out in his tent, and the skirts of his robe slipping off one by one, to one side and the other, revealed that nakedness which shame usually guards with such care—

upon the other. He then, having forged a
plot to bring them into subjection, judged
that he must first make a name for himself
through his cunning and bravery. To that end,
he first began to fight the beasts, so that at
some time he might be better able to do
the same regarding men. He then became
a mighty hunter, and through that difficult
exercise he hardened his body for labor and
hardship; he became bold and undaunted,
and by accustoming himself to killing beasts
and pursuing them even into the forests and
their most secluded retreats, his nature—
which was already haughty and hot-tempered—
became wild, inhuman, and bloodthirsty.
After he had thus begun to excel among those
of his own age, he made himself feared and
respected; and since no one dared to oppose
him, many sought his friendship and joined
him to follow his example. His authority
grew with his power, and seeing that there
was nothing more that could withstand him,
he brought his neighbors under the yoke,
and the peoples who were just beginning
to form themselves—and who had learned
the art of protecting themselves as little as
that of fighting others—under his violence.
To keep all these new nations in obedience,
and to take from them the thoughts of
ridding themselves of his yoke, he resolved
to build a city

<column-break/>

and to fortify himself there. The landscape
where he found himself was the most suitable
place in the world to carry out his intention;
therefore he remained there, and finding
on the bank of the Euphrates a city, which
those who had undertaken to build the fa-
mous Tower of Babel had begun there but
left unfinished, he put the finishing touches
to it and completed the construction. The
convenience of the location, the fertility of
the region, and the pleasantness of the air
soon attracted a great multitude of inhabi-
tants thither: thus Nimrod established it
as the capital of his kingdom, and made
himself increasingly powerful and formidable.
   His ambition was not yet satisfied; he ruled
indeed over the whole land of Babylon, but
that was not enough to accomplish his ex-
cessive designs. He then marched with an
army out of Babylonia and threw himself
into Assyria; for this is how the 11th verse
of the tenth chapter of Genesis is translated
by some learned Interpreters, and not ac-
cording to the common translation. <note>The author is debating whether Genesis 10:11 means "Asshur went out" or "He [Nimrod] went into Assyria."</note> ->*Out of
that land went forth Asshur*<-; taking the
word *Asshur* as the name of a person, and
confusing the same with *Asshur* the son of
Shem, of whom mention is made in verse 22,
and who, however, seems to have nothing
in common with the one whom Moses places
among the children of Ham. For this rea-
son, and for several others that are very
plausible, those Interpreters translate the
word *Asshur* in the Text as that of *Assyria*,
just as in the same book of Genesis Chapter 2
verse 14 and elsewhere; and what strongly
supports their opinion is that in the prophe-
cies of Micah, Assyria is called the land of
Nimrod. Nimrod then went from Babylonia to
Assyria; and having made himself powerful
there, he built on the bank of the Tigris
one of the largest and most beautiful cities
ever seen in the world; it was called Nineveh,
after *Ninus*, son of *Belus*

# HISTORY of the O. TESTAMENT. 22

Belus, the same as Nimrod. *Belus* means *Lord* in the Oriental tongue, and that name, which was given to Nimrod because he was the greatest Lord and the mightiest King in the world, is the only name preserved in the secular histories, <note>original: "ongewyde Historien," referring to non-sacred or extra-biblical historical accounts.</note> which have mentioned Nimrod only under the name of Belus. Regarding the city of Nineveh which Nimrod had built, the Prophet Jonah says that it was of three days' journey, which perhaps must be understood as the circumference of the city, which, according to an ancient historian,

<column-break/>

was four hundred and eighty stadia, <term>stadia<gloss>An ancient Greek unit of distance; 480 stadia is roughly 55-60 miles.</gloss></term> or as we say today, sixty miles of 1,000 paces. The extraordinary size of this city, added to the stateliness of its buildings and the beauty of its location, made it worthy to rule over the whole East. Thus it remained in a flourishing state for many centuries, and was formidable to its neighbors; but it has now been a long time since it ceased to exist, and barely the name of it remains.

## The Tower of Babel.
### Genesis Chapter XI. verses 2—9.

<margin>
The Year of the World 1757.
Before J.C. 2247.
</margin>
Some time before Nimrod, through an unbounded ambition, disturbed the peace of the nations and composed a sort of general monarchy out of many individual governments, the lineages of Japheth and Ham had stayed together and had settled in the fields watered by the Tigris, on the side of the mountains of Armenia, where the Ark rested after the Deluge. The children of Shem, who were of the blessed tribe, had moved a bit further upwards and settled in the land of the Chaldeans, according to what can be gathered from the eleventh chapter of Genesis, from the 10th to the 31st verse. Now, because the number of the households of Ham and Japheth had increased tremendously, a desire seized them to spread out much further, and thus to have more convenience and comfort. Leaving then the eastern bank of the Tigris, along which they had lived until then, they crossed that flood and came into a beautiful and vast region, which Moses calls the *land of Shinar*, which is the same as that which was afterwards called *Babylonia*. The beauty of this land, which formerly had been the earthly Paradise, took away their

<column-break/>

thoughts of going further: they settled down there, and to be there with more pleasure, and to make their society more agreeable, they built a city there. Vanity mingled itself herein, and wished also to have a part in it: a single city, to be able to house all their lineages, was not enough for them; there had to be something more remarkable, and that was accompanied by a proud magnificence. They then decided to make a Tower, whose top reached to *Heaven*, that is to say, a Tower so high that the top was lost from sight and seemed to vanish into the clouds. From the design of such an extraordinary height, one can judge the size which that tower must have had, and the thickness of its walls. They then immediately set themselves to work to carry out this great enterprise, which was solely an effect of ambition and pride. *Come*, they said, *let us build us a city, and a Tower, whose top may be in heaven, and let us make a name for ourselves*. The land yielded an earth that was suitable for making bricks, and it provided them with an abundance of bitumen <note>original: "lym," meaning glue or mortar, but referring to the biblical slime/bitumen used as mortar.</note> to serve them instead of clay or lime. They then baked bricks and laid the foundations of the city and of the Tower. The work proceeds; they make an alignment of the streets in the city, and the walls of the Tower are already raised very high. But God, who had thus far

# HISTORY of the O. TESTAMENT. 23

[God] had allowed them to proceed, but suddenly made them stop, and to thwart their pride, he confused their speech. They all spoke one and the same language, namely that of Noah, which was that of Adam, and has since been called Hebrew. <note>The author reflects a traditional belief that Hebrew was the original language of humanity before the confusion of tongues.</note> At that moment their languages were divided; they still possessed the use of speech, but their tongues could no longer come upon the same words that had previously been familiar and common to all; and new words came into their mouths of their own accord, without them being able to understand each other. Thus forced to separate from one another, they ceased their begun work; the city was not fully built, and of the Tower no more remained than was necessary to leave for them shame and disgrace for that attempted plan, and for future ages a terrible monument of divine justice against the vain efforts of mortals. After they were separated without having finished their work, they went one to one side and another to the other,

<column-break/>

and were scattered into many lands. And because Moses in the tenth chapter of Genesis indicates that this scattering of people happened in the time of Peleg, and because the genealogy found in the eleventh chapter, verses 10 to 17, shows that Peleg was born one hundred and one years after the Deluge, it follows that it was a little more than a hundred years after Noah left the Ark that the descendants of Ham and Japheth began to build the Tower and the city, which was called Babel, that name signifying as much as *confusion*, because God had confused the speech of the people who were building it there. From Babel, in the course of time, came the name Babylon, which has remained with it ever since; and Nimrod, having some time later brought all those various families under one government, completed the building of the city of Babylon, as noted in the preceding history, which Moses recounted beforehand in the tenth chapter and placed before this one.

# HISTORY of the O. TESTAMENT.

Belus, the same as Nimrod. Belus means Lord in the Eastern tongue <note>The name Belus is a Latinized form of 'Bel' or 'Baal,' a common Semitic title for a lord or deity.</note>, and that name, which was given to Nimrod because he was the greatest Lord and the most powerful King in the world, has only been preserved in the secular histories, which have mentioned Nimrod under no other name than Belus. Regarding the city of Nineveh which Nimrod had built, the Prophet Jonah says that it was a journey of three days, which perhaps must be understood as the circumference

<column-break/>

of the city, which, according to an ancient historian <note>Likely the Greek historian Diodorus Siculus, who wrote extensively on the dimensions of Nineveh.</note>, was four hundred and eighty stadia, or, as we speak today, sixty miles of 1,000 paces each. The immense size of this city, added to the stateliness of her buildings and the beauty of her location, made her worthy to rule over the entire East. Thus she was in a flourishing state for many centuries, and formidable to her neighbors; but it has now been a long time since she ceased to be, and barely even her name remains.

### The Tower of Babel.
#### Genesis Chapter XI. verses 2---9.

<margin>Year of the world 1757. Before J.C. 2247.</margin>
Some time before Nimrod, through an unbounded ambition, had disturbed the peace of the nations and composed a sort of general Monarchy out of many individual governments, the lineages of Japheth and Ham had remained together and had settled in the fields watered by the Tigris, on the side of the mountains of Armenia, where the Ark rested after the Deluge. The children of Shem, who were of the blessed tribe, had moved somewhat further upstream and settled in the land of the Chaldeans, according to what can be inferred from the eleventh chapter of Genesis, from the 10th to the 31st verse. Since the number of the households of Ham and Japheth had now greatly increased, a desire seized them to extend themselves much further, and thus to have more convenience and comfort. Leaving then the eastern bank of the Tigris, along which they had lived until then, they crossed that flood and came into a beautiful and vast region, which Moses calls the land of Shinar, which is the same as that which was later called Babylonia. The beauty of this land, which formerly had been the earthly Paradise, took away from them the

<column-break/>

thought of going further: they then settled there, and to be there with more pleasure, and to make their society more agreeable, they built a city there. Vanity mixed itself into this and wanted to have a part in it too: a single city, to be able to house all their lineages, was not enough for them; there had to be something more remarkable, and that was accompanied by a proud magnificence. It was then decided to make a Tower, whose top reached to Heaven, that is to say, a Tower so high that one would lose sight of the top, and it seemed to disappear into the clouds. From the design of such an extraordinary height, one can judge the size which that tower must have had, and the thickness of its walls. They then immediately set to work to carry out this great enterprise, which was solely a product of ambition and pride. "Come," they said, "let us build for ourselves a city and a Tower, whose top shall be in heaven, and let us make a name for ourselves." The land yielded an earth that was suitable for making bricks, and it provided them with an abundance of slime <note>The Dutch "lym" here refers to bitumen or asphalt, used as a binding mortar in ancient Mesopotamia.</note> to serve them instead of clay or lime. They then baked bricks and laid the foundations of the city and of the Tower. The work proceeds, an alignment of the streets in the city is made, and the walls of the Tower are already raised very high. But God, who until this point had

# HISTORY of the O. TESTAMENT.

had allowed them to proceed, then suddenly made them stop, and to thwart their pride, he confused their speech. They all spoke one and the same language, namely that of Noah, which was that of Adam, and since then has been called the Hebrew language. At that moment their languages were divided; they still possessed the use of speech, but their tongues could no longer find the same words that had previously been familiar and common to all; and new words came into their mouths of their own accord, without them being able to understand one another. Thus forced to separate from one another, they ceased their started work; the city was not fully built, and of the Tower nothing more remained than was necessary to leave behind for them shame and disgrace for that undertaken plan, and for future ages a terrifying monument of divine justice against the arrogant attempts of mortals. After they were separated without having completed their work, they went one to one side and another to the other,

<column-break/>

and were scattered into many lands. And since Moses in the tenth chapter of Genesis implies that this scattering of people happened in the time of Peleg <note>The name Peleg comes from a Hebrew root meaning "division," as the earth was divided in his days.</note>, and that from the genealogy found in the eleventh chapter verses 10 to 17, it appears that Peleg was born one hundred and one years after the Deluge, it follows that it was a little more than a hundred years after Noah left the Ark that the descendants of Ham and Japheth began to build the Tower and the city, which was called Babel, that name meaning as much as *confusion* <note>original: "verwarring"</note>, because God had confused the speech of the people who were building it there. From Babel, in the course of time, came the name of Babylon, which has remained with it ever since; and Nimrod, having some time later brought all those various families under one Government, completed the construction of the city of Babylon, as noted in the preceding history, which Moses recounted beforehand in the tenth chapter and placed before this one.

He departed, then, without knowing where he was going: God let him understand it in due course; but it was to an unknown land that the Lord called him, where he would have to be nothing other than a stranger and a traveler for all his life. They settled in a place in the region called *Moreh*, near an oak grove, which invited them with its shade to rest and to let their beasts of burden and flocks graze—which they carried with them, according to the custom of the Eastern peoples, especially in a time when the earth, which could not yet be populated everywhere, offered travelers entire lands that were completely wild and large fields that were entirely uncultivated. and fertile lands in the world, divided in some places by mountains and hills which, by their wide distance, create pleasant and rich valleys, and also provided with vast plains and spacious fields, through the middle of which the Jordan flows from Lebanon down to the sea of Sodom. Abraham had no children yet when God made those promises to him, and he was nearly eighty years old; Sarah his wife was also of great age and, moreover, barren. But the faith of that Patriarch was not hindered by such difficulties; he entrusted to God, who had made him the promise, the removal of those obstacles in such a manner as He saw fit; and just as he relied entirely on the Lord's guidance at his first departure, so he also left entirely to Him the care of fulfilling His word in the coming to pass of everything He had promised him. Someone other than Abraham might perhaps not have been satisfied that God promised the land of Canaan to his descendants in the future, and would have wanted it to be for himself, because Abraham saw himself excluded by this: but the greater faith is in a soul, the greater is the lack of concern regarding itself; and always satisfied with the peace of God and the hope of future things, it lets itself care little for the things of the present life; indeed, it even renounces the longing and desire for them when such is necessary to please God.

On his return from Egypt, he found that same altar still there and showed God the same reverence and service; he made a burnt offering smoke upon it and solemnly thanked the Lord for leading him so fortunately out of Egypt and allowing him to see again a place which He Himself had honored with such illustrious signs of His presence and where He had let His voice be heard.

Lot assisted Abraham in all these works of piety, and God increased his wealth and made his livestock multiply as well as those of Abraham. Such a great multitude of camels, oxen, donkeys, sheep, etc., often found it difficult enough to find sufficient pasture for food in one and the same place; and they often did not even find enough water in a land that is naturally somewhat dry and where there is very great heat. All of this sometimes birthed some jealousy between the herdsmen of Lot and those of Abraham, and from that jealousy, strife and quarreling often arose. These household disputes greatly saddened Abraham because he could easily foresee the consequences; he feared that the envy, passing imperceptibly from the servants to the masters, might bring about a cooling of their friendship and break the good understanding that had always existed between them. nephew: "See now," he said, "how our herdsmen daily clash and quarrel. We are brothers; I pray you, let there be no strife between us. Lot cast his eyes upon it, and his heart remained as fixed upon it as his sight: he longed to be in such a charming place and to see his flocks grazing in the plain and along the river that flowed through it. He then gave orders to depart and took his leave of Abraham; but he did not see what kind of snake lay hidden under those flowers, and he did not know that, just as that countryside appeared to the eye as the Garden of Eden, the Devil had also crept in there and had misled and corrupted all the inhabitants. While Abraham, meanwhile, did not yet know which way he should take, God appeared to him and spoke to him thus:

> *Lift up now your eyes, and look from the place where you are, northward and southward, and eastward and westward: for all this land that you see, I will give to you, and to your seed forever. Arise, walk through this land, in its length and in its breadth; for I will give it to you.*

Abraham, comforted by these words regarding the departure of Lot, saw well that he did not need to envy Lot for the choice he had made of the plain of Sodom; therefore, he struck his tent and moved toward the side of Mamre, not far from Hebron.

-> Genesis Chapter XIV. verses 8—12. <-

<margin>The Year of the world 2092. Before Christ 1912.</margin>The land of Canaan was, in the time of Abraham, inhabited by various nations who had their origin from the specific lineages of Ham, or of Canaan his son, and each of those nations had its cities and its King. They, weary of this servitude, decided to release themselves from it and jointly refused to pay him the customary homage in the thirteenth year. The King, provoked by this refusal, informed the King of Babylon <note>original: "Babel"</note> and two other Princes of Assyria of it; whereupon the four of them marched to the land of Canaan to make war against the five other Kings. The latter, therefore, gathering all their power together, marched out before them into a valley, where they thought they would be able to fight them with advantage. The attack was fierce on both sides, the fight stubborn, and the five Kings were conquered and defeated by the four foreign kings. He departed then, without knowing where he was going: God gave him to understand it in the time that followed; but it was to an unknown land that the Lord called him, where for his whole life he must be nothing other than a stranger and a traveler. He took with him Sarah his wife, and Lot his nephew, son of Haran his eldest brother. They went by Heaven's command to the land of Canaan, and after many days' journey they came to the place where, not long after, Shechem was built—a city famous for many remarkable occurrences mentioned in the Scripture. They settled at a place in the region called *Moreh*, near an oak grove, which invited them with its shade to rest and to let their pack animals and herds graze. These they carried with them according to the custom of the Eastern peoples, especially in a time when the earth, which could not yet be everywhere populated, offered travelers entire lands that were completely desolate and large fields that were entirely uncultivated. God appeared to Abraham in that wild and lonely place; and to reward him for the obedience with which that holy man had surrendered himself to the will of Heaven, God said to him: *To your seed (that is, your descendants) I will give this land where you currently find yourself.* This promise looked upon the whole land of Canaan, one of the most beauti-

<column-break/>

-ful and most fertile lands in the world. It is divided in some places by mountains and hills, which by their wide distance create pleasant and fat <note>In this context, "fat" means fertile or rich soil.</note> valleys, and is also provided with immense plains and spacious fields, through the middle of which the Jordan flows, from Lebanon down to the sea of Sodom <note>The "Sea of Sodom" refers to the Dead Sea.</note>. Abraham had no children yet when God made him those promises, and he was nearly eighty years old; Sarah his wife was also advanced in age, and moreover barren. But the faith of that Patriarch was not hindered by such difficulties; he committed to God, who had made him the promise, the removal of those obstacles in such a manner as seemed good to Him. And just as he relied entirely on the Lord's guidance at his first entry, so he also left entirely to Him the care of fulfilling His word and bringing to pass everything He had promised him. Someone other than Abraham would possibly not have been satisfied that God promised him the land of Canaan for his descendants in the future; he might have wanted it for himself, since Abraham saw himself excluded from owning it. But the greater faith is in a soul, the greater are the things of the future to that soul; it concerns itself little with the things of the present life, and even gives up the craving and desire for them when such is necessary to please God.

Lot stood by Abraham in all these works of piety, and God increased his wealth and made his livestock multiply, as well as that of Abraham. Such a great multitude of camels, oxen, donkeys, sheep, etc., often had difficulty finding sufficient pastures for food in one and the same place; and often they did not even find enough water in a land that is naturally somewhat dry and where one experiences very great heat. All of this sometimes gave rise to some jealousy between the shepherds of Lot and those of Abraham, and from that jealousy, strife and quarreling often arose. These domestic disputes greatly grieved Abraham, because he could easily foresee the consequences and feared that the envy, passing unintentionally from the servants to the masters, might bring about some cooling in their friendship and break the good understanding that had always existed between them. From the place where Abraham held this conversation with Lot, one could see many other lands, including the plain of Sodom. This was the most delightful landscape that the eye could behold, being watered by the Jordan, fertile like Egypt, and in a word, an image of the Garden of Eden—for that is how far Moses extends the concept which he has left us of that beautiful land. Lot cast his eyes upon it, and his heart remained as fixed upon it as his sight: he longed to be in such a charming place and to see his herds grazing in the plain and along the river that washed through it. The news of the defeat of the five Kings spread immediately throughout the whole land, and it came to Abraham's ears as well as others. Names are not always mystical, but divine Providence sometimes attaches very great mysteries to them, and did so especially in the person of this King, who, through the meeting or the union of these two words, Melchizedek and Salem, was established to be a prefigurement <note>Original: "voorbeeldsel." This Prince was also a Priest, and through the union of the Kingdom with the Priesthood in his person, he served as an illustrious sketch of Jesus Christ, King and Priest at the same time. In the capacity of Priest of the Most High God, Melchizedek gave the blessing to Abraham, and in his person, to his entire lineage; and Abraham, in recognition of that favor, gave him a tenth of all the spoils he had brought with him. The Kings whose protection Abraham had undertaken did not wish to leave him unrewarded for such a noble and extraordinary deed; and the King of Sodom urged him to keep all the spoils for himself, being satisfied if he could only have back the persons who had been taken from him. Abraham, even more noble in refusing what the King offered him, wished in no way to keep anything, but returned everything; and Lot returned to Sodom.

### Genesis Chapter XV. verses 9–17.

In the deed which Abraham had performed on behalf of the five kings, there shone forth such an excellent magnanimity that God did not wish to leave it unrewarded. Abraham had enjoyed no other advantage from the rich plunder he had wrested from the enemies than the glory of having returned it to the kings from whom it had been taken; and the reason he gave for his refusal was this: that he did not desire it to be said that a King of Sodom had made Abraham rich. It might have seemed as if some pride <note>The original Dutch *fierheyd* implies a sense of haughtiness or lofty spirit.</note> lay in that answer and in that refusal; but Abraham acted on other grounds in all of this; it was for God’s sake, and for the sake of the righteous person of Lot, and not for the kings and nations who were steeped in crimes, that Abraham had undertaken this great expedition, and it was from God alone that he expected his reward. God did not leave him long in that expectation, and no sooner had Abraham returned to the place where he had left his wife and all the other persons of his household, than God appeared to him in a vision and spoke to him thus: *Fear not Abraham, I am a shield, your reward is very great.* These words perfectly suited the state in which that holy man then found himself. He might have feared that the kings whom he had defeated, having jointly recovered

<column-break/>

themselves after a defeat which they had only to blame on their own imprudence, might suddenly return, attack his small band with all their might, and sacrifice everything to the edge of the sword. But God reassured him against that fear, which was nonetheless not without reason, and promised him His protection, and along with that protection a reward a thousand times greater than that which he had refused. This vision occurred by night, and God, having commanded Abraham to step outside his tent, ordered him to look toward heaven, to behold the stars, and to count them if he could. This was a task beyond human power. You have no children, God said to Abraham at that same moment; I shall give them to you, and shall cause such a numerous progeny to come forth from you that it will be just as impossible to make a count of them as of the stars. On this occasion, God wished to renew His covenant with Abraham; and He did it in a much more solemn manner than He had done before. He commanded him to take a heifer, a goat, and a ram, all three years old, to cut them in half, and to lay one half on one side and the other half on the other side, leaving a path between them. This was a ceremony customary among men in ancient times in the covenants they made together, as if by that symbol, which was of very great significance, they wished to say to one another that they were willing to be cut into pieces in this way if they failed in their faithfulness and broke the covenant. God also willed that Abraham should add a turtledove and a young pigeon to these three animals, which had to be cut through the middle and divided, as a symbol of simplicity <note>original: "eenvuldigheyd"; here meaning sincerity, integrity, or single-heartedness in keeping a contract.</note>, which ought to be the soul of all treaties and covenants; and for that reason, he did not have those cut into pieces as he had the other animals;

Abraham followed God’s command strictly; he cut the throats of the dove and the turtledove, and the heifer, the goat, and the ram he divided down the middle, and laid the halves opposite one another. They remained thus in the open air the whole day; a flight of birds of prey came swooping down upon them; but Abraham, who kept himself close by and was very attentive to the mystery of this ceremony, terrified them and drove them away. Because he had spent the night without sleep, owing to the vision he had had, and because he had tired himself during the day by the slaughtering and guarding of the animals, sleep overcame him toward evening, and God used that opportunity to reveal to him in a dream the evil and the good that would happen to his descendants: the servitude in which they would be in Egypt, their departure from the land of oppression and suffering, and finally, their entry into the land of Canaan, of which they would make themselves masters. <column-break/>

a thick darkness, in the midst of which Abraham saw a smoking oven, which gave off much smoke; at the same time there appeared a great flame, in the form of a torch, which passed between the halves of the animals that lay opposite each other. This flame was the image of God, who since then has often used that symbol as a sign of His presence; and the passage of that flame through the middle of those slaughtered and halved animals was the token of God’s inviolable promise that He would keep His covenant. The burning and smoking oven was the sign and the foretelling of the persecutions by Egypt against God’s people, which Moses and Jeremiah, perhaps in view of this ancient appearance, called an "iron furnace" <note>Original: "yzeren oven." This biblical metaphor (Deuteronomy 4:20) compares the suffering of the Israelites in Egypt to the intense heat used to smelt iron.</note>. But if this object was capable of terrifying and grieving Abraham, God again assured and comforted him through the mystical fire, which, while the oven burned and smoked, went through the middle of the divided animals, to give that Patriarch to understand that God would be mindful of His covenant at the time of the hottest and most terrible persecution against the children of Israel.

# God institutes Circumcision as a seal of His covenant with Abraham.
## Genesis Chapter XVII. verses 23–27.

<margin>
The year of the world 2107. Of Abraham 99. Before J.C. 1897.
</margin>
After God had made a covenant with Abraham, and had solemnly confirmed the same by the mystical fire that He had caused to pass through the middle of the animals which Abraham had cut in half and divided in two, He wished to add a visible mark to it, which would be the sign of the covenant for as long as that covenant lasted. He chose for this

<column-break/>

purpose Circumcision, a ceremony until that time unused, but since then become common among many peoples of the East descended from Abraham, who consider it an honor to be able to say that they are descended from him: while others have borrowed it from the Israelites, such as the Egyptians, and that out of a great reverence which they bore toward Joseph, because they owed the preservation of their entire nation to him. This ceremony, which had to be observed for almost all children of the male sex on the eighth day after their birth, was for the Jews a perpetual instruction of the corrupt state <note>This refers to the theological concept that humanity is born into a state of sin, requiring a ritual "cleansing" or marking to enter into a relationship with God.</note> in which all men are born, and

It was not until the eighth day that a Jewish child had to be circumcised, for since this work was very painful, it was necessary to wait until the child had become a little stronger to be able to endure it. Abraham himself was circumcised with all his household; he was ninety-nine years old when he received circumcision, and it was already twenty-four years since he had gone out from Chaldea and received the promises, and thirteen years had already passed since God, according to the wording of Scripture, had *credited his faith to him as righteousness*. The Turks <note>original: "Turken" — in this historical context, the author refers to Muslims generally, who traditionally trace their lineage to Abraham through Ishmael.</note>, descendants of Ishmael, consider it an honor not to circumcise their children before the age of thirteen, because Ishmael was circumcised at that age. On the day that God commanded Circumcision to Abraham, He changed his first name from *Abram*, meaning an *exalted Father*, to that of *Abraham*, which means as much as *Father of a multitude*: and the name of his wife, who was called *Sarai*, *my Princess*, to that of *Sarah*, *Princess*, to signify that through the birth of Isaac, the blessed son whom she was soon to bring into the world, she would become the *Princess of a great people*.

He then returned to his guests; meanwhile the food was prepared, served under the tree, and they held their meal together there in the open air under a cool shadow. Abraham did not suspect at all that any secret lay behind this; he thought that his three guests were truly eating for the sustenance of life: but because it happened through the dispensation of divine wisdom and omnipotence that the Son of God <note>The author interprets the "Lord" appearing to Abraham as a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ, a common historical theological view.</note>, and the two Angels who accompanied him, appeared there with borrowed bodies—which were miraculously formed from the air or from some other matter—so the food they took was no sooner in their mouths than God, by his infinite power, caused it to vanish into a fine and impalpable substance, like the air we breathe. The meal being ended, He who appeared most excellent, and to whom Abraham had spoken, asked where his wife was. She is in her tent, Abraham answered; (for it was the custom of the Eastern peoples that women had their own tents, which were separated from those of the men, even from those of their married husbands; as is seen in the history of Jacob, when he had departed from Laban.) *I will certainly*, continued he who had asked Abraham where his wife was, *return to you about this time of life (that is, a year from now), and Sarah shall have a son.* Sarah was barren, and far beyond the age of bearing children: she heard from behind in her tent what this stranger said, and she laughed at it, as if at a mere saying that had no substance in it. Abraham was startled upon hearing these words: he then noticed that it was the LORD himself who had appeared to him in a human form; and because he knew that God did not come to such terrible blows of his justice except as slowly as possible, and that he did nothing more gladly than to let himself be moved, he pleaded with him with all the motives that love could provide him, that he would let himself be reconciled toward those miserable cities. He besought him with a zeal that makes those who still read this history—as it is told by Moses after a lapse of three thousand and six hundred years—stand in wonderment: that if there were fifty righteous found in all those cities, he would please not destroy the cities for their sake. God promised it to him; but this number of righteous, however small it might be, was not to be found there. If five be lacking, Abraham said again, will you not then spare the rest for the sake of the forty-five? Yes, said the Lord, I will then not destroy those peoples. *But if only forty were to be found?* I will also not destroy them for the sake of the forty. Abraham then went on from forty to thirty, and from thirty to twenty, and finally came to the number of ten; but there were not ten righteous in all those cities: Lot was the only one. Abraham had no more to say. The Lord disappeared; the Angels continued their way to Sodom, and Abraham returned again to his tent, moved by the singular favor which God had shown him; filled with hope of having a son in a year's time, whom Sarah would bear to him in an aged life; and struck with pain and sadness over the thundering decree he had heard from the mouth of the Supreme Judge of the world against Sodom and the other neighboring cities, which were guilty of the same unbridled crimes.

### *Lot, having been made drunk by his daughters, commits incest with them.*

## Genesis Chapter XIX. verses 33---38.

<margin>
The same year. 2107 <note>This date refers to the "Anno Mundi" or "Year of the World," a traditional system counting years from the biblical creation.</note>
</margin>

Lot, having arrived at Zoar with his two daughters, was entirely safe there from the fire which fell from heaven and burned the entire region. Entering there, he brought with him all his purity and innocence, which could not be corrupted even in Sodom. The terror he had felt for the abominable crimes committed there had often made him lament the corruption of the human heart, which, when left to its own guidance, is capable of falling into the most hideous excesses. The Apostle Peter, speaking of Lot, says regarding this event: *This righteous man tormented his righteous soul day after day, by seeing and hearing the unrighteous works of these miserable Sodomites.* <note>Referencing 2 Peter 2:8.</note> But how little substance does the righteousness of man possess? Lot lost his own at Zoar; and neither the terrible judgments of God which he witnessed, nor the excellent grace which God showed him by sending two Angels to lead him out of Sodom and protect him from the flames of Heaven, could prevent him from committing two hideous crimes: drunkenness and incest. Not daring to remain in Zoar, out of fear that the inhabitants of that place—who were undoubtedly little less criminal than those of the four other cities—might bring a similar punishment upon themselves and their city, he departed from there and betook himself with his two daughters into a cave that was close by. These wretched daughters, finding themselves alone with their father, and already possessing minds corrupted by the in-

<column-break/>

fectious air of filth and unchastity which they had inhaled in Sodom, devised among themselves the most abominable and shameful plot that one could imagine. "Our lineage," they said, "will soon come to an end; our father is old, the men whom he had chosen as his sons-in-law perished in the destruction of Sodom, and we do not see that he will ever be able to give us any husbands: let us lie with him; by that means we shall preserve our name and our lineage." Even a moderate sense of shame could not help but blush at hearing such a conversation, and an ordinary virtue must shudder at such an existence. Lot receives from the hands of his daughters the deadly cup; he drinks and becomes drunk. His blood, which had been cooled by old age, was heated by the wine; and his reason was extinguished and murdered. He goes to bed, and the next day rises with incest. Ignorant of the crime into which he had fallen through his drunkenness, he allows himself to be seduced once more by the ruses of his youngest daughter, who, following the path of the eldest, persuades her wretched father to drink more than necessity required. The wine had the same effect on him as the night before, and the next day Lot found himself guilty of a second incest. These dishonorable daughters each brought a son into the world as the shameful fruit of their unrestrained passion. The son of the eldest was named *Moab*, from whom the *Moabites*—a people famous in Scripture for the constant wars they waged against the people of God—are descended. The son of the youngest received the name *Ben-Ammi*, who was the father and origin of the *Ammonites*, likewise a people who were enemies of the Jews, but who later—after having caused them innumerable disasters at various times, devastated their land, captured their cities, and made them tributary—were defeated by David, and finally completely exterminated in the following centuries.

## *King Abimelech returns Sarah, his wife, to Abraham, and gives him livestock, money, and servants.*

### Genesis Chapter XX. verse 14.

<margin>The same year.</margin>

Abraham had lived for a long time with all his household and his livestock in the plain of Mamre <note>A sacred grove or plain near Hebron where Abraham frequently camped.</note>, a region very well-suited for grazing. But that place, which was situated not far from Sodom, no longer appeared as charming to him as before, and he could not bring himself to live there any longer after Sodom and the other cities were burned. He then departed with all his people and traveled to the land of the Philistines, where a King named *Abimelech* reigned at that time, and whose capital city was *Gerar*. The vice of impurity was common in those days, and the virtue of modesty so rare among those unbelieving nations, that Abraham feared they would plot against his life to steal Sarah his wife from him. Her beauty was still preserved even at an age where usually nothing but faded traces can be seen on the faces of even the most beautiful women. He took recourse in a ruse which he had previously used when the famine in the land of Canaan forced him to retreat to Egypt, and which had served him well: namely, passing Sarah off as his sister. By doing so, he did indeed expose Sarah’s honor a little more than if she had passed for his wife, but in the meantime, he brought it about that his life was in greater safety. For however great the impurity of those peoples was, they had not yet fallen into that reckless lack of restraint—which is so common nowadays among Christians, to the shame of the holy name they bear—

<column-break/>

that they would commit adultery and wrest a wife away from her husband to make her a partner in a dishonorable and wicked shamelessness. To tell the truth, there was prudence and cleverness in this conduct of Abraham; but without doubt, there was not as much sincerity in it. The greatest Saints are not exactly so in all things, and if they sometimes deserve our admiration, there are other occurrences where it is necessary that we pity their weaknesses. Sarah was Abraham's niece <note>The text explores the complex family ties of the patriarchs; while Genesis 20:12 records Abraham calling her his half-sister, this author identifies her as the daughter of his half-brother.</note>, the daughter of Haran his half-brother, and the granddaughter of Terah, who had had two wives, from one of whom Haran was born, and from the other, Abraham. For that reason, Sarah could, according to the common idiom of the Hebrew language, indeed be called Abraham's sister, just as Lot, his nephew, is also often called his brother; but it was nonetheless an ambiguity under which Abraham hid the truth, which one could not approve of in a precise and strict moral teaching. In a general sense, he could call her his *Sister* and she him her *Brother*, because it was according to the custom of their language; but to answer a question with an ambiguous wording—and that in such circumstances as Abraham and Sarah might have found themselves, if they did so, which the Scripture nevertheless does not clearly say—is more worthy of reproach than imitation. Meanwhile, Abraham was permitted to be mindful of some security for the preservation of his life; for God Himself does not want one to tempt His providence to the detriment of the means which human prudence can suggest to us. And if he thereby exposed the honor of his wife a little too much, one can, in defense of that Patriarch, reasonably attribute this to the knowledge he had of the wise and prudent conduct of

Through this, Abimelech and the entire royal House regained the health which God had removed from them, in order to block, through that punishment, the design which that Monarch had upon Sarah’s chastity. Afterward, Abraham and Sarah returned again to the land of Canaan.

Abraham then did as Sarah had told him; he drove Hagar and Ishmael out of his house—the latter to punish him for his insolence against Isaac, and Hagar because she had been all too indulgent toward her son and had not taken enough care to restrain that turbulent and haughty nature which she necessarily must have perceived in him, and which he had inherited from her. They then went out of Abraham’s house early the next morning, having nothing with them but some small provision which he had given them for the way. The water they had taken with them began to fail them, and that in a dry and barren desert, where they could expect no assistance from anyone. In this scarcity of water, the desire to have it and the fear of not obtaining it caused Ishmael's thirst to increase more and more, so that he finally fainted from thirst and, exhausted by fatigue, became completely powerless to go further, standing almost at the point of breathing his last. Hagar could not behold her son in this extreme distress without being pierced through with sorrow; and after having tried all kinds of means in vain to come to his aid, she found herself forced to leave him under a tree, since she could not bear the sight of such a heartbreaking object, nor hear the last moans of a child who had been all her joy and hope. Thus weeping bitterly and moved by many

<column-break/>

various emotions, she remained standing a little way from the place where she had left her son; not even daring to turn her gaze there, she felt in her soul the most painful and sharpest pangs that a mother’s tenderness can feel in such instances. Every moment it seemed to her that her son was breathing his last; and because her troubled imagination presented him thus a thousand times dying, and yet not dead, she found herself between life and death, unable to seek comfort for a death she did not believe had yet come, and unable to find solace for a death she regarded as inevitable and near. Thereupon an Angel comes to dispel all that anguish; and this comfortless mother heard a voice from heaven, calling to her,

> *Hagar, do not fear, for God has heard the voice of the boy in the place where he is. Rise up, lift up the boy, and hold him fast with your hand, for I shall make him the head over a great nation.*

At that same moment God opened Hagar’s eyes, so that she saw a spring close by—whether it had been there before without God allowing Hagar to notice it, or whether He had made it appear there at once through a miracle of His omnipotence to quench Ishmael’s thirst. Hagar ran toward it and gave her son to drink from it, who, having thus regained his strength, continued his way with his mother, lived in the mountains of Paran, made himself powerful there, and having begotten children, according to God’s promise, became the head and origin of a great nation, which was called the *Ishmaelites* after his name.

God had shown many great favors to Abraham, but one of the most remarkable, and

<column-break/>

which included many others, was that He had given him, against all hope and through a great miracle, a son. This son was such as Abraham could have desired from God, if God had not anticipated his request, granting to that child all the qualities...

[...qualities] <note>The text begins mid-word, completing "hoedanigheden" (qualities) from the previous page.</note>, which made him dear and precious to his parents, and could make him prominent and respected by all the world. These qualities increased with his years, and the father’s tenderness found daily in Isaac some new cause to increase and grow even further, if such a thing were possible. But then a matter occurred no less amazing than terrifying; God commanded Abraham to sacrifice his son to Him. Far from hiding any part of the terror which Nature might find in such an act, He presented the matter to him under the most dreadful concept imaginable, as if, by commanding this of Abraham, He intended for his mind and heart to rebel against the command and prevent him from obeying. *Abraham, He said, Take now your son, your only one, whom you love, Isaac, and go hence to the land of Moriah, and offer him there for a burnt offering, upon one of the mountains which I shall tell you.* As many words, so many thunderclaps. That a father himself must take his own son, his only son, a son infinitely lovable, who was all his help and comfort, to cut his throat with his own hands and subsequently burn him to ashes—and that for this purpose this unhappy father had to lead his child far from his home, three days' journey away, to give grief more time to increase and to cause a miserable father a thousand deaths before his son even died—was to place before Abraham’s eyes a whole string of the most mournful and overwhelming thoughts possible. But it was not only Abraham’s heart that God thus roughly touched; He also attacked his faith, and with that intent He spoke the name of Isaac: *your son, your only one, whom you love*, in a word, *Isaac*; so that upon hearing that name, on which all the promises rested—*In Isaac shall your seed be called, and in your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed*—the faith of this Patriarch <term>Patriarch: a term for the biblical "founding fathers" like Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob</term> would be attacked and tested in the only place capable of supporting it: namely, the truth and faithfulness of God. Abraham received God’s command with reverence, and the next day, at the break of dawn, he set out with Isaac and two of his servants toward the place God had named. On the third day, he saw from afar the mountain on which he was to sacrifice his son. The sight of this object could not help but awaken his tenderness and plunge his soul into a new terror; but Abraham loved God even more than Isaac, and his soul, which was very intent on hearing the voice of Heaven, listened no longer to the voice of Nature. When they had all arrived at the foot of the mountain, Abraham did not want his servants to go any further; and whether he had some secret foreknowledge that he would soon return to them with Isaac, or whether—which is incomparably more likely—he spoke only of himself, he said in plural terms to express himself with more dignity and power (as one sees from various examples in Scripture): *Stay here, and I and the lad will go yonder; when we have worshipped, we will return to you.* Isaac went alone with his father; and since he was then in the full bloom of his age—for he was already over thirty years 

<column-break/>

old <note>The author follows a common tradition that Isaac was 33 years old, paralleling the age of Christ at his crucifixion.</note>—he took from the donkey led by the two servants the wood prepared for the burnt offering and carried it on his shoulders to the top of the mountain. But seeing no sacrificial animal with them, he asked Abraham *where the lamb for the burnt offering was*. Abraham, without being taken aback by this question, answered him *that God would provide Himself a lamb for a burnt offering*. In saying this, he had only Isaac in mind; but God, who directed this entire work, had put an answer into Abraham’s mouth that was to be proven true in an entirely different sense than this holy man had intended. They then came to the designated place; Abraham erected an altar there and arranged the wood he had prepared for the consumption of the burnt offering; the fire was entirely ready to be placed under the wood, and nothing else remained but to take the victim and bind him. Thereupon Abraham turned to Isaac, and with a voice which Divine Grace, triumphing over Nature, formed in his mouth, he said: "My son, it is you alone whom God has chosen; it is by His command that we have come here; He has commanded me to sacrifice you; your life is in His hands, and since He has today consecrated mine to make an offering of it to Him, receive then without resistance the blow that is to take your life; you shall find it again in God, and God Himself shall be your reward." Isaac obeyed the command of Heaven without difficulty; he offered his hands and feet for the bonds which his father threw around them and with which he tied him fast; and lying upon the altar, he stretched out his neck for the hand that was to give him the blow, and for the glittering blade already raised to cut his thread of life. God required no more; He desired only Abraham's obedience and Isaac’s submission; but He had reserved to Himself the right to stay the arm of the father and to spare the life of the son. Thereupon an Angel appeared before Abraham's eyes and cried: *Stop, do not stretch out your hand against the lad, and do him no harm; for now I know that you fear God, and have not withheld your son, your only one, from Me.* At these words Abraham stood still, and laying down the sword that was ready to shed Isaac's blood by the side of the altar, he unbound this voluntary and pure sacrifice, and received back the life of his precious child through a sort of resurrection, as a certain Apostle says <note>Referring to Hebrews 11:19.</note>. God caused him to find a sacrifice in his place to complete the ceremony; a ram, caught by its horns in the tangled thickets, waited there by a secret command of Providence; wherefore Abraham seized it to sacrifice it in Isaac's stead. The sacrifice was completed with that victim, and God, satisfied with Abraham, renewed His promises to him and sent him away again, full of joy and wonder at what had happened to him. God had very profound and mysterious intentions in all of this, the fulfillment of which He has shown us in Jesus Christ: yet with this distinction, that as the truth is above the image, He truly sacrificed His only Son for the reconciliation of the sins of this world; whereas Isaac was only sacrificed in the intention of his father; because the blood of a man was not sufficient for the sacrifice, but the blood of a God-Man alone was powerful enough to atone for our misdeeds.

### Sarah’s death.

#### Genesis Chapter XXIII. verse 19.

<margin>
The Year of the world 2145. Before J.C. 1859.

Sarah had the pleasure of seeing Abraham and Isaac return within a few days, although she had seen them depart without knowing the true reason for that journey, which could not have been known to her without causing a deadly torment. <note>The author suggests that if Sarah had known God commanded Abraham to sacrifice Isaac, the grief would have killed her.</note> But these three holy persons, after this had occurred, did not long have the comfort of being together; and God prepared a new subject of sorrow for Abraham. Sarah, his dearly beloved wife—who, just like himself, was full of trust in God and a prime example of modesty and piety—is snatched from him by death. She was one hundred twenty-seven years old, and thirty-six years had passed since she had brought Isaac into the world. Well satisfied then that she left her worthy spouse such a precious pledge of their marriage, she dies in the faith of the promises; and fully assured that God would fulfill them in His time, she joyfully leaves a land where she had lived so long as a stranger, and goes into Heaven to take possession of the rest and blessedness which God had caused her to hope for. Abraham could not behold the loss that befell him through the death of such a pious and holy woman without great heartache; and that heart, which had not shed a single tear over the sacrifice of Isaac, pours out sighs and tears over the death of Sarah. In the former, divine Grace stifled the affections of Nature, and in the latter, Nature—left to its freedom—innocently follows its

<column-break/>

inclination, without nonetheless exceeding the respect which one always owes to Grace. After these first movements of a distressed soul had passed, Abraham prepared himself to bury Sarah; and to do so with all the honor which was then, as it is today, customary to show to eminent persons, he desired that she should be placed in a private tomb, and not be cast among other dead in a common grave. But Abraham did not possess a thumb’s-breadth of land in all of Canaan as his own property, and the first possession which he intended to acquire there—and which was also the only one he ever had there—was a burial place that he bought for Sarah and himself. The prominent men of the city of Hebron, where Sarah had died, offered Abraham, in a very noble manner, each his own grave; but he flatly refused this, and however strongly they persisted in persuading him to accept their offer, he remained steadfast in his refusal: and he proposed to Ephron, one of the most distinguished among them, to buy from him a certain cave with two entrances, one in the front and the other in the back, which he had in a field called Machpelah. <note>The name Machpelah is often interpreted in Hebrew as "double" or "folded," hence the reference to two entrances.</note> Ephron, hearing this, immediately offered it to him along with the whole field as a gift: but Abraham, who had previously turned down the gifts of the King of Sodom, also refused this honorable and noble gift which this Hittite <note>original: "Hethiter"</note> wished to give him. Ephron, then compelled to yield to the pressing request of Abraham, sells him the field with the cave, and Abraham counted out to him the agreed price, namely four hundred shekels of silver, and subsequently buried the body of Sarah there. <term>Shekel: An ancient unit of weight used for currency; 400 silver shekels was a significant sum, emphasizing Abraham's desire for a legal, undisputed purchase.</term>

### *Rebekah gives water to Abraham's servant and draws water for his camels.*

## Genesis Chapter XXIV. verses 17—20.

Three or four years after the passing of Sarah, Abraham decided to arrange a marriage for his son Isaac; but not wishing for him to take a Canaanite woman, because the Canaanites were all idolaters who did not worship the true God, and moreover were descended from Ham and his son Canaan—whom, along with their lineage, Noah had condemned to an eternal curse through a heavenly inspiration—he resolved to seek a wife for his son among his own kin and family. Abraham had departed from the city of Ur of the Chaldeans and had left almost his entire kinship there; but that land was likewise very idolatrous, and the command Abraham had received to depart from there also did not allow him to turn his eye thither to seek a wife for his son, for he knew that such was not God's intention. Abraham had a brother named Nahor who had gone to live in Mesopotamia, where the city of Haran was located—in which he himself had lived for many years after he had moved from Ur of the Chaldeans by God's command. Nahor had left behind a son named Bethuel, who had several children; and although the worship of the true God was not kept pure and without a mixture of superstition and idolatry in those households, it was nevertheless not entirely extinguished there as it was nearly everywhere else. This was the reason that Abraham sought an alliance there for his son, since there is nothing that should more deeply concern

<column-break/>

parents regarding the marriage of their children than to ally them with families who make profession of fearing God and serving Him according to His Word. Abraham then commanded Eliezer, the chief of his servants and the steward of his house, to depart for Mesopotamia and to bring a wife from there for Isaac. And since Abraham was already very old and did not know what the outcome of Eliezer's journey would be, he made him swear solemnly upon the faith he had in the Messiah; for this was the purpose of the manner of the oath he had him take, which was that Eliezer had to place his hand under Abraham's hip <note>The "hip" or "thigh" was a common place for swearing oaths in the ancient Near East, often signifying an oath taken upon one's future descendants.</note>, because the Messiah, being destined to be born one day from Isaac's lineage, would thus come forth as if from the hip and loins of Abraham. He then made him swear that, whatever might happen, he would never bring Isaac back into Chaldea.

Eliezer then departed with a great procession, for the Scripture says that he took ten camels with him, from which it appears that he must also have had many servants in his entourage; and with this entire train, he arrived in Mesopotamia and at Haran, where Nahor lived. When he approached that city, he had prayed to God that He might be pleased to bless the undertaking for which he had come, and to make known to him—through certain signs which he named in his prayer—who the person was whom His providence had appointed as a wife for Isaac. God heard Eliezer's prayer; Rebekah, daughter of Bethuel, Abraham's nephew, came out of the city, carrying a jug on her shoulder to draw water. Eliezer spoke to her and asked her to give him water from her jug; she answered this request with a dignified grace, and showing her politeness even further, she offered to also draw water for the men who were in Eliezer's entourage and for his camels, which she did at the same time. God put the faith of Abraham once more to the test: Isaac was married, but his wife was barren; and he of whom it had been said to Abraham, *In Isaac shall your seed be called, and I will multiply your seed greatly*, had no children. It was a great cause of sorrow in that holy household, but nonetheless, it could not shake their faith in the promises of God. Isaac constantly poured out prayers to God to obtain for Rebekah that blessed fertility, which was to be all their joy and, in time, the happiness of the entire

<column-break/>

It is not a very uncommon thing for a woman to be pregnant with two children at once, but Rebekah's pregnancy was not according to the common course of Nature; it was one of the deepest mysteries of Providence; and it was not long before she became aware of it. These two children, whom Rebekah carried in her womb, waged a sort of war and jostled one another in a rough manner: and if this mother felt violent pains in her body because of it, the grief which her mind suffered on that account was no less. In this agitation and fear, she humbled herself very deeply before God, and after pouring out many sighs and tears at His feet, she received this answer, which made her understand the secret of this pregnancy: *Two nations are in your womb, and two nations shall be separated from your body; the one people shall be stronger than the other; and the elder shall serve the younger.* When the time for Rebekah’s labor had come, she gave birth to twins: the first came into the world entirely hairy and ruddy; the other followed him immediately, and as if he had wanted to be first, he had taken him by the heel. To the first, they gave the name *Esau*, meaning a *perfect man* <note>original: "volmaakt man." Some early biblical commentators interpreted the name Esau to mean "finished" or "complete," because he was born with the hair of a grown man.</note>, because it is not natural for a child who is just born to have hair on his body: and the other was called *Jacob*, as if one would say *heel-holder* or *supplanter* <note>original: "voetligter," literally one who trips another by the feet.</note>, because he had held his brother by the heel. The physical constitution of these two brothers was very different: Esau was of a strong and brave nature, suited for labor and to endure hardship; Jacob, on the other hand, was weak and tender, and not very capable of strenuous exercises, which is why he usually stayed with his mother in her tent, while his brother Esau was in the field and spent his time hunting. It happened once that coming home quite exhausted and powerless, he found Jacob busy preparing a certain dish of red pottage, for which he had a great desire to eat. Jacob, who was well acquainted with his brother's sensual nature, as well as his reckless and lighthearted mind, which was inclined to

<column-break/>

despise the privilege which his status as firstborn gave him regarding the spiritual blessings of which God had appointed those first Patriarchs as guardians, took advantage of this opportunity to ask Esau if he would surrender his birthright to him in exchange for eating the lentil pottage. This miserable man, who should rather have been willing to die of hunger and thirst than to listen to such an unfair proposal, joked with such a dignified and serious matter: *See, I am going to die*, he said, *and what use then is the birthright to me? I cede it to you, he continued, Let me gulp down some of that red, that red there!* <note>original: "dat roode, dat roode daar!" This reflects the Hebrew phrasing 'ha-adom ha-adom,' showing Esau's impatient hunger.</note> indicating by that doubled phrase his burning lust and desire for that dish. Jacob, taking this kind of frantic passion in which he saw him to eat that pottage to his advantage, made him swear that he surrendered his right of birthright to him. Esau swore so, and ate. This action of Jacob was not entirely within the rules of a holy morality; but God, whose wisdom often draws their greatest glory from the weaknesses, and even the fall of His children—as the Holy Scripture shows us through a thousand examples—fulfilled through this behavior of Jacob, which was quite self-serving and not very equitable, a part of the meaning of the Oracle <note>The "Oracle" refers to the divine prophecy Rebekah received during her pregnancy.</note> which had foretold to Rebekah that the younger would be above the older; and paved, so to speak, the way to all those great and wonderful events that were a consequence of the sale by which the light-minded Esau transferred his birthright to Jacob. The Apostle Paul shows us in the ninth chapter of his Epistle to the Romans the sublime insight of God in all these things, through a relation to the two peoples, Jews and Gentiles; and the advantage that these latter would one day have over the others in the spiritual blessings of the Gospel.

<meta>This page continues the narrative of the aging patriarch Isaac and the rivalry between his sons, Esau and Jacob. Having previously described the birth of the twins and Esau selling his birthright, the text now moves to the dramatic scene of the stolen blessing.</meta>

# HISTORY of the O. TESTAMENT.

Isaac’s years were advancing, and he found that he grew weaker daily, bowing under the weight of his old age. When he believed he had nearly come to the end of his life, he decided to fulfill one of the most significant duties of his life: to pass on the patriarchal blessing <note>The patriarchal blessing was considered a prophetic transmission of God's covenant and inheritance.</note> which he himself had received from his father, and in which were contained the promises God had made to Abraham for all his descendants, to the son who was to follow him in the inheritance. According to the natural course of things, it was the eldest son who should enjoy such a precious heritage; but Esau had stripped himself of his birthright for the sake of Jacob. God, in order to punish him for such unseemly contempt—which had sprung from a frivolous heart and an almost incomprehensible disorder of the mind—willed that the sale, which that wretched man had confirmed with an oath, should be fully binding. But Isaac, whether he had no knowledge of this transfer of the birthright from Esau to Jacob, or because he did not make much of it and had not considered all its consequences with particular attention, wished to grant the right of inheritance to his son Esau as the firstborn, and to leave him the patriarchal blessing in that capacity. It happened then that, wishing to eat of Esau’s venison, he commanded him to go out and get it, and then bring it to him prepared to eat; adding that he would then give him his blessing. Esau went out immediately, and taking his bow and arrows, set out for the hunt. He was no sooner outside than Rebekah—who had overheard from a corner what Isaac had said to Esau, and who always kept in her heart the oracle <note>referring to the prophecy in Genesis 25:23</note> which had given her to understand the priority of the younger over the elder—set all her tender affection on Jacob. He was, moreover, beloved for his mildness and simplicity of character. She ran immediately to inform him of what she had heard; and giving him her counsel regarding everything he had to do to prevent and hinder the outcome of Isaac’s intended favoritism toward Esau, she went quickly to prepare such food for Isaac as she knew he liked to eat, and then placed it in Jacob’s hands for him to bring. Esau was rough and hairy over his entire body, but Jacob was not; and as Rebekah rightly thought that Isaac, whose sight was entirely darkened by the weaknesses of old age, would lay his hands on those of his son, and on his arms and neck, in order that by

<column-break/>

feeling the hair on all parts of the body he might be better assured that it was truly Esau who presented himself before him, this mother, who loved her Jacob so heartily, used the cleverness of covering his hands and neck with pieces of goatskin, so that Isaac was deceived thereby. It was more difficult to change his voice; Jacob did his best as much as he could, yet he could not quite manage it, so that his father noticed that his speech sounded more like Jacob's voice than like that of Esau. But finding him nonetheless rough, and smelling the scent of Esau’s most precious garments, which Rebekah had made Jacob put on, he did not persist in the suspicion that the voice he heard was not Esau’s, but that of his brother Jacob. After he had then eaten of the food which Jacob had brought him, he had him draw near and kissed him. The lovely and pleasant scent which Esau’s clothes breathed out made him cry out in a sort of ecstasy: *See, the smell of my son is like the smell of a field which the Lord has blessed:* and turning then to Jacob; *My son,* he continued, *may God give you of the dew of heaven, and the fatness of the earth, and plenty of grain and new wine. Let peoples serve you, and nations bow down to you: be lord over your brothers, and let your mother's sons bow down to you: cursed be everyone who curses you, and blessed be everyone who blesses you.* This blessing presents to the mind at first glance nothing other than ideas of earthly and worldly things; but at that time everything happened to the patriarchs by way of examples and figures, according to what the Apostle Paul notes regarding this: so that under those earthly ideas, the great promise—namely that of the Messiah—together with the blessings essentially attached to it, was included. Esau came immediately afterward to receive his father's blessing, but it had already been given away; and although it was, according to Isaac’s intention, entirely meant for Esau, it was nonetheless such that God, correcting Isaac’s intention, confirmed His blessing in favor of Jacob, and fulfilled the entire extent of that blessing in his person and in that of his descendants; and that as well in the literal as in the mystical sense <note>original: "geheymduydenden zin," referring to an allegorical or spiritual interpretation.</note>. It was thus that God punished Esau for his godless misdeed, and through this judgment gave a fearsome example of His justice against those degenerate children of the world who value earthly advantages more than the honor of being in His covenant and possessing the favors of His Gospel.

->Genesis Chapter XXVIII, verses 11–14.<-
