<column-break/>

of God made in the covenant with his fathers Abraham and Isaac, he wished to take it out solely on Jacob, and turned all his spite and displeasure against him. The first thing that came to his mind was to rid himself of his brother, to prevent him from drawing any enjoyment from the blessing which their father had given him: but that which the fear of God could not have prevented in a mind accustomed to following its passions was restrained by a certain reverence which he bore for his father Isaac, who had but a short time to live; such that he, for that

Rebekah, fearful of the rising anger and the threats of Esau, and concerned for Jacob’s life, advised him to leave home for a time. To more easily obtain his father’s permission, she—being a wise and clever woman—represented to Isaac that she found daily cause for complaint against the women their son Esau had taken as wives from among the Canaanites. She added that if a similar misfortune should befall Jacob, and he too were to marry a Canaanite woman, she would die of a broken heart. Isaac declared himself to be of the same mind as his wife; thus it was decided between them that he should be sent to Mesopotamia, to their kin, and be commanded to marry one of the daughters of the house of Laban, Rebekah’s brother. Jacob decided without any resistance to follow the wise counsel of his mother, by which he had fared so well until then, and to depart from his father’s house. As he stood ready to leave, Isaac confirmed the blessing he had given him—which he never intended to retract, no matter how much Esau had pleaded for it—even after considering the trickery Jacob had used to seize his blessing; for Isaac well understood that all this had happened through a special arrangement of Providence. Jacob then departed from his father more like a fugitive than a son of the house, without any retinue or following of servants, as Rebekah did not wish to arouse suspicion in Esau, who had already conceived all too great a hatred against his brother. Therefore, she judged it a good means of pacifying him to let Jacob depart as a wretched soul <note>original: "elendige bloed," literally a "miserable blood," an old idiom for a person of no consequence or a poor wretch.</note> who is of no account. Night fell upon him in a desolate place, where he was forced to stop and lie down upon the earth

<column-break/>

to rest a while from the fatigue of walking; he then laid his head upon a stone, which served him as a pillow, and found himself thus exposed to the inclemency of the weather and the gloom of the open field, which was increased by that of the night and the darkness. But the state in which he found himself soon changed its appearance: the place where he lay was no longer a lonely wilderness, fit to inspire terror; but it became one of the most beautiful and glorious places he had ever seen in the world; for there appeared to his soul objects powerful enough to enrapture it with wonder and overwhelm it with joy. He was overcome by a heavy sleep, and when slumber had firmly closed his eyelids, his spirit saw in a vision a ladder, of which one end touched the earth and the other reached to Heaven: he lay at the foot of the ladder, and God stood at the upper end, and along the ladder he saw Angels of Heaven constantly ascending and descending. God, who appeared to him from the top of the ladder, said to him that He was the God of Abraham and Isaac, and would also be his God; He renewed to him the promises of a numerous and glorious progeny, which He had made to his fathers; He assured him that He would give to them the land of Canaan, where he now traveled as a stranger, as a possession, and that all nations of the earth would be blessed in his seed. Jacob was so struck by this vision—which was undoubtedly the most glorious and illustrious that God had ever shown to any man on earth—that, completely enraptured by wonder, he cried out: *How terrible is this place! <note>In 18th-century Dutch and English, "terrible" (vreeslyk) means "inspiring awe or dread" in a religious sense, rather than something bad.</note> that is, how awesome and how worthy of the humblest reverence of a creature: This is none other than a house of God, and this is the gate of Heaven!* Thus encouraged by what he had seen and heard, he continued his journey with joy to Mesopotamia, and came to Haran, the city where his mother Rebekah was born and where her kin resided.

### Jacob rolls the stone from the mouth of the well, and waters Laban's sheep.

->Genesis Chapter XXIX. 1–10.<-

<margin>The year of the world 2245; Jacob's age, 77; before Christ, 1759.</margin>
When Jacob had come near Haran, he encountered several flocks of livestock by a certain well where they had come to drink. This well was covered with a large stone, which was very heavy to remove. One was not permitted to lift it for just one flock at a time whenever one wished, because water being scarce in those regions, it had to be used sparingly so that everyone received their fair share. <note>This communal management of water sources was a vital social contract in arid ancient environments.</note> Therefore, the shepherds were accustomed to waiting for one another before opening the well; and when three or four of them were gathered together, they lifted the stone off and watered their flocks. Jacob addressed these shepherds and asked them where they were from: they said from Haran, which was the place where he was going and where he had his kinsmen. He then inquired if they knew Laban; and they answered yes: this was his uncle, his mother’s brother. "And how is he doing? Is it still well with him?" Jacob continued. "He is doing well," they said, "and look, there is Rachel his daughter coming with the sheep." Since Jacob understood the tending of livestock well, he noticed that they were in a bit of a hurry to water them and then drive them to the folds; and therefore he said, "Look, it is still high day; it is not yet time for the cattle to be gathered; water the sheep, and go, let them graze." While he was speaking thus, Rachel his cousin, daughter of Laban his uncle, arrived there with her father’s sheep. At that same time, Jacob ran to the stone that covered the well, rolled it away, and watered the sheep of Laban. Furthermore, he made himself known to Rachel, and, overcome with joy at such a favorable meeting, he became so emotional that tears sprang from his eyes. A similar 

<column-break/>

event—and possibly at the very same well—had previously happened to Eliezer, Abraham’s servant, when he had come to Haran regarding the marriage of Isaac and had met Rebekah there with her flock, and that happy beginning was answered by a prosperous outcome. <note>The author highlights the parallels between Jacob's meeting with Rachel and his mother Rebekah's meeting with Abraham's servant generations earlier.</note> It is likely that Jacob recalled all these things and took them as a good omen. Rachel, having learned from Jacob that he was her relative, ran quickly to bring this news to her father, who, seized by a tender affection for his sister and his nephew, did not have the patience to wait until he arrived, but ran to meet him to embrace him and to ask for news of Rebekah. Laban was by nature not a compassionate man from whom one could expect much politeness; rather, he was surly and greedy. Yet it seldom happens that nature is so completely extinguished in a soul that it does not occasionally bubble up again. Blood spoke for Jacob in the heart of Laban; he felt moved by the sight of his nephew and led him into his house with many signs of friendship. Laban could not tire of hearing the story Jacob told him regarding the state in which he had left his family; then the talk fell upon Rebekah, and then again upon Isaac; Esau also had his turn, and above all, the favors which God had daily shown to the house of his father were not forgotten. Laban soon noticed the merit of his nephew and therefore wished to keep him with him, with a view toward the profitable service he could draw from him. He therefore proposed to enter into a contract with him; but Jacob, who loved Rachel dearly, offered Laban to serve him seven years without any other reward than having Rachel as his wife. Laban struck the bargain with him, and Jacob served him all that time with no less cheerfulness than diligence, because the hope of marrying a person whom he tenderly loved was a great sweetening of his labor.

### Leah gives her son’s Mandrakes to Rachel.

#### Genesis Chapter XXX. verses 14. 15.

<margin>
Year of the world 2252. Of Jacob 84. Before J.C. 1752.
</margin>
When the seven-year service, to which Jacob had bound himself to Laban, had come to an end, Jacob demanded his daughter Rachel in marriage by virtue of his promise. Laban acted as if he granted her to him in good faith; but because he wanted to keep him in his service even longer, and feared that if Jacob were once married to the person he had set his mind on, he would leave him shortly thereafter, he deceived him. He had Leah, his eldest daughter, for whom Jacob felt no affection at all, lie in the bed where the marriage was to be consummated. Jacob, not having the slightest thought of the deceitful trick played upon him, found the next morning that it was Leah, and not Rachel, with whom he had lain. He brought his complaints about this to Laban, who gave him no other reason for this act than that it was not the custom of that land to marry off the younger daughters before the eldest. He further added that he only had to manage with Leah for that full week, and if he remained intent on also wanting to marry Rachel, he would give her to him, on the condition of serving him another seven years. At that time, it was not uncommon for a man to have several wives at once, and we do not see that God ever punished Abraham, nor Jacob, nor other Saints under the Old Covenant for this. There was in this a special dispensation, which religious reverence prevents us from investigating too deeply, and which has ceased under the Gospel. Since it is according to laws that we must arrange our lives, and not according to

<column-break/>

examples, except in so far as they conform to the laws; thus, the <term>polygamy</term> <note>The practice of having more than one wife at a time.</note> of the ancients cannot be cited today as a precedent to justify having multiple wives in marriage. It was much stranger that Jacob could decide to marry two sisters; but the Law, which has since forbidden this in the books of Moses, was not yet in effect in those bygone times, which still bordered closely on those in which the necessity to multiply the human race had made such marriages necessary. Since those times have changed entirely, and God has forbidden it with clear and express words, such unions can be regarded as nothing other than <term>incestuous</term> <note>original: "bloedſchandig" - literally 'blood-shaming' or incestuous.</note>. <margin>Year of the world 2259. Jacob 91. Before J.C. 1745.</margin> Jacob then accepted Laban’s proposal; he married Rachel and served another seven years to pay the dowry for his daughter to Laban, according to the custom of those times. But this marriage was not immediately as happy as Jacob had hoped; Rachel had no children, whereas God made the cohabitation with Leah fruitful. Through this inequality, God balanced the status of these two women; Rachel was indeed always the most beloved, but she was barren, which at that time was a great sorrow for a woman, even a kind of shame—especially for a woman of a lineage from which the Messiah was to be born, as everyone then could hope to be his mother. Leah was much less loved than Rachel, but she was already the mother of four sons, which was a great honor for her. Of those four sons, there were two, Levi and Judah, whom God had destined for the most prominent dignities that have ever been among His ancient people: namely, the Priesthood and the Royal State. Reuben was the eldest of all; having once gone into the field, he found there <term>mandrakes</term> <note>original: "Dudaim" - a plant traditionally associated with fertility in the ancient Near East.</note>, which he picked and brought to his mother. Jacob became daily aware of the unjust treatment of Laban: for that man acted constantly in bad faith, even though everything prospered for him as long as Jacob was in his house; his livestock had increased, and his wealth significantly multiplied; he knew well that he owed this to his son-in-law, who never spared himself in the management of his affairs; but he showed himself in no way grateful for it. He often made him great promises, but he never fulfilled them, and his aim was nothing else but to lead him astray and deceive him. Meanwhile, Jacob grew old, and his family became larger every year; this made him think of his own affairs, and it obliged him to request permission from his father-in-law to depart with his wives and children to the land of Canaan. This was highly reasonable; but Laban, seeing the loss he would suffer upon Jacob’s departure, urged him very strongly to stay, on such conditions as he himself would desire. Although Jacob could place no trust at all in someone who had deceived him so many times, he saw, how-

<column-break/>

ever, no chance to release himself from a matter that was so zealously requested of him. He then agreed to stay, and in place of a fixed and named wage, which Laban offered him, he proposed to take for himself all the speckled, spotted, and patched livestock that were among the sheep and goats: as this did not currently amount to a very great number, Laban willingly accepted this condition, and it was decided and established between them; that in the future it would also proceed on that basis, and that all the beasts from Laban’s herds that were born with such a variety of colors would belong to Jacob. This seemed in some way as if the matter were left to Divine Providence, to reward Jacob’s services more or less according to its pleasure. But Jacob devised a means to obtain a large number of spotted lambs and goats, which succeeded well for him. He took rods or twigs of green poplar wood, and of other trees, and he peeled the bark off a part of them, through which one saw white stripes of wood in various places: and when the sheep and goats became heated and were in season, he laid those rods in the gutters and watering troughs where the flock came to drink; and because this object was before their eyes when they were being leaped by the rams and bucks, the young that came from them were also spotted. Although the effect which followed the sight of these rods was not entirely natural, nevertheless, since it could assist Jacob’s design, and since Jacob [placed] these rods

But since God is the Supreme Judge of the world, He willed that Jacob, through this extraordinary means, should recover his losses from Laban, and He justified him sufficiently by the miraculous prosperity with which He accompanied him. Laban, who regretted that Jacob’s livestock increased so much because of this, wanted to change the conditions, and forced him to take the animals that would be born unspeckled as his wages, which turned out just as poorly for him as the first agreement. This caused him to conceive an incomprehensible displeasure against his son-in-law, which Jacob, having often noticed, made known to his wives, and proposed to them that it was necessary for him to secretly depart from Laban, without him noticing. They gave their consent, and Jacob was strengthened in his intention by a certain vision, in which God commanded him to depart and return again to Canaan. Laban was at that time away from home to have some other sheep shorn which he had, and which were not under Jacob's supervision. This was a favorable opportunity, and Jacob made use of it; he then departed with his entire household, without taking anything that belonged to his father-in-law: but Rachel took certain idols, called <term>Teraphim<note>Teraphim were small household figurines or "household gods" common in the ancient Near East, sometimes associated with inheritance rights or divination.</note></term>, which Laban had in his house, much more for the value of the material than for any remnant of superstition; for there is no likelihood at all that such a holy woman as Rachel was would have had any inclination toward idolatry, or that Jacob would have allowed any such thing in his house.

<column-break/>

Three days after Jacob’s departure, the news of it was brought to Laban, who immediately set out on his way and overtook him seven days’ journey from Haran, on the mountains of Gilead. His intention was to lead him back as a fugitive, or to plunder all his property; for he had strengthened himself to that end with a troop of people from his city, whom he brought with him: but God warned him through a dream that he should beware of attempting anything of the kind against Jacob. Coming to him, he met him with a sharp reproach for having gone away so silently. But Jacob could easily defend himself against all those complaints: however, there was one that hindered him somewhat; Jacob had taken every conceivable precaution that nothing might get among his livestock or other goods which belonged to Laban: meanwhile Laban complained that he had been robbed, and he said in the lawless <note>original: "spoorlooze," meaning godless or unprincipled</note> language of idolaters, that his gods (thus he called his little idols) had been stolen from him. Jacob, who knew nothing of this theft, took this complaint as a great injustice, and said at the same time that they were free to touch everything and search all his tents to see if they could be found. Rachel, who alone was guilty of it, went to fetch these Teraphim cleverly; she hid them under a camel’s saddle-gear, and went to sit on top of them. Laban came into his daughter's tent and searched all corners; but Rachel, feigning to be in such a state that the decency of her sex did not allow her to stand up from her place in the presence of a man, frustrated by this trickery the search her father might have made for his idols in the place where she had hidden them. Laban then apologized to Jacob, assured him of his friendship, and gave his blessing to his daughters; and after he had embraced them all, he returned again to Haran, and Jacob continued on his way.

his father's house, Esau had also departed from there. Although Holy Scripture gives no specific reason for this, Moses seems to give us some indication when he mentions in passing the constant misunderstanding between the wives of Esau and his mother Rebekah. It is very likely that as these quarrels and unrest increased, Esau was forced to move elsewhere to prevent further domestic strife. God’s wise Providence steered matters in this way so that when Jacob returned to his father’s house from Mesopotamia, he would not find Esau there, who had been the sole reason for his initial departure. There was yet another reason which the same Providence had in mind, one that had not occurred to Esau any more than the previous one: that Esau, having surrendered his birthright by an oath, had thereby forfeited the right he had to the land of Canaan, which was one of the future blessings and the primary inheritance of his lineage. Thus, God permitted Esau, through a kind of renunciation for himself and all his descendants, to leave and abandon any right or claim he might have made to the Promised Land, in order to settle in another country. He went to live in the mountains of Seir, near those of Gilead, through which Jacob was passing. Such close proximity caused Jacob such terror that he considered himself lost if Esau should learn of his passage; but God guided him, and His Angels encamped around him. For in that very place where he had, perhaps without his knowledge, come so close to Esau, his most dreaded enemy, he had a vision of a host of Angels who pitched their camp before his own. But since the Saints—no matter what special assurance God may have given them of His protection in the danger they faced—never neglected the means of human prudence and wisdom for fear of tempting God, Jacob, seeing the danger he was in, sent some people from his household to Esau with a great number of oxen, donkeys, sheep, and servants. This was done according to the custom of those times as a sign of submission and a request for his favor. Esau then set out with a retinue of four hundred men; and Jacob soon received news of this through the messengers he had sent to his brother. However, they could not tell him why Esau came with so many people, for he had revealed nothing to them, and Moses also says nothing of it in this history. Jacob’s fear increased, and all his people were in great unrest and distress. Jacob then turned to prayer, and with deep humility and burning zeal, bolstered by a living and firm faith in God’s promises, he burst forth thus:

> O God of my father Abraham, and God of my father Isaac; O Lord, who saidst unto me: Return unto thy country, and to thy kindred, and I will deal well with thee. I am not worthy of the least of all the mercies, and of all the truth, which thou hast shewed unto thy servant: deliver me, I pray thee, from the hand of my brother Esau.

Upon this, the night arrived, as if to double the fear and anguish in the heart of Jacob and all his kin. He, meanwhile, full of confidence in God’s promises, and always wise and prudent, set the necessary order. He gave commands to his entire company to move forward in such a manner that Esau—softened by the gifts he would find from place to place along the road, and by the deep respect shown to him—might be appeased by the time he met the wives and children of his brother (whom he had never seen) and finally Jacob himself. Being the object of Esau’s enmity, Jacob did not appear until the very last, after the others had gradually, and as if by degrees, caused Esau's heavy displeasure to subside. Jacob had remained alone, separated from his wives and children by a small stream that was at that place. Being thus brought to this extreme necessity, and buried in deep thoughts regarding the danger he was in, he saw—either in a dream, or in a vision, or in a kind of ecstasy, or in reality (for Holy Scripture does not express it clearly)—a man approaching him, who, seizing him by the body, wrestled bravely with him and sought to throw him to the ground. Jacob defended himself and offered resistance; the struggle became fierce, and the two combatants, standing bold against each other, held firm and steady in the wrestling, neither wishing to part nor able to throw the other down. Thereupon the dawn appeared and found the wrestlers still busy against one another. Therefore, he who had begun the struggle, as if he feared being recognized, wished to withdraw, and said to Jacob:
> Let me go.
Jacob, already accustomed to heavenly visions and inwardly illuminated by a light much more vivid than that of the dawn, perceived then that it was an Angel, or rather God’s Son Himself <note>Early modern commentators often identified the "Man" who wrestled with Jacob as a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ.</note>, who had appeared to him in a human form. Whereupon, renewing his zeal, he said to the one who hid a God beneath a human shape:
> I will not let thee go, except thou bless me.
This man then, to show Jacob what he could do, merely touched the joint of his hip, so that Jacob remained limping for the rest of his life; and at the same time, he said to him:
> Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel; for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed.
Thereupon he blessed Jacob and disappeared. Jacob, having taken courage from this rare and miraculous sign, joined his family and awaited the meeting with his brother Esau without further worry.

# HISTORY of the O. TESTAMENT.

After Jacob had left for his father's house, Esau had also departed from there. Holy Scripture gives no specific reason for this, but Moses nevertheless seems to suggest something to us when he mentions in passing the constant misunderstanding that existed between Esau’s wives and his mother Rebecca. It is very likely that as these quarrels and unrest increased, Esau was forced to move elsewhere to prevent further domestic strife. God’s wise Providence guided matters in this way so that when Jacob returned from Mesopotamia to his father's house, he would not find Esau there, who had been the sole reason for his departure. There was yet another reason that the same Providence had in mind, which, like the former, had not occurred to Esau: that by surrendering his birthright through an oath, Esau had thereby forfeited the right he had to the land of Canaan, which was one of the future blessings and, as it were, the chief inheritance of his lineage. Thus God permitted Esau, through a kind of renunciation for himself and all his descendants in the future, to leave the land and settle elsewhere, giving up the right and the claim he might have made on the Promised Land. He then went to live in the mountains of Seir, near those of Gilead, through which Jacob was passing. Such close proximity caused Jacob such terror that he considered himself lost if Esau learned of his passage. But God led him, and His Angels encamped around him; for in that very place where he had, perhaps without knowing it, come so close to Esau, his most fearsome enemy, he had a vision of a host of Angels who struck camp before his own army. However, since the Saints—no matter what special assurance God may have given them of His protection in the danger they found themselves—never neglected the means of human prudence and wisdom for fear of tempting God, Jacob, seeing the danger he was in, sent some people from his household to Esau with a large number of oxen, donkeys, sheep, and servants, according to the custom of those times, as a sign of submission and a request for his favor. Esau then set out with a following of four hundred men, and Jacob soon received the news from the messengers he had sent to his brother. But they could not tell him why Esau came with so many people, for he had revealed nothing to them, and Moses also says nothing of it in this history. Jacob’s fear increased, and all his people were in great unrest and anxiety. Jacob then turned to prayer, and with deep humility and burning zeal, strengthened by a living and firm faith in the promises of God, he burst out thus:

> O God of my father Abraham, and God of my father Isaac; O Lord, who said to me:

<column-break/>

> | Return to your country, and to your kindred, and I will deal well with you. I am unworthy of all these mercies, and of all the truth which You have shown to Your servant: deliver me, I pray, from the hand of my brother Esau.

Upon this, the night arrived, as if to double the fear and anguish in the heart of Jacob and all his people. He, meanwhile, full of confidence in God’s promises, and always wise and prudent, set the necessary order and gave the command to his entire company to move forward in such a manner that Esau—softened by the gifts he found from place to place on the road and by the deep respect shown to him—would be appeased when he met the wives and children of his brother, whom he had never yet seen, and finally Jacob himself. Being the object of Esau’s enmity, Jacob would appear only last, after the others had gradually, and as if by degrees, caused Esau's heavy displeasure to subside. Jacob remained alone, separated from his wives and children by a small stream that was at that place. Being thus brought to this extreme necessity and buried in deep thoughts regarding the danger he was in, he saw—either in a dream, or in a vision, or in a kind of trance, or in reality (for Holy Scripture does not express it clearly)—a man coming toward him, who, seizing him by the body, wrestled vigorously with him and sought to throw him to the ground. Jacob defended himself and offered resistance; the struggle became fierce, and the two combatants, standing brave and ready against each other, held fast and firm in the wrestling without wanting to part or one being able to throw the other underfoot. Then the dawn appeared and found the wrestlers still busy against one another; wherefore he who had begun the struggle, as if he feared he would be recognized, wished to withdraw and said to Jacob: *Let me go*. Jacob, already accustomed to heavenly visions and inwardly illuminated by a much more vivid light than that of the dawn, perceived then that it was an Angel, or rather God’s Son Himself <note>Many older commentaries interpreted the "Man" who wrestled with Jacob as a 'Christophany,' or an appearance of the pre-incarnate Christ</note>, who had appeared to him in a human form. Thereupon, renewing his zeal, he said to Him who concealed a God beneath a human shape: *I will not let you go unless you bless me*. This man then, to show Jacob what he was capable of, merely touched the socket of his hip, so that Jacob remained limping from it all his life long; and at the same time he said to him: *Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel; for you have behaved princely with God and with men, and have prevailed*. <note>The name Israel is interpreted here as 'Prince of God' or 'Striver with God.'</note> Subsequently, he blessed Jacob and disappeared. Jacob, having taken courage from this rare miraculous sign, joined his household and waited, without further worry, for the meeting with his brother Esau.

...relate, since the Patriarch stayed there for several years, and because a very remarkable thing happened there. Shechem was a city of Samaria, known in the Gospel under the name of *Sychar* <note>original: "Sichar"; see John 4:5</note>: it had, like almost all notable cities of that time, its own King, who was named *Hamor*, and the son who was to succeed him bore the same name as the city, whether the city had borrowed it from him, or he had taken it from the city of which he was Prince; at any rate, he was called *Shechem*. Jacob had encamped in that region; he had much livestock and was in great esteem throughout the land. He had a daughter named *Dinah*, who was still very young and endowed with great beauty. Curiosity, a common desire of persons of her age, once led her to go to Shechem on a certain feast day to see the daughters of that land. The young Prince caught sight of her, and struck by her beauty, he had the indiscretion to have that daughter carried off and to violate her. His passion was ignited even more by his crime, and having spoken of it to Hamor his father, he requested permission from him to marry her. When Jacob received the news of the misfortune that had befallen Dinah, his sons were absent, grazing their livestock in the field; but after they had returned, Jacob told them what had happened to their sister, which they heard with the greatest heartache and grief that one can imagine. Hamor, on the other hand, to prevent the consequences and at the same time to satisfy his son's passionate affection for Dinah through lawful means, had her hand requested from Jacob in marriage. Jacob called all his sons together, and it was decided to grant Dinah to Shechem on a certain condition, which was that Shechem and all his people should have themselves <term>circumcised</term> <note>original: "besnyden"; the ritual removal of the foreskin as a sign of God's covenant with Abraham's descendants</note>, because Jacob and all his sons, having received <term>circumcision</term> from God as a seal of His covenant, could not

<column-break/>

allow Dinah to be married off to an uncircumcised man: and if he would accept that condition for himself as well as for his people, they would then enter into a covenant with him to give their daughters to the Shechemites and to have their sons marry the daughters of the Shechemites. This proposal was made to Hamor and his son, who accepted it and had their people agree to it. Jacob proceeded in all this in good faith, but his children intended something else, which burst forth within a few days. At the same time, Hamor and Shechem and all the men of the city, following the example of their Prince and to please him, had themselves circumcised. Everyone wanted to be the first to be circumcised, such was the zeal and passion they had to show their Prince this token of their submission: so much so that after the lapse of three days, there was not a single man or boy in all of Shechem who had not been circumcised. Being in that state unable to take up arms for their defense, Simeon and Levi, two of Jacob's sons and full brothers of Dinah—being born of one and the same mother—entered the city with weapons in hand. Finding not a single person there capable of offering them resistance, they killed all who were male, from the house of the King down to the lowliest Shechemites; and they spared none but the small children, whom they led away captive along with a great multitude of women; they took back Dinah their sister, plundered the city, and devastated the entire land. Their other brothers had joined them to carry out this nefarious plot, by which, far from washing away the insult to their sister and lineage in the blood of the Shechemites as they had claimed, they defiled themselves with a stain that will never be erased from the memory of men.

### Genesis Chapter XXXV. verses 2, 3, 4.

It is easy to understand with what shame and heartache Jacob beheld this gruesome act of his children: he made bitter complaints to them about it and set before their eyes the danger into which they had brought themselves—the risk of seeing all the cities of Canaan rise up in arms to take revenge for the people of Shechem. But his sons had not looked so far ahead; they had only followed their own thirst for revenge, which made nothing seem too harsh or cruel to avenge the insult that Shechem had offered to their sister Dinah, and through her, to their entire lineage. A vehement passion is always a poor counselor; it believes it has the right to do anything to satisfy itself, and it holds Reason and Piety under its yoke. But after it has satisfied its lust, Piety and Reason—freed from their chains—come to exert all their power upon a mind that has not yet completely lost all sensitivity. Then, it is nothing but bitter remorse and a painful repentance that tears apart a soul that allowed itself to be carried away by its passions. The treacherous and inhuman deed of Jacob's sons was of such a nature that it was bound to produce these effects in their hearts, and furthermore, to bring down upon their heads the total ruin of their families alongside the judgments of God, just as Jacob, their wise father, made them fear. But God, who watched in a special way over the pre-
<meta>catchword: preservation</meta>

<column-break/>

servation of that holy man and his lineage—for whom He intended something great and extraordinary—wished to provide him with counsel in the agitation and distress in which He saw him. Through this, He intended to reassure Jacob against his fears and <term>to encourage him<note>original: "een hart onder den riem stecken," a Dutch idiom meaning to put a heart under the belt, or to give someone courage.</note></term>. *Arise*, He said to *Jacob, go up to Bethel and dwell there; and make there an altar to that God who appeared to you when you fled from the face of your brother Esau.* By giving Jacob this advice to quickly depart from the land of Shechem—to provide a kind of satisfaction to the people of that land through his departure, as they could only have felt indignation toward men who had committed such a terrible deed—He simultaneously pointed out the place where he should go, so as not to leave him in confusion and anxiety regarding the decision he had to make. By naming Bethel, God also wished to remind him that it was in that very place that He had appeared to him when he, fleeing from his father’s house to escape Esau's grudge, had lain down on the earth to sleep, having no other pillow than a stone. Jacob could not yet have forgotten that magnificent encounter—namely, the vision with which God had honored him during that meeting. But God, by those words, revived all the images of that great vision which time (and the many events of a different nature that had since befallen the Patriarch) had half-erased or buried under many other thoughts. He placed before Jacob’s eyes, to some extent, that <term>mysterious ladder<note>referring to the famous "Jacob's Ladder" from Genesis 28.</note></term>, which touched the earth with one end and heaven with the other, while the Angels climbed up and down it, and God stood at the top, His eyes fixed on Jacob, ready to descend Himself if necessary to guide and protect him. Jacob, having arrived at Bethel, erected an altar to God there to offer sacrifices of thanksgiving; and God appeared to him again in a vision, through which He confirmed all the promises He had made to him during various notable events. The faith of even the greatest Saint is subject to wavering, because, however holy, he is still a human; but God nevertheless always takes care that the faith of his children never completely fails. Jacob departed shortly thereafter from Bethel for Ephrath, a small town in the land of Canaan that has since been known by the name of Bethlehem. Generally, his adversities had something so remarkable and singular about them that it would be difficult to find anyone else who had such experiences. Jacob's sons thought thereafter of nothing else but how they could best hide this cruel deed from their father: therefore they slaughtered a he-goat, and having torn Joseph's coat in several places, they made it bloody with the blood of that goat, and sent it thus torn and smeared with blood to their father, pretending as if they had found it by chance in the field. As soon as Jacob saw it, he recognized it, and not doubting but that his dear child had been devoured by some wild animal, he mourned him as dead, and his grief was so great that it could have moved even the most unfeeling hearts.

Everything spoke for this woman, and there was nothing but innocence that spoke for Joseph; but the voice of innocence is far too weak to be heard amidst the riot of such violent passions as vengeance, anger, and the jealousy of a husband. Two years passed by before any mention of him was made to Pharaoh, and likely many more would have passed, had not God—who did not wish for such virtue as Joseph’s to remain any longer in the darkness of a dungeon—willed that an extraordinary opportunity to speak of him to that Supreme Monarch should come to light. Two years after he had granted mercy to his Chief Cupbearer, that Prince had a dream which troubled him greatly. It seemed to him that he stood on the bank of the Nile, that great and famous river which flows through Egypt and makes it one of the most fertile lands in the world, and that along this flood he saw seven young, very beautiful, fat cows grazing; after which seven others appeared to him that were hideous to behold and extraordinarily thin, which likewise went to graze along the riverbank and devoured the seven fat cows, so that they vanished entirely from his sight. Pharaoh awoke from this, but having fallen back into sleep a little while later, he had a second dream, quite like the first. He saw seven full and very beautiful ears of grain springing up from a single stalk; and close by these beautiful ears, seven other ears rose up, which were very thin and meager, and scorched by the East wind, and they swallowed up the first seven. These two dreams in one and the same night, so similar to each other and both so unusual, made a deep impression on Pharaoh's mind, for he rightly judged that it was not merely by chance that this had happened to him, and that he had retained such clear images of them: but to know what they might signify was a difficult task, and he could find no one who could give him such an explanation as he sought. Egypt, as well as Chaldea, was full of soothsayers and stargazers who made it their business to interpret dreams, and whose science consisted entirely in the credulity of the people and an unbounded boldness in covering their ignorance with grand speech. Pharaoh called them all together, but they could not answer his proposition. This Prince desired a precise explanation regarding everything he had dreamed, and no one was able to give it to him. The Chief Cupbearer then—more to win the favor of his King, whom he saw was troubled because no one could interpret his dreams, than to do Joseph a service—began to remember that he had previously known a Hebrew youth in the prison who had a wonderful understanding for interpreting dreams; he then recounted what had happened when he and the Baker were in the prison house, and how the outcome had entirely confirmed the interpretation that the young Hebrew had given them of their dreams. Something less than that would have been enough to stir in Pharaoh’s mind a great desire to see Joseph, so he commanded that he be fetched. Immediately

Joseph was let out of the prison and brought before Pharaoh. This Supreme Monarch asked him if he could interpret dreams; and Joseph answered with his usual modesty and humility, that such deep understanding came from God and not from man; but that he hoped God would be pleased to reveal the interpretation of the King's dreams to him. Thereupon Pharaoh recounted his two dreams to him; and Joseph began with a calm and unafraid countenance to tell him that those two dreams amounted to one and the same thing, and that God, who had sent them to the Monarch, had signified the very same outcomes to him through two different images only to better assure him of it. Subsequently, he took up all the concepts of those dreams and explained them with such good order and clarity that Pharaoh and his entire Court stood amazed. He said that the seven fat cows and the seven full ears of grain signified that there would be seven years of extraordinary abundance in succession; and that the seven thin cows and the thin and scorched ears signified seven infertile years of famine, during which all the grain that had been produced in the seven years of abundance would be consumed, without all the stores of those years being able to fill the terrible void <note>The Dutch *holte* literally means "hollow" or "cavity," here referring to the emptiness of the famine years.</note> of the years of scarcity; that this was what was signified by the thin cows that had devoured the fat ones and yet remained thin, and by the meager ears that had consumed the full ears of grain and had not become any fuller themselves. Pharaoh received this interpretation with the same reverence and the same trust as if it had come from God’s own mouth.

# HISTORY of the OLD TESTAMENT.

The Governor of On, or City-Ruler of Heliopolis <note>Heliopolis, the 'City of the Sun', was a major religious center in ancient Egypt</note>; for the designation in the Hebrew text, which means a sacrificial priest <note>original: 'Offerprieſter', referring to the Hebrew word 'Kohen'</note>, can also be understood as a Prince or Commander—at the least, a man of great authority. This Egyptian Lord, whose daughter Joseph took as his wife, bore a similar name to his former master who had bought him from the Ishmaelites; however, the first was the Captain of the King’s guards, or the Head of his bodyguard, while the other served in an office elsewhere. Joseph, having been thus raised to the highest honor and provided with sufficient authority to command obedience throughout all the land of Egypt, focused on nothing more than performing his duties properly. He took care of everything necessary to follow the advice he had given to Pharaoh. The seven years of abundance subsequently followed one after another through all of Egypt: everything overflowed with grain, and the Egyptians hardly knew where they would store such mountains of harvest any longer. Joseph had granaries built in various places, of such a great size as he deemed necessary; these were all filled up, and finally, the fertility came to an end.

<column-break/>

The lands brought forth no more; the farmer indeed tilled and sowed, but the heavens no longer granted a favorable influence to the fields. The harvest yielded ears of grain, but the ears withered on the stalk before they were filled with kernels; and for seven years in a row, either the husbandman’s hope was constantly betrayed, or the lands remained uncultivated. Egypt did not feel this immediately, for in the first years of this great barrenness, the scarcity was still compensated for by the abundance of the previous years—at least in some places and among the greater part of the people. But as the infertility of the lands persisted, there came a time of high prices, and subsequently, a famine. People then took refuge with the King, to pray that he would provide his people with sustenance; the King sent all the people to Joseph, and Joseph, opening the King’s granaries, had grain sold to all who came for it. People came from all of Egypt and all the surrounding lands, for the famine was there as well; such that Joseph’s agents <term>Faktoors</term><note>The Dutch 'Faktoors' refers to factors or business agents acting on Joseph's behalf</note> were constantly busy—some measuring out grain, and others calculating and receiving money.

# HISTORY of the OLD TESTAMENT. 59

The changes that age had wrought in his person made his current state so different from how one would have expected to find someone of his circumstances, that humanly speaking, it was impossible for his brothers to have recognized him in the person of the King of Egypt’s most prominent official. He left them in that ignorance and asked them where they came from, who they were, and what they had come to do in that land. He understood from their answer what he wished to know regarding his father and his dear brother Benjamin, without appearing to desire such information. But to give a sort of reproach and punishment to those who had committed such a vile deed <note>original: "snood feyt", referring to the brothers selling Joseph into slavery</note> against him, he told them that they were spies; so that, through various reminders, they might feel in their souls the pain of a crime that had been somewhat erased by time. He extended his objective even further, seeking to force them to bring Benjamin to him, and subsequently to draw his father with his entire household to him. There was no ground at all for Joseph’s complaint; but his great authority made him terrifying to these oppressed men. They defended themselves easily on that point, and Joseph showed himself willing to partially accept their excuses, so that he might not throw them into too great a state of consternation. He nevertheless had them put in prison as criminals of the State; but after three days, he released them again. To show them that they were not dealing with one of those worldly and frivolous men who make no difficulty of lying and deceiving, he assured them that he feared God, and thereby wished to give them to understand that he was no idolater, but a man who served the same God as they. Whether they understood his meaning completely, or only in part, is something not expressed in Scripture. Joseph did not wish to detain them any longer, for fear that his father and his household might suffer want through this absence; therefore he declared himself to them, saying that he would let them return with corn, under the promise that they would come to Egypt a second time and bring their youngest brother with them; and that meanwhile one of them would remain imprisoned as a hostage until they returned. These ten brothers heard this decision like a clap of thunder; their consciences reproached them for the inhumanity they had formerly committed against their brother, and they all agreed that it was through a punishment from God for this hideous crime that this misfortune befell them. Reuben, who was the eldest of all, and who had prevented Joseph from being killed by them, added his reproach to their remorse:
> Did I not say it to you, he said, when I said, 
> Do not sin against this youth; but you did not 
> listen; and behold, his blood is also being sought.
All this took place in Joseph’s presence, who, maintaining his tenderness and the internal agitation in which he found himself, acted as if he did not understand what they said, since he used an interpreter <term>interpreter: an intermediary used by Joseph to maintain his disguise as a high-ranking Egyptian official</term> to speak with them: but his heart drew him, and his emotion became so great that he could hardly step into another room quickly enough, where he gave free rein to his tears. After he had calmed down and recovered himself, he returned to his brothers and had one of them taken prisoner,

<column-break/>

and bound in his presence. This was Simeon, whose fierce and volatile nature—as had been evident in the murder of the Shechemites <note>Referring to the biblical event in Genesis 34 where Simeon and Levi slaughtered the inhabitants of Shechem</note>—had perhaps made him the most merciless and hard-hearted of all his brothers toward Joseph. It was not out of any particular vengefulness that Joseph had retained that he was taken; but if he had been more guilty than the others, it was only fair that if one had to be kept prisoner, it should be him above all others; so that he might have the opportunity to mourn all the longer for a crime which the tears of the longest and heaviest imprisonment could never erase. Simeon was then kept in custody, and all his brothers returned to Canaan and carried provisions to their households.

<margin>The same year.</margin>
It would be difficult to fully comprehend the nature of Jacob’s grief when, upon the arrival of his children from Egypt, he saw that one was missing from the number, and that the others had bound themselves to bring Benjamin along. He believed Joseph to be dead, he dared not be certain of Simeon’s return, they were taking Benjamin from him—the object of his greatest tenderness—and he did not know if he would ever see him again. All this brought that distressed father into an almost inconsolable state. He could not resolve to let Benjamin depart, but his children, when they were ready to make a second journey to Egypt, presented him with so many arguments to move him to do so, that he finally consented. He had his children take along everything most esteemed in that land as a gift for that mighty man who held their brother prisoner and who oversaw the sale of grain for the entire Kingdom. And since Jacob’s sons, after having placed the corn they had bought on their beasts of burden, had each found in his sack the money that had bought the corn—which they believed had happened through an oversight—their father commanded them to bring it back again, to give it once more to the King’s Receiver, and for each to take as much again to pay for the corn they were to fetch. After all these wise precautions they departed from Canaan, and Benjamin with them. Upon their arrival, Joseph cast his eyes upon Benjamin, his youngest brother and son of Rachel as he was; and he commanded his Steward to bring all those men to his house. They believed then that this was because of the money they had found in their sacks, and fearing that this would cause them much trouble, as if it had been done in bad faith, they recounted without disguise to the Steward how the matter had transpired. This man, who knew better than they, comforted them and encouraged them:
> Peace be unto you, he said, Fear not, your God and

These people did not know what to think of all these things, and it is easy to understand that their amazement must not have been small. Joseph

# HISTORY of the O. TESTAMENT. 62

Joseph suffered more from the restraint he put upon himself by not immediately granting the mercy requested of him, than Judah felt sorrow at the sight of Benjamin being taken forever from his father and brothers, or himself being separated from them and torn from his wife and children to end his days in slavery. Joseph could then no longer restrain himself, but since he was surrounded by many people, he commanded that all the people should go out, so that no stranger would be present when he made himself known to his brothers. Then tears burst from his eyes, and he gave a cry that was heard in the neighboring rooms, from where it was immediately reported to Pharaoh’s palace. After this first rush of tenderness and joy had passed, he spoke to his brothers thus: *I am Joseph: Does my father still live?* His brothers were so terrified to hear from the mouth of someone of such high rank and exalted state that it was Joseph speaking to them, that they were all as if shell-shocked <note>original: "verweezene," meaning stunned or bewildered as if one had lost their senses</note>; and they did not know what they should answer him. The amazement of seeing a brother alive whom they had long held for dead; the joy of finding a brother in the person of the mightiest Lord in Egypt—a Lord into whose disgrace they believed they had fallen—who revealed himself to them with great rewards of goodness and tenderness; and finally, the shame mixed with a fear to see that this Joseph, whose life they had wanted to take, and whom they had mercilessly thrown into a pit and subsequently sold as a slave to a troop of Ishmaelites <note>A nomadic trading people descended from Ishmael</note>, needed but to speak a word to have them all put to death; all these considerations welling up in their minds at once caused such a great turmoil that, unable to withstand the idea that the name of *Joseph* alone brought there, they could make no sound at all with their tongues, but remained utterly silent. Yet their faces and their

<column-break/>

eyes spoke enough for them, and revealed better than their words could have done what was passing in their hearts. Joseph, seeing them in this shame and amazement, which had made them as motionless as statues, encouraged them <note>original: "stak hen een hart onder den riem," a Dutch idiom literally meaning "tucked a heart under the belt"</note> and gave them heart: *Come near, I pray you*, he said, *come near to me.* At these words they took courage again; they threw themselves into Joseph’s arms, and enraptured by wonder and joy, they hardly knew whether they might believe their eyes and ears, so great was their consternation. After this first outpouring of tenderness and joy, which burst forth on both sides, Joseph spoke a few words to his brothers, in which he assured them that he held no vengefulness against them for the poor treatment they had formerly shown him, saying that what they had intended for evil, God had turned to good; and that it was God who had sent him into Egypt for the preservation of their lives and that of their households. Furthermore, he said that there were yet five years of infertility and high prices <term>dierte|dearth or famine</term> ahead, during which the famine would rage terribly in all the lands neighboring Egypt. To all these warnings he added that they should, without loss of time, return again to the land of Canaan to bring their father and their households to Egypt; and he assured them that he would take care of them and give them a land of their own to live in with their cattle. *Tell my Father*, he said, *of all my glory in Egypt, and all that you have seen; hurry, and bring my father down here.* Then ceasing to speak, he fell upon his brother Benjamin’s neck, and the two brothers, embracing each other with a special affection and emotion, wept on each other's necks, and did not release one another except to allow their other brothers the comfort of embracing Joseph and receiving his embraces, amidst a mutual joy mingled with tears.

->Genesis 47:1–12<-

one of his father’s wives <note>This likely refers to Bilhah or Zilpah, as the text notes Leah and Rachel had already died.</note> (for Leah and Rachel had died in Canaan) and his eleven brothers, and thus brought them from the land of Canaan into the heart of Egypt, to be admirers of his glory and to live off his bounty. After they had been together for some days, Joseph, who was called back to Pharaoh’s court by his office and the interests of the state, took leave of his father and his brothers. He told them that he would give the King an account of their arrival and inform him that their trade was to deal in livestock. He added that he did not doubt the King would want to see them, and he instructed them on how they should address him, especially regarding their trade as shepherds. His aim was to arrange things so that they might all remain in the land of Goshen and not be scattered in various places among the Egyptians; *For*, he said, *every shepherd is an*

<column-break/>

*abomination to the Egyptians*. It was not that all herders without distinction were hated people to the Egyptians; for it appears from this very history of Joseph that the Egyptians brought him their livestock in exchange for corn; and that Pharaoh suggested he choose the most capable and experienced of his brothers to appoint them as overseers of his own livestock. Rather, it was because the Egyptians—eating neither sheep, goats, nor oxen, and keeping livestock only for their milk or some other benefit whereby the lives of the animals (to whom they paid a superstitious reverence) were not taken—did not find the trade of their own herders hateful or shameful. In contrast, it was quite different with the shepherds of other nations, who used the meat of their livestock for food and slaughtered their sheep, goats, and oxen for sacrifices. Because the Egyptians viewed this as an act of godlessness, those shepherds were an abomination and a loathsome object to them.

### Joseph presents his father and five of his brothers to Pharaoh.

Returning from the land of Goshen, Joseph gave Pharaoh an account regarding his father and his brothers. This Prince, concerning himself with everything that involved the man to whom he owed the preservation of the majority of his people, the increase of his wealth, and the prerogatives of his crown, wished to know from him what trade his brothers practiced. Joseph answered him that they were shepherds: whereupon the Prince told him that he should choose the best land

<column-break/>

that was in Egypt to give to them. And since there was no better land than that of Goshen, nor any more suitable for grazing livestock than the region of Rameses, which was a part of the land of Goshen, Pharaoh set it aside for Joseph’s brothers. Subsequently, he requested to see them, and especially his father. Joseph immediately made this known to them, and Jacob came to the Court, followed by five of his sons; for it was not deemed advisable that he should bring all eleven of them. He asked Jacob several questions, and among others, how old he was. Jacob answered him with a dignified and solemn phrasing: *The days of the years of my pilgrimages* <note>original: "vreemdelingschappen," referring to his life as a sojourner or temporary resident in various lands</note> *are a hundred and thirty years*.

HISTORY OF THE O. TESTAMENT. 62

Joseph suffered more from the restraint he imposed upon himself—by not immediately granting the mercy requested of him—than Judah suffered grief in seeing Benjamin about to be taken from his father and brothers forever, or in seeing himself separated from them and torn from his wife and children to end his days in slavery. Joseph could then no longer contain himself; but because he was surrounded by many people, he ordered that everyone should leave, so that no stranger would be present when he made himself known to his brothers. Then the tears burst from his eyes, and he gave a cry so loud that it was heard in the neighboring rooms, from where the news was immediately carried into Pharaoh’s palace. After this first wave of tenderness and joy had passed, he addressed his brothers thus: *I am Joseph: Does my father still live?* His brothers were so terrified to hear from the mouth of someone of such high rank and exalted state that it was Joseph who spoke to them, that they were all as if stunned; and they did not know what they should answer him. The amazement of seeing a brother alive whom they had long held for dead; the joy of finding the most powerful Lord in Egypt—a Lord into whose disfavor they believed they had fallen—to be a brother who made himself known to them with great displays of goodness and tenderness; and finally, shame mixed with a fear of seeing that this Joseph, whose life they had wanted to take, whom they had mercilessly thrown into a pit and subsequently sold as a slave to a troop of Ishmaelites <note>The Ishmaelites were descendants of Ishmael; in this context, they were traveling merchants to whom Joseph’s brothers sold him for twenty pieces of silver.</note>, needed but to speak a single word to have them all put to death—all these considerations, welling up in their minds at once, caused such a great turmoil that they, unable to withstand the thoughts that the name *Joseph* alone brought forth, could make no sound at all with their tongues, but remained utterly silent. Yet their faces and their

<column-break/>

eyes spoke enough for them, and revealed better than their words could have done what was passing in their hearts. Joseph, seeing them in this shame and amazement, which had made them as motionless as statues, gave them heart and encouraged them: *Come near*, he said, *pray, come near to me*. At these words they took courage again; they threw themselves into Joseph’s arms, and, rapt with wonder and joy, they hardly knew whether they could believe their eyes and ears, so great was their agitation. After this first outpouring of tenderness and joy, which burst forth on both sides, Joseph spoke a few words to his brothers, in which he assured them that he held no vengefulness against them for the ill treatment they had formerly done to him. He said that what they had intended for evil, God had turned to good; and that it was God who had sent him to Egypt for the preservation of their lives and of their families. Furthermore, he said that there were yet five years of infertility and scarcity ahead, during which the famine would rage terribly in all the lands neighboring Egypt. To all these warnings he added that they should, without loss of time, return again to the land of Canaan to bring their father and their families into Egypt, and he assured them that he would take care of them and give them a land of their own to dwell in with their livestock: *Tell my father*, he said, *of all my glory in Egypt, and all that you have seen; hurry, and bring my father down here.* Then, ceasing his speech, he fell upon the neck of his brother Benjamin; and the two brothers, embracing each other with a special affection and emotion, wept on each other’s necks, and did not release one another except to allow their other brothers the comfort of embracing Joseph and receiving his embraces, amidst a mutual joy mingled with tears.

### *Jacob comes with his whole household into Egypt; and Joseph throws himself upon his father's neck.*
### Genesis Chapter 46, verse 29.

The King <note>Referring to the Pharaoh of Egypt.</note> was moved by Joseph’s joy and gave him new tokens of his goodwill on that occasion. Joseph repeated all this to his brothers and had them take a supply of provisions to carry to Canaan. He presented each of them with two robes <term>tabberden</term> <note>A "tabberd" was a long, formal gown or robe worn in the early modern period, here used to translate the biblical "changes of raiment."</note>, according to the custom of that time; but to Benjamin he gave five, and three hundred pieces of silver, and he had many wagons and beasts of burden travel with them. Joseph had already gone there to wait for them, and this son—the darling child of his father, showered with the favors of Heaven—enjoyed the joy of seeing his father again, by whom he was so tenderly loved; and Jacob enjoyed that of embracing a son, living and full of glory, whom he had mourned as dead. ...one of his father's wives <note>This likely refers to Bilhah or Zilpah, the handmaids who were also mothers to Jacob's children, as the text notes the primary wives were deceased.</note> (for Leah and Rachel had died in Canaan) and his eleven brothers, and thus brought them from the land of Canaan into the heart of Egypt, to be admirers of his glory and to live off his bounty. After they had been together for a few days, Joseph—who was called back to Pharaoh’s Court by his office and the interests of state—took leave of his father and his brothers. He told them that he would give the King an account of their arrival and inform him that their occupation was dealing with cattle. He added that he did not doubt the King would wish to see them, and he instructed them on how they should address him, particularly regarding their trade as shepherds. His objective was to arrange things so that they might all be left together in the land of Goshen and not be scattered in various places among the Egyptians; for, he said, *every shepherd is an

<column-break/>

abomination* <note>original: "grouwel"</note> *to the Egyptians.* Not that all shepherds without distinction were hated people among the Egyptians; for it appears from this very history of Joseph that the Egyptians brought him their cattle in exchange for corn; and that Pharaoh suggested he choose the most capable and experienced of his brothers to appoint them as overseers of his own livestock. Rather, it was because the Egyptians did not eat sheep, goats, or oxen, and kept no livestock except for their milk or some other benefit whereby the lives of the animals—to whom they paid a superstitious reverence—were not taken. For this reason, the occupation of their own shepherds was not considered hateful or shameful among them. Conversely, it was quite different with the shepherds of other nations, who used the meat of their livestock for food and slaughtered their sheep, goats, and oxen for sacrifices. The Egyptians regarded this as a form of godlessness, and consequently, those shepherds were an abomination and an object of loathing to them.

# Jacob’s last words to his sons.
## Joseph has the body of his father embalmed.
### Genesis Chapter XLIX, verses 1–28.
### Chapter L, verse 2.

<margin>
Same year. 2315.
<note>In the traditional biblical chronology used by the author, 2315 AM (Anno Mundi) refers to the years since the creation of the world.</note>
</margin>

When *Jacob* had given the blessing to *Ephraim* and *Manasseh*, he told *Joseph* that he felt himself drawing near to death; but that since Divine Providence had brought him into *Egypt* to end his days there, and because he had to leave his entire household there, he predicted to him as a certain matter that God would one day lead them out of that land to establish them in that of *Canaan*, which He had promised to him and his fathers for their descendants. *Jacob* subsequently gave to *Joseph* as a special gift—and above the inheritance that his lineage would have alongside all the others in the division of the land of *Canaan*—a piece of land which he, as he said, had won from the *Amorites* <term>Amorites: a powerful group of people who inhabited the land of Canaan before the arrival of the Israelites</term> with his sword and bow. This was the piece of land that he had bought from the children of *Hamor*, near *Shechem*, for a hundred pieces of silver; which likely (for *Moses* has not recounted everything that befell the Patriarchs) having been seized by some inhabitants of the land, signified under the general name of *Amorites*, when *Jacob* had left that land due to the murder which his sons had committed among the Shechemites, he forced them to return it after his homecoming. His strength decreased daily, and his sons saw with sorrow that this father, to whom God had so often appeared, and whom He had made a guardian of His <term>Oracles: divine revelations or messages from God</term> and promises, was now on the verge of being snatched away from them by death. On the day that they 

<column-break/>

were to lose him, he had them all come around his bed, and the Holy Spirit, with which he was filled, supporting his weak and dying nature within him, he delivered a long discourse to them, in which he predicted to each what would happen to his Tribe and lineage. It was something grand and extraordinary to see a greybeard of a hundred and forty-seven years on his deathbed surrounded by twelve sons, all well-formed men, who in a reverent and humble posture awaited his final blessing, and from his mouth understood the destiny of their generations. It seemed, when one heard him speak of so many events of things yet to come, and which were still wrapped in the darkness of what was far off, that he read such things from the very book of God’s decrees, so vivid and accurate was he in everything that he predicted to each of them. Thus it was God’s Spirit that revealed these future mysteries to him, which were impenetrable to all the understanding of a creature; and because he did nothing therein but lend his weak voice to the Holy Spirit, who enlightened his understanding and placed the ideas of future matters in his mind, so his heart found itself drawn forward by a supernatural light with which his soul was filled, and he had the freedom to deliberate what manner of blessings he would choose to give to each of his children. Yet, regardless of what effort Nature seemed to make in him, when the turn came to speak to *Joseph*, he could promise him nothing other than victory over his brothers and a long series of prosperity; but by no means did he take away from *Judah* the Scepter, which the Holy Spirit had placed in his hands, to cause it to pass into those of *Joseph*; and that extraordinary tenderness which he had always borne toward *Benjamin* could not grant him any special title of honor or dignities, to the favor—

would be taken from the mouth of that dear child. Everything was grand, everything was remarkable in Jacob’s prophecy to his twelve sons; but that which concerned Judah was the most excellent and noteworthy of all. Jacob predicted to him not only that the Scepter would come into his lineage and remain there for a long time, but also that the Messiah, that holy seed of Abraham in whom all nations of the earth would be blessed, would come forth from Judah, and that at a time when the Scepter would no longer be there, and that tribe would no longer provide Lawgivers to God’s people. *The Scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor a Lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh comes, and to him shall the obedience of the nations be.* <note>Original Dutch: "Silo." Shiloh is a title traditionally interpreted by both Jewish and Christian scholars as referring to the Messiah.</note> Jacob ended this long discourse that he gave to his sons by commanding them that, after his death, they should carry his body to Canaan and lay it to rest in the cave of Machpelah, where Abraham and Isaac were buried with their wives Sarah and Rebekah, and where he himself had buried Leah. After he had finished speaking, he gathered his feet together upon the bed and gave up the ghost. This was the end of one of the most beautiful lives in the world: glorious through the manifold appearances of God to this Patriarch, renowned for the constant adversities with which he was buffeted, and worthy to serve as an example for all believers through the patience, submission, and godliness which made it excellent until the very end.

Jacob had made Joseph promise with an oath that he would carry his corpse to Canaan after his death, to bury it in the grave of his fathers, Abraham and Isaac. It was not out of some vain and unfounded desire, such as worldly men sometimes have—preferring to lie in one grave rather than another—that he had so zealously desired to be carried to Canaan; rather, he had done so strictly for the same purpose that Abraham had when he purchased a burial site. These holy Patriarchs had received the promise from God that He would one day give this land to their children; and because faith presents the things one hopes for to the mind as if they were present, and makes the possession of them—no matter how far off it may still be—seem as if one had already obtained it, they viewed the land of Canaan from that time on as their own property. To demonstrate the faith they had placed in that promise, and all the others attached to it, Jacob wished to be buried in the grave of his fathers—less, to tell the truth, for his own sake than for the sake of his children and all those who were to be born of them in Egypt; so that they would not view Egypt as their fatherland, but that they would always direct their thoughts and desires toward the land of Canaan, the possession of which God had promised them.

<column-break/>

Thus Jacob, through a wisdom befitting his zeal and his faith, wished to lead the hearts of his children toward the land of promise by having them carry his body there, and by leaving them in his burial a certain pledge that God would one day bring them back from the land of Egypt into that of Canaan. People easily forget themselves in pleasant and luxurious places, and the vices of a land creep even more easily into hearts that have already taken root there. This was the matter about which Jacob was very concerned for his children: the land of Goshen was one of the most charming regions of Egypt, and Egypt was one of the most beautiful and convenient in the entire world—and often, one abandons their original purpose. Moreover, it was the most idolatrous land that could be under heaven: this wretched Egypt, as renowned for its wisdom as being the source of arts and sciences, was plunged into such dark and ghastly ignorance regarding religion that it made gods for itself out of everything—namely, out of oxen, sheep, vermin, and plants in the gardens. The holy Patriarch shuddered with horror at the contemplation of all these things. It is true, neither he nor his children had been deprived of the freedom to serve God without participating in idolatry; but he feared that evil examples would, gradually and over time, have a greater hold on the minds of his descendants than the instructions he left them, and that thus faith and godliness would be extinguished in his lineage. Since he could not speak to them forever while living, he wished at least to speak to them with the language of the dead, desiring that his grave should serve as a voice that constantly and unceasingly called out to them: *Never regard yourselves as anything other than strangers in Egypt, and always keep in mind that you must return to your fathers.* It was a common custom among the Egyptians, who were by nature grand and extravagant, to embalm the dead, even if they had not been of great standing during their lives. By that means, they preserved the corpses they wished to save from worms and decay for entire centuries, thus giving their outward form a kind of immortality. Joseph did not wish to withhold from his father’s body that honor, which was so common in that country. He called for men experienced and trained in the art of embalming corpses and provided them with an abundance of the most precious spices to perform a stately embalming. Forty days were spent on this preparation, so that the scent and the power of the dried goods used for it could better penetrate all the fleshy parts and even the innermost marrow, and so that nothing might remain in the whole body that could rot; after which the funeral procession took place.
