...observing the death of their Kings, which was to mourn them for seventy-two days, as is found among some ancient writers. *Moses*, it is true, speaks of seventy days spent in mourning for *Jacob*, but Holy Scripture often gives only a round account, and does not always take the numbers in the utmost strictness. <note>The author is reconciling the 70 days mentioned in Genesis 50:3 with the 72 days reported by historians like Diodorus Siculus for the mourning of Egyptian pharaohs.</note> However it may be with that matter, the mourning over *Jacob’s* death was general, just like that of the Kings, throughout all *Egypt*; and *Joseph* had the comfort of receiving from his *Sovereign* this new proof of his favor and esteem. After all the ceremonies were completed, *Joseph* sought nothing more than to fulfill the promise he had made to his father, to have his body carried to *Canaan* and to bury the same there in the tomb of his ancestors. He had the King addressed regarding this by some of the Courtiers who had the most access to that *Prince*, who represented to him that *Joseph* had bound himself by oath to perform these last funeral rites for his father. *Pharaoh* might possibly have found some difficulty in allowing *Joseph*, from whom he drew great service daily, to depart so far from the *Court*; but the affection he bore him did not permit him to refuse this journey; the more so because he saw that *Joseph* was bound to it by a solemn oath, and an oath, even among nations furthest alienated from the knowledge of the true *God*, has always been held as a holy and inviolable thing. *Joseph*, then, having obtained permission from the King to complete his father’s funeral, went to fetch his body from the land of *Goshen* <note>The region in Egypt where the Israelites were permitted to live and graze their livestock.</note>, and taking with him a stately retinue of men, wagons, and much other equipage, he set out with his brothers; and they together brought the body of *Jacob* into the land of *Canaan*, and bur-

<column-break/>

ied it in the double cave of the field of *Machpelah*, near *Hebron*, where his fathers, *Abraham* and *Isaac*, were buried. The *Canaanites* were astonished to see such a great multitude of *Egyptians* coming into their land to bury a dead man, and they marveled at the splendor of the funeral procession. After all the funeral services were performed, and after a lamentation of seven days had been held for *Jacob’s* death according to custom, *Joseph* gave the command to depart and return again to *Egypt*. His brothers took the road back to *Goshen*, where they had left their families and flocks; and he returned again to the *Court*, where he remained in great prestige all his life. This great authority which he held over all *Egypt* began to make his brothers anxious after *Jacob’s* death; they feared that, no longer being restrained by the respect he had shown his father, he would make them feel the sting of his displeasure, and avenge himself for the inhuman treatment they had once dealt him. He had indeed assured them of the contrary on the day he made himself known to them, and had since that time given them nothing but signs of unfeigned affection: but when one feels so guilty toward someone, as *Joseph’s* brothers were toward him, it can hardly be otherwise but that the remorseful mind imagines causes for fear where indeed no cause exists. *Joseph* then made new professions of friendship to his brothers, and after answering with tears of tenderness their request to forgive the injustices and the evil they had done him, he assured them that he would never do them anything but good, and promised them his protection. They then returned, comforted by his answer, and experienced the truth of his words in all kinds of occurrences.

### The cruel servitude of the children of Israel in Egypt.

#### Exodus Chapter 1, verses 10–16.

<margin>Joseph dies in the year of the world 2369, before J. C. 1535.</margin> <note>J.C. stands for Jesus Christ; the date refers to 1535 B.C.</note>
Joseph lived about fifty-four years after his father’s death, and after he had performed notable services for Egypt during the span of eighty years, he died beloved and honored by all men, at the age of one hundred and ten years. Shortly before his death, he said to his brothers, who had come to see him: *I die, but God will surely visit you, and he will cause you to go up out of this land, into the land which he swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Swear to me, that you shall carry up my bones from here.* His brothers promised him this with an oath; and thus this holy <term>Patriarch</term> <note>The Dutch 'Aartsvader' refers to the founding fathers of the Israelite nation.</note> died in the faith of God’s promise, just as his fathers had died, leaving to the whole world examples of kindness and patience; an example of chastity in those situations where that virtue is most attacked, and at an age where the alertness of the passions hardly leaves the mind time to consult with godliness; and to all state ministers of Princes, the art of behaving with such wisdom and neutrality that the Kings and the people are both made happy by their administration. They embalmed his corpse after the manner of the Egyptians, and just as they had embalmed the body of his father; and they subsequently laid it in a coffin, where it was left in Egypt until the <term>Exodus</term> <note>The departure of the Israelites from Egypt.</note> of the children of Israel, who carried it, along with those of the other Patriarchs, Jacob’s sons, with them to the land of Canaan, as one reads in the seventh chapter of the Acts of the Apostles. Meanwhile, the families of Jacob’s sons multiplied greatly in the land of Goshen. They had initially settled in the region

<column-break/>

of Rameses, but within a short time they grew so much that, spreading out on all sides, they filled the entire landscape. Such a numerous and powerful colony began to cause some suspicion at Pharaoh’s Court, and the children of Israel had reason to behave themselves wisely and cautiously, and never to step beyond the bounds of respect and obedience which subjects owe to their Sovereigns; for even if they did no harm, they *could* do so, and that was enough for a suspicious, unjust, and cruel statecraft to deem them criminal. All the services that Joseph had bestowed upon Egypt were forgotten; and all the promises that a wise and grateful King had made to Jacob’s sons for them and their descendants were no longer counted under a different reign. Men were intent on nothing else but to bring this poor people to ruin; and Pharaoh’s entire Council was busy seeking means to destroy them forever. The means of weapons naturally presents itself first to the minds of Sovereigns, who have them at hand whenever they wish, and turn them wherever they please: but this means does not always satisfy, and a Prince sometimes fears that he will soil his glory by the shedding of the blood of his people. Sometimes also a fear mingles in that such would lead to the ruin of state affairs; men fear that the subjects, if too much oppressed, will conspire with foreign Princes when they make war on the Kingdom; or that they, driven to the utmost necessity, will leave the land and seek refuge elsewhere with their neighbors. All these considerations occurred to Pharaoh. *Come on*, he said in his Council, *let us deal wisely against that people, lest it happen, if any war occur, that they join with our enemies and fight against us, or depart out of the land.* It was decided

To this end, one began to burden them with unusual taxes; this had a fine pretext, for the people in general must provide taxes for the maintenance and welfare of the State; and besides that, Pharaoh had new border cities like Pithom and Raamses built. But it did not stop there; an even heavier yoke was laid upon them, which was capable of suppressing both the spirit and the body: this was that they were forced to make clay bricks <note>The Dutch 'tichgeltsteenen' refers to the sun-dried mud bricks used in Egyptian monumental architecture.</note>, a menial and servile task, and besides that very troublesome, due to the great number of these stones that they were daily forced to deliver. They worked on this without ceasing, and with a diligence that ought to have won them the favor of their masters. Yet their destruction was decided, and their services were not valued. They found no kindness nor

<column-break/>

mercy with the King’s Deputies; but they were overwhelmed with cruel wrongs, and the rod fell upon them as upon wicked slaves or beasts of burden. Many succumbed under this inhuman treatment, but these wretched people were not yet being eradicated quickly enough, and a surer way had to be taken to see an end to them. Pharaoh forbade the use of any midwives other than Egyptian ones to assist the Jewish women in childbirth, and they had orders to smother all the children of the Hebrews who were boys at birth. These midwives shrank from such a barbaric command; they spared these young infants, and however heathen they were, they nevertheless wished to respect God’s laws, which were engraved in Nature, rather than obey the cruel orders of their sovereign. God therefore did not leave this unrewarded, but preserved them from the wrath of that unjust and raging Prince, and filled them with blessings.

This mother, completely despondent that she had thus placed her child at the mercy of the current, soon lost sight of him; but God had His eye on him, and His hand acted as a steersman for this little chest which carried such a precious pledge, and steered it close to the gates of Memphis. The Princess, Pharaoh’s daughter, had gone out from the city to bathe in a place by the river, designated for that purpose for persons of her rank; and while her young maidens walked along the bank out of respect, they saw a little chest that had drifted between the rushes and the reeds. Curiosity to see what was inside made them approach that spot; and having pulled in the chest, they found a swaddled infant lying within. This sight, for which they were not at all prepared, startled her immediately; but since they were not ignorant of the King’s command against the Hebrews, they did not doubt that it was one of their children, whom they had thus placed in the river to avoid the heartbreak of seeing him killed alongside others at the King’s command. It was the child's own mother whom she went to fetch, and Pharaoh’s daughter commanded her to take the little one and care for him, promising her a great reward once she had weaned him. The Princess herself gave this child the name of **Moses**, which in the Egyptian language <note>original: "Egiptische taal"</note> means someone who is saved from the water; and his mother, having taken him with her, took all care of him, as one can easily imagine; and after a certain time brought him back to Pharaoh’s daughter, according to the command this Princess had given her. This was a new cause of sorrow for the father and mother of Moses, that they had to hand him over a second time and expose him to the infectious air of an idolatrous Court; but they hoped that God Himself, who had saved his life from the waters of the flood, would also preserve his soul from the deadly impressions of error and vice; and their faith guided and supported them in both the one and the other, according to what the Apostle Paul remarks about it in his Epistle to the Hebrews <note>Reference to Hebrews 11:23-27, which praises the faith of Moses' parents and Moses himself.</note>.

of Moses, and of the faith which made him esteem the glory of being one of God’s people, even though it was oppressed and persecuted, higher than the honor of being called a son of Pharaoh’s daughter, and possessing the foremost dignities and riches of Egypt. He remained at Court until the age of forty years, having spent his youth learning all the arts and sciences which can make a man, destined for the highest rank, a complete person. In all this he excelled among those of his age, and although he was not as smooth of speech as is common—for he admits himself that he was impeded of tongue <note>The Dutch "belemmerd van tong" refers to Moses' speech impediment, often described in the Bible as being "slow of speech and tongue."</note>—one nevertheless perceived in what he spoke a certain elevation of spirit, which drew people in more powerfully than the most practiced eloquence. He was mighty, says St. Stephen <note>Referencing Acts 7:22, where Stephen recounts the history of Israel.</note> of him, in words and in works, wise in giving counsel and executing affairs, persuasive where necessary, and steadfast and undaunted in occurrences where it was required to show his bravery against the enemies of the State. In the midst of such an attractive state, which was capable of making a heart drunk with the pleasures of the world and causing it to forget what it owes to God and His Congregation <term>Congregation: from the Dutch 'Gemeynte,' referring to the community of the faithful</term>, Moses constantly thought of the sad condition of his brothers, the children of Israel; and having once come to the land of Goshen to see them, he had the sorrow of witnessing the injustice done to them and the constant hardships with which they were plagued. Among others, he saw an Egyptian who, behaving insolently toward an Israelite, mistreated him as one would a slave, without any reason, but solely out of a desire to oppress an unfortunate man who had nothing for his defense but his right and his lament. Moses was struck to the heart by this, and through a heroic impulse which God’s Spirit brought about in him—as if to serve as a sign of the deliverance he would one day grant to his people—he rescued the Hebrew from the hand of the Egyptian and took the life of that unbeliever. The next day, he met two Israelites who were quarreling with each other; Moses was saddened to see that there was so little harmony among his brothers, and that at a time when they were so heavily oppressed by persecution, there were still such private differences and disagreements between Hebrew and Hebrew. He therefore desired to know the cause of their quarrel; and the one who had been mistreated by the other having told him so, Moses rebuked the one who was in the wrong. But this unjust and angry person could not endure a rebuke, but asked Moses insolently if he wanted to kill him as he had killed the Egyptian the day before. Moses, seeing himself thus discovered and fearing the King’s wrath—which he knew would not forgive a Hebrew for the death of an Egyptian—did not dare return to the Court, but fled to the land of Midian. While he sat resting there by a water well, it happened that the daughters of a Priest of 그hat land came there to draw water for their flocks, but some shepherds, also having come there, treated these daughters rudely and wanted to prevent them. Moses, seeing this, stood up for them and drove the shepherds away. Having returned home, they told their father of this occurrence. Jethro

<column-break/>

asking where the man was who had done them such good service, had him fetched and brought into his house. They subsequently agreed that Moses would stay to live with Jethro, to oversee his livestock and to herd them; and some time later, he gave him his daughter Zipporah in marriage.

While Moses was grazing Jethro's flock in the wilderness of that land, he once went to Mount Horeb, and there he had a vision that amazed him and filled him with wonder. It was a bramble bush that burned without being consumed. Moses wanted to go there to behold this new miracle; but as he approached, he heard a voice from the midst of the bush, calling him twice by his name, crying out: *Do not come near; take your shoes off your feet, for the place where you stand is holy ground.* Moses perceived that it was God speaking to him, and that it was His appearance and presence which made that place holy and venerable. He then did as God commanded him, and covered his face out of reverence, for he feared to look upon God. Then God said to him that He had beheld the oppression of His people in Egypt, that He had come down to deliver them, and that He wished to use him for that great work. Forty years had now passed since Moses had left Egypt, and when he understood that God wanted to send him to speak to Pharaoh, his great humility made him answer that he was unworthy of that service, that he was not a man of eloquent speech but heavy of tongue, and that he requested that God be pleased to give that burden to another who could acquit himself of it better than he. But God persisted in the choice He had made of Moses, because the good result of His undertakings does not depend on the quality of His instruments which He employs, but that it is He Himself who makes the weakest and most despised instruments powerful. He then instructed Moses in everything he was to do; and to give him courage against the fear that the Hebrews themselves would not believe him when he said that God had appeared to him and commanded him to announce their upcoming deliverance, God said to him: "See to it that you perform in their presence all the wonders that I shall show you. *What is that in your hand?*" and he said, "*A staff.*" "*Throw it,*" God continued, "*to the ground*": and Moses threw it to the ground; whereupon it immediately turned into a snake. "*Grasp it,*" said the Lord, "*by its tail*"; and no sooner had Moses caught this snake than it returned to its previous form and became a staff. This first miracle was followed by another; Moses was commanded to put his hand into his bosom, and when he pulled it out again, it was entirely white with leprosy. He was ordered to put it in there again; he did so, and as soon as he had pulled it out again, it was healthy and pure like the rest of his body. By these two miracles which Moses saw, and for which God had granted him power to perform before the children of Israel, he took courage; and understanding that God wanted to add his brother Aaron as a helper in that great undertaking, he was quite gladdened; and departed after the ending of the vision with his flock from Mount Horeb, and returned again to his father-in-law.

# Aaron goes to meet Moses and joins him to go and deliver the people.

## Exodus Chapter IV. verses 27 – 29

Moses, having returned to his father-in-law, informed him of his intention to visit his brothers, the children of Israel, in the land of Egypt. The Scriptures do not mention whether he gave Jethro an account of the vision he had seen on Mount Horeb, or of the command he had received; there may have been reasons of wisdom and prudence to keep this secret from him; and Jethro agreed without difficulty that Moses should make the journey of which he had spoken. He took with him his wife and his two sons, Gershom and Eliezer. This latter son was not yet circumcised; one cannot say exactly what the reason for this was; but the respect one owes to the Saints <note>In this context, "Saints" refers to the holy patriarchs of the Bible.</note> does not allow one—when something irregular appears in matters that could serve as an accusation against them—to attribute it to their conduct, especially when it is wrapped by the Holy Spirit in the veil of silence within the Scriptures. One must not lightly imagine that a man as holy as Moses would have neglected the practice of circumcision in his household after such an express command as that which God had given to Abraham and all his descendants: to circumcise their male children on the eighth day after birth.

<margin>*The same year. 2513.</margin>
It is very likely that Moses' wife had not long ago given birth to this child, and that Moses, having departed as soon as she was fit to travel so as to delay as little as possible a journey upon which the comfort and deliverance of God’s people depended, had not dared to circumcise his child for fear that his life might have been in danger if he were exposed too soon to the hard-

<column-break/>

ships of a long journey; or that if he had waited until the child was entirely healed from the wound of circumcision, his departure might have been delayed too long. Indeed, the Israelites were exempted some time later from circumcising their children in the Wilderness so that their lives would not be endangered on that difficult journey which the people had to make; but neither Moses nor any other Hebrew had such a dispensation then; and the reason of prudence alone was not enough to make an exception regarding the Law. Moses then departed with Zipporah his wife and his two sons, and having stayed a while at an inn which he found on the way, the Lord met him and sought to kill him, because he had not immediately circumcised his child. Zipporah, terrified by this sight, took a stone knife and circumcised the child herself; then, quite angry with her husband because he had so hastened the journey that they could not circumcise their little son at home, she threw the portion of the foreskin which she had cut off at Moses' feet, saying to him, *You are a bridegroom of blood to me*, <note>original: "Gy zyt my een bloedbruydegom"</note> whether she meant to imply that she had saved his life through the blood of her son, and thus he had become her husband for a second time, or whether she meant that he would be the cause of the child's death, as she feared it would die on the way.

While Moses thus prepared himself to follow the commands God had given him, his brother in Egypt was commanded by the Lord to depart from there and to go to meet Moses in the wilderness of Midian. It does not appear from the Scriptures that God made known to him the cause of that journey, nor that He revealed to him His intention to use Moses for the deliverance of the Hebrews; this was a secret that God had entrusted to Moses alone, and which Aaron his brother had to learn from him. He then departed according to the command he had received, and he

#### Exodus Chapter V. verses 5---10.

<margin>The same year.</margin>
Aaron and Moses first came into the land of Goshen <note>A region in ancient Egypt assigned to the Israelites, located in the eastern Nile Delta.</note>, before they went to present themselves before Pharaoh. Upon their arrival, they gathered all the Elders of the people and gave them to understand that God would soon deliver them from their slavery, and that they were commanded by God to request their freedom from Pharaoh. Then they performed in the presence of the people the miraculous signs which God had commanded Moses to do to confirm their mission, and thereby find belief among the Hebrews. After they had seen all those wonders—namely, that the staff Moses had in his hand was changed into a snake, and the snake back into a staff; that Moses' hand, when he put it in his bosom, was immediately covered with leprosy, and in the next moment became as pure as the rest of his body—they felt convinced in their hearts that God, without whose power Moses could not have performed these miraculous signs (which exceeded natural ability), had

<column-break/>

truly sent him to set His people at liberty, and thus fulfill the promise He had made to Abraham, to deliver his descendants when they were oppressed and ill-treated in a foreign land. The Hebrews rejoiced to hear that God had not forgotten them, and that he was moved by their heavy distress. When Moses and Aaron then took their leave of them to go to Pharaoh, all the people overwhelmed them with blessings, and poured out wishes and prayers for the successful outcome of their service. They then went to Pharaoh, to present to him on God's behalf that he should allow the Hebrews to go out of his lands, saying:

Pharaoh heard these words with contempt and anger;

> *Who is the LORD*, he said, *whose voice I should obey to let Israel go? I do not know the LORD, nor this Jehovah of whom you speak*;

for Moses and Aaron called God by His own name of *Jehovah*, by which He has always been distinguished from the false gods of the idolaters. Kings do not always do what they might be able to do, or what their own conscience drives them to, because there is a greater King than they, who, without them realizing it, changes their heart somewhat and prevents them from taking a decision according to their own inclinations. Moses and Aaron then received from that Prince <note>Referring to Pharaoh</note> no other bad reception than an answer that was more an insult to God than terrifying to them. But no sooner had they departed, than Pharaoh gave the command to make the yoke of the Hebrews heavier and more unbearable. He had already long set them to work making bricks, which he used for the building of certain fortresses on the borders, and (as some have written) to erect those proud Pyramids or obelisks <note>The original Dutch uses *grafnaalden*, literally "grave-needles," a common historical term for obelisks or tall monuments.</note>, which have served as one of the greatest ornaments of Egypt and have been considered one of the wonders of the world. Until now, it had been customary to provide the children of Israel with the necessary wood and straw to bake the bricks, provided that they delivered to the King's officials a certain daily number, which was greater than what fair masters would have been able to demand. But after Moses and Aaron had gone away, the officials received orders to give no more wood or straw to the people, yet nevertheless to compel them to deliver the same number of bricks daily to the King as before. This was as much as putting this wretched people in a state of impossibility to perform the work required of them; but the greater their oppression was, the

<column-break/>

greater was the pleasure that Pharaoh took in it. The Hebrews, however, did not let their courage sink entirely at this new blow that pressed so heavily upon them, because they saw no means of being released from this command: therefore they doubled their diligence and alertness, and hastening first to make the set number of bricks daily, they spent the remainder of the day, or a part of the night, in gathering stubble to bake them. At the beginning, it was not exactly too difficult for them to find much of it in a land as abundantly fertile as that of Goshen, but the great quantity that was needed to bake so many bricks daily put the children of Israel in no state to fulfill what was demanded of them; and no skill, alertness, nor strength was powerful enough to resist such heavy necessity. All these calamities soon poured down upon Moses and Aaron; there were nothing but complaints and reproaches made to them, that they had been the cause of this latest aggravation and unjust severity; *You have made us*, it was said, *stink before Pharaoh and before his servants, putting a sword in their hands to kill us; may the Lord look upon you and judge!* <note>original: "stinkende gemaakt" - a literal translation of the biblical idiom meaning to make someone loathsome or odious.</note> These were in the beginning the consequences of the embassy of Aaron and Moses to the King of Egypt, being so difficult and sad in every respect that they were enough to frighten these two servants of the Most High, instead of strengthening their hope and encouraging them to pursue their petition for the freedom of the Hebrews.

...done beyond God’s command, He did not wish to leave them long in that distress and anxiety. He then spoke to Moses, and assured him that Pharaoh would let the people go, but that it would not be until extreme necessity forced him to do so, and the miraculous signs he would see compelled him. To help Moses believe this more firmly, and so that the Prophet might be able to convince the people with reason, God spoke to him of His covenant with Abraham, and of the explicit promise He had made to him to deliver his descendants from the servitude into which He had foretold they would one day fall in Egypt. God’s words are remarkable and well deserve to be quoted here:

> *I am the Lord, He said to Moses, and I appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as God Almighty; but by my name THE LORD <note>The original Dutch uses "HEERE," signifying the Tetragrammaton, the sacred four-letter name of God.</note> I was not known to them; that is to say, by that holy and adorable name, which perfectly signifies the faithfulness and unchangeability of that Supreme Being, in the fulfillment of His promise regarding the land of Canaan, in whose possession He had not yet placed them or their lineage until that time, but was finally about to do so, and through the fulfillment of that great promise, to hallow the Hebrew people as His own special people, and in that capacity to shower them with His temporal and spiritual favors. I will bring you out, He said, from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will rescue you from their bondage, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great judgments. And I will take you to be my people, and I will be a God to you; and you shall know that I am the Lord your God. And I will bring you into that land, over which I lifted my hand, to give it to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; and I will give it to you for a heritage, I THE LORD.*

These words set the minds of the Hebrews at ease again and drove away all doubts. Their yoke became easier to bear in the hope that it would soon be broken, and their difficulties were softened by the expectation of a deliverance which they regarded as nothing less than infallible.

Aaron and Moses, seeing them thus strengthened in spirit, returned again to Pharaoh. They found that Prince inaccessible to compassion and stubbornly set on not granting the Hebrews their freedom. They repeated to him the same matters they had said to him on the first journey, but it was in vain: this Prince mocked everything these Messengers of God could present to him to

<column-break/>

move him; and declaring what they said to him to be imagination and deceit—namely, that it was the Lord, the Master of Heaven and earth, who had sent them—he demanded that they prove it to him by some miraculous sign. Moses and Aaron desired nothing more than to make their mission evident before Pharaoh and all the Great Men of Egypt; they did so therefore, and Moses, turning to his brother Aaron, into whose hands he had placed the staff <note>This refers to the miraculous staff Moses used to perform God's wonders.</note> which he had with him when God appeared to him in the burning bush, commanded him to cast it down before Pharaoh. Aaron did so, and that staff became a dragon <note>original: "draak" — in 18th-century Dutch bibles, this term was often used for a large serpent or sea-monster.</note>. The King did not surrender to this miraculous sign, which nevertheless deserved all his attention and observation, and should have made him honor with awe the invisible hand that had produced it in this miraculous transformation. But instead, he sought only an opportunity to mislead and deceive himself: he summoned two famous Sorcerers, whose names the Apostle Paul has preserved for us <note>The sorcerers Jannes and Jambres are mentioned in 2 Timothy 3:8 as those who opposed Moses.</note>, *Jannes* and *Jambres*, to set them against Aaron and Moses. These conjurers deluded the eyes of the King and all the onlookers, and each having thrown their staff which they held in their hand to the ground, just as Aaron had, they appeared to the eyes of all the bystanders to have changed into two dragons. But God, who had permitted these Sorcerers to strike the eyes of the Egyptians with a kind of blindness in order to thwart the righteous and godly intention of His Servants, did not allow the lie and the deceit to obscure the greatness of the miracle that His hand had wrought. Aaron’s staff then—or the dragon that had come from that staff—hurled itself with force upon the two staffs of the conjurers, which appeared to be two dragons, and swallowed them up and devoured them, so that in a moment they disappeared before the eyes of the bystanders, and not the slightest trace of them remained; since the divine power had changed them into air, or some other fine and invisible matter, during the attack of the dragon that was formed from Aaron’s staff, which became a staff again as soon as Aaron laid his hand upon it. But neither the miracle of this transformation, nor the shame which must necessarily have seized the Sorcerers upon seeing their deceit frustrated and their staffs brought to nothing, could make Pharaoh change his purpose regarding the children of Israel; but on the contrary, he became more stubborn in keeping them in slavery, just as God had foretold to Moses.

“...river, which constitutes the beauty and wealth of your Kingdom, we shall change it into blood; and all the fish that are in this flood shall die, and people will not be able to drink of its waters, nor use them for any purpose in the Kingdom of Egypt.” Pharaoh should have trembled at this threat, had he carefully considered all its consequences; but God did not permit him to reflect upon it as wisely as was fitting. He remained stubborn in refusing the permission that had been requested of him; and God, provoked by this disdain and zealous for His honor, told Aaron to stretch out his hand and strike the waters of the river with the staff he held. Thereupon they were immediately changed into blood, presenting to the eye the most horrific spectacle ever witnessed: a river of blood. All the rivers of Egypt, its ponds, fountains, and streams underwent the same change, and not even a vessel of water was found in the houses of the Egyptians where the stroke of the staff that hit the Nile had not left its mark of power, and where the water did not turn to blood. All the fish of Egypt died, and the air became polluted, both by the blood covering the earth and by the dead fish, some of which lay washed up on the banks and some of which rotted while mixed in the blood. All Egypt beheld this terrible sight for seven days, realizing that this would cause the loss of all its inhabitants and livestock. People were in incredible distress, fearing they would die of thirst and struggling with other matters for which water is absolutely necessary. It would not have been difficult

<column-break/>

for Pharaoh to understand what this man could have done to him, who by the stroke of a staff had caused blood to flow throughout all Egypt: but this Prince was far too blinded by his passion to allow his vision to range so far. Instead of taking advantage of such a terrifying occurrence <note>Meaning, using the event as an opportunity to reconsider his stance and submit to God's command.</note>, he sought only to immerse himself deeper in his prejudices. He gave orders to his **Sorcerers** <term>Toveraars: magicians or court officials practiced in the occult</term> that they should attempt to do something similar. Water was then fetched from wherever possible, and it was likely from the land of Goshen where the Israelites lived, which was undoubtedly preserved from this plague just as it was from the others; and to this brought water, the two sorcerers <note>Traditional accounts often identify these two as Jannes and Jambres.</note>, whether by trickery or by the help of the Devil, made a change like the one Aaron had made in all the waters of the Kingdom: this water took on the color of blood, and possibly it even had the taste of it. But the difference was in every respect so great between the change which the Sorcerers made in a few drops of water, and that which Moses and Aaron had made solely by the stroke of a staff in an entire river, deep and wide like the Nile, and in all the waters of Egypt, that it was impossible not to perceive in the one the hand of God, and in the other the deception and weakness of a man. Yet God had given Pharaoh no eyes to see, nor a heart to understand. It was enough for him that he had been able to find some resemblance, however small and faint it might be, between the actions of his **Conjurors** <term>Bezweerdereren: those who attempt to control spirits or events through incantations</term> and those of Aaron and Moses, to restrain himself from believing that it was God who spoke and worked through them: and upon that, he rejected their request.

# The Second Plague of Egypt.
### Frogs scattered over the entire land.
## Exodus Chapter VIII. verses 1–8.

At the end of seven days, God withdrew His hand from over Egypt, and the waters of the entire land became pure and fresh, just as they were before. That which the terrible judgment of God—which had burst forth against the entire Kingdom—had not been able to produce in the heart of Pharaoh (to awaken there compassion toward the Hebrews), this mercy should have brought about. By causing the blood to retreat from all the rivers of the land, God showed a grace that ought to have moved Pharaoh to gratitude, leading him to grant the freedom that God demanded for His people. But Pharaoh looked upon everything, the good as well as the evil, with one and the same eye, and his heart was hardened <note>The Dutch "verstókt" refers to a spiritual state where a person becomes stubbornly insensible to divine warnings</note> by the one as much as by the other. As a pretext for his refusal, he told Moses and Aaron that his sorcerers <note>The court magicians or priests of Egypt who practiced the "secret arts"</note> had also changed their staffs into snakes and the water into blood; he therefore considered himself well-justified in not believing what they told him regarding God having sent them. But what could he say after he had seen that those same sorcerers had been unable to protect their staffs against Aaron’s, nor stop the blood that had flowed in the river for seven days, nor provide a single drop of fresh water to Egypt? It is an amazing thing that such stubbornness and rage can exist in a soul, hiding the truth from oneself and refusing to surrender to such clear evidence. The heart of man is an abyss which man himself does not yet know, and whose entire depth no one but God alone can see. Moses and

<column-break/>

Aaron received the command to return to Pharaoh again and to address him in the same manner as they had already done on three separate occasions, threatening him that if he persisted in his refusal to let the Hebrews depart, they would cover all of Egypt with frogs. They warned that no cities, villages, nor houses would be free of them; indeed, they would even be in his palace, in his chambers, and upon his bed. Pharaoh already had too much experience of what these two servants of God could do to doubt whether they would perform what they threatened. But this Prince was given over to a spirit of rejection, and godlessness had established its seat so firmly in his mind that it did not allow him to listen to reason for even a moment. God then commanded Moses to order Aaron to stretch out his hand and his staff over the rivers, the streams, and all the pools of Egypt, to bring forth millions of frogs and fill the entire land. This command did not require Aaron to traverse all of Egypt and strike every river and pool of the Realm with his staff; this would have required too much time, and such a long and difficult journey would have diminished the perceived greatness of the miracle. Furthermore, it was not properly the blow he struck that produced the miraculous signs, but it was God who worked all these wonders; Aaron’s staff was merely a given sign, upon which God executed throughout all of Egypt the things He had foretold through His servants. Aaron then struck the river, and at the same time an extraordinary multitude of frogs was formed in all the waters of the Realm. These swarmed out of the rivers, pools, and other such places in great troops, spreading everywhere until Egypt was covered with them. The cities became as full of them as the fields, and there was no amount of diligence or watchful oversight that [could keep] the doors

## The third plague of Egypt.
### Humans and beasts tormented by Lice.
#### Exodus Chapter VIII. verses 16–19.

After that behavior of Pharaoh toward Moses and Aaron, to which he had been forced to take refuge by praying them to deliver his land from the frogs, there seemed to be hope that, they having done what he wished, he would now desist from his severity against the Hebrews. But the heart of this Monarch was too proud to give himself over so quickly to the prayers which had been made on their behalf. He would have imagined that he lowered himself too far if he had shown such great respect for those Hebrew men, who requested him to allow their nation
<column-break/>
to go serve the God of their fathers in the wilderness. He had decided to keep this people in his shackles <note>original: "kluyfters," referring to bonds or heavy chains</note>, and he let himself be persuaded by an unwise vanity that it would have been detrimental to his honor to deviate somewhat from his first intent; and his flatterers did not fail to praise him highly for this resistance. Meanwhile, Moses and Aaron were not discouraged by the difficulties that occurred to them daily. They spoke to Pharaoh again, but their request was, just as before, very roughly refused. Aaron had that famous staff, with which he had already performed so many wonders, everywhere with him; Moses had placed it in his hand at God’s command, and Aaron made use of it only upon the word and command of Moses; for God had said to that Prophet <note>Moses</note> that he would be as a God to Aaron, and that Aaron would stand in service to him; and therefore it was that God always gave His commands immediately to Moses, and Moses subsequently gave those to Aaron. God then commanded Moses to say to Aaron, that he with his staff

staff should strike the dust of the earth, and that lice <note>The Dutch word 'luyzen' can refer to lice, gnats, or stinging midges; it represents the Third Plague</note> would come forth from it, which would fill all of Egypt. Until that time, Aaron had not stretched out his hand and his staff except over the waters: if he had always continued in the same manner, the Idolaters might perhaps have imagined that the power of the God of the Hebrews reached no further than the waters; just as many centuries later the Syrians, having been beaten by the Israelites in the narrow passes of the mountains, said—to comfort themselves over their defeat—that the God of Israel was a *God of the mountains*, and that if they could entice the people to fight on the plain, they would surely overcome them. But their imagination deceived them, and God showed those Unbelievers in a second battle which they lost in the field of Aphek, that He was no less the God of hosts in the plains than on the mountains and hills. The dust of the earth felt the staff by which it was struck, just as the waters of the river had felt it, and it was no less obedient to the commands of Him who moved this staff and struck with it wherever He willed. There was then formed from the dust of the earth throughout the whole land of Egypt a certain small stinging vermin, like lice, which attacked men and beasts. There was no age, no gender, nor status that went free; all were plagued by these crawling creatures, and all the diligence employed to guard against them was useless. The rich man was no less covered with them than the poor, and gold or purple <note>Referring to the expensive purple-dyed fabrics of the nobility</note> could excuse one as little as torn patches and old rags. It was the strict command of Him for whom all flesh is but dust and dung, that there should be no one among the Egyptians, from the beggar on the straw to the King on the throne, who would not fall prey to this vermin.

<column-break/>

And yet, after all this, the proud heart of Pharaoh could not resolve to humble itself under the hand of Him who, though he was most worthy of being crushed, had spared him until that day. He wished, according to his custom, to nullify the greatness of this miracle, and for that purpose summoned his Enchanters; but these wretched men, who had served as the Devil’s tools to resist the righteous intentions of Aaron and Moses, could obtain no help from Hell on this occasion to mimic Aaron’s deed, and, just like him, bring forth lice from the dust of the earth. One might think that they could have deluded the eyes of Pharaoh and the Egyptians, just as before, to make such vermin appear where they were not: but God was weary of enduring those deceptions, and willed that all the power of Hell should vanish before the most despised of all vermin. The Sorcerers confessed before Pharaoh that they could do nothing of the sort; *This is*, they said, *the finger of God* <note>original: "Dit is Gods vinger." Latin: *Digitus Dei*. This famous phrase indicates the magicians' recognition of a supernatural power beyond their own magic</note>. That which had preceded—the staff changed into a dragon, and the waters into blood, along with the frogs that covered Egypt—was likewise the finger of God; His power appeared very clearly in all those things; but the Devil and his servants hide the truth as much as they can, and when the Sorcerers were forced to acknowledge it in the miraculous production of lice, they did so in such a way as if to imply that everything Moses and Aaron had done until then did not exceed the power of Nature. Meanwhile, Pharaoh was no more persuaded by this miracle than by the others, but continued to harden his heart.

This threat should have made the Tyrant <note>Referring to Pharaoh</note> tremble, as sad experience had already taught him how terrible even the least of all vermin can be in the hands of a provoked God. Yet he paid no heed, but persisted in refusing freedom to the Hebrews. God even willed that Moses and Aaron, on that occasion, should stir up a sense of jealousy in the mind of that Prince, and that they should tell him that the land of Goshen, where the children of Israel were, would be free from all those insects with which the rest of Egypt was threatened. At first glance, this might lead someone to think that the other plagues had also extended to the land of Goshen; but such a thing is not at all probable, as it cannot be suspected that God’s people, for whose sake all these wonders were performed, would have suffered from them as much as the Egyptians. The reason, then, why God willed that this exception should be so expressly made known to Pharaoh on this occasion was so that he would pay more attention to it than he had done until now. It was intended that a kind of jealousy and shame—seeing that a small corner of his Kingdom would have more privilege than the places he honored with his presence, and the city where he had his palace—might make him cautious and thoughtful enough to prevent this occurrence. But all this was of no help; Pharaoh’s stubbornness prevailed, and the most powerful considerations had to give way to it. Then God caused a terrible multitude of various insects to come; Moses has mentioned neither the name nor the nature of them, and the Prophet who composed the seventy-eighth Psalm, in which mention is made of the plagues of Egypt, does not explain himself more clearly than Moses; nor does the Jewish historian <note>Likely referring to Flavius Josephus</note> speak more clearly of it than those two Prophets. Nevertheless, it is generally believed that the original word in Exodus and in the Psalm signifies flies or wasps rather than any other kind of creature, and especially those wasps or hornets that make a buzzing sound while flying, and whose sting is very fierce and painful. It was with this flying army that God went to battle against Pharaoh; it spread over all of Egypt, and humans and beasts suffered such discomfort from it that it is indescribable. One could not go into the field, nor remain in the cities: one saw entire swarms that darkened the sky, and they came flying into the houses, rooms, and most secluded chambers.

<column-break/>

It was no wind that drove them forward and carried them to and fro; but it was the breath of God’s wrath that brought them forth into the air, even into places that were the most inaccessible to winds and storms. Everywhere one found air to breathe, one found these insects and felt their stings. Pharaoh himself was so tormented by them that he knew of no counsel to protect himself or to find rest anywhere; all his recourse was to Moses and Aaron. And this Prince, unyielding due to a false statecraft and stubborn until that time in granting them nothing, did not realize that his rest and life were constantly in the hands of those two servants of God whose request he so proudly rejected. He felt, however, on this new occasion, his stubbornness waver, but his heart resisted it: and thus this miserable Prince found himself squeezed between his obstinacy not to let the people go and the dire necessity to ward off the scourge of God under which he was collapsing. In this strange state of mind, he decided to come to a kind of treaty with Moses and Aaron, which was to propose to them that the Hebrews should perform their sacrifices, which they wanted to go and do to God in the wilderness, within Egypt. But Moses refused this, because he well knew that such was not the intent of God, who intended to lead His people out of Egypt. There was yet another reason why he could not accept the King's offer, and upon which he also grounded his refusal, and that was that the Egyptians, having a horror <note>original: "grouwel"</note> of the sacrifice of sheep, oxen, and goats because of their superstitious reverence which they paid to those animals, would have thrown themselves with rage upon the Hebrews as loathsome and godless people, and would have stoned them. For these reasons, the latter of which Moses presented only to Pharaoh, he continued to request that the people might be permitted to go and sacrifice to God in the wilderness, three days' journey from Egypt. The King, seeing himself pressed and yet not wanting to allow the Hebrews to leave his land, pretended as if he consented to the request; and under a false promise he made to Moses and Aaron, or under a deceitful and doubtful assurance, he prayed them to obtain peace, so that the insects which plagued him might depart from his Kingdom and leave him and his people free to breathe. The two Prophets requested this of God, who granted their prayer. But Pharaoh resumed his harsh nature and paid no heed to what he had promised.

## The fifth plague of Egypt.

### A pestilence carries away all the livestock that was in the field.

### Exodus Chapter IX. verse 6.

<margin>The same year.</margin>
Egypt had not yet suffered any significant loss under the four preceding plagues; everything until now had consisted of various very difficult discomforts that had come upon the land; and as soon as God’s hand had stopped striking, all the evil was over, and the Egyptians found themselves back in their former state. Pharaoh perhaps imagined that he and his Kingdom would now be delivered; but

<column-break/>

God had yet other plagues prepared for him, which would strike him where people are usually most sensitive: namely, in their own interest and the loss of property. Egypt had a great abundance of animals, such as camels, oxen, sheep, donkeys, and above all horses, from which it drew great profits by selling them to foreigners, who made much of them. God then decided to take vengeance on these considerable goods collectively, because of Pharaoh’s hardheartedness against the children of Israel and the deceit he had committed against Moses and Aaron, since he had promised them to let the people go and yet held them back contrary to his promise. To that end, the Lord sent them for the seventh time back to that Prince to request the same thing of him.

<column-break/>

hour, and from all sides nothing was heard but talk of dead horses, and of entire herds of oxen, camels, donkeys, sheep, and goats, all of which had been swept away by a sudden pestilence against which no remedy could be found to protect a single beast. Those who are not accustomed to paying close attention to the right that God has over men and their possessions—and who do not know that there is an almost infinite number of occurrences where Divine Wisdom and Justice, working together, can involve many persons in the punishment that seemingly should have fallen upon only one alone—will stand amazed that all the Egyptians suffered such a great loss for a crime of which they were not guilty. Pharaoh was stubborn in not allowing the Hebrews to depart from his land, and therefore God was wroth with him and took His vengeance. But what could the people of Egypt do against it? It does not befit subjects to give counsel to their Kings and to govern their conduct; nor would Kings allow such a thing, and it would be nothing other than bringing unrest and disorder into the Government, and introducing anarchy <note>Original: "heerscheloosheyd," literally "rule-less-ness."</note>. Why then must they be punished for the mistakes that their Kings commit, and of which they themselves are innocent? The loss that Pharaoh and all the Egyptians had suffered regarding their livestock caused despair throughout the entire Kingdom; but Pharaoh consoled himself with the malicious pleasure of keeping the children of Israel in slavery. This pleasure had already cost him dearly, but it was still only half of the plagues which God had destined for Egypt, and the five yet to come were set to be much heavier than the first five. Moses and Aaron returned once more to Pharaoh and found him just as he was before. These ashes passed from their hands into those of God, where they multiplied almost infinitely and were carried through all the land of Egypt. The glowing hand of God’s wrath, which spread these ashes everywhere—even to the most remote places of the Kingdom—turned them into a penetrating poison which poisoned humans and beasts, and so corrupted their internal fluids that their bodies were covered with boils and blisters. It must have been ghastly, to see nothing in all of Egypt but half-rotted bodies, and from the poor man in his hut to the King in his palace and purple, not to find a single person who was not covered with pustules and boils. ### The seventh plague of Egypt.

->*Hail and fire mixed together devastate the whole land.*<-

->Exodus Chapter IX. verses 23—25.<-

<margin>The same year. 2513.</margin>
God continued by sending Aaron and Moses to Pharaoh to once again request the freedom of the Hebrews. If this Prince had not fallen into an extraordinary excess of mind and heart, he would have been able to see that God, who concerned Himself so much with the freedom of this people, could have given it to them Himself whenever it pleased Him; but it was written in the book of eternal decrees that Pharaoh would harden his heart more and more, so that God could make His power and justice against him, and His love toward the descendants of Israel, shine out all the more. This was what God had said to that Prince, with expressions that were capable of amazing him and making him tremble. This time, He said after Pharaoh was healed of his boils <note>The Dutch "zweeren" refers to the sores or boils of the sixth plague.</note>, *this time I will send all my plagues into your heart, that is, many calamities and disasters at once, which would pierce his soul with terror and pain: I will send them over your servants, and over your people, so that you may know that there is no one like Me on the whole earth: for now I have stretched out my hand, that I might strike you and your people with pestilence, and that you should be destroyed from the earth: But truly for this reason have I raised you up, for this reason have I still left you in existence, that*

<column-break/>

*I might show my power to you, and that my name might be told throughout the whole earth.* Moses and Aaron then declared to him with what disasters God threatened him, and told him that the next day terrible thunderclaps would come over all of Egypt, mixed with hail and fire, by which the grain would be beaten down, the trees broken, and the people and animals found in the field would be killed. They were still so charitable that they gave Pharaoh this advice: that he should cause all the livestock that was in the field to be gathered and kept locked up, so that they would not perish by this storm of fire and hail. Such great goodness, in men who had so much cause to complain about the hardheartedness and treachery of that Monarch, should have touched his heart and brought him to such considerations as his own interest and that of his Kingdom obliged him to take concerning the terrible destruction with which he was threatened; but this madman ran to his ruin, and nothing was powerful enough to stop him. The following day arrived, the sky darkened with thick clouds, the thunders roared, the lightnings shot down, the hail fell from all sides, a fire of a new kind, and until that day still unknown to the world, mixed itself among the hail, descended at once from heaven, and the hail and the fire seemed to contend who should be the first to devastate the earth; yet they both agreed to bruise the trees, to destroy the vineyards, and the barley which was almost ready to fill the hand of the reaper with its sheaves, as well as the

<column-break/>

that which Moses and Aaron had foretold to him the day before: that this plague had entered into his heart. God beheld and heard them, and immediately the thunder fell silent, the fire disappeared, the hail stopped, the air grew calm, and all the fields of Egypt came to rest and safety. But when the storm was over and the danger past, Pharaoh thought no more of his distress nor his promises, and he hardened his heart once again.

# The eighth plague of Egypt.

## *Locusts.*

### Exodus Chapter X. verses 13—15

<margin>
The same year. 2513.
</margin>

It seemed that Pharaoh had decided to put God’s patience to the ultimate test and to exhaust all the means He could use to punish the most stubborn rebellion. He had confessed to Moses and Aaron that he was guilty because he had not obeyed the repeated commands which they had presented to him on behalf of the God of Israel to let that people go, although he had promised no longer to oppose it. But for that, it would have been necessary for God to have changed his heart; for as long as God left him as he

<column-break/>

was, and in his own nature, he could be capable of nothing good, and it was almost as if God Himself had hardened him. Wherefore Moses, who saw this unyielding stubbornness of Pharaoh, often says that the Lord hardened his heart, solely for the reason that God, through His grace, did not soften and convert the hard and evil heart of this godless King. The Apostle Paul sets before our eyes the right of God’s supremacy in that regard and leads us before the feet of His adorable majesty to keep us in reverence and a humble silence: *God has mercy, he says, on whom He will, and hardens whom He will.* <note>A reference to Romans 9:18, explaining the theological concept of divine sovereignty and predestination.</note> Pharaoh, then, being left to his own guidance and remaining ever master of his heart, shows himself obstinate against God’s judgments; and it was necessary that God either cease insisting on the permission [to leave], which He so...

This latter course was indeed what **God** intended to do, and to that end He already had an eighth plague ready to pour out over Egypt. Moses and Aaron went to announce this to Pharaoh, and they did so with such power that the principal Lords of the Court, who were present, feared that all of Egypt would be destroyed. These were, meanwhile, only **Locusts** with which Egypt was threatened; but what is there so weak that it is not terrifying in the hands of **God** when He uses it as a punishment? Thus He Himself, through the Prophet **Joel**, calls the locusts, along with the beetle, the cankerworm, and the caterpillar, *His great army*. The hail of the previous plague had not yet taken everything away; and Moses gives us to understand that the wheat and some other grain, which had not yet shot up so high, were not entirely destroyed, because the ear <note>The Dutch "aair" refers to the head or spike of the grain containing the seeds.</note> had not yet appeared, being protected within the stalk, which, bowing under the violence of the storm, had afterwards risen again. But Moses and Aaron said to Pharaoh and those of his Court that whatever had escaped the violence of the hail would be eaten up by the locusts; and that there would be such a great number, and of such a terrible appearance, that the entire land would be covered with them, such as had never been seen before, nor would be seen in the future. One could not regard the threats of these Servants of **God** as words cast into the air; a deadly experience had all too often shown all of Egypt that they never threatened falsely. Pharaoh, however, did not allow himself to be moved by it, but the Egyptian Lords were terrified by it, and the fear of completely losing the little that remained to them in the field, and thus seeing the entire Kingdom overtaken by famine, caused them to advise the King to let the people go, and to allow them to serve the Lord their—

<column-break/>

—**God**, before they saw all of Egypt perish. Pharaoh accepted only a part of that advice, and having called Moses and Aaron, who had already left him, he told them that he allowed the men to go and serve **God** in the wilderness, pretending as if that was all they had requested of him; but regarding their wives, little children, and cattle, all those were to remain in Egypt. Moses and Aaron rejected this offer as being contrary to their purpose and to the command they had received from **God**; and the King, angered by their refusal, had them driven away from him. They were no sooner outside than **God** commanded Moses to stretch out his hand and his staff over the land of Egypt to bring the locusts: upon this movement made by Moses, **God** caused an East wind to rise, which lasted the whole day and the whole night following, and brought such a great multitude of locusts over the entire land that the earth was completely covered with them; they ate the grain crops, the meadows, and the leaves of the trees, leaving nothing behind, so that not the slightest greenery remained on the earth. Then Pharaoh, being troubled because he had brought this new devastation upon his Kingdom, sent for Moses and Aaron in haste, and as soon as he saw them, he cried out:
> I have sinned against the Lord your God and against you; 
and looking at Moses, 
> Forgive me, I pray, my sin only this once. 
Afterward, like a distraught man who cannot come to a firm decision, turning to Moses and Aaron together, he said to them: 
> Pray fervently to the Lord your God, that he may only take this death away from me. 
They then went out immediately and beseeched **God** for relief for this false penitent; and **God** immediately caused a West wind to blow, which took up the locusts and carried them to the Red Sea, so that not one remained in all of Egypt. But Pharaoh showed himself no more grateful for this favor than for the previous ones, nor did he keep his promise any better than before.

-> The ninth plague of Egypt. <-

# Thick Darkness.

-> Exodus Chapter X. verse 22, 23. <-

<column-break/>

<margin>The same year</margin> In all of Egypt, nothing was now left to be ravaged or destroyed; the rivers had no more fish, since they had been stifled by the blood; there was no more cattle on the land, for the pestilence or the hail had taken them away; the storm had mown down the flax and the barley, devastated the vineyards, and mangled and shattered the greater part of the trees; the locusts had destroyed the rest, and left scarcely a shadow of life upon the entire land of Egypt, such that everything seemed to be dead. Only the people remained, with several horses and some few other beasts that had been kept in the cities, and this was the sacrifice that Divine Justice reserved until the last. Yet before it came to that, **God** wished to perform another sign, only to strike the hearts of the Egyptians with a new and heavy terror: this was the dreary and thick darkness, which covered all of Egypt for three days. It was a kind

<column-break/>

of mourning, which **God** made this wretched Kingdom adopt for all that it had suffered, and an omen of what was still approaching them, which would surpass all the rest. Pharaoh, however, remaining stubborn and unyielding about letting the Hebrews depart with their families and their cattle from his land, because he found great profit in keeping them, wished only to grant permission to the Hebrew men to go and offer sacrifice in the wilderness, holding himself certain that if their wives and children remained in the land of Goshen, they would soon return of their own accord. Thereupon **God** said to Moses that he should stretch out his hand toward heaven, and that a great darkness would then come over all of Egypt: Moses lifted up his hand, in which he held the staff that had been used for so many miracles, and immediately such an excessive darkness spread over the entire land that there was nothing like it even in the darkest night; the Egyptians could not see one another, and for three days and nights that this darkness lasted, they dared not leave their houses. Meanwhile, the land of Goshen enjoyed, as before, a clear sky, and the sun hid not one of its rays: so that one could then say in a literal and proper sense, what **David** later said in a moral and spiritual sense,

meaning thereby that he would no longer do so of his own accord, as before, and without being requested by Pharaoh to do so, as happened not long thereafter.

# HISTORY of the O. TESTAMENT.

<image-desc>A detailed engraving depicting the biblical Exodus of the Israelites from Egypt. A vast multitude of people, including men, women, and children carrying bundles and leading livestock like cattle and sheep, are shown departing from a grand city. ...that illustrious passing through of the Angel. The Hebrews had been commanded to celebrate it for the first time at the fall of night, during which their lives were protected from the Angel’s sword, and in which they departed from the land of Egypt. They had roasted the lamb or the goat which they had slaughtered, and then ate it with their families, or in small groups, according to the number of people required to finish a year-old lamb or goat; for they were forbidden from leaving any of it behind. And they ate it with their loins girded <note>meaning their long robes were tucked into their belts to allow for easy movement</note> and a staff in hand, like travelers who do not have enough time to sit down; and they had to dip every bite into the juice of certain bitter herbs, which God had commanded them to prepare specifically for that purpose. From reading all these things, one can easily judge that God intended something more than a simple remembrance of the deliverance from Egypt. There is no Christian who does not know that God, in the institution of the first Passover <note>original: "Paasche"</note>, formed a prefiguration <note>a symbolic foreshadowing</note> of the death of Jesus Christ, who, according to the Apostle Paul, is our Passover, sacrificed for us. It is His blood that protects us from the sword of divine Justice when, through a living and sincere faith, we have made a spiritual sprinkling of it upon our souls, according to the teaching of that same Apostle, who for that very reason calls the blood of that mysterious Passover "the blood of sprinkling" <note>original: "het bloed der besprenginge"</note>.

God had also told the children of Israel on the day before their departure that they should borrow from the Egyptians, their neighbors, everything of value they had in their houses: whatever could be easily carried, such as fine linen, gold and silver vessels, and other such things; and at the same time, He had inclined the hearts of the Egyptians to refuse them nothing. Then came that night which cost so many lives in all of Egypt; and the Hebrews were commanded to depart immediately, and to do so with all possible speed—indeed, the Egyptians

<column-break/>

themselves, who considered themselves all lost if the children of Israel remained among them for even one hour longer, urged them to hurry. In this confusion and disorder, the Israelites had no opportunity to return to the Egyptians what they had borrowed from them the day before; nor did the Egyptians themselves, overcome with grief and terror, make any effort to have it back. However this may have been, one could not accuse the Hebrews of a crime, as if they had acted in bad faith or had robbed the Egyptians of their goods. For regarding bad faith, they were innocent of it, since they did not know when they borrowed those things that they would have no time to return them. And concerning the theft, God, who is the Lord and master of all our possessions, and who never relinquishes His right when He gives us the use of them, took them from the Egyptians to give them to the Israelites out of His pure and sole authority, as a certain Prophet suggests to us in the hundred and fifth Psalm. Moreover, one finds explicitly in the third chapter of Exodus that God said they would not go out empty-handed, but would plunder Egypt. The children of Israel, thus enriched by the booty and spoils of the Egyptians, departed with their families and all their livestock from the land of Goshen <note>the region in the Nile Delta where the Israelites had lived</note> on the night of the fourteenth day of the first month, which corresponds in part to our March <note>original: "Lentemaand," or Spring-month</note> and April <note>original: "Grasmaand," or Grass-month</note>. This was the four hundred and thirtieth year after Abraham’s calling, when God made him depart from Haran. For one must understand in this way what Moses says of the four hundred and thirty years, at the end of which the children of Israel went out of Egypt, and not from the time of their residence which they had there, because no more than two hundred and fifteen years had passed since the time that Jacob had moved there with his family.

Take also your flocks and your herds, as you have spoken; be gone, and bless me also.”* He wished that Moses and Aaron would leave him their blessing, without which he dared not believe himself to be safe. But what blessing could there be for a stubborn persecutor of God’s people? And how could these two Prophets have blessed a man whom the Lord had cursed? They left him then with his remorse and fear, and went quickly to bring the news of their approaching deliverance to the people of Israel.

The Angel, who was the executor of divine vengeance, had orders when he passed through the land of Goshen <note>The region in Egypt where the Israelites resided</note>, never to enter anywhere except into the houses of the Egyptians, and not to touch any family of the Israelites. But so that he could distinguish the houses of the latter from those of the others, God had commanded Moses to tell the Hebrews that every household should take a lamb or a goat, and that they, after having slaughtered it, should smear the side-posts and upper doorpost of their houses with that blood.

...that illustrious passing of the Angel. The Hebrews were commanded to celebrate it for the first time as night began—the night in which their lives were spared from the Angel’s sword, and in which they departed from the land of Egypt. They had roasted the lamb or the goat they had slaughtered and ate it then with their families, or in small groups, according to the number of people required to finish a year-old lamb or goat; for they were forbidden to leave any of it remaining. They ate it with their loins girded <note>meaning their robes were tucked into their belts to allow for easy movement</note> and a staff in hand, like travelers who do not have enough time to sit down; and they had to dip every bite into the juice of certain bitter herbs, which God had commanded them to prepare specifically for this purpose. One can easily judge from reading all these things that God intended something more than a simple reminder of the deliverance from Egypt; there is no Christian who does not know that God, in the institution of the first Passover, formed a clear prototype of the death of *Jesus Christ*, who, according to the *Apostle Paul*, *is our Passover, sacrificed for us*; it is his blood that protects us from the sword of divine Justice when, through a living and sincere faith, we have performed a spiritual sprinkling of it upon our souls. This is according to the teaching of that same *Apostle*, who for that very reason calls the blood of that mystical Passover *the blood of sprinkling*.

God had also told the children of Israel, on the day before their departure, to borrow from their Egyptian neighbors all the valuables they had in their houses—items that could be easily carried, such as fine linen, gold and silver vessels, and other similar things—and He had at the same time inclined the hearts of the Egyptians to refuse them nothing. Then came that night which cost so many lives across all of Egypt, and the Hebrews were given the order to depart immediately, and to do so with all possible haste: indeed, the Egyptians

<column-break/>

themselves, who considered themselves all lost if the children of Israel remained among them one hour longer, urged them to hurry. In this confusion and disorder, the Israelites had no opportunity to return to the Egyptians what they had borrowed the day before; nor did the Egyptians themselves, overcome with grief and terror, make any effort to get it back. Regardless of how this situation appeared, one cannot accuse the Hebrews of a crime, as if they had acted in bad faith or had robbed the Egyptians of their property. Regarding bad faith, they were innocent of it, since they did not know when they borrowed those items that they would not have time to return them; and regarding the theft, God—who is the Lord and master of all our goods and who never waives His rights when He gives us the use of them—took these things from the Egyptians to give them to the Israelites by His own pure and singular authority. As a certain Prophet suggests to us in the hundred and fifth Psalm: furthermore, one finds explicitly in the third chapter of *Exodus* that God said they would not go out empty-handed, but would plunder Egypt. The children of Israel, thus enriched by the booty and plunder of the Egyptians, departed with their families and all their livestock from the land of Goshen on the night of the fourteenth day of the first month. This date corresponds in part to our March <note>original: "Lentemaand," literally "Spring month"</note> and April <note>original: "Grasmaand," literally "Grass month"</note>. This was the four hundred and thirtieth year after *Abraham’s* calling, when God made him move from *Haran*; for one must understand this way what *Moses* says regarding the four hundred and thirty years—at the end of which the children of Israel left Egypt—and not as the length of their actual stay there, because no more than two hundred and fifteen years had passed since the time *Jacob* had moved there with his family.

There were two ways to go from Egypt to Canaan: one through the land of the Philistines, and the other through mountains and desert places. The first was the shortest, for it required little more than a week for a traveler; it was also the easiest, both because of the nature of the land and because provisions could easily be obtained there. The second, on the contrary, was very long and difficult, both because of the uneven and rough places one encountered there, and because it was an uninhabited land which provided travelers with no necessary requirements. God did not have his people take the first way because, as Moses says, he did not want to involve them in a war they would have had to wage against the Philistines, who would have contested their passage through their land. This reason was not the only one God had for doing this, but the holy **Historian** <note>Referring to Moses as the author of the Pentateuch.</note> satisfied himself with giving us that one, leaving it to the godly **Readers**, who attentively observe the consequences of this history, to trace and wonder at the deep wisdom of God in leading his people through a long and difficult path, and through uninhabitable deserts. The haste the **Hebrews** made to depart, and the confusion that must naturally exist among a multitude consisting of more than eleven hundred thousand people <note>The text estimates 1.1 million people; biblical accounts typically specify 600,000 men, plus women and children.</note>—men, women, and children alike—who brought much livestock with them and were burdened with a thousand various things, carrying among other items their unleavened lumps of dough wrapped in their clothes upon their shoulders, did not prevent Moses from remembering to take with him the bones of **Joseph**, that pious and holy **Patriarch**, who 

<column-break/>

had drawn Jacob and his children into Egypt; for Joseph had assured them by a prophetic spirit that God would visit them and cause them to depart from that land; and he had made them swear that they would carry his bones with them to Canaan.

The news of the departure of all these people soon reached **Pharaoh's** ears; it had happened with his permission, indeed one might even say by his command, for in the grief and terror in which he found himself when he saw his son and all the firstborn of the families of the entire Kingdom killed, he had not only granted the children of **Israel** the permission that Moses and **Aaron** had so often requested for them to depart from his lands, but it seemed to him to take too long before they were out, and the Egyptians urged them to go quickly. Notwithstanding all this, Pharaoh could not hear this news without vexation and grief: he had no sooner given this permission to the Hebrews than he wished to revoke it; but he did not dare out of fear that the same hand which had dealt the deadly blow to his son in his palace, and so to speak, at his side, might also strike him with a similar blow. But since then he had had time to take courage again, and when he knew that Moses and Aaron were no longer in his land, he believed that elsewhere they would not be as terrifying to him as they had been in Egypt. He then took a resolution to pursue the Hebrews as fugitives and bring them back into his Realm. To this end, he gathered as many people together as he could; his army was very numerous, and enough horses were still found in Egypt—after the destruction which the plague, the hail, and other scourges had caused there—to harness more than six hundred war chariots and to mount several troops. This entire army set out, with Pharaoh at the head of it, accompanied by all the **Nobles** of the Realm, and they pursued the children of Israel.
