The diligence with which God's people were forced to move forward meant that they soon found themselves close together. The Hebrews had entered the narrow paths and passes between two very high mountains when they noticed the Egyptians behind them, and they had the Red Sea before them. This sea is a large inlet between Arabia and Africa, about three hundred miles long, which had not received the name of the Red Sea from the color of its waters or its sand, as some have imagined without cause—for the waters of this sea are the same color as all others, and the sand likewise—but from the name of an ancient King, who ruled over the land bordering that sea, and who in the language of that land was called by a name which means red. This King was *Esau*, otherwise named *Edom*, which signifies red; for *Idumea* <note>The biblical kingdom of the Edomites, descendants of Esau.</note> lay on the coast of that sea, which for that reason the Hebrews also called the Sea of *Edom*. The people of Israel could not have found themselves in a more disadvantageous place, because it deprived them of all means to save themselves. Yet God had deliberately led them there, in order to perform for their sake an even more excellent miracle than all those He had performed in Egypt. They had the hard-heartedness and indiscretion to complain against Moses and Aaron, that they had made them leave Egypt, as if, they said, there were not enough graves in that land to bury them. Moses was not even upset by this scornful treatment, and God forgave the grief of this people for this grumbling, because they considered themselves lost without any hope of rescue. Moses sought to dispel their mis-

<column-break/>

trust and assured them that God was about to perform an unheard-of miracle for them. At the same time, he lifted his heart to God, and God answered him, commanding him to stretch out his staff over the sea and to strike it therewith. He does so, and the sea opens to two sides, offering the Hebrews a wide and broad path through which they could pass with their wives, children, cattle, and baggage, as if over a wide field. The waves show respect for a people beloved by God, who marched forward under His safe-conduct; they stand still on both sides and form, as it were, two mountains. Pharaoh arrived with his army when the Hebrews had already traveled far along this new path. He stood amazed when he saw that the sea was snatching them from his vengeance, but he did not have enough wisdom to keep himself from surrendering to such a fierce and terrible enemy. He recklessly, and like a man possessed, took that same path through which the Israelites had gone; and while his army made its way, the Israelites reached the other side. The waves, then no longer held back by fear of harming a single Hebrew or the slightest thing belonging to him, rushed down upon the Egyptians with a roar; and those mountains of water, which had risen on the right and on the left hand, crashing down upon them, they were all submerged in an instant, and not one of them escaped. Thus perished Pharaoh with his entire army by a most remarkable death; and such was the miserable end of that cruel Prince and persecutor of God's people.

In all this lies something too great for weak and narrow-minded thoughts, like ours, to be able to grasp. Therefore, unbelief has not failed to oppose this miracle, and the enemies of our Holy Scripture have attempted—with no other ground than the malice of their hearts—to make people who are as prejudiced as they, or of an unsteady and doubtful mind, believe that the Hebrews had only walked along the seacoast during the low tide <note>original: "ebbe"</note>, and that the Egyptians having arrived there too late, the high tide <note>original: "vloed"</note> had returned and caused them all to drown. Others, who hold the Scripture in greater reverence, do not deny the truth of the miracle, but dare to weaken and diminish it by denying that the children of Israel crossed the Red Sea from one bank to the other. They maintain, along with the former group, that the waters of the sea, in opening, made only a semi-circle, which began at the place where Moses stretched out his staff and, proceeding a little way into the sea, ended at some distance away on the same bank. But this is nothing other than creating difficulties where there are none. The wording of the Scripture in the account that Moses has left us of this miracle, as well as in the Psalms and various other places, everywhere gives us the idea of a passage that crossed the sea from one bank to the other; and it was no harder for God to make such a path through the sea than to simply pave one along its coast: especially because the Egyptians surely

<column-break/>

would not have failed to seek means to pursue the Hebrews by land, however difficult the passage in that place might have been, rather than put themselves in danger of following those who stood on the same bank by going through the sea.
When the Hebrews had reached the other side of this sea, they had the comfort of seeing that these conceited and bold enemies who had pursued them were submerged under the waves and drowned, and that the sea, courageous with this booty, carried them to their feet upon the shore. There were nothing but corpses, chariots, arrows, and spears seen bobbing on the waves, which, after playing their part for a time, washed up on the sand or were dashed against the rocks. Upon seeing all these wonders which God’s hand performed, the people felt drawn by joy and gratitude. Moses, giving them the first example of his holy rapture—with which they all ought to have been seized on such an extraordinary day—sang God’s praise at the head of all the people, and made the banks of the Red Sea echo with a divine song, which the Holy Spirit formed in his heart and in his mouth. All the people joined their voices to that of this holy man, and never has the earth seen so many people singing God’s praise together on a single day. Miriam, the sister of Moses and Aaron, surpassed others of her sex in demonstrating a holy joy, and all the women and daughters of Israel joining her, formed a music of voices that struck against one another in harmony, and were like a display and image of those of the Angels of Heaven, who sing their songs and call out to one another,

After that day, the Israelites saw the Egyptians no more, and they were delivered from all their fears.

### Exodus Chapter XVI. verses 14—20.

THE children of Israel continued their way under the leadership of Moses and Aaron, or rather under that of God, who Himself marked out the path for them by a miraculous cloud in the form of a column or pillar, which He had placed in the air from the first day of their journey. This cloud was dark and gloomy by day, as clouds naturally are, but at night it was bright, like a large ignited fire in the air, which illuminated the entire camp of the Hebrews. When it stood still, they also stood still and took up their camp there; and when God willed that they should depart, the pillar of cloud placed itself at the front of their army and moved ahead. But this so tangible proof of God’s love toward this people, and so many other miracles which He had performed for them, could not prevent them from frequently mistrusting His protection and help, and even falling into murmuring. After they had departed from the shore of the sea, where they had sung songs of praise to God, they arrived after a journey of three days at a certain place where

<column-break/>

they found nothing but bitter waters, which were impossible to drink, and therefore they gave that place the name *Mara* <note>From the Hebrew word 'Marah', meaning bitter.</note>. This seemed unexpected to them and made them upset, so that they began to complain against Moses, saying that he had led them there to make them die of thirst. They knew well that this Prophet did not move forward except by God’s command, and that therefore their grumbling was actually directed against God, and not against him, who was only His Servant. But the heart of man does not examine matters so closely when it believes it has cause for complaint. God took up the protection of His Prophet and provided for the needs of the people. Moses received a command to take some pieces of wood and throw them into that water; hereupon the water became sweet. It was not actually through the wood which Moses threw into it that this change came; for there is no wood in the world which in itself has the power to change the bitterness of a water source into sweetness; it was God Himself who immediately, and through His infinite power, had brought about that change.
A few days after God had thus miraculously preserved them from thirst, they began to believe that they would die of hunger. All the provisions they had brought with them from Egypt were exhausted, and they were traveling through a land that yielded no sustenance. Nothing more was needed to make them lapse into murmuring. The rock, insensible to a stick and the arm of a man, felt the hand of God which accompanied and strengthened that of Moses; and immediately, one saw the waters stream from its bosom and cover the earth. The Hebrews came running to this spectacle, and each hurried to quench his thirst with this springing water; but the water had soon made a brook, which took its course toward the camp and refreshed all the people. Moses gave to this famous place the names of *Massah* and *Meribah*, of which the first means *temptation*, and the second *strife* or *quarrel* <note>original: "Massah" and "Meriba". These Hebrew terms commemorate the people's lack of faith and their argument with Moses.</note>; in order to keep in memory through those two names the ingratitude of the Jews, who at that place *tempted God*, and had started a quarrel against Moses. The Apostle Paul teaches us that there was a mystery in this miracle: that the rock struck by Moses was a type <note>A "type" or "foreshadowing" is a person or event in the Old Testament believed to prefigure something in the New Testament.</note> of Jesus Christ, who was struck by the staff, or the curse of the law; and that the water which came out of the rock represented the healing and life-giving grace which flowed from Jesus Christ for the comfort and salvation of His people.

Israel expected nothing of the sort, and because it had no intention of attacking any of the lands through which it might pass, or those situated close by, it had not prepared itself to fight others or to defend itself. It had marched out of Egypt without weapons, but nevertheless, it could well have gathered some arms on the shore of the Red Sea when they came drifting there after the drowning of the Egyptians; also, they could have made some themselves, which was easy to do in a time when most weaponry, aside from a sword, consisted of spears and arrows, which are things easily obtained anywhere that lacks not for wood. And if, much later, one found in the army of the greatest Prince of Asia <note>Likely a reference to the Persian kings, such as Xerxes or Darius, as described by ancient Greek historians.</note> companies who had no other spears than long sticks, whose ends—in place of iron fittings—were hardened by fire, and who dared to present themselves with such spears before the army of Alexander, then one need not doubt that the necessity of protecting themselves led the Hebrews to find many means to provide themselves with weapons, and thus not be forced to appear naked in the sight of an enemy.

Moses chose from this great multitude of people who had departed from Egypt the most alert and strongest, and those whose courage was best known to him, and he gave Joshua the command over this army. He remained sufficiently assured that God fought for His people, but he also knew well that Reason and Faith do not allow one to neglect the natural and usual means for making an undertaking succeed, and that to act otherwise would be to tempt God. Joshua then placed himself at the head of all these people, and after having given the necessary orders, he marched straight toward the enemy. The battle was fierce and stubborn; the one side fought for their freedom, and the other for the honor of victory: then Amalek gave way before Israel, and then Israel had to yield, not be-

<column-break/>

ing able to withstand the attack of the Amalekites. Moses, accompanied by Aaron and Hur—a wise and godly person, whom Antiquity <note>Referring to ancient Jewish traditions, such as those found in the Targum or the writings of Josephus.</note> has believed to be the husband of Miriam, sister of Aaron and Moses—remained during this battle upon the top of a mountain, from where he could see what was happening in the press of the fight. It was there that this holy man, as if between heaven and earth, poured out fiery prayers to God for the happy outcome of the arms of Joshua and his people; and he held his hands raised with his heart, to thus request God’s assistance through supplication. The Scripture notes a most extraordinary thing regarding this: namely, that when the hands of Moses became weary from being raised so long and sometimes sank down, the Amalekites at that same time had the upper hand in the battle; whereas, when Moses raised his hands, Israel prevailed and struck the Amalekites. Aaron and Hur, perceiving this wonder, made a seat for Moses from stones which they quickly gathered together, and after he was seated upon it, they joined him, Aaron on one side and Hur on the other, and supported with their hands those of Moses, which thus remained constantly raised until the sun went down. It was then that the battle intensified, and the Israelites, feeling encouraged by a new bravery, attacked the enemies with force, striking down everything that came before them, and sacrificing everything to the edge of the sword. The victory was complete for Israel; the sword of Joshua had performed bravely, but it was the prayer of Moses that had conquered. God willed that His Prophet should put this great and illustrious event into writing, so that the memory of it would be preserved among His people from age to age. The defeat of the Amalekites was an invaluable benefit for the people of Israel. The honor of victory, with which men are generally immoderately infatuated and which often costs them so dearly, was in this instance the least of the Hebrews' concerns. Upon this battle hung nothing less than their total destruction; and had they lost it, they would have become far more miserable than they had been during a hundred years under the yoke and in the chains of Egypt. But God had not delivered them from Pharaoh to hand them over to Amalek, nor snatched them from the hands of a merciless tyrant to let them fall into those of a conceited victor who believed everything was permitted to him when nothing stood in his way. The Hebrews well perceived the greatness of this new favor, and struck by the terror of the danger they had been in, the happiness of seeing themselves completely delivered—and with such great glory and honor—produced extraordinary movements of joy and trust in their hearts. But what was most remarkable in all this was the piety of Moses; this holy man did not occupy himself merely with the simple reflections that a common virtue might easily make regarding the assistance of Heaven, which had so visibly favored the Hebrews; nor with those general and laudable thanksgivings that an entire people gives to God after an outstanding benefit: he desired that there should be something more powerful and notable. It was then the custom to prove one's gratitude to God through sacrifices, and on extraordinary occasions to erect altars at the very place where God had given some great and wondrous sign of his favor. Thus also when the Ark rested on the mountains of Armenia <note>This refers to the mountains of Ararat, which were often associated with the region of Armenia in older geographical descriptions.</note>, and Noah with his family having happily escaped the flood had stepped out of the Ark, and all the animals which he had enclosed there by God’s command had gone out, the first work he did was to build an altar to God in that same place, and to offer him a sacrifice of praise and thanksgiving. Abraham followed the same path, and when God had made him depart from Haran and brought him into Canaan, and showing him this beautiful land had promised to one day give it to his descendants,

<column-break/>

he built an altar at the very place where God had made him that promise. He did the same on various other occasions recorded in Genesis. This example was followed by Isaac; and Jacob, after the example of his fathers, built altars at the very place where God had honored him with some extraordinary favor. Moses did the same here, and his hands, which he had lifted to heaven on the day of battle, he now dedicated to the building of an altar to God, who had given him the victory. Never did a people run with greater joy to their cattle to choose victims for sacrifice, and never was a sacrifice made from a better heart. The priesthood was not yet attached to Aaron, as it later was by an express command of God, and Moses, who was the leader of the entire people, offered a sacrifice of thanksgiving in their name. This was still not enough; he wished to give the altar a name that would preserve the memory of the mighty assistance with which God had accompanied and blessed the arms of Israel in that great battle, so that those who had lent their hands and their bravery to fight against Amalek would not pride themselves on the victory they had carried away. He then named that altar THE LORD IS MY BANNER <note>In Hebrew: *Jehovah-Nissi*.</note>. This was a kind of inscription or motto which served to make the Hebrews understand that it was as if under God’s banner that they had fought, and that God was their Head and Commander-in-Chief, who had led them to battle and marched before them: that it was he who, from rank to rank and from company to company, had breathed courage and bravery into the Israelites, who were newcomers to war and people without experience: that it was he who had overturned the chariots of Amalek, brought terror among his troops, struck down the bravest at his feet, and defeated their entire host: and finally, that it was under his banner, under his hand, and under his sword that Israel had been victorious. On such occasions, where man so easily allows himself to be blinded by the glory that surrounds him, one cannot turn one's eyes away from it too much to be exhorted to raise them to God and to give the honor of the triumph to that Supreme Controller of all outcomes.

## Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, comes to visit him in the wilderness.

### Exodus Chapter XVIII. verses 5, 6, 7.

After the defeat of the Amalekites, Moses immediately relates the journey which Jethro, his father-in-law, made to visit him in the wilderness. The things that occurred while Jethro was with Moses lead one to believe that it was likely a year after that glorious victory over Amalek that Jethro came to him; for mention is made of a Council that Moses established from a certain number of persons, the most prominent of the people, to judge matters, so that by that means Moses would be partially relieved of the trouble he took to take notice of all the disputes and quarrels that arose among the people.

<column-break/>

Now it is such that in the first chapter of Deuteronomy it is indicated that this institution did not take place until shortly before they broke camp from Horeb; and from the tenth chapter of Numbers we see that the people did not depart from Horeb until the beginning of the second year after the exodus from Egypt. But since Jethro was a Priest in the land of Midian, which bordered that of the Amalekites, it could well be that Moses on this occasion, or for some other reasons unknown to us, wished to insert the history of his father-in-law's journey here. They had not seen each other since he had parted from them to go and deliver the people of Israel in Egypt; but Moses had sent his wife and two children back to him, who had lived with Jethro since that time. Jethro showed him that such a thing could ultimately only be harmful to him and the people: therefore, he advised him to choose a certain number of men of understanding who were known for their virtue, and especially those who were upright of heart, without being inclined to enrich themselves at the expense of their conscience; to whom he could leave the minor cases, while reserving the judgment of those of the greatest importance for himself. God had until now shown Moses nothing so great and so glorious as that which He allowed him to see a few days after the defeat of the Amalekites. The mountain range on which he was encamped with the entire people divided into two mountains, which are famous in Holy History; one was named Horeb, and the other Sinai. It was on the first that God had appeared to Moses in the burning bush and had given him the command to go to Egypt to deliver His people; and it was on this same mountain that the Hebrews were encamped when they were attacked by the army of Amalek. The other mountain had not yet been honored by any remarkable event, but God reserved one for it, which has made its name famous over the whole earth and through all ages of the world. It was an extraordinary appearance of God on this mountain, where He seemed to have descended from Heaven, and where He established His throne, as it were, for forty days and forty nights; a thing that had never happened in any place in the Universe, and which one has since

never seen again, not even on Mount Zion, although God had His Temple and Ark there. Moses was, in the meantime, to ensure that all the people sanctified themselves and washed their clothes with pure water, so that they might be in a condition to receive the laws and commands which God wished to give them, since He intended to establish a covenant with them. Moses recounted to the people everything he had understood from God; and the people, receiving with reverence the honor God wished to bestow upon them, purified themselves for two days so that they might be ready by the third to see God's Majesty appear on the top of the mountain. The Priests especially received a command to sanctify themselves, undoubtedly to offer sacrifices during those two days; for although God had not yet chosen the tribe of Levi to devote themselves to His service, and He had not yet placed the censer and Priesthood into the hands of Aaron and his sons, there were nonetheless Priests, whether they were the firstborn of the families (as is commonly believed) or the other sons without distinction. ...it originated from the fact that their ancestors had the custom of not accepting any proselyte <note>A 'Joodégenoot' or proselyte is a person of non-Jewish origin who has converted to Judaism.</note> without first circumcising him, and washing or baptizing him in water, and without offering an offering, just like their fathers, who—being already circumcised—did not enter into the covenant at the foot of Mount Sinai before they were first purified and as if baptized, and had offered sacrifices to God. Meanwhile, the people were forbidden under penalty of death to approach Mount Sinai too closely, or to allow any beast to approach it, during the entire time that God would be with Moses on the mountain: and so that they would know exactly how far they had to keep away from it, God commanded Moses to set boundaries <note>original: 'paalen', literally poles or stakes used as markers</note> all around, past which they were strictly forbidden to step, or even to stretch out their hand.

This being done, Moses commanded all the people that they should go out of their tents and remain outside the camp before the mountain, while he, seized with a holy fear, but full of trust in God’s goodness, who commanded him to approach, went straight to the mountain and climbed up a portion of it. The Prophet <note>A common title for Moses in historical texts.</note> thus approaching, God descended from Heaven to take His place at the appointed location. At His approach, the mountain began to shake and the foundations to groan, as if under the weight of a glory which the entire earth was unable to bear: the thunder crashed from all sides, the lightnings flashed every moment from a cloud, which was like God’s chariot, and the top of the mountain was suddenly on fire, so that the flames surrounded it on all sides; this occurred at the moment that God had descended. Moses stood still at the sight of such a terrifying object, and did not dare to proceed; possibly it was at that moment, when his heart was struck and carried away by fear, that he spoke those two words which the Apostle Paul has preserved for us in his Epistle to the Hebrews: *I am exceedingly afraid and trembling.* <note>Hebrews 12:21: "I am terrified and trembling."</note> Yet God encouraged him, because this fear was innocent, arising only from the sight of a Majesty before which even the Seraphim dare not appear without covering their faces, and in no way from any mistrust which Moses had of the love and protection of God, by whose command he went forward. God then called to him to climb to the top of the mountain, and the Prophet, strengthened and encouraged by the Lord's voice, continued his way; and passing through the lightnings, the gale, and the storm which covered Mount Sinai, he reached the top and stood as if across from God, and in His presence.

<margin>The same year.</margin>
While Moses was atop the mountain with God, the people, who stood below and some distance away, saw the peak of the mountain entirely in fire and flame, and heard the thunders and a resounding voice, like that of a trumpet. This sight, which was capable of striking the boldest hearts with terror, served to exalt the Majesty of God—who through this great approach to men seemed to have humbled Himself slightly—and to instill a wholesome fear of violating the laws of such an awesome Lawgiver, who did not appear except armed with His lightning and thunder, and surrounded by a fire powerful enough to consume the breakers of His laws to ashes. This piercing sound of the trumpet which was heard in the camp of the Hebrews made them regard God as

<column-break/>

a great King, who on a day of glory and pomp allows Himself to be seen in the midst of His legions, who, arrayed in battle order around His royal person, show themselves ready to attack at the first sign and at His first word. And these legions which God had with Him were the host of Angels, who had descended with Him from Heaven and had arranged themselves around His throne, from where He spoke His laws, just as Saint Stephen informs us in the seventh chapter of the Acts, and the Apostle Paul in the third chapter of his Epistle to the Galatians. After God had spoken the moral Law, or the Ten Commandments, He gave to Moses—who was as a Mediator or Spokesman between Him and the people, and who had descended from the mountain and climbed up again—many ordinances, both ceremonial and political, which are recounted in the twenty-first, twenty-second, and twenty-third chapters of the book of Exodus. Moses thereafter returned again to the children of Israel to read these to them, and they answered together with one voice: *All these words which the Lord has spoken, we will do.* God, giving His laws, promised to always acknowledge the Hebrews as His own and special people, and in that capacity to grant them His protection, to bless them on earth, and to make them blessed in all eternity; and the people bound themselves to bear reverence toward God’s laws, and to serve Him alone with all their strength. These were the general conditions of this covenant. When all the people had consented to this through this act of submission, Moses built an altar at the foot of the mountain and commanded all the Priests to prepare themselves for an offering; just as they had done before God had descended onto Mount Sinai. After they had offered the sacrifice, which was like the seal of this covenant, Moses took the blood of the victim and sprinkled the altar with it; then he took the book in which he had written the commands of God and read them for a second time; whereupon the people again bound themselves to keep them, crying out as at first: *All that the Lord has spoken, we will do and be obedient.* Moses then again took some of the same blood and sprinkled the people with it, crying with a loud voice: *Behold, this is the blood of the covenant, which the Lord has made with you concerning all these words.* He also desired that the children of Israel, to preserve the memory of this great work, should erect twelve high stones, like columns, at the foot of Mount Sinai according to the number of their tribes, so that these might serve as witnesses to the covenant they had entered into with God. After these ceremonies were completed, Moses resumed the path to the mountain and took with him, according to the command he had received from God before he had come down, Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, sons of Aaron, and seventy of the Elders of Israel. God had named this number of seventy persons from the nearly innumerable multitude of the people, perhaps to remind them thereby that their people, who had marched out of Egypt in such great numbers, had consisted entirely of this number of seventy when it had arrived there from Canaan <note>Refers to the seventy members of Jacob's household who originally entered Egypt (Genesis 46:27).</note>. All these men stood still about halfway up this mountain, from where they beheld the glory of God more closely and clearly than the people. And Moses, accompanied only by Joshua, went up to the peak, where he presented himself again before God, who shone there in His Majesty and glory.

<margin>The same year, the fourth month</margin>

**W**hen Moses had returned to the mountain, after he had solemnly ratified the covenant, God continued to instruct him regarding the matters belonging to that ancient Dispensation <note>original: "Huyshoudinge," referring to the religious and social administration of the Israelite nation.</note>. He spoke to him, among other things, of a Tabernacle <term>Tabernacle: A portable "Tent of Meeting" that served as a dwelling place for God's presence among the Israelites.</term>, which He desired the Hebrews to erect for Him in the wilderness, and of many other ordinances, all of which consisted of ceremonies and symbols. Finally, He gave him two stone tablets, on which He Himself had written—and as the Scripture says, had engraved with His own finger—the Ten Commandments, which He had made known to Moses during his first visit, and which that Prophet had presented to the people, along with many other laws, ceremonial as well as judicial and political. Moses, having received from the hands of God this precious gift, the two Tablets of the Testimony, descended from the mountain and returned again to the people, who had become very impatient because they had not seen him for such a long time.

Aaron and the other men who had gone out of the camp together with Moses when he ascended again to God, and who had remained halfway up the mountain, had descended again shortly thereafter and returned to the camp. But the presence of Aaron, whom God had used in Egypt to perform such great wonders, could not comfort the people regarding the absence of Moses; and when they saw that he delayed so long in returning—he who during his first journey had only made such a

<column-break/>

short stay on the mountain—they believed that God’s Majesty had either devoured him and that he had died, or that he had been taken up into Heaven. In short, they did not know what to think of him, seeing that it took so long before he returned to them. In this distress, there came into their minds the most foolish and godless thought that one could imagine. "We have Moses no more," they said, "to lead us, and it seems as if God Himself has withdrawn from us along with His Prophet. Let us make an image which we shall dedicate to God, so that God may make Himself present in that image; we shall then have a Leader and a refuge to which we can turn in our need, just as we did with Moses." These were purely Heathen thoughts, for it was not yet widely understood that idolaters believed their gods made themselves present in their statues. This unfaithful and senseless people ran at the same time to Aaron, as the most prominent among them, but not as to a High Priest, for it was not yet known that God had endowed him with that dignity <note>Aaron’s formal installation as High Priest is described later in the book of Leviticus.</note>. This man, who should have been terrified by such a proposal and should have preferred to suffer death a thousand times rather than allow the people to commit such a gruesome sin, allowed himself—one knows not how—to be swept away by the solicitation and the shouting of the people. He commanded them to bring him their ear-ornaments and other jewels of gold, and having received them, he melted them all together and made from them the image of a calf. It did not stop there; he built an altar before that idol and had it proclaimed throughout the entire camp: *Tomorrow shall be a feast to the LORD.* Thus it was that Aaron and the people believed they would be innocent of the crime of idolatry, because they intended to direct the service they showed to the golden Calf toward God, and that it was not strictly the image they served, but God Himself in the presence

# HISTORY of the O. TESTAMENT.

...the vanity of the image. The next day, nothing was seen but sacrifices, feasts, and rejoicings. One would have said that God Himself was in the camp, and that having come there in a visible form, He showed Himself to His people, now in one place and then in another; for Aaron, pointing to the idol, cried out: *These are your gods, Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt.* God beheld the idolatry of this people from the top of the mountain; He informed Moses of it and commanded him to descend in haste. *Go,* He said to him, *get down, for your people (God did not wish to say "My people," because an idolatrous people is His people no longer), your people whom you brought up out of the land of Egypt, have corrupted themselves: they have quickly turned aside from the way which I commanded them; they have made themselves a cast calf; and they have bowed down before it and offered sacrifices.* Meanwhile, it was not their intention to sacrifice to the golden calf itself, but to God in the presence of the golden calf; for Aaron had clearly declared this when he said there would be a feast to the Lord. But God did not wish to be served before an image, and therefore He left the honor and service, which they pretended to do for Him, entirely to the image. Moses was deeply grieved by this news, and seeing that God’s wrath was kindled and ready to consume this ungrateful and rebellious people, he prayed to the Lord to be reconciled and to forgive this great crime of the children of Israel, for the sake of the covenant He had made with their fathers; for as for the one He had made with them, they had broken it in the most shameful manner possible. God was moved by the prayer of Moses, and His anger was stilled. Then the Prophet, seeing Him appeased, departed from Him and went down to the people. When he and Joshua, who accompanied him, drew near, they heard a great noise throughout the entire camp; at first they did not know what to think of it, whether enemies had surprised them and attacked them, or whether it was something else. But coming closer, they noticed it was a noise of general rejoicing; they saw some people dancing; and when Moses came even closer, he saw the golden calf, before which this wretched people danced and leaped for joy. At the sight of this terrible object, Moses—who was otherwise so gentle and patient in all circumstances—was ignited with anger, and transported by a holy indignation, he impetuously threw the Tablets of the Law, which he held in his hands, to the ground and shattered them at the foot of the mountain; to signify thereby that of all the violations a people can commit against God’s Law, there is not one that so breaks the Lord’s covenant with His people as the worship paid to an image, even when this image is made in honor of God. Moses, having subsequently entered the camp, first gave Aaron such a reproach as he deserved for his too-great compliance with the disorderly and criminal desires of the Hebrews; furthermore, he rebuked the people sharply and took the golden calf, which he caused to be ground into dust; and scattering it upon the water, he made the children of Israel drink it, so as to instill in them all the more horror for this terrible idolatry. He also desired that those of the tribe

<column-break/>

of Levi—whom He had chosen on the mountain for the service of His altars and His sanctuary—should consecrate their hands by sacrificing a portion of these criminals to divine vengeance. The fear of God spread at the same time through the entire camp; the Levites took up their swords, and having received orders from Moses to go through the camp from gate to gate, sparing neither neighbor, nor friend, nor brother, they took the lives of three thousand people on that day of punishment and vengeance who fell under their hands and swords. But all this blood was not powerful enough to wash away such a great sin; and when Moses, having returned to the mountain, wished to speak for the people, God—who had previously granted his request that His fury should not be kindled instantly—would not promise him that He would not take other vengeance for it in the future. And to that which Moses said to Him with a burning zeal and a love that still strikes those who read this history with wonder: *Oh, this people has sinned a great sin; Now then, Lord, if You will forgive their sin: but if not, blot me now out of Your book, which You have written;* he received no other answer—he to whom God was not accustomed to refuse anything—than these terrible words: *Whoever has sinned against Me, I will blot him out of My book.* The Jews have since said that in all the disasters and miseries that have befallen their people, there has been an ounce of the golden calf <note>original: "once van 't gouden Kalf," referring to a Jewish rabbinic tradition that every punishment Israel suffers contains a small part of the punishment for the sin of the Golden Calf.</note>: yet this is nothing other than a ruse which they have used since the death of Jesus Christ to hide from their own sight the true cause of their miseries, which is the crime their people committed in putting the Messiah to death.

The people of Israel were in great consternation because of the wrath with which God seemed incensed against them on account of the golden calf; but God nevertheless had it told to them that He would not for that reason fail to bring them into the land of Canaan, and that He would send His Angel before them, who would march ahead of them and root out their enemies. Moses, meanwhile, who as a mediator frequently went back and forth from the camp of the Hebrews to God on Mount Sinai, and from Mount Sinai to the camp of the Hebrews, had a tent pitched outside the camp. This was not the tent where he lived with his family, much less was it the Tabernacle <term>Tabernacle: The portable dwelling place of God, the construction of which was commanded on the mountain.</term> of which God had given him the design on the mountain, in which the Ark of the Covenant, the Golden Altar, and many other things mentioned in Exodus from the twenty-fifth to the thirty-second chapter were to be; and even that holy Tabernacle, which was to be the dwelling place of God, was always to be placed in the middle of the camp. It was then a third Tent, entirely different from the other two, into which Moses entered to perform the duties of his office, and Joshua alone with him, in the capacity of his servant. God honored him with visible signs of His presence, through the pillar of cloud which descended and stayed in or above the door of that tent: and from there God spoke to His Prophet regarding such matters upon which he had to deliver a pronouncement to the people; and the people received such from the mouth of God with a very deep awe and a religious submission.

# *Moses brings the second tablets to the people, and his face shines with light.*

## Exodus Chapter XXXIV. verses 28, 29.

Since God, on His part, had not broken the covenant with the children of Israel—even though Moses had made them understand, by the breaking of the Tablets of Testimony, that their conduct regarding the golden Calf was a complete breach of the covenant on their part—He therefore wished to give him other tablets in place of the first. To that end, He commanded Moses to hew or smooth out two stone tablets and to come up the mountain with them the following morning. Moses did what God had commanded him, and having reached the summit of Mount Sinai, he saw God descend in a cloud, which came to rest and stood still before him. Moses was again with God for forty days and forty nights on that journey, without eating or drinking; and during that time God gave him His commands and renewed several ceremonial institutions which He had already given him when the Prophet was on Mount Sinai the first time. All these ceremonial laws actually served the primary purpose that God had in this dispensation, which was to set before the eyes of the Believers of that time a sort of tableau or depiction of future goods, and particularly to portray the Messiah therein, who, since the promise God made to Adam under the name of "the seed of the woman," and to Abraham under that of "a blessed seed" which would be the happiness of all nations, was the primary object of faith for the ancient Church and the most essential comfort for God’s children.

<column-break/>

This Law of ceremonies, shadows, and symbols was, rightly considered, nothing other than a means, or as the Apostle Paul says, a <term>schoolmaster<note>original: "tuchtmeefter." This refers to a "pedagogue," a guardian who led children to their lessons; Paul uses it to describe how the Law prepared people for Christ.</note></term>, to lead the ancient believers *to Christ, who was the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believed.* It is not very likely that God would have wished to descend, as He did several times upon the mountain, and occupy Himself there twice for forty days and forty nights with His Prophet over the construction of a tent with its poles and curtains, over the preparation of an altar and an ark, and over the manner of the priests' sacrifices, the fashion and number of their garments, and so many other matters of that nature, if He did not have very mysterious insights in all this, and if, by adding these ceremonial commands to the ancient institution of sacrifices, He had not intended to form a complete body of the Economy or the Covenant of Grace, since that which was alone beneficial to man after sin was kept as if under a cover or veil. God had also not made these institutions so numerous except so that the keeping of them would be more burdensome and difficult; it was a heavy and difficult yoke, the purpose of which was to humble a people who could not bear it, to make them long for the Redeemer. From this same insight, God expressly required them to keep the whole Law; and since this was an impossible task, the Jews saw themselves either entirely fallen out of God's Covenant, or fortunately forced to extend their desire and hope toward the promised Messiah, and thus to find the Covenant of Grace within the Covenant of Sinai. The Apostle Paul made this observation in his Epistle to the Galatians: *I through the Law,* he says, *am dead to the Law*; meaning by this that nothing had more caused him to abandon the hope of [attaining] life in the un-

<meta>This page continues the theological discussion regarding the nature of the Law and the Covenant of Grace, before moving into the physical construction of the Tabernacle.</meta>

# HISTORY of the OLD TESTAMENT.

...finding a way to keep the Law, than the covenant itself under which the Law promised life, which was a perfect keeping of all its commandments.

God then took from the hands of Moses the two stone tablets, which he had hewn and brought up the mountain; and He Himself wrote upon them, just as He had done on the first, the ten Commandments of the Law. The first words of the introduction which He placed at the head taught the children of Israel that the Covenant of Sinai was fundamentally the same as that which had been made with their fathers—which essentially differed nothing from the Covenant He had made with Adam after the sin, and under which all the other holy Patriarchs had lived—namely, the *Covenant of Grace*. God declared Himself first of all to be the God of that people: *I am the LORD, your God*. Now, it is such that God cannot be the God of a sinful man without showing him grace; for by calling Himself the God of a people solely in regard to the prosperity of this life, God would have been a thousand times more the God of the Babylonians, the Persians, the Greeks, and the Romans than of the Hebrews. These two words then, YOUR God, extend much further than the introduction of this people into the land of Canaan, and looked toward eternal goods: *He was not ashamed to be called their God, says a certain Apostle, for he had prepared a city;* <note>original: "Hebreeën 11:16" — Reference to the New Testament book of Hebrews.</note> and this city, according to that same Writer, is *Heaven*. In the second Commandment, God spoke of showing mercy; now, mercy and forgiveness are not the fruits of a

<column-break/>

Law which, without compassion, curses those who transgress the smallest matter. Moses brought to the people the two tablets of the Law, which were precious because of the hand that had engraved the Writing in them, but even more precious because of their holiness, and of an inestimable value for a sinful people, who found there in the first words that God called Himself *their God*, and who heard Him speak of *mercy* three lines lower. This Prophet did not know that any change had come upon his countenance during his stay of forty days and forty nights with God; but when he came down from the mountain with the two tablets in his hand and approached the camp, the children of Israel—who, seeing him arrive, had gone out to meet him—could not endure the radiance of his face, but were forced to cast down their eyes as if before the sun. Moses himself was amazed by this miracle, from which we can measure what the glory of the bodies of the resurrected Believers will one day be when they are received into Heaven to behold God’s face without shadows and without clouds. Moses, to accommodate himself to the children of Israel, covered his face with a veil, which he took off whenever he returned to God, and put on again when he came back to the people. This also did not happen without a mystery; yet everyone can see the application which the Apostle Paul made of this to the ministry of the Law and the administration of the Gospel in the third chapter of his second Epistle to the Corinthians.

# HISTORY of the O. TESTAMENT.

...had allowed that they, leaving Egypt, had provided themselves with many things, some of which were very precious, without knowing that these would one day be used for such a holy work. Moses then proposed to the entire people that everyone, according to the means they had, and out of a pure movement of zeal, should bring gifts of everything necessary for making the Tabernacle, and its ornaments, hangings, altars, and all the other things for which God had given the command and the design on Mount Sinai. To all this belonged planks, skins, precious fabrics, copper, silver, gold, and gemstones; all these things were found in abundance among the people, and love and zeal excelled above all else. Everyone was eager to seek out the rarest and most precious things, and to give the most. The women, who are by nature fond of their adornments, brought their rings, bracelets, and stones, with a willingness and joy that had not yet had an equal. For several days, nothing was seen being brought in but fabrics of purple and scarlet, or fine and beautiful webs of linen, or piles of gold and silver; and where those precious things were lacking, there were planks, skins, and other things of lesser value, though they were nevertheless as necessary as the most precious for putting into effect the design that God had given

<column-break/>

to be put into work: until Moses was finally forced to have it proclaimed throughout the whole Camp that they should stop bringing gifts and <term>heave-offerings<note>A specific type of offering (Hebrew: *terumah*) lifted up or presented to God; here refers to the voluntary contributions of the people.</note></term>, because more had already been received than was needed. Those who had any particular talent for working with their hands joyfully offered themselves to undertake some work for the Tabernacle. The women spun from the fine flax they had brought from Egypt, others worked on purple and scarlet; many spun goats' hair, and some occupied themselves with embroidery. The men, each in his own craft, put all their skill and ability to work to give the utmost perfection to the pieces they made: but among all the others there were two who were exceedingly famous; one was named Bezaleël, and the other Aholiab. God had granted them a very shrewd understanding, and a dexterity and capability for all those things, so that there was no one like them. For the knowledge of these two men was not limited to one or two kinds of handiwork; there was nothing in all the arts, which had to serve to make a Tabernacle of perfect beauty, that was unknown to them. Moses then gave them the oversight, and all the other craftsmen had to work under their direction and command.

### Exodus Chapter XXXVI. verses 8—18. Chapter XXXVII. verses 1—23.

# HISTORY of the O. TESTAMENT.

Israel would serve as a Temple; and to describe at length all its curtains, hooks, hangings, and everything else that served to cover or decorate it, of which Moses gave an accurate account in the book of Exodus. In the following, some of the most remarkable pieces, such as the Ark, the Altar, the Candlestick, and some others, will be discussed. For the present, it will suffice to say that the Tabernacle was to have a length of thirty <term>cubits<note>An ancient unit of measurement based on the length of the forearm, approximately 18 inches or 45 centimeters.</note></term> and a width of ten, and that it was to be divided into three sections, which the Scripture calls *Courts*. The first, being that through which one entered, was intended for the gathering of the people; the second, which was closed off only by a large curtain hanging from top to bottom, was for the Priests; and the third, which was all the way at the back and separated from the second by a second curtain, made of costly fabric and of artistic and excellent workmanship, was entered by no one. It was intended only to serve as a dwelling for God, who wished to have His Ark there as the glorious symbol of His presence, from where He revealed Himself to His people, and from where He gave His oracles from above the Mercy Seat and between the Cherubim, as we shall say in the continuation of this History when we explain the other printed illustrations. The Tabernacle in general, and particularly the second Court, called the *Sanctuary*, was a representation of the Church, which, considered in itself or in its nature, is the assembly of the Saints; the third, which was the hindmost of all, called the *Holy of Holies* or the *Most Holy Place*, was an example of Heaven, the palace and the throne of the Godhead, from where God reveals Himself to His Church. Entry to this last partition was forbidden to the people who gathered in the first, and even to the Priests, who were all sanctified persons and remained in the second; this is to teach us that we are all naturally removed from Heaven and from God, and that even those among men who are the holiest still retain so many remnants of their original impurity after their sanctification that there is not one who can rightly say they have enough holiness to approach God through their own righteousness and enter into Heaven. Meanwhile, this holy and awesome place was not so inaccessible to all men that the entrance was never open to any person. A man chosen by God and honored with the supreme dignity of the Priesthood was permitted to enter there once a year, carrying in a basin the blood of the sacrifices that had been offered at the entrance of the first Court, being a gateway or portal where the altar stood. God wished to signify by this symbol that the entrance to Heaven would stand open through the virtue and power of the holy and unblemished sacrifice, which would one day be offered outside the gates of Jerusalem, on Mount Calvary, for all the sins of mankind. The Apostle Paul noted some of the mysteries hidden under the form of the Tabernacle in his Epistle to the Hebrews; and it is not forbidden for a humble and sensible piety to make various other observations regarding it, to marvel more and more at the ways of God's wisdom in a Household <note>original: "Huyshoudinge" – referring to a divine arrangement or dispensation</note> that had only

<column-break/>

a shadow of the good things to come, and not the image itself, or the truth and substance of matters; and which could not receive its ultimate perfection except through the Household of the Gospel.

<margin>† Same year and same month.</margin>
No effort was spared to make the Tabernacle as perfect as possible; everything needed for it was available, and the workmen employed for it acquitted themselves with all required accuracy and skill. Bezaleel and Aholiab, who had the management and oversight of all the work, ensured that nothing was forgotten, and everything that was made showed signs of the craftsman's dexterity and the wise counsel of the Overseers: nothing remained unfinished. Besides the constant care that Bezaleel took to keep his eye on all the work, he himself worked on some of the principal pieces that deserved to be made by an artistic hand. Moses mentions several which Bezaleel took in hand, among which the Ark of the Covenant, the Table of Showbread, and the Golden Candlestick were particularly excellent. The Ark was a large chest, two and a half cubits long, half a cubit wide, and one and a half cubits high: it was made of <term>Shittim wood<note>original: "Sittim-hout"; likely acacia wood.</note></term>. This name is famous in Scripture, but it is not known exactly what kind of wood it was. Some take it for Cedar, but wrongly, because in the Hebrew text in Isaiah, in the 20th verse of the 40th chapter, a distinction is found between those two. Others take it for Pine wood, and others for Fir wood; some hold it for *Acacia*, which grows abundantly, according to the account of Jerome, in the deserts of Arabia, and seems to be signified by the name of Thorn-wood, because Acacia has thorns. Yet whatever it may have been, the Hebrews must have had much of this wood, because they used no other for the entire Tabernacle. Bezaleel overlaid all the wood of the Ark inside and out with gold plates, so that no wood was to be seen anywhere: he made a crown or rim of pure gold around it, with four rings, one at each corner, of the same metal, to be able to carry it from one place to another with poles of Shittim wood, which were likewise overlaid with gold. But all this could not compare to the splendor of the lid of the Ark, which was of pure gold, of the purest and finest that could be found; and at the two ends were two Cherubim of solid gold, whose faces were turned toward each other, yet slightly bowed, as if they wished to look into the Ark, and the wings of the two Cherubim were stretched out over the lid, so that they covered it entirely. In this, and all the rest, Bezaleel did nothing else than lend his hand and diligence to Moses to copy the design that God had given him, and he added nothing of his own to it: for God had expressly commanded not to add to or take away from the sketch which He Himself had given, but to conform in everything to the drawing: of such great weight is it in matters of Religion <note>original: "Gódsdienst" – Service to God</note> to mix nothing human therein, but to hold closely to God's Word. In another place, the mystery of the Ark, which in its entirety and in all its parts had a profound meaning, will be found described.

This work of art had its mysteries just like the others, and there will be occasion to mention something of them in the following, before we end the entire account of the Tabernacle.

## The Altar of Burnt Offerings, and the Copper Washbasin. The Priestly Garments.

### Exodus Chapter XXXVIII. verses 1-8. and Chapter XXXIX. verse 1. etc.

<margin>The same year, namely the first after the exodus from Egypt, around the final months.</margin>
Bezalel also made, to be placed alongside the Table in the Sanctuary, a golden Altar of Incense, the image of which will be seen in the following. The Altar spoken of here was for offering burnt offerings. God had commanded Moses to make it of the same wood as the Tabernacle, the Ark, the Table, and everything that was to be made of wood, and that was Shittim wood. It was of a square shape, namely five cubits in length, just as much in width, and three in height. Inside was a large copper grate, upon which the fire was placed to consume the sacrifices laid on that grate; and so that the wood surrounding it would not catch fire, it was overlaid with copper. Nevertheless, it is difficult to imagine how the great heat, which that copper absorbed from

<column-break/>

such a long and fierce fire, as that which must have been required to consume an entire ox, or many sacrifices at once, into ashes in the burnt offering, did not penetrate to the wood that was covered with these copper plates and burn it. Some take refuge here in a miracle, believing that the wood of the Altar could only have been preserved by a special Providence. But since it is not God’s custom to perform miracles without any necessity, and even less a miracle that would have to last as long as this one, one may suspect either that the copper covering the wood was so thick that the heat of the fire could not penetrate through it to damage the wood; or that the foresight of the Priests and Levites, and some other human means—of which the holy History is silent, as being matters that serve only to satisfy curiosity—prevented all accidents of that nature. This Altar was to be placed at the entrance of the Tabernacle, in a large courtyard, which was between the doors where the people gathered, where all the sacrifices were killed and all the offerings were made.

God had also commanded a large copper Washbasin <note>Also known as the Brazen Laver, used for ritual purification.</note> to be made, which was to be on the same grounds

set, and filled with water, so that the Priests might wash therein before they approached the altar and performed the service. This was also a piece of craftsmanship by Bezalel, and Moses says that he made it from the mirrors of the women who gathered at the door of the Tent of Meeting. This was a different tent than the Tabernacle, which we have already described here, and which was not erected until all the pieces of work, of which one sees the printed illustrations here, were made. It was therefore a special Tent, which until the time the Tabernacle was completed, was set up outside the Camp, where God revealed himself to Moses in a column of cloud, which descended before the door of this Tent every time Moses went there to give a pronouncement and pass judgment as if in a sort of Court of Justice, as we read in the thirty-third chapter of Exodus. The holiness of this place, which through the frequent appearances of God to Moses became the most venerable and awesome in the world, drew various groups of godly women to it, who at those hours when Moses was outside, went there and relieved one another like a kind of watch. It was these holy women who brought their mirrors to make the <term>brazen Laver<note>A large basin used by priests for ritual purification. In the Tabernacle, it stood between the altar and the sanctuary.</note></term> spoken of here. It was the custom of old to make mirrors of steel, or of polished copper, because the use of <term>foiled glass<note>Modern mirrors use a silver or tin-foil backing on glass; ancient mirrors were simply highly polished metal disks.</note></term> had not yet been invented as it is today; and although it would not have been difficult for these persons to have provided other copper for this work—since it appears from this entire History that the children of Israel had it in abundance—nevertheless they wished to dedicate their mirrors to this holy use through a spirit of humility, and to make an offering to God of that desire which is natural to the female sex: namely, to love adornments and to take pleasure in everything that can help to make their beauty stand out. In another place, one will see the full description of this Laver spoken of here, and the meaning of the same will be given there, which could well have been done here, if one did not seek to avoid repetitions of one and the same matter.

God had made known to Moses in what manner he desired the Priests to be clothed when they were to enter the Tabernacle to perform the service. This was also part of the ceremony, and it was well-suited to a Covenant of which all the outward parts were executed very magnificently and with the utmost precision. There were special garments for the High Priest, and others for the common Priests. This distinction served to make those persons whom God had consecrated to the service of his altars stand out among the Ministers of the Sanctuary, so that the dignity of the Priestly office was honored. But it was also a lesson for all the Priests to distinguish themselves from all other men by their good morals, and to be clothed with a special holiness, if

<column-break/>

they wished to properly discharge the duties of their office. And concerning the High Priest, God wished to teach him by such an excellent distinction in his clothing that he was even more obliged than all the other Ministers of holy things to excel above others in knowledge, godliness, and holiness. Moses had all those various types of garments made by the best craftsmen to be found among the children of Israel, and he gave them the pattern that he had received from the mouth of God himself on Mount Sinai. It is a reverence that men owe to God: to consider nothing mean or trivial among everything he commands; for even if the things in themselves have nothing great or very remarkable, they are nevertheless raised to a sublimity by the seal of Divine institution, which is above all the greatest and most magnificent things that one could find elsewhere. One must generally make this observation regarding the entire Mosaic Covenant, and in particular regarding the meticulous care God showed in making known to Moses the number, the fashion, and the colors of the garments of his Priests; these all being matters that at first glance seem so far below the Majesty of God that they could easily awaken thoughts in a worldly and frivolous mind that are not very respectful toward divine wisdom, and cause reckless and vain reasoning to rebel against the awe and submission which faith always maintains toward God—both in matters far removed from our usual imagination and in those which most agree with it. The gold, the purple, and the scarlet made several of the sacred garments stand out in luster, and others were made of the finest linen. Those which the High Priest had in common with the other Priests were the tunic of fine linen, the breeches, the sash, and the ornate turban, although in the latter two there was some difference: and the following four were for the High Priest alone: the sky-blue mantle of purple and scarlet, the <term>Ephod<note>An ornate vest-like garment worn by the High Priest, often associated with seeking divine oracles.</note></term>, the breastpiece, and the golden plate that was at the bottom of the turban and covered the High Priest's forehead. One will see the depiction thereof in the following, with the explanation alongside it. When the Priests did not go into the Sanctuary, or did not perform service concerning other things, they were dressed very simply, like other men; but it was expressly commanded them not to approach the altar and the Holy place without sacred garments; and it would have been a crime worthy of death if they had failed therein. Everything was strict in that Covenant, and one heard of nothing there but death. But nevertheless, it was Grace itself that had caused this <term>Dispensation<note>Original: "Huyſhouding" — referring to the theological system or era of the Old Testament law.</note></term> of severity to precede it, in order to make itself the more zealously desired, and to help God's people better understand the deficiency of a Covenant which at every moment set death somewhat before their eyes, and showed them life only at such a great distance that it could not be reached through the most perfect holiness.

# The Ark of the Covenant.

## Exodus Chapter 39, verse 35.

<margin>* In the same year, being the first after the exodus from Egypt, toward the end of it.</margin>
A little earlier, mention was made of the Ark, for which God had given the design to Moses and which was made by Bezalel; the explanation of its symbolic meanings has been reserved for this place, because its full illustration is shown here in its entirety. The Ark, taken as a whole, was a visible sign of God’s presence. The <term>Pagans<note>The original Dutch uses "Heydenen," referring to non-Abrahamic cultures of antiquity.</note></term> had statues of their gods, in which they imagined those gods were present after they had been consecrated with the usual ceremonies. God, who is a pure and infinite Spirit, did not want any image to be erected to Him. Moses gave the Hebrews to understand that it was for this reason that God had not appeared to them in any particular human form or any other shape: to prevent the urge they might have had to represent Him in the form He might have assumed in His appearances. For this same reason, wanting to give His people a visible sign of His presence, He chose an Ark or chest—a thing that would least of all come to people's minds as a way to make an image of God or a symbol of His presence. This was called the *Ark of the Testimony*, because the *Tables of the Law*, called the *Tables of the Testimony*, were placed inside it; or perhaps because they served the children of Israel as a magnificent testimony of God’s presence in their midst. It was for this reason that God, when promising His protection and favor to His Church through His Prophets, expressed Himself in phrases borrowed from the dwelling of the Ark among the chil-

<column-break/>

dren of Israel: *I will dwell in them, and I will walk among them; I will be their God, and they shall be my people.* The Ark also had another name, by which it is commonly known, and that is the *Ark of the Covenant*; because it was the pledge of God’s covenant with the Hebrews, serving as a summary and the center of their worship.

The two primary parts of this symbolic Ark were the body of the Ark or chest itself, and the lid. The first was made of <term>Shittim wood<note>original: "Sittimhout." This is wood from the acacia tree, known for being extremely durable and resistant to rot.</note></term>, entirely overlaid with gold. This was a representation of the Church, which in itself is made of humble material—for it consists of nothing but human beings—yet these are humans of great value to God, because they are, as it were, covered and clothed with faith. The value of faith surpasses all other virtues, just as gold is the most precious of all metals. Or, which is one and the same, the gold that covered all the wood of the Ark and was of the same nature as its lid, was the symbol of the righteousness of Jesus Christ, with which the Church is covered and clothed. Thus, the natural lowliness of the Church does not appear before the eyes of God; for since He never beholds her except in Jesus Christ, with whom she has a very powerful and intimate communion, she is in His eyes a glorious <term>Congregation<note>original: "Gemeynte." This can refer to a specific local church or the universal body of believers.</note></term>, having no spot or wrinkle or any such thing that could make her contemptible or unworthy to be received into Heaven. The overlay of gold that was around the Ark, and which increased its beauty, was a representation of the good works that ought to accompany our faith, serving as a precious and dear ornament to it.

Regarding the lid, called in the Scriptures the *Mercy Seat*, it was, according to the interpretation of the Apostle Paul, a brilliant symbol of our Lord Jesus Christ. The very name of *atonement* <note>The Dutch "Verzoendekfel" (Mercy Seat) literally means "Atonement-lid."</note> naturally leads us to these thoughts, because no one but Jesus Christ...

It is possible that, in view of this <term>symbolic model<note>The author uses "voorbeeldsel," referring to a "type" or "foreshadowing"—a common theological idea that Old Testament objects predicted New Testament truths.</note></term>, Holy Scripture expresses the forgiveness of our sins in various places through the concept of a cover, which hides them and conceals them from the eyes of divine Justice; and that Scripture intended to use this phrase, "to cover sins," to mean "to forgive sins"; and that it spoke of sins that are "covered" to signify sins which God does not punish. The material of the <term>Atonement Cover<note>In Dutch, "Verzoendeksel," often called the Mercy Seat in English bibles.</note></term> was not like that of the Ark—made of wood merely overlaid with gold—but was of pure and solid gold. This is because Jesus Christ, of whom it was a symbol, has nothing in Him that is base or contemptible as we do: He is a pure gold, precious in Himself, a Mediator without blemish and without lack. Two Cherubim of gold were placed on top of the atonement cover, having their faces turned toward one another, and both looking down upon the atonement cover. This represented the Angels, according to the allusion which the Apostle Peter notes regarding these words, which he speaks in view of the deep mys-

<column-break/>

tery of the Gospel: *the angels desire to look into these things.* He expresses this through a phrasing that suggests the Angels held their faces bowed down, just as they were depicted upon the atonement cover of the Ark. It was upon this Atonement Cover that God revealed Himself, and it is in and through Jesus Christ that God has revealed Himself to His Church, and has caused the Light of His grace and salvation to shine, just as one expressed it when speaking of God's appearances upon the atonement cover: *You who sit between the Cherubim,* it was said to Him, *shine forth.* Finally, this Atonement Cover was such that it did not protrude anywhere beyond the Ark, nor did it leave anything uncovered; for God had commanded that it be given exactly—no more and no less—the same length and the same breadth as the Ark. This was to give us to understand that Jesus Christ is essentially no reconciliation except for His <term>Congregation<note>The Dutch "Gemeynte" refers to the body of believers or the Church.</note></term>, which is His spiritual body, according to what the Apostle Paul says: that He is the Savior of His body, but not of those who are not truly His body and do not belong to His Congregation.

## The Table of the Showbread.

### Exodus Chapter 39, verse 36.

<margin>The same year.</margin>
This golden Table, which has already been mentioned in another place and whose full illustration is seen here, was no idle showpiece that served only for display. There was nothing in the Tabernacle which did not signify some beautiful moral lesson, or denote some mystery, and indeed often contained both together. We have just seen the hidden meanings of the Ark of the Covenant, which was like the summary of all the mysteries of Religion; and we shall now, in the ex-

<column-break/>

planation of this illustration, strive to discover what secret meaning might lie within this Table of the <term>Showbread<note>Literally "bread of display" or "bread of the presence." These were twelve loaves representing the twelve tribes of Israel.</note></term>. In general, it signifies that God provides us with our nourishment within His fellowship and within His Congregation, and that He sustains our life with the goods of His grace. *You prepare a table before my face,* David said to God in the twenty-third Psalm. This Table stood in the Sanctuary, which, more than any other part of the Tabernacle, was an image of the Church, because it is specifically in the Church that God gives this excellent nourishment which causes us to live unto eternity: and it did not stand with the Ark in the Holy of Holies, behind the veil, but in front of it, in the Sanctuary; because it is only in

The Sanctuary, or the Church which is still on earth and during this time is withheld from beholding God’s countenance, is where God prepares the table for His children, from which He feeds them: namely with His Word, His Sacraments, and the comforts of His Holy Spirit. In Heaven, just as in the <term>Holy of Holies<note>The innermost chamber of the Tabernacle, representing the immediate presence of God.</note></term> of the Tabernacle, there is no Table, because neither hunger nor thirst can reach there, as is said in the book of Revelation, and because the simple contemplation of God's countenance there is an eternal satisfaction for all the blessed. *As for me, I will behold thy face in righteousness: I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with thy likeness*, says David in one of his Psalms <note>Psalm 17:15</note>. The Table of the Sanctuary was, like the Ark, made of wood overlaid with gold, because the Church—in whose communion a Believer finds his nourishment, and which fundamentally consists of humans of the same nature as others—is, through her confession and through her virtues, the purest and most invaluable society that can be found on earth.

The loaves of bread which were to be placed on this Table were called *Showbread*, or in Hebrew *bread of faces* <note>original: "Toonbrooden" or "brooden van aangezigten"</note>, because they always remained uncovered and stood on display in God’s presence as a constant dedication made to Him. There were twelve loaves of fine flour, without leaven, stacked six and six upon each other, with a little incense on top of each stack. They remained standing thus from one Sabbath to the next, for every Sabbath they were renewed; and the Priests were to eat those which were taken away, after they had stood on the Table for an entire week.

<column-break/>

The Scripture calls these loaves a *holy offering*, and God explicitly declared that this should be an eternal ordinance. These unleavened loaves represented Jesus Christ, who was conceived without sin and is the true bread of life. The number of loaves, which corresponded with that of the twelve Tribes of Israel, signified that Jesus Christ is the spiritual and life-giving nourishment of His entire Community. The constant display of these loaves in God’s presence indicated that Jesus Christ always presents Himself before God in the capacity of our Mediator. The two stacks, consisting of twelve loaves, were an image of the ancient and new Church, and pointed out that Jesus Christ is the spiritual nourishment of them both. The incense placed on top of each stack as a sign of offering meant that Jesus Christ is the life-giving and healing bread of His Believers only by virtue of His sacrifice, according to what He Himself says in the Gospel of John: *The bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world* <note>John 6:51</note>. These loaves remained on the Table from one Sabbath to the next to signify that Jesus is the bread of His Community, from the Sabbath—or the rest of Grace of which the Apostle Paul speaks in the third chapter of the Epistle to the Hebrews—until the Sabbath, or heavenly rest, which is that of glory. In short, these loaves were intended for the Priests, who therein represented all true Believers, who are all sanctified in Jesus Christ and, as Scripture says, *made Priests unto God forever*.

## The Altar of burnt offerings, and the bronze Washing Vat. The vestments of the High Priest, and those of the common Priests.
### Exodus Chapter XXXIX. verse 39. and Chap. XL. verse 13.

<margin>The same year, in the last four months.</margin>
The two pieces that one sees depicted here also had their secret meanings, as well as the others. It seems at first glance highly surprising that under a Household where one had to offer many sacrifices to God daily, and at various occurrences a great number at once, there was nonetheless no more than one altar for all offerings. <column-break/>

there was no more than one Temple.
