Regarding the **Copper Washbasin** <note>Also known as the Brazen Laver.</note>, which stood in the same Outer Court as the **Altar of Burnt Offerings**, and which contained much water, its primary use was for the ministers of the Tabernacle to wash their hands and feet; because it was not permitted for the Priests to approach the Altar, or to enter the Sanctuary, with unclean hands and with feet that had contracted any substantial or ritual impurity by touching something unclean. One can easily observe the moral lesson hidden beneath this ceremony, and it is not difficult to understand that God, through this symbol—which was as the spirit and the very nature of the Law—intended to signify that to approach the Lord, one must be cleansed from the defilements of the earth. *I wash my hands in innocence;* said David to God, *and I go around your altar, O Lord.* The Apostle Paul also said, with the same intent, to the faithful Hebrews: *Let us draw near with a true heart, in full assurance of faith, our hearts being purified from an evil conscience, and the body being washed with pure water.* But there was even something more than this moral lesson in the institution of this Washbasin which God had made. The water of this copper vat represented the Holy Spirit, which is the spiritual water through which the impurities of our consciences are wiped away; and the mutual proximity of this vat full of water and the Altar of Burnt Offerings—which was colored and entirely red from the blood of the sacrifices—signified the necessity for these two things, the blood of the sacrifice and the washing of the Holy Spirit, to go together in the Church; and they signify clearly and under a foreshadowing what the Apostle John says in express words concerning our Lord Jesus Christ, that he came *through water and blood,*

<column-break/>

and as he immediately repeats once more to make that observation better understood, *not by water alone, but by water and blood,* that is to say, that he came to confirm his Covenant of Grace through the blood of his sacrifice, and through the Spirit of sanctification, with which he washes and purifies his Congregation. The Prophets often spoke of this mystical water, which God adds to the blood, just as the Washbasin is placed by the Altar; Ezekiel in particular seems to have signified in a very precise manner the mystery of this water from the court of the Tabernacle, and subsequently from the porch of the Temple (where Solomon had a massive vat placed, which in Scripture is called the <term>Molten Sea<note>A massive bronze basin described in 1 Kings 7, used by priests for ritual cleansing in Solomon's Temple.</note></term>), when he tells us in the forty-seventh chapter that he had seen waters flowing from under the threshold of the house, or the court of the Temple, and that intending to pass through them at the beginning, they only reached his ankles; that having come a second time he found they had risen to his knees; that at the third time, they came to his waist; and that those waters finally became a deep stream that one could not wade through, but which had to be swum across. It appears clearly from this that these waters signified the Holy Spirit, and the various measures which God has given thereof to his Congregation. Formerly in the court of the Tabernacle there was nothing but water in a washbasin; afterwards that water increased, and the <term>Synagogue<note>Here referring to the religious assembly of Israel under the Old Covenant.</note></term> had more of it under the ministry of the Prophets: it was much greater still in the time of John the Baptist and of Jesus Christ, up to the day of Pentecost: from that day on, the abundance of the gifts and graces of the Holy Spirit was a true flood, as can be seen in the twelfth chapter of the first Epistle to the Corinthians, and in a thousand other places in the writings of the New Testament.

The most remarkable thing that the High Priest wore, and that which made him stand out among all the other Priests, was firstly a golden plate, which was on the front of his Turban <note>The original Dutch uses 'Muts', referring to the priestly mitre or headdress</note>, and covered his forehead like a crown or royal head-ornament, with this inscription, which was engraved upon it in large letters: **HOLINESS TO THE LORD.** The second marked distinction between the garments of the High Priest and those of the common Priests was a sky-blue mantle or robe, which hung down almost to his ankles, and on whose lower hems were sewn matching pomegranates of sky-blue, purple, and scarlet color, mixed alternately with small golden bells, such that after one of those pomegranates a bell followed, and after a bell, a pomegranate, and this all around the robe. But the most remarkable of all is that which the Scripture calls the Ephod. It was a garment that covered only about half the body, being woven with threads of purple, scarlet, and sky-blue color, and stitched and adorned with gold, which the High Priest put on over the long sky-blue robe: it was opened and fastened on the shoulders, and had on either side, where it was secured by the shoulder-straps, two large stones, upon which the names of the twelve sons of Jacob were engraved—six on one side, and six on the other. To the Ephod was joined the Breastplate, which was made of similar material as the Ephod, being a span square, upon which twelve precious stones, three in a row, and four rows following one another, were set in gold. These twelve stones represented the twelve tribes of Israel, and on each was engraved the name of one of the twelve Patriarchs. The High Priest hung this plate full of gemstones on top of the Ephod by two golden chains, which, passing over his shoulders and coming forward again, were poked through two golden rings that were fixed to its bottom corners, and thus fastened around the waist. This precious ornament of the High Priest was called the Breastplate, because he wore it on his breast; it was also called the Urim and Thummim, meaning as much as *Lights and perfections*, because of the gemstones, which, being set close together, gave off a very great brilliance and filled the entire Breastplate, so that not the least empty space remained; according to these words of God to Moses: *You shall set in it settings of stones.* God revealed himself for a long time, and until the Babylonian captivity, through the *Urim* and *Thummim*; but since then the Lord God has no longer given his oracles to the High Priest, even though he, as before, wore the Ephod and the Breastplate adorned with twelve precious stones. The Jewish Teachers agree with the Christians in this; and Nehemiah clearly pointed this out in the seventh chapter of his book, when speaking of certain Priests who, after their return from Babylon to the Jewish land, had not been able to show by genealogical registers that they were of the Priestly tribe, says that they were forbidden to eat of the most holy things until a Priest stood up with Urim and Thummim; wishing thereby to give it to be understood that they had fallen forever from the right and the ministry of the Priesthood, because it would never happen under

<column-break/>

the second Temple that God would make known his oracles through the *Urim* and *Thummim*. Much effort has been spent to know exactly what this Oracle through the *Urim* and *Thummim* actually was, and one finds so many different opinions regarding this that it would be tedious to recount them: but it is very likely that people have fallen into all these vain speculations because they have been unwilling to accept the truth according to the simplicity of the words of the Scripture. God commands Moses in the twenty-eighth chapter of Exodus to make the Breastplate that was to be worn on the Ephod, and to fill it with gemstones; and after having indicated in detail everything that concerned that piece of work, he says to him in the 30th verse: *And you shall put in the breastplate of judgment the Urim and the Thummim, that they may be over Aaron’s heart when he goes in before the LORD;* this is nothing other than a repetition of what God had already said in the 28th and 29th verses, and a conclusion of everything that was indicated at length in the preceding verses. Consequently, that which God calls *Urim* and *Thummim* in this place, which were to be on the breastplate that Aaron had to wear on his chest, can have been nothing other than the same gemstones that were on the breastplate, and without which Aaron was not allowed to enter the Holy Place. When the High Priest then went into the Sanctuary, clothed with the Ephod, wearing on his heart, or on his breast, the Breastplate adorned with gemstones, to ask God for counsel regarding weighty and difficult matters, God gave him his answer, either by a living voice, as he did to Moses at the door of the Tabernacle, or inwardly in the mind of the High Priest: for the Scripture does not express itself clearly regarding the manner in which God spoke to his Servants, so that when it is said that God answered by the Urim and Thummim, it is to be understood that the Lord revealed his mind to the High Priest when he appeared before him with the Urim and Thummim on his breast.

Each of these garments had its own mysteries. The High Priest was a type <note>In the sense of a prophetic symbol or "foreshadowing"</note> of Jesus Christ, as the Apostle Paul explained this at length in the Epistle to the Hebrews, which alone is enough to make us understand that the consecrated garments of the High Priest all had a secret significance. It seems that Christ himself wished to make this known when he appeared to John in one of the visions of the book of Revelation, related in the first chapter, with a long garment down to the feet, and a golden girdle, which was unique to the High Priest. This girdle then, adorned with gold (to begin the explanation of the High Priest’s attire with it), represented that which is said of Jesus Christ in the eleventh chapter of Isaiah, that righteousness and truth should be the girdle of his loins. The long robe with which he was clothed was the symbol of the same righteousness of Christ, of which Isaiah prophesied in the sixty-first chapter, where he introduces the Savior speaking thus: *I will greatly rejoice in the LORD, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he has clothed me with the garments of salvation, he has covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decks himself with Priestly ornaments.* The Ephod, which was of purple and scarlet, stitched through with gold, and to which

## Moses erects the Tabernacle.

### Exodus Chapter XL. verses 17. 18.

<margin>
The year of the world 2514, the first day of the first month, in the second year after the Exodus from Egypt and before the birth of Jesus Christ 1490.
</margin>

THE children of Israel spent about six months working on the Tabernacle, and they had completed all the pieces of it at the end of the first year of their exodus from Egypt. During that time, Moses received from the hands of the craftsmen, or those to whom he had entrusted the oversight of all the work, everything that was completed: and after there was nothing left to be made, he began on the first day of the second year to gather all the pieces and join them together to erect the Tabernacle. The Hebrews then had, for the first time, the privilege of seeing a dwelling place for the God of Israel erected in their midst. Until that day, they had not properly had a consecrated place to offer their worship to God, and to be honored there with special signs of his presence. However, they had always been God's people and the object of his love and mercy, such that he had favorably accepted their worship, even though it had been offered to him in places which he himself had not specifically designated and consecrated for that purpose. The Apostle Stephen noted this in the formal and profound dis-

<column-break/>

course which he spoke in his defense before the Great Council <note>The Sanhedrin</note>. He was accused of having spoken irreverently of the Temple in Jerusalem, under the pretext that he wanted to give the Jews to understand that true religion would henceforth no longer be attached to that building, just as Jesus Christ had declared some years before to the Samaritan Woman, when he told her that the time was approaching when one would no longer worship the Heavenly Father in the Temple at Jerusalem above other places on earth. The Holy Martyr, wishing then to show the Jews that religion was not, as they falsely imagined, bound to the Temple, led them back to the earliest times of their nation, and told them that it was in the wilderness where their fathers had erected a Tabernacle to God; from which it followed that since religion existed before that time outside the Tabernacle and the Temple, one should not believe that it could not still exist without them, because God had reasons of wisdom not to bind his service to a certain place any longer. ### *Moses places those things in the Tabernacle which God had commanded to be set there.*

### Exodus, Chapter XL. verses 20—30.

<margin>The same year, and the same</margin>
After Moses had erected the Tabernacle and had hung the veil of tapestry which was to separate the Most Holy Place from the Holy Place, as well as that which was to make a partition between the Sanctuary and the forecourt of the people, he had those things brought into each part of the Tabernacle which God had commanded to be placed there. The Ark of the Covenant was placed in the Holy of Holies, and the Tables of the Law, which Moses had brought down from the mountain, were laid in the Ark. There was no place in the Tabernacle where the Tables, inscribed with the finger of God, could more worthily be; but even this did not happen without some mystery. We have seen that the body of the Ark represented the Church, and that the golden table that covered it, called the Mercy Seat <term>Verzoendekfel: The Atonement Cover or Mercy Seat, symbolizing God's grace covering the Law</term>, was an image of Jesus Christ. The Tables of the Law being laid in the Ark to be preserved there signified that the Church is the true storehouse of God’s Law, and that it is there that it is kept; but these Tables, being under the shadow and covering of the Mercy Seat, represent-

<column-break/>

-ed, firstly, that the Covenant of Sinai—of which the Tables of the Law are called the Testimony—was not given, so to speak, except under the shadow and protection of the Covenant of Grace, which was indicated in these words of the Law: 
> I am the LORD your God.... and showing mercy. <note>original: "Ik ben de HEERE uw Gód.... en doe barmhartigheyd." See Exodus 20:2-6.</note>

Secondly, this showed that the Church in general is never so holy that she has no need of grace, and that in particular no man is so righteous, or keeps God’s Law so faithfully, that he has no need of atonement to cover his transgressions; according to this upright confession of the Royal Prophet: 
> If You, Lord, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand? But there is forgiveness with You. <note>original: "Zo gy, Heere, de ongerechtigheyd gade flaat, wie zal beftaan? Maar by u is vergeevinge." Reference to Psalm 130:3-4.</note>

Regarding the golden pot that held the Manna, and the rod of Aaron which afterwards brought forth blossoms and bore almonds (as one reads in the seventeenth chapter of Numbers), which were also brought into the Most Holy place to be kept there, it was only long afterwards that they were placed there, and Moses speaks here only of the Ark and the Tables of the Law.

He placed in the Sanctuary the golden Altar, the Table of showbread, and the Lampstand, all of whose lamps he lit: and in all this he followed exactly the command that God had given him, this being repeated at least eight times in this chapter of Exodus, because in matters of Religion, nothing is more excellent than obedience. ### *Moses sets up the Court around the Tabernacle.*

<margin>The same year.</margin>

The cloud-column, which for many months had appeared above the tent where Moses held his judicial sessions and gave judgments, as we have indicated elsewhere, suddenly left this tent—which God had taken only for a certain time, and solely to speak His decrees and settlements there through the mouth of His Prophet—and came not merely to the door of the Tabernacle which Moses had set up, but went inside and filled it, to show that God indeed took possession of it, and that He henceforth wished to make it the place of His residence. but it was one and the same; inside and outside was the cloud, which is here called *the glory of the Lord*, just as in the first Book of Kings in the eighth chapter, because it was a miraculous token of God's appearance to His people. That same thing happened later in the dedication of Solomon’s Temple: *A cloud, says the holy History, filled the House of the LORD, and the Priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud; for the glory of the Lord had filled the House of God.* Both these appearances, which had so much in common with each other, signified in general the presence of God in His Church, which is His true Tabernacle and Temple, through the spiritual dedication and hallowing that has occurred for her in Christ. But they represented even more specifically the further fullness, so to speak, of the divine presence in the human nature of Jesus Christ, who called Himself *the Temple of God*, and in whom the Apostle Paul tells us that *all the fullness of the Godhead dwells*, not as a shadow and image, as in the ancient Tabernacle and in the first Temple, but bodily; that is to say, essentially and personally. In short, this manner of filling the Tabernacle by a cloud, rather than by a heavenly and miraculous radiance, showed what the nature of this Old Covenant was, namely a very dark and obscure Dispensation <term>Dispensation: A theological era or system through which God relates to humanity; here referring to the period of the Law before the Gospel.</term>, since the Light was reserved for another household <note>original: "Huys-houding," here referring to the administration or "economy" of the Gospel.</note>, namely that of the Gospel.

-># HISTORY of the O. TESTAMENT.<-

him on account of a multitude of matters that were to be observed among the Jews alone, but whose use under the Dispensation of the Gospel has come to a total end. In general, God's purpose in that almost infinite number of ceremonial ordinances was to lay such a heavy and hard yoke upon the necks of His people that they would feel the impossibility of bearing it, just as the Apostle Peter noted in the fifteenth chapter of the Acts of the Apostles: to the end that the believers of the ancient Dispensation, sighing under the weight that pressed upon them, would thereby be brought to that happy necessity of longing for the coming of the Messiah, who would relieve them of it. If God had not had mystical intentions in all these ceremonial laws, and if He had not pointed in everything to the Messiah and His graces—as if through so many different paths and under various symbols—the state of the Israelites after God had made a covenant with them on Mount Sinai would have been much less happy than before, and worse than the state of all the believers who had lived from Adam until Moses: for in those first ages of the world, the Church had but a very small number of ceremonies to maintain, and those of such a kind that their use did not occur daily, as it did after the covenant of Sinai and the erection of the Tabernacle.

Among the institutions of this famous Dispensation, where the mysteries of Grace presented themselves to the eyes of Faith under as many images and shadows as the ceremonial laws presented to the eyes of the Hebrews, one of the most remarkable was that of the <term>Levitisch Priesterdom</term> <note>Levitical Priesthood: The formal system of priests from the tribe of Levi established by God at Mount Sinai.</note>. Up until that time, for more than two thousand five hundred years, sacrifices had been offered to God without distinction by all the households of the believers; and in every household, all the sons of the house were born with a right to the Priesthood. In the beginning of the world, Abel offered as well as his eldest brother Cain; after the flood, Shem, who was the youngest of Noah's sons, offered just as his father Noah had done; Abraham, who was the youngest of his brothers, was also an Offerer; and Moses, though younger than Aaron, did not fail to perform Priestly duties. But this ancient and common right for all the households of God's children ended at the foot of Mount Sinai, and God assigned it to one family alone. Aaron was chosen by God for the supreme dignity of the Priesthood, and after him his eldest son; his other sons and their children after them were appointed as common Priests; such that after that time there was no man in Israel who dared to offer sacrifices to God on the

<column-break/>

Altar of Burnt Offering, nor lay a hand upon the censer, if he were not of Aaron's household. Now, just as this new and glorious distinction was in favor of Aaron and his children, so God wished to install them in their office in the most stately manner possible. To this end, He gave command to Moses that he should gather the people together at the entrance of the Tabernacle; which having been done, Moses gave them to understand the choice God had made of Aaron and his sons to place the Priestly office and the service of His altars into their hands. He then proceeded to their consecration, which occurred with great pomp and solemnity. He began with Aaron, whom he clothed with the Priestly garments and such robes as were unique to the High Priest alone: namely, the robe trimmed with pomegranates and golden bells; the Ephod with the breastplate, upon which the <term>Urim</term> and <term>Thummim</term> <note>Urim and Thummim: Sacred objects used by the High Priest to determine God's will, often translated as "Lights and Perfections."</note> were; the girdle embroidered with gold and purple; and the golden plate, which served him as a head ornament or crown, with this inscription: **HOLINESS TO THE LORD** <note>original: "DE HEYLYGHEYD DES HEEREN"</note>. After the consecration of Aaron, he performed that of his sons and likewise clothed them with their Priestly robes. Moses spent seven whole days with this solemnity, sacrificing various bulls and rams to God as an offering, of which he took the blood to use in various ways during this consecration. There was nothing in all that Moses did that did not contain some secret; but since it is impossible to enter here into a broad account of all those things, it will be enough to note these two, which first present themselves and occupy the mind of the reader. The first is that it was Moses, the Mediator of the Covenant of the Law, who consecrated the Priests; and the other, that he consecrated them through the blood of the sacrifices. The first shows that the Priestly office was separate from the quality of Mediator, to indicate the weakness of both: He who served the office of Mediator had no sacrifice to offer for the reconciliation of the people; and he who offered the sacrifices was no Mediator. But these two great offices are found united in Jesus Christ, who through this glorious union is the Savior of His Church. ...him because of a multitude of matters that were to be observed among the Jews alone, but whose use under the Dispensation <note>original: "Huyshoudinge," a theological term referring to the specific way God governs His people in a particular era.</note> of the Gospel has completely come to an end. In general, God's purpose in that almost infinite number of solemn ordinances was to place such a heavy and hard yoke upon the necks of His people that they would feel the impossibility of carrying it, just as the Apostle Peter noted in the fifteenth chapter of the Acts of the Apostles. This was done so that the believers of the ancient Dispensation, sighing under the weight that pressed upon them, would be brought to that happy necessity of longing for the coming of the Messiah, who would relieve them of it. If God had not had symbolic purposes in all these ceremonial laws, and if He had not pointed toward the Messiah and His graces in everything—through so many different ways and under various emblems—the state of the Israelites, after God had made a covenant with them on Mount Sinai, would have been much less happy than before. It would have been worse than the state of all the believers who lived from Adam until Moses; for in those first ages of the world, the Church had only a very small number of ceremonies to maintain, and those were of a kind that did not occur daily, as was the case after the covenant of Sinai and the establishment of the Tabernacle.

Among the institutions of this famous Dispensation, where the mysteries of Grace presented themselves to the eyes of Faith under as many images and shadows as the ceremonial laws displayed before the eyes of the Hebrews, one of the most remarkable was that of the Levitical Priesthood. Up until that time, for more than two thousand five hundred years, sacrifices had been offered to God without distinction by all the families of the believers; and in every family, all the sons of the house were born with a right to the Priesthood. In the beginning of the world, Abel offered as well as his eldest brother Cain; after the flood, Shem, who was the youngest of Noah’s sons, offered just as his father Noah had done; Abraham, who was the youngest of his brothers, was also a Sacrificer; and Moses, though younger than Aaron, did not fail to perform Priestly duties. But this ancient and common right for all the families of God’s children ended at the foot of Mount Sinai, and God assigned it to one lineage alone. Aaron was chosen by God for the supreme dignity of the Priesthood, and after him his eldest son; his other sons and their children after them were appointed as common priests; such that after that time there was no man in Israel who dared to offer sacrifices to God on the

<column-break/>

Altar of Burnt Offering, nor lay a hand upon the censer, if he were not of Aaron's family. Just as this new and glorious distinction was in favor of Aaron and his children, so God wished to install them in their office in the most stately manner possible. To this end, He gave command to Moses that he should gather the people together at the entrance of the Tabernacle; which being done, Moses informed them of the choice God had made of Aaron and his sons to place the Priestly office and the service of His altars into their hands. He then proceeded to their consecration, which took place with great pomp and solemnity. He began with Aaron, whom he clothed in the Priestly garments and such robes as were unique to the High Priest alone: namely, the robe trimmed with pomegranates and golden bells; the Ephod <note>A sacred vestment worn by the High Priest.</note> with the breastpiece, upon which were the Urim and Thummim; the girdle embroidered with gold and purple; and the golden plate, which served him as a head ornament or crown, with this inscription: HOLINESS TO THE LORD. After the consecration of Aaron, he performed that of his sons, clothing them likewise in their Priestly robes. Moses spent seven full days in this solemnity, offering various bulls and rams to God as a sacrifice, from which he took the blood to use in various ways during this consecration. There was nothing in all that Moses did that did not contain some mystery; but since it is impossible here to enter into a broad account of all those things, it will be enough to note these two, which first present themselves and occupy the reader’s mind: the first is that it was Moses, the Mediator of the Covenant of the Law, who consecrated the Priests; and the other is that he consecrated them through the blood of the victims. The first shows that the Priestly office was separated from the quality of Mediator, to point out the weakness of them both: He who served the office of Mediator had no sacrifice to offer for the reconciliation of the people; and he who offered the sacrifices was no Mediator. But these two great offices are found united in Jesus Christ, who through this glorious union is the Savior of His Church. The second, which concerns the sacrifices that Moses made for the consecration of Aaron and his sons, shows how little power the Priesthood had that, in its first institution, it needed a "foreign" sacrifice, so to speak; whereas the Priesthood and the sacrifice were found together in the person of Christ, who needed no foreign blood to be consecrated, but who did everything through His own blood. >*I sanctify myself for them, He said, so that they also may be sanctified in truth.*< <note>A reference to John 17:19.</note>

how the Ministers of the Sanctuary ought to walk in the ways of the Lord, to set an example for the entire Congregation. In all this, the right side was chosen to be marked with the blood of the sacrifices, because—there naturally being more strength in the right side than in the left—it has always been considered the primary side. God wished us to understand through this that we ought to offer all the strength and skill we possess to His service, and that such dedication serves as our dignity and glory.

<margin>The year of the world 2514, and the second year after the exodus from Egypt.</margin>
The consecration of Aaron and his sons was completed in seven days, and on the eighth, they together began the ministry of their Priesthood. That day, they offered various sacrifices of different kinds; Aaron first offered for his own sins, and then for those of the people, as is mentioned with explicit words regarding this first act of his Priesthood. It was a great imperfection in the Levitical Priesthood that its High Priest needed to make atonement for himself before he could offer any sacrifice for the expiation of the people's sins. But where does one find a man who is not a sinner, and who does not need to be reconciled with God through the blood of a sacrifice? This was a privilege for Jesus Christ alone, who was holy, innocent, undefiled, and separated from sinners, and who therefore did not need to offer for himself; for if such had been necessary, he could not have sanctified us through his own blood. Since impure and defiled blood is powerless to sanctify others and make atonement for their sins, according to the observations of the Apostle Paul in his Epistle to the Hebrews. Nothing, then, expressed the imperfection of Aaron’s priestly office so much as that of the Offerer himself—who was honored with the highest dignity in that Priesthood—as well as that great variety of sacrifices which he had to offer to God for his sins and the sins of others. Bulls, lambs, goats, turtledoves, and pigeons were all seized by the eager hand of the Priest, and the altar, which devoured and consumed them, never said, "It is enough": because all the blood in the world would not have been powerful enough to effect a true erasing of a single sin. For it is impossible, says the Apostle to the Hebrews, for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins; and the Law, with all its sacrifices, could not sanctify stained and unclean persons, except through a ceremonial purity, which always left the stain and uncleanness of sin remaining in the soul.

Meanwhile, because God, in all these sacrifices, had His eye upon that of Jesus Christ, of which they were representations, He accepted them favorably. At the sight of a victim falling under the Priest's knife and being offered to Him on the altar, He forgave the sins of the Priest and the people, and caused His blessings to descend upon them. He wished to give a credible assurance of this to the entire Church of Israel on the first day that Aaron and his sons began the ministry of their office: for after they had laid the victims on the altar to offer them as a burnt offering, one saw a

<column-break/>

miraculous flame descend from Heaven upon it, which completely consumed the flesh and the fat of the offerings. Nothing of this kind had been seen since the offering of Abel, and for more than two thousand years, all the burnt offerings which the holy Patriarchs had offered to God were consumed and turned to ash by no other fire than that which burned on their hearths and was used for the common purposes of life. But God wished to do something extraordinary for the sake of the Priesthood that He established with such great solemnity, to make it all the more venerable to all the children of Israel, and to give them for the future, and for the entire time this covenant would last, a great expectation of the offerings which they would present to God according to His institution and His word. About five hundred years later, on an occasion very similar to this, the same miraculous sign of a fire descending from Heaven onto the burnt offerings was seen at the consecration of Solomon’s Temple, and on various other special occasions, of which we shall have the opportunity to speak in the continuation of this work. The sons of Aaron preserved this fire, which had descended from Heaven, most religiously, in order to always use it for the burnt offerings, according to the command God had given them in the sixth chapter of this same book of Leviticus:

> The fire upon the altar,
> He had said, shall be kept burning thereon,
> it shall not be extinguished, but the Priest
> shall kindle wood on it every morning, and shall
> arrange the burnt offering upon it, and shall kindle
> the fat of the peace offerings upon it: the fire shall
> be kept burning continually upon the altar; **IT SHALL**
> **NOT BE EXTINGUISHED.**

This holy fire, whose miraculous descent brought such great honor to Aaron’s Priesthood and to the Tabernacle of Moses, was preserved until that day when a new fire of the same kind descended in the Temple of Jerusalem; and that remained in existence until the destruction of the Temple, or the Babylonian captivity. This pure flame, which had descended from Heaven upon the burnt offerings and which was never extinguished as long as the Tabernacle and the Temple lasted, was the symbol <note>The author uses the word "zinnebeeld," meaning a physical sign representing a spiritual reality.</note> of the Holy Spirit, the holy and mystical fire which ignites the hearts of the Believers, and there consumes the spiritual burnt offerings which they offer to God. This divine fire is never completely extinguished in the Church in general, or in a Believer in particular; and if it does not always give off the same light and the same heat, it nevertheless remains preserved under the ashes of human weaknesses and the inclinations that are still earthly, from which even the greatest saints are never entirely released. And it seems that the Apostle Paul had this mystery in mind when, with metaphorical and borrowed terms, he exhorted the Thessalonians not to quench the Spirit, so that they would be like spiritual Priests who always watch carefully for the preservation of this divine fire which has come into their souls from above.

Not long after Aaron and his sons were installed in the Priesthood, an astonishing and terrible thing occurred; Nadab and Abihu, Aaron’s two eldest sons, wishing to offer incense to God upon the golden altar which was in the Sanctuary, put fire in their censers which the Scripture calls *strange* <note>original: *vreemd*</note>, because it was not from that same fire which had been lit on the altar in the beginning, or which had descended from Heaven upon the burnt offerings, which the Priests were commanded to guard carefully so as to use it in the service of the altar. It was, then, with common and ordinary fire that Nadab and Abihu went to offer the incense, which they had likely taken from the coals under the kettles in which the Priests boiled the meat of the peace offerings. It would be difficult to discover the exact reason why they had not put the fire that was to be used solely for that purpose, and which was specifically kept for it, into their censers. Some believe

<column-break/>

that their minds were somewhat clouded by the vapors of wine, and they base their guess on this: that immediately after the punishment for the evil deed of these two Priests, God forbade Aaron and his sons from drinking wine upon pain of death whenever they were to enter the Tabernacle to perform their office. But this suspicion goes too far, and the guess upon which they lean is not conclusive enough to make that opinion respectable. So much was not required to make their deed criminal; the contempt of a command of God, however small the matter which He forbids or commands might seem in itself, can never be anything other than a great crime, because God’s authority in that regard is violated, and His infinite Majesty <term>Majesty: the supreme greatness and sovereignty of God</term> is offended and to some extent diminished by the boldness of a man who takes the liberty for himself to obey where and when it pleases him. Nadab and Abihu took the first fire they found in the Tabernacle and put it in their censers, and they persuaded themselves that it was all the same with what kind of fire they made their incense smoke. This was indeed true in itself and by nature: but that which is in itself indifferent is no longer so where there is a law. They gave too much place to Reason, and not enough to Faith: for in Religion it is always Faith, or God’s Word, with which one must consult, and not the cleverness of human wit. Thus God did not wish to leave this first wicked undertaking in the Priesthood unpunished. It was necessary to stop, at the very first, the bold liberty of man to introduce novelties <note>The author uses "novelties" to describe unauthorized changes to religious rituals</note> into the matters of Religion through some outstanding punishment; for without that, some change would have been made daily, and thus at last that manner which God had prescribed would no

...could have confessed more. The very nature of this covenant required great examples of severity. *It was a Dispensation of strictness*, established under the terrifying sound of thunder, and in the midst of lightning and flames that had covered Mount *Sinai*. It was a ministry of condemnation and death, *a killing letter* <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 3:6, contrasting the Mosaic Law with the New Covenant</note>, and a Law that pronounced a curse upon the slightest transgressions. God then took vengeance immediately and in a terrible manner for the contempt shown by *Nadab* and *Abihu* regarding the holy fire; and if the punishment did not entirely prevent their crime (for it never happens that the punishment precedes the transgression), it at least prevented them from completing it. They had as yet done nothing more than fill their censers with strange fire, but they had not yet made use of them; the offense was only half-committed. It was, nonetheless, already too much; the wicked intent was already fulfilled in the heart, and their hands were already all too guilty by the act’s beginning. The vengeance of Heaven overtook them in that state, and a fire, ignited in the blaze of God’s wrath, suddenly descended upon these miserable men and killed them in a moment. The fire of Heaven thus avenged the insult offered to the holy fire—which itself had descended from Heaven only a few days prior—and it made these criminals an offering to Justice, to punish in them the disdain for a fire which God, as an excellent sign of His reconciliation, had used to consume the burnt offerings. *Nadab* and *Abihu* fell dead with the censer in hand, at the entrance of the Court, and at the first step toward the Sanctuary: and the fire, which consumed their life in their entrails and in their marrow, left their bodies whole, and did not even burn their clothes: like that sort of lightning which, without burning the clothing or the body of a man, strikes the life in the bone and the heart, causing him to fall dead to the ground in an instant. *Aaron* beheld, without moving and without speaking a word, the fearsome death of his two children, the eldest of his household, of whom one should have followed him in the highest dignity, and the other should have been the head of the Priestly lineages; both of whom, a few months before, had the honor of being named by God Himself to climb Mount *Sinai* to a certain height in the company of *Moses*, while meanwhile the entire people of *Israel* were strictly forbidden even to approach the foot of the holy mountain. It was not through insensitivity or hardheartedness that *Aaron* showed no sign of grief at the mournful death of his two sons; the heart of a father is incapable of such cruelty; but the dignity of High Priest did not allow *Aaron* to mourn in God’s presence. However, it was not so with the people; astonishment and terror were visible on every face, and the mourning was general in *Israel*. *Moses* commanded *Aaron’s* next of kin, the sons of *Uzziel*, his uncle, to take up the corpses of *Nadab* and *Abihu* and carry them outside the Camp, where they were buried with their tunics and other Priestly clothing in the same state as the fire of Heaven had left them. This was done to show even better how unclean those bodies were, and even the clothes, no matter how much they had first been sanctified by the consecration; and thus to instill in the whole peo-

<column-break/>

-ple, but especially in the other Priests, a much greater terror for that crime.

<margin>The year of the world 2514, and the second month of the second year after the exodus from Egypt, etc.</margin>
The entire first month of the second year after the exodus of God's people from Egypt was spent in the institution of the ceremonial laws, which formed the external appearance and outward form of the Covenant of *Sinai*. During all that time, God spoke to *Moses* in the Tabernacle, which stood at the foot of the mountain, in the same place where *Moses* had erected it when it was completed; and the book of *Leviticus*, in which all the ceremonial laws are contained, covers the history of only one month. God subsequently commanded *Moses* and *Aaron* to count all the *Israelites* who were capable of bearing arms, from twenty to sixty years old. Each Tribe performed its counting separately, and the sum of each being brought to *Moses* to make a general calculation, it was found that the number of the men of *Israel*—calculating none others among them than those who had at least entered their twentieth year—amounted to six hundred three thousand five hundred fifty: the tribe of *Levi* was not included in this count, because the *Levites*, not being required to go to war like the other tribes, but being appointed solely for the service of the Tabernacle, were counted separately and set apart from all the others.

It is an amazing thing that this people had grown so uncommonly in such a short time. *Abraham*, who was the first root thereof, had had but one son, namely *Isaac*; from *Isaac* came *Jacob*; and from *Jacob* twelve sons and one daughter. When *Jacob* and his children moved from *Canaan* to *Egypt* in the time of *Joseph*, they numbered no more than seventy persons, or at most seventy-five, according to the calculation of St. *Stephen* <note>Referring to Acts 7:14</note>, who made the calculation in a different way than *Moses*; but both nonetheless according to the truth, because *Moses* included only those who were descended from *Jacob*, namely his sons and their children, as is stated in express words in the forty-sixth chapter of *Genesis* <note>The original text says "56th chapter," but Genesis only has 50; the author refers to Genesis 46</note>: whereas *Stephen* made his calculation a little differently, including also the persons who departed with *Jacob* to *Egypt* but were not of his descent and blood, namely the eleven wives of his sons; and *Jacob* himself he had not included in this number, nor *Joseph* with his wife and children, since they were already in *Egypt*. The people had been in *Egypt* only two hundred and ten years, and in that short span of time, notwithstanding that so many children had been killed and murdered by *Pharaoh’s* cruel command, it is found that from seventy persons a people of between twelve and fifteen hundred thousand souls or more had sprung; for there must have been at least that many, because there were six hundred and three or four thousand men capable of bearing arms, without counting those of an entire Tribe, nor the women, nor the children under twenty years of age. This was the fruit of the promise which God had made to *Abraham* when, already bowed under the weight of his years and having a wife almost as old as he, and moreover barren, he understood from the Lord that from him and *Sara* his wife a people would be born as numerous as the stars of heaven, wel-

...which one grows weary of counting because their number is so vast. Never has there been a lineage in the world that grew so tremendously in such a short time, and one must call Faith to the aid of reason to prevent the intellect from being hindered by the difficulties that such an extraordinary multiplication can cause in the mind. It was, then, through a special blessing upon Abraham’s blood that the descendants of that holy man were multiplied almost infinitely; but it was also a "prefigurement" or "foreshadowing" <note>A theological term meaning an event or person in the Old Testament that points toward a future reality in the New Testament.</note> that this occurred. Abraham was not only the Father of the Jews through physical procreation, but he was also the father in a spiritual and mystical sense of all Believers, of whatever nationality they might be, according to the teaching of the Apostle Paul in the fourth chapter of his Epistle to the Romans. This uncommon and miraculous increase of the descendants of this Patriarch in Egypt was a foreshadowing of the nearly countless multitude of the spiritual children of Abraham at the time of the Gospel covenant, even under the persecution and oppression of the Church. From a small number of people who had believed in Jesus Christ, there grew, through an uncommon blessing of God, under the hands and eyes of the Apostles, an exceedingly numerous Congregation. In Jerusalem at first, there was but a gathering of one hundred and twenty persons, and within a few days, the Christians were counted by hundreds and thousands. Judea soon became for the Church what Egypt had once been for the ancient Hebrews: a terrible scene of persecutions; but meanwhile, the Church grew daily, and the Gospel made such great progress that within a very short time Judea, Syria, and the other surrounding lands—indeed, the whole world—saw itself filled with Christians. In such a way that, just as truth is above the shadow, so the true people of God multiplied far beyond the prefigured people, and the *Israel according to the spirit* far beyond the *Israel according to the flesh*.

When Moses and Aaron had completed the census of the twelve Tribes of Israel, God wished to show them the form of their Army and the order of their march Himself. Until that day, the Hebrews had traveled in confusion, like a numerous crowd of men, women, and children, in the manner of traveling folk, without observing any other order than that each remained with his household, and each household with its Tribe. But God saw fit to give to this great multitude the appearance of a military host, to make them march with greater prestige and more security, no longer as a band of refugees fleeing from Egypt, but as a people going forth to conquer a Kingdom. To that end, He divided the twelve tribes into four different bodies or hosts, each of which consisted of three tribes; and in each of those hosts, the Tribe that held command marched in the middle of the two others. Each tribe had its own banner, and if one may believe the Jews, the banner of each was of the same color as the precious stone of the Breastplate <note>The *Hoshen*, a sacred breastplate worn by the High Priest, set with twelve stones representing the twelve tribes.</note> upon which the name of their Patriarch was engraved: but since this is nothing but a conjecture of the Rab-

<column-break/>

-bis, one cannot place much reliance upon it. Another of their conjectures is what they say regarding the sign or image that was painted on the banners of the four tribes that commanded the others: namely, a man in the banner of Reuben, a lion in that of Judah, an ox in that of Ephraim, and an eagle in that of Dan. It is true that one sees these four images in a vision which the Prophet Ezekiel relates in the first chapter of his revelations; but that is not proof regarding the banners of these four Tribes, about which the Jews have had several other observations that are even more vain and senseless. The Tribe of Judah camped at the front and had under its command those of Issachar and Zebulun, which together made up a host of one hundred eighty-six thousand and four hundred men. The Tribe of Dan, with those of Asher and Naphtali, which arranged themselves under its banner, made up the rearguard, which consisted of one hundred fifty-seven thousand six hundred. The six other tribes were at the sides: Reuben with Simeon and Gad, who camped under his banner, made up the right wing, consisting of one hundred fifty-one thousand four hundred and fifty; and on the left wing was the Tribe of Ephraim, under whose banner those of Manasseh and Benjamin had joined, to the number of one hundred and eight thousand one hundred men; which then all together yielded exactly the number of six hundred and three thousand five hundred and fifty who had been found in the census. In the midst of these numerous hosts, each of which could have made up a large army on its own, the Tribe of Levi camped, which God had dedicated to His service, for which reason they were also not counted with the others; and in the middle of that tribe the Tabernacle was placed, just like the Tent of the Commander-in-Chief in the armies of the Romans. And if we may judge by the arrangement and order observed at the time of Joshua in the crossing of the Jordan (as there is great probability for this), there was a space of a thousand paces on all sides between the Tribe of Levi and the others, out of reverence for the Tabernacle, which was the pavilion of God and the sanctified tent where His Ark, the illustrious sign of His presence, was placed. Such was the arrangement which the children of Israel maintained in their encampments during the thirty-nine years they were still in the wilderness, and they observed the same order in all their marches. They never broke camp from the place where they were except at God’s command, who showed them all their movements through the movement of the pillar of cloud. As long as it remained still above the Army, they also remained still; and at the first movement it made, whether by day or by night, everything was prepared to depart. When all the tents were rolled up and all the people ready to set out on the road, Moses approached the Ark and said to God, under whose guidance and protection they marched, these words:
> Rise up, LORD, and let your enemies be scattered, and let those who hate you flee from before your face.

And when the Priests who carried the Ark set it down, Moses spoke thus to God:
> Return, LORD, to the ten thousands of the thousands of Israel.

<margin>The same year</margin>
God had given several laws against the impurity of the flesh, and specifically against adultery. This crime cannot violate the sanctity of marriage without being one of the most heinous offenses that can be committed in civil society; and it gives such a harsh blow to true love and union that it is regarded in the world as one of the most punishable acts. All nations of the earth have been of this opinion; and the legislators who were least strict among the Heathens <note>The author refers here to non-Christian or "pagan" ancient civilizations like the Greeks or Romans.</note> condemned the act of adultery to the heaviest punishment. But as this sin naturally covers all persons who are guilty of it with shame, it imprints a yet fouler and deeper stain on women than on men: because modesty and virtue being seen as inherent and inseparable virtues of that sex, and the woman being dependent on the husband, the lack of faithfulness to her spouse is a crime in her that violates several laws at once. Just as all these observations ought to restrain all persons of this sex from polluting the purity of marriage by their conduct, so they should also oblige them to such a disciplined behavior that they give their husbands no cause to hold them suspect regarding any evil dealing. Nothing has ever been seen to instill such holy and righteous sentiments in women that could be compared to the

<column-break/>

institution of the **Water of Jealousy**, which God introduced among the children of Israel. He willed, first of all, that a man who had a strong suspicion of his wife—that she was misbehaving—and yet could not convict her of it, should have the right to accuse her before his authorities, and that upon that accusation, the woman should be sent to one of the Priests, appointed for that purpose, so that he might question her and proceed with her in the following manner.

This woman, who was suspected of adultery, presented herself before the Priest, having a cake of barley meal in her hands, upon which there was neither incense nor oil, as on the usual cakes offered to God; for incense being the symbol of a good name through its pleasant scent, and oil that of a sincere and peaceful mind, both were unsuitable for an offering which was the result of a bad name into which that woman had fallen, and of the jealousy of the man, which is called a *fury* <note>original: *grimmigheyd*. This refers to Proverbs 6:34: "For jealousy is the rage of a man."</note> by Solomon.

In this state, the Priest made her stand upright at the entrance of the Tabernacle, but nevertheless within the bounds of the first courtyard, for that is what Moses calls, *standing before the face of the Lord.* Subsequently, he took certain water, which is called *holy water*, because it was intended for nothing but a holy use; and this water was either that of the large copper wash-basin <term>laver|A massive bronze basin in the Tabernacle courtyard used by priests for ritual cleansing</term> which stood in the Courtyard of the Tabernacle, or more likely that mystical water, which is described in the nineteenth chapter of Numbers under the name of the *water of separation* <note>Also known as the Water of Cleansing, made with the ashes of a red heifer.</note>. The Priest, having taken this water in a small earthen vessel, gathered some of the dust that lay on the floor and mixed it into that water. Upon hearing these words, the woman—who had already sworn an oath that she was innocent of the crime her husband accused her of—had to answer twice in succession: *Amen, Amen,* to signify that she submitted with all her heart to all those curses, which she herself requested from God might come upon her, as severe as they were, if she had violated her marriage vows. All these ceremonies served to strike the accused woman with fear and terror, and to make her humbly confess the crime rather than expose herself to such a shameful death. If she continued to firmly deny the crime, the Priest offered her the vessel containing the water that was to demonstrate her innocence or put her to shame in her sin; and the woman, taking it from his hand, drank that mysterious drink, which was filled and, as it were, saturated with the curse the Priest had pronounced over her and had, in a sense, signed therein. This water, which the Scripture calls bitter <note>Original: "bitter." This refers to the 'Water of Bitterness' in Numbers 5:18.</note>, because of the bitterness of heart felt by the woman who had to drink it on that occasion, and which was even more bitter because of the miserable effects it produced, had barely descended into the bowels of the suspected woman before her innocence or guilt was immediately shown: If she was guilty, her face changed color, her eyes lost their luster, her belly swelled hideously, and those parts of her body which were most criminal were instantly seized by a rot, under which the entire body collapsed, and she lost her life in pain, remorse, and shame. But if the suspected person was innocent, this water—which could not be anything but very bitter even for the purest innocence—produced no such effect, and far from harming the health of the woman who had drunk it, she became only healthier and stronger, and it helped to make her more fruitful and the mother of many children. Such was the Water of Jealousy, and such were the various effects, all of which were so many miracles. It is not known when the Jews stopped using this water; yet if one can rely on their tradition, it remained in use long after their return from the Babylonian captivity: But there is great probability that since all the miracles seen in former times had come to an end with the destruction of the first Temple, this Water of Jealousy no longer had the same power under the second, and that the practice gradually fell away when it was seen to be nothing more than a mere ceremony.

Never was any people more willing to make holy offerings for divine service than the Israelites. When Moses wanted to have work begin on the Tabernacle, of which God had given him a design on Mount Sinai, many days long in the Camp of Israel, at the appointed place, a multitude of costly fab-

<column-break/>

rics were seen being brought, along with silver and gold, almost beyond counting; the weight of the gold amounted, according to the account Moses made of it in the thirty-eighth chapter of Exodus, to twenty-nine talents and seven hundred and thirty shekels; a talent now, when it is the name of a weight, weighed a hundred pounds, and a shekel half an ounce <note>The author provides these conversions to help the reader visualize the massive quantities of precious metals donated.</note>, which together made twenty-nine hundred and twenty-five pounds; the weight of the silver was one hundred talents and one thousand seven hundred and seventy-five shekels, or ten thousand and fifty-five pounds. The wealth of the Hebrews, however, was not exhausted by these great gifts, and so much silver and gold remained to them that on the day the altar was dedicated, the Leaders of Israel brought, each in the name of his tribe, costly gifts of gold and silver vessels for the religious service that was to be performed in the Tabernacle. The Leader of the tribe of Judah, who made the first offering, gave a silver charger <note>A large flat dish or plate.</note> weighing one hundred and thirty shekels, a silver sprinkling-bowl of seventy shekels, and a censer or golden vessel full of incense, of ten shekels. The Leaders of the other tribes each made a similar offering; and thus twelve chargers were received for the service of the Sanctuary, and as many sprinkling-bowls, all of silver, weighing two thousand four hundred shekels, and twelve golden censers of one hundred and twenty shekels. Nothing can better show us the wealth of Egypt than that vast abundance of gold and silver found in the tents of the Hebrews. It was mostly the loot and booty they had brought with them from the Egyptians, and which God, the Supreme Lord of all, had destined for His Sanctuary. The Israelites parted with it with a selflessness and joy that still serves to honor their memory, and which was the greatest act of piety and zeal they perhaps ever performed after their exodus from Egypt and in the wilderness. The nature of this ancient Dispensation required that there should be something magnificent in the outward practice of religion; God declared Himself to be the particular King of the Hebrews, and the Tabernacle, which He had erected, was like the tent of His glory and as His palace: and what is there so costly and of high value that ought not to serve to decorate a place God had chosen to dwell in Himself, and where He wished to give visible and most glorious signs of His presence? It is not that gold and silver are in themselves of greater value to God than the dust of the earth; but men hold them higher; and God, who in so many matters in that covenant adapted Himself to the manners and ideas of men, wished to be served in His Tabernacle with the splendor of the Kings of the earth. Yet the New Covenant has an entirely different character than the first, and as much as the one presented objects to the physical eyes that dazzled the sight with their costliness and luster, so much does the other love simplicity, and requires as Tabernacles those which are called by the Apostle Paul the Tabernacles of God in the spirit, which are the true Believers.

THE children of Israel journeyed from Mount Sinai, after they had been encamped there for eleven months, and were led to the wilderness of Paran by the pillar of cloud that went before them. They found themselves so exhausted by this journey, whether by the length of the road or by the roughness of the places through which they passed, that they murmured about it and complained against Moses. God punished them for this immediately, and caused a fire to go out from the earth, which spread over the outermost corners of their camp and consumed a great number of those rebels and defiant ones. <note>This location was named Taberah, meaning "burning."</note> They believed at once that it was all over for them, and according to their custom they took refuge with Moses, who prayed for them; whereupon the fire was immediately quenched and appeared no more. But no sooner was the people delivered from this great danger—which was the punishment for their criminal complaints—than they made themselves guilty of a new grumbling. They complained that for a year now they had eaten nothing but Manna, and because the delicacies of Egypt came to their minds, they longed to have eaten meat and fish again, which they had had there in abundance. This desire for meat became so strong in them that the Scripture notes they wept with displeasure because they could not obtain it, saying, *Who shall give us meat to eat?* Moses was sensibly touched, as he saw that the people were possessed by such a cowardly and earthly inclination. He would have liked to see them satisfied and their desire fulfilled by some means, so as to stop their grumbling. But, said he, *From where should I have the meat to give to all this people? For they weep against me, saying, Give us meat that we may eat.* God

<column-break/>

beheld the distress in which Moses was, and said to him that he would give meat to this people, not just for a day or two, but for a whole month. Moses was astonished to hear that an almost innumerable multitude of people in a wilderness could obtain so much meat that they could eat of it for a whole month; and although he was accustomed to miracles, he still could not understand by what means God would satisfy the craving of this people. *Six hundred thousand on foot*, he said, *is this people, without counting among them the women, the children under twenty, and the old men over sixty years, and You have said, I will give them meat, and they shall eat for a whole month. Shall sheep and cattle then be slaughtered for them, that there be enough for them; shall all the fish of the sea be gathered for them?* Since God had not yet declared in what manner he intended to satisfy the desire of the Hebrews, Moses could innocently present difficulties that arose from his ignorance and not from unbelief, for nowhere in Holy Scripture is he reproached for such a thing: but it happened to him much like the Holy Virgin, who said to the Angel out of astonishment and wonder: *How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?* <note>original: "Hoe zal dat weezen, dewyl ik geenen man bekenne?" This refers to Mary's response to Gabriel in Luke 1:34.</note> The Angel's answer to Mary, *No thing shall be impossible with God*, was the same that God gave to Moses: *Is the LORD’S hand then*, said he to him, *shortened? You shall now see whether my word shall happen to you or not.* The next day God caused a strong East wind to rise, which brought such a multitude of quails from the seaside that the earth around the camp of the Hebrews was covered with them for a day's journey. They gathered as many of these birds as they wanted, and they ate of them for several days, until God, provoked by the animal lust of this people, struck them with a plague that caused them to lose their lives while they had their mouths full of meat, and thought of nothing but their... <note>The text ends mid-sentence following the catchword "hunne" (their).</note>

<margin>The second year after the exodus from Egypt.</margin>
At a time when Moses was almost overwhelmed by cares and difficulties, and even more by the sorrow of hearing a new murmur in the Camp daily, he saw his sister Miriam and his brother Aaron also become rebellious and rise up against him. These two, envious of his honor and authority—yet without having the courage to dispute it with him openly—decided to start a quarrel with him because he had married a <term>Cushite<gloss>In this context, the text refers to an Ethiopian or Midianite woman, likely Zipporah.</gloss></term> or Ethiopian woman, instead of taking an Israelite wife. The aim of these two persons was to diminish the respect the entire people had for him and to force him into a public divorce from his wife. He had already been married to her for over forty years, but she had remained in Midian during that time with her father Jethro, who had only recently brought her and her two sons to Moses. God took up the defense of his Prophet, and He showed Himself more touched by the wrong done to him than Moses himself, who showed not the slightest sensitivity in a matter where self-love, bolstered by justice, could easily have shown its

<column-break/>

displeasure. God then declared Himself openly for Moses, and it was on this occasion that He gave him that testimony which has brought him so much honor, and which the Apostle Paul cited in his Epistle to the Hebrews: namely, that he was His faithful servant, to whom He had entrusted the entire management of His house. *Why then*, He added, *did you not fear to speak against my servant, against Moses?* God called him by name to better show how pleasing he was to Him. But as tender as His heart was toward Moses—who was unjustly accused and persecuted by his own relatives—so too His wrath was kindled against Miriam, who had been the primary cause of that quarrel. He struck her with a terrible leprosy, which brought a corruption over her entire body. Moses could not behold his sister, however guilty she was toward him, struck thus by the hand of the Lord without being overcome by heartache. He then prayed for her, and God was reconciled toward Miriam through his prayer, restoring her to her former state after seven days.

# HISTORY OF THE O. TESTAMENT.

...caught someone while he was busy looking for some firewood to bring into his tent. He was immediately seized as a criminal and brought before Moses. The case was entirely new and of such a nature that they did not know what judgment to pronounce against this transgressor. On the one hand, taken at its strictest and according to the letter, it was a violation of God's Law, because it strictly forbade doing any work on that day; but on the other hand, it was such a small thing this man had done, that this act could hardly be considered one of those regarded as labor of the hands. What increased the difficulty further was that the Law in the thirty-first chapter of Exodus, which commanded the keeping of the Sabbath, condemned those who profaned it to death; and yet it seemed uncommonly harsh to put a man to death for picking up a handful of wood, which he perhaps needed very much. They also did not know, assuming he must be killed, to what kind of punishment he should be condemned, because the Law had not declared itself on that point. In these doubts, Moses took his refuge in God, to hear from Him what He desired should be done in such a delicate matter. God's answer was that this man should be put to death and stoned; which at that time among the Jews was the most shameful punishment; for the cross was a foreign corporal punishment introduced into Judea by the Romans <note>The author clarifies that crucifixion, though well-known to his readers, was not a Jewish punishment during the time of Moses.</note>. 

->*That man shall surely be put to death*, God said to Moses, *and the whole congregation shall stone him with stones outside the camp*.<

This was the same sentence which God had pronounced a short time before over a blasphemer who had been brought before Moses, and about whom Moses had asked the Lord for advice, and received the answer,

->*that they should bring him outside the camp, and that the whole congregation should stone him*.<

One is not surprised that God condemned a blasphemer of His name to be overwhelmed with stones: for blasphemy is one of the greatest crimes one can commit, even when committed in circumstances most capable of diminishing the vileness thereof, such as those in which the curser, spoken of in the twenty-fourth chapter of Leviticus, found himself. But that God...

<column-break/>

...condemned a man to the same punishment for gathering a few small sticks of wood on the Sabbath day, and thus placed that act somewhat on par with blasphemy, is something that is amazing, and of which one does not see the reason immediately, although one must always remain certain of the justice of the matter, because God, who is the supreme Holiness, can never do anything but what is righteous. Meanwhile, it is not impossible to understand immediately, regarding the equality of the crimes, that it is not always by the equality of the punishments that one should judge them. Every day people are put to death on a gallows for very unequal matters, namely a thief, a murderer, and a hundred other wretches whose crimes are much greater in one than in the other. Often this depends on the insights which the wise and prudent Legislators had, to establish punishments for the smallest crimes that suit the most gruesome undertakings: And since God dealt with the Hebrews in the capacity of their particular, and so to speak, temporal Legislator, He also pronounced such sentences on certain cases, which do not always need to be followed for all times, nor for all places, nor for all peoples, because He pronounced them out of particular insights, specifically suiting the capacity of the temporal Legislator of the Jews. In that respect, then, He could command such a death against the violator of the Sabbath as pleased Him, without one being allowed to conclude therefrom that in all cases where the same punishment is commanded, there is also an equality of crimes. One must furthermore note that the Sabbath day, having become the actual sign and mark of the legal Covenant through God’s express institution, could not be profaned by the Jews without them making themselves violators of the Covenant itself. This is why the Prophet Ezekiel spoke to the Jews of his time about the profanation of the Sabbath as a crime that concerned the entire Covenant, and for which God had delivered them to their enemies and transported them to Babylon. From this perspective then, and for several other reasons which would be too long to trace here, the violator of the Sabbath was judged with the utmost severity and doomed to be stoned to death.

After he had recovered from his consternation, and his first movements of sorrow and heartache had given way to the necessity in which he found himself to answer these conspirators, he told them that the next morning they should all present themselves before the door of the Tabernacle, each with his censer, to see there who it would be that God would choose for the Priesthood. Such a gentle and wise conversation should have caused Korah and the Levites of his following to withdraw from the rebellion and ambition to which envy had driven them: but these demonstrations made no impression on their minds, and they went away from Moses with the same feelings and the same passions with which they had come.

The night, which is a fitting time for reflection, then came on, as if to provide them with a means to reconsider and come to a deep inner reflection of themselves; but they thought of nothing except to dispute the Priesthood with Aaron the following day. Morning having come, they each took a censer and incense to make it smoke before the entrance of the Tabernacle alongside Aaron, and subsequently to hear what God would command concerning it. Jesus Christ, in the third chapter of John's Gospel, explained the mystery of this serpent, which produced such miraculous effects, and told us that this prototype looked to him, and that it had been a foreshadowing of his exaltation on the cross for the salvation of all men, who, feeling the deadly wounds of sin, came to behold him with the eyes of faith on that cross, where he triumphed over the powers of Hell, wiped out the curse of sin, and reconciled divine justice: *Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up on a cross; that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.*

These ill-advised nations prepared themselves to dispute their passage. The Amorites were the first who confronted them because their land bordered the desert of Arabia; they held good positions and yielded to no other nations of that time in courage and bravery. The children of Israel sent emissaries to Sihon, their King, to request that he would allow them to pass freely through his land, upon the assurance they gave him that they would cause no disorder, nor even drink water from his wells. Sihon, listening only to those who breathed suspicion into him, refused the Jews <note>The author uses "Jews" here as a general term for the Israelites.</note> passage, and marched against them with his army to prevent and stop them from entering his lands. The people then defended themselves, and God gave them victory over the Amorites, and made them masters of his entire land within a few days. The King of Bashan <note>This was Og, legendary for his great stature.</note>, neighbor to the Amorites, having the imprudence to follow his example, suffered the same fate as he, and was defeated in a battle where he lost his land along with his life. The defeat of these two Kings brought a great consternation over all the land round about; and Balak, the King of the Moabites, deeming himself already lost like the other two, and seeing that the way of arms had succeeded so poorly for them, took recourse to an extraordinary means: namely, incantations and sorcery. This idolatrous prince expected to draw more help from Hell than from the earth, and from Devils more than from men. Far from his land, and on the bank of the Euphrates, lived a renowned sorcerer named Balaam, to whom he sent messengers with all haste to try and draw him to himself by the power of money, imagining that if he could obtain this man, he would accomplish more through his sorcery and incantations than with a great army. His messengers arrived at Pethor, the city of this Soothsayer in Mesopotamia; they delivered their message to him and made him very advantageous offers. Balaam requested time until the next day before he would give these emissaries a proper answer. God appeared to him in the night and forbade him to go to the King of Moab. He said as much to the messengers, who were thereafter necessitated to return without having been able to obtain anything from him. This troubled Balak greatly, for all his hope was in the sorcery of this Conjurer. However, he did not allow himself to be turned away by the first refusal, but sent other persons to Balaam with orders to make every possible plea to him and to promise him great riches to oblige him to come. These new emissaries neglected nothing they could think of that might be capable of persuading Balaam; and while they spoke very highly of the reward he could expect from the generosity of a King who sought him with such zeal, this man answered them with such expressions as seemed to show that he had a soul far too elevated to heed his own interest; and yet, therein he betrayed his own heart; for a certain Apostle <note>A reference to 2 Peter 2:15, which states that Balaam "loved the wages of unrighteousness."</note> said of him that he loved the reward of unrighteousness: but self-interest is such a cowardly and shameful passion that one dares not let it show, even in those actions where

<column-break/>
