God appeared to him in the night, just as the first time, and seeing in the heart of this false Prophet the secret desire he had to grant the King of Moab his request so that he might receive gifts, He delivered him over to his greed and allowed him to set out on his way, because He intended to use that man in matters that would be very glorious and renowned for God’s people. Balaam wished for nothing more than to be allowed to go to the King of Moab; he then gave his answer to the prince's messengers the next morning, and without any delay they departed together and took the road to Moab. The false Prophet was seated on a female donkey, the usual transport of those Eastern lands, especially in ancient times before excess and vanity had introduced the custom of having a great retinue; but it happened that his donkey, startled, suddenly swerved from the path without Balaam knowing the cause of it, or it being possible for him to make the donkey turn and proceed again. While he struck her vigorously to force her, he found himself in a narrow passage, lined on both sides with a wall that fenced off the vineyards that were in that place. The donkey meanwhile pressed with such force against one of those walls that she crushed and injured Balaam’s foot; he thereupon doubled his blows, and the donkey, instead of going forward, went to lie down on her belly. At that moment, God, by His omnipotence, formed speech upon the tongue and lips of this animal. The donkey spoke to the false Prophet, and after she had begun to speak to him, God opened Balaam’s eyes so that he saw an Angel with a drawn sword in his hand standing before him. It was this sight that had so terrified the donkey, and which likewise terrified the false Prophet. This Angel made Balaam realize that God saw well with what intent he had undertaken this journey—namely, out of a desire to enrich himself and, if possible, to do that which Balak requested of him. Balaam then wanted to turn back, loving his life even more than gifts; but the Angel commanded him to continue his journey, but to take great care that he spoke nothing except that which God should command him when he arrived in the land of the Moabites: thus Balaam continued his way.

Balak, meanwhile, waited with impatience for the arrival of Balaam, and having heard that he was on his way, he went to meet him to enter into conversation about matters he had to tell him, and to request all the help of his art in the danger that threatened him. This King testified by sacrifices and feasts the joy he had over the arrival of this supposed Prophet, and subsequently he brought him to a mountain from which one could see the Israelites, who were encamped some distance away. The prophet answered him boldly: "Shall I not take care to speak that which the LORD has put in my mouth?"

Balak, however, did not yet lose all hope of being able to have the people of Israel cursed by this hired prophet: He imagined that the place where he had led him was not entirely suitable for his purpose, because from there Balaam could see only a part of the army of the Hebrews. Behold, I have received a command to bless; since he blesses, I shall not reverse it..... There is no sorcery against Jacob, nor divination against Israel. Behold, this people shall rise up as an old lion, and it shall lift itself up as a young lion; it shall not lie down until it has eaten the prey, and drunk the blood of the slain.* Balak, stunned at hearing such language from the mouth of someone whom he had brought from so far, and in whom he had placed so much trust, entreated him that since he would not curse Israel, he should at least by no means bless them. But the prophet stood his ground and answered Balak once more, that he would say nothing but what the Lord commanded him to speak. This wretched prince, consumed no less by grief than by superstition, wished to try once more whether he might have better luck by bringing Balaam to a third mountain than on the first two. They used the same ceremony there of seven altars and such offerings as before; but all this served for nothing but to shame the Moabites, and to take away from them all hope that they could load with curses a people whom God protected, and whom he wished to overwhelm with blessings. Balaam himself dared no more to step aside as on the previous occasions to receive an answer from God; but filled and enraptured by an extraordinary inspiration, with which God wished to honor him to put the King of Moab all the more to shame, and to leave to the Church one of the greatest oracles that were ever spoken in favor of that ancient people, he said on that occasion things that have been a rich subject of reflection and exercise for the Jews, and still serve for the wonder and instruction of all Christians. This prophet, having thus served God's purpose against his own intention, departed to return again to his land; but the Hebrews, having fallen upon him in the land of Midian, from which he had not departed, took his life.

...last year on Mount Hor, and toward the end of the same year Moses laid his life down into God’s hands on Mount Nebo. The cause of the death of these two famous leaders of the Jews was a kind of doubt which they had in that year: whether God would once again bring water out of a rock for this ungrateful and rebellious nation, as he had done in the first year after the exodus from Egypt. The people found themselves in the wilderness of Kadesh, after the death of Miriam, without water; they made their complaints, according to their custom (as one sees in the twentieth chapter of <term>Numbers</term><note>The fourth book of the Bible, called "Numeri" in the original text, which contains the census and desert travels of the Israelites.</note>), against God and his two servants. God commanded them that they should speak to a rock that was in that place so that it would give out water; but they, fearing that their word would not be powerful enough to work such a great miracle upon the rock, did not dare to persist in speaking to it. They believed that to execute it better, they must use the same staff with which they had formerly struck the rock of Horeb. Moses and Aaron then took their usual staff together without an explicit command from God, and coming to the rock of Kadesh in the presence of the entire assembly, Moses, who had this fateful staff in his hand, struck the rock with it; and it was not until after the second blow, which immediately followed the first, that the water flowed out. God immediately expressed grievances over this, which made known how troubled he was by the mistrust these two ministers had shown. He reproached them that they had not shown proper reverence for his word and had been unbelieving:

> Because you, he said, did not believe me, to hallow me in the eyes of the children of Israel, therefore you shall not bring this assembly into the land which I have given them.

This was the sentence pronounced against the two holiest and most zealous servants God ever had in the world, which ought to fill with awe all those whom he does the honor of using in the service of his house. Aaron died first, possibly because he was the more guilty, and

<column-break/>

perhaps also for secret reasons which are not indicated in that place. Moses followed him not long after, and he was commanded by God to climb Mount Nebo, in the land of Moab, from where he could behold the greatest part of the land of Canaan—from the Jordan, which was close to that mountain, to Mount Lebanon, which was opposite it at the far end. "This is the land," the Lord said to him, "that I swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, saying: I will give it to your seed. I have caused you to see it with your eyes, but you shall not cross over there." Thereupon Moses closed his eyes, having nothing more to see in the world, after he had cast his gaze over this so desired and long-awaited land; and at that moment God separated his soul from this body of dust, to have it enter into his rest and into the possession of the heavenly and blessed Canaan, of which the other was but an imperfect image. The Prophet—whether it be the Priest Eleazar or Joshua—who described the death of Moses at the end of <term>Deuteronomy</term><note>The fifth book of the Bible; the original text uses the Latin name "Deuteronomium."</note>, suggests that God did the body of that prophet this special honor, that he buried it himself in a valley of that mountain, whether he used the service of angels for that purpose, or did it himself immediately through his omnipotence. However it may have been, the place where Moses was buried has never been known, and no man has ever been able to find his body nor his grave. One might think that God did this to deprive the children of Israel of the opportunity to make any object of idolatry from the body of this holy prophet, were it not known that this people never showed any inclination for such superstitions, even at the time when they were most given over to idolatry. But nevertheless, if it was for that reason that God hid the body of Moses, he has therein given us a lesson: that we must never show such honor to the dust and bones of even the greatest saints that tastes of superstition or leans toward the worship of idols.

All the people were very grieved over the death of Moses; each mourned him as his father, and together they lamented him as their general Redeemer and Protector. For an entire month in the camp, they did nothing but speak of the greatness of this loss, and made all the complaints that the bitterest grief is able to draw from the mouths of persons whose whole hearts are full of it. The usual mourning was seven days, but that of Moses was thirty, just as Aaron’s had been; and it ought to have been as long for Israel as the lives of all the people whom they both had led and protected for forty years, if it were to have any proportion to the merit of those two so excel-

After the memory of Moses had thus been shown the honor it was due, Joshua, who followed him in the government, thought of nothing else but completing the great work that Moses had left unfinished. He began this by sending men across the Jordan to spy out the land. Prudence does not permit one to enter an unknown land without first having taken all precautions possible to avoid falling into snares from which one could not rescue oneself. The children of Israel, it is true, marched under the eyes of God, and they were assured of his protection; but the same God who led them, and who always had his eye upon them as the most precious object he had in the world, is a wise God, who wills that all our deeds and our steps should also be so [wise], and who leaves the imprudent and reckless to the disorder of their own minds and thoughts. ...various places of the land, could more easily have given rise to some suspicion among peoples who were little used to seeing strangers travel through their land, and who were already all too much filled with distrust. The report of the miracles which God had performed in Egypt for the children of Israel had reached their ears long ago, and they had often heard tell of the victories which that people had achieved over the Kings of the Amorites, of Bashan, and of Moab, their neighbors. Terror spread through Canaan with that news, and the fear—which was all too well-founded—of suffering the same fate made them suspicious and distrustful toward all unknown people they saw. The two messengers sent by Joshua then departed secretly from the plains of Moab and crossed the Jordan. The first city they encountered on their way was Jericho; they had orders to spy out that place especially, because it being the closest to the Jordan, it would not have been prudent to leave it behind and travel inland; for that would have been the way to quickly find themselves surrounded on all sides and enclosed among the peoples of Canaan. These men fully acquitted themselves of their duty: after they had surveyed the fields, they entered the city and went to spend the night in a house where they were told that strangers were lodged; for the use of inns <note>The author notes that public houses of lodging were a relatively new development; in the era of the Patriarchs like Abraham, travelers typically relied on private hospitality.</note>, which three hundred years before, and in the time of the Patriarchs, seems to have been unknown, was not yet very common. It

<column-break/>

was noticed in Jericho that two strangers had come, and people immediately ran to the inn to look for them there. The woman of the house, named Rahab, being moved by a movement of God’s Spirit which enlightened her mind and touched her heart, concerned herself with the preservation of these two Israelites: she hid them on the roof under the <term>stalks of flax</term><note>original: "vlaſtóppelen". Flax was laid out on flat roofs to dry before being processed into linen.</note>, and said to those who had come to look for them that they had already left and gone out through the gate. God, who draws good from evil, saved Joshua's two spies through the lie of this woman, just as he had formerly saved a great number of the male children of the Hebrews in Egypt through the helpful lies of the midwives, whom Pharaoh had commanded to smother those little children. But what God allows to happen, and what succeeds well in the world because he directs it as it pleases him, ought not to serve as an example for us when it does not agree with his Law, which alone must be the rule of our actions. Joshua's spies promised Rahab that they would recognize the favor she showed them, and after having agreed with her upon the sign by which her house could be distinguished—which was to tie a scarlet cord to the window so that she might be spared during the taking of Jericho—she let them down at night with a rope through the window, so that they came down to the city wall, upon which Rahab's house was built; and while the people of Jericho sought them on one path, they escaped on another, and returned safely to their camp.

the state of the place. They recounted above all other things what an astonishment and terror they had perceived among the inhabitants, and they took as a certain omen of their victory the fear which those peoples showed, appearing unable to defend themselves behind their walls and bulwarks against the children of Israel. Joshua understood from the account which his spies gave him, that God through His providence was preparing a victory for him against the <term>Canaanites<note>The various ancient Semitic-speaking peoples inhabiting the region of Canaan before the arrival of the Israelites.</note></term>, which would not cost him dearly, and which was to pave the way for much greater conquests. As a wise man, he then wished to make use of the zeal which this news had ignited in the hearts of the Hebrews; and to that end, he gave orders that they should prepare to break camp within three days and march toward the Jordan. The city of Jericho lay on the opposite side, and the river was then very deep and wide, such that it was impossible to ford it. There was no bridge, and the art of building boats in haste was still little known in those times, when navigation was not yet nearly as common as it later became. But the people of Israel were accustomed to <term>miracles<note>Acts of divine intervention that bypass the laws of nature.</note></term>, and had often witnessed those great deeds of Heaven in their favor whenever the strength and industry of man were found too weak. Departing from Egypt, they had seen the sea open before them, offering them a wide path over the sand where the rays of the sun had never been able to penetrate. The past assured them of the future, and they did not doubt that what God had done for them through the service of Moses at the Red Sea, He would also do at the river by means of Joshua, who was appointed and chosen by God to follow Moses in leadership. Joshua, full of confidence in 그at good and mighty hand which had placed him over the Israelites, and assured by a revelation from Heaven,

<column-break/>

that *God would be with him, just as He had been with Moses*, and that He would cover him with honor on that day, immediately gave all the necessary orders to have that great multitude of men, women, animals, and baggage march straight toward the Jordan. He commanded the Priests to take the <term>Ark of the Covenant<note>A gold-covered wooden chest described in the Book of Exodus as containing the two stone tablets of the Ten Commandments.</note></term> and to go forward with that illustrious sign of God’s presence; and all the people were ordered to follow him according to the rank of their tribes, yet leaving out of reverence a space of two thousand paces between themselves and the Ark. Coming to the bank of the river, the Priests boldly set their feet upon the water, whereupon the waters of the Jordan immediately parted from one bank to the other; those coming from above stood still, and those from below, continuing their course as before, seemed to flee before the Ark, thus leaving their dry sands uncovered to make a new path for God's people. The Priests stood still to hold these heaped-up waters in awe, which, flowing down with a strong current, gradually felt their course slacken and finally could proceed no further, until the invisible dike that restrained them was removed. When the entire multitude had crossed over, Joshua commanded twelve men, one from each Tribe, to gather twelve large stones in the Jordan where the Ark had remained, and to set them up at the place in the river where the Priests who bore the Ark had stood still, as a monument to that miracle. Thereupon the Priests stepped forward, and as soon as they reached the bank, the waters of the Jordan rushed down upon the sands which had remained uncovered then for the first time, and these newly heaped-up mountains of water suddenly became level and resumed their usual course.

### ->*The Commander of the LORD’S army appears to Joshua.*<-

### Joshua Chapter V. verses 13, 14, 15.

<margin>The forty-first year after the exodus from Egypt.</margin>
The people crossed over the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month, exactly forty years less four days after the exodus from Egypt, which had occurred on the night of the fourteenth of that same month. Since that time, they had not circumcised any of their children, for fear that they might die from the pain of the cutting, which, because it had to be performed on the eighth day after birth, would have befallen a great number of them when they had to break camp, or when they were on the way between the mountains and other very rough passages. But after they had completed that very long and difficult journey, God commanded them to resume the practice of <term>circumcision<note>A ritual surgical removal of the foreskin, serving as a sign of the covenant between God and the Israelites.</note></term>, which had been suspended for forty years; and after crossing the Jordan, Joshua had all the men and male children of Israel who had been born after the exodus from Egypt circumcised. The place where this general circumcision of the Israelites took place was called <term>Gilgal<note>original: "Gilgal"</note></term>, which means "rolling," because Joshua said that on that day he had rolled away the reproach of Egypt from them. Four days later they held the <term>Passover<note>original: "Paassche" — the Jewish festival commemorating the liberation from Egypt.</note></term>, which in all likelihood was the first time they had celebrated it since they held it in Egypt on that night when they departed. The following day after Passover, they harvested the grain in the fields of Jericho, which was beginning to ripen, and immediately made cakes and unleavened bread from it. After they began to eat the fruits of the land of Canaan, the <term>Manna<note>The miraculous food provided by God to the Israelites during their forty years in the desert.</note></term>, which had fallen from Heaven every morning around their camp without fail—except only on the Sabbath day—ever since the second month of their exodus from Egypt, ceased entirely; for the people found enough to feed themselves, and God performs no miracles without necessity.

<column-break/>

After Joshua had devoted his first efforts to these duties of religion and piety, and after he had sanctified the entry of the Israelites into the land of Canaan through circumcision and the Passover, he turned all his thoughts to what was most necessary for him to do to make them masters of it. He then decided to undertake the siege of Jericho; they were encamped on the plain of that city, and it was advisable to make use of the consternation and terror into which the miraculous crossing of the Jordan had brought all the peoples of Canaan, and especially those of Jericho, which city found itself first exposed to the arms of the children of Israel. While Joshua thought on these things, and as he began to design the siege of that place, he had a vision which filled him with joy and a firm confidence. There came a man to him with a sword in his hand; Joshua thereupon approached and said with a bold and unhesitating voice: *Are you for us, or for our enemies?* No, answered the man, I am not of the enemies, but I am the *Commander of the army of the LORD*. There was no other Chief than Joshua, and God Himself who had given him that office. But a secret inspiration and an internal enlightenment of the Holy Spirit made Joshua recognize the one who thus spoke to him; so much so that he did not doubt that it was the Son of God Himself, who appeared to him in a vision under a human form, which He was one day truly to assume through the <term>Incarnation<note>The Christian doctrine that God became flesh in the person of Jesus Christ.</note></term>. He then immediately threw himself with his face to the earth, and with a humility of mind that was even greater and deeper than the prostration of his body, *What speaks my Lord,* he said, *to his servant!* Thereupon the *Commander of the army of the Lord* commanded him to take off his shoes, just as He had formerly commanded Moses at the burning bush;

## The Conquest of Jericho.

### Joshua Chapter VI. verses 20, 21.

<margin>The same year.</margin>
The inhabitants of Jericho, having seen their land covered with military bands for several days, expected a siege at any moment. All their hope of escape was placed in the height and strength of their walls, within which they kept themselves shut up, without letting any person go out, while their enemies, being masters of the field, mowed their corn and prepared themselves at their leisure to undertake the siege of that city. The method of storming places was still little known at that time, and it was enough to make a city almost invincible, or to keep an army before it for years, if it had thick and very high walls. Those of Jericho were both one and the other, being moreover guarded by a people who, placing all their hope therein, appeared in arms atop those walls to make them inaccessible to the enemy. But according to the manner in which Joshua began to besiege them, they did not need to throw a javelin or shoot a single arrow, for he kept himself with all his people beyond the reach of the bow, and the children of Israel on their part did not shoot a single arrow; so that one would have said they were there only to look at one another,

<column-break/>

the one to behold the high walls, occupied by weapons and covered with men; and the other to see a people who, having come from afar, occupied all their fields. What increased the strangeness of this spectacle for the people of Jericho was the movement which Joshua caused to be made around the city, at a distance that they could only reach with their sight. The entire army marched in battle order; after them came seven Priests, each having a trumpet in his hand, upon which they blew from time to time: they were followed by a small number of other Priests who carried the Ark of the Covenant, and an innumerable multitude of people came after them. Thus they went around the city, and this ceremony lasted six days in a row; they also continued with it on the seventh day, but instead of making only one circuit as on the other days, they made a circuit seven times without ceasing on that day, and always in the same manner. But when they had finished the last circuit, the Priests together made their trumpets sound, and all the people, who until that time had kept silent, made a great shout of joy and victory at that moment. This was the sign which God had given for the conquest of Jericho; and at the same time the walls, which were so strong and so firm, were cast down upon their foundations, and the city being open on all sides became a prey to the Israelites. They ran toward it in a crowd with weapons in hand; no one re-

God even did her the honor that He ordained her to be a mother of the *Messiah*, who after a long series of generations was born into a household descended from the marriage of *Rahab* with an *Israelite* from the Tribe of *Judah*, named *Salmon*, great-grandfather of *Jesse* <note>original: "Isaï"</note>, *David's* father.

### The punishment of Achan.

->*Joshua Chapter VII. verses 24, 25.*<-

<margin>

Nothing could better demonstrate how great God's wrath against *Jericho* was, than the strict commands which He had given to *Joshua* and all the people of *Israel*, to spare neither man nor beast, but to raze it to the ground, and to bury all that was precious and beautiful among the riches of that city in her ruins. It seemed as if all those things had previously made war against God, and that on this day of vengeance they were so burdened by His curse, that one could not keep a single one of them without dragging the curse along with oneself. God had reasons for all this which we ought to adore with a respectful silence, and which generally show us how terrible the stain of sin must be in His eyes, since it extends somewhat to everything that comes near the guilty, and that has any similarity or connection with him. The commands of God were made known to all the people, and *Joshua* gave

<column-break/>

a public command to all the *Israelites*, not to keep the very least thing of all the most precious and beautiful that they found in the city. It was a great temptation for the greed of victorious military bands, and even greater for troops who carried women and children with them, and who for forty years had been camped in dry deserts, that upon the first conquest of a land, for whose possession they had so long yearned, they might not take a single piece of gold or silver, or anything similar that was found in abundance under the hand of the soldier in the taking of such a rich city, without bringing themselves under the curse, and exposing themselves to the wrath of Heaven. But God wanted to curb in time the covetousness of a people, who were already all too earthly-minded <note>The original "aardich" here implies a focus on worldly or material goods rather than its modern meaning of "kind" or "pleasant".</note>, and to teach them that their true wealth would consist in the obedience which they showed to God. These commands were then followed, and the soldier, as well as his Commanders, showed a selflessness that one must wonder at in such a great multitude of people. *Joshua*, full of comfort and hope after such a happy success, moved from *Jericho*

...to *Ai*, a small city that lay not far off, and was called *Ai*. And this Commander of the Hebrews, not wishing to exhaust his troops in the siege of a place that, as he believed, could not offer much resistance, contented himself with sending only three thousand men from his army to capture it. But these three thousand men were beaten, and everyone who could save his life came fleeing to *Joshua*, bringing him the news of their defeat. This holy man was no less saddened than astonished; he sighed before God, and with a sensitivity that had no equal, he set before Him his distress and fear for this poor people, who would soon be destroyed by the Canaanites if God thus gave them over to the sword of the enemy. He found that God, since the capture of Jericho, had become angry with His people; however, not knowing the cause, the Lord told him that it was because someone had taken and kept some of the spoils of that city against His prohibition. *Joshua*, highly amazed at this, at the same time had all the Tribes draw lots, and it was found that this crime had been committed in the Tribe of *Judah*. This Tribe was set apart, and all its families were made to cast lots; thus coming from family to family, the lot fell upon a man named *Achan*. The man was seized, *Joshua* questioned him, and he confessed that among the spoils he had seen an elegant Babylonian cloak, two hundred shekels <note>original: "fikelen"</note> of silver, and a golden bar that

<column-break/>

weighed fifty shekels, and having seen these, had taken all this and hidden it under the earth in his tent. They ran to the place he had named and found there the deadly booty that had stirred God’s wrath against His people. *Achan* was condemned to be stoned immediately along with his children, who perhaps had some knowledge of their father's robbery, or who were guilty of other sins—for who is innocent of such? And God willed, to make *Achan's* punishment more remarkable, that his sons and daughters, whom He had spared until that time, should lose their lives alongside him, and be overwhelmed with stones together. All the beasts belonging to that wretched household were likewise put to death, and the bodies of *Achan* and his children were not removed from under the stones except to be burned and consumed to ashes. A great heap of stones was raised over those ashes to serve as a fearsome monument for posterity of God's wrath against the lust and greed of men, who, to satisfy this criminal passion, sacrifice the reverence and obedience they owe to His laws. God's wrath was appeased by the sentence carried out on *Achan*, and the people received grace again. *Joshua* had the city of *Ai* attacked for the second time, and having lured its inhabitants into an ambush <note>original: "laage"</note>, he hewed them to pieces, burned their city, and had their King hanged.

...to protect themselves from his weapons, they took recourse to a ruse that succeeded for them. They sent some of their people to him, who, pretending to be from distant lands, said that they had come to him upon hearing the report of what God had done for the people of Israel in the kingdoms of the Amorites, of Heshbon, and of Bashan, and in the crossing of the Jordan, in order to make a covenant with that people. And to give more credence to what they said—that they had come from very distant places—they had put on worn-out clothes and old shoes when leaving home, and had taken with them hard and moldy bread, as well as torn and patched leather skins to hold their wine. They said that their long journey was the cause of all this, and through this trickery and a feigned simplicity, they deceived Joshua, who, believing their words, entered into a covenant with them and promised by oath to let them live. Three days later, he learned that he had been deceived, and that it was the people of a city in that region who had come to surprise him. He was troubled by it, as were all the people with him; but the holiness of the oath, which Joshua and all the leaders of Israel had sworn to them, prevented them from being exterminated like those of Ai and Jericho. This oath was made based on a false declaration and was extorted through pure deception; but at that time, oaths were kept very strictly, and those loose moral lessons <note>A reference to the theological concept of "mental reservation" or "equivocation," which the author suggests was a later, less honorable development in ethics.</note>, which one turns and twists as one pleases and whose pronouncement is based on self-interest, were not yet known. Thus, the Gibeonites were allowed to live, and the only punishment they received for their deception was to be made slaves of the Jews, and to be made into hewers of wood and drawers of water <note>original: "houthouwers en waterputters"</note>. They received this sentence as a favor and submitted themselves willingly to it, both for themselves and for their descendants.

The covenant of peace that the Gibeonites made with the children of Israel caused suspicion among the kings of the other cities of Canaan, who saw that Joshua, through this treaty, suddenly gained a strong foothold in their territories; and that being master of the city of Gibeon, which was very prominent, and of several others belonging to it, he could easily enter their lands from there and besiege their cities. Adoni-zedek, King of Jerusalem, was one of those who took the greatest notice of all these things: He was one of the mightiest of that land, and he had no trouble forming an alliance with four other kings, his neighboring princes, for their common protection. These five Canaanite kings merged their forces into one and went to besiege the city of Gibeon. The Gibeonites immediately brought news of this to Joshua, who had retreated with his army to Gilgal, in the plain of Jericho, where he had left the women, children, and a portion of the people, so as not to exhaust them through the constant marches while he waged war. Joshua immediately set out with a portion of his troops and marched toward Gibeon. The enemies were encamped there and had expected nothing less than to see an army coming to attack them within such a short time. The disorder among them was great, and Joshua struck them with such courage and bravery that they could not recover. They then took flight; Joshua pursued them vigorously, and Heaven helped him to overtake the fleeing men, causing a heavy hail to fall on the road to slow their pace, which wounded them and struck them to the 

<column-break/>

earth, while they hurried to escape the sword of the victor. Meanwhile, the day was declining, and the approaching night threatened to hide the fleeing Canaanites from the hot zeal of the Israelites, who did not cease their pursuit. But Joshua, who fought for God and who conquered only through God's help, emboldened himself through a rapture of the Holy Spirit that encouraged him to command the Sun to stand still, so that he might carry away a complete victory: *Sun*, he said, *stand still at Gibeon; and you, Moon, in the valley of Ajalon*. At this word, the Sun stood still, as if to remain a spectator longer of the bravery and victory of God's people. The Moon remained immovable, and by an entirely new miracle, the order of day and night was found altered for several hours. Israel finished its conquest, and the five kings did not escape his victory except under the protection of a cave, into which they all went in the hope of saving their lives there. Joshua was informed of it while he continued to pursue the remnant of their defeated army: He commanded that large stones be rolled before the entrance of that hole, and that people be left there to guard them well. Upon his return, the five Canaanite kings were brought before him; he displayed them to all the principal commanders of his army, who, at his command, all placed their feet upon their necks, while he told them that God would grant them the favor of seeing the rest of their enemies thus under their feet. He then put the kings to death, and so that all the people might have the comfort of seeing the vengeance that God had taken upon these princes who had conspired against Him, he had them fastened to gallows <note>original: "mikken"</note>, where they hung until evening.

It had always been free to all believers to build altars to God in whatever place in the world they found themselves, until God had forbidden His people to offer him any sacrifices anywhere else but in the Tabernacle, on the copper altar that stood in one of its forecourts. But in the time of Joshua, a matter occurred that almost ignited a great war over this and would have been the beginning of a deadly schism. Two whole tribes and a half <note>Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh.</note> had taken possession of the land of the Amorites and that of Bashan, situated on this side of the Jordan, and had settled there during the lifetime of Moses, while the others sought dwelling places on the other side of that river, in the land of the Canaanites, which corresponded to their great number. To that end, it was necessary to fight the inhabitants of all those lands and wage a long and bloody war with them. Their brothers assisted them in this, according to the agreement made between them for that purpose, and the Scripture gives them the testimony that they performed their duty excellently and that they fought for the interest of the nine tribes as if it had been for themselves. When they no longer needed their help and saw themselves masters of the land of Canaan, Joshua publicly declared to the bands of these two tribes—which were those of Reuben and Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh—that he was very well satisfied with the zeal and bravery they had shown throughout the entire course of that war; and after having recommended them to always remain faithful to God and to strictly observe the laws of Moses, he gave them his bless-

Not long after, a rumor reached the children of Israel who lived in the land of Canaan, that the Reubenites and Gadites, with that part of the tribe of Manasseh which had its portion alongside them in the land of the Amorites, had built an altar of an immense size on their own territory, bordering the Jordan. This novelty was immediately perceived as an undertaking of very dangerous consequence, and as a sign of a split <note>The Hebrew word used in the Bible for this split often implies a religious rebellion or apostasy.</note> in both Religion and the State. The idolaters also built altars of an excessive height, and it is even believed that it was in opposition to that custom that God had forbidden in His Law the building of such a high altar to Him, so that one could not perform service upon it except by climbing up to it by high steps. It greatly troubled the Tribes of Israel to learn that their brothers had built such an altar, and being zealous for the honor of Religion, which they believed to be greatly offended by that act, they made themselves ready to avenge it by force of arms. When they were ready to march against those Tribes to tear down that suspicious altar, it was advised first to see if the matter could not be accomplished through a friendly representation and gentle means. Phinehas, son of Eleazar the High Priest, was chosen by all the assembled Tribes to express their complaint to the Reubenites, and the children of Gad and Manasseh, along with ten of their most prominent and distinguished leaders. Phinehas then departed with haste, accompanied

<column-break/>

by one of the Princes from each tribe, and the eleven of them crossed the Jordan and arrived in the land of the Reubenites. They made known to them the cause of their embassy, and made their complaint in the name of the ten other Tribes regarding this action, which seemed so irregular to them, and which they believed would be ruinous for Religion and the State. The Reubenites and the others who had sided with them listened to these complaints with great modesty and prudence, and took God as their witness that their intention had in no way been to offer any burnt offering, sacrifice, or grain offering on that altar. Rather, they only intended for it to be a monument <note>In the biblical text, this altar is named "Ed," meaning "Witness."</note> of their unity with the other Tribes of Israel in the service they performed to God on the altar of the Tabernacle, which they acknowledged to be the only one upon which one might lawfully offer sacrifices. Upon this, some powerful and heart-stirring speeches followed on both sides; and the Envoys of the Tribes, being completely satisfied with the godly answer of the Reubenites and Gadites, returned with this good news to Shiloh, where all the people awaited them, ready to march at the first command to fight their brothers. Everyone praised God that a matter, which could have had such deadly consequences for the entire nation, was so happily settled in its infancy through the wisdom and zeal of Phinehas; everyone departed well satisfied with the prudent conduct of the children of Ruben, Gad, and Manasseh, and the friendship and unity increased more and more among the twelve Tribes of Israel.

In six years, he conquered the largest part of Palestine and defeated thirty-one kings, each of whom—either individually or several at once—came to fight him and dispute his entry into their lands, or awaited him behind the walls of their cities. It is true, they were kings who ruled over only a small territory, yet they were kings nonetheless who fought for their altars, for their freedom, and for their lives; and they were attacked by bands of foreigners who had no precise knowledge of the places, and who, once beaten and cut down, had no allies <note>The text highlights the precarious position of the Israelites as invaders: a single defeat could have been total without divine aid.</note> nor places to retreat to against an unfortunate outcome and recover their strength. But God wished to show the Israelites, in those first six years of victories and triumphs, how much they ought to honor that mighty hand which could strike them down as easily as it had raised them up, should they make themselves unworthy of His protection. Now, to put the faithfulness of the Hebrews to the test and to keep them in a state of holy humility, God halted the rapid course of their conquests; and although Joshua lived ten full years after the first six which had been so glorious, the remainder of Palestine was not subjected to the Israelites, who still saw the Canaanite as master of his land and cities in many places. Joshua, nevertheless, made a division among the tribes of Israel of both the lands that were already conquered and those which were not yet, out of a certainty that they would all one day be captured, so that each Tribe might then know what portion of the lands and cities of Palestine would belong to it. But the greatest and most remarkable thing this holy man did in his entire life was the covenant which he desired all the people to solemnly renew with God shortly before his death. Many times he had perceived in this people a great inclination toward idolatry; that of the golden calf, of which he had been a witness alongside Moses, was not the only instance of which the Hebrews were guilty: they had since that time offered to Baal-Peor <note>A localized form of the god Baal worshipped by the Moabites.</note> and other idols, and Joshua feared that henceforth, being mingled among the rest of the Canaanites, or in great proximity to the Philistines and other idolatrous peoples, they would gradually accustom themselves to their superstitions and mix the service of their idols with that of the God of Israel—the strong and jealous God, who alone wishes to be worshipped because there is no one but He alone who deserves the adoration of the creature. **The loss** that the people suffered through the death of Joshua was not compensated for, as the death of Moses had been, by a successor who held the government over all the Tribes of Israel. Each Tribe had its own particular leaders, but there was not one

<column-break/>

tentions, Joshua called all the Tribes of Israel together. After presenting to them in few words the invaluable grace and favors which God had shown them since the day He called Abraham out of the land of the Chaldeans until the time He placed them in possession of Canaan, he asked them whether they would not swear that they would faithfully maintain the covenant which God had first made with their ancestors—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—and afterwards with themselves on Mount Sinai. The words of Joshua, with which he ended his speech in this place, are of a very singular emphasis, and indicate that in that sublime soul there was a certain concern and zeal for God's interests, at which one cannot marvel enough, nor present sufficiently for imitation. *If it be evil in your eyes*, he said, *to serve the LORD, choose you this day whom you will serve, whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the river Euphrates, or the gods of the Amorites in whose land you dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.* This great example, presented with all the zeal and power that the most vigilant godliness can add to words, drew the hearts of the Israelites; they all answered Joshua that they were of the same mind as he, and that they wished to serve no other gods than the God of their fathers. Joshua received this declaration with joy, and to make it more binding and credible, he commanded them—as Jacob had formerly done to his entire household when he departed from Shechem—that they should put away all the cast idols which were to be found among them. The people answered these words with new protestations that they wished to serve no other God than the LORD. Thus Joshua renewed God’s covenant with the people, and he wrote all these things in a book in which the Law of the Lord was also written; and according to the custom of that time, he set up a large stone under an oak tree that stood near the Tabernacle <note>The portable sanctuary used by the Israelites.</note>, to serve as a memorial of that covenant. Subsequently, he dismissed the entire assembly and died not long after at the age of one hundred and ten years, well satisfied that he left a people, whom he had seen wandering for forty years from one desert to another, as masters of the land of Canaan; and even more so that he had settled down in peace with his fathers, and was now about to enjoy a rest in Heaven, of which this rest into which he had led the children of Israel was but an imperfect reflection.

The first war they waged, in the same year that Joshua had died, was with a certain Canaanite King named Adoni-Bezek; this name signifies in the Hebrew language *Lord of Bezek*; but whether Bezek was the name of a city, or that of a particular region, is something that one cannot well say, and the knowledge of which can be of little use to us: all that can be said of it with certainty was that the land and the city where Adoni-Bezek reigned had fallen to the tribe of Judah as their portion, in the division which Joshua had made of the land of Canaan. Whether it was that this Tribe began to feel itself in a narrow strait, or that there was some other particular reason to make war upon that Prince, they took a resolution and prepared themselves to combat him. But before entangling themselves in such a great undertaking, they had the wise foresight to ask counsel of God, through the mediation of the High Priest Eleazar, to know if He approved of that war, and which Tribe should march up first and have the supreme command. The High Priest asked God for counsel through the Urim and Thummim <note>The Urim and Thummim were sacred objects—likely stones or lots—fastened to the High Priest’s breastplate and used to determine the divine will in matters of national importance.</note>, for thus it is that all the Commentators understand these words from the first verse in the Book of Judges, *that the children of Israel asked the LORD*. God gave His consent to this war, and named the Tribe of Judah to place itself at the head of the host and to have the command over it. The tribe of Simeon in particular joined with that of Judah in this expedition, which had as good an outcome as one could ever have expected. Adoni-Bezek, informed of the design of the Israelites, had quickly assembled his military bands,

<column-break/>

and because he was a proud and warlike Prince, he judged that he ought not to await the enemy behind the walls, but that it would be much more advantageous for him to march against them and offer them a battle in the open field. The two armies soon found themselves together; they fought on both sides with great bravery: the Canaanite, helped by the Perizzite, marched courageously under the eyes and the leadership of a bellicose King, formerly the terror and scourge of the neighboring Kings, seventy of whom had been forced to bow before him, whom he had made his prisoners; and the Hebrew went to battle, led and supported by the *Lord God of Hosts*. This being noted, it is not difficult to know on whose side the victory was. The Canaanites were before God but as victims which He Himself sacrificed to His vengeance; and the more stubborn they were in the fight, the more the earth was covered with their corpses, and the blood of the Uncircumcised flowed the more strongly under the sword of the Israelite. Ten thousand Canaanites or Perizzites lost their lives in that bloody fight, and Adoni-Bezek, seeing his army hewn to pieces, sought his safety in flight; but they pursued him so closely that he was taken prisoner and brought before Caleb and Othniel, heads of the army. God had commanded His people to show no mercy to the Canaanites; Adoni-Bezek tasted the effect of those strict commands; they cut off the thumbs of his hands and his toes, and this unbeliever found himself forced by the remorse of his conscience to confess that nothing happened to him therein except that which he himself had done to seventy Kings, whom he had conquered and taken prisoner in various wars. Thus God punished him justly for the cruelties which he had committed without reason against Princes who perhaps had been better than he.

The people of Israel did not enjoy rest for long after the victories achieved in the land of Canaan; and though they were successful in the war they waged against Adoni-Bezek, nevertheless that first prosperity soon ended, and their state became very miserable. All that still remained of the Canaanites in various places of Palestine took heart again and turned their weapons against them: from all sides, their lands were invaded, and through frequent raids, their cattle were taken, and their fields devastated. These hostilities lasted until a mighty King, against whom they were powerless to defend themselves, came to wage war in their land to bring them under the yoke. It was Cushan-Rishathaim, who came from deep within Mesopotamia to—without knowing it himself, as he was driven by his own ambition—avenge the contempt the Israelites showed toward God, and to punish them for their idolatry. They sighed and groaned under the servitude of the Syrians, and having repentance for their crimes, God filled Othniel, son of Kenaz and brother of Caleb, with strength and courage through His Spirit, so that he took up arms against the King of Syria and utterly defeated him in a field battle. The Jews were at rest for forty years after that victory, but abusing that long prosperity, they returned again to their first crimes. The North had formerly provided God with a host of Syrians to avenge His cause; and forty years later, the South sent Him the Moabites, who crossed the Jordan and made Judea subservient. To these new masters, it was subject for eighteen years—a long time for a people who had once been the terror of Moab, and who, despite Moab’s opposition, had marched through their lands as they pleased when coming out of Egypt. But then, God was for the Jew; and thereafter, He was for the Moabite. This time, the people again came to a realization of their sins, and no sooner had they converted back to God than God was moved by their oppression and gave them a Savior. It was one named Ehud, from the tribe of Benjamin, of whom the Scripture notes nothing else than that he was left-handed <note>Original: "flinks was." This term refers to being left-handed, which allowed Ehud to hide his weapon where it was not expected.</note>. The children of Israel sent him with several others to pay homage to the King of Moab for their servitude by delivering a gift, and God wished to make use of him to take that King’s life and, through his death, give freedom to the Israelites. Ehud hid a short sword under his cloak, which he had girded on his right

<column-break/>

side, in order to use it with his left hand in the plot he was turning over in his mind. He then departed with the other envoys, and they together brought their gift to Eglon, King of Moab. After having discharged their commission, they set out to return home and crossed the Jordan: but Ehud, leaving the others who were part of the embassy there, took the road back to Moab and, upon arriving at the Court, said that he had something of importance to say to the King. This Prince had him approach and commanded his people to leave. Ehud, finding him in his summer chamber where he had gone to catch the cool air, said to him upon approaching, *I have a word from God for you.* Eglon was an idolatrous Prince, but the God of Israel was at that time so well known to all the neighboring peoples of Egypt and Canaan through the unheard-of miracles He had performed for the Hebrews, that Eglon stood up from his seat or throne out of reverence to hear what Ehud had to say to him. Meanwhile, Ehud drew with his left hand—which he used as if it were his right—the sword he had hidden on his right side and thrust it into Eglon’s belly, which was so thick and fat that, as the fat closed around the blade, he could not pull the sword out. After this deed, he stepped out of the King’s chamber and, locking the door behind him, Eglon’s servants thought their Lord kept the room closed to relieve himself; meanwhile, Ehud found the opportunity to escape and thus returned with haste to Judea. The Jews immediately took up arms and, attacking the Moabites who were in their land, they hewed them to pieces everywhere at the passes and fords of the Jordan while they were hurrying there to cross that flood and return to their own land. Thus were the Hebrews delivered from the oppression of the Moabites. The act of Ehud was very unusual in all its circumstances, but just as one may not take it as an example, so one must not judge it too lightly. Ehud, raised up by God as the Scripture notes, may well have had something to say to Eglon on God’s behalf, and indeed may have said it; but which the holy Writer judged unnecessary to relate to us: and God, who is master of the lives of Kings as well as of other men, might cause the King of Moab to die by Ehud’s sword just as well as by any other means He could have used, had He judged it more fitting.

With such a terrifying force, Jabin waged war against the Hebrews, brought them under subjection, and ruled over them with violence for twenty years. WHEN Gideon saw that the man, whom he thought he had given food to eat, had caused a fire to come out of the rock, which consumed all the food, he noticed that it was a vision with which God had wished to honor him, and he cried out trembling: *Alas, Lord GOD, for I have seen an Angel of the LORD face to face!* <note>original: "Heere HEERE" — This reflects the Dutch rendering of the divine name YHWH.</note> But the Lord said to him: *Peace be unto you, Gideon, fear not, you shall not die.* Gideon, then full of confidence and wonder, wishing to testify his gratitude to God through an offering, built an altar at that same time, and God commanded him to break down the altar of Baal, upon which the people of his city made offerings, and to cut down a small grove <note>Specifically a sacred grove dedicated to Asherah, often associated with Baal worship.</note> that was nearby. Gideon took ten men with him and carried out that command by night, for fear that the people of his city would have prevented him by day; for the next day, seeing what he had done, they made a great outcry about it, and wanted the leader of

<column-break/>

...store it away quickly, and by that means preserve it from the raids which the Midianites had carried out in Judea for seven years, an Angel of God appeared to him and said: *The LORD is with you, you mighty Hero.* At these words, Gideon was moved by the disasters of his people and answered the Angel: *If the LORD be with us, why then has all this befallen us?* Go, said the Lord, who then spoke to Gideon himself, in this your strength with which I have filled you, and you shall deliver Israel. Gideon appealed to the fact that he was descended from one of the lowliest families of his Tribe, which was that of Manasseh, and that he was one of the least capable in his father’s house. He was given to understand that it would not be through those things that he would deliver Israel, but because God would be with him. Such a glorious vision, accompanied by so unexpected a conversation, produced a focused wonder in Gideon, who, to better assure himself of the truth of what his eyes saw and his ears heard, prayed the Lord who appeared to him (and whom he did not yet know) to be willing to tarry a few moments until he should return to him with something he could set before him; for he took him for a Prophet, raised up by God in an extraordinary way and sent to proclaim the deliverance of his people. The Lord granted his request, and shortly thereafter Gideon returned, bringing in a basket a young goat that he had boiled, and some unleavened cakes, to have the Prophet eat of them. Upon his arrival, he was told by the man for whom he had prepared this food to lay it upon a rock that was in that place. Gideon had no sooner done this than the man who appeared to him touched the meat and the cakes with the end of the staff he had in his hand, and immediately a fire came out of the rock and consumed it all. Then the Angel of the Lord disappeared, and Gideon, assured by this miracle that God had appeared to him, thought of nothing more than to carry out the commands he had received to deliver Israel from the oppression of the Midianites.

He prayed to Him for this purpose to confirm, by a new miracle, the assurance which He had already given him: to bless the weapons of the Israelites in his hands, and to make <term>Amalek and Midian</term><note>The Amalekites and Midianites were nomadic tribal groups who frequently raided Israelite territory during the period of the Judges.</note> fall under his sword. It did not arise from a basis of doubt and unbelief that Gideon requested this of God, unlike the unbelieving Jews in the time of Christ, who, although they saw him perform miracles daily, nevertheless wanted to compel him to show them some sign in the Heavens, or in the air, before they would believe in him. Gideon chose for himself—with such a humble and respectful confidence as that with which a child makes known the desire of his heart to a father by whom he is tenderly loved—the sign which he wished God might give him, to be assured of the happy outcome of his undertaking. "If

<column-break/>

you will deliver Israel through me," he said, "then I pray you that the fleece of a sheep, which I shall spread in the open air on the field and leave there the whole night, be full of dew the next morning, without any dew being perceived on the rest of the field." God granted him his request, and Gideon, having laid a woolen fleece in the open air as he had said, found it the next morning—when all the field had remained dry, as if it were day—so full of dew that he wrung a bowl full of water out of it. Rejoicing then that he had so easily obtained his desire, he took the liberty to make a second request: faith has its holy persistence, and provided that flesh and blood do not mix therein, God looks upon the same with pleasure in humble and fearful souls. Gideon requested of God that when he spread his fleece in the air for a second time, the dew might then fall in abundance on the whole field, and not one drop on the fleece. The matter happened just as he had wished; the following morning the field was covered with dew, and the fleece was as dry as when it was first laid there. These two miracles perfectly strengthened the faith of Gideon, who, thus assured of the assistance of Heaven, immediately gave all the necessary orders to march against the Midianites.

### Judges Chapter VII. verses 19--22.

<margin>

2759.

Gideon, surrendering himself to God's guidance and entrusting the entire outcome of the war against the Midianites to Him, marched toward them with the three hundred men who remained with him out of the thirty-two thousand who had originally come to him. God did not even want these three hundred men to go fight the enemy with conventional weapons; instead of the bow and arrow, He made each of them take a trumpet and an earthen jar with a burning torch inside. While Gideon arranged matters in this way, giving his followers the commands he had received from God himself, the Midianites and Amalekites remained still in their camp, having no thought that they could be attacked there. They were the flower and the very best of the military forces of many peoples of the East who had allied together to invade Judea with their army—a land where they believed nothing could offer them resistance—and they had their Kings and Princes with them. Meanwhile, it happened at night as Gideon approached that one of their soldiers dreamed he saw a barley loaf rolling into the camp with such great speed that it overturned the tents. He told this dream to his comrade, who then told him it was the sword of Gideon that would come to strike the Midianites and overturn all their tents. Gideon had sent his servant <note>The Dutch "jongen" here refers to a personal attendant or squire.</note> secretly at night to spy on the condition of the enemies and how they were encamped. This youth overheard the conversation these two soldiers were having, and returning quickly to Gideon, he gave him an account of what he had heard. This

<column-break/>

wise Commander understood from this that both the dream and the interpretation were from God, who had wanted to inform him of the coming defeat of the Midianites. He then proceeded at the same time with his three hundred men, each having a trumpet in their right hand and an earthen jar with a torch inside in their left; furthermore, he divided them into three groups, and placing himself at the head of one of these, he commanded them all to blow their trumpets as soon as he blew his, and at the same time to smash the jars they carried against each other so that the light of the torches would be seen everywhere. He arrived at midnight at one end of the camp, and giving the signal to his people with the sound of his trumpet, they all answered him with the sound of theirs at the place where they had approached the enemy; they broke their jars against each other and cried out together: *The sword of the LORD and of Gideon.* The enemies in their tents, half-asleep, heard these trumpets echoing from all sides, and opening their eyes, they saw everything around their camp as if on fire. The sudden surprise and the terror served to greatly magnify these sights, and the Midianites, agitated and in disorder, imagined the number of Israelites to be terrifyingly large and almost infinite; they thought they already saw them in their tents, and they struck each other dead as if they were enemies; furthermore, they abandoned their camp and sought their safety in flight. Gideon immediately dispatched messengers to all the neighboring cities, and people came running to meet him from all sides: the number of those fleeing decreased by the slaughter committed on all the roads, and the multitude of Hebrews pursuing them increased from hour to hour, and from moment to moment. This Abimelech was a proud and undaunted man who, in order to make himself master of the legitimate authority which his father had held over Israel, conspired against his brothers. They were the only ones who could rightfully claim the precedence in their House, where it had remained during the life of Gideon. To this end, he went to the inhabitants of Shechem, where his mother’s relatives lived; and having persuaded them to appoint him as their Chief and Commander, they provided him with money, with which he gathered and hired a band of vagabonds and scoundrels. Followed by these guests, who stood ready at his service, he went to the city where his brothers were, and falling upon them, he had them all killed upon a single stone, except for one named Jotham, the youngest of all, who found a means to hide himself. Such a wicked deed ought to have armed all the men of Israel against this Tyrant, if only to avenge the blood of a family whose father had been the salvation of their fatherland: but this abomination went unpunished, and from time to time after the murder of his brothers, Abimelech became more powerful and formidable. The young Jotham attempted to draw the Shechemites away from their unjust alliance with Abimelech, and having once come close to Mount Gerizim, he called out to them from a place where they could hear him. He attempted, through a figurative speech <note>This refers to Jotham's famous "Parable of the Trees" found in Judges 9.</note> that was no less meaningful than it was clever and which pleased them exceedingly well, to inspire in them a sense of justice and generosity, and to make them leave the following of Abimelech: but all this was in vain, and the citizens of Shechem remained by their first choice in favor of that Tyrant. It happened, however, not long thereafter, that they developed a loathing for him, and that a man who was powerful in Israel through his wealth and status hatched a plot to bring him to his fall. After the death of Abimelech, God appointed Tola, from the tribe of Issachar, as the Ruler of His people; he ruled Israel for twenty-three years and delivered them from their enemies. However, the inhabitants had the impertinence and hard-heartedness to refuse this. Gideon then continued his campaign as best he could; God supported him, and the strength of his people was not yet found to be exhausted. The enemies had no thought that they would be pursued so far, and they believed themselves to be in safety once they reached the desert. They stayed there quietly to catch their breath and to mourn their loss; but they were not a little dismayed to see the sword of the Lord and of Gideon, which came seeking them out in those remote places. They were still more than strong enough to have hewn Gideon and his three hundred men into pieces; but God, for this second time,

<column-break/>

just as with the first, struck their camp with terror, so that they did not know how to use their hands and swords to protect themselves. The earth was soon stained with their blood and covered with their dead. Zebah and Zalmunna, two of their kings who had escaped in the previous defeat, took flight again; Gideon pursued them, overtook them, and commanded Jether, his son, to pierce them with his sword. But this youth seemed terrified at the sight of these two princes, who requested of Gideon, as a kind of favor, that they might die by his own hand. Gideon sacrificed them to divine vengeance and subsequently returned with his brave heroes. In passing through, he punished the wantonness of the people of Succoth and Penuel who had refused him provisions, and joined again with the victorious bands of Israel, who were occupied only with gathering the loot of the Midianites. Thus, through the visible protection of God, the raids of the Eastern peoples into the land of Canaan ended, and the Hebrews were at rest for the forty years that Gideon lived after that glorious battle.

### Judges Chapter IX. verses 52, 53.

THE children of Israel felt so vividly the obligation they owed to Gideon for liberating them from the Midianites, and they were so filled with admiration for his bravery, that they wished to offer the sovereignty to him and his descendants for the future. But Gideon, no less humble and godly after his victory than he had been before it, refused a dignity that did not belong to him:

<column-break/>

but he said: "The LORD shall rule over you; He alone must be your Sovereign and King." It is a rare thing when men do not allow themselves to be carried away by ambition, and are not blinded by the glory of ruling. After such a noble and holy refusal, Gideon governed the Israelites for forty years under the guidance and command of God, their only Sovereign. Sarah and Hagar in the household of Abraham. <note>The OCR header likely contains a stray reference to an earlier chapter; the text actually concerns Abimelech and his brothers.</note> This Abimelech was a proud and undaunted man who, in order to seize the legitimate authority his father had held over Israel, conspired against his brothers. They were the only ones who could rightfully claim to maintain the leadership in their House, where it had remained during the life of Gideon. For this purpose, he went to the inhabitants of Shechem, where his mother’s relatives lived. Having persuaded them to appoint him as their Chief and Commander, they provided him with money, with which he gathered and hired a band of vagabonds and scoundrels. Followed by these guests, who stood ready at his service, he went to the city where his brothers were. Attacking them, he had them all killed upon a single stone, except for one named Jotham, the youngest of all, who found a way to hide himself. Such a wicked deed should have armed all the men of Israel against this Tyrant, if only to avenge the blood of a family whose father had been the savior of their fatherland. But this atrocity went unpunished, and from time to time after the murder of his brothers, Abimelech became more powerful and formidable.

Young Jotham attempted to draw the Shechemites away from their unjust alliance with Abimelech. Having once come near their city at Mount Gerizim, he called out to them from a place where they could hear him. He sought, through a veiled speech <note>This refers to the "Parable of the Trees," the oldest recorded parable in the Bible, where the bramble accepts the kingship that the noble trees refused.</note>—which was no less meaningful than it was clever and pleased them exceedingly—to instill in them a sense of justice and nobility, and to make them abandon Abimelech’s faction. But all this was in vain, and the citizens of Shechem stood by their initial choice in favor of that Tyrant. It happened, however, not long after, that they grew disgusted with him, and a man who was powerful in Israel through his wealth and prestige forged a plot to bring him down. This man was named Gaal, and his father Ebed; the Scripture says no more of him. He gathered among his kinsmen and in his city as many people as he could and marched straight toward Shechem. They

<column-break/>

were received there as people who came to deliver them from a Despot. But Abimelech, who was busy elsewhere, having received word of this, came marching quickly with his army. Since he was skilled in warfare, he found a way to lure Gaal and the citizens of Shechem outside the walls, after which he defeated them, took the city, and besieged the most prominent citizens in a tower where they had retreated, setting it on fire so that they all perished. Against the remaining inhabitants, he committed terrible cruelties. Following his atrocious and savage nature, he had the city of Shechem demolished and the site sown with salt, <note>Sowing a city with salt was a symbolic act indicating total destruction and a curse of perpetual desolation, meaning the land should never again be fertile or inhabited.</note> as a cursed ground that must no longer be inhabited. In such a terrible way did God punish the Shechemites for the criminal choice they had made of an Usurper and Tyrant, by the hands of that Tyrant himself, whom He nevertheless led to his death through all his prosperity, just like a sacrificial beast that is hung with garlands only to be slaughtered and offered up. Abimelech, puffed up by this victory, besieged a city called Thebez, which lay in the Tribe of Manasseh. His weapons had the result he expected, and the city was taken; but a large tower, to which a portion of the inhabitants had fled, was not yet captured. Abimelech went in person to storm it, and when he approached the door of the tower to set it on fire, a woman threw a piece of a millstone from above, which struck the Tyrant and crushed his skull. He was still ashamed to be killed by the hand of a woman, and turning to his armor-bearer, he commanded him to finish him off immediately and pierce him with his sword. This servant obeyed the command that shame and despair had torn from his master's mouth; and thus died this Despot, after having been for three years the scourge of his fatherland and a rod in the hand of God for the punishment of the sins of His people, who after Gideon’s death had again fallen into idolatry.

# Jephthah returning victorious from the Ammonites, is met by his daughter.
## Judges Chapter XI. verse 34. etc.

<margin>The year of the world 2794.</margin>
After the death of Abimelech, God appointed as Ruler of His people Tola, from the Tribe of Issachar, who ruled Israel for twenty-three years and delivered them from their enemies. But the Holy Scripture mentions nothing of the specific wars he waged, nor of other matters that occurred during his reign. After his death, God gave that dignity to Jair, the Gileadite, who served in the same office for twenty-two years. We have no knowledge at all of the matters that occurred in Judea in his time, nor of the wars he waged for the protection of his fatherland. All that one finds in the Scripture regarding this is that during the twenty-two years of his Judgeship, the people of Israel were not consistently faithful to God, and that in the last four or five years they gave themselves over so entirely to idolatry that they had never before done anything of the like. God complain-

<column-break/>

ed that this miserable people had so completely rejected Him and no longer served Him; and when they wished to take their refuge in Him to pray, as they had done at other times, that He might be pleased to deliver them from the enemies who waged war against them from all sides, God gave them this terrible answer, which was harsher than any He had ever given them in their previous idolatries: *You have forsaken me, therefore I will deliver you no more: Go, and cry out to the gods whom you have chosen; let them deliver you in the time of your distress.* One can easily imagine how great the consternation of the children of Israel must have been upon hearing these words; a thunderclap could not have made someone more stunned or amazed. They nevertheless persevered in seeking mercy, for there was no other means of escape left for them, and they knew that God is full of compassion, and that if He is in His wrath for a moment, He is in His favor for a whole lifetime. Driven from his father's house, finding himself without property and without protection, this man had retreated to a land which the Scripture calls Tob, located on the borders of Arabia and adjacent to the Ammonites. God sought him out in that refuge and gave him the Government of Israel. At that time, the Ammonites were the most formidable enemies the Jews had. The King of the children of Ammon renewed against them an old quarrel over matters that had occurred nearly three hundred years prior, demanding that the Hebrews return to him certain places which they had taken long ago when coming out of Egypt. Jephthah sent Envoys to him to let him know that his claim was poorly founded, and thus to turn him away from his intention to make war upon the Jews. Yet this King remained fixed in his first intention, because he did not believe the Hebrews were capable of resisting him. But God wished to foil the injustice of that Prince and to humble the pride of the children of Ammon through the weapons of the Israelites. Jephthah placed himself at the head of their host and led them against the enemy, whom he went to seek out even unto the borders of their own land. Becoming sorrowful over his daughter’s and his own misfortune, he cried out: *Alas, my daughter! you have brought me very low, and you are among those who trouble me; for I have opened my mouth to the LORD, and I shall not be able to go back.* This wise and respectful daughter, upon hearing these words, restrained her displays of joy to give place to her submission and obedience in a matter that concerned God. She consented to her father’s vow, and requested only as a final favor that she might be allowed to go with her companions for two months to bewail her virginity <note>In this historical context, dying childless was considered a great tragedy for a family line.</note>. But the men of Ephraim were generally proud and conceited, and because their Tribe was one of the most numerous and powerful, they abused their power and assumed a kind of command and authority over those who were weaker than they, especially over the Tribe of Manasseh, who descended from one and the same father alongside them.
