...with a brave and bold step, roaring at Samson to devour him. Samson awaited him undaunted, and even more courageous than the lion, fell upon him and seized him with such violence that he tore him to pieces, just as one would have done to a young goat. He then left him lying dead on the earth and continued his way to Timnath. Some days later, returning along that same path, he saw the body of that lion lying a little to the side; he turned aside to inspect it and saw that a swarm of bees had settled in the lion’s mouth and was making honey there. He took some out, ate of it, and also gave some to his father and mother, who ate of this honey without knowing where their son had obtained it. The marriage of Samson was concluded, and he married his wife; a wedding feast was held for several days according to the usual custom, and thirty young men of the Philistines were invited to that feast. It was the custom of that land to mingle some sharp-witted amusements of the mind among the good cheer and other festivities; and since the Oriental peoples naturally have a very vivid imagination and a clever intellect, they took pleasure in exercising their wit through clever questions, the meaning of which was wrapped in metaphorical speech; and whoever had the quickness to discover and reveal it won a certain prize set for that purpose. Samson made his riddle from the honey he had found in the lion and presented it to his guests thus: *Food came out of the eater, and sweetness came out of the strong.* They turned every which way to discover the meaning of this riddle, but it was impossible for the Philistines to understand anything of it. They exercised their senses on it during the seven days spent with the wedding, but on the last day they were no wiser than the first. They were ashamed that they should see themselves defeated in this game by Samson, and they could not

<column-break/>

decide but to pay him, as a punishment for their lack of understanding and cleverness, the prize that had been agreed between them in case they could not solve the riddle he gave. In this predicament, they decided to entice Samson's wife to their side, to discover the meaning of the riddle through her. This woman showed herself willing to do them the service they desired. She spoke to her husband privately about it, and Samson, who had no suspicion in that regard, explained to his wife what that saying meant. She told it again to the Philistines, and they, joyful over the explanation this woman had given them—just as if they had the honor of having found the secret themselves—brought this answer to Samson. But he, well understanding that it was his wife who had untangled the whole knot for them, reproached them for it as a trick for which they should be ashamed. The agreement brought with it that if they explained his riddle, he would then give each one a coat and a cloak: thereupon the Spirit of the Lord came mightily upon Samson, so that he departed in haste and alone killed thirty Philistines in one of their cities called Ashkelon, whose coats and cloaks he took and handed to those of Timnath who had won them from him. This deed must not be judged by the usual rules <note>The author explains that Samson’s actions are part of a divine plan against an oppressive nation, rather than standard criminal behavior</note>. God is master of the lives of all men, and He takes it from those whom it pleases Him. The Philistines were a people whom He had long ago doomed to death, and who would have been exterminated nearly three centuries earlier if God had not preserved them in the land of Canaan to be like thorns, as the Scripture says, in the sides of the Israelites whenever they should come to deviate from their duty; and Samson was raised up by God in an extraordinary way to break these thorns, after God had used them against the Hebrews.

### Judges Chapter XV. verses 4, 5.

<margin>

Samson's wife had already shown her treachery toward her husband from the first days of her marriage by revealing the secret he had entrusted to her. Therefore, displeased by such disorderly conduct, he had withdrawn to his own home; but while he was in his father's house, his wife—believing herself abandoned by him, or using that as a pretext to separate from him—married one of those to whom she had explained the meaning of the riddle. Samson, who knew nothing of his wife’s bad conduct, returned to Timnath some time later; however, he found her married to another, and having complained to his father-in-law about it as a hideous wrong done to him, this man answered him that he had a second daughter, who was even more beautiful than the eldest, and that he would give her to him if he wished to take her as a wife. But Samson took no satisfaction in this answer, and because he sought nothing but an opportunity to attack the Philistines and to curb their pride, he took this as a cause to burn their grain, which was almost ready to be cut, and of which even a portion already stood in sheaves. The means he used for this was very singular and entirely unusual. He took three hundred foxes; this number seems very strange to those who do not notice that Judea, being a land full of mountains and hills and occupied almost everywhere with vineyards, was therefore very capable of feeding a great multitude of those animals; it also appears from several places in Scripture that there was a very large number of them and that they often did much damage there. Samson had the skill to gather them, either himself or through the help of those he employed in various places, to the number of three hundred. He then tied them two by two, tail to tail, and in the place where the tails were tied together, he placed a torch. When he had prepared these three hundred foxes in this way, he lit all those torches with fire and let the beasts run into the grain of the Philistines. It is the custom in hot countries to let the grain become exceptionally ripe in the field, until the straw has no more greenness or moisture; and in such a state was the grain when Samson intended...

## *Samson kills a thousand Philistines with an ass's jawbone.*

### Judges Chapter XV. verse 15.

<margin>The same year.</margin>
One might think that Samson should have been satisfied enough that he had thus avenged himself upon the Philistines' corn for the insult done to him at Timnah, and that the Philistines themselves had punished Samson’s wife and her father, who alone were guilty. But it was not his own interests that Samson sought to avenge; it was merely an opportunity and a pretext; he regarded all the Philistines as oppressors of his people, and he knew that God, by means of him, intended if not to utterly destroy them, at least to weaken them and humble their pride. This observation must be made in the history of Samson, in which one sees nothing that is not outside the common and ordinary ways. Thus the Scripture says, speaking of him *several times*, that the *Spirit of the Lord came mightily upon him*, to give us to understand that outside of those extraordinary outpourings of the divine Spirit, which enraptured him, he was but a man like others, peaceful,

<column-break/>

quiet, and busy with his office, just as all the Judges who had ruled God’s people before him had been. Samson then, guided by this Spirit and from such an insight as we have stated, proceeded to do harm to the Philistines. They themselves provided him with the opportunity through the vengefulness they expressed for the loss of their harvest. After that exploit, he had gone into the mountains of Judah, which were very well-suited to provide various hiding places for fugitives, as one sees in the history of David. The Philistines gave notice of this to the men of that tribe, who, being afraid of people much more powerful than themselves and who had become their masters, went to seek Samson in their mountains: they were three thousand men strong, so greatly did they fear either that they would miss him or that he would escape them if they had already caught him: for their intention was not to kill him. They found him by the rock of Etam <note>original: "Elams"; likely a variation of Etam, where Samson took refuge.</note>, and after he had made them promise with an oath that they would not kill him, he surrendered himself into their hands and allowed them to bind him as they wished. It was a great cowardice on the part of these men of Judah to act thus with one of their brothers, an Israelite who sacrificed himself for the protection of all the people; but a false

They then brought Samson into that city to the Philistines, who were more joyful to see this prisoner arrive, bound with two new ropes, than if they had won a battle. Seeing him approach, they shouted with joy and ran toward him like people possessed. But the Spirit of God came mightily upon Samson, and the ropes with which he was bound fell broken to the earth, like linen threads singed by fire and burned in several places. Samson saw lying at his feet a donkey's jawbone <note>original: "ezels kinnebakken"</note> that was not yet fully dry; he grabbed it and fell upon the Philistines, striking with it all who came before him. As many blows as he dealt, so many dead there were. <column-break/>

wrath. He grew weary of striking and killing, and his hands, which God had made fit for battle—as David says somewhere <note>A reference to Psalm 144:1, "Praise be to the Lord... who trains my hands for war."</note>—finally felt that they were made of flesh and blood and began to weaken. The entire body lost its strength, and thirst began to consume it almost entirely. The Philistines had fled; Samson had nothing left to fight but weakness and thirst. He feared that his enemies might notice this and attack him. He prayed to God to come to his aid in this great need, and not to allow him to fall into the hands of those <term>Uncircumcised</term> <note>A term used by the Israelites to distinguish themselves from neighboring peoples like the Philistines who did not share their religious covenant.</note>, nor that he should die of thirst after a miraculous deliverance. His prayer was heard; God opened one of the large molars of the donkey's jawbone, and a stream of water came flowing out of it. Samson drank from it and regained his strength. The Scripture speaks here of Samson's reign and says that he judged Israel for twenty years, because it was perhaps this great deed that made him known as a man whom God had given to His people to serve in the office of Governor <note>original: "Overheer"</note> among them and to protect them from the oppression of the Philistines.

Arriving at Gaza, he took lodging with a woman who kept a public inn. The Hebrew word signifies both a woman of an immoral life and also a hostess or innkeeper; but one owes this respect to a man whom the Apostle <note>This refers to the Apostle Paul, or the author of the Book of Hebrews, who includes Samson in the "Hall of Faith" in Hebrews 11:32.</note> has placed on the list of the greatest Saints of the Old Law: that one should not, based on the mere ambiguity of a word, accuse him of a dishonest transaction of which his history has not charged him. Samson was recognized in this house, and word was immediately given to the rulers of the city, who thereupon had the gates closed and laid an ambush of people just outside the city to seize him when he should go out. For it seems that they feared, after what they had seen him do with the donkey’s jawbone <note>original: "ezels kinnebakken"</note>, to come and attack him in his room; and they believed that through this caution they could easily and without danger make themselves master of him, and that he would not be able to escape. All this took place at night, and Samson, quiet and peaceful in his room, slept until midnight. Then he awoke, and stepping out of his inn, he went to the city gate, which he found closed, yet without a guard, because it was not judged necessary to watch it after it had been well-secured. Samson was not even dismayed by this, but seized the doors with their posts, and wrenching them from their place, he laid them upon his shoulders and carried them far away from the city, to the top of a hill. There is no human strength capable of doing such a thing, but it was easy for that God who had given power to one man to change all the waters of Egypt into blood by the mere stroke of a staff, and to pave a way through the middle of the sea, to grant strength to the arms of another to tear loose the fixed posts and

<column-break/>

heavy doors of a city gate, and to carry them as far as he wished. It is somewhat difficult to understand why Samson was not satisfied with breaking or wrenching out the locks of this gate, since it was enough merely to open them to leave the city, without there being any necessity for him to burden himself with such an unwieldy load. But although it is not given to us, poor mortals, to extend our sight to all the ways and deeds of a man whom God’s Spirit leads where He wills, and whom He makes to work as He wills, we can nevertheless reasonably believe that God’s purpose was to show the Philistines, in the person of a man as strong and extraordinary as Samson was, what He was capable of doing if He wished to deliver His people from their oppression. For He had taken the lives of a thousand Philistines through a single man, and a man who was himself unarmed, having nothing but a bone or jawbone in his hands; and that same man tore loose the heavy doors of the gate of one of their cities, and without any other necessity than to show them his strength and thus mock their weakness, he carried those same doors, which he had taken from them, away to the top of a mountain. God could have made for Himself an entire army of such strong heroes as Samson, and without making that miracle so general, what could He not have done if He had willed to cast the Philistines to the earth and to have destroyed them forever, just as He had done nearly three hundred years before to various nations of that same land of Canaan? But He was satisfied with humbling the pride of those Unbelievers, who relied on their Idols and spoke scornfully of the God of Israel. He had need of the Philistines to punish the rebelliousness of His people through them, and the time had not yet come to throw these rods into the fire <note>A metaphor meaning the Philistines were the "rod" of punishment that God was not yet ready to destroy.</note> and to make Abraham’s offspring master of all Palestine.

# *Samson is betrayed by Delilah, who has his hair cut off, and thereby takes away all his strength.*

## Chapter 16 of the Book of Judges, verses 18, 19.

<margin>
Around the year of the world 2885; 1119 B.C. <note>original: "voor J. C." (Before Jesus Christ)</note>
</margin>

Samson’s father and mother had, as much as was possible for them, opposed the plan he had to marry a Philistine woman: and the Scripture gives us to understand that they did not know that this came from God, whose Spirit guided Samson through paths that are not common for other men. Without doubt, we must attribute to the same cause the suit which Samson brought about eighteen years later to Delilah, another Philistine, as well as the very singular affection he bore for her. The sacred History of the book of Judges, whose condensed reports often only let us see things briefly, tells us only that *Samson loved a woman whose name was Delilah*; and because of this, most commentators have believed that she was not his wife, but that he kept an immoral relationship with her. Meanwhile, the Holy Scripture nowhere charges him with that crime, and the Apostle Paul, on the contrary, has placed Samson in the rank of the most excellent Saints of God’s ancient people in his Epistle to the Hebrews, according to the observation we made in the preceding history. This is not to say that the Saints, whose praise the Apostle mentions, were without faults, and St. Paul did not intend to count all their actions among holy works. It happens all too often that the human side is found in the Saint, and the faith which made those of whom the Apostle speaks with wonder so famous was not always powerful enough in

<column-break/>

them, to banish all human passions from their hearts, or to keep them constantly under the yoke. But nevertheless, it would be something very unusual if God had abandoned a man like Samson so much to the passion of unchastity that, stepping down from the exalted seat of Israel <note>Samson served as a Judge, the highest leadership position in Israel at the time.</note>, he would have pursued a lewd woman in the cities of the Philistines: and it would have been even more wonderful <note>In this context, "wonderful" means "astonishing" or "miraculous."</note> if God had allowed him to keep that miraculous strength which He had granted him at a time when that Hero had defiled the holiness of his religion and, in the most shameful manner, tarnished the glory of his Naziriteship <term>Naziriteship: A sacred vow of consecration to God, which included never cutting one's hair and abstaining from wine.</term>, which was the foundation of his strength. It is then much more believable that Delilah was Samson's lawful wife, and that the wording in the book of Judges—that he loved Delilah—means nothing other than that he had an extraordinary fondness and affection for her, as what follows here will show only too clearly. The objection made that Samson did not take Delilah home with him can only be of very little importance to those who know that everything related about Samson is beyond common rules, and that even regarding the things we know, we are ignorant of all the particulars and the primary circumstances. We do not know then whether Samson brought Delilah to his home among the Jews or not; and whether she embraced the Jewish religion, as some Rabbis have believed, or whether she always remained an idolater: all that the Scripture tells us of it is that Samson loved her very much, and that he had gone to see her in one of the cities of the Philistines. This great man had affections for this wicked woman which one cannot read without astonishment. She conspired with the Philistines to plunge him into his destruction; the extraordinary strength of Samson struck them with terror, and they did not know

One would have to be very foolish to imagine that Samson's strength originally resided in his hair and had a human basis. It was not the long hair of the Nazirite vow <note>A Nazirite was a person consecrated to God who, among other requirements, was forbidden from cutting their hair</note> that gave him that extraordinary strength; for if that were the case, then all Nazirites would have had that strength, whereas it belonged to Samson alone and was never found in anyone else. The strength of this hero was a pure miracle; but God, who wished to preserve this strength for him as long as he himself kept the hair of his Naziriteship, would not let him keep it for a single moment after he had scorned and desecrated his status as a Nazirite.

God, who had still destined him for something great, did not wish to restore his strength to him all at once; but to honor the Naziriteship <note>A Nazirite was a person consecrated to God by a vow, which included not cutting their hair and abstaining from wine.</note> to which God Himself had dedicated him before his birth, and to make him better understand how criminal he had been by desecrating the holiness of that consecration, the Lord willed that his powers should not return except in proportion to the regrowth of his hair. The Philistines did not yet notice the return of Samson’s strength, nor did they even think of it; and he kept what he could do hidden, so as not to give his enemies any suspicion through any deed that might be too conspicuous. But the opportunity to demonstrate his new strength was not long in coming. The Philistines held a great feast in honor of their god Dagon <note>Dagon was a major Philistine deity, often depicted as half-man, half-fish.</note>, and nothing was seen there but sacrifices, banquets, and festivities. ### *Judges Chapter XIX. verses 26—30. and Chap. XXI. verse 23.*

<margin>Around the year of the world 2887.</margin>
Corruption grew daily among the Hebrews along with idolatry; they forsook God, and God likewise forsook them, and gave them over to their own passions. The Book of Judges relates, after the death of Samson, the history of a woman whose son was named Micah, of the tribe of Ephraim; he, having returned to his mother the eleven hundred pieces of silver which he had taken from her, caused this woman—who was so overjoyed at the recovery of this sum, which she had completely given up for

<column-break/>

spectacle and pastime for all those people. They were not satisfied merely with feasting their eyes on this object, upon which revenge, contempt, and false zeal simultaneously found something to satisfy themselves; but they insulted him further with everything that the sharpest mockery could devise, and they jested with him like someone who is pushed and turned from all sides to make him even more ridiculous. Samson felt this insult less for himself than for his God, who was so visibly touched in the proud and arrogant triumph which the idolaters held over Him to honor their Idol. He sighed for it in God’s presence from the bottom of his heart, and he prayed to the Lord that He would strengthen him in an extraordinary way, so that by the death of these idolaters he might avenge the insult they offered him, even if he should lose his own life in the process. Having a mind full of these thoughts, and being entirely set on sacrificing the final remnant of his life for the defense of God’s honor and the benefit of his people, he requested the lad who led him to bring him into the middle of the two pillars that supported the entire building. As soon as he was at the place where he could stretch out his arms around the two columns and embrace them, he turned inward to God and offered this prayer:
> Lord GOD, remember me, I pray thee, and strengthen me, I pray thee, only this once, O God, that I may be at once avenged of the Philistines for my two eyes.

Saying this, he embraced both pillars; and he bowed himself with might, so that the entire house collapsed and crushed the Philistines, numbering three thousand persons. He himself lost his life along with the others, but he found it again in God, who would not have restored his former strength to do a deed that can only be regarded as a miracle if the vengeance which Samson took on the Philistines in his death had not been pleasing to Him, just as He had considered pleasant those deeds which he had done in his life.

About four months later, the Levite <note>A Levite was a member of the Tribe of Levi, set apart for religious duties but not necessarily a priest.</note> traveled to Bethlehem to fetch his wife back. He was received with great affection at the house of his father-in-law; indeed, they did everything they could to keep him there for a while, attempting to postpone his departure from one day to the next. However, he finally departed with his wife and took the road to Gibeah, a city of the Tribe of Benjamin. Since it was already late before he left his father-in-law—who had wanted to keep him yet another day, pointing out that the sun was already descending—night overtook him near Gibeah, so that they were forced to stay still there. And whether it was that there was no inn for the convenience of strangers in that city, or that this Levite did not see fit to take lodging there, he decided to spend the night in the street. An honest old man who lived in that city, yet was born in the same region as the Levite, obliged him to stay overnight at his house, where he was received and entertained with all possible courtesy. But the same thing that had happened in Sodom <note>A reference to Genesis 19, where the men of Sodom surrounded Lot's house.</note> to the two Angels whom Lot had met in the street and brought into his home, befell this Levite as well: the inhabitants of Gibeah came knocking at the door at night, wishing to seize his guest from him to commit a crime of the most extreme infamy with him. The good old man, moved and distressed that such a wicked violence was being done at his door, offered his daughter to these villains, not considering that he committed a great sin by thus exposing the honor of his daughter to shame. The Levite, for his part, being only concerned with protecting himself, surrendered his wife to these raving people. The next morning they found her back, and she sank down dead before the door

Now, to take revenge for such a loathsome crime, this Levite resolved to do something that finds no parallel in all History <note>original: "Hiſtoriën"</note>, and which leaves the reader stunned and amazed: he cut the body of this, his concubine <note>The original Dutch uses "bywyf," referring to a secondary wife or concubine.</note>, into twelve pieces and sent one to each tribe with a precise account of everything that had happened to him. In all the tribes of Israel, there was a horror of such an excessively wicked deed; and they collectively took a resolution to execute punishment for it. They demanded of those of Benjamin that they should deliver the guilty ones to them, to punish them as an example to others. The Benjaminites—who ought to have been the first to wipe away the shame they had brought upon the whole nation in general and their Tribe in particular by the death penalty of these villains—refused this. Consequently, it came to an open war; the men of Benjamin, no less proud than unjust, had the audacity to wage that war alone against the other tribes; and what is even rarer, their army, which consisted of twenty-six or twenty-seven thousand men, defeated that of the allied Tribes, which amounted to four hundred thousand, of whom twenty-two thousand were killed in the first battle. In the second, they lost another eighteen thousand men, and the victory remained entirely on the side of the children of Benjamin. It was a terrible judgment of God <note>original: "oordeel Góds"</note> against this unfaithful and idolatrous people, arming tribe against tribe and turning sword against sword to avenge Himself for their rebellion. The wisdom and godliness of Ruth—on whom everyone had their eyes as a foreign woman, which was a rarity in Israel—soon became known, and gained her the respect and affection of all who knew her. The affairs of Naomi's house were in complete disorder; an absence of ten years was enough to cause great changes in estates of little significance, as the land Elimelech had owned in Bethlehem might well have been. But the Moabitess <note>A woman from the land of Moab; the Moabites were often seen as outsiders or enemies of Israel, making Ruth's integration significant.</note> bore these inconveniences with a patience and gentleness that made her more and more respected and loved by her mother-in-law. It was then the time of the barley harvest, and Ruth went to the field, like the poor daughters, to collect some ears of grain. Good Providence led her to a field belonging to Boaz, who by that same Providence was brought there when Ruth arrived. He learned from his reapers that she was the Moabitess who had recently arrived with Naomi; and the charity of Boaz, stirring him to notice the needy state in which that family found itself, gave orders to his people to intentionally let some handfuls fall, and not to prevent this stranger from gleaning. Thus it was easy for Ruth to soon have her hands full, and to collect much more grain through her gleaning than one could usually find in so little time. This was what Boaz intended, and Ruth made such good use of it that, having beaten out the ears she had collected with a stick, she found an ephah <note>An ephah is an ancient Hebrew dry measure, roughly 22 liters or about 6 gallons.</note> of grain from it. Rejoicing over such a good encounter, she brought the grain to her mother-in-law, who was surprised to see that her daughter-in-law had collected such a great quantity of barley in one day. Naomi asked her in which area she had been, and she—

<column-break/>

understood from the answer that it was in the field of Boaz that Ruth had collected all that barley. She told her that Boaz was of her kinship, and she gave her to understand how she should behave to make herself known to him. Ruth followed her mother-in-law's advice exactly, and Boaz declared that by right of kinship with her deceased husband, the son of Elimelech, he wished to take her as his wife; but he added that there was another in Bethlehem who was more closely related to her, to whom this right first belonged, but that if that man refused, he himself would then marry her. Boaz then went to the city gate <note>In the ancient world, the city gate was the site of the local court and the center of public life.</note> where all legal cases were judged, and having sat down with the elders, the kinsman of Elimelech, of whom Boaz had spoken to Ruth, passed by. Boaz stopped him and proposed to him in the presence of the entire assembly whether he, as the closest relative of Elimelech, wished to redeem <note>In Hebrew law, a "kinsman-redeemer" had the right and duty to buy back family land and care for widows.</note> a certain piece of land that had formerly belonged to him. This man answered, yes; then Boaz told him that he must then also marry Ruth, the widow of Elimelech's son, to revive the name of his deceased kinsman in his inheritance, according to the institutions of Moses. This man said that he could not marry her, and therefore ceded his right to redeem the field to Boaz; saying this, he took off his shoe and gave it to Boaz, as a sign of transfer, according to the custom of that time on such occasions. Boaz took all the people present as witnesses to what had happened, and declared that he would redeem the piece of land and marry Ruth the Moabitess. The marriage was performed, and all the people accompanied it with their well-wishes: *The LORD*, they cried, *make this woman who comes into your house like Rachel and like Leah, who both built the house of Israel! Act mightily in Ephrathah, and make your name famous in Bethlehem!* God poured out his blessing particularly over this marriage and caused a son to be born from it named Obed, whom the virtuous Naomi had the comfort of seeing and raising, and who was the father of Jesse, the father of David.

The year of the world 2848, before J.C. 1156.

We do not read in holy history that God, after Samson's death, gave his people any of those extraordinary men who distinguished themselves by their victories. The principal dignity in civil government was held for forty years by the High Priest Eli, who was the only one in whom these two great offices <note>The offices of High Priest and Judge/Leader of Israel.</note> were united in the first centuries of the Jewish Commonwealth. Under his priesthood, an event occurred that made it very famous in the Scriptures, and that was the birth of Samuel, and the appearance with which God honored him in his childhood. His father, named Elkanah and of the lineage of the Levites, had married two wives, which at that time was no dishonor for a man, nor an uncommon thing. One of these women,

It was anciently among the women of Israel a great sorrow to have no children, and her barrenness made her somewhat despised, as was seen more than ten centuries later in the time of Zechariah and Elizabeth. Hannah was very sensitive to this sorrow, and once at a certain time when she had gone from the city of Ramathaim-Zophim, where she lived, to Shiloh, where the Tabernacle of God stood, she appeared in a prayer which lasted quite long, so dejected and unusually distressed that Eli took notice of it; and because he did not know her and saw that she only moved her lips, he believed that her head was disturbed by wine. He had the imprudence to reveal his thoughts to her and add a rebuke, as he believed the matter deserved. Hannah heard this with great modesty and respect, and said to the High Priest that it was a bitter heartache which had thus caused her to pour out her soul in prayers and tears before the Lord. The crime of Eli was that he had shown all too much indulgence toward his two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, who committed deeds of the greatest shame for men who had the honor of serving in the highest dignities of the priesthood. <note>Hophni and Phinehas were known for taking meat from sacrifices by force and for their misconduct at the entrance of the Tabernacle.</note> Samuel was in an incomprehensible state of shock when he heard the calamities God prepared for an old Priest, who was otherwise very godly and for whom he held a deep respect. Eli asked him what God had revealed to him; Samuel seemed distraught and did not dare give Eli such a sad account. The other, however, urged him and adjured him to hide nothing from him: the youth obeyed and recounted everything he had heard: and Eli received this decision with a submission that exceeds human strength: *He is the LORD,* he said, *let Him do what is good in His eyes.*

## The Death of Eli the High Priest.

### I Samuel Chapter IV. verse 18.

<margin>
The year of the world 2881. Before J.C. 1116.
</margin>

The abominable crimes of Hophni and Phinehas, both sons of the High Priest, had so kindled God's wrath that He had sent a Prophet to Eli to tell him that He would cause those villains to die, that He would transfer the High Priesthood from their family into another, and that no one of his lineage would reach a great old age. He had revealed the same matter to the young Samuel, who, being urged by the High Priest to recount the revelation he had received, could not release himself from giving him an account of God's threats over that wretched household. The time approached then for God to avenge the crimes of shameful unchastity which had been committed even within His Sanctuary, and to give a terrifying example of justice to indulgent fathers <note>The original Dutch uses "ooglukende vaders," literally "eye-closing fathers," referring to parents who turn a blind eye to their children's faults.</note> who show an excessive leniency regarding the misdeeds of their children, or who punish them only very faintly. The Jews were then at war with the Philistines. These peoples, who were the remnants of the ancient Canaanites whom Joshua had destroyed, and whose lands and cities the Hebrews possessed, maintained an irreconcilable hatred against God's people and sought only to oppress them. The opportunities for this presented themselves only too often because this people, by provoking God with their idolatries, were delivered by Him to their neighbors, who repeatedly came to make war upon them and subdued them. He thereafter sent them Saviors <note>These "Saviors" refer to the biblical Judges (Richteren) who were raised up to lead Israel out of oppression.</note>, but their land, weakened by so much loss, often found itself unable to resist the Philistines, who took those times to take now one city, and then

<column-break/>

the other away, and thus to bring them entirely under the yoke; and their wars always turned out well or poorly against the children of Israel, according to whether God resisted this people or was favorable. The time in these last years of Eli was then altogether suitable for the Philistines to wage war against the Hebrews; God was angry with the Rulers and with the people, and no more was needed to make the Philistines victors. They came into the field with an army, the Israelites also marched out with all the people they could gather, the battle began, and the Philistines struck down the Israelites, who lost four thousand men there. Consternation spread through the camp, and it was decided, as a last resort, that they would fetch the Ark of God from Shiloh <note>Shiloh was the central place of worship for Israel before the Temple was built in Jerusalem.</note>, to place the entire army in safety under the protection of the Ark, and to be able to deliver a second battle with better fortune. The Ark arrived with Hophni and Phinehas, the two principal Heads of the Priesthood, but at the same time the most criminal. Through this new reinforcement, in which the Jews placed greater trust than in an entire army, they believed themselves invincible; and seeing it arrive, they made such a great shouting that all the Philistines were astonished by it. And their astonishment increased when they understood that the cause of this uncommon cry was that it was said that the God of the Jews had come into their camp. This saying made the Philistines think of the wonders which that mighty and terrible God had formerly performed for that same people in Egypt and in Canaan; such that they already believed themselves defeated. But God, who intended for them that day the greatest victory they had ever carried away, allowed them to take courage again, and to draw themselves up in battle array to fight with such stoutheartedness and bravery as is commonly seen in people who have won a battle against their enemies. ## Dagon falls down before the Ark of God.

### I Samuel Chapter V. verse 4.

<margin>
* The same year. 2888 after the creation of the world.
</margin>

Nothing was lacking from the victory of the Philistines to make it complete; they had hewn the army of the Hebrews to pieces and made the Ark of God a prisoner. But they soon found that this conquest, which they considered the greatest cause for their triumph, was more ruinous to them than the loss of a field battle. Within a few days, they saw this captive Ark triumph over their gods and cause incurable plagues in their land. The principal idol of the Philistines was called *Dagon*, which is a name formed from another word meaning a fish <note>Original: "vifch." This refers to the Hebrew word 'dag,' meaning fish.</note>; because that idol had the body of a fish, but the head and hands of a human. The Philistines had brought the Ark to Ashdod and placed it in the temple of their god as a trophy of victory where they came to show him their submission. God, who through an exercise of His wrath against the Israelites had allowed His Ark to be taken from them, could not endure that it should remain at the feet of an idol; so it was that when the temple where it was placed was opened the next day,

<column-break/>

the idol was found fallen to the earth on its face before the Ark. The idolaters were astonished by this accident; but as they did not immediately take any special notice of it, they raised their god up again and restored him to his place, taking every necessary precaution to prevent such an accident in the future. Yet their precaution was in vain; Dagon could not stand before the Ark, and falling a second time from his place, he was found the next day not only stretched out upon the earth as on the previous day, but his head and both his hands were cut off and lay separated from the body on the threshold of the door. The idolaters then saw that it had not happened by a natural accident, such as one sees happening daily, that Dagon had fallen before the Ark the first time; and they were convinced that it was the God of Israel who, to bring honor to His Ark, had caused Dagon to plunge down before it, and had thus come to scorn their god even in his own temple and upon his throne. They were very distressed by this and decided no longer to leave the Ark of the God of Israel in the temple of their idols. The shame and disgrace it brought them to see that their god was without hands and without a head—indeed, nothing more than a deformed and ugly trunk—was

### I Samuel Chapter VI. verses 10, 11, 12.
### Chapter VII. verses 5, 6. and Chapter X. verse 1.

<margin>The same year. 2888.</margin>
The Jews were so weakened by the loss of the two battles which the Philistines had won against them, that they dared not risk a third, nor make any attempt to retake the Ark that had been carried away from them. But although the weakness in which they found themselves thus left the Ark a captive in the hands of those uncircumcised ones, the Ark itself fought for its own freedom through the afflictions it caused those who held it in their power. They acknowledged this to their great shame, and they were forced—after having kept it for seven months—to return it of their own accord, out of fear that it might cause them all to perish. Their princes consulted about this with the priests of their gods, who were collectively of the opinion that the Ark must be sent back

<column-break/>

and a gift added to it as a sign of the submission which these idol-worshippers—who, after what had happened to Dagon, already considered all their gods lost—wished to show to the God of Israel. Since the Ark had been among them, the land had been plagued by a terrible multitude of mice that ate all their fields bare; and the plague of hemorrhoids had so afflicted these peoples that neither rich nor poor escaped it. Based on this, the priests imagined that one must offer to the Ark of God such figures as represented the very things through which it had taken vengeance on the Philistines. And because their land was divided into five governorships <note>the five lordships or city-states of the Philistines: Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron</note>, it was decided to make five golden likenesses of that part of the body where the hemorrhoids arise, and just as many golden images of mice, and to put them together in a small chest on the side of the Ark upon a wagon. And to better assure themselves whether all the disasters, the cause of which they attributed to the Ark, indeed proceeded from it, or whether they had only happened by chance, those same priests thought it best that two nursing cows should be harnessed to the wagon on which the Ark was placed, and their calves led away from them back to the stall as soon as the cows were harnessed to the wagon, which they would allow no man to drive. They requested a truce of seven days to see if they might be rescued, with the promise that if this did not happen within that time, they would then submit to the law Nahash had prescribed for them. The messengers from Jabesh came to Saul; he was still living as a private citizen at that time, and they found him coming from the field with his oxen. All the people in his city were as if drowned in tears over the sorrowful state to which the city of Jabesh had been brought. Saul was moved by it like all the others; and God’s Spirit filled him through His inspiration, to take the protection of that city upon himself. He quickly gathered all the Tribes together, and placing himself at their head, he marched straight toward the Ammonites, surprised them in their camp, and hewed them to pieces. This first campaign of Saul's earned him the respect and admiration of all the people, and Samuel took this opportunity to entirely resign his office and deliver it into the hands of the new King.

This Prince was no less grieved than stunned by the disgrace into which he had fallen; he humbled himself, but the decree was irrevocable. The Philistines were stunned to see men coming to bring them death while they lay behind inaccessible rocks: Jonathan and his armor-bearer killed all who came before them; the rest took flight, bringing turmoil and terror into the army. Saul was informed of the enemies' disorder, the cause of which was unknown to him; he marched straight toward them and carried out a great slaughter among them. Thereupon, he himself carried out the judgments of Heaven upon that Prince: he thrust the steel into his body, and to make the offering—which he made to God's wrath through the death of the Amalekite—the greater and more stately, he hewed him into several pieces, leaving Saul there under the remorse and gnawing pain of knowing that he would never see him again for the rest of his life. For the rest, one must not judge Samuel's conduct in this incident as one commonly judges the actions of men: but one must look upon this holy man as a Servant of God; and God, who is the Supreme Judge of the world, speaks His decrees—which can never be anything but just—against whom He wills, and has them executed by whom it pleases Him, and in such a manner as it pleases Him.

The sweet-sounding tone made an impression on the King’s mind and stilled the violence of his internal turmoil. David conducted himself so prudently and wisely at the Court that he thereby gained the respect of all the Great Lords, and especially that of the King, who made him his Armor-bearer <note>original: "Wapendraager"</note> and desired to have him always by his side.

THE victory which Saul had achieved some years earlier through the extraordinary bravery of Jonathan <note>Jonathan was King Saul’s eldest son and a close friend of David.</note> over the Philistines had not weakened them so much that they could not, some time later, take up arms again to wage war against Israel. Indeed, they had become so mighty, and Saul so weak, that the Jews greatly dreaded coming to a pitched battle with them. The two armies remained encamped in sight of each other for some time, separated only by a small valley situated between two mountains, one of which was occupied by the Philistines and the other by the Hebrews. For many days, the Hebrews suffered the vexation of seeing a terrible giant named Goliath appear. Coming out from the enemy's camp, he challenged the Israelites to find someone from their army who dared to fight him, so that this private duel might settle the war between the two nations. To this arrogant pride, he added many blasphemies against the God of the Hebrews; yet no one dared to accept his challenge or commit the common cause—which was, in a sense, the cause of God—to a fight where the Jews could bring nothing but a very unequal power against that of the Philistines. David was then with his father; and whether the envy of the courtiers had played a foul trick on him with Saul, or whether the King, through the eccentricity of a damaged and troubled mind, had quickly developed a distaste for him, David had not been at Court for a long time. He had resumed his original way of life with his father at Bethlehem, which was tending the sheep. His brothers had joined the army, and Jesse <note>The original Dutch text uses "Isai," the name for Jesse.</note> sent David to bring them some refreshments and to learn how they were faring.

<column-break/>

Arriving there, he found the entire army in great consternation, arising from the arrogant and godless threats of Goliath; and a little while later, he saw that giant appear, who, according to his custom, came to mock the Israelites. David’s zeal was ignited upon seeing the Philistine and hearing his blasphemies, and he asked here and there, as someone who had just arrived, what the King would do for the man who dared to go and fight this giant. He was told that the King would enrich him with wealth and honor, and give him his daughter. David spoke of this matter so often and with so many people that the rumor of it reached the King’s ears, who then commanded that this young man be brought to him. The changes that years might have made in David’s person, his shepherd's clothing—so different from that of a courtier—the distraction of mind that could only be very great in a troubled King buried in his melancholy, and finally the short time this youth had previously stayed with Saul, caused the King not to recognize him; and David had his reasons for not revealing who he was. The King asked him some questions regarding the fight of which they spoke, and David answered with so much piety, wisdom, and courage that Saul allowed himself to be persuaded to permit him to go and fight the Philistine. The King desired that David should put on his own armor, from which one can gather that since the time he was brought to Saul to play the harp for him, he must have grown significantly; for Saul was a tall man, and there must have been some similarity in the physical stature of the youth with his own to make him try to fit his armor on him. **D**avid’s victory over Goliath was followed by that of the entire host of Israel over the Philistines. They were so dismayed by the death of their giant, who for many days had been the terror of the Israelites, that fear spread among them at the same time, and they became powerless to offer any spirited resistance. The Jews, on the other hand, encouraged by David’s victory and firmly believing that God fought for them, viewed their victory as something of which they were certain. They ran toward the host of the Philistines, not as an army they had to fight,

The means for this were naturally very easy; but God, who did not want David to perish, brought various considerations to Saul’s mind which restrained him from using any means that he could easily have put into effect to rid himself of a youth whose merit stood in his way. Politics mingled in this, and by presenting Saul with various means to carry out his design, it did nothing but delay the execution thereof, and finally make it impossible. Saul could not refuse the honor that David’s great deed deserved. One had to give the Victor of Goliath offices that could outweigh such great merit; for all the world would have blamed the King if he had done otherwise: and he believed that by elevating him in such a manner, he would not lack opportunities to rid himself of him whenever he wished: and God, to comfort David for the suspicion and injustices of Saul, caused him to find in the person of Jonathan, the King's son, a sincere friend, who, full of respect and admiration for David, swore an eternal friendship to him, and was his protector before the King all his life.

THE hatred of Saul against David increased daily, and he wished for nothing with greater zeal than his destruction. David was still at the Court, and Saul still pretended to take the same pleasure in seeing him play the harp as he had found in it previously. The troublesome ailment

<column-break/>

of this Prince remained with him, and from time to time he suffered such violent fits <note>A reference to the "evil spirit" or melancholy that the Bible describes as afflicting Saul.</note> that they seemed to deprive him of all his reason. But instead of humbling himself before God, who had sent him this ailment as a punishment for his misdeeds, he wanted, on the contrary, to make it serve the criminal design that was constantly in his head: to kill David. One is often willing to excuse the errors of a man who is in such a state, and one attributes to a distraction of the mind those deeds whose origin is often hidden in the heart. This was a blending of everything: namely, the cunning of the serpent with its venom, so as to commit the most cowardly and wicked deed without losing the reputation of his innocence in the eyes of everyone. On a certain day, then, while David played the harp for the King—who appeared to be completely insane and in the state of someone who knows not what he does—Saul, who during these fits of madness (which were sometimes merely feigned) held a spear in his hand, sought to transfix David. David, through the sweet sound of his harp, was attempting to quiet and calm the mind of the Prince; but God turned the shot aside, and David received no harm from it. This had already happened twice; and although the Scripture, which is generally not long-winded in recounting the circumstances of matters unless they are essential, does not tell us how this act of Saul's was regarded, nor in what way he tried to prevent the opinion people might form to the detriment of his honor; yet one need not doubt that he attributed the violent and irregular action of his hand entirely to the disturbance of his senses. There is even reason to believe that David himself, whatever reasons he might otherwise have had to suspect something more than a mere disturbance of spirit, was of such a mind—along with others—because after escaping such great danger twice, he exposed himself to it yet a third time. But besides the fact that noble souls are generally not suspicious, David saw himself showered with the King's favors, who had recently granted him new offices and employed him in the most weighty matters of his Kingdom. What is more, the King, who had promised his eldest daughter in marriage to the one who should overcome Goliath, having given her to another against his promise,

<column-break/>

had since caused David to marry Michal, his second daughter. For this Princess had conceived such a particular esteem for David that she regarded him as a man worthy to be her husband; so the King pretended to be very well pleased that, through the marriage with his second daughter, he could fulfill the promise he had made to David to have him marry his eldest after the death of the terrible Philistine. But Saul, ever intent on means to bring about David's end, believed that in concluding this marriage he had found one that was perfectly suited to that purpose. In ancient times, it was the custom that men gave a dowry to the women, and obtained them through sums of money or such other conditions as they agreed upon with their fathers: one sees a very old and famous example of this in the history of Jacob, who served Laban for seven years for each of his daughters, and elsewhere one finds yet other examples of it. Saul then proposed to David that he should go and kill a hundred Philistines, and that as a certain proof thereof, he should deliver as many foreskins to him. This was intended to make him perish in the undertaking, which was full of very great danger; but David was not at all dismayed by this, and having chosen some men from his following, whose courage and bravery were known to him, he attacked the Philistines and killed two hundred of them, of which he brought such proofs to Saul as he had demanded for the death of a hundred. The marriage was thereupon performed, and David having become the King's son-in-law, it seemed that his life would henceforth be in safety: and yet it remained always in danger as before. Saul, seeing no more convenient means to take it from him than the way which he had already twice attempted in vain—which was to kill him himself by the cast of a spear while David played the harp before him—attempted such a thing for the third time; but David evaded the shot, and Saul had the shame of having wanted to kill his son-in-law, and the cruel sorrow of not having been able to carry it out.

Saul, having missed for the third time the chance to kill David with a spear, and being unable to resolve to let him live any longer, now spared nothing to rid himself of him, and took recourse to open violence after having employed craftiness and cunning in vain. David was the most faithful of his subjects, the best Commander he had among his troops, and moreover his son-in-law: but Saul, although he was King, judged that his own prestige was being eclipsed by his subject, and could not endure to see in his Kingdom a person of merit who caused himself to be esteemed and honored by all the world. Holy Scripture seems to indicate that he was not even considering a secret escape when he was told that his house was surrounded by armed men to seize him, so certain did he feel of his innocence. However, his wife Michal showed him the danger he was in and persuaded him, for the sake of saving his life, to flee through a window. God permitted that he was not discovered by Saul’s men, and thus he escaped this snare which, by all appearances, would have been fatal to him. The men whom the King had dispatched entered the house under the pretext of having a strict order to compel David to appear before the King in haste. The Princess, approaching them, said that David was sick and could not rise from his bed. These messengers then brought this answer back to the King, and the King commanded them to go into David’s chamber, and in case he was so sick that he could not rise, to bring him to the Court along with his bed, in whatever state it might be. To carry out this command, they returned to David’s home, and Michal, his spouse, let these men come by her husband’s bed. The first time, they had gone no further than the chamber door, where they thought they saw David in his bed; but this second time, when they approached it, they saw that Michal had played a trick on them, and that what they had mistaken for David was nothing but

<column-break/>

an image which the Princess had laid in his place and cleverly dressed up to make them believe it was a person. The Scripture says that she took an image or *Teraphim* <note>original: "Teraphim" - Hebrew: household idols or figurines</note>, and that having placed a goatskin at the bolster, she covered it with a cloth, so that this presentation looked very much like a person. These Teraphim were, among the Syrians and other Eastern peoples, the same as what the household gods or tutelary deities <note>original: "beschermgoden"</note> later were among the Greeks and Romans. Mention was first made of them in the history of Laban, from whom Rachel stole them when she fled with Jacob her husband to Mesopotamia; and mention is also made of them in the Book of Judges, in the passage where the story of Micah and the Levite, whom he had taken into his service, is recounted. One owes it to the piety and faith of David—whom the Scripture never reproached for any act of idolatry—to have the respect to believe that he either did not know that these Teraphim were in his house (just as Jacob had not known that Rachel had the Teraphim of her father Laban among her things and in his tent), or that it was simply an image that his wife had brought there and which was kept as a piece of art <term>kabinétstuk|a decorative object or collector's item kept for its beauty rather than for worship</term>, without making any superstitious use of it. Through this ruse, Michal thwarted Saul’s persecutions and saved David’s life.

Achimelech had no suspicion at all regarding the truth of this story, for David was one of the first officers of the Crown and the King’s son-in-law. He asked Achimelech for some refreshments, but the Priest was not at that moment able to provide him with any; and David seemed in such a hurry, and desired moreover that his arrival at Nob should be kept so secret, that Achimelech could not, nor did he dare to, send to his friends to request from them that which he would gladly have given to a man of such rank and merit. In this predicament, he took the <term>Showbread<note>Also called the 'Bread of the Presence,' these were twelve loaves placed weekly on a golden table in the Tabernacle. Normally, they were reserved strictly for the priests.</note></term>, which had been removed that day from the golden Table of the Sanctuary to be replaced by others according to the law of Moses; and although it was permitted to no one but the Priests to eat that holy bread, the High Priest nevertheless judged that in such a necessity as this, which concerned the interest and welfare of the State, he might well give those loaves to the King’s official and those of his following, after the assurance David gave him that neither he nor the men who accompanied him had defiled themselves, and that it was already the third or fourth day since they had been with their wives. Not that a lawful cohabitation is not always—according to the words of the Apostle Paul to the Hebrews—an undefiled bed; but since the Priests, who daily approach the altars, even though they were married, were nevertheless in some cases not permitted to touch their wives, because the marriage bed could on certain occasions be stained by a ceremonial impurity (as one sees in several of the laws of Moses), Achimelech desired that there should be at least as much of that kind of ceremonial purity in those men—to whom necessity alone allowed the giving of bread intended only for the holiest persons—as one could expect in people such as they were. The action of this High Priest was something unusual, but nevertheless, we do not read that when Saul put him to death because he had given this small assistance to David and his people, he charged him as a crime that he had given him the Showbread to eat: and Jesus Christ, the supreme and infallible Judge of the deeds of men, far from condemning this action, on the contrary openly approved it, as being in accordance with the sense and meaning of the Lawgiver. David also asked Achimelech for a weapon, for he did not even have his sword with him. Those who are accustomed to seeing persons of noble birth, especially those who hold some command among the troops, never appear in public without their swords, and therefore think that such has been the custom at all times, are surprised by this; but in ancient times it was not the custom, even among Military Commanders, never to go out except with a sword at one’s side, unless one had some duty of office to perform: and that was why David said to Achimelech that his departure had been so hasty that he had not had time to take his sword with him. Achimelech had no other weapons with him than Goliath’s sword, which was kept in the Tabernacle as a glorious trophy of the victory achieved over the Philistines; and since there was no man on earth who better deserved to wear that sword than he who had won it by his bravery, and

<column-break/>

who had been the very first to use it to strike off the Philistine's head, the Priest gave it to him; and David immediately departed with his people and continued his way and his flight.

<margin>The same year.</margin>
David fled from Nob to the land of the Philistines and took refuge at the Court of Achis, King of Gath. It is not known what reason he had for this; but the necessity of withdrawing from Saul's territory as quickly as he could, and the belief he had (though with far too little grounds) that he would not be known in the cities of the Philistines, were likely the principal reasons that made him take this decision. The fear of danger in battles and skirmishes does not disturb great souls who give themselves over to the protection of their nation or strive to uphold its honor; but it is a rare thing, and almost without example, that a man who sees himself persecuted by his own King, and who at every moment runs the risk of having his life taken, takes such steps which reveal nothing but a disturbance of the mind. Never had the Philistines had a more formidable enemy than David, and the famous Goliath, who for a long time had served them as a source of mockery against the Hebrews, but whose life David had taken through a skill and bravery that amazed the whole world, was from Gath—the very same city where David went to seek a hiding place. But he was soon recognized, and they said to the King: *Is this not David, the King of the land, in whose honor they sang in the dances and called to one another, Saul has slain his thousands, but David his ten thousands?* He then realized the mistake he had made in fleeing to the Philistines, and seeing no other means to save his life than to play the part of a man who has lost his mind, he changed his appearance; falling now to the ground, and then again scratching at the posts of the door, he meanwhile let his spit run into his beard, such that he was taken for a madman. Achis, feeling a loathing at the sight of this object, could not believe that it was that David of whom people spoke with such fame, and commanded that he should be let go.

Saul meanwhile, having learned from Doeg (one of his officials who by all misfortune happened to be at Nob when David passed through there) all that the High Priest had done for him, was in a fierce rage over it; and to take a terrible revenge for it, he wished to go to Nob himself to have the cruel decrees he had made against Achimelech and the other Priests carried out in his presence, even though they had had no hand in the act of their High Priest. Saul complained to him about what he had done for David—whom he called nothing else but "the son of Jesse"—and he accused Achimelech of having conspired against his person and royal dignity. The High Priest, being stunned by a complaint for which he had given no cause, answered the King wisely: that among all the officials of his house he knew no man more faithful to him than David, who had the honor of being his son-in-law, and to whom he could not have refused his request since, according to his word, he was passing through there on the express command of the King. But Saul was too much prejudiced by the poisonous report of Doeg, and by the rage he felt against David, to listen to the truth and the validity of the reasons which had moved Achimelech.

<summary>David receives the sacred Showbread and Goliath's sword from Achimelech at Nob before fleeing to Gath, where he narrowly escapes King Achis by feigning madness. King Saul, informed by Doeg the Edomite, prepares to execute the priests of Nob for their perceived conspiracy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the account of King Saul’s descent into paranoia and his pursuit of David. It follows the previous page where David had received the holy Showbread and Goliath's sword from the High Priest Ahimelech at Nob under the pretense of being on a royal mission.</meta>

### HISTORY of the O. TESTAMENT.

Saul was determined to act this way, to listen only to his own anger, and refused to be persuaded of the High Priest's innocence. He wanted, at any cost, for the High Priest to be found guilty, because he wished to sacrifice some of the most prominent leaders to his fury and vent his courage upon them, for lack of the one he truly desired, who had escaped him. He commanded his henchmen at the same time to fall upon Ahimelech and the other Priests, to sacrifice them to his vengeance, *“because their hand,”* he said in giving this inhuman command, *“is also with David, and because they knew that he was fleeing and did not reveal it to my ears.”* The commands of Kings are held as inviolable, and one owes them great obedience; but this obedience has its limits, and Saul’s henchmen did not believe they were free to overstep those boundaries which their conscience and their religion dictated to them on this occasion regarding their Prince’s command. They refused to serve his rage against the Priests of the Lord and to shed such pure and precious blood before the eyes of God. Doeg, who under a false appearance of being a Jewish proselyte <note>A convert to Judaism.</note> retained the Edomite heart given to him by his birth, was present at this refusal; the King turned to him and commanded him to strike all those Priests with the edge of the sword. This command was no sooner given than the rogue drew his sword, and like a mad lion rushing upon the venerable High Priest, he plunged the steel into his breast; and thus stained with the blood of this victim, he also thrust it into the bodies of the others, eighty-five in number. This slaughter passed from the Priests to the people: men, women, great and small, everything was sacrificed to the sword of the Tyrant, who did not leave even a single beast alive. Never had such fury extended further, but Saul was forsaken by God, whose vengeance sometimes, to punish the ingratitude and sins of His people, makes use even of those who are appointed to protect them.

<margin>The same year. 2944.</margin>
The mortal danger David had faced at the court of Achish <note>The King of Gath, a Philistine city.</note> forced him to vacate the land of the Philistines, fearing he would be no less recognized in other cities than in Gath. But whether he did not judge it advisable to distance himself from Judea to seek refuge in foreign lands and wait there until God had changed Saul’s heart toward him, or whether Providence directed matters to the point where they had to be to achieve the great purpose God had for him when He had him anointed by Samuel, or for other reasons which the Holy Scripture does not name, he returned again to his own land and chose the mountains of Judah as his refuge. The occupation of shepherd that he had practiced in his youth had given him a particular knowledge of all the places in the surrounding mountains of Bethlehem suitable for hiding fugitives, and such places were there in great number, because in those wildernesses there are a multitude of caves, many of which run very deep under the earth and between the rocks. His first refuge was the cave of Adullam, where his brothers and his father’s relatives came to find him; also to him came all those whose affairs had declined and who were troubled by their creditors, such that he gathered about four hundred men with him. His intention was not to create an uprising in the State

<column-break/>

and stir up a civil war there, even though the Kingdom was intended for him, and he had been anointed to that end by the Prophet Samuel more than ten years before; but he only wanted to prevent his enemies, taking advantage of his weakness, from easily attempting to capture him and deliver him to Saul. As soon as he had obtained this small assistance, he considered that nothing required greater haste than to provide for the safety of his father and his family, as he was constantly fearful of Saul’s unjust dealings and violence; for after what that Prince had done to the wretched city of Nob and the Priests of the Lord, David saw clearly that there could be no safety in Bethlehem for his father’s household and his brothers. He then took them with him and led them to the land of Moab, where the King of the Moabites received them with great generosity and gave to him and his kin such a place of refuge in his lands as he desired. However, God did not wish to leave him there long, but sent him His Prophet Gad to command him to return again to the land of Judah. David saw well that it was not without danger to venture again within Saul’s territory, but one is always in safety, as he himself has told us in his Psalms, when one walks under God’s oversight. Saul was soon informed of David’s arrival and prepared himself to have him seized. It happened meanwhile that the Philistines invaded the land with armed force and plundered the threshing floors of Keilah, in the Tribe of Judah. The inhabitants of that city begged David, who was not far off, to come to their aid with his people. He did not know if this was perhaps a trap set to deliver him to Saul once he was shut up within that city—which should have appealed to the King for relief rather than to him—or if they were acting in good faith. He had with him the Priest Abiathar, son of Ahimelech, whom God had miraculously preserved from the hands of Saul when he had all the other Priests who were at Nob killed. And since David wished to undertake nothing in such a delicate matter without asking God for advice through His Priest, the Lord had him told that he should march against the Philistines and that he would defeat them. He then set out and drove the enemies away from Keilah and defeated them completely. Saul soon had news of it, and rejoicing to hear that David had entered a city, as he said, provided with gates and bars, he imagined that he would not escape him, and he prepared to go and besiege him there. But God had David told that if he stayed there longer, the inhabitants of that city, however much they were indebted to him, would deliver him to Saul. He then hastened to depart from there with his band, which had increased by two hundred men and now consisted of six hundred. The Scripture says that they *“went wherever they could go,”* just like people who do not know whom to trust or where to hide. They then withdrew to the wilderness of Ziph; and the inhabitants of those mountains immediately let Saul know this and offered to deliver David to him. But God, who protected him, inspired him to leave that place and go to another mountain, called the wilderness of Maon, which likewise lay in the Tribe of Judah. Saul marched with his people directly toward that place, and because he had many people with him, David saw himself surrounded on all sides, without

## *David shows Saul from a distance a corner of his cloak that he had cut in the cave, without Saul having noticed it.*

### I Samuel Chapter XXIV. verses 9–12.

<margin>The same year, 2944.</margin> <note>This date follows the "Anno Mundi" system, counting years from the creation of the world.</note>
If Saul had wisely reflected on the wondrous way God had protected David from his persecutions until that time, he would have ceased his intention of relentlessly hunting him down to take the life of someone whose only crime was being loved and esteemed, and deserving that such was his lot. But it was a judgment of God upon Saul that he was incapable of reflection, and that he plunged himself into his own ruin by seeking that of another. David, not daring to remain long in one place for fear of betrayal or of being overwhelmed by Saul’s troops, was constantly wandering from one wilderness to another. All places seemed safe to him as long as he was far from them, but everywhere he saw his destruction, if God did not take care to keep and protect him. He had moved from the wilderness of Maon to that of Engedi; it was nothing but rocks, precipices, and inaccessible places, except for the wild goats <note>original: "steenbokken," referring to the Nubian Ibex</note> and other such wild animals, according to the description that Holy Scripture gives us of it. Saul did not let himself be deterred by such an unfavorable state of the landscape, and because his mistrust made him fear that if he sent his people into those difficult and rugged places, they would return without 

<column-break/>

bringing David to him—due to the secret understanding <note>A suspected conspiracy or sympathy among the soldiers for David.</note> they might hold with that supposed rebel—he wanted to go and seek him in person. Undoubtedly it was a degradation of the royal state to see a King running from wilderness to wilderness and through inaccessible paths to catch one man; but everything tastes sweet to revenge, and it finds nothing too base or unbecoming if only it can be satisfied. David was hidden with his men in a cave, and Saul, thinking they were elsewhere, had imprudently gone in to relieve himself <note>original: "om zyn gevoeg te doen," a polite contemporary euphemism for using the bathroom</note>. His supposed enemy took that opportunity to softly cut a corner <note>original: "slip," referring to the edge or hem of the garment.</note> from his cloak, without Saul—whose mind was occupied with thoughts that did not allow him to take any notice of the place where he had gone—noticing in the least what was happening at his side. He then left the cave with as little notice as he had entered it, and his people, weary of searching for David in nearly inaccessible places, utterly despaired of finding him there; and he himself gave up hope, as did the others, and turned his thoughts elsewhere. When they had all moved away a little, and David saw them at such a distance that it was not very likely they would return to him—due to the great difficulty of the passage—he wanted to show the King how poorly founded were the complaints he made of David plotting against his life, and at once erase the impression which such ghastly accusations might have made on a large part of his soldiers, who did not fully [know] the piety and nobility of David...

David had reason to complain, but not to take revenge, and he thanked God shortly thereafter that He had prevented him from carrying out such a violent resolution. Nabal was married to a woman named Abigail, who was as wise and prudent as her husband was foolish; she was informed by one of her servants of the unjust answer that Nabal had given to David’s people, and this servant, who was one of the shepherds of Nabal’s flock, gave witness to Abigail that they had received nothing but good service from the soldiers who were with David in those mountains, without having any reason to complain that any wrong had ever been done to them by him. Abigail understood immediately that this was a matter that could plunge her husband and his house, indeed all of them, into ruin; and seeing that she must not lose any time, she had her people gather two hundred loaves of bread, two leather skins of wine, five prepared sheep, and many other foodstuffs, which she had loaded onto donkeys, which she sent ahead of her to make a gift of them to David. David then resumed the way to his wilderness, and Abigail the way to Carmel. Upon her return she found Nabal in the merriment of a feast, not knowing what his wife had done to keep him and his whole house alive. The state in which she saw him, full of wine and immersed in his pleasures, did not allow her to tell him anything of her journey; but the next day she gave him an account of it. Thereupon this man was so struck by the danger he had run without knowing anything of it, that he remained as if immovable; the Scripture says that his heart became like a stone in his bosom; and ten days later he died. David recognized that God, who had prevented his hands from taking revenge on Nabal, had Himself taken vengeance through the ways of His Providence; and he had conceived such a great esteem for the wisdom and the understanding that he had perceived in this entire conduct of Abigail, who was moreover very beautiful, that he requested her hand in marriage, and married her shortly thereafter.

David was not dismayed at the sight of this army, and instead of fleeing elsewhere, he made the boldest and rarest decision ever heard of: to sneak into the enemy camp at night and make his way even to the King’s tent. Doubtless, he was aware of the army’s arrangement, the carelessness of Saul, and the negligence of his people in guarding the camp and the King. He revealed his plan to two of his best friends—namely, Ahimelech the Hittite <note>A non-Israelite warrior serving David</note> and Abishai, the brother of Joab. To this it must be added that this Prince, rejected by God and left to the governance of his own heart, lost all the fruit of this work by taking his final refuge in those black arts <note>Original: "zwartekonft"; referring here to necromancy or sorcery</note> which were summoned up from Hell. The Soothsayer at first made great difficulty in admitting that she employed that art, and she said to the one who spoke that he could not be unaware of what Saul had done to root out the Sorcerers and all those who had a divining spirit from the land; she complained about this man, saying he had come to set a trap for her destruction. She did not know it was Saul himself to whom she spoke. But this man encouraged her, and the woman—not wishing to lose the profit of her art, since usually such a sort of people do not practice their juggling act except for gain—having begun to put her sorcery to work, the man who had come to her for advice asked if she saw anyone appearing. Upon seeing him appear, she realized that he who came to her for advice was Saul; she was entirely terrified by this and gave a great cry, believing her life was lost.
