If this Prince had used even a little of his reason, he would have been able to notice from these first words the crudeness of the deception with which he was being misled; for the rest of the Saints after this life does not depend on such a small thing that it is in the power of a sorceress to disturb it, according to the wise remarks of the Author of the *Questions on the Old and New Testament* <note>Original: "Vraagen over 't Oude en Nieuwe Testament"; referring to the *Quaestiones Veteris et Novi Testamenti*, a work once attributed to St. Augustine but likely by a contemporary known as Ambrosiaster</note>, which one finds among the works of Augustine. One did not even need to be a devil to predict such things in some way, which one could, so to speak, grasp with the hand. It was clearly evident that Saul was a Prince abandoned by God; one saw the military might of the Philistines and the dismay of Israel; it was known among men and devils that David was to reign after Saul's death; but there was little appearance that he would ascend the throne as long as Jonathan, the presumed heir to the Crown and David's bosom friend, lived. Such was the mournful end of a Prince whose reign had had very glorious beginnings, but whose continuation was stained by such crimes that made him the object of God’s wrath—whose authority and laws ought to be respected by Sovereigns no less than those Sovereigns, who have all their exalted state from Him, wish to be respected and obeyed by their people.

The inhabitants of Jabesh-Gilead owed their freedom, property, and lives to Saul, who had come to their aid against the Ammonites, and through that glorious expedition had begun the service of his Kingly office. The memory of that great obligation was not erased from their minds, and after forty years they still retained all the feeling for it, which a favor of inestimable value for that city deserved. After the defeat, the entire army had fled and left the bodies of Saul and his sons among the other dead, without daring to go look for them and take them up to bury them. The Philistines, who had remained masters of the field, had recognized the corpses of Saul and his three sons among the dead while stripping them; and after having robbed them of their weapons—which they subsequently sent around all their cities with the head of Saul to serve as a trophy of victory among their peoples—they brought them to one of their cities called Beth-shan and hung them on the walls for display. But the inhabitants of Jabesh-Gilead could not endure that the bodies of their King and of their Princes should remain unburied, and serve any longer as a mockery and reproach to the Philistines. They then decided to go and take them away by night: this was a bold and dangerous undertaking, but there was found within Jabesh a company of valiant men who were courageous enough to carry this out. Their alertness and courage overcame all danger, and they had the honor of returning with this precious spoil which they had wrested from the enemies. They brought these corpses to their city, where they were first burned before the honor of burial was given to their bones. The custom of burning the dead was very common among the Romans, but it was not the practice of the Jews, and this is the first example of it found in the Scripture, and possibly the oldest that one reads of in any History. While David, with his band of six hundred Hebrews, was busy pursuing the Amalekites—who had plundered and burned Ziklag—the Philistines engaged Saul in a field battle. The raid of the Amalekites served at that time as one of the secret driving forces of divine Providence, as they arrived at the right moment to pull David out of one of the worst positions he had ever found himself in his entire life, and from which one cannot conceive how he could have saved himself without staining his good name, which God did not allow to be defiled. David had already taken refuge in the states of Achish <note>The Philistine King of Gath</note> for fourteen months, and that King, a few days before the battle was held, had ordered David and the Hebrews in his retinue to join his army. Achish had no such mistrust at all; he held such a high opinion of the integrity of this Commander that he judged him incapable of such false dealings. If this King had not been deceived in his thoughts, then David and his six hundred Hebrews would have had to fight against Israel, lending their bravery and swords to the Philistines to bring God's people under the yoke and shed the blood of their brothers. God had then sent the Amalekites at the right time to remove all cause for Philistine mistrust against David, and also so that he would turn his weapons against Amalek, who was as much an enemy of the Philistines as of the Jews. And to confirm this story of Saul's death with evidence, he showed David the crown he had taken from the King's head and an armlet that Saul had worn on his arm. David was bitterly grieved over the death of Saul and Jonathan, and he felt himself very vividly struck by the loss that the people of Israel had suffered in that battle. His soldiers whom he had with him also testified that they were very moved by it, and they all mingled their lamentations and tears together and fasted that entire day. The Amalekite, meanwhile, who had hurried so much to bring this sad news and who claimed the honor of a crime he had not committed, awaited the reward that his greedy and dishonorable heart had expected from David once his first tears had dried. But this holy man had, all his life, held too much respect for his King and had too elevated and noble feelings in his heart to reward a villain who boasted of having taken his life. Having then called him to himself, he said to him:

And thereupon he called one of his people and commanded him to fall upon that man and kill him. David showed, through this wise and noble conduct, that however much change Saul’s death must bring to his own state—since it called him back from his exile to his fatherland and left the throne vacant for him—such great advantages were nevertheless not powerful enough to make any impression on his mind that was contrary to the submission he owed to God and the deep respect he had always borne for his King.

After Saul's death, David asked God for counsel through the Priest Abiathar, who had remained with him constantly, to know whether he should return to the land of Israel, and to which city. But the Spirit of God does not conform to the judgment and thoughts of men, and because it blows where it wishes, it often moves those whom it fills with its light and inspires with its divine fire to do such things which the wisdom and considerations of the flesh—which is a true enmity against God—judges unbecoming for a wise man, under the pretext that they do not always remain within the usual rules of the Wise of this world.

If the Ark in the house of Obed-Edom had been an abundant source of blessings, it was no less so in that of David. This Prince was prosperous in all his undertakings, and God daily added some new happiness to his reign. David, for his part, was so sensitive to this that, to show his gratitude to God, he made a resolution to build Him a glorious Temple; he made his intention known to the Prophet Nathan, and spoke to him thus: *I dwell in a house of cedar, and the Ark of God dwells only in a Tabernacle, and in the midst of curtains.* Nathan was as if enraptured to see such exalted and holy thoughts in that Prince, and therefore told him that he should simply carry out his intention, not doubting that it would be very pleasing to God. However, the Prophet said this of himself, and the following night God revealed Himself to him, to command him to tell David that the Lord indeed approved of his intention, but nevertheless did not want him to execute it, because having spent his whole life in heavy wars, his hands had shed much blood. To nonetheless not leave the godly intention of David without some reward, Nathan had orders to tell him that God was about to give him a son whose reign would be peaceful and illustrious, and that this son, the greatest and most distinguished of all Kings, would build him a house.

<column-break/>

David, comforted by this promise, desisted from his intention to found a Temple, and contented himself with making some preparations for it, leaving them to the son who was to follow him, and who would have the honor of carrying out such a great design. Around that time, David had a war with those of Zobah, and God so blessed his arms that he defeated their army, took a vast number of prisoners, and caused twenty-two thousand men of the bands of the King of Damascus, who had come to the aid of the King of Zobah, to fall; furthermore, he made all those peoples tributary. After he had returned from that glorious campaign, the Edomites also tested the strength of his arms and lost eighteen thousand men in a battle. Amidst all these victories, he remembered the tender friendship that had formerly existed between him and Jonathan. This Prince had left a son named Mephibosheth, who was lame in both his feet: David had him brought to him, and assuring him of his favor, he had all the goods that had belonged to the house of Saul restored to him, and had him always eat at his table like the Princes, his sons. Nahash, King of the Ammonites, whom Saul had caused to retreat from Jabesh with great loss at the beginning of his reign, had given protection in his lands to David when he was being persecuted by Saul. This Prince happened to die, and David, receiving news of it, sent Ambassadors to Hanun his son, to offer condolences and to perform the duties of a sincere friendship and gratitude. This new King took this honorable and noble conduct of David toward him poorly, and puffed up by false reasons and a suspicious statecraft, he allowed himself to be convinced by those of his Council that David, under the cloak of an embassy, hid an evil intention against him, that he aimed at his Kingdom, and that it was to spy out the ways and fortifications that he had sent these Ambassadors. There was no validity in all these reasons, but for that they did not fail to make an impression on the mind of Hanun, so that they also drove him to an act that, above all others, conflicted with statesmanship and justice, and that was to violate the law of nations in an unseemly manner in the persons of the Ambassadors, whose office from all times, even among the least civilized and roughest peoples, has been regarded as sacred. Hanun had the beards of David's Ambassadors half-shaved off, and their clothes cut off as far as the buttocks, after which he sent them back to Judea. They let the King know what kind of treatment they had been given, and David sent them word that they should stay at Jericho until their beards had grown again, so that they would not be seen in Jerusalem in such a shameful state. Meanwhile, the Ammonites saw well that by such an insulting act they had brought a war with David upon their necks; to be able to defend themselves against such a mighty enemy, they had thirty-three thousand Syrians come to their aid. David did not go out in this war in person, but he contented himself with sending Joab and Abishai, to whom he gave the command over his troops. The Ammonites, seeing themselves the strongest in number, believed that if they made two armies, one of which consisted of their own military force and the other of that of the Syrians, they would then [defeat] the army of the Israelites...

## *David, walking upon a flat roof, sees Bathsheba bathing, and is seized with an unchaste inclination toward her.*

### II. Samuel Chapter XI. verses 2—4.

<margin>The year of the world 2962. Before J. C. 1035.</margin>
The history of David has, until now, shown us nothing but great virtues in his person; but the most perfect holiness found on earth is subject to stumbles, and, so to speak, to eclipses, which make it almost entirely disappear. A year after the great victory which the army of Israel, led by Joab and Abishai, had achieved over the Ammonites, David again sent his military bands against them under the leadership of the same commanders, who besieged Rabbah, the capital of the Kingdom. This Prince, blessed and favored by Heaven, remained meanwhile in Jerusalem, soothed by the sweetness of such a happy and glorious reign as his was. But it once happened that, having gone to take the fresh air on a flat roof of his Palace, he saw from afar a woman who was bathing, and who had not possessed the caution which persons of her sex <note>original: "persoonen van haare kunne"</note> ought always to have on such occasions—to avoid being seen from any place, and to ensure that no one’s wandering gaze from one side or the other could reach her. That of David was in this state; he walked upon the flat of his roof, and his eyes, which he

<column-break/>

allowed to wander here and there without any intent, happened to fall upon this woman, who was entering the bath. She was of an uncommon beauty, and the impulse of unchastity, welling up in the heart of the King through this unexpected object, darkened all his reasonable understanding, and brought his virtue and piety under the yoke. He learned that this woman was Bathsheba, and that she was married to one of the officers of his army named Uriah, who was at the siege of Rabbah. The temptation of sin, that sin which had already occupied David's heart, immediately made him think that he was King, and virtue did not have the strength to remind him that he was a subject of God, and that he consequently had to respect the Law which forbade adultery. He misused the power that the status of King gave him and had Bathsheba brought to him. He learned shortly thereafter that she was pregnant; and whether it was that he was ashamed to have stained his Royal state through adultery, or that he feared—which is more likely—that he could not save the life of Bathsheba (who by the Law of Moses <note>The Mosaic Law prescribed the death penalty for both parties involved in adultery.</note> was doomed to the death penalty for the crime of adultery) without exposing himself too much, he immediately gave orders to summon Uriah from the army. This man, who did not know the reason why he was summoned, came and immediately presented himself to the King. David asked him some questions regarding the army and the siege, and after speaking with him as long as he judged necessary to maintain decorum, he commanded him to go home. Uriah, who was of a tender piety and a strict virtue, judged that it did not befit him to go sleep in his house, and the...

We owe the memory of the Saints <note>In this context, "Saints" refers to the holy figures of the Bible, such as David.</note> this respect: not to dwell too extensively upon their failings, nor to show them from every side in such a way that their excesses are seen at their clearest; but meanwhile, we ought to make prudent observations for ourselves regarding the natural corruption of the human heart, which caused the purest faith and the liveliest piety of a David, and many other Saints, to succumb, to the end that even their fall should serve to confirm us in virtue, and that we should learn from all those sad examples that our faith and our piety are never out of danger, so long as the passions lie as if asleep around our hearts, because often no more than a word, or a glance of the eyes, as with David, is needed to awaken them.

was deeply affected. David was immediately so moved by the sickness of this child that nothing was able to drive away his heartache or remove his fear; he not only fasted and poured out prayers to God for several days, but he also could not be persuaded to join those of his Court at the table. He remained in his room, where, giving himself over to his grief, he lay stretched out upon the ground and spent whole nights there. This sorrow was undoubtedly too powerful to have been produced by nature and the simple love of a father alone: the heart could not yet have formed such strong bonds with a child that was only just born to give itself over to such an excess of mourning and dejection. When reason gives even a little aid to fatherly weakness, it will easily prevent one from stepping into an extravagance in such instances—an extravagance that does not honor a man, much less a Hero such as David was, or a Prophet and a Saint. It must, therefore, necessarily have been that something more than a father’s tenderness lay in this grief, which had nothing common or mediocre about it; piety undoubtedly had a greater share in it than Nature. David was convinced within himself that the deadly illness of this child was a blow struck by the hand of God in His wrath, and it could not help but make him very faint-hearted when he viewed the child as a victim being offered, in a sense, in his place. He saw that God, who had told him through His Prophet, *You shall not die*, was now taking away the life of the child while sparing that of the father. Seeing the child sick and near death, he did everything that piety could inspire him to do to ward off, through his prayers, the blow that was about to fall upon his son. But when he saw that God had ordained otherwise, he offered up his will to that of God, holding himself certain that God had not remitted the eternal punishment of the guilty father’s sin only to transfer it onto his child, who was innocent. David’s Courtiers stood amazed to see such a sudden change in the Prince, noticing that he was comforted in an instant over a death, the mere fear of which had overwhelmed him with sadness; but he gave them a reason for it that ought to serve us as a lesson in resignation and humility:

> While the child was still alive, he said, I fasted and wept; for I said, Who knows, the LORD may be gracious to me, that the child may live? But now he is dead, why should I now

But God was preparing torments for David that were even more terrible than the death of this child, and two years later he saw in his household those horrific calamities with which Nathan had threatened him. He gave himself over to his raging lust, thinking of nothing but the means to satisfy it, in defiance of all divine and human laws. The hellish Spirit lent him the counsel of another villain like himself; and God, who wished to carry out those terrible judgments against David with which He had threatened him, and to punish one sinner through another, allowed in His wrath that the brother should dishonor the sister. Thus, in the palace of the King of Israel, one of the most abominable crimes was committed—one that could only occur in the houses of the most shameless among the Heathens and Unbelievers. two years later, having prepared a great feast in the country on the day of the sheep-shearing (following the simple manner and custom of that time), he invited all the Princes his brothers and many other Nobles of the Court. The wretched Amnon, who imagined that Absalom no longer thought of the past because he had forgotten it himself—as sinners do who move from one passion to another and from this crime to that—allowed himself to attend this banquet. # David, fleeing from Absalom, is cursed with insults by Shimei.

### II. Samuel Chapter XVI. verses 5—13.

However loathsome Amnon's offense was, it was not for Absalom to take revenge for it. It is true that the honor of his sister, violated by Amnon, concerned him deeply, but he should have let the justice of the King his father act against him, and not have committed a murder—indeed, a fratricide—to avenge an incestuous act. But it seems that David had to be weighed down by torments and grief of a very uncommon nature

<column-break/>

after he himself had fallen into such horrific crimes as his adultery with Bathsheba and the death of Uriah. The death of Amnon, however guilty he was, provided David with a new cause for mourning and tears. What increased the anguish of his soul on that occasion was that if the dead man was his son, the murderer was likewise his son; he could not avenge the death of the one through the punishment of the other without filling his house with his own blood. Meanwhile, it was to be feared for Absalom that the King's justice might one day gain the upper hand over the father's love, and that the voice of Nature would be found too weak to be heard beneath that of the laws, which demanded his condemnation. The safest course for him, then, was to leave the Kingdom immediately and seek a refuge in foreign lands.

The people generally love changes, and since there is no Government so perfect that restless and difficult Spirits cannot find something to say against it, one sometimes imagines an improvement by changing Masters. Absalom had, besides that, a very distinguished appearance, and was nonetheless very familiar in his dealings with the people; and David began to yield somewhat under the weight of the years of a life that had been full of turmoil. ### Absalom's death.

#### II. Samuel Chapter XVIII. verses 9--14.

<margin>

The first steps that Absalom took to climb the throne of his father succeeded as he wished. Jerusalem opened its gates to him, and those who most condemned the rebellion dared not refuse the rebel the obedience which he unjustly demanded. But God, who did not intend to destroy David, and who only wanted to discipline him further for the great crime he had committed through adultery with Bathsheba, did not allow Absalom to draw from this initial success of his rebellion those advantages which he might naturally, and according to the state of affairs, have expected. He did not make use of the prudent advice which Ahithophel, the shrewdest politician of his time, gave him; this man wanted Absalom to have pursued David in his flight without giving him time to recover. But the Usurper <note>original: "Geweldenaar" — meaning one who takes power by force or a tyrant.</note>, seeing himself master of the throne, was all too well 

<column-break/>

pleased that he should have pursued a King who was almost abandoned and whom he did not believe was powerful enough to harm him. He extended his contempt for David even further, and to add incest to his rebellion, he abused the wives of the King his father. Yes, he had the impudence to commit this dishonorable debauchery in the sight of the Sun, and to some extent before the eyes of all the people, having a tent pitched on the flat roof of the royal Palace, to commit such crimes as a common sense of shame cannot hear told without blushing. This was one of the calamities which the Prophet Nathan had foretold to David, and this prophecy, as unlikely as it was then, could not fail to be fulfilled because it came from God. The dethroned King meanwhile, who to save his life had gone to one of the most remote corners of his Kingdom on the other side of the Jordan, did not fail to make use of the time the rebel gave him to work toward his restoration. At that time, he found himself at the head of an army powerful enough to protect him. He wished to command it in person, but everyone advised him against it, fearing that he might be captured or killed in the battle. The King listened to the reasoning and the pleas of his subjects, and he handed over command of his troops to Joab, expressly ordering him before the entire army to spare the person of Absalom and not to take his life. The army of these rebels was much more numerous than that of the King, and if God had not been for David, the victory would likely have gone to Absalom. The two armies came to blows, and they fought on both sides with great bravery; but finally, that of Absalom—which, through the great loss it suffered, was constantly diminishing—was forced to retreat. Absalom led his troops into battle with an undaunted heart, and he was in the thick of the fray just as much as the least of his commanders; but finally, the hour had come when the mutiny and the Mutineer both had to be suppressed at once. This Prince was forced to take flight, and having thrown himself into a nearby forest to save himself, his hair, which swung over his shoulders, became entangled between two thick branches under which Absalom had to stoop to ride through with his mule; such that he found himself fixed to these boughs by his long and strong hair, where his mule, which ran on without stopping, left him hanging between heaven and earth. Such an accident could hardly happen today, because one would not easily find someone with such long and thick hair as would be required to thus entwine itself around the branches of a tree and be able to carry the weight of the entire body. But the hair of Absalom was altogether something rare, for the Scripture notes that this Prince had it cut from time to time,

<column-break/>

and that it weighed two hundred <term>shekels<note>Original: "fikelen". An ancient unit of weight used by the Israelites.</note></term> according to the King’s weight, which would be about six pounds, if the shekel of the King’s weight was the same as that which formerly, and in the Books of Moses, was called the shekel of the Sanctuary: but if it weighed only half as much, as is generally believed, then Absalom’s head of hair would still have weighed three pounds. The oils or balsams which were used at that time among the Eastern peoples, and with which they coated the hair so thickly that it sometimes almost dripped from it, served in no small way to add a heavy weight to it, which could not be anything but very great in hair that was exceptionally long and thick. But be that as it may, Absalom remained hanging by his hair, and Joab, who was pursuing him, having been informed of this, came running and struck three arrows into his heart, which brought death to this Prince. Joab then immediately had the retreat sounded, and having reassembled his troops, he sent messengers to the King to make known to him the winning of the field battle. David asked the one who brought him the news whether Absalom was also killed, and when he was told that the Prince had lost his life, he was so saddened by it that he was heard crying out as he went: *My son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! O that I, I, had died for you, Absalom, my son, my son!* Joab, being informed of the King’s extraordinary mourning over Absalom’s death, hastened to point out to him that such a thing would be powerful enough to cool the zeal which his subjects had shown for his restoration. The King listened to the wise remarks of this General, and having tempered his grief, he openly testified how well satisfied he was with the bravery of his troops, and he set out on his way to return again to Jerusalem.

### *The head of the rebel Sheba, who was besieged by Joab in the city of Abel, is thrown to him over the city wall.*

### II Samuel Chapter XX. verse 22.

<margin>The same year 2981</margin>
The death of Absalom ought to have been followed by the execution of a great number of the principal conspirators who had sided with him; and even if a King were not like another man, prone to revenge, nevertheless the laws and politics usually require examples of justice and severity against rebellious subjects to prevent similar disorder in the State. But the gentleness and magnanimity of the King prevailed over all the reasons of a disturbed mind and a fearful policy, and he granted pardon to all the guilty: indeed, he even forgave the insolent and bold Shimei, who had so cruelly insulted him. The latter, terrified of the danger in which he saw himself after the death of Absalom, was one of the first who came running to David to pray for his mercy, and he brought a thousand men of his Tribe, which was that of Benjamin, with him. The King granted mercy to this villain, who had deserved the punishment of death. Abishai judged

<column-break/>

Why should I put a man of Israel to death today, now that the Lord has restored me to the throne?" David knew better than anyone else the greatness of Shimei’s crime, but he also knew that he himself was a thousand times more guilty before God, and he saw that it was a day of grace for him, since God gave him back the Kingdom that he had already nearly lost, and for that reason he found himself unable to refuse grace to anyone. This sensible woman went to make this proposal to the prominent men of Abel, who thereupon seized the Mutineer and cut off his head, which they threw over the walls to the besiegers. As soon as Joab had seen it, he broke off the siege, and all the disturbances ended at the same time in the Kingdom.

->II. Samuel XXI. vs. 1.<-

The King did not doubt that there must be an uncommon cause for which God was thus angered against his people, and having asked Him through the Priest—who was clothed with the Ephod and wore the Urim and Thummim <note>The Urim and Thummim were sacred objects used by the High Priest to determine God's will; their exact nature remains a mystery to historians.</note> on his breast—the Lord answered that it was on account of Saul and his bloody house, because he had put the Gibeonites to death. These were descendants of the first Gibeonites who had come to Joshua, and who, through a hasty decision by him and the chief leaders of Israel, had obtained the promise that he would do them no harm, provided that they and their cities would stand under the power of the Israelites <note>original: "overyling" — referring to the event in Joshua 9 where the Gibeonites tricked the Israelites into a treaty.</note>. This covenant was confirmed by a solemn oath, and since that time the Gibeonites had remained among the Jews as a sort of servants or slaves, without the faith of that ancient treaty ever being violated. But under the pretense that the Gibeonites were a remnant of those Canaanite nations which the Jews, according to the command given to them, were to exterminate, Saul wished to demonstrate his zeal by stirring up a violent persecution against them, notwithstanding the solemn oath that his ancestors had sworn to them. God had never demanded the execution of those first and ancient commands—given for the destruction of all the peoples of Palestine—to the detriment of this oath; and this King, who had little insight into the duties of the conscience of Sovereigns, did not observe that an oath solemnly made in the name of the State, and ratified by the descendants of those who swore it (especially when such is done for the benefit of subjects), also binds the conscience of those who ascend the throne after them. False zeal does not care for many such considerations; but believing on the contrary that

<column-break/>

it was a meritorious work before God to exceed the bounds of a wise and regulated piety, Saul put these poor Gibeonites to death, who had no other bulwark than their innocence and the faith of the first treaty, strengthened by long possession. This unjust and violent dealing displeased God, who cannot let the violation of an oath made in His name go unpunished; and through a judgment that is almost incomprehensible to human reason, and of which the specific motives and grounds are unknown to us, He severely punished the people for the perjury of the King, and that even long after the death of the guilty party. David then asked the Gibeonites, who remained after the slaughter Saul had committed among them, what satisfaction they desired, so that they might subsequently pray for the entire Realm, which God had stricken for their sake. They answered that it was not a matter of silver or gold for them, but only that it might please the King to deliver to them seven sons of Saul, to hang them on gallows. David granted them their request, however unusual it was; but sparing Mephibosheth, so as not to violate the oath he had sworn to his father Jonathan never to destroy his lineage, he took two sons from one of Saul’s wives named Rizpah, and five from Merab, Saul’s daughter—whom Michal her sister and David's consort (who never had children) had adopted <note>The text clarifies a biblical discrepancy: while 2 Samuel 21:8 mentions Michal, Merab is traditionally identified as the biological mother of these five sons.</note>—and he handed all seven over to the Gibeonites. They had them hanged on gallows which they had erected on a mountain before Gibeah, the city of Saul, to appease God’s wrath: and by that means Judea was delivered from the famine.

God's scourges <term>scourges: divine punishments or afflictions</term> followed shortly after one another in Judea, and the civil wars, followed by a famine of three years, could not but cause a very great destruction there. Nothing more was missing but the plague to further devastate this Kingdom, against which God had long been angered. David soon brought the same upon the land through an act that ignited God's wrath anew. David found himself peaceful and at rest in his States since the defeat of Absalom and the death of Sheba, and after a few years, his Kingdom hardly felt the loss it had suffered. David tasted with all too great a pleasure the honor of reigning, and in prosperity his heart did not retain that inward humility from which the Kings of the world should never consider themselves exempt. He decided to have his people counted, in order to know the entire military power of his Kingdom. Joab, to whom he revealed this intention, tried to dissuade him from it; but the King remained by his first decision and commanded Joab to carry it out. At the end of ten months, the census was completed, and it was found that in the entire Kingdom there were more than thirteen hundred thousand men capable of bearing arms. God became angry with David because he had commanded this census out of a motive of pride and vanity, and He had him informed by the Prophet Gad that he might choose one from these three 

<column-break/>

scourges: namely, either a famine of seven years throughout his entire Kingdom; or to flee from place to place for three months before the sword of a conquering enemy; or that the plague should rage in his land for three days in a row. David answered the Prophet: *I am in great distress: let us fall into the hand of the Lord, for his mercies are many; but let me not fall into the hand of men.* He then chose a plague of three days over the other scourges. Immediately the Plague came into the cities and onto the land throughout the entire Kingdom, and snatched away seventy thousand people in less than one day. An Angel made this scourge fly in all directions and spread with an incredible speed, and just as he was ready to strike the city of Jerusalem—which, being the most populous place in the Kingdom, was about to see its streets and houses full of the dead or dying—God had compassion for these poor people, and said to the Angel who was doing the destruction: *It is enough, withdraw your hand.* The Angel stood still, and the plague did not proceed in Jerusalem. David built an altar at the place where the Angel had stopped, which was the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite, and at that same place, not long after, the Temple of Solomon was founded.

When he was seen to decline daily in this manner, and that there were several sons capable of succeeding him in the government, Adonijah, who after Absalom's death was the eldest of all, imagined that the Kingdom [belonged] to him by right of his birth...

His cunning did not extend to inviting Solomon, who, suspecting nothing, would no more than the others have guarded himself against the snare being set for them: but God does not allow men to always do what they otherwise could, when such might serve to the detriment of His purpose; He had a plan for Solomon that was incomprehensible to the political maneuvering of Adonijah, and even the hasty steps of that impatient Prince to rule were to remove him from the throne forever, and caused Solomon to ascend it sooner than he could have done if matters had taken their usual and natural course. The Prophet Nathan, the Priest Zadok, and many other persons of standing had no part at all in Adonijah's plot, and their respectful devotion to David had not permitted them to get involved in that party, nor to do anything to the detriment of the King's objective. The Priest Zadok and the Prophet Nathan received the command to carry out the King's orders; and these two men of God, accompanied by all the Officers of the Crown who had not been invited to Adonijah's banquet, had Solomon mount the King's mule, as David had commanded, and led him with great ceremony to the place David had named for them; and Zadok, who had taken a horn of oil from the Tabernacle, anointed him publicly, amidst the sound of trumpets and the acclamations of the people, who cried from all sides: *Long live King Solomon.* Solomon was subsequently led with this grand procession to the royal Palace to take possession of the throne there, and the joy was so great throughout the city of Jerusalem that the sacred Writer <note>The biblical author of the Book of Kings</note> could only express it by borrowing from hyperbole <term>hyperbole: a figure of speech using exaggeration for emphasis</term> the strength which natural wording lacked, saying that the earth split from the sound of the joy. Adonijah's invited guests, hearing this unusual sound within Jerusalem, wanted to know what it was; and understanding that it was the anointing and crowning of Solomon, whom David had appointed as his Successor, they quickly dispersed, and took flight, one to one side and another to the other, for fear of being taken into custody and punished by the new King. Adonijah ran to the Tabernacle as the readiest and surest hiding place he could find, and grabbed the horns of the bronze altar <note>original: "kóperen altaar"</note> that stood in the forecourt. Solomon was informed of this, and had it said to that Prince that he granted him mercy and gave assurance for his life, provided that in the future he would conduct himself so as to give no evil suspicion of his loyalty and zeal. Adonijah then came to thank the King, and Solomon confirmed to him with his own mouth the assurance he had granted him.

## Solomon has the Temple built. Solomon has the golden Altar, the Table of Showbread, and other holy vessels made.
### 1 Kings Chapter 6, verse 1 etc. and Chapter 7, verse 48.

<margin>The Year of the World 2993. Before J.C. 1011.</margin> <note>Early modern historians often used the "Year of the World" (Anno Mundi) to date events from the biblical creation. J.C. refers to Jesus Christ.</note>
Solomon had requested nothing from God but wisdom, and God, to reward him for the lack of concern that Prince had shown regarding the riches of the earth, gave him such an abundance of them that the like had never been seen under any reign. Silver had become so common in Judea that it was hardly valued, and one can scarcely imagine the immeasurable amount of gold found there, which increased from year to year. Solomon hallowed all these treasures through the use he made of them to build the most magnificent Temple the world had ever seen, and the first that God had ever possessed there. David, who had desired to be allowed to found it, but to whom God had said that this honor was reserved for Solomon, had left his son some costly preparations: but Solomon designed such a magnificent and glorious plan for the Temple he wished to build, that for its completion an

<column-break/>

uncommon abundance of all kinds of precious things was required, and it was necessary to have workmen almost beyond number to prepare the materials or to join them together. He wished to use for this building only the most beautiful stones that could be found, and there were eighty thousand men at work, either to hew them from the quarries or to polish them and further work them, so that Art and Nature, conspiring together as if in competition, might contribute to this building everything that each had most perfect. All the wood had to be either cedar or fir, but primarily the most precious of all timber. It grew in abundance on Mount Lebanon, which lay in the territory of the King of Tyre; and Solomon, having obtained permission from that Prince to have as much of it cut as he desired, employed thirty thousand men, both to cut down the cedars and to <term>dress</term> <note>original: "bediffelen." This refers to the trimming and squaring of timber for construction.</note> them. They relieved each other from month to month; there were constantly ten thousand at work on Mount Lebanon, besides the workmen whom Hiram, King of Tyre, had sent there in great numbers from his lands at Solomon's request, as people who had some particular knowledge and skill for that work. In all this, such a wonderful order was maintained, and all the measurements and regular divisions of the stones and the wood, which were to be used for the erection of this building, were so well taken, that when they went to join and set them up, neither axe nor hammer was needed to make any

to make changes, and to join this almost infinite number of worked stones and wood together. History does not provide us with another example of a building of such magnitude and splendor as this, and the master builders who had the primary oversight must have possessed a skill and capability that bordered on the miraculous. The construction of the Temple was begun in the fourth year of Solomon's reign and finished in the eleventh, such that seven years were spent on it, regardless of the speed with which it was carried out and the great number of workmen who labored upon it; which alone is enough to give us a very grand idea of this building. It might nevertheless seem small in comparison to the forty-six years which the Jews, according to the Evangelist John, said to Christ had been spent on the building of the second Temple, which was much less in splendor and costliness than this one of Solomon. <note>original: "zesënveertig jaaren... Evangelist Joannes" — This refers to John 2:20, where the Jews contest Jesus' claim about destroying and raising the temple.</note> But that was not steady labor, nor were many thousands of people employed as they were when this King had the Temple built, of which the description is given here. These were only some changes and decorations which Herod had made to the second Temple, which had been built in the time of Zerubbabel by a poor people who had only shortly before returned from a long captivity. After the death of Herod, which occurred about thirty years before the Jews spoke those words to Christ, those improvements had been resumed several times to add all possible ornaments to the second Temple; but all of this could not match the luster and splendor of the first; and Solomon, the wisest and richest of all Kings, had been able to make a much more splendid and costly Temple in seven years than the entire nation could have built in half a century after their return from the Babylonian captivity, and under the rule of the Romans, who, through new taxes with which they burdened Judea, were able to further exhaust that meager wealth which a long series of civil wars had already consumed there.

Just as Solomon followed the form of the Tabernacle, of which God had given the sketch to Moses, in the shape of the Temple, so he also did regarding the holy vessels that were to be placed in the Temple. There was only the Ark of the Covenant which he did not change, but kept exactly as Moses had left it; but concerning the other pieces, these were changed, and he had new ones made according to the fashion of the first, which did not seem costly or large enough to him to correspond with the splendor of the Temple he was building. In the Holy Place of the Tabernacle, there had been only one golden lampstand, the description and costliness of which we have seen previously; but Solomon had ten made, which were placed five in a row on either side of the holy place; and in place of one golden Table that stood in the same place in Moses' Tabernacle, Solomon had ten made, [2 Chron. 4:8] which were arranged in the same manner as the lampstands, five on the right and five on the left hand. However, there was only one, which was the middle one, upon which the showbread was to be placed; the nine others were occupied with golden vessels which Solomon had made in great multitude for the service of the Temple, such as basins, censers, wash-

<column-break/>

basins, etc., which were of matchless costliness. He also changed the golden Altar that stood in the Sanctuary and had another made that had more agreement with the size and costliness of the other holy vessels. But he did not do regarding the Altar as he had done regarding the Table and Lampstand of Moses, the number of which he had increased, making ten tables for one, and ten lampstands likewise for one; for he made only one golden Altar for the incense, just as he also made no more than one bronze Altar for the burnt offerings. If this Prince had aimed for nothing other than the splendor of the Temple, he would have made as many golden altars as he had golden lampstands and tables; but the heavenly wisdom with which he was filled caused him, in the entire management of this holy building and all its vessels, to make a distinction between that which served only for ornament and splendor, and that under which a mystery was hidden.

In things of the first sort, he had complete freedom to do as he saw fit, but in those that were of a higher character and whose institution was of a secret significance, he had to conform entirely to the prescription that God had given to Moses, and according to which 그 servant—who was faithful in all the House of God—had built the Tabernacle. Therefore, Solomon could, without deviating in any way from the intent of the Holy Spirit, increase the number of golden tables in the Sanctuary, provided that he did not divide the twelve loaves of showbread (which always had to stand on one table) among the others; but that those nine were kept for another use: thus, the mystery of the Table of showbread, the explanation of which we have seen elsewhere, remained intact. And with respect to the nine lampstands which this wise Prince added to the one God had commanded Moses to make for the Tabernacle, this increase did not diminish the mystery, which consisted in representing the spiritual light which Jesus Christ pours out into His Church, whether through Himself or through His Ministers, who are like so many symbolic Lampstands beside Christ, represented by the middle Lampstand, which Josephus, in the eighth book of his *Jewish Antiquities*, calls the great Lampstand, and of which he says that it alone burned steadily day and night.

But Solomon could not have multiplied the Altar of incense, nor the Altar of burnt offerings, without spoiling the mysteries thereof, which were to represent through the latter that in the Church there is but one single Altar upon which an atoning sacrifice for the sins of the world could be offered to God; and through the former, that there is also no more than one Altar from whence the spiritual incense of our prayers rises to God with a sweet fragrance. Both these altars were a prototype of Jesus Christ, under two different respects, namely, of sacrifice and intercession, but nonetheless both joined together in His person and applicable to no one else. This, then, was the reason why Solomon, however much splendor he wished to add to the Temple, did not increase the number of the Altars, but religiously adhered to unity regarding the one as well as the other, to which Moses had adhered in the building of the Tabernacle.

### I. Kings Chapter VII. verse 15. etc.

**T**he bronze Altar, which God had commanded Moses to make for the burnt offerings, did not seem to Solomon to have enough proportionality with the size of the Temple's courtyard, nor with the preciousness of the other sacred furnishings which he manufactured for such a magnificent building. The first Altar was only five cubits long, and just as wide, and its height was only three cubits. Solomon then had one made that was more than three times as large, for it was twenty cubits in its length, twenty in its width, and ten cubits in its height, so that it was like a small bronze mountain that rose in the middle of the courtyard, and thus from all sides displayed to the eyes of the bystanders the sacrifices which the Priests offered to God there, and the burnt offerings they burned in His honor. The sacred writer of the second book of Chronicles, who gives us the measurement of that altar in the fourth chapter, mentions nothing of the manner in which the Priests approached it to perform the service; for because it was more than twice as high as the usual height of a man, it was not possible for the Priests to lay the offerings upon it and arrange them there for a burnt offering without climbing very high, and yet God had forbidden in the twentieth chapter of Exodus to climb up to His altar with steps. But either this prohibition had regard to such steps whose treads were so high and far apart, like those on the altars of the idolaters, that those who climbed up

<column-break/>

were forced to set their legs so far apart that decency and modesty were thereby offended; and not to such whose low treads provided an easy ascent, in which one saw nothing other than that he who climbed up merely lifted his foot—or Solomon had an almost imperceptible ramp made from all sides of the Temple floor to a certain height of the altar, along which the Priests gradually came to the place where they had to perform the service without stairs or steps. Now, to give to this piece of work, and all others of that same material of which Solomon had made an excellent sketch, all the beauty they could have, he had a Brass Founder <term>Geelgieter (a master craftsman who casts objects in yellow metals like brass or bronze)</term>, the most skillful to be found, come from Tyre. He was named Hiram, a Jew by descent but a subject of the King of Tyre, and residing in the city of that name. This excellent and incomparable man in his art cast two bronze pillars of very rare size and beauty: they were twelve cubits in circumference and eighteen in height, which made thirty cubits; for otherwise it seems it cannot be understood what is said in the holy Books of the length of these pillars, which the second book of Chronicles says was thirty-five cubits, and the first book of Kings says was eighteen. They had, moreover, pedestals and capitals of a very skillful make, where one saw in raised work four hundred pomegranates in two rows, which seemed to hang down from the top of the pillars, with much other interwoven sculpture, in which the art and neatness so excelled that one could not grow weary of marveling at the hand of the master craftsman who had worked on them. These two pillars were placed with the altar of burnt offerings, and the molten sea (of which will be spoken in the following print illustration), in the large courtyard, the one on the right...

## The Molten Sea.
### I. Kings Chapter VII. verse 23, 24. etc.

Moses had, by God’s command, placed a bronze washbasin in the courtyard of the Tabernacle, which always had to be full of water, so that the Priests might wash their hands and feet therewith before they performed their service. In place of this washbasin, whose shape and size corresponded with the place where it stood, Solomon had a bronze vessel made for the same use, of a size and beauty fitting the splendor of that Monarch. This vessel, which the Scripture calls *the molten Sea* <term>molten Sea: a massive bronze basin used for ritual purification, signifying the vast amount of water it held</term>, because of the quantity of water which it held, was of a round shape, having a circumference of thirty cubits and a height of five: Its thickness was a handbreadth; and to make the rim wider and more pleasing to the eye, there were buds or protrusions under it that surrounded it all around, arranged ten to every cubit of width, and that in two rows, likewise of cast work. This Sea stood upon twelve bronze oxen, whose hindquarters were tucked under this washbasin, while their forequarters showed themselves all around, arranged three by three, looking toward the four quarters of the world. Ten bronze stands, of which each was four cubits long, four wide,

<column-break/>

and three high, supported this great structure; these stands were decorated with much costly sculpture, and on the frames that were between the wreaths one saw lions, oxen, Cherubim, and various other additions of excellent workmanship.

Although this large water vessel, which appeared like a small sea in the portico of the Temple, was enough to wash everything that had to be cleansed by water in the holy use prescribed by the Law of Moses, Solomon nevertheless added ten other bronze washbasins thereto, much smaller indeed, but still large enough to each hold four or five hogsheads <term>hogsheads: an old liquid measurement (Dutch: oxhoofden), here indicating the large capacity of the smaller basins</term> of water: they stood on stands of the same material, and were placed five on the right and five on the left side of the Temple, which was no small ornament for the portico where they were thus arranged. All this great quantity of water at the entrance of God’s Temple gave the Israelites in general, and the sanctified Ministers in particular, to understand with what purity one must approach God and devote oneself to worship and prayer, and how much we all need to be washed and cleansed of our sins by the pure water of Grace and of the Holy Spirit to approach God, according to the express words of the Apostle to the He- <note>The text cuts off mid-word; it likely refers to the Epistle to the Hebrews.</note>

## The Dedication of the Temple.

### I. Kings Chapter VIII. verses 3—21

<margin>
The year of the world 3001. Before J.C. 1003.
</margin>

After the Temple was completed, and nothing was lacking of all that was required for divine service, Solomon cared for nothing more than to perform its dedication. He chose for this ceremony the most suitable time of the entire year, in order to draw a great multitude of people to it and thereby increase the solemnity; it was the seventh month, in which two of the greatest high festivals of the ancient Church, namely the Feast of Atonement and that of the Tabernacles, happened to fall. This month corresponds in part with our "Autumn-month" <note>September</note> and "Wine-month" <note>October</note>, and it is the same in which, according to the most common and best-founded opinion among Theologians, the world—the only Palace in some measure worthy of God, and which he himself has consecrated—was created. It is also the same month, according to the most probable opinion, in which God’s Son came into the world with that venerable and holy body, which he signified by the name of Temple in the Gospel of John, when, to express both his death and resurrection, he said to the Jews, *that they would one day break down that Temple, but that he would raise it up again in three days.* In this month then, which was so remarkable and so full of mystery, and around the time of the Feast of Tabernacles, the Temple was dedicated to God through Solomon’s wisdom and zeal. This Temple was in itself, in its parts, and in its arrangement, a collection of all the mysteries which Grace has since placed in perfect clarity under the Dispensation of the Gospel.

<column-break/>

The Priests carried the Ark of the Covenant with great pomp and stateliness out of the Tabernacle, where it had been encamped for more than four hundred years, into the Sanctuary that Solomon had prepared to be a place of rest for it. This Sanctuary was the most illustrious and brilliant representation of the glory of the third Heaven <note>In ancient theology, the "third heaven" was considered the dwelling place of God Himself, beyond the atmosphere and the stars</note> that has ever existed on earth. The Tables of the Law, which God himself had written and given to Moses on Mount Sinai, were enclosed in this holy Ark as the holiest pledge one had in the world, and the only one worthy to be kept in an Ark that served as a throne for God. It was, as it were, the foundation or the spiritual center of his Covenant, through the privilege it had of being the most expressive foreshadowing of Jesus Christ and the communion of his Church with him, which He ever gave to his people. It is inconceivable how many bulls, rams, and other such sacrificial victims were offered during this transfer of the Ark; the holy Scripture says in one place that because of the multitude they could neither be numbered nor counted; and in another, that Solomon offered twenty-two thousand cattle and one hundred and twenty thousand sheep for the dedication of the Temple: never was so much blood shed at one time to make the Divinity favorable. God showed himself moved by these signs of godliness and zeal, which the King and the people gave him on this occasion; and hardly had the Priests, who had brought the Ark into the Most Holy place, returned to join the entire assembly waiting for them in the Court, when a miraculous cloud came to overshadow the Temple, to signify that God, of whom 그 cloud was the token, was...

### I. Kings Chapter VIII. verses 6, 7.

THE golden table <note>The author refers here to the Mercy Seat or the lid of the Ark.</note> that covered the Ark of the Covenant was overshadowed by two golden Cherubim, placed at both ends, and having their wings extended over the entire Ark. Moses had placed them there by an express command from God, and since there was nothing in the entire construction of the Ark which did not have its mystery, so these two Cherubim were also placed there for mystical and very profound purposes. Solomon followed this model, and for the same reasons, had two large Cherubim made of olive wood, which were overlaid with gold and placed in the Holy of Holies behind the veil, at the place where the Ark stood. They were ten cubits high, and their wings, which they had extended, were

<column-break/>

each five cubits long, such that the end of the wing of one Cherub touched the wall to the South, and the wing of the other Cherub touched the wall to the North, which then spanned the entire width of the Oracle, <term>Oracle (Aanspraak-plaats): literally "the place of speaking," referring to the Holy of Holies where God spoke to His people.</term> or the Most Holy Place, which was twenty cubits; the two other wings met in the middle of this Divine chamber and covered the Ark of the Covenant, which was placed under the wings of the Cherubim as if under a kind of vault. They stood upright on their feet, and their faces were turned toward the interior of the Most Holy place. One need not fear then that they, not worshipping the Angels, would worship their images, and that they would make these Cherubim the object of their attention and devotion: just as they indeed never allowed themselves to be carried away to such a foul misuse of these two images, however holy and venerable these were always esteemed by them.

### The City of Jerusalem.

The city of Jerusalem, known throughout the whole world for so many centuries, did not become famous because it was the capital of a great Empire, like Babylon in the East, and long after that the city of Rome in the West. Its domain extended only over a small region, and it gave its laws only to a single people, who, content with the inheritance of their fathers, usually kept themselves within the narrow borders of Palestine, and did not carry their weapons elsewhere, except when the necessity to defend their own land forced them to wage war on someone else's soil. That which caused the fame of Jerusalem, then, and placed it upon such an exalted step that no city has ever been able to

<column-break/>

reach, is that God chose it out of all the other cities of the world to make it, if one may speak thus, His Royal Court, and to have His Palace and His Throne there. Until that time when Solomon, by his commands, built the famous Temple there—which was the wonder of the whole earth and the glory of Judea—the city of Jerusalem had nothing special or remarkable; it yielded in antiquity, wealth, and power not only to many cities of Egypt, Assyria, and many other lands, but it also had, so to speak, at its gates the cities of Tyre and Sidon, which far surpassed it in all those things. Its old name, Jebus <note>The city was controlled by the Jebusites until King David conquered it.</note>, shows that it owed its origin to the Jebusites, who were a people of Palestine; and it would be difficult to climb much higher back to the time of Melchizedek <note>A priest-king mentioned in Genesis; tradition often identifies his city, "Salem," with Jerusalem.</note>, to recognize it there under the name

It is not appropriate here to show how little ground there is for that opinion, however common it may be among Scholars; but if it were as certain as it is doubtful, it would nonetheless be true that this city in those ancient times had nothing that significantly distinguished it from a hundred others whose names were already very famous then. Its position was very advantageous for placing it beyond the danger of being easily attacked by hostile bands in those early times, when the main power of a place consisted in being built on mountains of difficult access; for it was situated on two mountains, close to each other. On the lowest mountain stood that which was actually called the city of Jerusalem, and on the other, which was Mount Zion, the fortress was built which the Jebusites, because of its advantageous position, judged unconquerable, but which David nevertheless made himself master of, and which since then for that reason was called the City of David. Afterward, the valley which formed a separation between those two mountains was also built upon, such that it was but one city, but which nevertheless always remained distinguished by the two names of the lower city and the upper city. Because the Temple was in this latter <note>The "upper city."</note>, the Apostle Paul made an allusion to it when he spoke in his Epistle to the Galatians of the true Christian Congregation, the true and only House of God, under the name of the *Jerusalem that is above*, which, says he, *is the mother of us all*. <column-break/>

In Scripture, mention is made of the ancient walls of that city, and the great number of its towers, which, being built around their entire circumference at a certain distance from each other, made it unusually strong with the help of Nature and the terrain. But its strength consisted less in its mountains and bulwarks than in the protection of God, who, even by the fact that he had made it his own city and had his Temple there, seemed to have an interest in protecting it. He did so as long as Jerusalem remained faithful to him, but when it made itself unworthy of the honor it had of being the City of God, God caused terrible enemies to come against it, who besieged and took the place as a rebellious city that was abandoned by God; once it was a King of Egypt who made himself master of it; then it was a King of Babylon <note>original: "Babel"</note> who took it and laid it in the dust: at another time it fell under the power of the cruel Antiochus; and finally, after many fatal revolutions, having been subject to the Romans for more than a century, Titus came to besiege it, took it, filled it with the blood of its citizens, turned it entirely into ruins, had the plow go over it as over a field, and since that time it has never been able to be rebuilt, and has remained no more than a vain name in the memory of men.

twenty wide, and thirty high; but above those thirty cubits <note>original: "ellen" — an ancient unit of length based on the forearm, usually about 18 inches.</note> there were two more stories, which together made a building one hundred and twenty cubits high, as we read in the second book of Chronicles. The Temple faced West, and the large door through which one entered faced East, so that its position would be exactly contrary to those which the Idolaters gave to their Temples, which all faced East, as have those of the Christians since the reign of Constantine. The interior of the Temple was divided into two parts, of which the room one first entered had a length of forty cubits and spanned the entire width of the building, which was twenty cubits. It was in this spacious hall that the golden Altar, the Table of Shewbread, the golden Candlestick, and all the other holy vessels, of which we have already spoken, stood. This part was called the Temple, or the Sanctuary, into which no one but the Priests might enter. Beyond this holy and venerable place was a second which was infinitely more so, and which was therefore called the Holy of Holies, or the Oracle <note>original: "Aanspraakplaats" — literally 'the place of speaking,' referring to where God's voice was heard.</note>, because God made Himself present there above the Mercy Seat, and from this illustrious Throne gave His Oracles and answers to the High Priest, who came to ask Him for counsel through the Urim and Thummim <note>Hebrew terms for sacred lots used by the High Priest to determine God's will.</note>, as has been related by us in the description of the Tabernacle. This Most Holy place was half the size of the first, and of a square shape, being twenty cubits in length, twenty in width, and the same in height. The walls were entirely paneled with cedar wood, but this wood, however beautiful and precious it was, could not be seen anywhere; it was covered from top to bottom with golden plates, which were fastened to it with nails of the same metal. The floor and the ceiling were likewise overlaid with it, and all these pieces of gold were so thick and heavy that the sacred Writer of the second book of Chronicles estimates the weight of the golden plates of the Holy of Holies at six hundred talents, or sixty thousand pounds. The Temple, or the Sanctuary, although twice as large as the Oracle, also glittered on all sides, and from top to bottom, with gold;

<column-break/>

and in order not to go into a detailed and entirely accurate description here of so many riches, which today would exhaust all the treasures of the very largest Kingdom, it will be enough to say that David had left to his son Solomon, for the adornment and preciousness of the Temple, three thousand talents of gold, and seven thousand talents of silver. The imagination strains and almost sinks in forming an idea of such immense riches, which were still increased daily by the extraordinary sums brought into the King’s treasuries from all sides, and by the great quantity of gold and silver which his fleet brought him annually from the land of Ophir; whether this was the Taprobane of the ancients, today the island of Ceylon <note>Now known as Sri Lanka.</note> in the East Indies; or the Golden Chersonesus, which is today called Malacca, lying on the other side of the Ganges; or finally, a certain place on the western coasts of Africa near the side of Ethiopia; for none of all these opinions, about which the Scholars of our time differ, are fixed and certain. To this large and costly edifice of the Temple, which contained the Sanctuary and the Holy of Holies, several very high buildings were joined on both sides, of a magnificence equal to that of the Temple, in which were many rooms that increased its adornment, and upon which it is believed that Jesus Christ had his eye when he said in the Gospel of John, *that in his father’s house were many dwellings.* <note>John 14:2.</note> Nothing will be said here of the immensely large and wide Forecourt that was at the entrance of the Temple, because it has already been spoken of in the description of the Altar of burnt offerings, the Molten Sea, and the two bronze pillars, which were placed in that Forecourt. We pass over here a thousand other things, each of which could pleasantly occupy the Reader, because the narrow limits within which one is confined in these Histories leave the opportunity to the holy curiosity of those who wish to know more about it to inform themselves more broadly by reading the divine Books, and that of Josephus, who wrote very accurately and beautifully about it in his Jewish Antiquities.

## *Description of the Feast of Tabernacles. The Queen of Sheba, drawn by Solomon’s great name, comes to Jerusalem.*

### I. Kings Chapter VIII. verse 65. and Chap. X. verse 1. 2. etc.

On the occasion of the Dedication of the Temple, which Solomon wisely caused to coincide with the Feast of Tabernacles, the description of that High Festival is given here, which was one of the very greatest held in Judea. One sees the institution of it in several places in the Books of Moses, and one finds the observance of it renewed with great stateliness after the return from the Babylonian captivity, in the eighth chapter of the book of Nehemiah. The Feast of Tabernacles <note>original: "Loofhutten-feest" — literally 'Feast of Leafy Huts.' Also known as Sukkot.</note>, so named because of the huts of green branches in which the people camped for an entire week, was one of the three great High Festivals for the celebration of which the Jews

<column-break/>

came from all the cities of Judea to Jerusalem. And just as in the two other Feasts, namely, Passover and Pentecost, God intended thereby to bring to His people's memory some prominent event each time, such as the deliverance from Egypt at Passover, and the Covenant of Sinai at Pentecost; so He had also instituted the Feast of Tabernacles to remind the Jews that their ancestors had lived in huts or tents in the desert, to bring to their minds thereby, as in a single moment and as with one glance, the most wonderful care He had taken of their ancestors during forty years while they had been as wanderers in the deserts of Arabia, and the unspeakable goodness He had had for them, giving them in place of those tents, which were inconvenient and unstable dwellings, houses and cities in the land of Canaan. Yet this Feast served not only, any more than those of Passover and Pentecost, to renew the memory of past matters, but it also raised the mind to the contemplation of future goods. For just as the Jewish Passover was an example of the spiritual and blessed— <note>The text continues on the next page, likely explaining the Christian fulfillment of these festivals.</note>

life-giving Passover, the truth of which we have in Jesus Christ; and just as the Feast of Pentecost <note>original: "Pingsterfeest" — the author is drawing a parallel between the Jewish harvest festival and the Christian celebration of the Holy Spirit's descent.</note> was a foreshadowing of the New Law, which the Spirit of grace and truth would cause to be heard in the Church through the service of the holy Apostles, who were filled with the Holy Spirit on that day; so the Feast of Tabernacles <note>original: "Loofhutten-feest" — also known as Sukkot, a festival where Israelites lived in temporary shelters to remember their desert wanderings.</note> also symbolized that the Church had not yet arrived at that state of perfection and permanence which was intended for her, and that God did not leave her under the Law—as if under a Tabernacle—except for a time, in expectation of a spiritual Canaan, where she would enjoy a new rest, and where her state would be firm and certain, indeed, entirely unchangeable. This is the state of the Church under Grace, a state so different from that in which she was seen under the Law, as the condition of the carnal and outward Israel—when it possessed houses and cities in the land of Canaan—differed from the sorrowful state in which it had been when it encamped only in tents. This Feast lasted seven days, all of which were days of joy and gladness. The public places of Jerusalem were filled with huts, which were prettily and skillfully woven from the branches of various kinds of trees. One saw them at all the city gates; and the roofs of the houses, which were made flat, were occupied by these pavilions, which by their greenery created a kind of delightful landscape out of the city, where the simplicity of Nature, standing out through a hundred pretty shapes which art had devised, presented thousands upon thousands of objects to the eye, which, all alike and yet all different, drew curiosity to themselves from every side, and everywhere presented some ornament to the sight. During all that time, no one was seen appearing in the streets except with Myrtle, Olive, Palm, or Willow branches, bound together and interspersed among each other like bouquets of flowers. They even brought these into the Temple, where

<column-break/>

from all sides one heard the redoubled cry of <term>Hosanna</term> <note>original: "Geef dóch heyl, óf Behoud dóch" — the author translates the Hebrew phrase as "Please grant salvation" or "Save now."</note>, which was shouted out by people of every age, sex, or status, amidst the sweet raptures of joy. The last day of the Feast, which, like the first, was a day of rest—on whichever day of the week it happened to fall—was added to the seven preceding ones; and it was celebrated with so much state that the Jews gave it the name of *Great*, as one observes from their books, and also sees in the seventh chapter of the Evangelist John, where it is said, *that on the last and great day of the Feast, Jesus being in Jerusalem cried out: if anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink*. On that day then, which formed the conclusion of this Feast, the Jews went in a great multitude out of the city to draw water with all kinds of demonstrations of joy from the fountain of Siloam, which was at the city gate. They applied to this these words of the Prophet Isaiah in the twelfth chapter: *You shall draw water with joy from the fountains of Salvation*, and they called this ceremony *drawing the Holy Spirit*. The Feast of the dedication of Solomon’s Temple, which had begun seven days before that of the Tabernacles, was followed by this one, and on the eighth day of this latter feast, the King gave the people leave to depart. Each then returned again to his own land to give an account of the splendor of the Temple, and to recount the rarest and most unusual things he had seen at that great Festival.

It was not only in the building of the Temple that Solomon’s glory shone: his Palace, his Throne, his household furniture, his vessels, his retinue—everything was precious and magnificent, even to the point of being astonishing. But what was even more worthy of wonder was the Prince himself, whose understanding, shrewdness, and wisdom—qualities a thousand times more excellent and precious than all the riches of the earth—had no equal in all the preceding centuries. All these things together—
