combined to make the reign of Solomon the most magnificent that had ever been, and they earned for this Monarch a respect that carried his name and glory throughout the whole world. Through the account of so many wonders, curiosity was awakened in the hearts of men, and people from all sides were drawn to Jerusalem to see them. The Queen of Sheba was so struck by everything that Fame proclaimed of him, that she could not resist the desire to be convinced of it by her own eyes. The land where she ruled was located far from Judea; our Savior says in the Gospel that it was at the ends of the earth: it is true that there is a degree of hyperbole in this expression, it being a common and inexhaustible figure of speech among the Oriental peoples, as appears from a multitude of texts in the Holy Scripture, and especially from the book of Job, which is full of it; but nevertheless, these words of Jesus Christ indicate that the land of this Queen—whether one places it with some in Ethiopia, or is content with others to place it in the farthest parts of Arabia—was far enough from Judea for her journey to be regarded as an amazing feat, especially for a person of her gender and status. She departed from her land with a large and distinguished retinue, carrying with her precious gifts to honor Solomon, namely fragrant and choice spices, an immense quantity of gold, and precious stones; and many camels came in her train, laden with all the most precious things that the hot regions of the South <note>The "South" likely refers to the Sabean kingdom in modern-day Yemen or the Aksumite Empire in Ethiopia.</note> could produce. Having arrived at Jerusalem, she saw all those magnificent buildings which Solomon had caused to be founded, and that abundance of wealth which shone out in all the works that this Monarch had caused to be made at unheard-of cost; the arrangement of his house, the great number of his officials, the splendor and delicacies of his table, his servants, chariots, stables, gardens, and a thousand other things which cannot be described; and she stood amazed at it. This Queen had almost as much trouble believing her eyes as she had had in her own land believing what had been brought to her by rumor: She confessed that everything that had been said of it, though surpassing probability, was not to be compared to what she beheld. But that which even more amazed this Queen, and seemed to exhaust her wonder, was the alertness of spirit, and the extensive knowledge and science which she perceived in Solomon. This was what had seemed to her, in the stories she had heard of him, the most un-

<column-break/>

believable, and it was primarily in this that she found Solomon much greater than rumor had depicted him. She held several conversations with him about the most difficult subjects of Nature, and she had also prepared some profound questions <note>original: "diepziunige vraagen" — traditionally understood as riddles or ethical puzzles meant to test a ruler's wisdom.</note> that were unfathomable to any other wit than that of this Monarch: but Solomon solved the darkest difficulties she proposed with such neatness and accuracy, and he spoke to her with so great a wisdom and understanding on all kinds of subjects, that there was nothing upon which he did not give her complete satisfaction. She could not tire of hearing his conversation, and she often envied his servants the happiness of hearing a King speak whose spirit, surpassing that of all the wise men and Philosophers of the world, made him the wonder of the whole earth. She herself made this noble declaration to him:

>You have with wisdom and goodness surpassed the report that I heard. Blessed are your men, blessed are these your servants, who stand continually before your face, who hear your wisdom! Blessed be the LORD your God, who has had delight in you, to set you on the throne of Israel: Because the LORD loves Israel forever, therefore has He made you King, to do justice and righteousness.<-

It would be difficult to say whether this Queen had knowledge of the true God; or whether it was but a vain desire to manifest her love for the sciences that spurred her to undertake such a great journey, and made her speak with such respect for Solomon's wisdom. The Holy Scripture has told us nothing in this regard, but nevertheless, probability leans more toward giving us good thoughts of her faith and godliness, than to leaving her buried among the supposed Sages of Heathendom. The praise which Christ seems to give to the zeal she had to hear Solomon's wisdom serves in no small way to foster such a high opinion of her. But, as we have said, one can conclude nothing certain on this matter: so that after having given the deserved praise to the Queen’s dignified and noble desire for Solomon's wisdom, her example ought to encourage all the world to strive for knowledge of the purest and truly heavenly wisdom that has ever been seen on earth, which is that of Jesus Christ, and to meditate attentively on the profoundest mysteries of Grace.

Solomon gave an example of this <note>The "example" refers to the great heights of wisdom and glory mentioned on the previous page.</note>; and surpassed all others who came after him in it. But the remainder of his life did not correspond with such a good beginning; his heart gave way amidst the prosperity that accompanied his reign. Having been accustomed for a long time to seeing nothing but his own glory, he gradually lost sight of God’s Glory, and, enchanted by the splendor of human greatness, he forgot that within the Monarch, and beneath the Majesty that surrounded him, was enclosed a poor and miserable creature, little different from a Nothing, who ought to have remained eternally subject to his Creator and God, and who should have placed all his boast in obeying Him. The love for foreign women carried away his heart, and as one passion draws another, this poor Prince soon passed from this irregular love of women to a contempt for Religion, and to idolatry. Besides the daughter of Pharaoh, whom he had married—instead of taking no person for a wife except from his own nation—he took many others; indeed, it even seemed as if he intentionally sought them out among the idolatrous nations, to add the unbridled nature of the mind and Religion to that of the heart. He then had brought to him Moabite, Ammonite, Edomite, Sidonian, and Hittite wives: nations regarding whom God had expressly forbidden His people to take their women in marriage. These wives brought a Heathen and idolatrous heart with them into the Palace, and into the bed of the King; and his heart, possessed by the love he bore them, imperceptibly corrupted his mind, and allowed idolatry to creep in. The first step toward sin always costs the most, and the others follow of their own accord. As soon as Solomon had begun to turn away from the Lord, and once he had overcome the horror which his understanding and a remnant of the fear of God gave him toward idolatry, his heart was no longer able to 

<column-break/>

defend itself; idolatry needed only to place such an object before his eyes as it desired, for he immediately made his God of it. The Moabite woman presented him with the Idol Chemosh <note>original: "Kamos"</note>, which she had brought with her from her land, and this Prince had the weakness to bow his knee before it. The Ammonite woman drew him to Milcom, and made him worship Molech. The Sidonian woman persuaded him to the service of Ashtoreth <note>original: "Astoreth"</note>; such that he had as many gods as he had wives of various nationalities. History provides us with no example of such a rare deviation, and whether it was a matter of pleasing them or a superstition, Solomon was highly criminal, and differed as much from himself as innocence can differ from crime, and wisdom from folly. God punished him for his unfaithfulness, and told him that He would tear the Kingdom—which He had given him entirely over the twelve tribes of Israel—and that He would pull ten away from it, which would become rebellious against Rehoboam, the son and heir of this Prince, and form a separate Kingdom; but that for the sake of David, and for the sake of the covenant He had made with him, He would leave one tribe to his son, over which he would reign. God allowed Solomon to reign peacefully over the entire land until the end of his life, as he had always done. This particular mercy which God showed to this Sovereign, after such frequent and loathsome idolatry, is no small proof to support the opinion of those who believe that this King did penance for his sin, although such is not explicitly recounted in the holy History. Solomon's reign was happy and peaceful from the beginning to the end, and in the period of forty years that this Prince was on the Throne, he saw neither internal nor external wars in his States. The wonder which his people had for him kept them in awe and obedience; and that outstanding prosperity, which should naturally have brought upon him the envy of other Kings, took away from them any thought of undertaking anything against such a mighty and formidable Prince. Holy Scripture makes mention of three enemies of Solomon, but enemies who were powerless and weak, and dared attempt nothing during his life. One was an Edomite Prince, named Hadad, who, having neither lands nor people since the slaughter which Joab, David’s General, had carried out in the land of Edom, had gone to Egypt to King Pharaoh, who had him marry the sister of the Queen, his wife. The other was one named Rezon, who had been in the service of Hadadezer, King of Zobah, and who had afterwards become King of Damascus. But these were more like rods which God held ready in Idumea and Syria to strike Israel with when the time to use them should come, rather than enemies who caused Solomon any trouble. The third was of his own nation, and from the number of his subjects; his name was Jeroboam, son of a widow from the city of Zeredah in the Tribe of Ephraim, a man without standing or authority, in himself incapable of making any movement in the State, but nonetheless appointed by God to bring about a great change in it, and to take more than two-thirds of the Kingdom away from the Royal House. Solomon, who did not yet know that he would have such a mighty enemy in Jeroboam, had raised him from the lowly state of his birth and given him an office in his State; and through the first elevation of this man, he promoted him himself, without knowing it, toward the Throne which God was preparing for him, and he thus sowed the first seed of the deadly discord that was shortly to tear the Kingdom of Israel apart. But such are men: their short and dark sight does not penetrate into the future, and when they, either without intention or with a particular insight,

<column-break/>

do something, then there is a higher hand that governs their conduct quite differently than they intend. Solomon had a certain space called <term>Millo</term> <note>Millo refers to a specific fortification or landfill project in the City of David intended to strengthen the defenses between the temple and the palace.</note>, which was on Mount Zion between the Temple and the royal Palace, filled in and built upon. The people took no pleasure in this change, and therefore murmured. Jeroboam was one of those who had oversight over this work, and who fostered the discontent of the people. Solomon having gained knowledge of this, Jeroboam was forced to leave his administration and depart from Jerusalem. As he went alone, he was met on the road by a Prophet named Ahijah, who lived in Shiloh, and on 그날 <note>The Dutch "dien dag" means "that day."</note> wore a new garment. This Prophet had been sent to him on God's behalf to foretell what was destined for him, and what a great change of State Providence was preparing for him. Ahijah then, walking on the field alone with Jeroboam, took the new garment he was wearing and, tearing it into twelve pieces, gave ten of them to Jeroboam, and spoke to him these words: *Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Behold, I will tear the kingdom out of the hand of Solomon, and will give ten tribes to you; but I will not take anything of this kingdom out of his hand, but out of the hand of his son I will take it, and I will give you ten tribes thereof.* It was the custom of God to thus represent through some tangible thing the events which He foretold through His Prophets, so that their predictions would be clearer and more easily make an impression on the minds; the books of Jeremiah and Ezekiel are full of such examples, and one finds them everywhere in Scripture. The new garment, which God had intentionally made the Prophet take, was the symbol of the beauty and strength in which the Kingdom of Israel then found itself; it was at that time in its state of perfection; until the time of Solomon, something had been lacking, but under his reign, nothing was missing; and if there ever was a flourishing state in the world of which one might have promised a long duration, and whose luster would never be extinguished by time, which erases everything, it was beyond doubt the Kingdom of Israel, as mighty and rich as it was during the life of this King. But God gave this Kingdom no time to grow old and wear out by itself through its duration, like a new cloth that gradually consumes and wears out of its own accord: God had decided in His wrath to make it perish in its greatest strength, and to rend it apart by an unexpected and terrible schism, which brought it, as it were, but two finger-breadths from its total ruin.

The man of God did nothing therein but follow the commands given to him; for God had explicitly forbidden him to eat or drink within Bethel, as if in that godless city there was no food that was not defiled, since it had become the site of the golden Calf and the center of idol-

<column-break/>

atry. God had likewise forbidden him to return from Bethel by the same way he had come. This prohibition had its mystery <note>meaning a hidden spiritual purpose</note>, and might well have regarded the contagion of idolatry, to signify how dangerous it is to return from an idolatrous people with the same sincerity and purity of heart and mind with which one had approached them. But whatever the intent may have been, that which is always of the greatest weight, both in the commands and the prohibitions God has given us, is not to try to search out the hidden purposes thereof, but to humbly submit oneself to them and do what God commands. The Prophet was precise in following all of this; he departed from Bethel without having eaten or drunk there, and he returned by another way. The news of what had happened to Jeroboam and his altar spread immediately through the city, and everyone knew at the same time that the Prophet who had come from Judah was [departing] from Bethel again.

The prophecy was fulfilled, and God, who as the Jews say, holds the keys of the rain <note>A reference to a common rabbinic teaching that God retains personal control over three "keys": birth, resurrection, and rain.</note> in his hands, closed the heavens during all that time, so that not a drop of water fell. This woman testified to him that she had nothing at all left but a little meal and a little oil, from which she intended to bake a cake with the wood she had been looking for, to eat it with her child, after which she had nothing more to be able to live on. No sooner had Elijah avenged the service of the true God through the death of the Priests of Baal, than he climbed to the top of Carmel accompanied by a young man who served him. There, separated from all the people and being as it were between Heaven and earth, he poured out his soul in prayers to God, to beseech Him to have compassion on His people, who were perishing through a drought and famine of three years. He bowed his face to the earth and placed his head between his knees, as if he did not dare to lift it toward Heaven to request any favor from God for a people as guilty as that of Israel, and to pray that He would be pleased to send a fruitful rain upon a land that had been defiled by so many

<column-break/>

crimes. Such is generally the disposition of the minds of the Righteous; the holier their souls are, the more humble they become, and they fear that in their reverence they will fall short before that supreme Majesty, whom even the Angels dare not approach without covering their faces with their wings. In this posture of respect and humiliation, Elijah worshiped God in silence, while his heart spoke to Him, and requested from Him that necessary and long-desired rain for the land of Israel. Thus had Moses formerly made his prayer to God in the pressing danger of the Israelites on the shore of the Red Sea. He, being in a deep seclusion of mind while all the people burst out in complaints and murmurs, spoke not a single word, and God showed that He had heard his cry to Him. This internal language of a praying soul is that which is always best heard in Heaven; whereas without the language of the heart, all the words of the mouth vanish into the air and never reach God. After Elijah had thus prayed in the secret of his heart, he broke the silence to call to the youth who accompanied him, telling him to go a few steps from there and turn his gaze toward the sea, to see if any clouds were rising. The youth, having gone there, returned and said that he had seen nothing; therefore he commanded him to return again, up to seven times. On the seventh journey, there appeared

This was the sign and the precursor of a heavy rain, and the Prophet, who had already seen it in the spirit arising from the source of mercy, gave orders to his servant to quickly inform Ahab—who had left him and gone to a certain place in the field to eat—and tell him that he must have his chariot harnessed with all speed, lest he be overtaken by the rain. Meanwhile, the small cloud that the young man had seen rising from the sea grew larger and larger; new ones joined it from all sides, the sky was immediately covered with them, and God, as the Scripture says elsewhere, brought the rain out of His storehouses and poured it out in abundance over the whole land. The King hurried to Jezreel, and the Spirit of the Lord took Elijah and carried him as if on the wings of the wind into that city. The Prophet, through such a swift run, outpaced Ahab’s chariot, and having arrived at Jezreel, he saw with a heart full of wonder and gratitude that rain, for which he had prayed to God with such zeal, pouring down like streams, whereby life was restored to the fields of Israel, where a drought of three years, which had left almost no greenery, had spread the sorrowful image of death everywhere.

<margin>The year of the world 3096. Before J.C. 908.</margin>

Ahab, having returned from Carmel, gave Jezebel an account of everything that had happened, and how Elijah had caused all the prophets of Baal to be killed. This Princess, no less superstitious than she was cruel, showed herself so affected by this that she sent a message to Elijah with an oath, declaring that she would put him to death the next day, around that same hour. The Prophet feared the execution of this threat, and since prudence is not contrary to zeal, he did what Jesus Christ later advised His Apostles to do in similar instances, which was to flee from one place to another to keep his life in safety. Elijah then went out of the city at once and traveled to the wilderness of Beersheba, in the land of Judah, and sent away the young man who accompanied him. After he had traveled an entire day through these desolate places, he sat down under a broom tree <note>Original: "jeneverboom." While literally a juniper, in Biblical translations this refers to the broom tree (*Retama raetam*).</note> and fell asleep, saying to God, in deep sorrow over seeing the corruption of the Israelites and the rage of Ahab and Jezebel against the servants of God:

> It is enough; now, LORD, take my life; for I am no better than my fathers.

Thereupon an Angel came and woke him. Elijah was amazed by this sight, and looking behind him, he saw a cake baked on coals and a jar of water, which the Angel had brought there. The Prophet ate and drank, but because he was weary and his heart was overwhelmed by sorrow, he soon fell back asleep. The Angel of the Lord came to him again, and waking him a second time, told him to stand up and eat, because he still had a great journey to complete. Elijah then ate of the cake again and drank from the jar of water, and having been strengthened by this food—the power of which God miraculously increased—he traveled forty days and forty nights without eating or drinking, until he came to Mount Horeb, famous in the history of the ancient people of Israel for the appearances of God to Moses, and for the Law of Mount Sinai, which

<column-break/>

was a part of the wilderness of Horeb. The Prophet having arrived there, went into a cave, and God, who had led him there by His Spirit, appeared to him in a vision and asked him why he had come to hide himself in this remote and uninhabitable place. Elijah answered that it was out of a zeal he had for Him, which had not permitted him to behold the godlessness practiced among the Israelites to the detriment of His honor without complaining to Ahab and Jezebel about it; thus he had brought the hatred of those powers upon himself and was persecuted for that reason, just like the other Prophets who were inspired by the same spirit and zeal as he. *They have broken down your altars,* he said, *and killed your Prophets, and I alone am left.* It seems indeed that the greatness of his sorrow had made him forget at that moment that there were still a hundred other Prophets whom the godly Obadiah had secretly snatched from the rage of the persecutors by hiding them in caves: or if he did think of them, he dared not count them as living, since they showed themselves as little in the land of Israel to withstand Ahab and the Priests of Baal as if they had truly been dead. God commanded him to go out of this cave and stand outside on the mountain: at the same time, He caused a mighty wind to pass before the Prophet, which made a terrible crashing on the mountain and among the rocks; but the Holy Scripture says that God was not in that wind. This fearsome wind was followed by an earthquake; yet the Scripture gives us to understand that God was not in that earthquake either. Next, a great fire appeared, but God was not in that fire either. Finally, there came the whistling of a gentle silence; and the Prophet, who until that time had not dared to show himself, seeing that it was nothing but a soft blowing of a wind, more fit to refresh the air and make it pleasant than to stir up a storm, stepped forward and stood at the entrance of the cave, having covered his face with one of the edges of his mantle out of reverence. God was in this gentle whistling and asked Elijah, as before, what he was doing there. Elijah gave Him the same answer; and God comforted him by saying that He had caused seven thousand to remain in Israel—that is, a significant number of persons—who had not bowed their knees to Baal and whose mouths had not kissed him. God thus showed His Prophet, through this mysterious vision, with what gentleness He supports the weaknesses of His children when they do not always have enough courage to openly confess His name. He accommodates Himself to them, and on that occasion He does what Christ said: that He will not break the bruised reed, nor extinguish the smoking wick. He comes in a refreshing whisper, and not in the stormy wind of His judgments, or in the fire of His wrath, to strike with fear and trembling those souls who have more need to be comforted than to be made afraid and terrified. When the Lord said to Elijah that He had still kept such a large number of Israelites from the idolatry of Baal, He thereby gave that Prophet, and in his person the entire Church, to understand that His Grace always watches over the welfare of His elect, and that He, when it pleases Him, miraculously preserves His believers in and among idolatrous lands.

God had commanded Elijah on the mountain to go to Damascus and to anoint Hazael as King over Syria, and from there to travel to the land of Israel and anoint Jehu, the son of Nimshi, to be King over the ten Tribes at some future time; and likewise to perform the anointing of Elisha, the son of Shaphat, to be a Prophet in his place. Elijah then left his desert and cave, and going to the land of Israel, he met Elisha, who was tilling the land with twelve yoke of oxen, and was himself behind one of the plows. Elijah went to him and threw his mantle upon him, as if to accept him into the office of the Prophets by that act; he declared to him the command he had to summon him to this calling and to confirm him in this dignity. It was in truth the greatest honor that could befall anyone on earth, to enter into such close communion with God and to receive the oracles directly from His mouth. But in such difficult times as those were, performing the ministry of a Prophet was almost the same as dedicating oneself to a martyr’s death. Elisha, however, did not let himself be deterred by the danger to which this office would expose him; but immediately leaving his oxen and agriculture, he only requested permission from Elijah to take leave of his father and mother. Since this request of Elisha’s did not arise from any sorrow at leaving them, but only from a movement of respect and affection toward his parents, the Prophet allowed it and waited meanwhile in the same place where they were. Elisha did not fail to return, and upon his return, he sacrificed a pair of the oxen with which he had plowed the land, and with the wood of the plow, he cooked the meat of those animals and gave a feast of it to the people who gathered there; after which he set out on his way with the Prophet Elijah.

Some time afterward, it happened that Benhadad, King of Syria, under the pretext of some displeasure he had conceived against the King of Israel, brought a great army into the field against him; and accompanied by thirty-two Kings, his neighbors and allies, he came to besiege Samaria. Ahab, seeing himself unable to defend himself against such a terrible army, made several proposals for a treaty to Benhadad, all of which were rejected by that proud and unjust Prince. But just as Benhadad was preparing everything to attack the place, a Prophet came to Ahab, who was in the utmost distress along with all the leaders of Israel, and told him that God would deliver the Syrians into their hands; that to strike them, he need do nothing else but have them attacked by the young servants of the provincial governors <note>original: "voetjongens der Landvoogden"</note>; so much did God despise that ambitious military force with which the Syrian flattered his pride. Ahab immediately gathered all the body-servants of his Court, who numbered two hundred and thirty-two, and having at the same time made a count of the people in Samaria capable of bearing arms, it was found that there were seven thousand men. The gate was then opened at noon; the young servants went out first, and the seven thousand warriors followed to support them. Benhadad was enjoying himself in his camp with eating and drinking, along with 

<column-break/>

his thirty-two Kings and the principal commanders of his army; men came to tell him that the besieged had made a sortie; he then sent people to observe them; and these people were struck down by the young servants who had marched out first. Thereupon the whole army fell into alarm, the King saved himself by flight, and the entire army was hewn to pieces.

A year later, Benhadad came again to make war on the King of Israel with an army just as numerous as the previous year; and because his flatterers had whispered to him that the reason they had been defeated the year before in the land of Samaria—which is full of mountains and hills—was that the God of Israel was a *God of the mountains*, he let himself be persuaded that if he drew the Israelites onto a plain, not one of them would escape. He then went to encamp in the plain of Aphek, and the troops of Israel also marched thither; the Scripture says that they were but like two small flocks of goats <note>original: "twee geyten-kudden"</note> in comparison to the Syrians, who covered a vast area of the land. But God had an interest in this war, and it concerned His glory to show these idolatrous nations that the God of Israel, who is God of the whole earth, was no less powerful and victorious in the plain than on the mountains. The battle began, and the Syrians lost it. The earth was soon covered with blood and the dead, and Holy Scripture relates that the children of Israel slew one hundred thousand foot soldiers of the Syrian army in that famous struggle. Benhadad had fled this terrible slaughter, and some Syrians, having cleverly persuaded Ahab to show mercy to them and their King, then brought him to him; and Ahab, treating him as a brother, spared his life and made a covenant with him. This generosity, which was an encroachment on God's prerogatives—to whom alone Ahab owed the victory—displeased God to the highest degree; so much so that He had a Prophet announce to him that since he had let a man escape who was worthy of death, his life would have to pay for that of the King of Syria. Ahab, ever light-minded and godless, mocked the prophecy of the Prophet;

Ahab could not be restrained by all the calamities which Micaiah predicted for him from making war against the King of Syria; and flattered by the deceptive assurances which his Prophets gave him, he made the final decision with Jehoshaphat, and was only concerned with giving the necessary orders for a pitched battle. ### II. Kings Chapter I. verse 10.

Jehoshaphat, King of Judah, having been delivered by divine Providence from the great danger in which he had found himself during the battle against the Syrians, returned to Jerusalem. He was one of the most pious Kings of Judea, led by his zeal to tear down several of those unholy groves and high places where the people still offered sacrifices, despite the prohibition God had given against offering sacrifices anywhere else but in the Temple at Jerusalem and upon the Altar of burnt offerings. To this great act of piety, he also added that he sent Priests and Levites to all the cities of his Kingdom to instruct the people in God’s Law, which had not been properly observed in previous reigns; and he reigned twenty-five years in Jerusalem, enriched with blessings with which God mercifully rewarded his piety. The Kingdom of Israel did not have the good fortune of seeing Kings on its throne who allowed piety and the service of the true God to prevail for so long.

<column-break/>

Ahab, who had fallen before Ramoth in Gilead, had left a son named *Ahaziah*, who, following in his father’s footsteps, gave himself over to idolatry just as he had; and to those impieties, which were already all too prevalent in Israel, he added this one: <margin>The year of the world 3108. Before J.C. 896.</margin> that having once fallen through a lattice <note>A decorative window grating or railing.</note> in his chamber and thus received a mortal wound, instead of taking his refuge in God, he turned to a new idol from the land of the Philistines, named *Baal-Zebub*, to know if he would recover from that sickness. This new act of idolatry toward a god who until that time had been unknown or despised by the Israelites, aroused the wrath of a zealous God, who saw superstition breaking in from all sides of the Kingdom of the ten Tribes under godless Kings, who daily introduced it and subsequently caused the people to follow it. God then sent an Angel to Elijah to command him to go and meet the messengers whom Ahaziah had sent to Baal-Zebub, and to say to them: >*Is it because there is no God in Israel that you go to inquire of Baal-Zebub, the god of Ekron? Therefore now thus says the LORD: You shall not come down from that bed on which you have gone up, but you shall surely die.*< These men returned in haste, and as soon as the King saw them return—

Thus, on this occasion, Elijah was only the mouth which God used to curse these two Captains of an abominable King, and God lent Elijah His hand and arm to immediately punish those who were doomed to death by the mouth of this Prophet.

# HISTORY of the O. TESTAMENT.

The manner in which God took him from the earth was no less a miracle than the ascent itself. That of Enoch <note>Enoch was a patriarch before the Great Flood who, according to Genesis 5:24, "walked with God" and was taken by Him without dying.</note> had nothing of grandeur other than the greatness of the wonder; for that a creature of flesh and dust is transported to those regions where even our sight cannot reach, and that he makes a path from here to the firmament, and from there extends beyond the stars, is something in which our imagination loses itself, and faith alone can compensate for the lack of our insight. But in this ascent of Elijah to Heaven there was, if such a thing is possible, something even more remarkable and rare. He traveled with Elisha, that holy man whom he had anointed some years before to be Prophet in his place. Several Prophets, less renowned than these two, but nonetheless enlightened by God's Spirit—who used them as He judged necessary—had some secret intuition of the upcoming ascent of the Prophet Elijah. They had made this known to Elisha, his worthy disciple, who had answered them that he knew it as well as they; meanwhile, he kept close to him and did not lose him from his sight for a single moment. Elijah wished to test his disciple to see if he was steadfast in his resolution to stay with him until the end; and the command, which Elijah said he had received, was undoubtedly a conditional command, in case Elisha left him; for one must not do this injustice to a Saint, who was almost at that moment to be carried alive to Heaven, to believe that he would have taken refuge in a lie in order to rid himself of someone whom he might have commanded by right, or sent away from him in some other manner. But be that as it may, the Kings who commanded this army all three went together to the <term>Prophet</term>. <term>Elisha</term> immediately addressed the King of <term>Israel</term> with the authority and dignity of a true Man of God. *What have I to do with you?* he said to him, *Go to the prophets of your father, and of your mother.* <note>Elisha is rebuking King Jehoram for his family's history of idolatry and worship of Baal.</note> Nevertheless, out of regard for <term>Jehoshaphat</term>, who was a godly and zealous Prince for the purity of the service of God, <term>Elisha</term> showed himself willing to do what these Kings requested of him. He had someone brought to him who played a stringed instrument, to bring his spirit to rest as if by that means, which had been troubled because of the sharp rebuke he had given to the godless King of <term>Israel</term>; and the Spirit of God coming over <term>Elisha</term> while this musician played, the <term>Prophet</term> commanded that they should make many ditches along a brook that was completely dried up, and he told them that they would see that this brook and the ditches would be filled with water, without

<column-break/>

wind, and without rain; adding further thereto that God would deliver the <term>Moabites</term> into their hands. The commands of the <term>Prophet</term> were immediately followed, and the next day the water came, and the earth was filled with it. The <term>Moabites</term> had meanwhile approached to surprise the army of the King of <term>Israel</term>, in the great distress in which they believed it to have been brought; but they were themselves defeated, and driven to flight: whereupon the King of <term>Moab</term>, giving himself over to his despair, took his eldest son, who was to reign after him, and made a burnt offering of him upon the walls of his city. <note>This desperate act was an attempt to appease his gods and likely horrified the besieging armies into retreating.</note>

   About that time it happened that the widow of one of the <term>Sons or Pupils of the Prophets</term> <note>These were communities of disciples who studied under the great prophets.</note>, finding herself entirely unable to pay the debts which her husband had left behind, was so heavily beset by one of her creditors that he had come to take her children and make them his slaves. This was indeed a right that was given to creditors by the Laws of God, under certain regulations and conditions added thereto <note>Under Mosaic law (Exodus 21), debt could be settled through physical labor or servitude for a limited time.</note>: but meanwhile it was a hard case for one already sufficiently oppressed by the loss of her husband, that she saw her children, the only comfort left to her, thus being taken away. She made her complaint about it to the <term>Prophet Elisha</term>, who, moved with compassion for the household of a man who had lived in the fear of God, and who in his life had been honored with the title of <term>Son of the Prophets</term>, asked this widow what she had in her house that she could turn into money. She gave him as an answer, that she had nothing in her house but a jar of oil. <term>Elisha</term> then commanded her that she should go and borrow empty vessels from all her neighbors, and see to it that she got not a few; and that she should then shut herself in the house with her sons,

# Naaman healed of his leprosy by
# Elisha.
## II. Kings Chapter V. verse 1 — 14.

Elisha continued to make his service remarkable through some new miracle. At <term>Shunem</term> <note>A village in the territory of Issachar, north of Jezreel.</note> in the Tribe of Issachar, he was hosted by a certain man and woman who, having no children, had obtained a young son from God through his prayer. When this boy had grown somewhat, it happened one day that he went out to his father in the field, who was busy with the harvest; while there, such a severe headache seized him that he died of it that same day. Elisha was then on Mount Carmel, and the Shunammite woman, having come to him in haste to bring him the news of her son's death, he gave his staff to <term>Gehazi</term> <note>Elisha’s servant.</note>, commanding him to go quickly to Shunem and lay it upon the face of the dead child. Gehazi carried out his master's command, but the dead boy did not recover. Elisha arrived shortly thereafter himself, and having closed the door of his room, into which the child had been brought, he prayed fervently to God that it might please Him to raise the boy up again. He then lay upon the dead child, as <term>Elijah</term> <note>original: "Elisa", likely a printer's error for "Elia" (Elijah), referring to the similar miracle in 1 Kings 17.</note> had done previously in a similar instance; whereupon a slight warmth came into the boy, which was as a forerunner of

<column-break/>

the life which God was about to give back to him. The Prophet then walked back and forth across the room twice, and climbing onto the bed again, he lay upon the child once more, whose life returning, he sneezed seven times and opened his eyes.

This miracle was soon followed by another. At Gilgal, during a time of famine, there was a company of the <term>Sons or Disciples of the Prophets</term> <note>A school or community of prophets living and studying together under a leader.</note> who believed they had all been poisoned by some harmful plants which had been put into a pottage among other herbs. Elisha took a handful of flour, which he threw into the pot, and immediately the soup lost that bitterness which had caused so much distress to those who had eaten of it. Furthermore, the Prophet fed a hundred persons with twenty barley loaves, and much was still left over, because the loaves were miraculously multiplied while eating: just as happened long afterward under the hands of Jesus Christ, when he satisfied five thousand people with five barley loaves.

All these miracles made Elisha very renowned among his people, and a certain young Israelite girl, who had been carried away captive to Syria, served to make him known in that land as well, through an event that brought him an immortal name. One of the chief lords of Syria, named <term>Naaman</term>, was <term>leprous</term> <note>In the Bible, "leprosy" (melaatsheyd) often referred to various serious skin diseases, not just the modern Hansen's disease.</note>; and although that ailment among foreign nations was not, as

As among the Jews, <term>leprosy</term> <note>In biblical times, leprosy referred to various skin diseases that rendered a person ritually "unclean" and required social isolation.</note> was a sufficient reason to exclude anyone infected with it from all public offices, it was nonetheless a blemish and a kind of dishonor. Naaman had used all the remedies that medical art could provide against such a difficult ailment in vain; however, having understood from this Israelite girl, who was in the service of his wife, that there was a Prophet in the land of Israel who could unfailingly heal him if he went to him, he departed to visit Elisha, carrying letters of recommendation from the King his master to the King of Israel. When this Prince had read them, he seemed very surprised that the King of Syria sent his Army Commander to him to be healed of his leprosy; and he conceived a suspicion that it was a snare which that King was laying for him, to take from it a pretext to wage war against him. Elisha, having understood the concern of the King on account of those letters, and at the same time Naaman's arrival, immediately sent someone to tell that Syrian that he should just

<column-break/>

come to him to be healed. Naaman went there, and Elisha commanded him to plunge himself seven times in succession into the Jordan. He imagined that Elisha was mocking him, and, quite incensed, made a resolution to return at once to Syria. But some of his people, pointing out to him that he ought at least to make a trial of such an easy remedy as the Prophet had prescribed for him, he allowed himself to be persuaded and went to wash himself seven times in the Jordan. The hand of God was with him and healed him of his leprosy. He, delighted by this miracle and full of gratitude for such a great favor, returned again to Elisha and strongly urged him to accept some gifts; but the Prophet refused them. To this miraculous healing of the body, Grace also added that of the soul. Naaman became a participant in the Covenant and renounced idolatry, to henceforth serve no one in the land of Syria, where he returned, but the God of Israel, whom he had not known until that time.

Naaman had no sooner departed from Elisha than Gehazi ran after him to cunningly demand a <term>talent of silver</term> <note>A talent was a heavy unit of weight; a talent of silver was a very large sum of money, roughly equivalent to several years' wages for a laborer.</note> and two changes of clothing from him in his master's name, under a pretext that he invented. Naaman received this request with joy and gave the servant of the Prophet two talents and two garments. Upon his return, Elisha asked him where he had been; and Gehazi had the audacity to answer that he had been nowhere.

<column-break/>

But he stood amazed when he saw that God had revealed everything he had done to the Prophet; and to punish him for his greed and lies, Elisha announced to him that the leprosy of Naaman would cling to him and his entire lineage forever. Immediately, this miserable man saw himself covered with leprosy and did not show himself to Elisha again.

Holy Scripture continues from here with another miracle of Elisha. The King of Syria had marched into the land of Israel with an army and had secretly laid an ambush to surprise the King of Israel at a place where he was known to have to pass through. Elisha made this known to the King of Israel, who immediately sent troops to take up a position there. Other decisions were made in the Council of the King of Syria, all of which were discovered. The Syrian imagined that he was being betrayed by someone from his Council; but he was assured of the contrary, and told that the man who revealed all his designs to the King of Israel was a certain Prophet in that land. The King of Syria then sent a large band of cavalry to seize him at Dothan, in the Tribe of Zebulon or Manasseh, where the Prophet was then staying. These people came by night and besieged the city; the next morning very early, Elisha's servant came to him, very afraid, to bring him this news. At the same time, at the prayer of the Prophet, the Lord opened the eyes of this young man, so that he saw a mountain full of fiery horses and chariots surrounding Elisha. The enemies meanwhile having come down to capture him, he prayed God to strike them with blindness; and subsequently coming to them, he said to them by way of mockery and derision, that he would bring them to the man they sought. Thereupon he led them to Samaria. When the King of Israel saw these Syrians enclosed within his city, he wanted to sacrifice them all to the sword: but the Prophet prevented him from doing so, and brought it about that Joram sent them back, after having given them all kinds of good hospitality.

Some time after this, the same King of Syria came again into the land of Israel and besieged Samaria. Because this siege lasted a long time, and because the city had perhaps not been sufficiently provided with food, such a great famine arose that a <term>donkey’s head</term> <note>Considered an "unclean" animal under Jewish law, eating it—let alone paying a high price for it—signaled the ultimate level of desperation.</note> was sold for one hundred and twenty <term>guilders</term>, and a small measure of dove-droppings for nearly three <term>rijksdaalders</term> <note>The original Dutch uses 'gulden' and 'ryksdaalder', 17th-century currencies, to help the reader of the time understand the exorbitant prices during the biblical famine.</note>. The besieged were finally brought to such a terrible state of need that they ate one another, and there were two women who entered into a cruel pact with each other to eat their own children. The one of these miserable mothers who was the first to surrender hers shared it with the other; but when she expected that the other would in her turn produce her son to be eaten, she refused to do so. The first, now carried away by grief and despair, ran to make her complaint to the King about this faithless woman who had thus deceived her; she found him as he was inspecting the walls of the city, and having thrown herself at his feet, she told him the cause of her grief which pierced her heart, and sought justice from him. The Prince shuddered upon hearing this matter, and without passing judgment on such a hideous quarrel, his pity for his people suddenly changed into a raging wrath against Elisha. He swore that he would have his head cut off before the day was out, and quickly sent someone to seize him. Perhaps he held a grudge against that Prophet because the year before he had been the cause that they

<column-break/>

had not put to death the Syrians, who had imprudently entered Samaria like a flock of birds into a fowler’s net: or perhaps he was angry because the Prophet had not delivered Samaria through some miracle, or warded off the famine. The Spirit of God revealed to Elisha that someone was coming by the King's command to cut off his head. The Prophet then had his door shut; and while the King's messengers were attempting to enter, the King himself arrived—having reconsidered the injustice of his command—to prevent its execution and to speak with Elisha, who was thus miraculously saved from the death which seemed inevitable.

But when they arrived in the camp, they found not a single man. The Syrians, terrified by a great noise, like that of chariots, horses, and a mighty army, which they imagined they heard, had fled with great haste, out of fear of being overwhelmed by this army, which they believed to be Egyptians and other peoples come to the aid of the King of Israel. These four lepers ate and drank in the first tent they entered, and they found gold and silver there, which they took away to hide. They then went into another tent, where they likewise took and carried away various things: they would have gone back and forth in the camp even more, had they not feared being discovered by some people from Samaria and being punished for keeping this notable news of the breaking of the siege hidden for so long. They then returned to the city without delay. The report they brought there appeared incredible to everyone. But the King, having sent out two men on horseback to go and inspect the camp of the Syrians, they soon returned with confirmation of the news which the four lepers had brought. All the people who were within Samaria marched out to see this wonder, and to obtain their share of the booty from the enemy army. So many valuables and such a great multitude of all kinds of provisions were found there, that from all sides nothing but cloth, linen, and foodstuffs were brought from the camp to the

## II. Kings Chapter IX. verses 30--37.

Since the King of Israel and his people had no true gratitude for the deliverance which God had granted to the city of Samaria, and since they continued to offend him through their horrible idolatries <note>The worship of false gods, specifically Baal, which was promoted by the royal house</note>, the Lord decided to punish that Kingdom with a famine of seven years. Elisha had warned the Shunammite woman <note>A woman from Shunem whom Elisha had befriended</note>, whose child he had raised from the dead, about this; and she, on the advice of the Prophet, had moved with her household from her land to that of the Philistines. Seven years later, she returned to the land of Israel and appeared before the King to be restored to her estate. At that time, the King was being told by Gehazi, who had been in Elisha's service, of all those wonders which he had seen his master perform, and he was just at the account of the bringing to life of the Shunammite's child when he saw her arrive. "See there, My Lord King," he said, "this is the woman, and this is her son, whom Elisha brought back to life." The King desired that she herself should tell him in what manner Elisha had performed such a great miracle; after which he granted her what she requested of him.

Around that time it happened that Ben-hadad, that King of Syria who had so often made war against the King of Israel, 

<column-break/>

fell ill at Damascus, and Elisha went there at the same time, moved by the Spirit of God. Ben-hadad, having heard of his arrival, sent Hazael, one of his chief officials, to him to ask whether he would recover from this illness. The Prophet gave such an answer from which one could conclude that the illness was not exactly fatal, but nevertheless, he said clearly that the King would not recover from it. While Elisha looked intently at Hazael as he spoke, he showed a great agitation on his face, even to the point of weeping. Hazael, startled by the Prophet’s sadness, asked him for the cause: "It is," he said, "because I know what evil you will do to the children of Israel; you will set their strongholds on fire, kill their young men with the sword, dash their young children to pieces, and rip open their pregnant women." Hazael, amazed to hear the Prophet speak thus, cried out: "What is your servant, who is but a dog, that he should do this great thing?" "Yes," Elisha answered, "The LORD has shown me that you shall be King over Syria." Hazael then returned to the King and made him believe that he would recover from his illness; yet the next day he smothered him in his bed and reigned after him in his place.

To this end, he gave an order to all the priests of Baal, who were scattered in various places throughout the entire Kingdom, that they should present themselves in Samaria on a certain day, *“for I have,”* said he, *“a great sacrifice to Baal.”* Men then came there from all sides, and not a single one of those priests remained behind; they all came running to this ceremony, as if to a magnificent triumph that their god had achieved over the Lord in the Kingdom of Israel. The Temple of Baal was filled with people, the priests dressed themselves in their priestly garments at the King’s command, everything was prepared for the sacrifice, the victims were brought, the priests laid their hands upon them, the blood was shed, the burnt offering smoked upon the altar, and the idolater rejoiced to see that the god he worshiped was being served publicly and with splendor in the capital of the Kingdom, under the eyes and by the authority of the new King. After the idolaters had been put to death, the idol itself was also brought forward; it was immediately plucked from its place, broken into pieces, and cast into the fire. They also tore down the Temple of Baal and turned that place into latrines <note>original: "heymelyke gemakken," literally secret conveniences; Jehu turned the site of the pagan temple into a public sewer to ensure it would remain ritually unclean and disgraced forever.</note>, deeming it unworthy to serve any more honorable use after it had attracted such infamous and wicked impurity through an abominable idolatry. This Temple was never rebuilt thereafter, and Jehu had the honor at the beginning of his reign in Israel of casting down that idol of jealousy <note>original: "belgzugt," referring to the provocative nature of false idols that incite God's jealousy</note> which Jezebel had brought with her from Sidon, and which the wretched Ahab had confirmed there by his authority. After this great deed, there remained nothing left for Jehu to do but to likewise tear down the golden calves of Jeroboam; but this superstitious service had gained a sort of privilege in the minds of all the Kings of Israel, whereby the purest knowledge they could have possessed was extinguished in their souls. And notwithstanding the warnings and rebukes of the Prophets against the golden calves of Dan and Bethel, the politics of schism <term>schism: the political and religious split between the northern kingdom of Israel and the southern kingdom of Judah</term> always held the upper hand in the minds of those Princes over the interests of religion and the duties of conscience.

At that time Elisha became ill, and the King of Israel came to visit him; finding him in danger of dying, he said while weeping: *My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its horsemen*; as if he meant to say, "You are the guidance, the strength, and the protection of the Realm." The Prophets thus had certain particular ways of foretelling the future; and since God had only revealed to Elisha that Joash would be victorious over the Syrians as many times as he struck the earth with his arrows, without prescribing that he should inform the King how many times he must strike, Elisha was troubled that he had stopped after three strikes. He saw clearly that in three battles with the Syrians, Joash would not gain enough advantage to destroy that great Kingdom of Syria, which had constantly brought so many calamities upon God’s people. Elisha died of that illness, and although he deserved the greatest honors of burial to be given to his memory, nevertheless the Holy Scripture, through the simple and abbreviated manner in which it speaks of it, gives us sufficiently to understand that the Prophet was brought to the earth without any special sign of honor or distinction, for it tells us only that Elisha died, and that they buried him.

Not long thereafter, some war-bands of the Moabites entered Judea to raid and plunder the countryside; meanwhile it happened that some people were going to bury a dead man. As soon as the dead man touched the bones of the Prophet, he became alive again and stood upright on his feet. ...shadow of the Apostles, on the road where they passed by. But it belongs to a wise and sensible piety to make a distinction between the almighty hand which brought forth all those miracles, and that which gave nothing more than the occasion for them; to the end that one ascribes to God alone the glory of those great wonders, and shows reverence in the bones and ashes of the Saints to the Grace that sanctified them, without attributing any other honor to those bones and ashes than that which consists in the imitation of the virtues of those great Saints.

The holy Writer of the second book of Chronicles relates a very remarkable matter in the life of King Joash <note>original: "Joas"</note>, which was passed over in the book of Kings, and which it was felt ought to be inserted here, so as not to deviate too far from the thread of the Biblical History proposed here. Joash had walked in the ways of the Lord as long as the Priest Jehoiada <note>original: "Jojada"</note>, to whom he owed his life and crown, was still living. But this holy and wise High Priest, who had performed all the remarkable services for Religion and the State that one could expect from someone of that rank, finally died at the age of one hundred and thirty years, leaving behind the most excellent reputation a man could leave. Joash, no longer having before his eyes that great example which the High Priest had always given him, allowed his heart—which was not sufficiently established in the holy resolve never to deviate from the paths of godliness in which Jehoiada had raised him from his tender youth—to be led astray by a company of flatterers, who persuaded him to reintroduce the worship of Baal, which Jehoiada had banished, into his Kingdom. The Prophets did everything possible to restore order and to persuade the King that he should not allow his reign to be stained with an act so contrary to the Laws of Religion. They set before his eyes the calamities which those impieties would bring upon his Kingdom and his person, and they forgot nothing to instill in him feelings of loyalty, which he owed to the goodness of a God who had given him a refuge from the cruelties of Athaliah <note>original: "Athalia"</note> in His own Temple, and caused him to ascend the throne as if by a miracle. But Joash was insensitive to all this; he restored the sacred groves of the idol-<column-break/>aters, the service of false gods was legalized by the scandalous example of the Great Men and the King, and the worship of the true God was as if smothered under the terrible progress of idolatry. Among those who resisted this with the most courage, the High Priest Zechariah <note>original: "Zacharia"</note>, who had followed in the office and zeal of his father Jehoiada, showed himself particularly praiseworthy. He used all the authority which the supreme ministry of the Church gave him over his nation; but he found in the people, as well as in the King and the principal Lords of the Court, such a monstrous inclination toward idolatry that he could gain nothing over minds so prejudiced. At a certain time when he spoke to them in the Temple against such hideous impieties, he was suddenly seized by an extraordinary movement of the Holy Spirit, which caused him to speak thus to the people from an elevated place where he stood in the Temple: *Why do you transgress the commandments of the LORD? therefore you shall not prosper: because you have forsaken the LORD, he shall also forsake you.* At these words, their wickedness burst out with a fierce rage against the rebuke; they fell upon the High Priest, dragged him close to the gate of the Temple, and overwhelmed him with stones between the gate and the altar. Joash saw this hideous deed committed within Jerusalem, indeed within the Temple, and he did not wash away the stain of it with the blood of the guilty: but God was Himself the avenger of it; just as Zechariah had said while dying: *The LORD shall see it, and require it.* <note>The Hebrew phrase implies seeking an account or vengeance for the blood spilled.</note> The following year an army came out of Syria to make Jerusalem and Judea bear the punishment for their abominations. Since it was God who had called the Syrian to defend His cause, it was not necessary that they assemble a large army, as at other times, nor that the King himself come in person. With a very small number of troops, the Syrians defeated a large army of the King of Judah, because God fought with them, and for Himself. Judea was plundered by its enemies, and the treasures of the King were sent to Damascus to the King of Syria. The principal Lords of the Kingdom of Judah lost their lives in that war, and if the King survived this loss, it was only to be delivered over to his sorrow and to his own servants, who finally conspired against him and killed him on his bed.

...extends so far as to grant the power to make changes in Divine Worship to the detriment of godly laws, or that it leaves them free to command what God has forbidden and to forbid what He has commanded; and that if the Lord sometimes permits Kings to abuse their power without punishing them instantly, as He did with <term>Azariah<gloss>Also known as Uzziah</gloss></term>, the vengeance, though long delayed, is no less certain, since God is no less just at one time, nor less zealous for His prerogatives, than at another. Azariah reigned fifty-two years, and left as his successor his son Jotham, who reigned sixteen years, and likewise did not deviate from the service of the true God to chase after <term>Idols<gloss>Images or gods worshipped instead of the Creator</gloss></term>, as some of the Kings his ancestors had done, and as all those of Israel did.

<margin>The year of the world 3262. Before J.C. 742.</margin>
Piety is not hereditary in families; Jotham had a son named <term>Ahaz<gloss>original: "Achaz"</gloss></term>, who succeeded him in the government, yet immersed himself in idolatry. He walked in the footsteps of the godless Kings of the Kingdom of Israel, and to all the superstitions of previous reigns, he added the service of <term>Moloch<gloss>original: "Moloch" or "Milkom"</gloss></term>, whom God had so expressly forbidden in the laws of Moses. Since the unholy reign of Ahaz, this worship was introduced into Judah and persisted there, despite all warnings and threats of the Prophets, until the destruction of Jerusalem and the downfall of the entire Kingdom. Moloch, or Milcom, as he is called in other places of Scripture, was an Idol of the Ammonites—the god for whom that people had the greatest reverence and in whom they placed their greatest trust. This name of Moloch means <note>original: "Koning"</note> "King" in the language of those peoples, and since the oldest idolatry was that of the Sun, it was specifically the Sun which was worshipped under the name of Moloch, because the Sun was regarded by those idolaters as the King of the Universe, on account of its great influence on all the products of Nature. The Sidonians worshipped this heavenly light

<column-break/>

under a similar name, namely that of <term>Baal<gloss>A Canaanite title meaning Lord or Master</gloss></term>, for Baal means <note>original: "Heer, óf Oppervórst"</note> "Lord" or "Sovereign." In some lands of Assyria, the Sun was also honored under the names of <term>Adrammelech<gloss>Meaning "Magnificent King"</gloss></term> or <term>Anammelech<gloss>Meaning "King who Answers"</gloss></term>, both of which mean roughly the same thing; and one can say in general that there have been few peoples who did not worship it as the greatest of their gods. The worship rendered to him under the name of Moloch was the most superstitious and the most terrible of all: it consisted primarily in showing very great honor to that Idol through fire, which is the element on earth that most closely resembles the nature of the Sun, and which somewhat represents the heat and light of that star. But this worship, which occurred to Moloch or to the Sun in the fire, was performed in two ways; the simplest was to light two large fires close to each other and to walk back and forth between them, thrusting hands and feet into the flames: this was called a consecration or purification, and one considered oneself very well purified when this exercise had been repeated several times. The other way to honor Moloch, of which Holy Scripture speaks most, and which is also the most criminal, was to offer living people to the burning flames that were lit for that godless and terrifying use. For the fathers threw their sons and daughters into them, to be thus burned entirely alive; and it was then that this invention of beating on drums <note>This refers to the "Tophet," where drums were used to drown out screams.</note> during these human sacrifices came into practice, so that the pitiful crying might not be heard, and the bystanders thereby be made faint-hearted. Ahaz introduced these impieties into his Kingdom and gave an example of them himself, making his son pass through the fire, whether this occurred simply in the first of these two ways to consecrate his son to the Idol, or whether it occurred in the other manner, and that he actually delivered one of his children to the flames; for the Interpreters differ in their opinion regarding this.

### II. Kings Chapter XVIII. verse 4.

The wickednesses of <note>The text mentions "Achab" (Ahab), the notorious King of Israel, likely referring to the lingering influence of his idolatrous house upon Judah, or perhaps as a scribe's comparison to King Ahaz’s similar sins.</note> Ahab and all his people brought upon the Kingdom of Judah a terrible war, under which it seemed to sink entirely. Pekah, son of Remaliah, King of Israel, turned his weapons against his brothers, the children of Judah, and in a battle which he waged against them, one hundred and twenty thousand men of Judah were killed; and Pekah, returning again to Samaria, carried two hundred thousand, both men and women, captive with him. One can hardly imagine how such a multitude of people could exist in so small a land as the Kingdom of Judah was; but one can also easily think that it must have been little better than a desert after more than three hundred thousand souls were taken from it. God, meanwhile, not wishing to destroy this Kingdom entirely, although it had deserved it only too well, sent a Prophet named Oded to the King of Samaria, to command him to send those two hundred thousand people, whom he had carried away, back to Judah. Ahaz having died some time later, Hezekiah his son reigned in his place. This was a King whom God in His mercy gave to Jerusalem, to prevent <term>Religion<gloss>Refers here specifically to the worship of the God of Israel</gloss></term> from being completely stifled and extinguished. Hezekiah began his reign with the tearing down of all the places which were dedicated to the Idols. He had all the statues found in the land shattered; he rooted out all the <term>High Places<gloss>Elevated sites used for unauthorized or pagan sacrificial worship</gloss></term>, cut down the groves, overturned the altars, and left no trace of idolatry in the entire Kingdom. There was also an abuse concerning the <term>Copper Serpent<gloss>The Nehushtan; originally a symbol of healing, it had become an object of worship</gloss></term> which had crept in, which he

did not wish to let take root. Moses, by God’s command in the wilderness, had made a serpent of copper to set up before the sight of all the Israelites who were bitten by the fiery serpents; but from the book of Numbers, where that history is told, until this place in the life of Hezekiah, which comprises a time of about eight hundred years, there is no mention made of it at all in the Scripture, and one does not perceive at all where this image of the serpent had remained. Meanwhile, it appears by this act of Hezekiah regarding this copper serpent, that it must have been preserved in some place in the Temple, or the city of Jerusalem, to serve the children of Israel as a distinguished memorial of the miraculous healing which God had formerly wrought for their fathers through this image. This was the only use made of it for many centuries, but superstition increasing in these latter times, had made of this monument of antiquity—which was truly holy to some extent, and of such a nature that it impressed feelings of wonder and gratitude toward the infinite goodness of God upon the minds of the Jews—an object of religion, to which they attached a sort of godliness and reverence. Hezekiah could not endure that they burned incense before this copper image, however venerable it might otherwise be, for it was made by God’s express command and had served for a miraculous healing of the Israelites; yes, what is more, it was arranged by a profound insight of God as an emphatic <term>foreshadowing<gloss>A prophetic symbol or "type"</gloss></term> of our Lord Jesus Christ. He had this serpent shattered, calling it out of contempt <term>Nehushtan<gloss>original: "Nehuſtan"</gloss></term>, that is, a piece of copper. ### II. Kings Chapter XIX. verse 35.

<margin>The year of the world 3291. 713 B.C.</margin> Eight years after the downfall of the Kingdom of Israel, Sennacherib <note>original: "Sanherib"</note>, King of Assyria, son and successor of Shalmaneser, led his armies against Judea. The beginnings of this war were very favorable to him; he took without much effort the first places he attacked in Judea, and being master of the field, he advanced almost as much as he wished. Within a short time, he approached close to Jerusalem, the capital of the Realm and the only city capable of offering much resistance. King Hezekiah, finding himself not strong enough to do battle with him, turned all his care toward reinforcing that place, to make it as capable as possible of enduring a siege—which he feared he could not escape, regardless of his conduct toward Sennacherib to that end. This proud and ambitious Prince had not come from so far merely to set limits to his glory by taking a few cities and to content himself with the treasures Hezekiah had sent him. Sennacherib sent from Lachish, where he remained with his army, three of his chief commanders to demand the surrender of Jerusalem. Hezekiah <note>original: "Hizkia"</note> seemed struck by the threat of Isaiah <note>original: "Jeſaia"</note>: the desire to live is natural to man, and it is a rare thing when Grace, which makes saints, extinguishes it so completely in them that it does not well up again when one believes death to be near. Hezekiah was not yet free from that weakness, which cannot be considered sinful as long as it does not weaken the desire and hope for the other life in a soul. This Prince could also not but have many reasons, even arising from piety, to wish that God let him stay a little longer in the world. He saw that the Kingdom, for which the irreligion of the King his father, and some other of his ancestors, had been so destructive, had need of a King who was zealous for the purity of Religion; and since he and his whole people had received an excellent favor from the protection of God, it befitted his piety to wish that he might live, to testify his gratitude to God for it even longer at the head of his whole Kingdom; almost in that same spirit as David said, *Let my soul live, and it shall praise you.* God was sensitive to the heartache and the sorrow of Hezekiah, and heard his prayer. Isaiah came to tell him that he should not die, and that God gave him fifteen more years of life. Hezekiah asked him whether the Lord would not be pleased to confirm that grace through some miraculous sign. The Prophet said to him "Yes," and proposed to him at once whether he desired that the Sun should so hasten its course that the shadow of Ahaz's <note>original: "Achaz"</note> sundial went forward ten degrees, or whether he would rather that the sun moved back ten degrees. Hezekiah chose the latter, which appeared more wonderful to him than the former. Isaiah then prayed to the Lord that it might please Him to work such a great wonder; and Hezekiah had the pleasure of seeing, for his sake and solely for his comfort and for the strengthening of his faith, a miracle the like of which had never been seen before, and which has never been seen since: namely, that the Sun returned, and that the shadow on the Sundial of King Ahaz went backward ten degrees. The use of Sundials <note>original: "Uurwyzeren," literally hour-indicators</note>, where all the hours of the day are indicated by a needle upon which the Sun shines, was at that time so rare that they had not yet been seen in Italy or in Greece, much less would they have been known in other regions of Europe that were more remote and less civilized by science. The Egyptians and Chaldeans, the first Mathematicians and Astronomers of the world, had first invented the division of the day into a certain number of small parts to which the name of "hours" was later given, and they had subsequently devised that ingenious art of indicating those hours or degrees by the shadow of sundials; but the use thereof was not yet common, and it was a rare thing that King Ahaz, father of Hezekiah, had one made on the wall of the Palace: and therefore special mention is made of that Sundial in the miracle that God performed for Hezekiah on that occasion. Since this miracle is of such a nature that great difficulties arise from it, the Interpreters are divided into various opinions regarding the manner in which this matter might have occurred; but without

<column-break/>

entering into that investigation here, it is enough to note that the opinion of those who believed that the change of which is spoken consisted only in the shadow of Ahaz's Sundial, is clearly contradicted by the account of this history found in the second book of Chronicles, where it is said that the King of Babylon sent Envoys to Hezekiah to inquire after the miraculous sign that had happened; and by what is recounted in the thirty-eighth chapter of Isaiah, that the *Sun returned ten degrees.*

The arrival of the Envoys of the King of Babylon at Jerusalem to congratulate Hezekiah on his miraculous healing was something so unusual that all Judea was amazed by it: Hezekiah in particular, who had the full honor of that embassy, expressed great joy because of it: and in order to give the Babylonian Lords the highest possible idea of the greatness and excellence of his Kingdom, he showed them everything that was most outstanding with him; his gold, his silver, his precious stones, the choicest spices that grew in Judea or the surrounding lands and were so esteemed and sought after by the whole East; his treasuries, his armories—in short, there was nothing that he did not show them. It is considered on such occasions in the Courts of Princes a duty of propriety and politeness to show to strangers all the rarest and most beautiful things one has. The ambition to have oneself spoken of by strangers because of something remarkable flatters man in a pleasant way, and the world considers that enough to justify its use. Hezekiah also allowed himself to be deceived by this, and took no heed that he longed too much for fame, and himself took too much pleasure in the praise which the Envoys of Babylon gave to his glory and luster. Isaiah came to warn him about this, and showed him that there was a certain pride in that dealing for which God—who loves nothing so much, even among the greatest Kings of the earth, as an inward humility—was very angry. The Prophet asked Hezekiah from where those men had come? *They have come*, answered the King, *from far countries, from Babylon.* Isaiah asked him further what they had seen in his house: *There is nothing in my treasures*, said the King, *that I have not shown them.*

Thereupon the Prophet pronounced this judgment over him:
> "The time shall come, says the Lord, that
> everything that is in your house, and everything that your
> fathers have gathered there until this day,
> your gold, your silver, all your wealth, shall be carried
> to Babylon; yes, all your children shall be led
> thither as slaves.

The decrees of God are always just, as the Scripture says, but without doubt this is one of the strictest, because God has wanted to give us to understand—what His Scriptures have told us so many times—that it pleases Him to humble a heart that exalts itself, and that the more virtues are united in a mind like that of Hezekiah, so much more humility ought to be found therein. But this godly Prince, through the answer he gave to the Prophet, showed sufficiently that it was only through a sort of surprise that vain ambition had crept into his heart:
> "The

Thus Manasseh, through a miracle of Grace, learned to know the God of his fathers within Babylon, whom he had not known in Jerusalem; and he returned with an enlightened understanding and holy inclinations from the land of the Unbelievers, where he had dragged his vices and errors with him.

Original taint always passes from the father to the children, for this is the constant and irrevocable law of all the children of Adam; and often, various criminal inclinations and seeds of vice creep into children alongside that natural impurity, so that one sees the crimes of their deceased fathers reborn in them. Josiah also had all the people solemnly renew the covenant with God, just as Joshua <note>original: "Josua"</note> had done shortly before his death. His piety likewise excelled in the celebration of the Passover <note>original: "Paaschfeest"</note>, which he had held with such generosity and great expense that nothing like it had ever been seen, even under the reign of Solomon. Josiah gave to the people for sacrifice thirty thousand lambs and young goats, and three thousand cattle, besides the other sacrifices given by the Lords of the Court and other wealthy and generous persons, which also amounted to several thousand. This holy King, having received a new confirmation from God through the prophetess Huldah <note>original: "Hulda"</note> that the curses written in the book of Moses against Judea were soon to be fulfilled, received that prediction from the Prophetess with deep reverence; but he had the comfort of understanding that God spared him from seeing those great disasters, and that he would depart from the world in peace before those sad and calamitous times came.
