<margin>The year of the world 3416. before J. C. 588.</margin>
Nebuchadnezzar departs from Babylon with a great army; he enters the land of Judah and marches directly upon Jerusalem to seek the rebel, who kept himself enclosed there with his men of war to defend the place.

Meanwhile, the King of Babylon begins the siege and, according to the custom of that time, throws up mounds and fortifications before the city to create approaches and to storm the walls with good progress. The place was strong by its position, for it lay very high and was difficult for the siege engines to approach: the walls were high and thick, and strengthened by a multitude of towers built close to one another; and because it was only in the protection of that city that Zedekiah had placed his trust, it was guarded by his best troops. All this made the conquest very difficult; the siege lasted eighteen months, but finally the day arrived which God had destined for its downfall. The enemy made a breach in the wall; the besieged despaired of their safety, and the King, having fled by night, was pursued and taken prisoner in the plains of Jericho. The Babylonians then entered Jerusalem from all sides, and with them came rage and murder. Its streets and squares were immediately filled with the dead, and the air with the mournful lamentations of the conquered, along with the fierce and terrible shouting of the conquerors. Everywhere there was nothing but filthiness, cruelties, and the plundering of houses. And the Temple—that Temple so precious in its materials, so magnificent in its arrangement, so artistic in its making, so

<column-break/>

wonderful in everything, that Palace of the God of Israel and the Lord of the world—is laid open to the insatiable greed of the soldier. The Bronze Sea <note>original: "kópere Zee" — a massive bronze basin used for ritual washing in the Temple court.</note>, the altar, and its pillars are broken into pieces to be carried to Babylon. The gold, the ornaments, the sacred tools, even the Ark of the Covenant—so precious by its nature and of an inestimable value for the honor of having served God as a throne for nine hundred years in his Tabernacle or in his Temple—become a prey to the Babylonians. The sacred Tablets of the Covenant <note>The stone tablets inscribed with the Ten Commandments.</note> are thrown among common stones and buried with them under the ruins of the entire building. They overload King Zedekiah with chains and gouge out his eyes, after first having slaughtered his sons in his presence. They then carry him, with the nobles of the Realm and the greatest part of the people, to Babylon: and they allow no one to remain in the whole land except some families of farmers and vinedressers, solely so that the lands would not lie entirely unplanted and fallow. Such was the end of the Kingdom of Judah and Jerusalem, and of the Temple; a deserved punishment of divine Justice for the long and ancient idolatry of the Kings and the people; a punishment nonetheless all too mild for such heavy crimes, had God not intended mercy for a race from which he had decided to bring forth the Messiah one day. This decree which God had made, and with which he had maintained the hope of Israel for many centuries, prevented Judea from being ruined forever then; and it was the cause that God, wanting to deliver it from a criminal people with whom it had long been burdened as with an uncomfortable pack, transported them in such a way to the land of Babylon that he kept them there as in a place of safety, to bring them back again—

<margin>The year of the world 3442.</margin> Babylon was enriched by the spoils of Jerusalem, and Nebuchadnezzar brought in greater honor through the conquest of the Kingdom of Judah than through the seizing of any other land. But this Prince took far too much courage from this glory and became too puffed up by it. He imagined that he had triumphed over the God of Judah himself by the casting down of His Palace and His Temple: but in Babylon he soon felt the formidable hand of that God whom he thought he had conquered at Jerusalem. God struck him with a certain malady of the mind <note>The author refers to the period of madness described in the Book of Daniel, where Nebuchadnezzar lived like a beast of the field.</note>, which placed him among the rank of the beasts and made him an object of contempt and mockery to his Court and people. His son Evil-Merodach <note>Also known as Amel-Marduk, reigned c. 562–560 BC.</note> ascended the Throne after him. At that time, thirty-seven years had passed since Jehoiachin, King of Judah, had been a prisoner in Babylon; it is not known what special bond existed between him and Evil-Merodach. Jewish tradition states that they had been in prison together for a time, and that Nebuchadnezzar had placed his son there for certain matters that occurred under the administration of this Prince during his father’s insanity; but this is a pure Jewish tradition which has no foundation in History. Whatever the causes of the new King’s friendship toward Jehoiachin may have been, he released him from his chains and gave him back his freedom. He extended his mercy even further and gave to the

<column-break/>

Jehoiachin also had the honor of eating at the King’s table, and he received, moreover, an annual sum for the maintenance of his house for all his life. It was a great comfort for the captive Jews in Babylon to see that their King was held in such high regard there, and it was a means which God wished to use to make their state less miserable. The heat of His wrath had already passed somewhat, through the vengeance He had taken for the crimes of the Jews; and if in those first years of their servitude it had not entirely cooled, it was because He judged it necessary for their well-being to keep them under the rod of His chastisement, and that He wished to make their deliverance, after a long captivity, more glorious. But amidst all the loss that the Royal house had suffered in these last wars, God always preserved for David a lamp <note>The "lamp of David" is a biblical metaphor for the continuation of the Davidic lineage (cf. 1 Kings 11:36).</note> in Babylon, which He had allowed to be extinguished in Jerusalem, so that in Judea there might once again be Kings of his descent, and above all so that the Messiah, the spiritual King, who was to come forth from there at a certain time, might be born in the following centuries from the blood of that illustrious House and restore the Kingdom of Israel in a much nobler and more glorious sense.

It was a great comfort for this people in their calamities that they could say of them not only that they would one day come to an end, but also that they could see the entire duration beforehand from afar and without fear of being mistaken: for every month, every week, indeed every day of their captivity, was a shortening of the account of the seventy years, at the end of which their freedom was to be restored to them. To give the Jews their freedom, Babylon had to be laid in chains and the whole world, so to speak, turned upside down. Cyrus, born in somewhat humble circumstances, made a great name for himself through his deeds of war and political virtues. Zerubbabel, an illustrious descendant of the Royal line, and Jeshua the High Priest, set out with all these people; God serves as their guide, and under His guidance and watch they come into Canaan, and behold their ancestral lands again, yet above all Jerusalem, the object of their most tender desires during their long absence, and the source of the greatest comfort after their return, though it presented nothing to their eyes but ruined walls and collapsed houses. They even held a fondness for the very dust and rubble, and Mount Zion, where the Temple had stood, presented to their minds, from the midst of the ruins, the pleasant idea of God’s covenant with them, and of His presence in the midst of His people. They began at once to erect an altar to God, to offer sacrifices to Him. This holy practice, which was like the center point in which all the lines of the Mosaic religion <term>Mosaic religion: The system of laws and worship established through Moses in the Torah.</term> were united, had been entirely ceased during the captivity, because it was not permitted for this people to erect altars to God in a foreign land: one can therefore easily understand with what joy the Priests consecrated their hands anew to offer sacrifices, and what a comfort it must have been to this people to be able to offer that duty of their gratitude and zeal to God again. Meanwhile, Zerubbabel and Jeshua made the necessary preparations to build the house of the Lord. The work was great in itself, and it could not be otherwise than very difficult for a people who had recently returned from a long captivity. But God had already provided for this, by instilling such a noble generosity in Cyrus <note>Cyrus the Great, the Persian king who conquered Babylon and permitted the Jews to return to Jerusalem.</note> that he had the gold and silver vessels, which had formerly served for the Temple of Jerusalem and which Nebuchadnezzar had carried away to Babylon, returned to the people. God blessed the diligence and industriousness of the people in building the walls of Jerusalem, and fifty days <note>Though the biblical text in Nehemiah 6:15 mentions 52 days, this author records fifty.</note> after Nehemiah had resumed the labor, they were completed. It is true, they built from all sides at once, and a countless multitude of people devoted their hands with zeal to this work, while others kept themselves in arms all around to prevent their enemies from entering; but nonetheless, one could then truly say according to the letter, with the 127th *Psalm, Unless the LORD builds the house, its builders labor in vain: unless the LORD guards the city, the watchman stays awake in vain*. The people acknowledged this and were sensible of it; for Ezra, wishing to gather them five days later to perform a public act of godliness, they all came running together in a multitude to the place where he had appointed them, to hear from the mouth of that holy man everything he had to present to them. Ezra went thither, accompanied by all the Leaders of the people, and having climbed upon a raised wooden platform, so as to be seen by all and heard more easily from all sides, he took, says the holy Writer, *the Book of the Law*, whether these were the five books of Moses, which usually made up only one scroll, or whether it was the fifth book alone, which is like a short summary of the four; and he read from it from early morning until noon before the whole people. Nehemiah suggests that Ezra explained the meaning while reading. Some believe that this referred to the literal text, regarding certain words that could not be so easily understood by those among the Jews who were born in the land of Babylon and were not accustomed to speaking Hebrew. But since one cannot reasonably doubt that the Jews in their state of captivity would have had the divine books in their original language, and that the fathers would have had the children read them, especially since they knew that at the end of seventy years they were to be restored to Judea; so it is not probable that Ezra, on that solemn day, would have interrupted the reading of the Holy Scripture every time to explain the Hebrew words through Chaldean <note>original: "Chaldeesche" — referring to Aramaic, the language adopted by many Jews during the exile.</note> idioms. However, this much is certain, that he gave the people an understanding of the matters according as they were more or less obscure, and the weight of the subject required it. Ezra was an intelligent Priest, and perfectly experienced in the practice of the Law, and moreover inspired by that same Spirit who had foretold to Moses the things which he wrote. Meanwhile, this holy Teacher used a certain manner for the interpretation of Scripture which equally makes known his humility and wisdom, and should serve as an example to all Interpreters of the divine Books; this was *to explain Scripture by Scripture*; because, as Augustine <note>original: "Augustus" — referring to Saint Augustine of Hippo, who championed the principle of "Scriptura sacra sui ipsius interpres" (Sacred Scripture is its own interpreter).</note> wisely remarked, what Scripture says somewhat obscurely in one place, it gives to be understood clearly in another. One need only read it with attention, without bending its words through any prejudice toward that sense which one has previously imagined, and then, when comparing the obscure places against the clear ones, one will perceive the meaning enclosed in the first without much effort. It is not easy to know in what time the matters related in the book of Esther occurred, or who King Ahasuerus <note>Original: "Ahasueros". Traditionally identified as Xerxes I, though the author debates this below.</note> was. The Interpreters differ so much in their opinions regarding this that it is not advisable to trouble the Reader with it here. The most probable opinion, and that which is followed by most, is that Ahasuerus was that same Monarch who is also called Darius Hystaspes <note>Darius the Great, who ruled the Persian Empire at its peak.</note>. One sees in all the ancient Histories of the Kings of the East that one and the same Prince had many names, and those of Ahasuerus or Cyaxares, which both mean Lord or Overlord, were titles of greatness rather than the proper name of the person, just like that of Pharaoh among the Egyptians, and that of Caesar or Augustus among the Romans. The city of Susa <note>Original: "Susan".</note>, where the Palace of King Ahasuerus stood, was the capital of Susiana, a prominent province situated between Babylonia and Persia; and as it appears from Greek History that a certain King of Susiana, named Astyages <note>Original: "Astibaras".</note>, had allied himself with Nebu-

Ezra went there, accompanied by all the leaders of the people, and having climbed upon a high wooden platform so as to be seen by all and more easily heard from all sides, he took—as the holy Writer says—*the Book of the Law*. Whether these were the five books of Moses, which usually made up only one scroll, or whether it was the fifth book alone, which serves as a summary of the other four, he read from it from early morning until noon before the entire people. Nehemiah suggests that Ezra explained the meaning while reading. Some believe this referred to the literal text, regarding certain words that could not be easily understood by those among the Jews who were born in the land of Babylon and were not accustomed to speaking Hebrew. But since one cannot reasonably doubt that the Jews in their state of captivity would have possessed the divine books in their original language, and that the fathers would have had the children read them—especially since they knew that at the end of seventy years they were to be restored to Judea—it is not probable that Ezra, on that solemn day, would have interrupted the reading of Holy Scripture every time to explain Hebrew words through Chaldean <note>Aramaic, the common tongue of the Persian Empire and Babylon.</note> expressions. However, it is certain that he gave the people an understanding of the matters according to whether they were more or less obscure, as the weight of the subject required. Ezra was a wise Priest, perfectly experienced in the practice of the Law, and moreover inspired by that same Spirit who had foretold to Moses the things he wrote. Meanwhile, this holy Teacher used a certain method for interpreting the Scripture that reveals his humility and wisdom equally, and which ought to serve as an example to all Interpreters of the divine Books; this was *to explain Scripture by Scripture*. This is because, as Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo, the influential early Christian theologian.</note> wisely remarked, what the Scripture says somewhat obscurely in one place, it makes clearly understood in another. One only needs to read it with attention, without bending its words through any prejudice toward a meaning one has previously imagined, and then, by comparing the obscure passages against the clear ones, one will perceive the meaning enclosed in the former without much trouble. He then said to the King that he felt the man whom the King wished to honor should be dressed in royal robes, have the royal crown placed on his head, and be set upon the horse that the King was accustomed to ride; that he should thus be led through the entire city of Susa accompanied by a great retinue, and that one of the greatest Lords of the Kingdom, holding the horse by the bridle, should walk ahead and cry out that this was how the King honored that man. Haman had no sooner finished speaking than the King commanded him to do everything he had proposed for Mordecai, and to lead the horse himself through the streets of the city. Here, there was nothing for him to do but to obey or bring death upon his own neck. Haman then had the King’s horse brought to Mordecai, and after dressing him in the royal robe, he himself led him with this pomp through the entire city. One can easily imagine with what shame and despair this proud man viewed that astonishing elevation of Mordecai, which caused himself to sink so low. His spite was further increased by the fact that he himself had advised the King to show such great honor to someone who, far from being the one he intended, was the man for whom he held the greatest hatred in the world. But God often pleases thus to shame the thoughts of the proud, and to turn the proposals of their vanity against themselves.

...the King was moved. The hour of the banquet to which Esther had invited the King, and where Haman alone of all the Great Men of the Realm was permitted to be found, having come, Ahasuerus betook himself there, as he had done the day before, with his Favorite. When Esther judged the time appropriate to make her petition to the King, she showed him in few words the miserable state of the Jews in his Realm, who by virtue of the last decree, which had come out in the King’s name against them, were all to be murdered, to satisfy the hatred of the irreconcilable enemy who had promoted that decree. She added to this that she herself being a Jew by birth, her life could also not be safe; and thereupon she prayed the King to have compassion on her and her people. Ahasuerus stood amazed to hear the Queen speak thus, and all his tender affection welling up for her at that moment, he asked who that man was, whom she said was the cause of the decree, which had been issued a few days before against the Jews. "It is Haman," she said, "this wicked Haman, who oppresses and persecutes my people." No more was needed to make the King enraged against him. This Prince nevertheless wished to place some moments of respite between the complaints of the Queen and the condemnation of the guilty one. The accuser was his consort, a woman whom he tenderly loved; and the accused was his chief favorite, who possessed all his good affection. All this created in his mind a sort of conflict, which not allowing him to take a decision on the spot, he stepped out of the hall, and went to walk alone in the garden, as if to listen with more freedom to the arguments of both. Haman meanwhile, who saw no outcome except in the compassion of the Queen, went to throw himself at her feet upon the bed <note>In ancient Persian custom, diners reclined on elaborate couches or 'beds' rather than sitting in chairs.</note> where she was seated during the meal, according to the custom of those times, to desire mercy from her, and to pray her that she herself would request the King’s goodness for him. At the same time Ahasuerus returns

<column-break/>

from the garden with the decision, which the interest of the Queen and the justice of her cause—strengthened by God Himself, who had spoken in the King's heart in her favor—had caused him to take against Haman; and seeing that Haman had added yet this to his first crimes, that he had violated the respect which a subject like him owed to his Queen, by climbing upon the sacred bed on which she was seated, he pronounced his death sentence as he approached. Scarcely was this judgment spoken, or they covered Haman's face, as unworthy to behold the King; so as to hide from the eyes of that Sovereign the face of someone who had fallen into his disgrace. Then one of the King's Chamberlains who had served at the table said that in the courtyard of Haman's house stood a gallows which he had caused to be erected there for Mordecai: *Hang him on it*, said the King. Immediately this wretched man is led away, and they hang him in his own courtyard, before his windows, on the gallows which he had caused to be made the day before, thinking to delight his envious and cruel eyes with the death penalty of Mordecai. All the goods of Haman were declared forfeited and given to Mordecai; the King honored him with the principal offices of his Court; he revoked the harsh decree that Haman had extorted from him through deceit against the Jews, who henceforth were honored and respected through the whole Realm; and the blessing of God was with Esther and Mordecai until the end of their lives. God showed through this remarkable example of His righteous severity against a conceited and proud Favorite—who to satisfy his private vengefulness had led the King to give such an unjust command—with what wisdom and modesty the Great should use the access they have to Princes, and how very criminal they are before God when they move him by their counsel to the oppression of their subjects.

The afflictions and the patience <term>patience: from the Dutch 'lydzaamheyd', meaning long-suffering or steadfast endurance under trial</term> of Job are so famous in the Church that one can generally say they are unknown to no one. This holy man, who by all appearances lived before the exodus of the Jews from the land of Egypt, lived in the land of Uz, on the borders of desert Arabia, and was in great esteem among the people of the land. He possessed an immense wealth, which primarily consisted, according to the manner of ancient times, and even more

The Holy Scripture says that he had seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen, and five hundred female donkeys. God had given him seven sons and three daughters, who lived together in such a perfect harmony that this father in that respect, as well as regarding other qualities which could make children lovable, had nothing more to wish for. But that which is even more excellent and more noteworthy was Job himself. One found in him a penetrating understanding and an extensive knowledge, which seemed to leave him ignorant of nothing: the speeches in his Book are a public proof of it, and that which made those sciences stand out even more was the modesty with which he possessed them, which made him say in a certain place in his book that he only knew the outer ends of God’s ways, and which made him cry out in the contemplation of His works: *What a small piece of the matter have we heard from him!* His virtue and godliness were to be esteemed even higher than his knowledge. ...stood likewise in his mind, and the insignificance of the one never caused him to lose anything of the goodness of his cause, nor did the pomp and splendor of the other allow him to gain anything in a wicked matter. His wise and orderly conduct served as an example to his people, and his tender and compassionate heart regarding the misfortunes of others caused the most wretched to find comfort in his charity and assistance. Such dignified and very numerous virtues sprouted from a foundation of godliness and fear of God, which made the righteous Job the most perfect man then on earth, according to the testimony that God Himself gave him. But it was this very rare and perfect piety of Job that brought all his misfortunes upon his head, just as that same piety had previously brought him so many favors and blessings. The hellish Spirit <note>The "hellish Spirit" refers to Satan.</note>, always ready to bring men to ruin, beheld with an envy and fury—fitting the bottomless depth of his malice—the holiness of Job, but he did not know how he might catch him in his snares and nets. It was not strictly that Job was incapable of being tempted; Adam had allowed himself to be caught in the earthly Paradise, in the midst of the radiant knowledge and original righteousness that surrounded him; but God, who for reasons of His adorable wisdom had then permitted Adam to be tempted, made Job inaccessible to the evil Spirit. This the Holy Scripture makes understood through metaphorical figures of speech <note>original: "oneygentlyke ſpreekwyzen"</note>, in that sort of dialogue between God and Satan, where it has the hellish Spirit say that he could not approach Job because God had surrounded him, his household, and his goods as if with a hedge <note>original: "betuyninge"</note>, so that it was impossible to draw near to them. God thereupon exposes the goods and the household of that holy man and delivers them over to the Tempter, to show that Job’s piety did not sprout from self-interest, as the

<column-break/>

Devil accused him of, and to teach all the righteous that they should love God with a love so pure and free from earthly interests that—whether He favors them with prosperity during this life, or takes away all their goods and leaves them with nothing but the hope of possessing Him in eternity—they should nevertheless always love Him and place His will above all other things. As soon as God had lifted the barrier, so to speak, which protected the household and goods of Job, only to enclose his person within it, Satan departed and caused a band of Sabeans <note>A nomadic tribe from South Arabia.</note> to come, who took away Job’s oxen and donkeys and struck down his servants who were tending them. In another place, he caused lightning to fall upon his sheep and shepherds, and everything perished through the heat of the flames. From another side, three bands of Chaldeans <note>An ethnic group from Mesopotamia.</note> came to attack the camels and carried them away. Job’s children had gathered in a house where they were eating together to maintain the lovely harmony that had always existed among them. Satan came to overwhelm them there, and having raised a terrifying wind against which nothing could stand, the house was thereby thrown down, and all of Job’s children were crushed under the ruins. The tidings of such a sequence of misfortunes were all brought to Job on a single day, and shortly after one another. This holy man was not insensitive to this, but his sadness served only to humble him, and while it humbled him before God, it increased his true greatness.

> Naked I came, he said, into the world, and naked I shall go out of it again. *The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away: blessed be the name of the Lord!*

The Apostle James sets this example forth as a model of patience and surrender to God’s will, and one cannot remind oneself of this case too often, or have the mind too full of it.

Satan was greatly astonished to find such a profound unconcern for all things in Job, seeing that the loss of his children and possessions had not been able to snatch a single word of displeasure from his mouth; but he did not allow himself to be deterred by this, and he did not lose hope of making him succumb if he might have permission to touch his body. God gave him that permission, reserving for Himself only the life of His servant, which He forbade the evil Spirit to touch, leaving him almost master of all the rest. It was then that the Enemy thought he would triumph; he struck Job with a plague that covered his entire body, and the malignancy of which was so great that he could find relief from it neither day nor night. His ailment became sharper daily, instead of diminishing, and the mere sight of him repelled the persons from whom he might otherwise have expected some service. Job’s understanding was too clear and elevated not to realize that such an uncommon ailment in itself, and in all its circumstances, came from further away than common and natural causes, and his faith made him see the invisible hand of God that struck him. Full of these thoughts, he persisted in humbling himself in God’s presence, and he went to sit down in the dust and ashes, as the original text of the Scripture says. This was formerly among the Eastern peoples the sign of a heart deeply humbled under great sorrows, and the Prophecy of *Jonah* provides us with a remarkable example of this in the person of the King of *Nineveh*, who, terrified by the threats of that Prophet, laid aside his royal robes and, covering himself with sackcloth, sat in the ashes. Of all the persons of his household, no one remained to Job but his Wife, whose heart and feelings differed greatly from those of this Righteous man. This light-minded and godless woman approached him in this state where he was in such high need of comfort; but instead of giving it to him, she mocked him, and this admirable gentleness, which this holy man displayed in the midst of all his calamities, she labeled as a weakness or stupidity. The modesty with which Job bore these harsh adversities she regarded as a restraint unbecoming for a man of such station as Job had been in, and as a vain virtue of a philosopher; indeed, she extended her godlessness so far that she advised him to pour out his grief in unrestrained complaints, and to maintain no more reverence for the Providence of a God who thus abandoned him to such terrible calamities. The answer that Job gave to this wretched woman is of incomparable value:

> *You speak*, he said, *as one of the foolish women: Shall we receive good from God, and not evil?*

The news of Job’s misfortunes spread in all directions, and he was visited by three of his friends of high standing, who came from various places in *Arabia* or *Idumea* <note>Idumea is the Greek name for the land of Edom, located south of the Dead Sea.</note>. One was *Eliphaz* of *Teman*, who is believed to have been that *Eliphaz* spoken of in *Genesis*, and who was a son of Esau: The other was *Bildad* of *Shuah*, who was one of the sons that *Abraham* fathered by *Keturah*, his second wife: and the third was named *Zophar* of *Naamath*, who likely also was from one

<column-break/>

of the lineages descended from *Abraham*. This is pointed out here in passing, as it serves to show that the knowledge of the true God, which was preserved in those households—and of which these three friends of Job gave very excellent proof in the conversations they held with him—was an effect of the blessing which God continued to pour out over the descendants of *Abraham*, and of the diligence which that holy Patriarch had applied to teaching his household well, according to the glorious testimony which God gave him regarding this in these words:

> *For I have known him, so that he may command his children and his household after him, and they shall keep the way of the LORD, to do righteousness and justice.*

The friends of Job, all three having come to him, found his state so mournful that for several days they could not recover from the astonishment in which they were. They wept as soon as they saw him; they tore their clothes, as was customary to do in cases of heavy affliction, and they remained sitting on the earth or in the ashes for seven days, just like Job, without being able to hardly open their mouths, so incredibly great was their sorrow. Meanwhile, Job’s ailments continued without reduction or pause, and the violence of them was so exceedingly fierce that it wrung some impatient complaints from his mouth: He wished that he had never been born. This was the only time that this holy man was found to be but a man; but the Devil did not long have cause to rejoice that he had overcome Job’s patience: for Job recognized his error and repented of it. The conversations which he held with his three friends, and which make up the largest part of his book, are of inestimable value. His friends could not imagine that he had not brought these misfortunes upon himself through some great sins: but he contested that reckless prejudice, and he did so sometimes with such wording that seemed to wound the humility of a creature of dust and ashes, and did not seem to agree well with the rules of a precise godliness; but as soon as one has grasped his thoughts and well-considered the subject that causes him to speak, one can without difficulty notice the fairness of all his discourses. Finally, God crowned Job’s steadfast perseverance; He gave him his health back, and twice as many goods as he had lost; such that he had fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, a thousand yoke of oxen, and a thousand female donkeys: and concerning his sons and daughters, God gave him the same number that he had had before; and since the first were not lost to him—seeing as he was to find them again one day in Heaven—it was a doubling of this number as well as of the other, when he received just as many children back as he first had. Job lived a hundred and forty years after his restoration, so that he likely lived twice as many years as he was old when his misfortunes befell him, since it pleased the divine goodness to give him all other things double; and then, according to that calculation, he would have reached seventy years when God put him to the test so sharply. Thus he spent the remainder of his days in a long series of prosperities, being the wonder of all his neighbors, and the glory of his age.

## Isaiah Chapter VI. verses 1—7.

<margin>The year of the world 3244. Before J.C. 760.</margin>
There has been no Prophet in the entire ancient Dispensation <note>original: "aaloude Bedeelinge"; a term used to describe the era of the Old Testament before the coming of Christ</note> with whom God held conversation for a longer time, and to whom He revealed Himself with more clarity and discovery of the mysteries of the New Covenant, than the Prophet Isaiah. It appears from the beginning of his book that he prophesied under the reign of four Kings of Judah; which can account for a span of nearly a hundred years. And regarding the nature of his predictions, they are everywhere so vivid, so remarkable, and accompanied by so many circumstances, that they might seem to have been written after the outcome of the events, if one were not assured by irreproachable evidence that they preceded them—some even by more than seven or eight centuries. For that reason, some of the Church Fathers <note>original: "Oudvaderen"</note> have given him the name of the "fifth Evangelist"; and one never finishes reading his Prophecy without wonder, and without carrying away some new knowledge. But besides the spirit of Prophecy, with which God favored him for so long and in such great measure, he was honored with several miraculous visions, in which God appeared to him, to speak to him in a visible form, as it were, regarding matters concerning his office. The vision related in this chapter is one of the most illustrious found in the Scriptures. It appeared to him in an ecstasy <note>original: "verrukkinge"; a state of spiritual trance or being "carried away" by the Spirit</note> through which

<column-break/>

God drew up his spirit, so that he saw the Lord in the Temple at Jerusalem, seated on a high throne, and clothed with a garment whose hems <note>original: "zoomen"; often translated as the "train" of His robe</note> filled the Temple. Around that throne he saw a company of Seraphim <note>term: Seraphim (fiery angelic beings who stand in the immediate presence of God)</note> of a very singular form; for they each had six wings, of which two served to cover their faces, and two to cover their feet, and with the other two they flew. They called out to one another: *Holy, Holy, Holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory;* and their cry made such a piercing sound that the posts of the thresholds of the Temple moved because of it. A smoke filled the entire house at the same time, and the Prophet, amazed by such a magnificent sight, and terrified to find himself so close to the Seraphim, indeed to God Himself, cried out: *Woe is me! for I perish, because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people that is unclean of lips; for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts!* These were the natural perceptions of a sinful soul who saw himself in the presence of a holy God, whose face the Angels themselves—however pure and zealous for His service they may be—dare not behold, but cover their feet and face with their wings, while through the movement of their two other wings they stir each other up to praise God, and fill Heaven with their songs of praise. But no sooner had the Prophet lamented his corruption, and expressed a painful sorrow of heart that, having defiled lips, he could not join his voice with those of the Seraphim to glorify the thrice-Holy God, than he saw one of the Seraphim fly to the altar where the Priests always kept the fire, and take from it a glowing coal with the tongs, with which this Seraph came to the Prophet, who stayed at the door of the Temple, and [touched] his

Jeremiah received the burden of these threats, while at the Court and in the city, men thought of nothing but satisfying their passions and lusts; and everything that the Prophet foretold of the coming calamities was dismissed as whims and fantasies. Finally, people grew tired of it, and the Jews—as if one could bring disasters upon oneself simply by constantly predicting them—became so embittered against Jeremiah that they viewed him as an enemy. The Nobles of the Realm complained about it to Zedekiah, and that King, who was no more righteous than they were, allowed them to take the Prophet into custody. But, just as the Apostle Paul said in the midst of his bonds, that the word of God was not bound <note>A reference to 2 Timothy 2:9.</note>, Jeremiah continued prophesying as before; and the more he saw the time approaching that was destined in God’s counsel for the destruction of Jerusalem, the more vivid and powerful were his predictions. They wished to have him put to death, but God had assured him that He would protect his life and, in that regard, surround him as if with a bronze wall. This wall was invisible to the Prophet’s enemies, yet they nonetheless perceived that something held them back; for when they gave free rein to their grudge and hatred to plunge Jeremiah—who was defended by no one—into his ruin, they in no way did to him what they had gladly desired. Their last resort was to throw him into a deep pit, which had formerly held water, but now contained nothing but mire. They did not doubt that he would die there, and indeed, how could one remain alive in a place that already possesses all the horrors of death and is worse than a grave? Before they did this, they had gone to the King to complain that the Prophet continued to predict the downfall of their nation, and that the people were so terrified by this that they lost all courage; and Zedekiah had already handed the Prophet over to them, so that they might do with him what they wished. After they had thrown him into this pit, one of the King’s Chamberlains, named Ebed-Melech, distressed by seeing that a man—whose only crime was to exhort the people to seek to avert the judgments of God against Jerusalem and Judea through deep humiliation accompanied by a pious life—informed the King of what the Nobles of the Court had done. It had to be a Stranger, a Moor <note>original: "Moorman"; the biblical text identifies Ebed-Melech as an Ethiopian.</note>, who had mercy on a Prophet of the Lord and preserved his life, while all the hearts of the Jews were closed to compassion, and no one dared speak for oppressed innocence. God put it into the King’s heart that he should not let the purest and brightest light of Israel be extinguished in the mud: he commanded his Chamberlain to take thirty men from his bodyguard and pull Jeremiah up out of the pit. They went there in haste, and having thrown him some old rags to place under his armpits—where the ropes to pull him up would pass—so that he would not be hurt by them, they drew him out of this pool. After he was put in a condition to appear before the King, who had commanded that the Prophet be brought to him,

<column-break/>

he arrived and foretold to that Prince everything that would happen to him if he did not heed his salutary counsel. But the exhortations of Jeremiah were rejected, and God delivered Jerusalem, the King, and the Kingdom over to the army of the Chaldeans.

<margin>*The Year of the World 3399. Before Christ 605.</margin>
Long before the Nobles of the Realm of Judah committed that inhuman deed against Jeremiah, the history of which has just been related based on the preceding illustration <note>Referring to the engraving on the page</note>, and which ought to have been placed after this one, he had the sorrow of seeing his prophecies treated with the greatest contempt during the reign of the previous King. God had commanded him to write these in a book, and the Prophet had dictated them to Baruch, who served him as a scribe, in order to then bring them to the King, so that he might read them at his leisure and with proper reflection in his cabinet. Jehoiakim occupied the Throne of Judea at that time. He was a Prince without religion, or at least one who observed none other than an idolatrous service. His history has already been seen previously, and mention is made of him here only to give an account of a particular act concerning Jeremiah. This Prophet, having had his predictions against the Kingdom of Judah written down by Baruch, his faithful Disciple, this writing was brought to Jehoiakim, who, having shut himself in his chamber with one of his Secretaries, had it read to him. But he became so annoyed and irritable because he heard nothing but talk of calamities, and because in that writing nothing was to be found but threats, predictions of sieges, the taking of cities, and the downfall of all Judea, that he could not endure it being read to the end. He then took a penknife from the table, cut the book into pieces with it, and threw them into a fire before which he was sitting. This act indicated that there was in this Prince a depth of levity and godlessness that is scarcely comprehensible. But when the mind has already strayed from God’s ways and one has plunged oneself into vice, one is no longer well able to think of the future; and being occupied only with the present, which strokes and flatters the senses, one cannot listen to the prediction of sad disasters that are approaching. The prophecies of Jeremiah, however, were not lost with his book; they remained ever written with clear strokes in the mind of the Prophet, and they soon appeared again on paper or parchment, by an express command of God, just as the first time. The original draft remained ever preserved in the Book of God’s decrees, and the execution thereof could not fail to follow, and to show itself as if in large letters before the eyes of all the world. God added new additions to the predictions which Jehoiakim had burned, and it was from these that this wicked King—to whom they were read or recounted by Jeremiah himself—learned of the miserable misfortunes that were destined for him and were soon to fall upon his head. He understood that he would leave no son to follow him in the Royal dignity; that Jerusalem, his people, and he himself would be delivered to the King of Babylon; and that no burial would be permitted for his dead body, but that it would be cast away to lie exposed to the heat by day and the cold by night. ### Ezekiel Chapter I. verses 4, 5, 6, etc.

The Prophet Ezekiel, a contemporary of Jeremiah, was carried away to Babylon during the time of Jehoiachin (or Jeconiah), who was himself also carried there as a prisoner with his Royal House and a great multitude of Jewish families during the first time that Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem. The people who were thus led away into captivity considered their state all the more miserable because their brothers were still in Judea, tasting their ancestral lands and the sweetness of freedom there, while they themselves were deprived of all this. But they did not see that the same avenging hand of that strong and jealous God, who had taken them from their land, was ready to strike the same blows upon the remainder of the entire nation, whose crimes were multiplied daily. This was what Ezekiel sought to make them understand, while Jeremiah threatened the King and the people of Jerusalem with the same; so that these two Prophets, who at one and the same time—the one in Babylonia and the other in Judea—predicted the same histories, mutually added a very significant weight to each other's prophecies, which ought to have persuaded the most

<column-break/>

unbelieving hearts. Ezekiel recounts here an utterly wondrous vision, yet very difficult for the mind to grasp, which he had by the banks of the river Chebar <note>A canal in Mesopotamia where Jewish exiles were settled.</note> in the land of Babylon, in the fifth year of the first captive deportation. It was a chariot with four wheels of an immense height, and all around full of eyes. It was drawn by four creatures, all of one likeness, but each having four different kinds of faces. The first was the face of a man; the second, which was on the right side, represented the face of a lion; the third, on the left side, was the countenance <note>original: "trooni," an archaic term for face or mask.</note> of an ox; and the fourth and hindmost was the visage of an eagle. The feet of these creatures were like those of an ox, and they stood upright and glistened like polished bronze. They also had four wings, of which two served them to cover their bodies, and the other two to fly; and from under their wings, arms came out like those of a man. Their eyes flickered like a flame, and between those creatures, one saw the form of a fire going forth, which gave off a glistening light; and this chariot moved forward, or stood still, according to how the Spirit, which animated the creatures and which spread even into the wheels, made them go. Above this extraordinary chariot, and over the heads of the creatures, one saw a brilliant crystal <note>original: "kristal," referring to the "terrible crystal" or firmament described in the text.</note>, fearsome to behold; and in 그 expanse <term>expanse|firmament</term> there appeared a throne, which had the luster and color of a sapphire, upon which the likeness of a man appeared. This Throne was as if surrounded by flames, and one saw there

The Prophet ends this magnificent description by saying that it was the appearance or the *likeness of the Glory of the LORD*; upon beholding which, he fell with his face to the earth, and then heard a voice speaking to him, commanding him to prophesy to his people. There is no part of this great depiction, consisting of so many different features gathered from so far and wide, so small that it does not have its own particular significance. It is impossible to unravel <note>original: "ontzwachtelen," literally to unswaddle or unwrap.</note> them all in such a small space as this, and therefore it is our task only to point out the general purpose of this vision and to say but a little about its most excellent parts. The opening of the entire mystery depends absolutely on the observation made by Ezekiel: that it was an image of the glory of God; for this leads us immediately to believe that God reveals Himself in that Majesty and dominion with which He rules the world, and particularly His Church. He does nothing there but what He wills, and all second causes are in His hand, just like this mystical chariot, which was moved only by the

<column-break/>

It is the Spirit of God, His Providence, His influence, that moves everything as it pleases Him, and which, when He wills, brings the swiftest movement to a standstill. This was a great subject to present to the Prophet amidst the confusion in which affairs then stood, and in all those fierce movements of the Chaldeans against God’s people. The creatures formed from the mystical likeness of so many images of different kinds were the symbols of the Angels, and each of these forms represented them in some of their qualities. The face of the man was the sign of their intelligence; that of the lion was the image of their zeal and alertness; that of the ox, the symbol of their steadfastness and tireless diligence in all the services for which God uses them; and the form of the eagle signified their readiness and speed, as is depicted for us in the 103rd and 104th Psalm. We learn from the Scripture regarding all these matters that God has often used the service of Angels for the benefit of His Church; and for 그 reason the Apostle Paul gave them the name of *ministering Spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation.*

Eleven years after Jeconiah, otherwise called Jehoiachin, was led with a portion of his people to the land of Babylon, Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem for the second time, and brought all the inhabitants and the people of Judea into his Kingdom. The Prophet Ezekiel, who was among the number of those

<column-break/>

who were involved in the first captive deportation, also saw this second one. He had often foretold it in Babylon, just as Jeremiah did not cease to threaten the Jews in Jerusalem daily with it; but the certainty which the Prophets had of a history that was yet to come did not prevent them from being just as sensitive to the lashes with which God chastised His people as if they had not seen them from afar, and as if they had been overtaken by them like the bulk of men, whose sight goes no further than the present. God had told the Jews that their captivity would last seventy years, but that at the end of that time they would return again to their land. The promises of God are always certain,

more certain, because God is unchangeable in His will, and always mighty to do that which He desires. But when one finds themselves as sinful as the Jews were, then mists <note>The author uses "mists" as a metaphor for spiritual doubt and confusion arising from a guilty conscience.</note> arise from the depths of the soul, which often cause one not to have such clear and distinct ideas of all these things. The Jews saw, besides that, how great and fearsome the power of Babylon <note>original: "Babel"</note> was, which gave laws to the entire East, and they were a ruined people, weakened by their scattering, and pressed under the chains of their slavery. One was at least often dismayed by this, but God wanted to lift the hope of His people through a wondrous vision, which He showed to Ezekiel. He showed him a valley that was entirely covered with bones, and He led him through and around them; so that the Prophet saw that they were human bones, and that they were very dry. Thereupon God asked him if he believed that these bones would live again. Ezekiel answered humbly:

> Lord GOD, you know.

God commanded him to speak to those bones, and to say to them:

> You dry bones, hear the word of the LORD. Thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I will bring the spirit into you, and you shall live; and I will lay sinews upon you, and make flesh come upon you, and draw skin over you, and give the spirit in you, and you shall live.

Ezekiel did as God commanded him, and while he spoke to these bones, he saw them move with a great noise, and seek one another, so that one bone approached the other, and each set itself into its joint. Immediately sinews were formed, the flesh surrounded them, and skin came over them: but life was still lacking. Ezekiel received

<column-break/>

the command to continue prophesying, and to command the wind or spirit of life to come and animate these bodies. He did so, and with that same authority with which he had spoken to the bones, he said to the spirit:

> You spirit, come from the four winds, and breathe into these slain ones, that they may live.

Upon this saying, the spirit came into them, and they became alive, and stood on their feet; and it was such a multitude of people, like a very great army. God did not leave the Prophet to struggle to find the secret hidden beneath this vision; but He explained it to him Himself as follows:

> These bones are the entire House of Israel. They say, "our bones are dried up, our hope is lost, we are cut off." Therefore say to them, "Thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I will open your graves, O my people, and I will bring you into the land of Israel."

Isaiah had long before predicted their return from captivity under the same idea of a resurrection:

> Your dead shall live, he said to Jerusalem, they shall arise: awake and rejoice, you who dwell in the dust, for your dew shall be as the dew of the herbs, the land shall cast out the deceased, and the earth shall no longer keep her slain covered.

But even if the vision of Ezekiel did not, at first glance, refer to the resurrection of our bodies on the Last Day, the resurrection of the dead is nevertheless assumed therein as a known and certain truth, the possibility of which is in God's hands; for otherwise He would not have given to His Prophet and to His people—to assure them of their future deliverance—a symbol of a resurrection that was impossible. That would have run directly contrary to His purpose, and His people would have become more and more confirmed in their fear that they would never see an end to their slavery.

He led him in the spirit into the land of Israel, and set him upon a high mountain, where there was as the building of a city, situated toward the South. This was Mount Zion on which the Temple was built, which by the size of its circumference, and the height of its walls, seemed a city; and the Prophet says that this mountain with this great building lay toward the South, because Judea is situated south of Babylonia. Ezekiel entered this building, and found at the gate a man whose appearance or radiance was like that of copper <note>The Dutch "koper" can mean copper, brass, or bronze; in biblical contexts, it usually refers to a glowing bronze appearance.</note>. The allusion which St. John makes to this description, in the first chapter of his Revelation, gives us to understand that it was Jesus Christ. This man had a measuring reed in his hand, and after having commanded the Prophet that he should pay close attention to everything he would see, to afterwards give an account of it to the house of Israel, he set himself to measuring with this reed. He began with a wall that ran all around, and was found to be one reed in width, and one reed in height. He came then to the gate that looked toward the East, to which one went up by steps, and he measured the threshold which was one reed wide. From there he went to the chambers, the porch, the walls of the building, the facade, the inner court, indeed there was nothing that he did not pass through and measure. It was a Temple built nearly according to the sketch of that which the Chaldeans had thrown to the ground; but much larger. The description which the Prophet began in the fortieth chapter thereof, provides material for several long chapters, of which one could not well give a neat account here, no matter how much one might shrink it down. The principal aim of such an accurate and powerful showing of a Temple, was to make Ezekiel see that the Temple of Zion would be rebuilt. The destruction of the Temple was the thing that went most to the heart of the Prophet and the people: the bitter complaints that they make of it in the 74th and 79th Psalms, are a public proof of it, and the Church <note>The author uses "the Church" to refer to the assembly of the faithful in the Old Testament.</note> would have little regarded her return to Judea, if God’s Temple had not been built up again. This also happened, as we have seen elsewhere, by *Zerubbabel*, and the diligence of the Priest *Jeshua*. But there was such a great difference between the first Temple and this second one,

<column-break/>

that those who had seen it could not refrain from shedding tears, because they found it to differ so much in everything from the last <note>referring to the superior glory of Solomon's original temple compared to the one rebuilt after the exile.</note>. It could then not be otherwise but that God’s aim, in the description which he gave of it to Ezekiel, reached further than to this second building. He also mixed into it from time to time some matters, which in no way could be applied to a material Temple. One shall touch upon only two of them here, after which the godly and enlightened Reader can arrange his judgment concerning all the rest. In the 44th chapter, where mention is made of the Temple that was shown to Ezekiel, it is said, *that no strangers nor uncircumcised of heart might enter therein*. That which is said there of strangers, could not refer to the earthly Temple, for in that of *Zerubbabel*, as well as in that of *Solomon*, there was a court for foreigners, which was called the *Court of the Gentiles*: and concerning the uncircumcised of heart, who has ever been able to know them so, that entrance to the Temple was granted to them alone? <note>The author argues that since human guards cannot see into the heart to know who is "uncircumcised of heart," this must refer to a spiritual reality rather than a physical building.</note> It appears then clearly that these things concern the Christian Church, which is the spiritual Temple of God, consisting of the fellow citizens of the saints, as the Apostle *Paul* says to the *Ephesians*, and of the *Assembly of the firstborn*, and the spirits of the perfect *righteous*, as the same Apostle calls them in his Epistle to the Hebrews. That which Ezekiel relates in the forty-seventh chapter of the waters that flowed out from the gate of the Temple, of their increase, and of the fishermen who stayed on the banks of those waters, and there made a great catch of fish, can just as little fit the Temple of *Zerubbabel*, or any similar one; but clearly looks to the Christian Church, the abundance of the graces of the Holy Spirit, and the wonderful success of the preaching of the Apostles. One therefore needs not wonder that God gave such a great measure of the extent of the Temple to Ezekiel; they were symbols that in general showed that the Christian Church would extend incomparably further than the Jewish. But God wrapped all those mysteries in images borrowed from the material Temple of Zion, because it has always been the habit of the Holy Spirit to show the most weighty truths of the Evangelical Covenant under familiar depictions.

While they were being instructed under the guidance of their masters in the knowledge of the language of the land and the manners of the Court, so as to be capable of serving the Prince's person, Nebuchadnezzar had a very strange and unusual dream, by which his mind was greatly troubled. But God, who had sent it to the King, allowed him to forget it entirely, so that nothing remained in his mind except a strong desire to recall it to his memory. Nebuchadnezzar then summoned the magicians and astrologers <note>original: "Starrekykers" — literally "star-gazers," a common 17th-century term for astrologers</note> who were most famous in the presumed science of divination, and in the whole world none were more esteemed than the Chaldeans; but their art could never go so far as to discover in the darkness of the past a dream that had vanished. The desire to recall it grew in Nebuchadnezzar's mind because of the impossibility in which all the diviners of his Kingdom found themselves to satisfy it. God willed it so, in order to prepare a greater honor and fame for Daniel, to whom He was about to reveal the dream. The King indeed had reason to be angry with his diviners; for if they had, as they boasted, the art of foretelling the future, which is not yet and often very far ahead, why could they not, with the same eyes that penetrated so far into the darkness where the future hides, discover the past, which was present only a few hours before? The King's wrath went so far that he sentenced all the Wise Men of his kingdom to death. Daniel requested a stay of that decree from the one to whom its execution was entrusted, since he hoped to be able to do himself what the King desired. He immediately made his intention known to his three dear friends, Shadrach,

<column-break/>

Meshach, and Abednego; and after all four had humbled themselves very deeply before God and prayed to Him for His spirit of revelation and understanding for Daniel, Daniel went to tell the King that he would make known the dream he had had. The King, delighted by this offer, sat down to listen, and Daniel then taking the floor, told him that the dream about which the King showed himself troubled was that he had seen a large statue, whose head was of gold; the chest and arms of silver; the belly and thighs of copper <note>The Dutch "koper" can refer to copper, brass, or bronze; in the context of the four monarchies, it traditionally signifies the bronze age of the Greeks</note>, the legs of iron, and the feet partly of iron and partly of clay: that while the King beheld this strange statue, he had seen that a small stone was cut out of a mountain without hands, and that it struck the statue with such force at its feet that it was thereby broken into pieces and ground to dust. This was the dream; and the interpretation which Daniel added to it was that this statue represented the four great Monarchies; namely, that of the Babylonians, shown by the golden head; that of the Medes and Persians, signified by the silver chest and arms; that of the Greeks, depicted by the copper belly and thighs; and the fourth, being the Roman Monarchy, sketched by the iron legs. With regard to the small stone that was cut out of the mountain and had struck down the statue, Daniel gave Nebuchadnezzar to understand that it was the symbol <note>original: "voorbeeldsel"</note> of a King who would destroy the last Empire and establish His own, which would extend much further than all the others and be of eternal duration. And this King is Jesus Christ, born of a virgin, small and despised in the eyes of the world, but nevertheless so highly exalted and so powerful that His Kingdom extends over the whole earth, and of His Kingdom there shall be no end, as the Angel said to Mary.

->Daniel Chapter III. verses 23–25.<-

<margin>The year of the world 3417.</margin>
King Nebuchadnezzar stood so amazed at the purity and greatness of Daniel’s understanding, who had interpreted his dream for him, that his conscience forced him to make this excellent declaration to Daniel, to the honor of the God of the Hebrews: *It is the truth that your God is a God of gods, and a Lord of kings, who reveals secrets.* He subsequently placed Daniel in a high position, and upon his recommendation, gave very prestigious offices in his provinces to Daniel’s companions Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. But this Prince did not always maintain such a favorable affection toward these Hebrews. A few years later, the opportunity arose to show how much the zeal of a false religion could influence his mind, and how little security there always is for God's children who live under the dominion of an idolatrous King. Nebuchadnezzar had a golden image made, sixty cubits high and six wide, to make his people worship it. It is not known whether it was his own likeness, or whether it was in honor of his deceased father King Nabopolassar, or in honor of Bel <note>The chief god of Babylon, also known as Marduk</note>, the god who was most highly esteemed by the Babylonians, that he had erected this exceedingly costly statue; Scholars are divided among those three opinions, and it is of little importance to take a side in that dispute. After the image was completed and placed in the middle of a field

<column-break/>

to be seen, honored, and worshipped by everyone, the King had it dedicated with all imaginable splendor, and to the sound of trumpets, shawms <note>original: "schalmeyen" — an early woodwind instrument</note>, flutes, zithers <note>original: "cyters" — a stringed instrument similar to a lyre or harp</note>, and all kinds of music; and he commanded that when one heard the sound of all those instruments, one should not fail to fall down and worship the image, on pain of being cast into a large burning furnace, that being a common corporal punishment of the Chaldeans, as appears from the twenty-ninth chapter of Jeremiah. The King had summoned all the Governors <note>original: "Landvoogden" — or Satraps</note> and other Lords of the Empire to attend this ceremony; since Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego held high offices in Babylonia, they were also summoned and came to the Court. No mention is made of Daniel during this event, who held a significant position with the King, but either Providence sent him elsewhere from Babylon at that time, or if he were there, in that high state in which he found himself, they did not dare to treat him as harshly as those three other Hebrews when they were brought before Nebuchadnezzar. Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, then, were among the number of Lords and Authorities of the Empire who were present at the dedication of the image; but when that disastrous moment arrived in which this multitude of people, with <margin>Dan. 3. v. 14. 15. 16. 17. 18.</margin> whom the field was covered, fell down together before this idol, these three Hebrews did not change their posture, but remained standing as before. Complaints were immediately made about this to the King, who, having had them brought before him, asked them whether they did not know that he had commanded all his subjects to fall down before the golden image. They answered that it was not unknown to them, but that they could not obey him in a matter over which God would be angered. The Prince threatened them that he would have them cast into the furnace, and said with a proud arrogance that it would be seen whether the God, whom they feared to anger, would deliver them.

The King saw this as well as all the others, and full of amazement and wonder, he called the three Hebrews by their names and commanded them to come out of the furnace. They came to him, and it was found that neither on their persons, nor on their hair, was there the slightest mark or singeing from the fire. God does not always perform such miracles for His children; martyrdom would then become all too common, and one would find little difficulty in exposing oneself to it: but those of His confessors whom God does not deliver from the flames, or any other kind of death, He delivers from the hellish fire and eternal pains.

In all histories, both sacred and secular, one finds no example of such a punishment as this, which God brought upon Nebuchadnezzar. This Prince ruled the entire East, and Egypt in the South had recently experienced the power of his arms. The city of Babylon, the seat of his Empire, was through its great glory the wonder of the whole world, and at the same time the terror thereof through the laws which it gave to a hundred different nations; and everything that was most capable of flattering ambition and vanity, Nebuchadnezzar found in the prosperity of his reign. He would have been happy if, while the whole world beheld him with

Yet so that he should not be ignorant of the hand that was about to strike him down from this high peak of honor—from where all other men seemed small to him, and where he beheld himself as if between Heaven and earth, and closer to a God than to a man, with excessive pleasure—God wished to warn him through a dream which He sent to him. Evil-Merodach followed his father Nebuchadnezzar in the reign, and after him Belshazzar ascended the Throne of Babylon. Nebuchadnezzar, a year later, walking on a flat roof of his Palace, from where he could see the greatness and glory of Babylon, was so enchanted by this sight that he expressed this to the people of his Court who were with him; but hardly had he begun to say: *Is this not the great Babylon that I have built for a royal house, by the strength of my power, and for the honor of my glory?* or the decree that had been foretold to him was pronounced over him by a voice from Heaven, and in the same hour this King was thrust out from the company of men; he ate grass like the oxen, he was exposed to the rain and the dew of heaven, his body became entirely hairy, and the nails of his hands and feet grew like birds' claws. After the passing of seven years, his senses and understanding returned to him, he gave to God, whom he had not acknowledged, the honor, and God showed him the mercy of putting him back on the Throne. Unless one wishes to deny that God holds all the hearts of men, those of Kings as well as those of the peoples, in His hand, and that He makes them descend as low as He wills, just as He raises them as high as He pleases, one would have difficulty understanding how such an extraordinary change could have come into the heart of that Prince, and that the persons of his House and Court could have left him so, that he spent seven years among the beasts, and ate grass with them. But all things are possible with God, and His Justice has so many means to punish men, that the best use we can make of our intellect is that we learn, at the sight of His judgments, when they seem incomprehensible to us, to keep ourselves in a respectful silence, striving to avoid them through deep humility and an earnest repentance of the crimes which they can bring upon us.

Holy Scripture does not mention why Daniel had left the Court or what he did; but there is great probability that after the death of Nebuchadnezzar he had retired from the Court and state affairs, especially since he was already old by that time; for if his age had been only ten years when he was taken from Judea to Babylon, he must have been more than eighty when Belshazzar prepared this meal. The King then sent for him, and Daniel read this writing; and found there these three words, MENE, TEKEL, PERES <note>Aramaic: Numbered, Weighed, Divided</note>, which he explained thus:

This terrifying sentence was carried out that very same night; the city was taken, and King Belshazzar was killed in his palace.

# Daniel thrown into the lions' den by command of Darius without suffering any harm.
## Daniel Chapter VI. verses 17—23.

---

<margin>
The year of the world 3466. 538 B.C.
</margin>
Darius, King of the Medes, otherwise named Cyaxares <note>Ancient historians often identify the biblical Darius the Mede with Cyaxares II</note>, uncle of Cyrus, was with him at the siege of Babylon. Since he was already of great age, Cyrus wished to give him the honor of taking that city, and to leave the primary government of it to him. For that reason, Cyrus and Darius in the Prophecy of Daniel

<column-break/>

are joined together, and in the same chapter of the book of Ezra, the Decree which was given by Cyrus in the first year of his reign is attributed to Darius and Cyrus together. In this first year of Cyrus and Darius, and probably before they had issued that decree in favor of the Jews, a few days or months after the taking of Babylon, Darius appointed new Governors or Satraps <term>Stadhouder: a regional governor or lieutenant acting on behalf of the monarch</term>. The great prestige that Daniel had held under the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, and the new respect he had gained by reading and explaining the words which a divine hand had written on the wall of the previous King's hall, made him known to Darius as

<image-desc>An engraving depicting the biblical scene of Daniel in the lions' den. ...him as one of the most worthy persons to serve in the highest offices. He then gave him the most prestigious position of all, which required not only great ability but also perfect integrity. He appointed him over all the **Governors** <term>Stadhouders: provincial rulers or satraps</term> of the provinces, so that they should give an account to him of all the most noteworthy things that occurred in their administration, for he was tasked with overseeing their conduct. Such an exalted status, which eclipsed the splendor of all the Great Men of the Empire, could not help but provoke much envy. They therefore deliberated how to plunge Daniel into ruin; and because his conduct was irreproachable, they decided to set a trap for him regarding his religion. They proposed to Darius that it befitted his greatness to make an edict that not one of his subjects, for a period of thirty days, should make any request to anyone in the entire Kingdom except to him alone, without even excepting the prayers which those idolaters offered to their gods. This was one of the most cunning and excessive flatteries by which these wicked sycophants sought to instill in this new King the idea that all the interests of his people were in his hands, and that he alone was sufficient to ensure the happiness of his subjects. We, who are filled with a concept of the Divinity and who are accustomed to living under more regulated governments, have difficulty understanding how it could be possible that a Prince could allow himself to be persuaded to issue such an unreasonable prohibition. But when one considers that on that very same Throne of Babylon there had sat Kings who wished to be regarded as Gods, then this prohibition of Darius will no longer seem so strange to us. The command was then drawn up, and a proclamation of it was made throughout the entire Kingdom. Daniel was spied upon, and it was found that three times a day he went to his chamber, where he opened the windows on the side which

<column-break/>

looked toward Judea, and each time offered his prayer there, with his face turned toward Jerusalem. Complaints were made about this to the King, and Daniel being summoned, was so far from denying the supposed crime with which he was charged, that he considered it an honor. Darius, grieved that he could not save Daniel because of the **irrevocability of the law** <note>The laws of the Medes and Persians were famously unchangeable once enacted</note>, said to him when he was led to the pit: *Your God, whom you continually honor, deliver you.* Daniel was then thrown to the lions, and then a stone was placed on the mouth of the pit, which was sealed with the King's ring. The lions respected the Prophet of the Lord and did him no harm. The King, meanwhile, was so troubled that he had thus delivered an innocent and righteous man, whose merit he otherwise held in high esteem, that he could not sleep for the entire night. Very early in the morning, he wanted to go to the pit himself to see if the God whom Daniel worshiped had preserved him from the mouth and claws of the lions. Upon arriving, he called out to Daniel twice by name, and he heard with amazement and wonder Daniel's voice answering him. Immediately he had the pit opened, and the Prophet having been pulled out without having suffered the least injury from the teeth or claws of the fierce beasts, related to the King that God had sent an Angel who had delivered him. Thereupon the wrath of Darius was kindled against Daniel's enemies, who had been the cause of him being thrown to the lions; and he commanded that they themselves should be thrown to those beasts. Scarcely had they touched the floor of the pit before the lions sprang upon these miserable wretches and tore them into a thousand pieces. Kings diminish their dignity when they usurp God's prerogative; and to obey them in such instances is the same as elevating them above God and making idols of them.

Daniel, after having related the two preceding histories one after another, returns to the reign of Belshazzar, and relates a wondrous vision which he had in the first year of that King. God showed him by night four great beasts that came up out of the sea. The first was like a lion, and had eagle's wings; but its wings were plucked out, and it raised itself upright on its feet like a man. Thereafter appeared at the side another beast, which resembled a bear; it had three rows of teeth, and it was said to the same that it should stand up and satiate itself with flesh. This beast was followed by a third, resembling a leopard, and it had four wings and four heads. Finally, there appeared a fourth beast, uncommonly strong, which had great iron teeth and crushed everything, and trampled the remainder with its feet. It also had ten horns, and from the midst of the horns a small one came up, before which three of the previous ones were torn out; and that horn had eyes like human eyes, and a

<column-break/>

mouth that spoke great things. Daniel then saw a Throne of fire appear, upon which the Ancient of Days <note>A title for God the Father</note>, the eternal God, surrounded by a thousand million Angels, was seated. The beast which spoke the great words was killed, and its body cast into the fire, and the power which the other beasts had was taken from them, yet they were nevertheless kept in life until a certain time. Then appeared the Son of Man, who having approached the Ancient of Days, received an extraordinary reception, and the dominion over all peoples was given to him forever. Daniel's mind was so filled with this vision that he could not distinguish the ideas thereof; but an Angel pulled him out of this difficulty, and unraveled everything for him. They were the four great Monarchies <term>Monarchyen: the successive world empires of Babylon, Persia, Greece, and Rome</term> that were depicted there, especially the last, being that of the Romans, with all its circumstances. But what is of the greatest importance for us to note in our present state is the reign that was given to the Son of Man: for this Son of Man was Jesus Christ, who said to God his Father in the seventeenth chapter of St. John: *I have glorified thee on the earth; I have finished the work which thou gavest me to do; and now glorify me, O Father, with thine own self with the glory which I had with thee before the world was.* That is the time in which the Heavenly Father, answering the prayer of his well-beloved Son, addressed him with these words of the second Psalm: *Thou art my Son, today I have begotten thee. Heaven, and those on the earth, and those under the earth: and every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is the Lord, to the glory of God the Father. <margin>The year of the world 3452. Before J.C. 552.</margin>
Three years after God had shown Daniel in Babylon the vision of the four fierce beasts, the description of which we have just seen, He caused him to see another in the city of Susa, where the Prophet was then located.
