This proud and raging ram pushed with its horns against the West, against the North, and thereafter also against the South: the other beasts could not withstand him, nor protect themselves from his strikes, so that he did whatever he wished and made himself very powerful. Thereafter came a he-goat from the West with such speed that he did not seem to touch the earth, and this goat had a very large horn between its eyes. He ran with all his might at the ram; and having cast him to the ground, he trampled him under his feet, without anyone being able to deliver him from the violence of the goat. He subsequently became uncommonly great, and then his large horn broke, and four horns came up in its place, stretching toward the four parts of the world. But out of one of the four horns came a little one, which became exceedingly great, toward the South, toward the East, and toward the <note>original: "cierlyk land"</note> pleasant land <note>A biblical term for the land of Israel.</note>. —man who called out to the Angel Gabriel to explain it to him. This man was Jesus Christ, the Prince of the Angels, who appeared thus in a human form in anticipation of His future Incarnation. Gabriel then came to the Prophet and unfolded for him all the secrets of that vision. He told him that the ram with two horns represented the Monarchy of the Medes and Persians, and the he-goat the Monarchy of the Greeks; that the great horn between its eyes signified the first King of that mighty Monarchy, who was to throw down that of the Persians and Medes and turn it upside down; that the horns which had come up after that first great and terrible one—before which nothing could stand—was broken, signified four Kings who would come forth in place of that first one, but would not have the power and might that the first had; finally, that after all those Kings, one would arise who, no less cunning than cruel, would cause incredible evil and let his rage burst forth primarily against Judea and the holy people; that he would desecrate the Temple and, through his terrible persecutions or other craftily devised means, bring many Jews to apostasy. To these accurate and well-connected explanations nothing else was lacking but to mention the names of the persons to make it look much more like a history than a shadowed and obscure prophecy. The outcome, which has answered the prophecy in everything, has shown us that it was Alexander <note>Alexander the Great.</note> who was represented by the great horn before which nothing could stand, and that Darius, King of the Persians—attacked, struck, pursued, cast to the ground, and stripped of power and movement by Alexander—was that ram, formerly so proud and so mighty that he had been the terror of the greatest part of the known world. The horn of the goat, which after becoming so exceedingly great finally broke, clearly signified the death of Alexander, which occurred after the conquest of all Asia, when that Monarch had climbed to the highest peak of his glory. From the Sovereignty which he left behind, four great Monarchies arose, which were possessed by the foremost Commanders of his army. Antigonus reigned in Asia; Philip in Macedonia and the rest of Greece; Ptolemy in Egypt; and Seleucus in Syria. Finally, the cruel Antiochus <note>Antiochus IV Epiphanes.</note> came, the true image of the Antichrist, descended from Seleucus, to complete Daniel’s vision and fulfill the Angel’s interpretation. Never had Judea suffered such heavy persecutions as those it endured under that godless reign, and God’s people had never, even in their captivity, seen religion in greater danger of being suppressed, nor beheld a greater multitude of apostates who, through the crafts and cruelties of Antiochus within the span of five or six years, renounced their faith.

### Daniel Chapter X, verses 5–10, and Chapter XII, verses 5, 6, 7.

<margin>
The year of the world 3466.
</margin>
Fourteen years after the vision Daniel had of the goat and the ram, in the year that Babylon was captured <note>The fall of Babylon to the Medes and Persians occurred in 539 BCE.</note>, which was the first of the reign of Darius the Mede, the Prophet reflected that it was the seventieth year of the captivity. Upon this, he redoubled his humble prayers before God, pleading with Him that He would have compassion on His people and restore their freedom to them. God was mindful of His promise, which He had made to bring His people back from servitude in Judea after seventy years, and He assured Daniel that he would soon see the fulfillment of it. But God did even more; He revealed to His Prophet the greatest events that had ever been signified in His <term>Oracles</term> <note>Prophetic messages or divine revelations.</note>. This was the exact timing of the coming of the Messiah, who, shown from so far off, was the expectation of so many centuries, and the glory and blessedness of Israel. The oracles of the Prophets had postponed that coming until the latter days, but as if God

<column-break/>

had wished to advance the time thereof, He revealed to Daniel that after seventy <term>weeks of years</term> <note>A prophetic calculation where each "day" of a week represents a year, totaling 490 years.</note>—just as many as the captivity of Babylon had lasted in single years—the Messiah would come. These were four hundred and ninety years, beginning from the day of the decree which gave the Jews permission to return again to Judea, and there to rebuild Jerusalem and the Temple. Herein an unbelieving Jew <note>This reflects the 17th-century Christian perspective of the author, seeking to prove that Jesus was the fulfillment of Hebrew prophecy.</note> finds the conviction of his error; and if he were not blinded to the highest degree, he would see without difficulty that such an exact prediction, expressed in such simple and absolute terms, and which God made dependent on no condition, must necessarily have been fulfilled in the signified time. Whether this Oracle refers to the decree of Cyrus, or to that of Darius Hystaspes, or finally to that of Artaxerxes, it is something in which a modern Jew has no interest in reconciling his faith to the oracle. Let him begin his calculation after whichever of the three decrees he wishes; he will find that the end of the four hundred and ninety years, which were to pass from that decree until the coming of the Messiah, falls precisely in that century in which History indicates the life of that Christ whom we worship, and that more than sixteen centuries have passed since the time in which the seventy weeks of Daniel ended. What then would have become of God’s promise? Should all the other predictions of Daniel be fulfilled down to the smallest circumstances, and should this one, the most remarkable of all—this one upon which the mercy of God has always had its eye, and which it has renewed so many times from the fall of Adam until the time it ceased sending Prophets—alone have remained unfulfilled? One must have reached the point where one does not shrink from denying the most manifest and certain truths when one dares to call this into doubt.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Daniel’s prophetic visions. HISTORY of the O. TESTAMENT. 283

In the third year of Cyrus, God showed Daniel a vision that had some commonality with the previous revelation, and in which He pointed out the principal histories that were to occur during the time of these seventy weeks of years. Daniel was then—whether in reality or in a vision—on the bank of the Tigris, and saw there a Man clothed in linen, having a belt of fine gold around his waist; his face flashed like lightning, and his eyes appeared like fiery torches; his body was like turquoise <note>Original: "turkois." In many English translations of Daniel 10:6, this is rendered as "beryl" or "chrysolite."</note>, his arms and feet were like polished copper, and his voice made a noise like that of a great multitude of people. One can easily understand who this man of such majesty must have been; and when one compares this description to the one found of Jesus Christ in the Book of Revelation, one is quickly persuaded that it was the same who appeared to the Prophet, as He had already done in other visions, and who is called Michael, the Prince of Angels, in the 13th verse. Daniel could not endure the sight of such an illustrious Prince, who glittered so with glory; he fell down on his face, and having stretched his hands to the earth, he waited to stand up until the Angel who spoke to him had encouraged him to do so. Having then risen upright, that most glorious Man who had appeared to him approached and touched his lips: Daniel, having thereby gathered some courage, opened his mouth and said to him who spoke to him:

> *How can my lord’s servant speak with my lord? For as for me, from now on no strength remains in me, and no breath is left in me.*

But he whom Daniel saw in the form of a man touched him a second time and commanded him not to fear. He subsequently revealed to him the things that were to happen to the Church on account of the Princes, her enemies, which one can see at length in the eleventh chapter of the Prophecy of Daniel, and which are continued until the end of that book. Everything was thus opened before the eyes of the Prophet, and God gave him a clear understanding, which extended to the furthest reaches of future matters.

The persecution which God foretold to Daniel that would come under the reign of Antiochus Epiphanes—the illustrious, or the cruel <note>A wordplay on his title: "Epiphanes" means "The Illustrious," but his detractors called him "Epimanes," meaning "The Madman" or "The Cruel."</note>—was set to bring such great devastation upon the people that God Himself declared that nothing like it had yet been seen. But for that reason, God had appointed a short time, and fixed it at three and a half years, at the end of which deliverance was promised to the people. It was Michael, their protector, who would bring it about—namely, that so desired and so necessary deliverance, which would be for the people like a resurrection; for it is under that great and stately imagery that it was shown to Daniel. *Many of those,* said the man clothed in linen, *who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, these to eternal life, and those to contempt and to eternal horror.* These words will one day be proven true according to the letter in the greatest and final resurrection, according to the assurance which Christ gave us

<column-break/>

in the fifth chapter of the Gospel of John, and according to a hundred other texts of Scripture: but at first glance, and in a figurative sense, one could regard them as a prophecy of the restoration of the faithful, who had succumbed through weakness during the persecution of Antiochus, or who kept themselves hidden or buried as if in caves: these were they who would awake to eternal life. The others, on the contrary, who after the persecution had nothing to expect but shame and eternal disgrace, were the cowardly deserters of Moses' laws, who, by following the Tyrant—either to be rewarded with offices and gifts or out of other human considerations—had abandoned the religion of their fathers. The Angel, or the Man clothed in linen, added further that in those happy times of calm and safety, the Teachers, who had instructed others in God’s laws and had made them walk in the way of righteousness, would shine like the brightness of the firmament, and like the stars, forever and ever. This was the glory that the Teachers of the Law and such other wise and enlightened persons would have before God and before the eyes of the whole Congregation, they who had applied their knowledge and diligence to instruct the people in their duty and to strengthen them in those times of anguish and offense. The Prophet was told that those words were closed up and sealed until the time of the end; to give us to understand that God always—sometimes more, and sometimes less, as He sees fit—leaves some obscurity in the prophecies, and that the opening thereof does not truly happen except at the time of their fulfillment. Daniel subsequently saw on the bank of the Tigris, where he had this great vision, two men, one on this side and the other on that side, and in the middle of that wide river the man clothed in linen, whom he had already seen in the beginning, and who now stood upon the water, whom he asked when these things would happen. This man lifted both his hands toward Heaven, and he swore by Him who lives forever that all those things would be fulfilled, and that it would be *after a time, times, and half a time.* These involved and enigmatic words signify three and a half years, *which was the time of the principal oppression of the Church and Religion under Antiochus, and the abolition of the worship and the sacrifices in the Temple at Jerusalem.* Because this arrogant and cruel Tyrant was the archetype of the Antichrist, the Apostle John, speaking of him and of the persecutions he would cause the Church to suffer, borrowed many images and prophetic expressions from these visions of Daniel. And the book of Revelation, which, like the visions of this Prophet of old, was a closed and sealed book, is opened daily by the outcomes that unwrap the mysteries. Happy is he who pays heed to it, and who, in the midst of the confusions that the spirit of error and persecution spreads in all parts of the world, preserves the purity of his faith and listens only to his duty.

> *Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life.*

## The first six minor Prophets,
### *Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, and Micah.*

JUST as there is no natural or inherent greatness in creation, so too it has no true greatness, except insofar as it partakes in that of God, who alone is great; because He alone is completely perfect. But God, taking delight in humbling Himself and descending, as it were, to us, it is the intellectual knowledge and other perfections that He leaves in the soul which alone create a true and genuine distinction between men. The Prophets under the Old Covenant <note>Original: "Bedeelinge," referring to the era of the Old Testament law.</note> are even as the Apostles under the New, being those to whom God spoke intimately, and upon whom He bestowed a much greater outpouring of grace and knowledge. Such a glorious distinction has made them all great in the Church and prominent in all the ages of the world. But since we barely know them except through the Scriptures they left behind, the practice was introduced—first among the Jews and subsequently among Christians—of distinguishing between "major" and "minor" Prophets. Moses should have been placed at the head of those called "major," since he wrote more than all the others, and his writings even served as a primary Text for all who came after him; and next to him should have been added Joshua, Samuel, David, and others from whom we have divine Scriptures in the books of the Old Testament. Nevertheless, those usually designated by the name of "major" are only these four: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel. The twelve that follow are called the minor Prophets, because the prophecy of nearly all twelve is very short and requires little time to be read through.

<column-break/>

Hosea, who is the first in the ranking that has been made, lived under the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, Kings of Judah, being a contemporary of the Prophet Isaiah. He was commanded to direct his addresses specifically to the ten breakaway Tribes who made up the Kingdom of Israel or Samaria, and to reproach them for their impieties, which he did in a very vivid manner. He threatened them with the disasters and calamities that befell them not long after Shalmaneser, King of the Assyrians, had made himself master of their land and led them into captivity in Assyria. Hosea also prophesied to the Kingdom of Judah, which was no less criminal than the other; and under the symbol of a marriage which God caused the Prophet to enter into with an unchaste woman <note>Scholars debate if this marriage was a literal event or a symbolic vision intended to mirror Israel's unfaithfulness to God.</note>, the Lord gave His people to understand that He would reject them, and that He would call the Gentiles <note>Original: "Heydenen."</note> in their place.

Joel, who is believed to have lived alongside Hosea under the reign of Uzziah, prophesied in the Kingdom of Judah. On the occasion of a great famine and various other plagues which God had brought upon this sinful Kingdom, he gave the Jews very powerful exhortations to repentance. And just as the Prophets mixed the promise of the Messiah into all the great comforts which they presented to the Church of their time, so Joel foretold the times of the Gospel <note>Original: "Evangelium."</note>, and specifically that extraordinary outpouring of God’s Spirit which was to occur in that dispensation of salvation and grace. This was so gloriously fulfilled on the day of Pentecost that St. Peter applied this prophecy of the Prophet Joel to it:

> I will pour out of my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, etc.

God, who is free in the choice He makes of men, and when it pleases Him to use

HISTORY OF THE O. TESTAMENT. 285

He makes use of the weakest and most unfit to carry out His great designs; He took from among the cattle herders of a city in Judea called Tekoa, *Amos*, who was a cowherd, to make him His Prophet. He sent him to the ten tribes of Israel to rebuke them for their idolatries, the injustice of their rulers, and the horrific excesses in eating and drinking practiced among the people. He also prophesied of the times of the Gospel; the Apostle James <note>Original: "Apostel Jakobus."</note> relates a prediction by this Prophet in the fifteenth chapter of the Acts of the Apostles, which concerned the restoration of the Church by the Messiah.

*Obadiah* prophesied around that same time; his prophecy is very short and looked only toward the future destruction of the Edomites; but under that image, God foretold the spiritual victory of the Church over her enemies through the Messiah.

<column-break/>

*Jonah* began to prophesy at the same time as Hosea, or a little before. He prophesied in the Kingdom of Israel, and God having subsequently commanded him to go to Nineveh, he was troubled by this; but we shall soon have the opportunity to speak more broadly of his prophecy.

*Micah* was a contemporary of Isaiah, with whom his style has great similarity. He prophesied the fall of the Kingdom of Israel and that of Judah, and he often mingled predictions regarding the Messiah into his prophecy. One of the most prominent is that of the fifth chapter, where he foretold that the Messiah would be born in Bethlehem. This entire fifth chapter is, among others, of a wonderful beauty and profundity, and the times of the Gospel are so well depicted therein that one can perceive nearly all its various stages—namely, its beginning and its miraculous progress.

# De zes andere kleyne Profeeten
## Nahum, Habakuk, Zephanja, Haggai, Zacharia, en Maleachi.

---

*Nahum* lived at the time when the Assyrians led the ten tribes captive to Assyria. He prophesied against Nineveh, the capital of that vast Empire; and he foretold her fall, which she had avoided for a time when, upon hearing the terrifying threat of Jonah that she would be destroyed within forty days, she humbled herself.

*Habakkuk* lived at the same time as Jeremiah, and foretold to Judea all the calamities that befell her shortly thereafter through the weapons of the Chaldeans <note>The Neo-Babylonian Empire.</note>. He comforts the people by the assurance he gives them of God’s assistance, and upon this he says the words which the Apostle Paul quotes in several places in his Epistles—

<column-break/>

—*that the just shall live by his faith.* <note>Original: "dat de regtvaerdige door zyn geloove zal leeven." A reference to Habakkuk 2:4.</note> He ends his prophecy with a long and fervent prayer, which makes up the third part of his book, and in which one perceives a loftiness of thought and expression that gives an idea of God's greatness, capable of instilling in us the reverence owed to His eternal Majesty.

*Zephaniah* lived shortly after Habakkuk; he sharply rebuked the Jews for their crimes and threatened them, like all the other prophets of his time, with the army of the Chaldeans and all the disasters that befell that people. But finally, he comforted them and gave hope that God would not abandon them forever, but that He would bring them back from the captivity of Babylon <note>Original: "Babel."</note>.

*Haggai* was one of those who returned with Zerubbabel from the Babylonian captivity in the first year of the reign of Cyrus. The following year, God revealed Himself to him, and ful—

<note>The sentence begins mid-thought from the previous page</note> filled him with the spirit of Prophecy. Encouraged then by this Holy Spirit, he began to rebuke the Jews; for they had more zeal to build houses for themselves, and to vault them <note>The author refers to "ceiled houses," meaning finished with decorative woodwork</note>, than to complete the house of the Lord. When they labored upon it, and it began to take the shape of a Temple, some who saw what had already been built thought it so beautiful that they could not express enough joy; but others, who had seen the first Temple <note>Solomon's Temple, destroyed by the Babylonians</note>, found this one so meager in comparison that they wept bitterly. It was then that Haggai spoke that oracle which has since become so famous, and which the Apostle Paul applies to the Covenant of Grace in his Epistle to the Hebrews: *Yet once more, it will be a little while; and I will shake the heavens, and the earth, and the sea, and the dry land: yes, I will shake all nations, and they shall come to the desire of all nations <note>Original: "de wensch aller heydenen."</note>, and I will fill this House with glory. Mine is the silver, and mine is the gold, says the Lord of Hosts.* "*The glory of this latter House shall be greater than the former; and in this place I will give peace.*" Everything in this oracle speaks of the Messiah; and this second Temple, into which He so often entered, and where He so many times made Himself heard, was more honored by His presence than Solomon’s Temple was by the splendor of its construction and the immeasurable riches with which it was filled.

Zechariah prophesied at the same time as Haggai, following the Babylonian captivity. His book is the longest of the twelve minor Prophets, and one of the most profound in the entire Old Testament. The vision he relates in the third chapter of the High Priest Joshua, clothed in filthy garments, and of the struggle between the Angel of the Lord and Satan, contains great mysteries, which the Apostle Jude also points out through an allu-

<column-break/>

sion that clearly refers to this divine word, in the struggle of the Archangel Michael with the Devil. The prophecy of the same chapter, where Zechariah speaks of a spiritual Sprout <note>The "Branch," a Messianic title</note> who would spring from his place, and build the Temple of the Lord, and be both Priest and King at once, is beyond dispute one of the most profound passages, highly worthy of the attention of faithful souls, to be found in all the writings of the Prophets. One could say much more, but no sooner has one spoken two words of Zechariah than one must move to Malachi, who appears as the last.

Malachi lived and prophesied during that same period and was the last of all the Prophets whom God sent to His ancient people; from him until John the Baptist, the Spirit of Prophecy was given to no one. We also see that Malachi wrote as one who was providing the conclusion to the Book of the Old Testament. The prediction seen at the beginning of the third chapter, where he points out that the Messiah would enter the second Temple and that He would send His Angel—being John the Baptist—before Him, gives such great clarity to the words of Haggai that these two joined together create a light as pure as the sun at high noon for any soul not entirely blinded by prejudice or enchanted by delusion. The fourth chapter contains in brief the predictions of the rejection of the Jews, the destruction of Jerusalem, and the happiness of those among that unbelieving people who would recognize Jesus Christ; and finally, a short but vivid description of John the Baptist. One cannot read these Prophecies, thus linked and following one another, without seeing the entire Gospel within them, and without pitying the misfortune of a people who still daily read them in the Prophets' own language and yet see nothing of it, nor understand it.

Jonah was from Gath-Hepher, a city of the tribe of Zebulun, in Galilee. Since the Jews, and especially the Scholars, could not have been ignorant of a matter so clearly pointed out in Scripture, it is inconceivable that the Pharisees, who said to Nicodemus in the seventh chapter of John that no Prophet had arisen from Galilee, would have meant it in the sense usually attributed to their words. What they meant to say is that *the Prophet*, namely the Messiah, would not come out of Galilee, for He had to be from Bethlehem in the Tribe of Judah; and that therefore Jesus being a Galilean, as they believed, could not be the Prophet. Nathanael had these same thoughts when, upon Philip's saying that he had found the Messiah, he immediately made this objection: "But he of whom you speak is from Nazareth in Galilee; and can anything good come out of Nazareth, or can such a great good emerge from there?" Jonah was not only called, like the other Prophets, to rebuke the ten Tribes for their

<column-break/>

idolatries, but God also gave him a command to proclaim to the Ninevites the fall of their city and their total destruction. Nineveh was the capital of the mighty empire of the Assyrians, under whom all the other states and kingdoms of the East trembled. Her long and exceptional prosperity had plunged her people into all kinds of vices, and God—who often in His wrath casts down and overturns Empires that seemed destined to last forever—had decided to let this one stand a while longer, to use it later against the idolatrous Tribes of Israel. But to prevent the sentence upon the Ninevites from being hastened by their crimes, God wished to send them one of His Prophets, who through terrible threats of Heaven's judgments upon the city, would cause the King and the people to turn back from the lawlessness in which they were sunken. Jonah was chosen for this service, which was of a new kind and entirely uncommon. "*Arise*," said the Lord to him, "*go to the great city of Nineveh, and preach against it, for her wickedness has come up before my face.*" The Prophet was astonished to receive such an order, for which there was no precedent; and whether it was that he was jealous of the honor God showed to a people who were not of His covenant, or that he feared God would grant them forgiveness if they humbled themselves,

He thought of nothing but means to escape this burden. The disturbance of his mind clouded the conceptions he otherwise should have had of the immensity of God, who is present everywhere; and he imagined that by boarding a vessel which he found ready to sail from Japho <note>Modern Jaffa</note>, or Joppa, for the land of Tarshish <note>original: "Tharſis"</note> (since called *Tartessus*, today known as Cadiz, near the Strait of Gibraltar, according to the opinion of several commentators, and according to others, on the coast of Africa), he might somewhat steal himself away from God’s sight, or at least that God would not fetch him from so far, but would give His command to someone else. Yet Jonah was not a little astonished when, having gone aboard, he found that the sea would not carry a ship which served as a hiding place for a fugitive and a rebel, whom the God of the sea and the earth, the Master of the world, pursued and wished to prevent from escaping. The storm increased steadily, and the tempest became so ghastly that it was believed something extraordinary must lie behind it. In the midst of this great danger lay Jonah, who had gone down into the ship and was in a deep sleep. People ran to him to wake him, and he saw that all the people in the ship

<column-break/>

were ready to cast lots, to determine and cast overboard the man found to be the cause of that storm; for God willed that they should all believe there was a great criminal among them, for whose sake the sea raged so violently. The lot fell upon Jonah, who immediately confessed that he was guilty. They did everything they could to save him, and attempted to reach land by rowing; but the storm became heavier and heavier, so that they were forced to throw him into the sea, just as he himself desired. God, who did not wish him to perish, caused a great fish to be at hand to receive him. The Hebrew word of the text of this history, and the Greek of the Gospel where the same is cited, indicate only that it was a "great fish," and it is suspected that it may have been the *Lamia* fish <note>Historically, the "Lamia" was often identified by naturalists as a Great White Shark</note>, since the entire body of a man in full armor was once found within one. For regarding the whale, the whole world agrees that its throat is much too narrow to swallow a whole man. Jonah was then preserved in this fish, as in a place of safety, as we shall see in the continuation of this history, and the storm subsided entirely.

One must judge these words by the meaning Jesus Christ used when He spoke of the time He Himself remained in the grave until the third day, a span of about thirty-eight hours. For, in a natural sense, it is impossible for someone to live so long in the belly of an animal, whose natural heat would consume all food in much less time. The light of the Holy Spirit penetrated into the depths of this dungeon to illuminate Jonah there, while he made very Godly observations on the state in which he found himself. His sighs and prayers made a way through this abyss to God and ascended to Heaven. On the third day, the fish received a command from God to spit the Prophet out onto the shore, and Jonah saw the light again, healthy and unharmed, without anything from that physical prison remaining with him except the memory of having been enclosed therein, and the joy and gratitude of having come out. Christ has pointed out to us in the Gospel that Jonah’s exit from the belly of the fish on the third day was a type <note>A 'type' or 'prefiguration' is a person or event in the Old Testament believed to foreshadow something in the New Testament.</note> of His resurrection from the grave on the third day after His death; and He shows us through that profound application to this history that God, in the Old Testament, created various shadows of the mysteries of Grace, which we, with our limited understanding, often cannot trace.

After Jonah had come out of the belly of the fish, he received a command for the second time to go to Nineveh and to cry out in the squares and streets of that great city that it would be overturned forty days after his preaching. He was not slow to obey, and having arrived at Nineveh, he went everywhere, crying aloud that Nineveh was to be destroyed within forty days. The size of this city was something rare; Holy Scripture says it was a journey of three days, and this is likely to be 

<column-break/>

understood as its circumference. Secular writers have spoken of it in almost the same way, for one finds those who have written that it covered twenty-four miles in circumference. That which God says at the end of this history—that there were more than one hundred and twenty thousand people in it who knew no distinction between their right and their left hand <note>This biblical phrase usually refers to young children or the innocent who cannot yet discern right from wrong.</note>—likewise shows that it must have been exceedingly large and very populated. Jonah, accustomed to finding among the tribes of Israel nothing but people who paid no heed to the protests of the Prophets and the threats that accompanied them, believed that the people of Nineveh would have struck dead an enemy who pronounced curses over their city. Yet he voluntarily exposed himself to the one as well as the other, to offer himself in the service of God, who had sent him to that people. But God had already provided for this, and holding the passions—which might have flared up against the Prophet at his sight and voice—as if they were chained, He made the Ninevites and the King himself attentive to Jonah’s preaching. They came to a serious reflection on the irregularity of their morals, and noticing that they had deserved all the calamities with which that man threatened them, they sighed and wept over it. The King himself showed his people by his own example what they ought to do to turn away the disasters with which they were threatened. He had a general fast proclaimed; they all clothed themselves in sackcloth and sat down in the ashes; they neither ate nor drank that whole day, indeed, not even the little children or the beasts. Everything within Nineveh bore the signs of mourning and amazement, and looking at them, one would have said they were all people who, having been condemned to death, only waited for the hour to be led away to punishment. [God] saw this great humbling, and although it might not have been joined with true faith, and though the fear of God’s judgments—awakened out of self-love—might have played as much a part in it as the hatred of sin, He nevertheless took heed of it. One would expect an entirely different sentiment from a Prophet, but one sees there man as he is in himself: namely, that false fastidiousness that seeks honor in all things, and those secret, selfish insights to observe one’s own interests where one ought to prioritize those of others and submit one’s own entirely to those of God. Jonah feared that he would be regarded as a false prophet; and since God had only given him the command to proclaim to the Ninevites that they and their city would perish within forty days—without showing him that the threat was conditional in case they did not repent—he had spoken of Nineveh’s downfall to those he came to as a certain and infallible matter. Nevertheless, it could be that these feelings were not entirely human, and that he had the honor of God, who had imposed this threat upon him, more in view than his own. ### The elder Tobias loses his sight.
### Tobit Chapter II. verses 9, 10.

<margin>The year of the world 3286.</margin>
One finds mentioned in this History two persons who bore the name Tobias <note>In many English Bibles, the father is called Tobit and the son Tobias, though the original Dutch follows the Vulgate tradition of using Tobias for both.</note>: the one was the father, and the other the son, who themselves described their history. The elder Tobias was, according to his account, led from Galilee to Assyria while still very young by Enemessar <note>original: "Enemessar," a variation of the name Shalmaneser V.</note>, who subsequently honored him with his favor. He made such good use of the wealth he obtained either from that Prince or through the office of Purveyor of the—

<column-break/>

—him to pity him, and to marvel at God’s goodness with which He accommodated this untimely agitation of the Prophet, and at His gentleness with which He brought him back from his straying. Jonah had, as well as he could, put up a small hut to shield himself somewhat from the sting of the sun, which shines burningly hot in that country. At the foot of this shelter, God caused a plant to grow, which shot up so high in a single night that it shaded the Prophet’s hut. In Hebrew, this plant is called *Kikajon*, and Hieronymus <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the translator of the Latin Vulgate.</note> translated this word as *ivy*, which had not yet been used in his translation of the Bible in that place, as seen in a letter from Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a contemporary of Jerome.</note> in which he writes to Jerome that when the book of Jonah was once read in a certain Church in the presence of the Bishop, the people, upon hearing the word *ivy*, cried out as if at a novelty. The most common opinion today among the Learned is that this plant was what is called *Palma Christi* <note>original: "Palma Christi," Latin for "Palm of Christ," referring to the Castor Oil plant (*Ricinus communis*).</note> or also the *Wonder-tree*, because it has very broad leaves and grows as high as a small fig tree; it is called *Kiki* in Arabic, which corresponds to the name *Kikayon*, and it is certain that it is very common in various Eastern lands. This plant, whose shade had been so pleasant to Jonah, withered all at once because God had appointed a worm that gnawed through the root in one night. This served as a lesson which God gave to the Prophet, because he showed himself so offended by this sudden withering of a little tree, the sight of which had been so pleasant and the shade so convenient to him. God instructed him through this symbol: *Is it right for you to be angry,* He said to him, *about the wonder-tree?* Yes, said Jonah, *even unto death.* God allowed His Prophet to have such excessive sensitivity about it so that the conviction could better penetrate his mind.
> *You are thus distressed, the Lord replied, over the wonder-tree for which you have not labored, and which came up in a night and perished in a night; and should I not spare that great city Nineveh, in which there are more than one hundred and twenty thousand people who do not know the difference between their right hand and their left hand?*

One can learn from no one but God alone how tender and compassionate He is regarding our calamities; and since our conversion always stills His wrath, it can never be too ready nor too powerful. We can then end this History no better than by saying with the Prophet to God: *Turn us, and we shall be turned.* <note>A reference to Lamentations 5:21.</note> Amen.

...to the memory of a deceased person, to have no burial; and the Pagans had the foolishness to imagine that the souls whose bodies were not buried suffered greatly thereby, and that they wandered around these miserable corpses and elsewhere without being able to find any rest as long as the bodies remained in that state. The elder Tobit, in these circumstances, was very diligent in performing this difficult work of burying the dead, even at the risk of his own life. Meanwhile, he did not forget to care for the living; and once, on the feast of Pentecost, when he gave a meal to many poor people whom his son had brought to him at his command, he was told that in the city (it was Nineveh where he lived)

<column-break/>

one of his countrymen had been strangled and cast into the street. He immediately rose from the table and went to retrieve the corpse, which he brought to his home in order to bury it by night. Afterward, he washed himself and finished his meal in sadness. When night came, Tobit buried the dead, and because he was very weary, he lay down by a wall of his house; he did not wish to enter, as he said, because he had become "unclean" <note>According to Jewish Law (Numbers 19), touching a corpse made a person ritually impure for seven days, preventing them from entering holy spaces or touching sacred things.</note> by touching the dead body. Such an example [of devotion] had never been seen; but while he slept, hot dung fell from the nest of a sparrow or swallow into his eyes, from which a film developed that made him blind.

And a long time afterward, Tobit, seeing that his years were advancing and judging that he did not have much time left to live, called his son to him to give him great exhortations of godliness and to command him to care for the poor. On this occasion, he also revealed to him what he had kept secret until that time: that he had lent ten talents of silver <note>original: "tien talenten zilvers." young; therefore his father wished to provide him with an Overseer <term>Overseer: a guide or traveling companion responsible for the safety of a minor</term>. He immediately brought this man to his father, who asked him from where and who he was. The stranger answered that he was Azarias, son of the great Ananias, who was a kinsman of Tobit. This supposed Azarias was, as the story relates, an Angel named Raphael. One finds several examples of godly people who, upon certain occasions where the heart was carried away by self-interest, spoke an untruth; but this is the first time that such a thing is found mentioned of an Angel. The elder Tobit agreed with him and entrusted the guidance of his son to this stranger, who presented himself as one of his kin. Within a short time, it marched through Mesopotamia, and having crossed the Euphrates, it spread out like a stream in Syria, so that the kingdoms of Tyre and Sidon were on the verge of being flooded by the same. The Priest, who at that time held the highest dignity of the Priesthood, was named Joachim; he, in this pressing danger, had an extraordinary fast proclaimed throughout all Judea; and what was something singular, they even covered the altar with a sack <note>Sackcloth, a coarse fabric used as a symbol of mourning or extreme penitence</note>. The Jews then put themselves in a state to protect their land and occupied all the passes where they thought they could stop the enemy host. Holofernes, who had command over it, became very angry, seeing that the Jews dared to stand in their own defense. The beauty of this Israelite woman made Holofernes give more credit to her words than he likely would have done had they come from someone else. the wicked and shameful proposal which these 
scoundrels made to her: to follow their cursed
will, or else they would accuse her of unchastity 
committed with a young man who had fled upon
their arrival. Innocence is often unsettled by a 
slight assault, but a dignified virtue does not 
fail to remain steadfast in the midst of danger. 
That of Susanna was of such a nature: this 
holy woman immediately saw what was coming
upon her if she were accused by two men of such
status as these; but she paid more heed to her
honor and her duty than to the danger that 
threatened her; and lifting her eyes toward Heaven, 
to implore God for His assistance in such a 
delicate case, she gave a loud cry, so that her 
people might come to her aid. The Elders then 
cried out as well, and one of them ran to the door
of the garden, as if he had wanted to pursue the
guilty party to seize him. The household staff
came running, the Elders accused Susanna, and
Susanna had nothing for her defense but her 
conscience and her God.

### The History of Bel and the Dragon.
->VERSES 2—21.<-

---

The Babylonians worshipped an idol named *Bel*, and it is certain that of all the gods of these idolaters, it was this one to whom they paid the most reverence. We have elsewhere noted that this was the Baal of the Sidonians, who later became the idol of the ten Tribes of Israel, and from there passed into the Kingdom of Judah. We have also said that the Eastern peoples sometimes under this name, and sometimes under that of Moloch, worshipped the Sun, which was regarded by all the Heathens as the greatest of all gods, the Lord and King of the world; as still happens today in Persia and other countries of the East. A great image had been dedicated to that god Bel in Babylon, and his Temple was the most prominent of all. King Cyrus, who, like his entire people, showed a particular devotion to this Idol, was displeased that Daniel did not worship him. Daniel answered the King that he made profession

<column-break/>

of worshipping no one but the true God, and that Bel was not such. The King then countered Daniel, saying that Bel daily consumed a great quantity of food brought to him, which a dead and inanimate image could not do; for the Author says that every day they set before that idol twelve measures of flour, forty sheep, and six vessels of wine; this was served to him in the evening, and in the morning it was found that everything had been eaten. It is true that the Unbelievers were so prejudiced regarding their idols that one must often stand amazed at how such foolish and absurd thoughts could enter the human mind; but God willed it so, to frustrate godlessness through itself, according to what the Apostle Paul noted in the first chapter of his Epistle to the Romans. But that the idolaters and the King of Babylon could believe in good faith—to the point that they dared to put the matter seriously to the test—that an image of gold and silver truly ate the food brought to him, is something that exceeds the imagination. The writer of this history seems to have had his eye on a certain text of Jeremiah, in which he foretells, according to the usual language of the Prophets, the fall and ruin of Babylon and her gods, especially Bel, who was the protector-god of the city. <margin>Jeremiah 51:44</margin>
The 51st chapter is set down thus: *I will punish, says the Lord, Bel in Babylon, and I will bring out of his mouth what he has swallowed.* However, the actual meaning of this prophecy is that Babylon would be destroyed; that Bel—who was considered the cause of all her prosperity—would no longer have worshippers; and that those immense treasures which the Kings of that great Empire had brought into the Temple of that god from all the regions they had conquered, as magnificent trophies of victory which they sacrificed to him (as one observes from the history of those nations), would be carried away from Babylon. But Daniel (to return to our story), after the usual foods had been set before Bel, secretly had the floor of the Temple strewn with ashes. After the door was closed, it was sealed for greater security with the King’s ring. The next morning, the King went with Daniel to the Temple; the food that had been brought there the evening before was gone. The King, seeing the table empty, assumed that since the door was closed and sealed, Bel must have eaten the food. But Daniel began to laugh and held the King back from entering, pointing out to him the footprints of men, women, and children on the floor. It was subsequently shown that the priests of Bel had entered and exited with their families through secret doors. This discovery had such a profound effect on the King’s mind that he sentenced the priests of Bel and their families to death, and ordered the Idol and his temple to be demolished.

# Daniel causes a Dragon of immense size, which was worshipped by the Babylonians, to die.

## The History of Bel and the Dragon. verses 22—26.

The Babylonians also worshipped a Dragon <note>The "Dragon" mentioned here is often interpreted by historians as a large serpent, a creature frequently deified in ancient Near Eastern and Egyptian religions.</note> of an extraordinary size. It is well known that the Devil, who has caused himself to be worshipped under a thousand different forms, has also influenced many peoples to make gods out of snakes; history is full of such examples, and even today among the unbelieving <note>A common 18th-century term for non-Christian or "pagan" cultures.</note> one still finds peoples who are enchanted by that superstition. The basis of this idolatry was, firstly, that the Gods presented themselves wherever it pleased them; and secondly, that there were harmful gods, always inclined to do evil to men, just as there were also good-natured and benevolent ones. Based on this, it was believed that one must offer sacrifices to both:

<column-break/>

to the good, to thank them for their favors and to pray that they would persevere in their care for mankind; and to the others, whose evil inclinations they feared, to soften them, and—through the incense and sacrifices offered to them—to prevent their wicked designs against the poor humans, who had nothing but submission and prayers for their protection against such harsh Deities. Snakes were of this number; and because people daily perceived the deadly effects of their venom and bites, especially in the East and in the South <note>Referring to the Levant, Mesopotamia, and Africa.</note>—where those animals are most venomous and where one finds many terrifying species unknown in Europe—it was believed that the surest means to guard against them was to build them Temples and altars, and to honor them as gods. By keeping some of these animals in such Temples for a long time, they were seen in several places to grow to an immense size. It is upon this that the writer of this history looked when he says that King Cyrus presented this Dragon to Daniel as an object that deserved his worship.

->The Prayer of Manasseh in Chains<-

### The Prayer of Manasseh in his chains.

Manasseh, son of Hezekiah, had so degenerated from the godliness of the King his father that he seemed to oppose him in everything, and gave himself over to idolatry with as great a passion as Hezekiah had used diligence to root it out of his Kingdom. God, angered at this Prince because of this, caused Nebuchadnezzar to come from Babylonia for the first time: having taken Jerusalem, he led Manasseh away as a prisoner. The writer of the second book of Chronicles, relating this history, says briefly in the 33rd chapter that Manasseh humbled himself under the hand of God, who had struck him, and that having acknowledged and wept for his crimes, the Lord

<column-break/>

took pity on him and brought him back to Judea and to the Throne. Another writer <note>A reference to the author of the apocryphal "Prayer of Manasseh"</note> has described the penitent outpourings of this Prince in his imprisonment in such a way that one sees very well depicted therein the remorse of a sinner who accuses and condemns himself with great and holy severity, and expects neither salvation nor mercy except from God’s pure compassion. There is no human who ought not to have such feelings as are expressed in this prayer; they are all borrowed from various texts of Holy Scripture, especially from the Psalms and the Prophets. But since the pure source of all knowledge is there, one must also go there to draw, in order to learn to know God’s greatness and man’s misery, which are very well shown in this prayer of Manasseh.

One might think that her condition under the reign of the Kings was more fortunate; but what wars, and what disorder in Religion and the State, did one not see arise at various times among that people, until finally the ten tribes of Israel were carried away captive to Assyria, and not long thereafter the two others, who made up the Kingdom of Judah, to Babylon? The pinnacle of the destruction of the ancient Jewish **Church** <note>The author uses the Dutch word 'Kerk' (Church) to refer to the community of Israel, common in period literature to show continuity between the Old and New Testaments</note> was the deadly war which the Chaldeans came to inflict upon her; she then saw Jerusalem destroyed, the Temple demolished, the altars crushed, and the practice of Religion abolished. Having been captive in Babylonia for a span of seventy years—a long time for a people who had fallen from such a height—she regained her freedom, with permission to return to Judea. But this poor Church had so much trouble recovering and restoring herself that the difficulties seemed insurmountable. The Writer who composed this History relates the heavy persecutions which the Church suffered under the reign of Antiochus, surnamed *Epiphanes*; he was descended from Seleucus Nicanor, one of the Generals of Alexander, and he reigned over Syria, upon which Judea was dependent at that time. This Antiochus was, in the vision of Daniel mentioned just now, signified by that *little horn* which came forth after the four large ones on the head of the goat, and was to do an unspeakable evil to the Church. This prophecy was fulfilled in all its parts; the Jews had in the person of that Prince an irreconcilable enemy, who seemed pregnant only with a desire and longing to destroy them to the ground. Never has one seen greater violence and rage, and never has God’s people suffered so much. But that which made their condition most piteous was the violent assault of Antiochus against Religion. He deprived Onias, who was a godly Priest, of the High Priesthood, to provide it to a certain Jason, a wicked and godless man. He defiled and desecrated the Temple, plundered its treasures, and committed unheard-of debaucheries there: he even had an Idol placed upon God’s altar. All the people dissolved in tears; public Religion ceased, sacrifices were no longer offered; and the History is full of the impieties of that Prince, and of the misfortunes of that poor people, which seemed destined to perish under that cruel persecution.

### *Mattathias, father of Judas Maccabeus, kills a Jew who was sacrificing to the Idols.*

#### 1 Maccabees 2, verse 24.

Antiochus was not satisfied with stripping the Jews of the free exercise of their Religion, but he also wished to compel them to do things that were entirely contrary to it. He knew that this people very religiously observed the avoidance of foods forbidden by the Laws of Moses, and especially the eating of swine's flesh: therefore he forced them to it with violence. But that which embittered him even more against the Jews was the unyielding aversion they showed toward all kinds of idolatry. The Babylonian captivity had had such an effect on them; for in their ancient histories one sees how uncommonly inclined they were to that crime. The books of Judges and Kings are full of those mournful examples. They had hardly abandoned their Idols before they took them up again; the Prophets, who zealously rebuked them on God's behalf, were not heard, and God finally—after many severe punishments which he sent them, now in this way and then in that, to draw them away from that abominable sin—had to destroy their city and Temple, and lead them to Babylon. This hard blow, foretold for a long time and never believed, fortunately caused them to abandon that foolish passion, and they finally learned in the lands of the Idolaters to loathe Idolatry. Antiochus wanted to compel them to resume it: many yielded before his severities and persecutions; but there was also a great number of upright Israelites who, far from being willing to please the Tyrant, or looking only to their own peace and self-interest, were instead more and more strengthened in their holy pur-

<column-break/>

-pose of being faithful to God, and not sacrificing to Idols. Among those who in those distressed times let their zeal for Religion be seen, Mattathias, the Head of a Priestly family, stood out with his five sons, of whom Judas, surnamed the Maccabee <note>The surname 'Maccabee' is traditionally thought to be derived from the Aramaic word 'maqqaba', meaning 'hammer', in recognition of his fierce leadership in battle</note>, earned himself a name through his great deeds that will never die in the memory of men. Mattathias lived in Jerusalem, but he was so saddened by the destruction of that city, and even more by that of the Temple, that he could no longer remain living there. He then betook himself with his children to a remote place, which the Historian calls Modin <note>Modin was an ancient village located between Jerusalem and Lydda, famous as the starting point of the Maccabean Revolt</note>. There this holy man mourned the misfortunes of the Church <note>original: "Kerke"; the author uses this term to refer to the assembly of faithful Israelites</note>, he prayed and fasted, and his children followed his example. However, the rage of the persecutors soon came to find them there, and there followed an order from Antiochus to all those who had retreated to Modin that they must offer incense to the Idols. There were those who were cowardly enough to obey his orders. The authority of Sovereigns is hallowed, and one finds people so small of understanding that they imagine Kings are Kings in all things, and that their subjects have nothing to do but to show obedience in everything. One sees others who love Religion no further than they can reconcile it with their interests, and who go no further in God's ways than when the danger of losing their peace, property, or life comes before their eyes. Mattathias, urged like all the others, gave this noble answer to those who spoke to him on the King's behalf and presented the example of those who had already obeyed: *Even if all the nations that are in the House and Kingdom of the King obeyed him, and every one of them fell away from the Religion, yet will I and my sons and my brothers walk in the covenant of our fathers. ### I. Maccabees Chapter II. verses 49—69 and Chap. IV.

AFTER the Priest Mattathias had killed a certain Jew, who wished to sacrifice to the Idols, out of a zeal for the true God, there was no safety for him except in flight. He then withdrew with his sons, and a great number of other persons, to the deserts of Judea, just as David had done in former times to preserve his life from the persecution of Saul. Many others in various places likewise took flight, so that the cities became like deserts, and the deserts were populated like cities. But they did not remain long in peace; Antiochus sent troops there; and because these poor people dared not defend themselves on the Sabbath day, for fear of profaning it, the Persecutors made them all die without mercy. Mattathias and his sons, who were hidden in other places, heard of the death of their brothers with the utmost sorrow. But to the end that their enemies might not again

<column-break/>

avail themselves of the easy means they had found to put the people to the sword on a day on which the former, through an all too great reverence for the Sabbath, had all allowed themselves to be struck dead, without even having dared to block the mouths of the caves, it was decided that they would defend themselves on the Sabbath as well as on other days of the week; and at the same time Mattathias and his sons took up arms to resist the tyranny. They were soon followed by a great multitude of people, who could no longer withstand the iniquities and cruelties of Antiochus, and their courage made itself known in various occurrences. One cannot recount those in this short summary of the History of God's people; but those who have the curiosity to be informed thereof can read the history in the first Book of the Maccabees, and in the *Jewish Antiquities* of Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus was a first-century historian whose "Antiquities of the Jews" is a primary source for this period of history.</note>.

Mattathias died not long after, at the age of one hundred and forty-six years, leaving five sons, all of a particular and exemplary godliness. He gave them exhortations on his deathbed, fitting for the great zeal which he had shown for the divine Laws during all the time of his life. He laid before them how very necessary it was for them in that time of persecution to remain steadfast in the fear of God, and to keep the interests of Religion always before their eyes and in their hearts. ...stepping back to the histories of their ancestors, he chose the most prominent examples from them to compose a complete picture of all kinds of virtues. The faith of Abraham, the chastity of Joseph, the zeal of Phinehas, the bravery of Joshua, the fervor of Elijah, the untainted integrity of the three Hebrew youths <note>Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, also known by their Babylonian names Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego.</note>, from whom all the respect they bore the King of Babylon could not extort a single grain of incense for the Idols, and who preferred to be thrown into the glowing furnace than to show such a cowardly compliance toward that great Prince who had favored them with benefits and honored them with the most prestigious offices of his Realm: and finally, the steadfastness of Daniel. All these great examples Mattathias presented to his children; and he zealously commanded them that they should all with one accord be concerned with the protection of their Religion and their people. He charged them in particular to listen to the counsel of Simeon, one among them; and in matters of war to follow the leadership of Judas, surnamed Maccabeus, in whom that wise father had found all the qualities necessary to make a General. The outcome soon proved that Mattathias had not been deceived in his judgment regarding his children. Simeon and Judas distinguished themselves among the others, and this latter especially, in the wars he waged against the troops of Antiochus, gave such signs of his bravery and courage that he became the admiration of his people and the terror of his enemies.

Judas achieved many other remarkable advantages over the enemies in that same year, and defeated Gorgias, who with five thousand men on foot and a thousand on horse—all chosen people—had camped close to Emmaus; and lost three thousand of his own on the spot. But the victory which brought him more honor, and his people more benefit, was the one he achieved the following year over the army of Lysias. This General commanded an army of sixty thousand men on foot and five thousand on horse, the finest troops of Syria. Antiochus caused this formidable army to march against Jerusalem: Judas had only ten thousand men, but he had God on his side. Strengthened then by such a mighty

<column-break/>

assistance, which he invoked anew with great zeal, he set out against the enemy. This march will seem reckless to those who judge matters only by the usual principles of reason and human wisdom. But if Heathendom has seen amazing deeds, and those that run against common rules, performed by their Heroes; why should the Church not also have her Heroes, who, full of a much greater courage than that of all others, and guided by a much more exalted knowledge than theirs, have carried out such enterprises which to all appearances could not have succeeded for them? God blessed the arms of the Jews, the small number overcame the large, and the army of Lysias was cut to pieces. That of the Jews then marched to Jerusalem, which by that great victory was delivered from the calamities that threatened it. The victorious people entered the city, led by Judas Maccabeus. Jerusalem was abandoned by inhabitants, the Temple half destroyed, the altar of the Lord profaned, and the shrubs grew like thickets in the courtyards. The godly and brave Chief of Israel dedicated his victorious hands, and those of his brave soldiers, to set the ruins of the Sanctuary upright again.

They tore down the altar which the idol-worshippers had profaned, and they made a new one again. They purified the courtyard and made it fit again for the use for which it was intended: they made new vessels for the service of the Temple. The Priests resumed their office; they offered sacrifices again, and made incense smoke on the altar of incense. This was the use that Judas Maccabeus made of his victory. He knew that he had to thank God alone for it, therefore he also wanted to pay him homage for that reason, and apply his first cares to the restoration of Religion. Acts of that nature bring more honor to Princes than their victories, and nothing is more becoming for the greatness and Majesty of Kings than to be mindful in their highest elevation that there is a King above them, whose servants they only are, and whose interests they ought to stand for, and cause his laws to be honored by the people.

### The death of the godless Antiochus.

#### I. Maccabees Chapter VI.

The happy progress of the Maccabees awakened the old enemies of God’s people, the Idumeans <note>Descendants of Esau, the brother of Jacob; their kingdom, Edom, was located south of the Dead Sea.</note>, among whom the enmity against the Jews was as if hereditary, since the hatred that Esau, from whom they were descended, had borne toward Jacob. But Judas Maccabeus was no less prosperous in this war than he had been in the previous ones, and his weapons, blessed everywhere by Heaven, were as victorious in Idumea as in Judea. When he returned from this illustrious expedition, he found the Ammonites in arms against the Jews; their army was very strong, but Judas the Maccabee was accustomed to seeing a large number bow under a small one. The Lord of hosts fought for him, and caused him to win many battles from the Ammonites. Having returned to his land, he found matters in many places in a very piteous

<column-break/>

state. The enemies had fallen into the land of Gilead, and had brought it to the utmost necessity: and from another side, troops had come from Tyre and Sidon who were devastating Galilee. But Judas promptly set everything in order: he sent his brother Simon to the aid of the Galileans, and he himself with Jonathan, his other brother, set out to protect the land of Gilead. God caused them both to be prosperous in their expeditions. Simon drove the Syrians and Sidonians out of Galilee, and Judas defeated the army of the enemies in Gileaditis <note>The region of Gilead, east of the Jordan River.</note>, over which Timotheus commanded.

While these things were occurring in Judea, Antiochus was involved in other wars on his side of the Euphrates, and made an expedition to Persia which turned out badly for him. His intention was to surprise the city of Elymais, or Persepolis, to take from there the riches which were said to have been dedicated to one of its Temples by Alexander <note>Alexander the Great.</note>, and were held to be of an invaluable price. But the inhabitants of that magnificent city, informed of the march and design of Antiochus, had [prepared] themselves...

Persecutors of the Church a remarkable example of despair, to which God abandons such fierce enemies of His truth; who, after having unmercifully oppressed His people, closed or demolished God's Temples, and halted the public service which His faithful worshippers perform for Him, would willingly, in the hour of their death, buy off the violence committed by them with all their blood. The Christian Church has seen a multitude of similar examples, such as that of the cruel Antiochus in his death. Lactantius <note>Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325), an early Christian author who wrote "De Mortibus Persecutorum" (On the Deaths of the Persecutors).</note> composed an entire booklet in the third century regarding the miserable death of the Persecutors. The following centuries have provided only too much material to increase the account which that wise and godly writer made thereof nearly fourteen centuries ago. Each century, one more, another less, adds new examples to it. But even if God permits at all times that new "Antiochuses" rise up against His Church, He Himself will be the comfort and strength of the persecuted Believers in all ages of the world, and until the end of time; and according to His promise, He will always prevent the gates of Hell from prevailing against His Church.

The Kings of Syria were very powerful, and because their Empire extended very far, it was not difficult for them to bring large armies into the field. The matter was of the utmost consequence for **Antiochus Eupator** <note>The young son of Antiochus Epiphanes, reigning under the regency of Lysias.</note>; it concerned an entire Kingdom, and he saw well that if he gave the Jews time to strengthen themselves, it would later fall very hard upon him to bring them under subjection. He then gathered, both from his own lands and from those of neighboring Princes, an army of one hundred thousand men on foot, and twenty thousand on horseback, to which he further added thirty-two **Elephants** equipped for war, each of which carried a tower or castle on its back, containing about thirty men who shot with bows. The mere sight of these animals brought terror to the troops; they were armored with copper plates, and the master who sat upon them governed them so skillfully that they moved between the battle lines, where each was followed by a thousand footmen and five hundred horsemen. All of this made a terrible noise, and one can imagine what kind of disorder could be caused in an army that was much smaller in number by thirty-two such Elephants, supported by nearly fifty thousand men, when they came charging from many sides at once and made various attacks. With these thoughts, and full of courage, he pierced through the great troop of cavalry and infantry that surrounded the Elephant and served as a bulwark, and he killed to the right and to the left everything that stood in his way. Thus he came like a bolt of lightning to the Elephant, and because he could strike it nowhere that it was not covered with iron armor, he went beneath the belly of the animal and thrust his dagger into it. The Elephant falls upon receiving that stab and crashes to the earth before **Eleazar** had time to move out from under it; thus he perished, crushed under the overwhelming weight of such a hideous beast, which, due to the tower with the men it carried, was as heavy as a mountain. It is not known whether the King was indeed in that tower, but the Historian says that **Judas Maccabeus**, finding himself unable to endure such a fierce and dangerous fight any longer, withdrew with his troops, without the enemy army gaining any other advantage from the retreat than that it was no longer prevented from laying siege to the fortress of **Sion**, which was besieged by the troops of the Maccabees. He also took **Bethsura** and besieged **Jerusalem**; but since provisions began to fail him for such a numerous army as his, because there were few supplies in the land because it was a **Sabbath year** <note>The "Shemitah" or Sabbatical year, during which the land was required to lie fallow according to Mosaic law (Leviticus 25:1-7).</note>, he was forced to march away to prevent the changes that had arisen in Syria during his absence, and he made a covenant with the Jews, according to which he allowed them the exercise of their **Religion** entirely freely.

### 1 Maccabees Chapter 9, verses 37–41.

Antiochus Eupator did not sit long on the throne of Syria; God brought an enemy from Rome who stripped him of that dignity. This was Demetrius, son of Seleucus Philopator, his kinsman, who had been sent as a hostage in place of Antiochus Epiphanes <note>Antiochus Epiphanes had been a hostage in Rome earlier; Demetrius was his nephew and the rightful heir to the throne.</note>. Having fled from there when he understood that Antiochus was dead, Demetrius departed from Rome to make war against the king’s son. Antiochus and Lysias, his General, were taken prisoner—either by their own people or by a party from the army of Demetrius. Demetrius, not wishing to see them, commanded those who brought them to him that they should be killed, which was carried out immediately. Upon his arrival in Syria, several ungodly Jews who had forsaken their religion came to him, along with Alcimus, and requested the High Priesthood for that wicked man, who was not even of priestly descent. Demetrius granted him that illustrious office as a reward for the vile services he had rendered and the malicious report he had given regarding the state of affairs in Judea; for he, with other dishonorable men in his retinue, had given the king a poisonous account full of hateful exaggerations and falsehoods. Demetrius sent Bacchides, one of the principal lords of his court in whom he placed complete trust, to that region and gave him the governorship of the province. When Bacchides arrived in the land, he drew several persons of distinction to himself under a false pretense of entering into a treaty; but he broke his 

<column-break/>

word immediately and put as many as sixty of them to death in a single day. This treachery showed the whole world what was to be expected from a man who began his rule with such an exceptionally wicked act. His affairs soon called him back to the King, and he left Alcimus in his place. This villain strove to secure the High Priesthood, which the Jews were by no means willing to allow him; and seeing that he would never achieve his goal as long as Judas Maccabeus was so powerful, he went to King Demetrius to voice his complaints. Demetrius sent Nicanor, one of his Generals and a sworn enemy of the Jews, to hew them all to pieces. Nicanor attempted to surprise Judas and his brothers through crafty proposals; but Judas the Maccabee, having perceived that it was a snare <term>snare: a trap or trick intended to catch an enemy off guard</term> which Nicanor had set for them, wisely withdrew and subsequently took the necessary precautions for his safety. Nicanor, seeing that craft and deceit had not succeeded, resorted to arms; but his troops were defeated, and he himself was killed in the battle. Judas Maccabeus, finding no security for his country—which had become the stage for the persecutions of the Kings of Syria—placed himself under the protection of the Romans. They, following their old custom of never refusing friendship or alliance to any people, made a treaty with the Jews. Nevertheless, Demetrius did not cease to pursue the war against Judea; he sent Bacchides and Alcimus back there with a large military force. Having arrived in the land of Judah, they marched straight toward the Maccabees; however, the army of the latter was so small in comparison to the enemy’s that most lost their courage, such that the army of Israel scattered in all directions, and only eight hundred men remained. The enemies, wishing to take advantage of this dispersion, pressed the others to fight; and Judas, considering that he could not avoid this...

With these thoughts, and full of courage, he pierced through the great troop of cavalry and infantry surrounding the Elephant, which served as a bulwark, and he killed to the right and the left everything that stood in his way. Thus he came like a lightning bolt to the Elephant, and because he could hit him nowhere that was not covered with iron armor, he went under the belly of the animal and thrust his dagger into it. The Elephant fell upon receiving that stab and crashed to the earth before Eleazar had time to get out from under it; thus he died crushed under the overwhelming weight of such a monstrous beast, which, because of the tower with people it carried, was as heavy as a mountain. It is not known whether the King was indeed in that tower, but the Historian says that Judas Maccabeus, finding himself unable to sustain such a fierce and dangerous fight any longer, withdrew with his bands, without the enemy army gaining any other advantage from the retreat than that it was no longer prevented from laying siege to the fortress of Sion <note>This refers to the Acra, the Syrian-held citadel in Jerusalem, which the Jews had been besieging.</note>, which was besieged by the bands of the Maccabees. He <note>Antiochus Eupator</note> also took Beth-zur and besieged Jerusalem; but as provisions began to fail him for such a numerous army as his, since there was little supply in the land because it was a Sabbatical year <note>Every seventh year, the land was left fallow according to Jewish law, meaning no crops were harvested.</note>, he was forced to depart to prevent the changes that had arisen in Syria during his absence, and he made a covenant with the Jews, according to which he left them entirely free to practice their religion.

<summary>This page describes the Battle of Beth Zechariah, where the Syrian King Antiochus Eupator deployed war elephants against the forces of Judas Maccabeus. It highlights the heroic but fatal action of Eleazar Auran, who crushed himself beneath an elephant to slay it, and the subsequent peace treaty that restored Jewish religious freedom due to a Sabbatical year famine.</summary>
