## **I. Maccabees Chapter IX. verses 37—41.**

Antiochus Eupator did not sit long upon the throne of Syria; God caused an enemy to come from Rome who stripped him of that dignity. This was Demetrius, son of Seleucus Philopator, his kinsman, who, having been sent as a hostage in place of Antiochus Epiphanes (who had fled from there), departed from Rome when he understood that Antiochus had died, in order to wage war against his son. Antiochus and Lysias, his Commander-in-Chief, were taken prisoner, either by their own people or by a party from the army of Demetrius; the latter, not wishing to see them, commanded those who brought them to him that they should be killed, which was carried out immediately. Upon his arrival in Syria, several godless Jews who had forsaken their religion <note>These "godless Jews" were the Hellenizing faction who sought to integrate Greek customs into Jewish life, often at the expense of traditional law.</note> came to him along with Alcimus, and requested the High Priesthood for that wicked man, who was not even of priestly descent. Demetrius granted him that illustrious office as a reward for the foul services he had rendered him and the malicious report he had given regarding the state of affairs in Judea; for he, with other dishonorable men in his retinue, had given him a poisonous account full of hateful exaggerations and falsehoods. Demetrius sent Bacchides, one of the primary Lords of his Court in whom he placed total confidence, thither, and gave him the governorship of that province. When Bacchides had entered the land, he drew several persons of distinction to himself under a false pretense of entering into a treaty; but he broke his

<column-break/>

word immediately and caused some sixty of them to die in a single day. This treachery showed the whole world what was to be expected from a man who began his reign with such an exceedingly wicked deed. His affairs called him back to the King, and he left Alcimus in his place. This villain strove to secure the High Priesthood, which the Jews would by no means grant him; and seeing that he would never achieve his aim as long as Judas Maccabeus was so powerful, he went to King Demetrius to make his complaint. Demetrius sent Nicanor, one of his Generals and a sworn enemy of the Jews, to hew them all into pieces. Nicanor attempted to surprise Judas and his brothers through cunning propositions; but Judas the Maccabee, having perceived that it was a snare <note>The "snare" refers to Nicanor's attempt to capture Judas during a peaceful parley.</note> Nicanor had set for them, wisely withdrew and subsequently took the necessary precautions for his safety. Nicanor, seeing that his trickery and deceit had not succeeded, resorted to arms; but his troops were defeated, and he himself was killed in the battle. Judas Maccabeus, finding no security for his land, which had become the stage for the persecutions of the Kings of Syria, placed himself under the protection of the Romans, who, according to their old custom of never refusing their friendship and alliance to any people, made a treaty with the Jews. <note>This was the first formal diplomatic contact between the Maccabean state and the Roman Republic, intended to deter Syrian aggression.</note> Demetrius did not, however, cease to pursue the war against Judea; he sent Bacchides and Alcimus there again with a great military force. Having arrived in the land of Judah, they marched straight toward the Maccabees; yet the army of the latter was so small in comparison to the enemy's that most lost their courage, such that the army of Israel scattered in all directions, and no more than eight hundred men remained. The enemies, wishing to take advantage of this dispersal, pressured the others to fight, and Judas, judging that he could not avoid

[Judas], who could not [retreat] without staining his reputation with a blemish, risked the battle. The situation immediately turned in his favor; he broke through the right wing of the enemy, over which Bacchides <note>A Syrian general and governor under King Demetrius I Soter.</note> commanded, and drove them so far away that they could not recover. But Alcimus <note>An apostate Jew and Syrian-appointed High Priest who opposed the Maccabees.</note>, who was with the left wing, fell upon the Jews and attacked them from behind. The fight was fierce on both sides, and after having lasted from morning until evening, it ended with the death of the brave and undaunted Judas Maccabeus, whose loss was followed by the loss of the battle. All the people wept bitterly and bestowed the office of Commander-in-Chief upon Jonathan, brother of Judas, who had also acquitted himself bravely in all those wars. Since the army had to be regrouped before they dared appear before the enemy, Jonathan and his brother Simon, followed by all those who were with them, retreated to the wilderness near Lake Asphalti-
<column-break/>
-tes, or the Lake of Sodom <note>Better known today as the Dead Sea; "Asphaltites" refers to the bitumen (asphalt) that often surfaced there.</note>; and meanwhile, they charged their brother John to request the Nabateans <note>An Arab people of the Levant, often allies of the Maccabees.</note>, their friends, that they might leave their baggage, which was extensive, with them. The children of Ambri <note>Also known as the sons of Jambri, a desert tribe.</note>, having obtained knowledge of this, ambushed John on the road, seized all the baggage, and took his life. A few days later, Jonathan and Simon heard that a great wedding was being prepared in the house of Ambri for a marriage to a daughter of one of the prominent lords of the land of Canaan. The Maccabees then laid an ambush behind a mountain, and while the procession of that great wedding passed by, they attacked them and killed many people. The rest fled to the mountains, everything was taken as loot, and the wedding of the children of Ambri was thus turned into mourning, and their music into lamentations.

## Simon erects a very magnificent tomb for his brother Jonathan.

### 1 Maccabees Chapter 13. verses 25—30.

A son of Antiochus, who was named Alexander <note>Alexander Balas, a pretender who claimed to be the son of Antiochus IV Epiphanes.</note>, could not endure that Demetrius had made himself master of the Kingdom of Syria, of which he said he was the heir, and therefore attempted to regain it by force of arms. Demetrius, therefore, sought to enter into an alliance with the Jews, since he could not again enter into war against them without risking the loss of all his lands. Alexander, for his part, also did everything possible to win the Jews to his side. Thus, the Jews saw the throne seeking their favor through two Princes, each of whom would have sought their destruction if the one had not been in the other's way. They chose the alliance with Alexander over that of Demetrius;
<column-break/>
but while these two rivals disputed the crown with each other, Jonathan improved Jerusalem and rebuilt the walls of Zion. The beginnings of this war were fortunate for Alexander, who defeated Demetrius in the first battle. Ptolemy <note>Ptolemy VI Philometor.</note>, King of Egypt, involved himself in this war, and after having given his daughter in marriage to Alexander, he took her back from him along with the Kingdom; but having died a few years later, Demetrius made himself powerful in Judea. God allowed, however, that he was more favorable to the Jews than before. Jonathan went to visit him now with a large embassy at Ptolemais <note>The coastal city of Acre.</note>, where he had arrived. The King received him favorably and confirmed him in the High Priesthood, which office he served, and Demetrius restored to Judea its liberties and privileges, provided that three hundred talents of silver were given to him annually as an acknowledgment; but not long after, he broke his word and became an enemy of the Jews, despite the great services which— <note>original: "wel-" / catchword: "ke" (which)</note>

...with orders to the High Priest and the other Priests to deliver that money to him, so that it might be brought to Syria. Everyone was distressed, seeing that Seleucus <note>Seleucus IV Philopator, ruler of the Seleucid Empire from 187 to 175 BCE.</note> wished to make himself master of the sacred treasures. Onias the High Priest <note>Onias III, known for his piety and opposition to the Hellenization of Judea.</note> seemed even more moved by this than all the others, and the heartache he felt was so clearly depicted on his face that it was capable of inspiring sadness even in those least sensitive to this misfortune; for he saw the consequences of it better than anyone else, and was more concerned with the disasters facing his people. He presented Heliodorus with every argument he could to turn him from his intention, and to move him to represent to the King the reasons the Jews had for not surrendering those treasures, the greatest part of which had been entrusted to the Priests by private individuals <note>The Temple acted as a sort of bank for widows and orphans, keeping their savings safe under religious protection.</note>. But greed, when armed with absolute power, cannot be stopped by any reasons. Heliodorus insisted, come what may, on carrying out the orders he had brought; and Onias and the other Priests could do nothing more to preserve the sacred treasures than to pour out tears and prayers at God's feet in His Sanctuary. Heliodorus arrived with his soldiers,

<column-break/>

and intended to force open the door of the place where the treasure chest was kept. There was no one who stood against his orders, and they expected nothing else than to see all those riches taken away by the hands of those wicked men. But immediately there appeared a horse, upon which sat a terrifying man clothed in golden armor; and the horse, attacking Heliodorus with a charge, struck him with its front hooves; at the same time, two young men appeared, shining with glory, who, flanking Heliodorus, struck him incessantly with rods. Heliodorus fell suddenly to the ground, entirely overcome by darkness; he was picked up and placed in a litter, and carried out of the Temple. Some of his friends ran to Onias to beg him to pray for his life. The High Priest prayed for him, and while he prayed, the two Angels <note>original: "Engelen"</note> appeared again before Heliodorus and told him that he should thank the High Priest Onias, because it was through his prayer that he had regained his life. By this means the treasures of the Temple were preserved, and the Priesthood of Onias was made very illustrious.

### 2 Maccabees Chapter 5, verses 2, 3.

<margin>2 Maccabees 5:1</margin>
Under the reign of Antiochus <note>Antiochus IV Epiphanes, the successor of Seleucus, whose reign was marked by severe persecution of the Jews.</note>, not long after that Prince had ascended the throne of Syria, there were seen for forty days above the city of Jerusalem riders in the sky, riding in troops, dressed in golden robes and armed with spears; they were set in battle formation, charging and fighting against one another; one saw the clashing of shields, the shooting of arrows, the flickering of naked swords, the shining of hel-

<column-break/>

mets and breastplates, and everything that one was accustomed to seeing in battles according to the custom of those times. Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century historian whose works are vital for understanding Jewish history under Roman rule.</note> relates in his book *The Jewish War* <note>original: "Joodfche Oorlogen"</note> that in his time armies and other such signs also appeared in the sky as omens of the war which the Romans waged in Judea shortly thereafter, and of the disasters with which God threatened the Jews. The persecutions which Antiochus Epiphanes prepared for this people were so terrible, and had such a deadly aftermath, that it could well be that God had wanted to warn the Jews of them through these signs. He had even had them foretold more than three hundred years earlier by the pen of Daniel <note>A reference to the prophecies in the Book of Daniel concerning the "vile person" and the desecration of the sanctuary.</note>; but they had

<meta>This page continues the discussion of divine warnings and the onset of the persecution of the Jews under the Seleucid King Antiochus IV Epiphanes, following the failed attempt by Heliodorus to plunder the Temple.</meta>

# HISTORY of the O. TESTAMENT.

...did not pay attention to those prophecies. There then had to be something more vivid and visible to wake them from the carelessness into which man naturally falls. Such predictions and signs are not intended to prevent the events they signify; rather, they are like sketches of future things which God sets before the eyes of the Believers beforehand. These are sketches which His wise and almighty hand has drawn according to the Principal <note>In this context, the 'Principal' refers to the actual historical event or the divine reality that the 'sketch' or sign is foreshadowing.</note> that is to come, and according to the design He has made in His decrees. But when those events are once [established] in the eternal and unchange-

<column-break/>

-able council of God's purpose, they cannot fail to happen in the same way, and in all their circumstances, as they have been decided. The purpose, then, of such miraculous signs—which depict history before the eyes of men, just as prophecies first imagined them to the mind—is that the people whom God threatens with His judgments might reflect in advance upon the crimes that provoke God's wrath against them; and that through a deep humiliation <note>This refers to 'humility' or 'abasement'—a formal act of repentance before God to seek mercy.</note>, they might cause the effects of His vengeance to be beneficial to them.

### II. Machabees Chapter VI. verse 18. etc. <note>The original Dutch text labels this as the 'III' book, but the reference and story belong to 2 Maccabees.</note>

The persecutions of Antiochus <note>Antiochus IV Epiphanes, the Seleucid king who attempted to suppress Jewish religious laws.</note> against the Jews were not of a single kind; he sought to uproot their religion by desecrating the Temple, breaking the altars, and causing public worship to cease. But he was not yet satisfied with that; he also wanted to stifle religion within their hearts and bring the Jews to violate the laws of their fathers. He found in them an insurmountable aversion to eating pork, because the Law <note>The Mosaic Law (Leviticus 11) strictly prohibited the consumption of swine.</note> forbade it to them. Antiochus therefore resolved to force them to it; and when the executors of his cruelties could not move the persons they addressed to eat those forbidden foods voluntarily, they thrust the same into their mouths by force, to have the malicious pleasure of tormenting them through that contact—which, however, was no sin for the Jews, because their hearts had no part in it, but rather held a holy horror for

<column-break/>

the same. Among those who on that occasion gave outstanding examples of their steadfastness was a venerable old man named Eleazar, a Teacher of the Law, whose zeal served as a blessing to the entire Church. He was urged by every conceivable means to eat pork, but he refused very strongly. The violence was redoubled; and he became all the firmer in his resolve to show his indignation against the urgent request made of him. He was told that death would be the punishment for his disobedience: he chose it, without even a second thought, rather than the crime which was demanded of him, and he went at the same time to the place of torture as a voluntary sacrifice <note>original: "vrywillyg flagtóffer"</note>, without waiting until he was dragged there. When he went there with a steadfastness that amazed his persecutors, he was addressed along the way by some Jews who were his friends, and who—through a sinful compliance—believed that one should adapt to the times and take a middle path between the laws of God and the King's command, by pretending as if one were eating the forbidden food. They spoke to him to persuade him to allow clean meat, prepared by himself beforehand, to be brought to him to eat, and that he should meanwhile feign as if he were eating from the King's sacrifices

<meta>This page continues the narrative of the Jewish resistance to the Hellenistic persecution led by Antiochus IV Epiphanes. It specifically follows the story of Eleazar, an elderly scribe who has just been pressured to eat forbidden meat and offered a chance to fake his compliance to save his life.</meta>

# HISTORY of the O. TESTAMENT.

...the intent that the people would believe that he, in order to save his life, had eaten of the defiled foods <note>Original: "verontreynigde spyzen." This refers to pork or meat sacrificed to Greek idols, which was forbidden under Jewish dietary laws.</note>. But this holy man rejected this cunning proposal as a temptation from the Devil. He saw immediately that it was not enough to be innocent before God if one gave pretexts for scandal to others; and he preferred to die rather than give offense to his brothers, or to hide himself under a sidelong deviation <note>An indirect way of avoiding the law through deception or a loophole.</note> which is viewed by an upright and pure mind as a betrayal of the truth. He declared that it would be too high a price to pay for a few years of life, to buy them at the cost of the edifying example which one owes to one's brothers. Therefore, he remained unyielding to the end against everything his so-called friends might propose to him. But we must hear him speak for himself. *“It does not benefit our old age,” he said, “to pretend, lest many young people, thinking that Eleazar—now being ninety years old—had gone over to Heathenism, should also be misled by me because of this pretense of mine and because of this short and fleeting span of life; and that I should thus bring a curse and a stain upon my old age. For even if I were to be delivered from the punishment of men for the present, I would still not escape—neither living nor dying—the hands of the Almighty.”* The rage of the persecutors, which for that short moment had shown a feigned and deceptive gentleness, came upon hearing these words with greater violence

<column-break/>

welling up again than before. They brought Eleazar forth to the place of punishment, and this holy Martyr left in the hands of the executioners the remains of a body made of dust and clay, while his soul, which only parted from it for a time, went to take possession in Heaven of a life full of glory and blessedness. As long as the Church <note>The author uses the word "Kerk" (Church) to describe the community of the faithful in the Old Testament, applying Christian terminology to Jewish history.</note> shall see persecutors, God's children—who rejoice that they suffer for His name—will find false friends everywhere, like those of Eleazar, who, not knowing what noble feelings of godliness are, nor wherein the simplicity of true zeal consists, will advise those heavenly souls to do what they themselves feel in their hearts of flesh and earth. Through worldly insights and the deceits of the ancient serpent <note>A common biblical reference to the Devil.</note>, they will try to move the Believers to conceal their true convictions and hide them from their persecutors, who often show that they are quite willing to be deceived. But the example of Eleazar, which is deemed worthy through all the Laws of the Gospel and the commandments of Jesus Christ, should always be kept before the eyes of true believers in similar occurrences; and the honor of suffering martyrdom for matters that are in themselves of a thousand times more importance than those for which the aged Eleazar went to his execution, shall be in all ages of the Church a powerful motivation for those whom God has called to this test, to glorify Him through their sufferings.

Following the martyrdom of the elderly scribe Eleazar, the narrative now shifts to the famous story of the seven brothers and their mother, as recorded in 2 Maccabees and historically attributed to the "Jewish Historian" (Josephus) in the work known as 4 Maccabees.</meta>

# HISTORY of the O. TESTAMENT.

...sealed their zeal and faithfulness to God’s laws with their blood. The persecutors wished to force this family to eat pork, but neither their tricks nor their threats could have any effect on them. Seeing the great unity in their sentiments and in their speech, one would have said that one and the same heart animated them all, and that the spirit of the mother had passed into her seven sons along with the blood from which they were formerly formed in her womb. But their feelings had a higher origin than that earthly birth, and the mother and her sons were all guided by one and the same spirit, which was the one God had given them. The Writer of the second book of the Maccabees has nothing more excellent than this history, which is not only confirmed by the famous Jewish Historian <note>This likely refers to Flavius Josephus, to whom the work "4 Maccabees" (a philosophical discourse on the martyrdom of these brothers) was traditionally but incorrectly attributed.</note>, who wrote an entire separate treatise on it, but it is also believed, and with reason, that this is the wonderful history which the Apostle Paul had in mind when, in his Epistle to the Hebrews, speaking of various Martyrs, he said:

> Others were tortured <note>original: "uytgerekt geworden," literally "stretched out," referring to the rack.</note>, not accepting the offered release, so that they might obtain a better resurrection.

Upon the refusal which the mother and her seven sons gave the King to eat pork, Antiochus ordered that they should be scourged; this was but a beginning of the punishment. Their bodies were thereafter miserably carved by lashings with sinews or straps of ox-hide; but these pains served only to stir up their zeal all the more, and to make them say with greater boldness than ever that they would much rather die than violate the Laws of God. The King, angered by that answer, ordered that the tongue of the one who had spoken first should be cut out, and the extremities of his hands and feet be lopped off, in the sight of his brothers. After he had been thus maimed, he ordered that he should be fried in a glowing pan, which stood ready there on the fire, while he was still alive. All his brothers beheld this cruel punishment with as little dismay as if they had been insensible, and they instead encouraged one another and their mother to die steadfastly. From the first, they proceeded to the second, who offered himself for punishment with the same intrepidity as his brother, saying to the King with his final breath these excellent words:

> You villain, you may take the present life from us, but the King of the world shall raise us up, who die for his laws, unto an eternal resurrection of life.

Yet these words made no impression at all on Antiochus, and this holy Martyr died by the same punishment as his brother. After him came the third; they demanded his tongue to cut it off, and he offered it immediately, saying with a boldness that filled all the bystanders with wonder:

> All my limbs I have received from Heaven, and I despise them for the sake of God’s laws, hoping that I shall receive the same back from Him.

Next they took the fourth, who, full of comfort and hope, turning to this cruel King—who had the dishonorable curiosity to wish to be present at this punishment—addressed him thus:

> It is better to exchange the hope that is of men and to wait for the hope that is of God, to be raised up again by Him; but for you there shall be no resurrection to life.

The fifth was treated like the four pre-

<column-break/>

ceding ones, and in the midst of his pains he said to the King:

> You have power among men, and although you are mortal, yet you do what you will: but do not imagine that our race is forsaken by God. Just wait, and you shall behold God’s great power, how he will torment you and your offspring.

The sixth, who was delivered over to the same torments, said:

> Do not wander in vain; for we suffer these things for our own sake, because we have sinned against our God; however, things have happened to us that are worthy of wonder. But you, do not imagine that you shall be innocent, since you have undertaken to fight against God.

The mother of these holy Martyrs was present at all their punishments, and far from requesting any mercy from the Tyrant out of compassion, or advising her children to have any regard for their own lives or her own, she encouraged them to remain steadfast until their last breath. When the King saw that no one remained but her and the last of her sons, he attempted to win him over with flattering promises: but this youth showed nothing but a disdain for the King’s flatteries. The Tyrant, thus rebuffed and ashamed that he was disappointed in his aim, addressed the mother, proposing to her that she should at least protect this son, the only one of the seven remaining to her, by exhorting him to obey his commands. The mother, on the contrary, gave her dear child very lively and emphatic exhortations to follow the example of his brothers; and this lad then addressed Antiochus with the most powerful words to make him have an abhorrence of his cruelties. But the Prince, forsaken by God and delivered over to the spirit of persecution, doubled his gruesome rage against this Martyr. He ended this bloody day’s work with the death of the mother, who by her steadfastness and zeal completed that holy glory with which her entire family had been crowned that day by the hands of the executioners; leaving thus to the Church the greatest example of perseverance and love for God’s laws that has ever been seen in the world.

The third book of the Maccabees is a History of the persecutions which the Jews in Egypt suffered under the reign of Ptolemy Philopator, forty or fifty years before those which Antiochus Epiphanes caused in Judea. This book ought then to have preceded, but under a different title than that of Maccabees, because those illustrious Jews, of whom Judas was the first to bear this name, did not take that surname until long after the events related in this book. Ptolemy, nicknamed out of mockery, or by irony <note>original: "tegenwaarheyd," meaning a contradiction or antiphrasis.</note>, Philopator or "Father-lover" because he had killed his father, reigned in Egypt. He waged war against Antiochus the Great, King of Syria and father of the cruel Antiochus, whom he defeated in a pitched battle where those two Kings even fought in person. After this great victory, Ptolemy received embassies from all sides, and the Jews as well as other nations who were under the Kings of Syria also sent him a delegation. This victorious Prince, praised by everyone and tickling himself with his own fame, wished to see Judea for once, and especially the city of Jerusalem, famous in the East for many centuries. Arriving there, he performed thank-offerings for his...

It was presented to him that the most remote part of the Temple, before which a purple curtain with various embroidery always hung, was inaccessible to all persons, even to the Priests themselves, and that no one but the High Priest alone might enter there once a year. In contrast, He never abandons or surrenders His Church—the true House of the living God, the pillar and support of the truth—to her enemies; for in all ages it has been seen that He has performed astonishing miracles for her to prevent her downfall.

# P R E F A C E .

It would detain the reader far too long with this preface if we were to point out everything here that deserves deep consideration in the life of Jesus Christ. We shall say nothing then of His death, because too much would have to be said if one were to delve into that subject. It will be enough to admonish the Christian reader that, in order to profit from reading the History of the New Testament, he must never separate it from that of the Old. The New is entirely in the Old; and the Old is brought forth again, so to speak, and completed by the New, which in reality is nothing but a fulfillment of the first, and a history of the events that were pointed out in the prophecies of the Prophets. The books of the Jews are those of the Christians; and would to God that the books of the Christians were also those of the Jews! They shall, however, be one day; their Prophets have foretold it to them, and our Apostles have confirmed it: Israel shall remain stubborn and unbelieving, according to the words of the Apostle Paul, until the fullness of the Gentiles <note>A reference to Romans 11:25-26 regarding the "fullness of the Gentiles" and the salvation of Israel.</note>, whom God wishes to save, shall have entered into the Church; but then all Israel shall be saved; and God will forgive them their rebelliousness, just as He has forgiven the Gentiles their idolatry. Meanwhile, we see these poor people, formerly the sole object of God's love, but for more than sixteen hundred years <note>This indicates the text was likely written in the late 17th or early 18th century, calculating from the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 AD.</note> the object of His wrath, miserably passing their days between life and death—a people who have not perished in their dispersion, because God preserves them to one day in...

### The Evangelist Matthew.

Before we begin the History of the Gospel, and proceed to the account of the most remarkable deeds contained therein, we have deemed it useful first to give a sketch here of the divine Writers, who have left us these histories in writing. One finds four who applied themselves to this holy work, and therefore bear the name of Evangelists, namely Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Two of these four, Matthew and John, were Apostles; concerning the other two, they were either from the number of those who accompanied Jesus Christ with the twelve Apostles, as some of the Ancients <note>original: "Aalouden," referring to the early Church Fathers</note> have believed, or they were at least among the first who were converted by their preaching, and whom God filled with such an abundance of His grace, that they could rightly be called, as has been done, Apostles of the second rank.

Matthew, otherwise called Levi, was a Tax Collector <note>original: "Tóllenaar," a publican who collected taxes for the Roman authorities</note> in Capernaum, where the Lord, having encountered him one day while passing by the Custom House, commanded him to leave his office and follow Him; which Levi did with a readiness and joy that came from a higher hand than the word of a man; for his eyes saw nothing but a man who spoke to him, but his heart felt that it was God's word. From that day he was constantly with Jesus; he heard him preach in Judea and in Galilee; he saw him perform all his miracles; he was with him when they captured him in the garden of Gethsemane; and if sorrow or fear had allowed him to follow Christ even to Mount Calvary, he would have seen him die on the cross, just as he saw him resurrected again three days later. He received, like the other

<column-break/>

Apostles, the Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost; and he preached, as well as they, the Gospel which he has left us in writing. This is all that we know of it with certainty. Tradition has wanted to go even further, and name the time and place in which Matthew would have described his Gospel; but if one considers with a little attention what is said thereof, one finds no firm ground for it. Still less stability is there in what is added further, that this Evangelist wrote his book in Hebrew. Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the scholar famous for the Latin Vulgate translation</note> indeed relates that he had seen it in that language, which was a "new Hebrew" <note>likely referring to Aramaic, the vernacular of the time</note> such as was spoken in the time of the Apostles; but why could the same not have been a translation for the use of the peoples who spoke that language? This Gospel is currently still had in Hebrew, whether this be the same that Jerome had seen, or another; but all the world agrees therein that it is nothing but a translation, like the Syriac, the Arabic, and a hundred others. It is not well conceivable that God would have allowed the Original Text of such a remarkable book to be lost, and nothing but a translation thereof to remain for us. Greek is the language of the New Testament; it is that in which all the Apostles wrote, even those who, like Peter, were properly Apostles of the Jews; and that also when they wrote directly to the Jews, as Peter did in his two Epistles, and Paul in that to the Hebrews. Would Matthew then have had a greater reason than all the other Apostles, especially those two, in the three Epistles which they addressed to the Jews, to write his Gospel in their language? But this dispute has already detained us too long; if one were to accept as true everything that Tradition—bold in inventing, and often little enlightened regarding such subjects—has dared to spread, which lie buried in a deep antiquity,

## The Evangelist Matthew.

Before we begin the History of the Gospel, and proceed to the account of the most remarkable deeds contained therein, we have judged it useful to first give here a sketch of the divine Authors, who have left us these histories in writing. One finds four who devoted themselves to this holy work, and therefore bear the name of Evangelists, namely Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Two of these four, Matthew and John, were Apostles: regarding the other two, they were either of the number of those who accompanied Jesus Christ along with the twelve Apostles, as some of the Ancients <note>The "Ancients" refers to the Church Fathers and early Christian writers.</note> believed, or they were at least among the first who were converted by their preaching, and whom God filled with such an abundance of His grace that one could rightly call them, as has been done, Apostles of the second rank.

HISTORY of the NEW TESTAMENT.

one would need a measure of gullibility, which reason would not always find satisfying.

Matthew begins his Gospel with the genealogy of Jesus, and moves swiftly from his birth to his preaching ministry, which Jesus did not begin before the thirtieth year of his age; for until that time he had lived as a private citizen <term>private citizen: an "ampteloos persoon" refers to someone not holding a public office or religious position.</term>, remaining in Nazareth in the lowly state of a carpenter's household, until the time destined in God’s Council had come to begin that great service: he was introduced into it by the baptism he received from John the Baptist, and he ended the same in the middle of the fourth year, which was the thirty-third of his life.

But in those three and a half years, which the History of the Gospel contains, there was nothing but preachings and miracles throughout the entire land of Judea, and that of Galilee.

Matthew related some of these, which are also found in Mark and Luke; John, who wrote last, adds many others, and he assures us that Jesus Christ spoke and did so many great and divine things, that if one had wanted to relate them all, the world would have been filled with the books that would have been written about them. <note>original: "de waereld vervuld zoude geweest zyn van de boeken" — a reference to the hyperbole in John 21:25.</note>

<column-break/>

Nevertheless, one clearly sees from this short account that Jesus is both the Messiah and God’s Son. The first truth appears everywhere in this Gospel, where, when one examines it thoroughly, one perceives an exact similarity and agreement until the very end, between the person and deeds of Jesus Christ and the nearly innumerable Oracles <note>Oracles: Here referring to the Old Testament prophecies.</note>, which for four thousand years had not ceased, each through some particular trait, to depict and signify him.

To this first truth, which presents itself to us naturally and, so to speak, without one searching for it, in the simple narrative of the History of Jesus Christ, one finds that other doctrine, the foundation of salvation: that Jesus is the Son of God, joined by a necessary bond.

This divine truth is seen shining everywhere in this Gospel; and from the first chapter, where we read that *Jesus would save his people from their sins*; and that he would be an *Emmanuel*, God and man, until the last where we see him worshipped by his Disciples, while he commands them to baptize in his name, as well as in that of the Father and the Holy Spirit; everywhere we find that Jesus *is God*, just as we everywhere find that he is the *Messiah*.

### The Evangelist Mark.

Regarding the person of this Evangelist, nothing is held with absolute certainty, to know whether it was the same Mark spoken of in the twelfth chapter of the Acts of the Apostles, and whom Paul, in the Epistle to the Colossians, says was the cousin of Barnabas; or another, whom Peter, at the end of his first Epistle, calls his son. Tradition <note>Tradition: Referring to "Overlévering," the historical accounts of the early Church not found in the Bible.</note> holds that it was this latter one, but this Tradition wavers so unsteadily in everything, that one can

<column-break/>

rely on it with no certainty.

Thus, it also grossly contradicts itself regarding the time in which it claims Mark wrote his Gospel. Sometimes it tells us, on the testimony of Clement of Alexandria <note>Clement of Alexandria (c. 150–215 AD) was a prominent theologian and teacher in the early Church.</note>, a dignified and very ancient writer, that this Evangelist wrote during the life of Peter, whose beloved disciple and faithful traveling companion he was; and at another time it claims, believing Irenaeus <note>Irenaeus (c. 130–202 AD) was a Greek bishop known for his role in guiding and expanding Christian communities.</note>—even older than Clement and of greater name—that it was not until after the death of Peter and Paul that Mark gave this precious gift to the Church.

But these are all matters of little importance, which have fallen from our pen rather than us judging them worthy of a place in this

# HISTORY of the N. TESTAMENT.

to find in this work, where we have intended nothing but the edification of the Christian reader. It is enough, then, that one knows that the Gospel which bears the name of Mark, as well as the three others, is a product of the Holy Spirit, who guided the hand and pen of this Evangelist. This alone is what constitutes the excellence of the Holy Books and gives them the authority they possess to subject our faith to them, and not the names of their authors, however famous they may have been in the Church. In regards to the language in which Mark wrote, the earliest antiquity <note>referring to the early Church Fathers and scholars of the first few centuries AD</note> never doubted, nor said otherwise, than that it was Greek. In following centuries, there were some who wished to award that honor to Latin; and because the heart often has certain tender interests that involve the mind in its cause, people have been found who, after that fanciful dream, wished to make a history of it and present it as truth.

Since it is likely that Mark did not write his Gospel until that of Matthew, and probably that of Luke, had already seen the light, he did not—as the first two did—recount the genealogy of Jesus Christ. What they had written was sufficient to show that Jesus, the son of Mary, was truly descended from David, according to the prophecies seen in the Prophets. Therefore, Mark began the History of the Gospel differently than the first two Evangelists, and he chose to have it follow immediately upon the prophecy of Malachi, which closes the gate of the Old

<column-break/>

Testament, as if to link it together with the book of that Prophet. Malachi had ended his prophecy thus:
> *Behold, I send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD. And he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers, lest I come and smite the earth with a curse.* <note>original: Malachi 4:5-6. The author uses the name 'Elias,' the Greek/Latin form of 'Elijah.'</note>

These words clearly signify John the Baptist; thereupon Mark comes five hundred years after Malachi, and linking the fulfillment to the prophecy, he makes it the beginning of his Gospel.
> *The beginning,* he says, *of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God; as it is written in the Prophets: Behold, I send my messenger before your face.* <note>Mark 1:1-2</note>

He continues by speaking briefly of John the Baptist, and then passes over, like Matthew and Luke, to the baptism of Jesus Christ. Furthermore, until the end, he maintains almost the same order as the first, and it seems as if he has done nothing but abridge him—whether that was indeed his intention in many places to expand somewhat more on others, or that the Holy Spirit, who enlightened him with the same understanding as Matthew, often caused him to agree with him, as Micah once did with Isaiah. <note>Micah 4 and Isaiah 2 contain nearly identical passages, a parallel the author uses to explain similarities between Gospels without assuming one simply copied the other.</note> But one need not view Mark as a mere abridger of Matthew, as such does not seem exalted enough for an inspired <term>inspired: "aangeblaazen," literally "breathed into," referring to divine inspiration</term> writer who is himself an original narrator; besides, this opinion is clearly contradicted by a close comparison of one Gospel with the other.

## The Evangelist Luke.

Some have believed that Luke was one of those seventy disciples whom Jesus

<column-break/>

formerly sent out to preach in the cities of Judea; but that opinion is without any foundation. All that is known for certain regarding the person of this Evangelist is that he was from Antioch, the capital of Syria, that he was a physician, and that he accompanied the Apostle Paul,

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Evangelists, moving from the Gospel of Mark to a detailed examination of Luke’s Gospel—specifically its timing, sources, and its unique genealogy of Jesus—before transitioning to the Gospel of John.</meta>

# HISTORY of the N. TESTAMENT.

who <note>The author refers to the Apostle Paul here.</note> in some of his Epistles gives him the praiseworthy title of his fellow laborer, and that he is also the author of the book of the Acts of the Apostles. Everything that tradition adds to this is either very uncertain or evidently false; and in this work, we shall attempt to avoid all such matters. In the arrangement of the Evangelists, Luke has been given the third place, but there is more probability that he ought to have been placed first, if one considers the time in which he might have written his History. It is true, nothing certain can be said about it: but the conjectures one might draw from the Preface or Introduction, which this divine Historian placed at the head of his Gospel, give cause to judge that he wrote before all the others. He says that what induced him to publish this account of the life and death of Jesus Christ was that there were already many books in the world in which these matters were described. If those writings had come from a reliable hand, and if they had been the work of an Apostle, or another such writer whom the Church could have completely trusted, Luke would have—as he gives clearly enough to understand to his noble Theophilus <note>original: "waarden Theophilus." Theophilus, meaning "friend of God," was the person to whom Luke addressed both his Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles.</note>, to whom he dedicates his History—left it at that; which then seems to be clear proof that the Gospels of Matthew and Mark had not yet appeared. But because they were writings mixed with truth and falsehood, as those usually are which are composed from the accounts of private persons and based on traditions that change and multiply by deviating from their origin, Luke did not judge it advisable to leave the Church in danger any longer of mixing truth with lies in matters of such great importance for the faith, such as all those concerning the life, the teaching, and the miracles of Christ. He likewise declares in that short preface that everything he would write in his History, he had heard from the very mouths of the Apostles, who had been eyewitnesses to it. But although this manner of informing himself was entirely through human means, one must nevertheless regard it here as nothing other than subordinate to a much more vivid and certain knowledge than that which the fertility of memory could provide to the mind of this Evangelist. It was then the Holy Spirit who, when he described this History, brought to his mind everything he had understood from the Apostles, and who guided his hand and pen in all truth. Otherwise, Luke would be but a human historian. The Apostles themselves, Matthew and John, who were witnesses of everything they recount, are divine historians

<column-break/>

only because they wrote under the guidance, and as if under the eyes, of the Holy Spirit, just like Moses, Joshua, Samuel, and others in the Old Law <note>The Old Testament</note>, who left us the histories of matters which they themselves had seen and heard, and whose hands were guided by the Holy Spirit, of which they were the instruments.

Luke begins his Gospel, as we have also seen with Mark, with the history of John the Baptist, but he traces it from further back and recounts the most important circumstances. He then comes to the birth of Jesus Christ, regarding which he also informs us of several matters that are found nowhere else, such as, for example, everything he relates of Zechariah and Elizabeth, the sending of the Angel to Mary, and many other things which Matthew contents himself, so it seems, with merely touching upon in passing, possibly because he judged it sufficient that they were already described in a Gospel. These two Evangelists, Matthew and Luke, have each described the genealogy <term>genealogy: a record of ancestry</term> of Jesus Christ, and shown us his descent from David along different lines. Matthew made one of the ancestors of Joseph, who was betrothed to Mary and was publicly known to have sprung from the Royal House of David; for God had so directed it in His wisdom, because although Jesus was not descended from Joseph, Joseph was nevertheless regarded by all men as his father; wherefore it was necessary that he also be from the House of that ancient King of Judah, so that Christ himself could be seen as having sprung from it, even by those who were ignorant of the mystery of his conception in the womb of the blessed Virgin. But because he had to be so in truth, so that the common people would not be misled by a mere appearance, Luke set up the genealogy of the Holy Virgin, who, as well as Joseph, was descended from David, but along different branches: for Joseph was properly only the son-in-law of Heli. In all the rest of this Gospel, one finds in various places almost the same subjects and matters as in Matthew and Mark. The wisdom of the Holy Spirit did not permit the Evangelists to all recount nothing but one and the same things, so that they might not be suspected of having copied one another: but that same wisdom nevertheless willed that they often recounted the very same matters, so that they would not appear to be differing historians, especially in everything concerning the death and the resurrection of Jesus Christ, which being the primary aim of this entire History and that upon which faith is particularly attentive, is recounted by all four Evangelists with the most essential circumstances.

### The Evangelist John

THE extensive remarks which one has been forced to make on the Gospel of Luke oblige us to greatly shorten those concerning John: also, his name is so great and renowned that one may well pass over speaking of his person. Coming then immediately to his Gospel, we shall here repeat what has already been said in another

<column-break/>

place: that John did not write until long after the three other Evangelists. Therefore, he also took an entirely different path than they did, so as not to repeat the same things without necessity, since the Church was sufficiently informed of them, and because the writings of the other holy historians did not need to be confirmed by his, regardless of the great weight of everything that came from the pen of this Apostle, who had had the honor of being the beloved disciple of Jesus

->JOHN<-

...to have been <insert>a witness</insert> of Jesus Christ, and to have followed Him alone even to Mount Calvary. But just as the Lord, speaking of Himself, said that He had a much greater testimony than that of John the Baptist, so too the three Evangelists who had written first all likewise had a much greater testimony than that of the Apostle John, because it was the Holy Spirit Himself who stood surety for their Histories, being the primary Author thereof. The specific reason why John wrote his Gospel was the emerging heresy of Cerinthus and Ebion <note>Cerinthus and Ebion were early Gnostic and Jewish-Christian teachers who argued that Jesus was a mere human and not eternally divine.</note>, and some others who contested the Divinity of Jesus Christ, placing him in the rank of a mere creature—one who was indeed great and excellent in truth, but nevertheless a creature who had a beginning. To dispel this error, which overthrows the entire foundation of the faith, John begins his Gospel with a flight, so to speak, so high that the Church Fathers gave him the name of an Eagle <note>The eagle is the traditional symbol for John because his Gospel "soars" to the heights of theology regarding the divine nature of Christ.</note>. *In the beginning*, he says, *was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things were made by the same, and without the same was not any thing made that was made.* And a bit lower: *The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth.* When one does not see in such a magnificent and lofty eulogy of Jesus Christ a Son

<column-break/>

of God who was with God His Father before creation, who from that time on was God just like His Father, and who created the world just as He did; then it must be because one has sworn to oneself to close one's eyes to the truth, in order to strengthen oneself in error. The entire sequence of this Gospel agrees with this great beginning; everywhere Jesus Christ is called God’s Son and equal to God; and one sees him in various places maintaining against the Jews that he was in the world before Abraham was born; and that he was no blasphemer, or unjust usurper of the Divinity, when he said that God was his own father, and he was God’s son. One also hears him saying to his Father in the sublime prayer which occupies the entire seventeenth Chapter, *that he had the glory with him before the world was:* which clearly indicates a substantial and actual existence, by which Jesus Christ existed before the world, and consequently from all eternity: for according to the language of Scripture, that which was before the world is eternal. John also recounted various conversations and miracles of Christ which are not found in the other Evangelists; and he has thus left in this Divine Book a living and pure light to the Church, which creates the most pleasant joy during this life, and shall shine unto eternity.

In the West, a Commonwealth <note>The Roman Republic.</note> arose which in a short time made itself known and feared in Asia, and the Monarchy of the Greeks—weakened by the divisions made after Alexander’s death—was gradually overwhelmed by the **Romans**, who a few centuries later saw themselves as Masters of the en-

It can sometimes happen through human accidents that someone loses their speech, but no one suspected anything of the kind in the change that had come over Zacharias's tongue; and he himself dispelled those thoughts from the minds of the bystanders, giving them clearly to understand through signs—which were sufficient to remove all suspicion in that regard—that his silence arose from a much higher source than natural causes, and that he had seen a vision. Each man then judged this miracle according to his own understanding; but all were bound to draw from it a good omen for their nation, and believe that God was preparing a great and singular event for them. Zacharias could indeed have made known through writing what had happened to him, but either he had an express command to remain silent, or he wisely judged that since God had brought him to silence, he ought to maintain it in every respect, and withhold his hand from writing the things he had seen and what the Angel of the Lord had told him, however comforting the matters he had heard might be. This disbelief of Zacharias at the first news of the **Gospel** <note>The "good news" of the coming Messiah.</note>, the silence to which he was doomed, and all the other circumstances of that appearance, had their Divine mysteries. This ancient and so excellent House had, since the Babylonian captivity, gradually become as if extinct, such that for some time nothing remained of the illustrious lineage of Jesse <note>Jesse was the father of King David; the "stump of Jesse" refers to the prophecy in Isaiah 11:1.</note> but an almost dead stump, whose roots were hidden beneath the earth. She was descended from David through Solomon and the other Kings of Judah, his sons and descendants; because Salathiel, son of Jechonias and father of Zerubbabel, at the time of the Babylonian captivity was married to a Princess descended from Nathan, in whose person the branch of the royal House likely ended, and through that marriage was incorporated into the branch of the Kings of Judah, which was that of Solomon. The godly Elizabeth, amazed by this quickening that occurred within her womb, did not know at first to what she should attribute the cause; but the Holy Spirit, with whom she was immediately filled, did not leave her searching for long. He gave her to understand that in that young and poor daughter—her cousin from Nazareth—she saw the mother of God’s Son, and in some measure the Son of God Himself, who took on the form of a man in the chaste womb of Mary. Elizabeth, illuminated by such a pure and sublime light of revelation, surrendered herself to the holy rapture of her joy, and exalted the state of the holy Virgin above everything that the world of happy women had ever beheld, or would ever see again. She calls her the mother of her Lord, and after having given her faith the praise it deserved, she assures her—through the prompting of the Holy Spirit who inspired her and made her speak—that everything the Lord had told the blessed Virgin through His Angel was destined to be fulfilled. The Spirit then passed from Elizabeth into the holy Virgin, like a flame that gradually increases and multiplies, and which, without leaving its first subject, passes at the same time to another. Mary was then, in her turn, also seized by the Holy Spirit, and in the loftiness and greatness of the thoughts with which her soul found itself suddenly filled, she spoke the holiest song that ever came from the mouth of a creature. It is far too excellent not to be recounted here in its entirety, since its brevity allows us to insert it into this history.

*My soul,* she cried out, *magnifies the Lord; and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior;*

<column-break/>

*because he has regarded the lowliness of his handmaiden. Behold, from now on all generations shall call me blessed: for he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name. His mercy is from generation to generation over those who fear him. He has performed a powerful work by his arm; he has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts; he has pulled down the mighty from their thrones, and the lowly he has exalted. He has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty. He has taken up Israel his servant, so that he might be mindful of his mercy (as he spoke to our fathers, namely to Abraham and his seed) forever.* <note>This song is traditionally known as the "Magnificat," taken from its first word in the Latin translation.</note> One sees in the beginning of this short hymn of praise a wonderful power: a soul full of God that nevertheless feels its own nothingness, and which, in the height of its exaltation, recognizes its natural lowliness. One finds there a heart permeated with love and gratitude toward God—indeed, a heart which drinks in great draughts of the sweetness of grace and mercy. But one also sees there a mind which, rising above human reach, penetrates into the future and discovers there the most wonderful events that were to follow the birth of that divine Son, who began to be formed in the womb of Mary; namely, the rejection of the proud Synagogue <note>In this 18th-century context, "the proud Synagogue" refers to the Jewish religious establishment that contemporary Christian authors believed would be replaced by the Church.</note>; the calling of the Gentiles <term>Gentiles: non-Jewish people</term> who were held in contempt by the Jewish people; and finally the wealth and infinite extension of mercy over the entire Church, the only true Israel, and the only true heir to the blessing of the Patriarchs. Mary stayed three months with Elizabeth, after which she returned again to Nazareth in Galilee, full of hope and faith, carrying in her body Him who, through His omnipotence, carries and supports the Universe.

## *Zechariah writes in a writing tablet the name that shall be given to his son, and prophesies immediately thereafter.*

### Luke, Chapter I. verses 63—79

<margin>The year of the world 4004. <note>This date follows traditional biblical chronologies common in the 17th and 18th centuries, which calculated the age of the earth from the moment of creation.</note> Six months before the birth of J. C. <note>Jesus Christ.</note></margin>
After the holy Virgin had departed from Hebron to return again to Nazareth, Elizabeth reached the end of her time and gave birth to a son, just as the Angel had foretold to Zechariah. The birth of this child left the whole world <note>Used here to mean the local community and all who heard of it.</note> standing in wonder, and everyone in the small town of Hebron sought to express to Zechariah and Elizabeth—who were held in high regard there—the joy they felt at seeing that God had given them a son in their old age. After eight days had passed, the child, according to the Law of Moses, had to be circumcised; and since it was a custom to delay the giving of a name to small children until the day of circumcision, just as Christians have since been accustomed to doing at Baptism, the kinsmen <note>original: "bloedvrinden," literally "blood-friends" or close relatives.</note> of that lineage wanted him to carry the name of his father and be called Zechariah. It was believed that it would be a double comfort for that old and nearly exhausted father to see himself live on somewhat in his child, and to pass his name to this son who was to follow him in his household and in the Priesthood. But this was not God's intent, and Zechariah, who had already been instructed by the Angel regarding the name God wished him to be given, settled the dispute that had arisen between his relatives and his wife over it. The friends all thought it good, as we have just said, that he should be named Zechariah; but Elizabeth opposed it and wanted him to be named *John* <note>original: "Joannes"</note>, even though there was no one among her entire kindred of that name. The simple way in which Luke relates this event

<column-break/>

gives reason to believe that Elizabeth followed her own impulse in this, without having consulted her husband about it, for she would have said as much to end that small dispute. But God had put it into the heart of that holy woman to choose such a name for her son as he must bear. They therefore approached Zechariah to ask him by signs what name he wanted to give to his son; and he gestured to them that they should fetch a writing tablet <note>original: "tafelboekje," a small portable tablet often coated in wax for writing.</note> to write the name he desired in it; for since he had seen the vision of the Angel in the Temple, he had not only remained mute until that day, but he must also have been deaf, as one had to make oneself understood to him through gestures and signs. A writing tablet was then handed to him, and he wrote in it that he desired the child to be called John. Because people were convinced by the way all this happened that it was not a pre-arranged plan between Zechariah and Elizabeth, they stood amazed that they both agreed on the choice of a name that was foreign to their family: but they were even more astonished when they saw that Zechariah, after he had written the name of his son, had also regained his speech. It was clearly understood that it was the finger of God <note>A biblical idiom for divine intervention or power.</note>, a miracle of His omnipotence—indeed, a miracle beneath which some great secret lay hidden; for everything regarding the birth of this child was far too remarkable not to understand that God had a very uncommon purpose there. Zechariah's kinsmen would not have been able to discover this on their own, but this holy man pulled back the curtain that kept the secret hidden from the eyes of the whole world, and in a song—which his piety, his faith, and the light of the Holy Spirit formed in his heart and on his lips—he unfolded all the greatest and deepest things that the...

One can read that divine Song in the book of Luke itself, the full wording of which we cannot recount here without depriving ourselves of the space to examine it in its most illustrious parts. Zechariah begins by glorifying God because He had taken pity on His people, and because He was ready to redeem them by raising up, as He was soon to do, *the horn of salvation in the house of His servant David*. <note>The "horn of salvation" is a biblical metaphor for a kingly power or a mighty savior, as the horn represents the strength of an animal.</note> These words referred to the child whom Mary still held hidden within her body, who, formed from the blood of David through the immediate action of the Holy Spirit, was destined to redeem His Church and bring salvation into the world. Zechariah also added in his song that as God redeemed His people from the hand of their enemies, the love and fear of God would be the first fruits of this glorious freedom, just as they had been its ultimate purpose. All of this—freedom and holiness—was Evangelical; any other kind of freedom was unbecoming for the Messiah, and any other

<column-break/>

holiness than that of the heart and the spirit was far too earthly to have fellowship with a freedom that was entirely spiritual. Thereupon the Holy Spirit causes Zechariah to turn briefly and cast his eyes upon the precious child whom Grace had given him: *And you, little child,* he says, *shall be called a Prophet of the Most High; for you shall go before the face of the Lord to prepare His ways.* Thereafter, rising from that child to the Messiah himself, he depicts this Messiah—the Savior and King of His people—as a Sun appearing above the horizon, which in a short time fills the whole earth with its light: *Through the tender mercy,* he says, *of our God, by which the dayspring from on high has visited us; to appear to those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death; to guide our feet into the way of peace.* <note>The "dayspring" or "rising sun" (original: *opgang*) refers to Christ bringing spiritual light to a dark world.</note> Thus ends the Hymn of Praise of Zechariah, and thus the tongue of this holy man, which had been bound for nine whole months, served as an instrument for God’s Spirit to prophesy of the upcoming wonders of the Gospel.

# God sends an Angel to Joseph to dispel the suspicion he had conceived regarding the pregnancy of Mary, his betrothed.

## Matthew, Chapter I. verses 20—24.

When God sent the Angel to the holy Virgin to announce to her that she would be the mother of the Messiah, she was already betrothed to a man of her Tribe and lineage, named Joseph. This was one of the secret insights of God’s wisdom, who, having intended to have His son born of a Virgin, nevertheless did not wish to expose him

<column-break/>

to being regarded as an illegitimate child, as the whole world would have done if he had been born outside of marriage. That stain which would then have fallen upon his birth would have been held against him all his life—indeed, it would have rendered him unfit for the ministry for which he was intended. His mother, then, had to have a husband, although he <note>The Christ child.</note> was to have no earthly father; because if he, to be born a man like all others, had to be formed from human blood, it was then necessary that this blood—naturally impure in all the children of Adam—leave behind all its impurity under the working of the Holy Spirit. It was necessary that this God-man, who came to break the power of sin, never felt the slightest contagion of it, so that he might be as holy

Since Mary's three-month stay in Hebron—after she was betrothed to Joseph—had delayed the consummation of her marriage, and since she had already conceived her divine child before her departure from Galilee, Joseph began to notice her pregnancy after she had arrived back in Nazareth. He was entirely ignorant of the Angel’s message; Mary’s humility could have kept this secret from him, and God—whose wisdom governed this entire undertaking, managing even the slightest circumstances—had not allowed him to know anything of what had occurred regarding that matter until then, neither in Nazareth with his bride, nor in Hebron with Zechariah and Elizabeth. Joseph was utterly bewildered, seeing that Mary was pregnant: the perfect virtue of that person had never allowed him to harbor any suspicion against her; but his eyes belied the esteem he had for her; and though his heart wanted him to believe she was innocent, he could not prevent his judgment and intellect from regarding her as guilty. Another person, less charitable than he, would have made his complaint to the authorities; but Joseph was of a gentle and polite nature, who preferred to cover another's faults. The Hebrews express this excellent quality through the word *righteous* <note>original: "rechtvaerdig"; in this context, it refers to a "just" man who balances adherence to the Law with mercy and kindness.</note>, and St. Matthew, following their language in speaking of Joseph’s gentleness, tells us that he, *since he was righteous, did not*

<column-break/>

*wish to make her a public example; but was minded to put her away secretly and without any rumor.* This was the only path a man of his character could take, but this path, however honorable and gentle it was, nevertheless exposed Mary’s name and reputation too much, had God—who was the guarantor of her innocence—left her under such an unjust suspicion. It happened then, while Joseph pondered all these thoughts in his mind and was on the point of breaking his marriage, that an Angel appeared to him at night in a dream, to help him out of the error in which he was stuck, and to assure him that the pregnancy of his betrothed was a pure miracle of the Holy Spirit; that she would bring a son into the world, whose name should be JESUS, because He would save His people from their sins; and that what had happened to Mary was that which had been foretold by the Prophet: *that a Virgin would become pregnant, and that she would bear a son, who would be Emmanuel, a God with us* <note>original: "Emmanuël, een Gód met ons"; a reference to the prophecy in Isaiah 7:14.</note>. Joseph, instructed by this revelation of a truth that was unknown to him, gained as much reverence for his bride as he had had bad suspicion, and he completed his marriage, at least as far as the outward ceremonies were concerned; for through the reverence he bore her, she remained always a virgin. Thus Mary passed publicly as his wife, and He was believed by all the world to be Joseph’s son, until finally, in the course of time, the Church was instructed in the secret of His birth.

what is made of it, and that it is in no way probable that so many writers who described Roman history or the life of Augustus would have forgotten such a notable matter as the registration of all the households of the Empire, there is almost no doubt that this command only concerned Judea, taken as a whole, which then included Galilee. The Greek wording of Luke is used in this sense in several places in the translation of the LXX <note>original: "LXX. Overzetteren"; the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, and by himself as well in the 21st chapter of his Gospel, to signify the entire Jewish Land. And the reason why he used such an extensive wording here is that he wanted to distinguish this first registration from the one that occurred in Judea some time later—not everywhere, but only in certain places. Augustus's intent, when he commanded this description of all the Jewish households, could have been nothing other than an effect of his statecraft, to flatter his ambition or to satisfy his greed; but God had a particular purpose in it, upon which the vain desire of the Roman was gloriously focused, without him knowing anything of it himself. It was from this great and sublime insight that God put it into the Emperor's heart to command that every family should be registered in its own Tribe, and in the city where its earliest ancestors had lived. Rome had no interest in observing such a specific order in that registration, and it would have been more natural and convenient to do so by villages and cities (as is done today), without making families come from one province to another, such as from Judea to Galilee, and from Galilee to Judea. But God, who presided over the Emperor's Council, would not allow the tribes and the lineages to be confused with one another—a state of confusion to which He has since abandoned them, from which one

<column-break/>

finds it impossible to rescue oneself. And He particularly wanted a renowned decree to come from Rome, which drew Joseph and Mary out of Nazareth and sent them to Bethlehem in Judea, exactly within the timeframe that the Holy Virgin’s term was coming to an end. Jesus was not to be born in Galilee or in Nazareth; yet Mary spent the days and months of her pregnancy there peacefully, busy pondering the favors with which God had overwhelmed her, and focusing her observations on the treasure of grace and glory that she carried in her chaste body. But it does not appear to us that she had any thought of going to Bethlehem to unburden herself of that precious treasure. Possibly she had not even understood the sense of the prophecy of Micah <note>original: "Orakels van Micha"; specifically Micah 5:2, which predicts the Messiah's birth in Bethlehem.</note>, which had named Bethlehem as the place from which the Messiah was to come, because those words do not in themselves give such a clear idea of a person's birth that Joseph and Mary, seeing that God still let them remain in Nazareth, would have had any other insights regarding it. Or it could be that they waited there with patience until God gave them the command to depart from there and go to Bethlehem, so that Mary would have her childbed there. God did this at the proper time, and He did it through such a public and well-known means that the arrival of Mary and Joseph in Bethlehem could remain unknown to no one. Indeed, He also wanted their arrival in that place, for such a reason as this which forced them to make the journey, to serve as an eternal proof for them, to show that they were both descended from the House of David and were recognized as such by their entire nation. One must either be incapable of wondering at anything, or one must here recognize the wonders of God’s adorable wisdom, which steered all these things thus to the fulfillment of His prophecies and to the glory of Jesus Christ.

</columns>

# The birth of Jesus at Bethlehem.

## Luke, Chapter II. verses 6, 7.

<margin>
The year of the world 4000; or according to the common Chronology, which is the one followed throughout this entire work, the year of the world 4004.
</margin>

THE city of Bethlehem was so small, and so many people had arrived from all sides because of the registration that took place by the Emperor's command, that Joseph and Mary could find no accommodation. The inns at that time were not as common as they are today, and since the primary aim of those who keep them is to draw profit from the persons whom they house, people who can only afford small expenses are not the ones most preferred for reception. All these reasons were the cause that Joseph and Mary could obtain no lodging in a public inn, and people had the hard-heartedness to tell them, when they appeared there, that there was no room for them. They bore this rejection with patience, and they went with many other poor people of their station into a kind of public hall, to wait there until they could give their names for the registration taking place at Bethlehem. It must have been that no more families lived in that city who were descended from the lineage of David, or all the ancient heritage of that House must have been scattered,

<column-break/>

since Joseph and Mary, who had sprung from it, found no friend or kinsman there who took them in; for it is not very probable that, Mary being so far advanced in her pregnancy, Joseph and she did not use every possible diligence to be able to enter the house of one or the other. But this too was God’s plan regarding His Son, who, coming into the world to teach men humility and to labor toward the weighty work of our salvation under the deepest humiliation, had to encounter poverty and disdain with the first step of His life. Mary was then forced to go with Joseph into a place that stood open to everyone, and where she could not be without much discomfort. She was overtaken there at night by labor, and she saw in her arms a son for whom she did not even have a simple cradle. Nevertheless, she wrapped him in swaddling clothes as well as she could and laid him in a manger, so that what Jesus Christ said later became literally true: that the Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head. Thus, in Bethlehem, in the greatest poverty, was born this Branch of Jesse <note>original: "Spruyt van Isai"; a reference to the messianic prophecy in Isaiah 11:1.</note>, who was to be full of glory; this Jesus who would reign eternally over the House of Jacob and climb the Throne promised to David His father, and from which the royal seat upon which that famous king...

The Church did not lose anything through her long wait for the Messiah. His birth, his life, and his death, which were as if present before God's eyes, previously constituted the happiness of the Faithful, whose faith beheld those things in the promises. The Church has gained everything through the coming of the Messiah, in whom all the promises of God have had their fulfillment; and the birth of Jesus at Bethlehem has been the salvation of the old and new world, just as it shall be the glory of divine wisdom and mercy for all eternity.

And He particularly wanted a renowned decree to come from Rome, which made Joseph and Mary travel out of Nazareth and go to Bethlehem in Judea, exactly within the span of time that the holy Virgin's term was coming to an end. Jesus was not to be born in Galilee and in Nazareth, and yet Mary spent the days and months of her pregnancy there peacefully, busy contemplating the favors with which God had overwhelmed her, and letting her observations rest upon the treasure of grace and glory that she carried in her chaste body; but it does not appear to us that she had any thoughts of going to unburden herself of that precious treasure in Bethlehem. Possibly she had not even understood the sense of the Oracle of Micah <note>A reference to the prophet Micah (5:2), who foretold the Messiah would come from Bethlehem.</note>, which had named Bethlehem as the place from which the Messiah was to come, because that wording in itself does not give such a clear idea of the birth of a man that Joseph and Mary—seeing that God still let them remain in Nazareth—could have had no other insights regarding it. Or it could be that they waited there with patience until God gave them the command to depart from there and to go to Bethlehem, so that Mary would hold her childbed there. God did this at the proper time, and He did it through such a public and notorious means that the arrival of Mary and Joseph in Bethlehem could remain unknown to no one. Indeed, He also wanted their arrival in that place—for such a cause as this which necessitated their journey—to serve as an eternal proof for them, to demonstrate that they were both descended from the House of David, and were recognized as such by their entire nation. One must either be incapable of wondering at anything, or one must acknowledge here the miracles of God's adorable wisdom, which governed all these things thus for the fulfillment of His Oracles, and for the glory of Jesus Christ.
