# The birth of Jesus in Bethlehem.
## Luke, Chapter II. verse 6, 7.

<margin>The year of the world 4000. Or according to the common Chronology, which is the one followed throughout this entire work, the year of the world 4004.</margin>
The city of Bethlehem was so small, and so many people had arrived from all sides because of the registration that took place by the Emperor's command, that Joseph and Mary could find no lodging. The inns were not as common at that time as they are today, and since the main aim of those who keep them is to profit from the persons they house, the people who can only spend small amounts are not those whom one most prefers to receive. All these reasons were the cause that Joseph and Mary could obtain no lodging in a public inn, and people had the hard-heartedness to tell them when they appeared there *that there was no room for them.* They bore this rejection with patience, and they went with many other poor people of their station into a kind of public Hall <note>Likely referring to a communal shelter or stable area.</note>, to wait there until they could give their names for the registration that was taking place in Bethlehem. It must have been that no more households lived in that city that were descended from the lineage of David, or all the ancient heritage of that House must have been scattered,

<column-break/>

since Joseph and Mary, who were sprung from it, found no friend or kinsman there who took them in; for it is not very probable that Mary, being thus far advanced in her pregnancy, and Joseph did not use every possible diligence to be able to come into the house of one or the other. But this too was God's plan regarding His Son, who, coming into the world to teach men humility, and to labor for the momentous work of our salvation under the deepest humiliation, had to meet poverty and disdain with the first steps of His life. Mary was then forced to go with Joseph into a place that stood open to everyone, and where she could not be but with much discomfort. She was overtaken there at night by the time of birth, and she saw in her arms a son for whom she did not even have a simple cradle. Nevertheless, she swaddled him as well as she could, and laid him in a manger, so that what Jesus Christ said later became true according to the letter: *that the Son of man had nothing whereon to lay his head.* Thus was born in Bethlehem in the greatest poverty this Shoot of *Jesse* <note>original: "Isai"; Jesse was the father of King David.</note>, who was to be full of glory; this Jesus who would reign eternally over the House of Jacob, and climb upon the Throne that was promised to David His father, and of which the royal seat upon which that renowned

One might wonder why God, who from the beginning of the

<column-break/>

world had promised the <term>Savior<note>original: "Zaligmaaker"</note></term> under the mysterious name of the *Seed* or the *Son of the Woman*, waited so long to send him. Curiosity, always restless and sometimes presumptuous, would very much like to be told the reasons God had for doing so: but it ought to be enough for us that he can have had none but very great reasons for it; since he is infinitely wise, and that it is not for us, poor miserable creatures—who run the risk of going astray as soon as we wish to raise ourselves from the earth with our own understanding—to fathom God's secrets, and to know the times and seasons which the Heavenly Father has in his power. The Church has lost nothing by her long wait for the Messiah. His birth, his life, his death, which were all-present before God's eyes, previously constituted the happiness of the Faithful, whose faith beheld those things in the promises. The Church has gained everything by the coming of the Messiah, in whom all the promises of God have had their fulfillment, and the birth of Jesus at Bethlehem has been the salvation of the old and new world, just as it shall be the glory of divine wisdom and mercy for all eternity.

## An Angel announces the birth of Jesus Christ to the Shepherds.
### (Luke, Chapter II. verses 9--12.)

<margin>The same year.</margin>
God wished to mark the lowly birth of Jesus Christ with wonder-signs of a very singular nature, such as have never been seen regarding any other birth: He sent an Angel to the Shepherds who kept the night-watch over their flock in the field, to tell them

<column-break/>

that the Savior was born in Bethlehem, that they must hasten to go see him, and that they would find him wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger. God wished to make him known in this way at the moment he appeared in the world, and he wished, to do him the greater honor and to make the tidings of his birth more certain, that an Angel should be the first proclaimer thereof. But the choice God made of the persons to whom he had these tidings announced—namely, Shepherds who were busy guarding their flocks...

Indeed, he himself once took this as a subject of thanksgiving and praise when, reflecting with sadness on the unbelief of the Synagogue and noting with joy the zeal of the people to hear his preaching, he said to God: *I thank you, O Father, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding, and have revealed them to little children: Yes Father, for so it was pleasing in your sight.* The Angel who spoke to the Shepherds had no sooner made this great news known to them than there appeared in the Sky an innumerable multitude of Angels, who, all raising a divine tone, made the air echo with this new song: *Glory to God in the highest heavens, peace on earth, and among men goodwill.* To be able to see all the beauty of this language of the Angels, and to understand the deep meaning of their song, one would need to have knowledge equal to theirs; but what we can perceive of it with our eyes of flesh and dust makes us know and understand that the incarnation of the eternal Word is that work among all God's works from which he draws the most glory, and that which most deserves to occupy the contemplation of the Angels of Heaven, who, to see it more closely, approached the earth at the moment that God was revealed in the flesh. They taught us that the eternal God had become man only to bring the peace of Heaven to the earth, by reconciling men with God; and that from being objects of his wrath, which they all naturally were since sin had become inseparable from their birth, they were henceforth to be objects of his love. The Shepherds beheld this host of Angels with wonder and heard their divine Song with joy. But as soon as these holy Spirits vanished from their sight—

<column-break/>

Having then come to the place indicated to them by the Angel, they found Joseph and Mary there, and beside them the infant, who was lying in a manger. Their faith was not offended by seeing in such a despised state the one whom the Prophet <note>Referring to the prophecy in Isaiah 9:6.</note> had designated by the name of *Wonderful*, and whom he had called *Mighty God*, *Prince of Peace*, and *Father of Eternity*. A light even more powerful and pure than that which had shone around the Angels who appeared to them made them see, in the weakness of a newborn child, the greatness of a God who had destined him for the execution of the deepest decrees of his wisdom and mercy. Their faith then animating their zeal, they worshiped God's Son in the little child of Mary, and returned home entirely gladdened, glorifying God for what they had heard and seen. Joseph and Mary were likewise full of wonder, seeing a troop of Shepherds arrive all at once, who at that hour, and in the middle of the night, left their flocks in the open field to run in haste to Bethlehem and see a child born somewhere in a corner of a Hall or public place. But they were even more amazed when they heard from the mouths of these Shepherds that an Angel had brought them the news of this birth, and told them that this child was the Messiah, the King of Israel, and the Savior of the world; and when these Shepherds added further that they had seen a heavenly host of Angels whose song they recounted. Such great and wonderful things could not fail to make a deep impression on the minds of these holy persons, and therefore the Scripture tells us, *that Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart.*

Eight days after the birth of this divine child, who had been the wonder of the Angels and the subject of their songs, Joseph and Mary prepared themselves to have him circumcised. When God had instituted circumcision to be a sanctified sign of his Covenant, he had commanded that from that time forward, as long as that Covenant should last, all male children born in that holy lineage should be circumcised on the eighth day. This cutting could not be performed on a child of such a tender age without causing him great pain, and without sometimes, when he was very weak and delicate, putting his life at risk, as it indeed often happened that some children died from it. God had taken into account all those dangers to which circumcision exposed the infants when he exempted the Jews from circumcising those who were born in the Wilderness during the forty years they wandered in those deserts. And we understand from their <term>Rabbis<note>Jewish teachers and scholars of the law.</note></term> that it was an ancient custom among them not to endanger a child's life in a family where several had already died under the knife, or from the wound of circumcision. But if it is true that there were Jews who, without explicit permission from the Lawgiver, dared to exempt themselves from a custom so strictly commanded by God, it was undoubtedly during a time of laxity and irreligion, and in families where more attention was paid to nature than to piety. Never could a child be dearer to his parents than this one was to Joseph and Mary, and never were there so many reasons to be concerned for such a precious life; but
*Part II.*

<column-break/>

duty here took precedence over all fear; such a tenderness, which could never be too great and was as piercing as it could possibly be, was powerful enough to arise in the hearts of Mary and Joseph. Even more powerful considerations, and of a higher rank than those, could have restrained them from having their child circumcised—namely, the very purposes God had in the institution of this holy ceremony. There were, as in nearly all legal ceremonies, moral and <term>mystical<note>Original Dutch: "geheymduydende," referring to symbolic or hidden spiritual meanings.</note></term> aspects: the moral intentions God had in commanding circumcision were that he signaled to his people that they were all born in sin and, to some extent, outside his covenant; since a God who is infinitely wise can have no covenant with a sinner who is still actively in his uncleanness. This is why the Apostle Paul, speaking of the Jews, said *that they were by nature children of wrath, even as others*. <note>A reference to the New Testament book of Ephesians 2:3.</note> Circumcision, then, symbolized the cutting away we ought to do of our vices, to truly be in the covenant of God and to enjoy all the privileges it contains. This is what the Prophets called *the circumcision of the heart*, of which they spoke many times and which they so often recommended to the Israelites as the truth and substance, of which the circumcision of the body was but a shadow. This is what made the Apostle Paul say *that he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is circumcision that which is outward in the flesh: but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision of the heart, in the spirit of grace and holiness, is the true circumcision.* <note>A reference to the New Testament book of Romans 2:28-29.</note> The mystical purposes God had in choosing this holy ceremony were that he made known to his people that it was through the washing, which was once to take place, of all the sins of his children in a blood of infinite value, that we would receive...

Now, God did not wish to make this exception for his Son, because this eternal Son, becoming man in the lineage of Abraham, was born a subject of the Law; and since he had to bear the yoke thereof his whole life long, according to the teaching of the Apostle Paul to the Galatians, it was necessary that he begin this by receiving circumcision, because, according to the observation of that same Apostle in the same Epistle, anyone who is circumcised must keep the whole Law.

a law in the book of Leviticus, according to which women who had given birth to a son were commanded to keep themselves separate from the holy assemblies for forty days, and at the end of that time to present themselves before the Lord in the Temple at Jerusalem, with the offering of a lamb, or a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons, for the purification of her impurity. This law was based on the fact that since all children are born with the original stain of sin, the mother who brings them into the world is to some extent defiled thereby, however otherwise holy the marriage might be, according to what the Apostle Paul said to the Hebrews, *that marriage is honorable among all, and the bed undefiled*. This impurity of a woman in childbed was only a ceremonial impurity, like many others of the same kind pertaining to the female sex: but since it took its origin from the connection she had with the impurity of sin, which is natural to all the children of Adam, it had to be removed and purified through an offering, according to the <term>Law of shadows</term> <note>The "Law of shadows" refers to the Old Testament ceremonies and laws which Christian theologians viewed as "foreshadowing" the spiritual truths revealed in the New Testament.</note>. Until those happy times, which were like a prelude to the abundant outpouring of the Holy Spirit in the <term>dispensation of the Gospel<note>The 'dispensation' refers to the specific way God deals with humanity during the era of the New Testament.</note></term>, there had been no men or women in Israel inspired by the spirit of prophecy, according to what we have noted elsewhere; but God, who had foretold in one of the oracles of Joel that in the last days he would pour out his Spirit on his servants and handmaids—as he clearly did on the day of Pentecost—began with the birth of the Savior to give glorious signs thereof in all those holy persons who prophesied on his behalf, among whose number was Anna. In Jerusalem at that time, there were many God-fearing people who, paying attention to the predictions of the Prophets in which God had designated the time of the Messiah's coming, waited with a holy impatience to see him appear. <column-break/>

The news of this wonder spread as far as faith allowed it to be received and publicized; but irreligion, joined with the ignorance and prejudice which were so common in the <term>Synagogue<note>In this context, 'the Synagogue' refers to the Jewish religious establishment and community of the time.</note></term> at that time, meant that few people were moved by all these stories or convinced of their truth. People began already then to see too much lowliness in the son of Mary and Joseph to believe that all the glorious predictions which the Prophets had made of the Messiah referred to him. Thus, the God-fearing and enlightened souls, who were few in number, found themselves forced to keep the great opinion they had of this child closed within their own bosoms; so that this first light, which God caused to rise in a small number of chosen souls at the time of the birth of Jesus Christ, was almost imperceptibly lost in the darkness of the Synagogue, while Jesus was hidden in Egypt or unknown in Nazareth until the day of his Baptism.

### The Adoration of the Wise Men from the East in Bethlehem.

### Matthew, Chapter II, verses 1, 2, etc.

<margin>The same year 4000, or according to common reckoning 4004, since the creation of the world. <note>original: "gemeene rekening" - referring to the Ussher chronology, a 17th-century chronology of the history of the world.</note></margin>
WE place, after the forty days of the purification of the holy Virgin and the song of Simeon, the arrival of the Wise Men in Bethlehem, which common opinion has caused to arrive there before that time; because it does not seem to us that this view can agree with the narrative found in the Evangelists Matthew and Luke of various matters concerning the first days of the life of Jesus Christ. Matthew says that immediately after the Wise Men had

<column-break/>

departed from Bethlehem, an Angel came to warn Joseph and Mary that they should flee hastily with the child to Egypt, to hide him from the cruelty of Herod, who wanted to have him killed. Now it appears from the preceding history that, having brought Jesus to Jerusalem, they took the way from there to Nazareth, where they lived, and from which they had not traveled shortly before except to have themselves registered at Bethlehem. One also reads in Matthew that Joseph and Mary, having been in Egypt for some time, an Angel came to bring them the news that Herod had died, and further commanded them to go back to the land of Israel; whereupon they made a decision to return again to Bethlehem, from which place they [fled] to Egypt...

# HISTORY of the N. TESTAMENT.

<columns>

had departed; but when they had set out on their way, they received another warning from Heaven to withdraw to Nazareth. This all shows that it is not probable that Jesus would have been visited by the Wise Men before Joseph and Mary brought him into the Temple, but that it was some time thereafter; without one being able to know the exact time, nor in what manner Joseph and Mary, after they had come to Nazareth, left that place again to return to Bethlehem, where it appears they were when they departed for Egypt.

The journey of the Wise Men to Bethlehem is not known to us except through St. Matthew, who is the only one of the Evangelists who speaks of it, and that still in a very brief manner. It happened, he says, when Jesus was born, that a new star appeared in the East, which some Wise Men or <term>Astronomers<note>The original Dutch 'Sterrekundigen' refers to the Magi, who were learned men from the East, often understood as practitioners of astronomy and astrology.</note></term> from that land having seen, they wondered at it, and enlightened by a supernatural light, which showed them that there was something divine in that appearance, they said to one another that this star signified the birth of a King who was worthy of their submission. They thereupon made a resolution to undertake a great journey, under the guidance of this star, which showed them the way from afar, to go into Judea to see the King whom Heaven had given to the Earth. In all this there is nothing that is not divine: the appearance of the star, the reasoning of the Wise Men, their resolution, and the movement of the star that went before them. They went straight toward Jerusalem, because, it being the capital of Judea, they believed they could more easily find out there than elsewhere in what place the child was whom they sought. They inquired about it upon their arrival, and were heard asking, just as strangers and unknowns arriving somewhere in a city would do in such a case:
> Where is the born King of the Jews? For we have seen his star in the East, and have come to worship him.

The rumor of the arrival of these strangers, and of their question, spreads immediately through the city, and everyone speaks and reasons about it according to their understanding. The news of it also came to the Court of Herod, and the cunning and shrewd King, seeing that something uncommon and something not human lay hidden beneath it, and knowing moreover that it was around the time predicted by the ancient <term>Oracles<note>In this context, 'Oracles' refers to the Old Testament prophecies concerning the Messiah.</note></term> regarding the coming of the Messiah, feared being deprived of his Royal state,

<column-break/>

and forced to yield the Throne of Judea to its legitimate King, upon whom the whole Nation had had its eye for a long time, as upon the one who was to bring all their happiness. Herod then called together the Priests and Teachers of the Law, who unanimously told him that the Messiah must be born in Bethlehem; and although he did not want to show that he took any interest in the rumor circulating about the arrival of the Wise Men and their conversation, in order not to make known his fear and anxiety, he nevertheless had these strangers brought to him secretly, and asked them several questions regarding their journey; after which, having given them permission to go to Bethlehem, he wanted them to promise him that upon their return they would bring him word of what they had learned concerning the child they sought. After they had departed from Jerusalem, the star they had seen before appeared to them again on the road, and standing still at Bethlehem, and as if descending above the house where the child was, so that they would not go looking for him elsewhere, they went into the place indicated by the star and found there this divine child, for whose birth Heaven took so much pains to make it stand out. The high esteem they had conceived of him was in no way diminished by the lowly state in which they found him. The Holy Spirit, which enlightened them, made them see through that lowliness the loftiness of a God, and upon seeing him, being seized with reverence and zeal, they fell down at his feet and gave to Jesus in his cradle the same adorations they would have given him if they had seen him on his magnificent Throne, where he is worshipped by the Universe today. They offered him as a sign of their submission, *Gold, frankincense, and myrrh,* which they had brought from their land, because it was the best and worthiest to be offered to him. Whether they came from Persia or from Arabia, both of which lie to the East of Judea, would be impossible to determine for certain. Likewise, nothing certain can be said about their number; Tradition sets it at three, but it is completely unknown from where it has taken this. With just as little basis, it also gives them the title of Kings, and goes so far as to tell us their names. However, the Evangelist Matthew remains entirely silent about that, and it matters little to the Church to know anything more about it.

## Joseph and Mary flee with the child Jesus to Egypt.
### Matthew, Chapter II, verses 13–15.

<margin>The same year.</margin>
The arrival of the Wise Men in Bethlehem was something so great and unusual that it could not be otherwise than that Joseph and Mary must have been amazed and gladdened by it. But this joy, of seeing their divine child worshipped by the Wise Men who had come from the East specifically for that purpose, was very soon disturbed; for hardly had they departed from Bethlehem to return again to their country, when an Angel came to warn Joseph in a vision at night of the plot Herod was hatching to make this child, who was all their delight, just

as he was one day to be all their happiness, die. It was therefore necessary to hide him from that Tyrant, and to hasten to conceal him from his cruelty. But the Angel made them take a resolution regarding what they were to do:
> *Rise up,* he said to Joseph, *and take the young child and his mother, and flee into Egypt, and be there until I shall tell you.*
Thus Mary saw beginning to be fulfilled what Simeon had foretold to her,
> *that a sword would pierce through her soul.*
That Oracle had a deep and wide-reaching meaning, and although it primarily referred to the death of Jesus, it also looked toward the persecutions that were to be inflicted upon him—

Jesus was then still only a child sucking his mother's breasts; and nonetheless one sees a storm suddenly rise against him, namely a King who had sworn his destruction. What then did Mary have to expect in the life of a child who so early began to be the target of the fiercest hatred? And what sad thoughts must her heart, startled by an unexpected danger, have caused to well up in her mind, to spread over all the years of his life? It is true, she saw clearly that God concerned Himself with the preservation of this child, and that He Himself had chosen a refuge for him, but they had to go seek it so far away, and among so many dangers, that she needed all her faith for her support, so as not to doubt whether she should follow the angel's counsel. It would have been easy for God to have found another hiding place for His Son, and to have protected him from Herod's persecution by other means; but He willed that Egypt, which in former times had shed the blood of the sons of the Hebrews, and which, to utterly destroy their race, caused them to be smothered in the cradle <note>A reference to Pharaoh's decree in Exodus to kill Hebrew male infants.</note>, should now protect from a monster of cruelty the life of a child who would raise the glory of Israel to such a peak,

Since Joseph and Mary remained with Jesus in that land until the death of Herod, which according to the reckoning of the best <term>chronologists<note>Scholars who study historical dates and timelines to align biblical events with secular history.</note></term>, occurred two years after the birth of our Savior, one can guess, according to what we have said regarding the time of the arrival of the Wise Men in Bethlehem, that Jesus had been in Egypt for about a year and a half; thus suffering in his tender youth with Joseph and Mary the hardships and inconveniences of a long exile.

The profound silence of Scripture regarding this matter does not allow us to know for certain what the cause of this second journey was, and it would be nothing more than a guess, although it would not be an entirely ill-founded conjecture <note>original: "giffing"</note> to say that they were exhorted to it from Heaven by an Angel, just as had happened to them during several other events. God's purpose in all this was to hide His Son, in a sense, in a corner of Galilee, so that by becoming unrecognizable to His countrymen there, the Oracles—which had foretold that He would be despised and rejected by His people—might be fulfilled. Indeed, the prejudice which the Jews had conceived regarding Jesus dwelling in Nazareth had such power over their minds that it was impossible for them to rid themselves of it; and every time He demonstrated with such great evidence through His miracles that He was the Messiah, they countered it by saying: *But this man is from Galilee, and can any good thing come out of Nazareth?* The Evangelist Matthew has, so to speak, led us to the very door of God's Counsel to let us see there the deep purpose He had regarding the child Jesus, when, speaking of His return to Nazareth in Galilee, he tells us that this happened so that the Prophecies might be fulfilled, which had depicted Him as someone who would be

At the age of twelve, Joseph and Mary took Him with them to Jerusalem to celebrate the Feast of the Passover there, just as all fathers were accustomed to bringing their children there when they began to reach such years of being capable of understanding the mystery of that ceremony. After the Holy Days had ended, everyone returned to their own home; and Joseph and Mary, with their kinsfolk and other persons of their acquaintance, resumed the road to Nazareth. The men formed several groups <note>original: "tróppen"</note> that were separate from the women; and the women likewise went by themselves, without their fathers and husbands; but concerning the small children, they were free to join either the men or the women as they preferred, because modesty and propriety, upon which this custom was solely based, could not be violated by it. When these groups departed from Jerusalem, Jesus, without anyone noticing, became separated from them and remained in the city. Joseph and Mary each soon noticed that Jesus was not in their group, but because neither had any suspicion that He had remained in Jerusalem, Mary thought He was in Joseph's group, and Joseph that He was in that of the women. But toward evening they noticed their mistake, and set about searching for Jesus on all sides, but found Him nowhere. Grieved then that they had lost Him, they returned again to Jerusalem to inquire after Him there, and three days later they found Him in the Temple, seated among the Teachers of the Law, instructing them through many great and profound questions which He put to them, according to the manner of teaching at that time, and with so much understanding that all who heard Him were astonished. Joseph and Mary having come to Him, respectfully made their complaints to Him that He had thus left them without warning: but He answered them with a power and dignity that was entirely divine: *Did you not know that I must be about my Father’s business?* <note>original: "in de dingen myns Vaders" — literally "in the things of my Father," often translated as "in my Father's house" or "about my Father's business."</note> Yet the Evangelist Luke indicates that Joseph and Mary did not fully understand the meaning of this answer.

<margin>

John the Baptist made himself famous from day to day through the fiery zeal of his preaching, and through the holiness of his life. However, he lacked one thing which *Elijah* <note>original: "Elias"</note>, of whom he was a perfect image, had possessed, and which had been common to him with many other Prophets of his time, and that was the gift of miracles. *John the Baptist* performed none; that quality would have exalted him all too high, and perhaps too easily caused him to pass for the *Messiah* who was then so near; for the time had come that *Jesus Christ*, who kept Himself hidden in *Nazareth* as if in secret, had to manifest Himself to *Israel* and begin His ministry. It was at that age <note>Likely referring to the age of thirty, the traditional age for entering the priesthood.</note> that the Priests entered into their offices, and were confirmed therein by washing, anointing, and sacrifices. He trembled with a holy and reverent fear at the approach of such an exalted person, and ashamed to find himself thus at the side of *Christ* of whom he was only a Servant, and to see that the Lord of glory, the King of Heaven and Earth, came to place His sanctified head under his hands to receive Baptism, he could not sufficiently express his amazement to Him, nor almost resolve to obey Him. *I need to be baptized by you*, he was heard to say, *and do you come to me?* The Lord therefore found Himself compelled to command that he should baptize Him. *Allow it*, He says, *for thus it becomes us to fulfill all righteousness;*

"It befits you to lend your hand to this ceremony in the performance of your office; and it becomes me, through this act of humility, to accept a Ministry that shall be nothing other than a continuous humiliation, in which I shall fulfill the entire will of my Father, and bring the righteousness of the ages to the earth." It is an arrogance, a stubbornness, too stiff and under a pretext of humility, to push away a work that God imposes on us, however unworthy we may be of it. John then no longer hesitates to do what the Lord requires of him. The Messiah descends into the water, and John baptizes him. At the sight of this baptism, which opened the great and glorious path of his Ministry for Jesus Christ, Heaven opens itself, and the Holy Spirit descends in the visible form of a dove, which comes to rest upon his head; and at the same time, the banks of the

<column-break/>

Jordan echo with a voice coming forth from God’s Throne, through which the eternal Father gives this glorious declaration in honor of Jesus Christ: *This is my Son, my beloved, in whom I am well pleased.* Never had the Trinity appeared together in such a visible way. The Son is baptized, the Holy Spirit descends upon him, and the Father crowns that most glorious ceremony with his testimony. Thus the Gospel, which took its first milestone from the day of Jesus’ Baptism, is not the work of one divine person alone, but of the entire Trinity; it is for this reason that the three Persons constantly appear there, each in their rank and the duties that fit them; and it is also for that reason that Baptism, by which we are incorporated into the fellowship of the Church, is administered in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

### *Jesus is led by the Holy Spirit into the Wilderness, where after a fast of forty days, the Devil comes to him to tempt him.*

#### Matthew, Chapter IV, verses 1–11. <note>The original text lists verses I--II, which in this period's notation often signified 1 through 11.</note>

<margin>
The year of the world 4034, and the 30th of the life of J.C.
</margin>
After Jesus Christ had been baptized by John the Baptist, the Holy Spirit, with which he was filled, seized him and took him up by such a powerful impression, as he had sometimes done to the Prophets, whom he transported from one place to another, as one sees in the history of the Prophet Elijah <note>original: "Elias"</note>. The place to which Jesus was led was a ghastly wilderness inhabited only by wild beasts. This was to let Christ—who at the first entrance of his ministry found himself as if outside the world, in a place where everything was lacking and which was fit for nothing but to provoke terror—know that henceforth he would be rejected by men, deprived of all the innocent sweetnesses of life, and exposed to the fury of his enemies, which was even more to be feared than that of the cruel beasts. The Lord sanctified this lonely wilderness through a fast of forty days, and through constant meditations: and since he was steadily in communion with God his Father, these uninhabited places became for him a true Bethel <note>Bethel means "House of God" in Hebrew, referring to the place where the patriarch Jacob had his vision of a ladder to heaven.</note>, a house of God, a Paradise on earth. But this Paradise was no less accessible to the Devil than that of Adam. In the first, he had entered under the form of a serpent, and through his cunning had caused the temptation to flow into the minds of our first parents, dragging them into crime. After the temptation was over, Jesus returned again to Nazareth. We do not know what occurred in those first months of his ministry; we only see that a little before the first Passover (which will have been about six months after his baptism, if it is true, as we have touched upon elsewhere, that he would have been born toward the end of the harvest month <note>Dutch: "Herfstmaand," an old name for September, suggesting an autumn birth for Jesus rather than mid-winter.</note>) he returned from Galilee to Judea, to the place where John was baptizing. The Gospel, speaking of that journey, says that John the Baptist made Christ known to Andrew and some others, and that Andrew subsequently introduced him to Simon his brother, whose name the Lord changed from Simon to that of Peter, under which he has since become so famous. These two disciples followed him with Philip and some others; but he had not yet drawn them to himself through an explicit calling, nor made them his Apostles. He did so shortly thereafter when, returning from Galilee, he saw Peter and Andrew in a small boat busy fishing from the shore of Lake Gennesaret <note>Also known as the Sea of Galilee.</note>, for they had returned to their primary trade, which was that of fishermen. Jesus, who was walking along the shore, saw them as they cast their net into the sea, and called to them that they should leave their net and boat and follow him. It was no great thing to leave a small boat and a net; yet it was much to give up everything,

<column-break/>

and to leave a profession by which one, however modest it may be, earns one’s living, in order to surrender oneself to a poor man such as Jesus Christ was, in whom one saw no apparent possibility of being able to place anyone in even the slightest state of prosperity. But a secret power drew them from their profession and bound them to another, where the cross and oppression would accompany them. Christ, calling them, promised to make them *Fishers of men*: one could not exactly say what kind of ideas those words brought to their minds, yet it is hard to believe that their thoughts rose to that miraculous outcome which their ministry had for the conversion of mankind, when they, with the spiritual net of preaching, brought men in multitudes into the Church of God's Son. Walking a few paces further from there, he saw another fishing boat lying still close to the shore, in which were an elderly man and two others much younger, who were together repairing their nets to go fishing. It was Zebedee, with his two sons James and John. Jesus called them, just as he had called the two other fishermen who accompanied him. The Evangelists who recount this calling do not add, as in the preceding one, that Jesus said to James and John that he would make them fishers of men, but they say only that he called them. It is not the aim of the motivation that makes the power of the calling, but it is the power of the one who calls. The motivation comes afterward, and the interest which the soul finds in obeying joins with the duty of obedience, which is always the strongest in a soul where Grace is at work, although that same grace never leaves obedience without encouraging it

### Jesus Christ, being invited with his Disciples to a wedding at Cana in Galilee, changes the water into Wine there.

->John, Chapter II. verse 2–9.<-

<margin>The year of the world 4034. In the 30th year of Jesus Christ.</margin>
A few days after the calling of Peter and Andrew, and the two sons of Zebedee, a marriage took place at Cana, where Jesus was invited with his Disciples; and since marriage is holy by its institution, which took its origin from God himself and in the state of innocence <note>This refers to the belief that marriage was established by God in Eden before the Fall of Man.</note>, Jesus did not refuse to be present there. It has always been the custom, even among the most orderly people, on such occasions to have friends and kinsmen come together, and to take all the innocent pleasure of a feast, which each person arranges to be larger or smaller according to his means. But it was also anciently a custom that, in order to prevent any excess being committed during the merriment of the wine, and so that one guest should not have reason to complain about another, someone was chosen from the company to whom was entrusted the power to maintain good order regarding everything needed at the meal. He to whom this charge was given was called the *King* or *Overseer* of the Feast, and the Greek word in

<column-break/>

this history, which has been translated by the word *Steward* <note>original: "Hofmeeſter" — or "Governor of the Feast." The Greek term is "architriklinos."</note>, actually signifies someone who is the Ruler of the table, or the Head of the banquet. After the meal had lasted some time, those who served the guests saw that wine was beginning to fail; the holy Virgin, being informed of this, as someone who was of the kinship, or who had a great interest in that house, immediately made this known to her son, whether she merely wanted to unburden herself of the anxiety she felt about it, or whether she wanted to nudge <note>original: "aanporren"</note> the charity of Jesus—of whose power she was not ignorant—from the sidelines to perform a miracle, to save the household from the shame into which it would undoubtedly have had to fall, if in a land where wine was so common, it had completely failed. Whether Mary showed herself too eager regarding a matter which was fundamentally earthly, and consequently too minor to take so much interest in; or whether she did not rely as much as she ought on the wisdom of Jesus Christ, and imagined that he did not care enough about what she told him, is something the Evangelist has wished to leave us ignorant of; but he nevertheless gives us to understand, through the answer that Jesus gave to his mother, that he was not entirely satisfied with it:
> Woman, he says, what have I to do with you? my hour has not yet come. <note>original: "Vrouw, zeyd hy, wat heb ik met u te doen? myn uur is nóg niet gekomen."</note>

Jesus departed with His mother and His Disciples from Cana to Capernaum; but they were there only a few days, because He wished to go to Jerusalem to be there for the Passover feast. This was a respect that one could easily show to Moses's Laws, both for their holiness and to prevent the accusations that would surely have been thrown at Him for despising the institutions of that Prophet, had He neglected to appear at the Feasts of Passover, Pentecost, and Tabernacles <note>original: "Loverhutten" — literally "leaf-huts," referring to the Jewish festival of Sukkot</note>. Having then arrived in Jerusalem, He went immediately to the Temple; but it pained Him to see that it was desecrated by an unseemly trade in various kinds of animals and the exchanging of money. This abuse, which one would hardly have tolerated in the temples of idols, had gradually crept into God's Temple under the cloak of religion. Those who came from afar could not bring animals for the sacrifices with them, and those who did not have them with them found all kinds of livestock there, namely oxen and sheep for those who could well afford them; and doves and turtledoves for the poor who had nothing to buy a lamb or sheep with. The exchanging of money, of which there were several types in Judea since the Romans had introduced their coinage there, was also very convenient. All this took place in the outermost court, which was a large plaza within the first enclosure of the Temple, but nonetheless separated from that plaza where the

Jesus could not tolerate that greed and avarice showed themselves with such insolence in that holy place, and that the House of God was being made into a place of trade. His zeal was awakened and ignited at the sight of such a violent desecration; and seeing at his feet in the forecourt of the Temple many of those cords with which the sheep and lambs, brought there for sale as sacrifices, had been tied, he picked up some of them and made a whip out of them, with which he drove the animals that were still for sale out of the Temple; he overturned the money-changers' tables, and he commanded those who carried doves to take them away and leave, not wanting to touch them himself, for fear that the doves, starting to fly, would have caused a commotion and riot in the Temple, which was already all too great. No one, however bold he might be, dared to oppose such a holy act; each was convinced in his own mind of the wrong they all had done by coming to conduct an unseemly trade in a place that should serve only for a holy use,

<column-break/>

and where one ought to come only with great reverence. But if the interest and greed of the buyers and sellers did not dare open their mouths to complain, the vanity of the persons of rank who allowed this transgression could not endure seeing themselves rebuked by an act that could not be considered just without the continuation of that shameful trade being condemned. They then approached Jesus, and not daring to directly approve or condemn his action, they asked him by what right he presumed to change such an established custom, and to set himself against the permission granted by the Masters of the Temple. Jesus Christ somewhat disregarded this question, and answered it only through a complex prophecy in figurative speech, which they did not understand—indeed, even the Disciples did not, until after his resurrection: *Destroy this Temple*, he said, *and in three days I will raise it up.* He meant to say that if they did not then know who he was, and what his authority was, they would one day be able to know it, when he, after they had committed against his body—the true Temple of the Godhead—that cruel and bitter outrage of tearing it down and delivering it to death, would then raise the same from the grave on the third day.

## The conversation of Jesus Christ with Nicodemus.

### John, Chapter III. verses 1 -- 11.

<margin>The 30th year of J. C.</margin>
The act that Jesus Christ had performed in the Temple was followed by many miracles which he did in Jerusalem, and which drew the wonder of the common people to him. Among others, there was a man of great standing named Nicodemus, a Counselor of the great Sanhedrin <note>The Sanhedrin was the supreme judicial and administrative council of the Jewish people in Jerusalem.</note>, and of the sect of the Pharisees, who especially wished to know him and to hold a secret

<column-break/>

conversation with him. He had a sincere desire to be instructed and to work toward his salvation; but he was still one of those unsteady souls who drift between duty and self-interest, and who, having long stood in doubt between God and the world, do not know which of the two they will choose. In this state of mind, mixed with good and evil, Nicodemus chose the nighttime as the most convenient for his status to go to Jesus. He said to him, as soon as he spoke to him, that he recognized him as a Teacher sent from God, because it was impossible that anyone who was not sent by God could perform the miracles

Christ had already contested this destructive prejudice when, in the first chapter of this Gospel, speaking of those who had a right to the benefits of His Covenant, he said *that they were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.* He taught Nicodemus the same thing here, and after reproaching him that, being a Teacher in Israel, he found this language of being born again and being born of water so strange—even though the Jews themselves used those expressions, albeit in a much lesser and lower sense, when they spoke of the baptism of their proselytes <note>Proselytes were non-Jews who converted to Judaism; their initiation often involved a ritual washing or baptism which was seen as a "new birth" into the community.</note>—he continued with his instructions. Nicodemus did not leave him without being convinced that Jesus was the Messiah; he showed this on several occasions, and demonstrated it especially in the care he took regarding His burial.

When the Lord, in order not to bring the jealousy of such a powerful sect upon himself so soon, decided to move further away from Jerusalem and go to Galilee. To that end, he had to travel through the land of Samaria; and since the heat in that season, between Passover and Pentecost, was already great, Jesus felt his strength diminish through the difficulty of the journey, so that he became weary from the heat and grew thirsty. He then found himself by a well, which was near the city of Sichem, which at that time was called Sichar; and he sat down on the edge of that well to rest a while, and meanwhile to wait until someone coming to draw water might allow him to ask for a drink, for the spring was too deep to be able to scoop from it by hand. It would have been easy for Christ to prevent himself from becoming weary or thirsty, and it would have been no less easy for him to have quenched his thirst through a miracle. But he had not taken on human nature in order to avoid feeling its weaknesses, and he did not keep the glory of God hidden under the cover of weak flesh simply to use his infinite power to prevent his own needs. While he sat there waiting, a woman came with a pitcher to draw water. Jesus asked her for a drink; she noticed that he was a Jew, and wondered that he, being of a nation that had the utmost aversion to the Samaritans, asked her for water from her pitcher. Christ answered her that if she knew who it was who asked this of her, she would have anticipated him by desiring living water from him. This woman understood nothing of this conversation; she believed that Jesus spoke of a water of such a nature as that of the well, or of that same water. Naturally, our minds recoil before the mysteries of Grace, and as long as God does not lift it up by his divine light, it is unable to reach the spiritual sense, of which it sees nothing but the letter, and the husk that hides the secret. -ually the mind of the Samaritan woman; she noticed from what he told her regarding the man with whom she lived, and concerning all her previous life, that this person drew the knowledge of everything he had told her from Heaven. Jesus gave this woman to understand that this difference was of little importance, because the entire earth was to become the Temple of the Lord through the abolition of the ceremonial Law, which bound religion more to one place than to another; such that without going further into the investigation of a dispute which might have made the mind of a woman, who was biased toward her own nation, hesitate, the Lord answered her with so much wisdom and power that she was convinced that he was the Messiah. His Disciples, who had left him a little while before by his command to go buy food in the city, arriving then, were surprised to find their Master in conversation with a woman. They then offered him something to eat, but he refused it, saying that he had another food to eat. They did not understand what he meant by that, but he explained it to them, saying that his food was to do the will of his Father, who had sent him for the conversion of sinners. The woman, who meanwhile had returned to the city to make it known there that she had encountered the Messiah, came back followed by a multitude of people, who, having heard Jesus Christ, recognized him as the Messiah, the King of Israel, the Savior of the world: so that in the holy joy of their souls they said to the woman who had brought them to him:

> *We no longer believe because of your saying, and because of the conversation he held with you to reveal your previous life, but we ourselves have heard him, and know that this is truly the Christ, the Savior of the world.*

## Jesus miraculously heals all kinds of ailments.

### Matthew, Chapter IV. verses 23, 24.

<margin>The year of the world 4034, and the 30th year of J. C.</margin>
The miracles were the essential marks of the Messiah. The Prophets had indicated as much in their predictions of him, and it appears from various texts of the Gospel that the Jews were of the opinion that the Messiah, coming into the world, would perform not only miracles, but also of various kinds. It was indeed consistent with God's wisdom that this happened thus. All the world had an interest in knowing the Messiah, so as to be able to believe in him; but the greater the interest was in knowing him, so much more important was it not to be deceived therein, by taking a deceiver and seducer for the true Messiah, or through ignorance to place him on the same level as the

<column-break/>

common sort of men. To prevent all these misfortunes, the surest means was for the Messiah to distinguish himself through his miracles. This path could not be held in suspicion, since it came directly from God, who alone has the power to produce effects of which one finds no origin in Nature, because he alone is above Nature, to do everything he wills. But since many Prophets had performed various miracles without anyone being able to conclude, to the honor of any of those uncommon men, that he was the Messiah, it was necessary that it appear publicly that Jesus Christ performed miracles to convince the world that he was the Messiah: because it is not conceivable that God would have wanted to lend his hand to work directly himself, at the will and word of a man, solely to favor a deceiver. Therefore, it was always by that proof, which was of such evidence and power that unbelief could bring nothing against it, that Jesus Christ

Galilee sees him perform all these wonders; Judea finds evidence of them everywhere; <term>Decapolis<note>A group of ten cities on the eastern frontier of the Roman Empire in the Levant, largely inhabited by Greeks.</note></term>, Syria, and other neighboring lands all draw benefit from his charity, and from the power he has to restore health to the sick in a moment: and his name and fame thus spread far and wide through his miracles, and bring everywhere a conviction that Jesus is the Messiah.

# Jesus Christ preaches on a mountain before a multitude of people who had followed him.
## Matthew, Chapters V, VI, and VIII.

<margin>The same year.</margin>
Jesus Christ often went into the silence of a remote district to seek the freedom to maintain communion with God through meditation and prayer. But the zeal of some, and the curiosity of others, constantly disturbed his solitude, and brought very numerous crowds to him in the wilderness. Because his wisdom and charity allowed all occurrences to manifest for the advancement of the salvation of men, by giving them instructions, he delivered on a certain day—before a great multitude of people who had flowed together to him from many places on a mountain—one of the greatest and most useful discourses found in the <term>Gospel<note>Literally "Good News," referring here to the accounts of the life of Jesus.</note></term>. He began by making them understand how blessed the poor in spirit were, namely such humble and <term>fearful<note>In this context, "fearful" means reverent or God-fearing.</note></term> souls,

<column-break/>

who, struck by the feeling of their natural poverty, do not cease to long and sigh for grace, who always hunger and thirst after righteousness, and who, when God calls them to it, suffer persecution for the Gospel. Furthermore, he proceeds to the reforming of many abuses which the Jewish Teachers committed in the instruction of souls regarding some important parts of moral teaching, granting a criminal freedom to the mind regarding the keeping of various parts of the Ten Commandments, about which those ignorant Teachers gave an overly broad explanation. As for example, regarding the prohibition of murder, they said that it only looked upon the outward act by which one took the life of a man; but concerning the secret movements of the heart, which gives itself over to hatred or revenge, that was, according to their opinion, of little importance when the execution did not follow. Thus they also made almost no account of the outbursts of anger, and all the bitter words which it causes to be brought forth—

—larger than theirs, and yet to step out of that tribunal. Through such unfair behavior, love is broken, and one always has a thousand seeds of enmity and discord ready, which give birth to resentment at the first occasion; from resentment arises a coolness that breaks off social interaction; and finally, public enmities follow, and quarrels without end and without number. One tickles oneself with good qualities that one does not possess because one does not want to see the bad ones that one indeed has; and thus one grows old and dies in one's great defects, whether because one did not want to notice them before they had taken over the whole heart, or because the heart—crafty, malicious, and flattering itself in its vices—has borrowed pretexts from the intellect so as not to condemn those defects most strictly and drive them from the mind forever.

# **Our Savior heals a leper**
# **whom he met near Capernaum.**

### Matthew, Chapter VIII, verses 1, 2.

<margin>The same year.</margin>
When the Lord had finished that excellent and incomparable discourse, which occupies three large chapters in the Gospel of Matthew, the people who had heard it were carried away with wonder at seeing so much knowledge and holiness at once. They had, moreover, perceived in Jesus Christ, while he spoke to them, a certain dignity and power in all his words that mastered their hearts and prevented their passions—naturally so sensitive and restless regarding their own interest—from—

<column-break/>

—opposing a doctrine that came to challenge them in their strongholds and showed not the slightest compliance toward them. They had never seen anything like it in their most famous Teachers <note>Referring to the Scribes and Pharisees.</note>, so that they perceived a very great distinction between Him and them. When he went down from the mountain, accompanied by that great multitude of people who had come to seek him there, he took the path to Capernaum, which was not far from that mountain. His fame, which was already very well known, and this great crowd of people following him, made a leper who was on the road believe that Jesus could heal him of his leprosy. With this confidence, he approaches him and throws himself down at his feet, with these words: *Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.* Well then, Jesus answered, stretching out his hand and touching him: *I will, be made clean.* At that moment, the leprosy disappears, and—

It was not the visible hand which the Lord stretched out to the leper that caused his healing; it was the invisible hand of God—of which the movement and action of the human hand was a tangible sign—that had wrought this miracle. But Jesus, by stretching out his hand, had awakened the faith of the leper, and by that means placed him fully in a state to obtain the grace he requested. This act was performed before the eyes of a great multitude, and our Savior saw clearly that it could not remain a secret; nor was it his intention that it should be so. Nevertheless, he commanded the man whom he had healed to say nothing of it to anyone before he had shown himself to the Priest, who, according to the laws of Moses, had to inspect the lepers to see if they were indeed healed before he allowed them to appear in the holy gatherings. <note>In ancient Israel, leprosy was not only a medical condition but a ritual one; a priest had to officially certify a person as "clean" before they could rejoin society and worship.</note> But our Savior, by this command, was urging diligence and speed rather than silence and the keeping of a secret. It is possible that the man would have wanted to remain with him, finding the joy that a grateful heart feels in

<column-break/>

beholding, for as long as possible, the person to whom he considers himself bound for a great favor, in order to testify through a holy zeal the earnestness with which he acknowledged the happiness he owed him for his healing. But Jesus Christ did not wish to tolerate a man who was generally known to be a leper by his side, so as not to give those who were ignorant of the miracle, or who doubted it, any suspicion that he allowed an unclean person in his company. He also wanted this man to show the reverence due to the Law of Moses by presenting himself to the Priest, and for that leper to then offer the customary sacrifice for his cleansing. This served at once to make the miracle all the more certain and indisputable, by having it confirmed by someone who, far from favoring him, belonged to a group where the Lord Jesus found only envious men, who were set upon diminishing the fame of his deeds, and were accustomed, in his regard, to call good evil, as Isaiah said, and light darkness. <note>A reference to Isaiah 5:20: "Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness."</note>

But this great humility in the Centurion was the effect of the high esteem which he had for Jesus Christ, and this esteem was the fruit of his faith, which was in him in a much higher degree than in all the others. He then went to the most prominent Jews in that city, to pray them that they would request a favor from Jesus for him, which he himself did not dare to ask. Because this Commander was very beloved by the Jews of Capernaum, since he had done them many good services, and through his prestige and his gifts, had helped them to build a Synagogue <note>original: "Synagoge"</note>, they went at his request to pray Jesus that he would restore health to the servant of this Centurion. The Lord answered them, *I will come and heal him*. The Centurion was immediately informed of this; but instead of being pleased that Jesus had set out on his way to come to him, he immediately sent his friends to meet him, to request him to spare the trouble, having them say that he did not know himself worthy that the Lord should come into his house; and that it was enough that he but spoke a word for the healing of the

On the occasion of this rare faith of a Centurion, who was a Gentile <term>Gentile: A person of non-Jewish origin; in the New Testament, often used for Greeks or Romans.</term> by birth, and until that time also in religion, Christ predicted the upcoming conversion of the Gentiles, and even gave it to be understood that they would surpass the Jews through the greatness of their faith and zeal. *Many,* he said, *shall come from the East and the West, and shall sit with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the Kingdom of Heaven; but the children of the Kingdom,* which were the Jews, *shall be cast out into the outer darkness, where there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth*. Thereafter, turning to the friends whom the Centurion had sent, he granted him his request. *Go thy way,* he said, *and be it done unto you as you have believed*; and at that same hour the servant became healthy.

It is highly surprising, since the Jews ate no pork and were forbidden by specific ordinances of the Synagogue from grazing those animals on their lands, that such a large multitude of them was found in that region. <note>The Mosaic law (Leviticus 11:7) strictly forbade the eating of pork, and later rabbinical laws restricted even the raising of pigs.</note> But these people had, in many matters, deviated so far from the strictness of the ordinances, and had become so greedy, that it is not strange that in a land so far distant from Jerusalem—the center of the Laws and Religion—as Gadara was, which bordered the

<column-break/>

It could also be that these pigs belonged to heathen families who lived in Gadara and Gergesa, because they were border towns. Jesus Christ, the Lord and Master of all things, who has absolute right over them, allowed the demons to enter the bodies of those beasts to show his power and to punish the guilty owners through the loss of the swine. Disorder and madness entered into them; the pigs could not live with the evil spirit that drove them; they no longer heeded their pastures, they no longer feared their herders; they ran in all directions, and finding neither in running nor in standing still any rest or relief, they plunged themselves into the sea and were smothered in the water’s waves.

THE Gadarenes were so distressed by the loss of their swine, and they had such a fear that the stay of Jesus among them would cause them even greater damage, that they begged him to depart from their borders. Such are naturally the inclinations of men whose hearts are not sanctified by Grace; they place an earthly interest above the spiritual goods of the Gospel, and they say to Jesus Christ, like those ungodly ones of whom Job speaks, *Lord, depart from us, for we have no desire for the knowledge of your ways*, <note>original: "Heere, wyk van ons, want aan de kennisse uwer wegen hebben wy geenen lust" — a reference to Job 21:14.</note> as soon as it should cost their covetousness or the affection they bear toward the world

When God departs from us, he leaves us with nothing, even if he lets us keep all other things, because all of those together—yes, even the whole world—cannot compensate us for the loss of him. When the paralytic had been brought onto the roof, an opening was made at the place where the tiles lay, and the sick man was lowered from there on his small bed, into the middle of the assembly. <note>Middle Eastern houses of this period typically had flat roofs accessible by an external staircase, allowing for the unusual entrance described here.</note> It must be that Jesus was then on the highest floor of the house, as it was customary at that time to go to the upper rooms of the dwelling when any number of persons gathered to hear a renowned man speak on matters of Religion. The books of the Jews report this ancient custom, and we find some trace of it in the first Chapter of the Acts, where we read that the Apostles were gathered with the Believers of Jerusalem in the Upper Room; and in the 20th Chapter we see the Apostle Paul preaching to a large assembly in Troas in a hall that was on the third story. If one were to judge the actions of these people according to the rules of human conduct, one might find some impertinence in it; but faith does not concern itself with the reasonings produced by a false delicacy; it is bold without yet being reckless, and that which it cannot acquire with ease, it snatches as if by force

That of the sick man was no less great, and also had its reward. *Son, he said to him, your sins are forgiven you.* Curiosity had drawn the Scribes and Pharisees, who had mingled among the crowd, to Jesus. They were offended to hear him speak with such authority, and they said to themselves, not wishing to speak aloud, perhaps so as not to make themselves known: *Who can forgive sins but God alone?* The Lord knew their thoughts, and turning to them he said, *Why do you think evil in your hearts? What is easier to say to the paralytic: Your sins are forgiven you; or to say, Arise, and walk?* Without doubt, a divine authority was required for both. *But so that you may know that the Son of Man has power to forgive sin on the earth, Arise, he said to the paralytic, and take up your bed, and go hence to your house.* Immediately the afflicted man stood up; he took his bed and went away, glorifying God for all the mercies He had shown him. This miracle stunned all who saw it, and full of wonder, they cried out as they left the house, *We have never seen the like! We have seen incredible things today!*

Matthew, otherwise called Levi, was of that number—a Jew by birth, but by trade a servant of the Roman tyranny, and a tool of oppression. Christ saw him in passing, sitting at the tax office, and said to him with masterly authority, *Follow me.* This word pulled him away from his writing desk. Matthew concerned himself no longer with his office or his money; he left everything for Christ’s sake; he stood up and followed him. Jesus entered the city with this tax collector <term>tax collector (original: tóllenaar); these men were often Jews who collected taxes for the Roman occupiers and were widely hated for their perceived greed and betrayal of their people</term>, whom the power of his calling was about to withdraw from the world; and Matthew, overcome with joy, prepared a feast, to which he invited his best friends, who were mostly all tax collectors, and Jesus was also invited there with his Disciples. It was not the choice dishes which Levi had prepared that drew Jesus Christ there; his most delicious food was, as he himself said, to labor for the conversion of sinners, for which the Heavenly Father had sent him to earth. He knew that there were persons at that banquet who were in the highest need of his teachings, and who would receive them with more reverence than a thousand others who encountered him daily and saw him perform miracles. His conduct, however, was poorly tolerated by the Scribes and Pharisees. The holiness of a hypocrite consists entirely in the skill of covering his own vices, and in rebuking the most innocent actions if they displease him slightly and he can cast them in a false light. Gener-

<column-break/>

-ally the Jews were offended whenever they saw someone of good name and reputation keeping company with the tax collectors, whom they all regarded as people of a very evil character. It was enough for slander to defile Christ that he ate at the same table with that sort of people, and in their house. The Pharisees complained about it to his Disciples, and with a vanity fitting their great hypocrisy, they said to them: *Why does your Master eat with the tax collectors and sinners?* The Lord himself answered that unjust accusation: *Those who are healthy have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. Go then, and learn what it means: I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; for I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.* The Scribes and Pharisees were themselves those "righteous" ones in their own conceit, to whom the Lord had not come to bring his grace; they had too high an opinion of themselves to believe they had any need of it. It would have been giving that which is holy to the dogs, and casting pearls before swine, to preach to such conceited men self-contempt and the renunciation of their own righteousness, so that they might find salvation and life in Jesus Christ alone. But those whom Jesus had come to call, and whose hearts his Grace, triumphing over them, led to repentance, were those humble and fearful souls who, like those tax collectors and sinners, casting their eyes over the disorders of their former lives, were sighing for their salvation.

...had been at hand. The dead man, who was being taken to be buried, was a young man, the only son of a widow. Nature is moved and troubled by the death of a son, and grief—always clever at finding reasons to justify its tears in the loss of someone who is mourned—found several in this case which are only rarely met with all at once. A young man snatched away by death in the flower of his age, at a time when the most pleasant hopes were built upon him; an only son who possessed all the tenderness of a heart that cannot divide its affection among several children; and a mother and widow who feels the barely healed wound of her heart, which the death of her husband had made there, open once again; all this placed this mother in a most sorrowful state. The Lord Jesus, who saw her following her son’s bier <note>original: "doodbaar"</note> in great desolation, was moved with compassion by it, and approaching her, he said with a love that the woman could not have expected from a stranger who seemed only to be passing by by chance: *Woman, do not weep:* then turning to the bier, he touched it. Those who carried it stood still. Thereupon, he turns to the dead man, and just as if he had spoken to a living person, *Young man,* he says, *arise.* The dead man heard the voice of him who speaks to things which are no more, as if

<column-break/>

they once were; he raised himself up, and sat upright on the bier, which was a kind of open bed on which the Jews were accustomed to carry their dead to the grave, where they then placed them, wound and swaddled in a shroud, without laying them in a coffin, as we do nowadays. This young man having thus sat upright, as if he had only just awakened from a deep sleep, began to speak; and Jesus gave him back to his mother. The persons who were in this procession were terrified, and the Evangelist Luke says that *fear seized them,* because it is natural to fear when one finds oneself so close to a power whose dominion extends over death. But because that fear was also an effect of wonder, it pressed praise and glory from the mouths of that multitude for the glorification of God, who had sent such a great Prophet to his people. *Surely,* they cried, *a great Prophet has risen among us, and God has visited his people.* This miracle alone, so divine in itself and in all its circumstances, ought to have opened the eyes of all the world regarding Jesus Christ, and converted all of Judea; but the heart of man does not surrender itself so easily to such weighty truths as those of the Gospel; and a hundred miracles like that will never make a Christian, unless God, through the same power that raises the dead, works faith in the soul.

Around that time was the second Passover after the Baptism of Jesus Christ; the barley was then ripe, and the Lord walking through a field overgrown with it, his Disciples, who had become faint from being long without food, plucked some ears of grain, which they rubbed between their hands and ate the grain thereof. Since it was the day after Passover, for that reason called by the Evangelist Luke the *second-first Sabbath* <note>original: "tweede eerste Sabbath"; a technical term in the Gospel of Luke for the first Sabbath after the second day of Passover</note>, that is, the *first* of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, and the *second* in respect to the preceding day, which was a feast, being the first day of Passover, the Pharisees deemed it evil that Jesus’s Disciples ate of the first fruits of the harvest before an offering of the firstfruits had been brought into the Temple, which was not accustomed to happen until the day after. This was a difficulty which an idle superstition and a jealous desire to criticize another's conduct had caused to arise, but Christ set the law of necessity, which is above ceremonial institutions, against it, and proved this by the example of the Priest Ahimelech, also called Abiathar, who in a case of necessity had given the showbread to David and his people, which had been taken that day from the Table of the Sanctuary, and which might be eaten by no one but the Priests.

A short time later, the daughter of a man named Jairus, who was a Ruler of one of the Synagogues in Capernaum, became so ill that at every moment it was believed she lay dying. Jairus ran immediately to Jesus, and falling down at his feet, he earnestly begged him to please come and lay his hands on his daughter, who, as he said, was already dead. Upon leaving the house of Jairus, Jesus met two blind men, who having understood that it was he who was passing by, called out to him, *You Son of David, have mercy on us?* This title of *Son of David*, which these blind men gave to Christ, signifies that he was generally recognized by everyone as being descended from David. When he had come into the house where he was staying, he asked them if they believed that he could do what they requested of him; they answered, *Yes Lord*: thereupon he touched their eyes, saying *Let it be done to you according to your faith*; and immediately they received their sight again. From there he traveled through the land, and went about in all the cities and villages, leaving everywhere signs of his power and love. He was moved, seeing in those people the zeal which they showed to hear him, and he looked upon them with compassion, like sheep that were abandoned by their Shepherds. He gave his Disciples to understand that he saw a great harvest before his eyes, but that the number of laborers, who were capable of being used for it, was very small, and he commanded them that they should pray to God, the Lord of the harvest, the master of hearts and cal—

Their names are so famous in the Church that it hardly seems necessary to recount them here: but one owes them the honor of not omitting such in a History where they, next to Jesus Christ, have the greatest role to play. ## **John** the Baptist sends two of his **Disciples** from his prison to **Jesus**, to ask him if he was the **Messiah**,

### Matthew, Chapter XI. verses 2–7

<margin>The 31st year of J.C., being the 2nd of his Ministry.</margin> Since the Disciples, whom **Jesus Christ** sent out into the land of **Israel**, were not to be occupied for long with that first mission, he did not want them to take anything with them which they did not absolutely need on their way: no other garment than that which they wore on their bodies, no other shoes than those which they had on their feet, and no staff in reserve, besides the one on which they leaned while walking. He told them that everywhere they went they would find people who would take care of them, but he also gave them to understand that they would meet people everywhere who would oppose them; and from this he took the opportunity to foretell that they were to suffer persecutions when he would one day use them for a greater ministry. All of this is recounted at length by **Matthew** in the tenth chapter, which is one of those whose reading is most useful for the Church, to teach her

<column-break/>

to suffer patiently and holily.
While the twelve **Disciples** were busy preaching in the cities of **Judea**, **Christ** continued on his part with teaching in other places. **John** the Baptist was at that time imprisoned by order of **Herod** the **Tetrarch** <term>Tetrarch: a governor of one of four divisions of a country or province; in this case, a ruler of a portion of the Herodian Kingdom.</term> of **Galilee**. This Prince led an immoral life with **Herodias**, his sister-in-law; and **John**, having come through the wilderness of **Judea** into the land of **Galilee**, could not hear such an infamous relationship spoken of without publicly condemning it. When Kings have abandoned themselves to some passion, however criminal it may be, they believe it is a violation of the respect owed to their dignity if anyone remarks upon their conduct, and they want such a mixing of other matters to always be added to what is presented to them, so that under all those embellishments they can hardly recognize the vices from which one attempts to turn them away. But the zeal of **John** the Baptist, just like that of **Elijah** <note>original: "Elias"</note> formerly at the Court of **Ahab** and **Jezebel**, was incapable of such concealment. **Herod**, and even more **Herodias**, who made herself infamous by her devotion to immorality, could not tolerate the reproach and rebukes of that holy man, and therefore placed him in a dungeon.

He was, however, allowed the freedom to be visited by his disciples, who, coming to him to receive his teachings, gave him an account of the miracles with which the Lord **Jesus** filled **Judea** and **Galilee**. A hidden concern for the reputation of their master mingled with this account <note>John’s disciples were likely protective of John's status and perhaps jealous of Jesus’s growing fame.</note>. **John** had already condemned such indiscreet zeal on another occasion; but the heart is not so easily detached from a firm bond, and these Disciples, conflicted by various prejudices, did not yet dare to firmly imagine that **Jesus** was the **Messiah**. **John**, then, more to leave them in no doubt regarding this than to be perfectly instructed himself, sent two of his Disciples to **Jesus**, to learn from his own mouth whether he was the **Messiah** who was to come, or whether they were to expect another. It seems a wonderful thing that **John the Baptist** had this question put to his Head, after all he had seen of **Jesus Christ** on that day when he baptized him, and after such express testimonies as he himself had already given him. But as has been said, it was for the edification and instruction of his wavering and doubting Disciples that this holy man made such an inquiry, and not to assure himself. **Jesus**, seeing these messengers from **John the Baptist** arrive, and having heard their question, instead of answering them, turned to the sick and the possessed, who had come to be healed by him, and at the same time gave health back to the sick, delivered the possessed, and granted sight to many blind people. After he had then performed all these miracles in their presence;

<column-break/>
