Tell him that the blind see, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, and that the Gospel is proclaimed to the poor. By this gathering of so many wonders, which were all designated by the Prophet **Isaiah** in the 35th and 61st chapters of his Prophecy as the marks of the **Messiah**, **Christ** answered more powerfully to the question of **John’s** Disciples than through his words. The testimony that someone gives of himself can be suspect, but that of so many miracles cannot be so; for it is the testimony of **God** himself. After these Disciples had gone away, **Christ** gave of **John the Baptist**, of his knowledge, and of his zeal, the greatest eulogy that was ever given regarding any man. He said that of all the Prophets which the world had seen until that time, **John the Baptist** was the greatest: he praised his unshakable steadfastness and perseverance in performing his office, so that one could not accuse him of ever having shown himself fickle in anything, or of being like a reed which is moved by the wind <note>A metaphor for someone easily swayed by public opinion or hardship.</note>. He also gave this testimony to the happy effect of his preaching, that since the beginning of his ministry the Kingdom of Heaven had suffered violence, and that the violent—whose fervor arose not from blood and passions, but from a divine zeal that ignited them—had taken it: From the days of **John the Baptist** until now, he said, the Kingdom of Heaven suffers violence, and the violent take it by force <note>A difficult passage often interpreted as meaning that the Kingdom is seized by those who seek it with great spiritual urgency and effort.</note>.

However accurate the Jewish historian <note>This refers to Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), the most famous historian of the Jewish people in antiquity.</note> may have been in recounting the most remarkable events that occurred among his countrymen, he nevertheless skipped many things that one would think should not have been forgotten in his history. For example, he said nothing of the miracle which was seen in his time, or a little before, at the pool of **Bethesda**, when an Angel descended to stir the water. He remains silent on the infamous massacre of the infants in **Bethlehem**, and a hundred other similar matters that all deserved to be pointed out. He hardly mentions a word of **John the Baptist** or of **Jesus Christ**, although they both should have had the greatest part in a work intended to preserve the memory of the most remarkable things seen among that ancient people for posterity. We make this observation here only to show how absurd the conclusion is which the enemies of the Christian religion try to draw from the silence of **Josephus** regarding various matters related by our Evangelists; as if one should hold them suspect because they are not found in his books. Such are also the two histories which the Evangelist **Luke** mentions in passing in the thirteenth chapter of his Gospel, and of which **Josephus** makes no mention: namely, the death of certain **Galileans** whom **Pilate** had killed, and that of certain persons who were crushed by the fall of the **Tower of Siloam**. The first had likely just happened when the Disciples, speaking with **Christ**, brought him news of the **Galileans** whose blood **Pilate** had mixed with their sacrifices.

<column-break/>

Such a short and condensed account of a deed that caused much noise in **Jerusalem** now shows us only the cruelty of that Governor <note>Pontius Pilate, the Roman prefect of Judea.</note>, who, for his ambition or vengefulness, caused the sacrifice of who knows how many **Galileans** who had come to **Jerusalem** to offer their sacrifices to God. They were subjects of **Herod**, the Tetrarch <note>A "Tetrarch" was a governor of a fourth part of a province; Herod Antipas ruled Galilee at this time.</note> of **Galilee**; but **Pilate**, who was his enemy at that time, showed himself ready to let his vengefulness against their Prince fall upon these miserable victims whom he found, as if under his hand, in **Jerusalem**. It is not known what pretext he may have had for committing this inhumanity. Statecraft rarely lacks a cloak for Princes who make their power serve the fulfillment of their passions. The observation which **Jesus Christ** made on this act of **Pilate** was that these **Galileans** were no greater sinners than the other Jews, and that they would all, sooner or later, perish if they did not repent of their crimes. To this sad history, he added a pitiful case that had befallen some people who were no guiltier than those whom misfortune had not struck. These were eighteen persons who were crushed under the collapse of the tower of the pool of **Siloam**. *Do you suppose*, he said, *that those eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them, were debtors* <note>original: "schuldenaars" — in this context, it refers to those who owe a debt of sin to God's justice.</note> *or had angered God more than all the men who live in Jerusalem? I tell you, no: but unless you repent, you shall all likewise perish.* It is naturally difficult for us to restrain ourselves from passing a negative judgment on the virtue of those whom we see fall into heavy misfortunes; because a secret malice, which we all have, to dig into another’s faults, causes us in such instances to look for the smallest stains we can perceive; less to honor the divine justice that has punished them than to flatter ourselves with those thoughts.

## ->The Tower of Siloam crushes eighteen persons under its ruins.<-

<margin>

However accurate the Jewish historian <note>original: "Joodſche Hiſtoriſchryver" — referring to Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Roman-Jewish scholar whose works are vital for understanding first-century Judea.</note> may have been in recounting the most remarkable events that occurred among his people, he nevertheless skipped many things that one would think should not have been forgotten in his history. For example, he said nothing of the miracle seen in his time, or shortly before, at the pool of Bethesda, when an angel descended to stir the water. Christ found few good listeners, and the number of those who drew benefit from his preaching was everywhere but small: he had foreseen this long ago, and already seven or eight centuries before had complained about it in the prophecy of Isaiah. <note>The text quotes a combination of Isaiah 53:1 and 65:2.</note> *Who, he said to God his Father, has heard our preaching; and to whom is the arm of the Lord revealed: I have stretched out my hands all day long to a rebellious people, a people constantly provoking me.* In some, the fickleness of spirit and the little attention paid to the word preached to them causes it to vanish from their minds almost as soon as the sermon is finished, just like a seed which the birds pick up almost as soon as it is sown. In others is a heart of stone, a hardened heart, which nevertheless hides under an appearance of godliness, like a rock covered with a little soil: the preaching does indeed have some effect, but the ground of that heart being so bad, the word can take no root, and at the first persecution the godliness withers and the faith is lost. Others allow the word of the Gospel to be choked in their minds by an infinite multitude of matters and worldly occupations. The smallest number are those of honest and pious hearts, reborn through grace, who receive the word in their innermost being, keep it steadily, and through a public confession of the Gospel bring forth all the fruits of true faith; one, it is true, more, and another less, according as the grace is greater in the one than in the other, but all nevertheless in abundance, and they together yield fruits worthy of the holy seed that produced them.

After Jesus had given all these instructions to his Disciples, he went to **Nazareth**, where he had been brought up from his childhood, but he was received very poorly there. The memory of the lowly state in which he had always been seen in the house of **Joseph** inspired in them such a great contempt for his person that he was forced by their unbelief to depart from there quite soon, after he had healed only a few sick people.

At that time, **Herod Antipas**, son of Herod the Great and **Prince of Galilee**, prepared a

<column-break/>

banquet to celebrate the anniversary of his birth, or that of his elevation to the Government; for the Ancients gave the name of "birthday" as much to the day on which a Prince began to reign as to the day on which he was born. The **dances**, which among worldly people have always made up a part of the merriment of the greatest feasts, were not forgotten at this festival. Among those who drew attention to themselves through this art—where vanity, luxury, and many other passions unite to distract the mind and often cause dangerous impulses to creep into the heart—the **daughter of Herodias** <note>Historically known as Salome, though not named in the Gospel account.</note> excelled above all others through her skill and graceful manner.

The criminal relationship which Herod maintained with her mother made him view the dance of this daughter with more pleasure; and his heart, which was always inclined to please Herodias (who had led him astray), took the opportunity to place her under obligation. He showed her daughter such honor for a worthless thing as one could hardly have shown to the most heroic deed in the world. He told her that she should demand whatever she desired, and that he would give it to her, even if it were **half of his Kingdom**. One can well believe that there was exaggeration in this offer; but even if Herod had promised much less, it would nonetheless have been an unseemly humiliation for a Prince to be so lavish in squandering his favors for the sake of a dance that had pleased him.

# The Beheading of John the Baptist.
## Matthew, Chapter XIV. verses 8–11.

<margin>The same year.</margin>
The offer which the <term>Tetrarch: a title for a ruler of a quarter-province in the Roman Empire, in this case, Herod Antipas.</term> of Galilee made to Herodias’s daughter was too great for her not to take advantage of it. This young daughter then asked her mother for advice on what she should demand; and this wicked woman, seeing nothing in the world that could give her more pleasure than the death of John the Baptist, advised her daughter to request that Herod give her the head of that holy man, whom he had held prisoner for some time, as a gift. This request came to Herod unexpectedly; he had indeed wished John out of the world, for he was an all too strict rebuker of his irregularities; but certain considerations of propriety and worldly honor, which men possess so as not to defile themselves with deeds that could bring too great a slander upon them—and from which Sovereign Princes themselves, however powerful they may be to do as they please, do not easily dare to exempt themselves—restrained Herod, and prevented him from listening to what his thirst for revenge, ignited by the rage of his debauchery, might have inspired in him against John the Baptist. Contented then that he had put John in prison, he let him spend his life there in a despised state, entirely separated from the company of men. John preached no more, and his tongue, doomed to eternal silence, no longer disturbed the dishonorable relationship of Herod with Herodias. But just as the honor of women has something that is even more easily offended than that of men, so the resentment which they conceive against those who reproach them for their evil conduct is usually more violent and fierce, and that affront is always the last thing they for-

<column-break/>

give. Herod found himself pressed between the impulse of lust, which did not allow him to deny anything to the desire of Herodias, and the shame of having someone’s head struck off whose only crime was that he, as a true Servant of God, had rebuked the sin. In this precarious state—both for the heart, which wanted Herod to surrender without hesitation, and for the understanding and reason, which opposed it and wanted Herod to spare the life of that holy man—a wicked oath, with which this Prince had accompanied his promise, caused him to give in to the foul demand made of him. The *King*, say the Evangelists, *was saddened*, but because of the oath he had made, *and out of consideration for those who sat with him, he would not refuse her*; for possibly these guests, as subservient courtiers entangled by self-interest, favored the longing of a woman upon whom their fortune depended by some word or physical sign. Herod then granted the daughter the head of John the Baptist, and gave orders at the same time to behead him in the dungeon. Thus this holy victim is sacrificed to the revenge of a second Jezebel <note>original: "Jefábel". Jezebel was a queen in the Old Testament notorious for her wickedness and persecution of prophets; the author uses her here as a moral archetype for Herodias.</note>, dishonored by her lewd life: the executioners placed this head, the most precious that has ever been in the world next to that of Jesus Christ, on a platter; and the daughter who had demanded it receives this platter in her hands, the sight of which alone should have struck her with terror, and her mind, which had turned to crime so early, should have been pinched with such remorse that it would not depart until the end of her life. But as the mother was, so was the daughter; she looked upon the head of John as that of a monster from which she had delivered mankind, and she did not hand over that platter, the profit and trophy of her dance, except to offer it to her mother. This was, for the heart of this cruel woman, the most pleasant dish that had yet been served to her. She delighted...

### The Pool of Bethesda, and the healing of the sick man of thirty-eight years.

#### John, Chapter V. verses 2–8.

Since St. John wrote after the three other Evangelists, his Gospel contains some particulars which are not found in the others. However, one should not regard this in them as an omission, strictly speaking, for John himself would then not be free of it, since he says in a certain place that in those few years of the ministry of Jesus Christ, so many remarkable things had occurred that if one had wanted to describe them all, even the world itself would not contain those books <note>original: "de waereld zelve die boeken niet zoude vatten." This refers to the famous hyperbole at the end of the Gospel of John (21:25) regarding the extent of Jesus' deeds.</note>. God, then, willed that we should have the history of some, and that the Evangelist John in particular should relate a good number of them which are of a quite extraordinary nature. The one given here is entirely of that kind. He tells us that in Jerusalem, near the sheep gate, or sheep market, there was a certain building called <term>Bethesda: from the Hebrew "Beit Hesda," meaning House of Mercy</term> in Hebrew, as if one were to say a house of mercy, and that in the same place, near the pool, five galleries or halls were built for the convenience of the sick and the crippled. The water was brought into this pool from the same spring from which the famous stream of <term>Siloam: an ancient spring-fed pool in Jerusalem, often associated with healing</term> had its origin. This pool might at first have been intended for many services for the convenience of the inhabitants; but the Evangelist John mentions nothing of that, as it was a matter of little concern to the Church...

<column-break/>

...had made thunder. The disciples of John, who had continually come to visit their master in prison, having heard of his death, came to fetch his body and buried it.

---

...and he gives us an account of a certain miracle which happened in that pool and was seen nowhere else. This was that at certain times—whether those were set times or not—the water of this pool was seen to be suddenly troubled and moved in a very singular manner, and that the first sick person who was then dipped into it was immediately made healthy, of whatever disease he was afflicted with. It was an Angel who made this violent disturbance in the water, and who brought this supernatural power to heal all kinds of ailments down from Heaven. But since God, who is free in all His favors, does not extend them further than it pleases Him, He had willed to limit the effect of this pool to the first who entered the water, and not extended it to others who might enter after him. Since we know nothing of this miracle except solely through the account of John, and since that Apostle has not informed us further about it, it is impossible to say when it began and when it ended. It is probable that this miracle did not last long, and that if it had its beginning some years before the ministry of Jesus Christ, it would have ceased around the time of His ministry. What is strange in this case (for one need not conceal it) is that neither <term>Josephus: Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian whose works provide much of our knowledge of 1st-century Judea.</term> nor any other Jewish writer mentions anything of these miraculous healings which occurred in this pool. But besides the fact that the silence of writers is not in itself a sufficient reason against the account which a reputable historian gives of a matter that happened in his time; the Jews have perhaps intentionally kept a deep silence regarding...

A few days later, Jesus found him in the Temple and made himself known to him, for Jesus had slipped away unnoticed from the multitude of people when he had healed him; and he spoke these words to him, so remarkable for all sinners to whom God has shown grace: *See, you have become well; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you.*

### John, Chapter VI. verses 10–13.

The Jews, superstitious to the highest degree regarding the keeping of the Sabbath day, were offended because they saw the paralyzed man walking on that day with his little bed in his hands; for they believed that the smallest thing which one carried was a profanation of the Sabbath. Jesus Christ defended the act of that man, and his own, and on that occasion held a conversation with them in which he showed that he had received all power from his Father, and that being his own Son, and God as well as he, he would be the general Judge of the world

<column-break/>

on the day of the general Resurrection of the good and the evil, foretold in the 12th chapter of Daniel and believed in all ages of the Church. He pointed the unbelieving Jews to the testimony which John the Baptist had given of him, whom he calls a burning and shining lamp <note>original: "kaers," literally "candle," but historically used to translate the Greek 'lychnos' (lamp) in John 5:35</note>, at whose radiance all Judea had wondered and rejoiced; and he gave them to understand that they could also learn the same from Moses, who had likewise spoken of him and pointed to him in his prophecies.

<margin>the year 32 of J. C., the 2nd of his ministry.</margin>
After this discourse which Christ gave in Jerusalem, the Evangelist John relates the miracle of the multiplication of the loaves, which occurred a little before his third Passover, a year before his death. He had crossed the Sea of Tiberias, and many people having followed him, he went with his disciples up a mountain, where all the people followed him to bring many sick, all of whom he healed.

But since it was already late, and it was a long way from that mountain to the places where these people—who were already weary from the journey—could find something to eat, Christ was moved with compassion for them. He did not want to put them in danger of any mishaps that might have befallen them on their return. He then asked Philip, one of his disciples whose faith he wished to test, where one could obtain enough bread in that wilderness to feed such a great multitude. Philip answered him that even if one ran to the surrounding villages to buy two hundred pennies' <note>original: "penningen," referring to denarii</note> worth of bread (or about sixty guilders of our modern currency <note>The author is providing a 17th or 18th-century equivalent for his contemporary readers</note>), there would still not be enough to give everyone even a small piece. Andrew, the brother of Peter, then said that there was a young boy who had five barley loaves and two small fish; but, he added, what are these among so many? Jesus commanded that all the people should sit down in small groups or companies. He then took the loaves and blessed them; afterward, he broke them, and the disciples took them from his hands and distributed them along with the fish to all these groups. They all ate until they were satisfied, and after the meal, so much bread was left over that twelve baskets were filled with it. Everyone was so amazed by the greatness of this miracle that they did not doubt that Jesus was the Messiah: "This is truly the Prophet," they said, "who was to come into the world."

Jesus Christ crossed the sea again and arrived at Capernaum. Those who had followed him on the mountain also came to him; and since they had not seen him go aboard a ship to cross with his disciples, and therefore believed he had taken a long detour by land, they were very surprised to see him there so soon. Addressing him, they said, "Master, when

<column-break/>

did you come here?" Jesus rebuked them, saying that they did not have such a great longing except out of a vain curiosity to see him perform miracles, or out of a desire to eat of the loaves, like those he had miraculously multiplied on the mountain. He took this opportunity to exhort them to have higher thoughts and more spiritual feelings; he spoke to them of a bread whose excellence he exalted infinitely above that of the Manna with which God had fed their fathers in the wilderness, and which he said had come down from Heaven to give life to the world. These coarse and earthly people understood nothing of what he spoke to them and said to him, "Lord, give us this bread always," with just as great an ignorance as the Samaritan woman who, when Christ spoke to her of a water that would quench thirst forever, had said: "Lord, give me that water, so that I no longer need to come to draw from this fountain." The Lord Jesus answered these ignorant Jews that he himself was this bread of life of which he spoke, and that everyone who ate of that bread would have eternal life, and that he would raise him up on the last day. People were amazed to hear Christ say that he would give himself to be eaten: understanding without faith is blind in the mysteries of salvation. Jesus answered that his words must be taken in a spiritual sense if one wished to find life in them, and that the eating of his flesh would not benefit them if he were to give it to them in such a sense as they imagined. "The words that I speak to you are spirit and life; and my body is set to be carried from the earth to Heaven. Does this offend you? What would it be, then, if you saw the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?"

### Peter, seeing Jesus walking on the sea, steps out at his word from the little ship to go to him over the waves, but begins to sink.

### Matthew, Chapter XIV. verses 24--31.

<margin>The 32nd year of J. C. and the 3rd of his ministry.</margin>
Before Jesus Christ held that conversation before the crowd of people who had gathered around him at Capernaum, which one reads in the same chapter of the Evangelist John, he had given a command to his disciples that they should go aboard a ship and cross the sea. They could hardly bring themselves to do so because he was not going with them, and they could not live without him. But they had to yield to his will; for obedience is always the principal thing in religion. They then entered a small ship and sailed to the other shore, where they hoped Jesus would come to them. The Lord, after they had departed, finding himself alone as he had desired, climbed a nearby mountain to be there in his solitude and to enter into conversation with his Father through prayer, as well as to avoid the multitude of people, knowing (as the Evangelist John says) that they would come to make him King by force. Meanwhile, his disciples had set

<column-break/>

sail, and their little ship was already in the open sea when night fell upon them. Around four or five o'clock in the morning, which is the time the Evangelist Matthew denotes by the name of the *fourth watch of the night* <note>The Jews had by then adopted the custom from the Romans of dividing the twelve hours of the night into four watches of three hours each</note>, the disciples happened to look out from the deck by chance and without any particular intent, as travelers are accustomed to do, especially around those hours. They saw a man appearing from afar, walking on the waves, and keeping almost the same course as their vessel. They were troubled at the sight of this object, and immediately imagining that it was some ghost <note>original: "spooksel," meaning a phantom or spirit</note>, they gave a great cry because of the fear that seized them. This supposed ghost meanwhile continued on its way, and when it had come a little closer, they saw it stepping a bit faster slightly to the side of them, as if to pull ahead of them. Captured then by that first thought that it was a ghost—because it is an unheard-of thing for a man to walk on water—they did not even think of Jesus, who had given them no indication of his intention, and whom they still believed to be on land. Such is the power of prejudices; they bind the human understanding so strongly to the subjects they present to it, that it is not able to turn its sight elsewhere, and its...

The greatest Saints are nothing as long as they have no faith, and they have cause to fear in all circumstances as soon as they stand on their own alone. When Jesus was in the vessel, the sea, which had been troubled the whole night, began to calm, and the wind died down. The crew and the travelers who were crossing with the Disciples, enraptured with wonder at the rarities <note>In this context, "rarities" refers to miraculous or extraordinary events.</note> which they had seen, came to throw themselves down at the feet of Jesus and worshipped him, saying, *Truly, thou art the Son of God*. ## The Canaanite Woman.
### Matthew, Chapter XV. verse 22–28.

<margin>The 32nd year of J. C. <note>Jesus Christ</note> which was the 3rd of his ministry.</margin>
Jesus having returned to Upper Galilee, people brought him the sick from all sides, many of whom were healed by merely touching the hem of his garment. But some Pharisees who had come from Jerusalem to Galilee reproached him for allowing his Disciples to eat without first having washed their hands, which they regarded as a crime in religion, because their tradition dictated that if one consumed pure foods with unwashed hands, these foods thereby became unclean, just as

<column-break/>

those which were forbidden by the laws of Moses. But Christ closed the mouths of those hypocrites by convincing them that they nullified God's commandments through their traditions and ordinances. God had commanded children to honor their father and mother—that is, not only to show them reverence but also to help them in all necessary matters; and they, to the detriment of that law which has its foundation even in Nature, exempted from that duty a son who had made a vow of his goods to the Temple or for some other religious use; and they called this the <term>Korban</term> <note>original: "Korban," a Hebrew word meaning a gift or offering dedicated to God</note>, or the promised gift. In this way, they intended that a son whose father was poor and in need of assistance might freely say to him, *That which might have been of use to you from me is a gift, I have vowed it*,

...and may no longer touch it. <meta>This completes a sentence regarding the Pharisaic laws of ritual purity mentioned on the preceding page.</meta> He subsequently gave his Disciples to understand that it was not eating without having washed the hands—which made the food one consumed unclean—nor anything of that which enters into a person’s body as necessary nourishment, provided it was used moderately and with thanksgiving; but that it is the evil thoughts and the evil desires that arise in the heart, and manifest themselves in words and deeds, which defile people and make them guilty. Jesus then departed from the region of Gennesaret, where he was then located, to go deeper into Galilee to the borders of Tyre and Sidon. He wanted his arrival there to be kept secret, out of that great humility which made him shun the rumors and the multitude of people; but his fame, which traveled everywhere before him, immediately sounded out the news of his arrival. A woman of that land, a Heathen <note>A Gentile, specifically a Syrophoenician or Canaanite woman, not of the Jewish faith.</note> by birth and religion, had a daughter who was possessed by the Devil; and upon the favorable reports that had spread about Jesus Christ, she emboldened herself—though she was an absolute stranger to God’s people—to go and request the healing of her daughter from him. *Lord*, she cried out to him, *thou son of David, have mercy on me; my daughter is grievously possessed by the Devil.* Jesus, usually so kind-hearted and gentle toward all persons who came to make such requests of him, at first showed nothing but indifference and disregard toward this unfortunate mother; He did not answer her a word. Nevertheless, she did not lose hope of being heard, but continuing alongside the Disciples and following him, she did not stop speaking the same words,

<column-break/>

until the Disciples became annoyed by it. It vexes a person quickly when he constantly hears one and the same request in his ears, and he calls such a thing a nuisance: but God loves nothing so much as such a holy stubbornness of faith <note>The author uses "holy stubbornness" (heylige hardnekkigheyd) to describe persistent, unyielding prayer.</note> to never cease one's request, and it is to that perseverance that he allows his blessing to be snatched from him. Christ then finally answered this Canaanite woman, but he did so in such a manner that seemed more intended to rebuff her than to encourage her. *I am not sent*, he said to her, *but unto the lost sheep of the house of Israel, and you are a stranger.* Her faith told her that Jesus was master of his graces, and that his love was too great to be so narrowly limited to the blood of Abraham <note>Referring to the Jewish people as descendants of the patriarch Abraham.</note> that only those who were of that blessed lineage could have a share in it. Despite that answer, she then came to Jesus Christ, and throwing herself down at his feet, she said to him, *Lord help me.* But it is not fitting, the Lord said to her, *to take the children's bread, and to cast it to the dogs.* It is true, Lord, she replied, *yet the dogs also eat of the crumbs which fall from their masters' table.* Christ marveled at this answer. *O Woman*, he cried out, *great is thy faith: be it unto thee even as thou wilt:* and at that hour her daughter was delivered. Everything was great in the conduct of this Canaanite woman: her perseverance, her humility, her hope, her zeal; but Jesus praised only her faith, because it was the source and origin of all other virtues, which are always more or less lively in a soul, according to whether faith is more or less great or deep-rooted there.

## The Transfiguration.

### Matthew, Chapter XVII. verses 1—7.

<margin>
† 32nd year of J. C. <note>Jesus Christ</note> and the 3rd of his ministry.
</margin>
Jesus returned from the borders of Tyre and Sidon again along the Sea of Galilee, and after healing many blind, lame, deaf, and others with infirmities there, he once again fed four thousand people with seven loaves of bread, and then departed from there by ship to the land of Dalmanutha in Upper Galilee, bordering Decapolis <note>A group of ten cities on the eastern frontier of the Roman Empire</note>. He found Pharisees there who desired of him, as others had already done before, that he would show them some sign in the sky. Such an unreasonable request, which—after the great number of miracles he performed daily and in all places—could be nothing other than the effect of matchless unbelief, made him sigh deeply, and he dismissed them, as he had done the others, until after his resurrection. He came from there again into Lower Galilee, and commanded his Disciples to beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which was their teaching and tradition; and of the leaven of the Sadducees, which is called the *leaven of Herod* by the Evangelist Mark, because that Prince, being very lustful and living as one who believes in no other life after this, could in essence have no other sentiments than those of the Sadducees, who denied the immortality of the soul and the resurrection of the body. From there, our Savior went again to Upper Galilee, and went to the region of the city of Caesarea, which was named after Philip <note>Caesarea Philippi</note>, and was situated near Mount Lebanon. Some days later he took Peter, James, and John with him, and brought them up a high mountain. It is generally believed that it was Mount Tabor, but just as one could not easily prove that opinion, so also there is so little at stake in contradicting it, that it

<column-break/>

is not worth the trouble to dwell upon it. When they had come to the place where Christ intended to go, such a wonderful change was suddenly perceived in his person that the Evangelists say he was changed in appearance <note>Original: "van gedaante veranderd," often translated as "transfigured"</note>. The body of Jesus Christ, it is true, remained the same as it was, and lost nothing of its human form, but it was surrounded by such great glory that the earth had never beheld anything like it in a body of flesh. His face shone like the sun, and his clothes became white as snow, and glittering like the light. At that moment Heaven opened, and Moses and Elijah descended from there to speak with Christ. Elijah had his own body with which he had been carried to Heaven in a fiery chariot: Moses had laid his down on the earth, and as if in God's hands, who alone and without human help had given him a burial: but God provided him with another, whether made of air or of nothing <note>The author is speculating on the nature of Moses’s appearance, as Moses died in the Old Testament while Elijah was taken up alive</note>, for that time that this Prophet was to be with Christ on the mountain. The Holy Scripture does not say how these two Prophets were recognized by the Disciples of Jesus; it could be that it was from their words, but it could also be that the three Apostles understood this from the mouth of Christ. Peter, struck by a spectacle capable of drawing the gaze of the Angels toward it, immediately cried out with his usual alertness of spirit: *Lord, it is good that we are here; let us make three tabernacles here, one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah*; but Mark and Luke give us to understand that Peter *did not know what he was saying*; for his mind being enraptured by wonder, his heart alone, without direction or enlightenment, made his tongue speak. Scarcely had Peter finished these words when there appeared a glittering cloud that overshadowed them all, and out of the midst of that cloud, which was like the throne of God, came a loud

### The parable of a King who settles accounts with his servants for what they owe him.

### Matthew, Chapter XVIII. verses 23 — 34

<margin>The same year. Toward the end</margin>
There is hardly anything regarding which self-love is more sensitive than wrongdoing. The heart helps the memory remember a crime; and a sincere forgiveness, especially if it

<column-break/>

The Apostle Peter was, regarding that matter, in that preoccupation with which the heart so flutters itself: that if someone whom we have already forgiven once comes to offend us again, he makes himself unworthy of forgiveness. how he should conduct himself henceforth. "Lord," he said to him, "*how many times shall my brother, or as we might say in general, anyone, sin against me, and I forgive him? Up to seven times?*" He meant to ask if there should not be some limit in that matter. Christ answered him no, but that one must forgive as often as one was offended, "*I say unto you, not seven times, but seventy times seven.*" Yet, to provide a detailed teaching on such a weighty subject, Christ added a parable, in which he expressed his thoughts in a very vivid manner, capable of instilling a powerful impression in anyone. "*A certain King*," he said, "*wished to settle accounts with his servants; among them all was one who owed him ten thousand talents.*" This sum, which is very large and astonishing (for it amounts to nearly fifteen million <note>The author likely calculates this based on 18th-century Dutch guilders; a 'talent' was the highest unit of currency in the ancient world, representing an astronomical debt.</note>), is set here to represent an immeasurable sum which an ordinary person could never pay. This man, seeing himself unable to satisfy the debt, took refuge in the King's mercy, who generously cleared him of his debt. But this debtor—so fortunate to have found such compassion in his creditor as he could never have expected—met upon leaving one of his fellow servants who owed him a hundred Denarii (or shillings according to the Dutch currency <note>original: "fchellingen volgens de Hollándfche munt"</note>), being a sum that was in no way comparable to that which he himself had been forgiven; and he demanded payment with such hard-heartedness that he threatened to choke him if he did not pay him immediately. The man, seized with fear, fell down at his feet before him and begged him to have patience, promising to pay everything. This rude man would listen to nothing, but threw his debtor into prison, there

<column-break/>

to spend his time in misery until he should have paid him. The King, having heard of this dealing, immediately summoned the servant whom he had forgiven his entire debt, and said to him: 
"You scoundrel that you are, I forgave you all that great debt because you begged me to have compassion on you: should you then not also have had mercy on your fellow servant, who begged you on his knees, and owed you only a very small sum?" The King, being then wroth, had him seized and led to prison, with the command that he should not be let out until he had paid the very last penny. "*So*," Jesus Christ continued, "*shall also my Heavenly Father do unto you, if you do not each from the heart forgive his brother his trespasses.*" The end of this parable, where one sees a King who withdraws the favor previously shown to a servant, might lead one to think that God indeed revokes the forgiveness he has granted someone for their sins. But God's forgiveness is fundamentally irrevocable, because it always rests upon the merit of Jesus Christ, of which a believer, once that merit is applied to them, is never deprived. One must therefore consider that this is a parable, and that one must never draw anything further from a parable than the ideas that naturally serve the purpose for which it was spoken. This idea of a revoked forgiveness is only fitting here to connect the literal sense together. And regarding the moral or hidden sense, that rests entirely on the conclusion that Christ draws from it: namely, that God will not forgive us our sins if we do not forgive and release those who have offended us from all grounds of complaint we might have against them.

***

### Little children are brought to Jesus, upon whose heads he lays his hands.
#### Matthew, Chapter XIX. verses 13-15.

<margin>Around the end of the 3rd year of the Ministry of J.C.</margin>
The greatest part of the discourses and conversations of Jesus Christ took place in Galilee, but he also often came to Judea, and to Jerusalem, so that there would be no city of the Jews where he did not make himself known. After he had given the teachings recounted in the previous history, to recommend the forgiveness of wrongs, he went from Galilee, where he then was, to the borders of Judea, along the Jordan, and much people followed him. He had no sooner arrived there than some Pharisees came to ask him a cunning question, with the intent to ensnare him. It concerned divorce, a subject hateful in itself, and over which the two principal schools of Judea—namely those of Hillel and Shammai <note>Hillel and Shammai were famous rival rabbis; Hillel's school was generally more liberal, while Shammai's was more conservative.</note>—were at odds with one another. The latter maintained that a man could not divorce his wife except for adultery; and the former claimed that one was permitted to do so for much lesser matters, such as some unseemly words or deeds that a man had heard his wife speak or seen her do. Indeed, according to the principles of that school, the freedom of divorce was extended much further, and it had come to such excess that a woman some-

<column-break/>

times saw herself cast out by her husband solely because of some displeasure in the household. Christ answered the Pharisees by drawing the matter back to the first institution of marriage, and he showed that in view of that holy institution—which was established by God himself in the earthly Paradise when he united man and woman such that he made of two persons but one—there was nothing but adultery which could lawfully break that union. During this conversation, several small children were brought to him, so that he might give them his blessing by laying his hands on their heads, according to the custom of that nation. This custom was derived from the Patriarch Jacob, who, wishing to give his blessing on his deathbed to Ephraim and Manasseh, the two sons of Joseph, had them approach and laid his hands upon their heads. Because the crowd was large, and Jesus may have been tired, his disciples—for these or similar reasons—sought to hold back those who brought these children to him. The disciples did this not out of hardheartedness or a lack of love, but human reasoning and a certain mistaken concern for their Master led them to deny this comfort to those fathers who

Our Savior, noticing this, commanded that they should not be hindered. *“Let the little children,”* he said, *“come to me, for of such as these—those who are like children—is the Kingdom of Heaven.”* It is a right given by birth to children born into God's covenant. The children of the Faithful are, according to the words of the Apostle Paul, holy. If they, then, despite the original sin with which they are born, are children of the covenant and sons of the Kingdom, then the Sacrament which serves as the entrance and the visible sign—Circumcision under the Law, and Baptism under the Gospel—also rightfully belongs to them. Thereupon, Christ had those little children brought to him, and having laid his hands upon them, he gave them his blessing.

### A rich Young Man who had come to Christ, goes away from him sorrowful.

### Matthew, Chapter XIX. vers. 16--22.

<margin>The same year being the 32nd of Jesus Christ, toward the end.</margin> AFTER Christ had blessed the children who had been brought to him, he crossed the Jordan and took his way toward the city of Jericho. A young man, whom the Evangelist Luke calls a *Ruler* <note>The Dutch "Oversten" refers to a person of high social standing or a magistrate.</note>, came to meet him, to request that he might tell him what he must do to be saved. This behavior was fine and excellent in someone of that age who was very wealthy. It is a rare thing to find such inclinations in persons who have every opportunity they could wish for to satisfy their desires, and to whom the world presents itself with all its charms. It was not out of an

<column-break/>

idle ambition that this young Gentleman came to ask that question of Christ; his conduct was undoubtedly sincere, since he dared to answer Christ that he had been careful from his youth to keep the commandments of God. This is even more certain since Mark relates that the Lord, casting his eyes upon him, *loved* him; for that is a sure proof that he was no hypocrite who possessed only sham virtues. Upon addressing Christ, he gave him the title of *good*: “*Good Master*,” he said, “*what shall I do that I may inherit eternal life?*” The Lord Jesus caught him at that word, and as if he had wanted to rebuke him for giving him that title: “*Why do you call me good?*” he said, “*none is good but God.*” This was not a reprimand, but it was a lesson to teach him that Jesus was not merely a sensible and wise Teacher, as that young man had intended to imply by calling him good; but that he also

After this first passing admonition, Jesus added to it, *If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments.* This answer agreed with the style of the Prophets and the Law, whose general conclusion was: *Do these things, and you shall live.* The young man did not even seem upset by this saying; he only asked Christ which commandments he meant. The Lord named the Ten Commandments to him, and especially those of the second Table <note>The "Second Table" of the Ten Commandments refers to the laws governing human relationships, such as honoring parents and forbidding murder or theft.</note>: *Honor your father and mother; You shall not kill,* and the others. He only meant to say that until that time he had been of blameless conduct, and during his entire life had been diligent in keeping God's Law. Christ, looking upon this young Lord, and especially beholding him through the light of his Divinity, did not reproach him as a hypocrite or a conceited person; he satisfied himself by telling him that one thing still failed him, which was to immediately rid himself of all his goods and give them to the poor; *Then come hither,* he said, *and follow me.* Possibly this was the only thing which this Rich man was unable to do for

<column-break/>

his salvation, and it will also have been for this reason that Jesus proposed it to him; to show us thereby that often no more than one weakness is needed in a man to cause him to be lost, and that the world does not exactly need to hold the heart fast from all sides to prevent it from lifting itself up to God; but that it is enough if it is held strongly by one thing alone. The young man felt the sting with which Christ's words had struck him in the heart, and he went away sorrowful, because he had many possessions. He would gladly have gone to Heaven, but his wealth served as a counterweight to keep him on the earth; and being unable to decide to buy eternal life with the loss of all his goods, nor to amuse and please himself henceforth, as before, with his wealth, he went away sorrowful and quite dejected. Christ then made this remark to his Disciples: that it was very difficult, and almost impossible—especially in those first times when the Church had none but a humbled and abased <note>Original Dutch: *vernietigden*, meaning "brought to nothing" or "emptied," likely referencing the theological concept of *kenosis* or Christ's humility.</note> Jesus as its leader—that rich and powerful persons should enter into the Church, which he called the Kingdom of Heaven, and consequently into Heaven, which is the pinnacle of that Kingdom. *Truly, I say to you that a rich man shall hardly enter into the Kingdom of Heaven. It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the Kingdom of God:* for that, an extraordinary grace from God is required, for whom nothing is impossible.

## The Lord Jesus teaches the Jews in Jerusalem at the Feast of Tabernacles
### John, Chapter VII. verses 14, 15.

<margin>The 33rd year of J. C., which was the 4th and final year of his ministry.</margin>

THE Feast of Tabernacles <note>Also known as Sukkot, a major Jewish autumn festival commemorating the protection of the Israelites in the wilderness.</note> was one of the three great High Festivals for which the Jews were required to travel annually from all the cities of Palestine to Jerusalem to celebrate. Jesus Christ was in Galilee at the time this Feast occurred, which was around the middle of September <note>Original Dutch: *Herffstmaand*, literally "Autumn-month."</note>; and this month of which we speak here, in which the events related in the seventh chapter of the Evangelist John took place, was the one just preceding the Passover at which the Lord Jesus was crucified. His kinsmen suggested that he go with them to Jerusalem; but he had certain reasons to refuse this, and to wait with that journey until they had departed. Because he did not arrive there for that reason during the first days of the Feast, which lasted an entire week, the Jews in Jerusalem asked one another if they knew whether he would come there. Everyone was in great anticipation to see him there, some out of curiosity, and others from a motive of piety and zeal. Opinions were divided concerning him: some maintained that he was a good man and a true Prophet; others, conversely, held him to be a Deceiver. After the Feast was about half over, Jesus arrived, and having gone to the Temple, he delivered an excellent discourse there. His listeners were amazed to hear him speak with such profound understanding, so that they asked each other in total astonishment, *How does this man know the scriptures, since he has never learned them?* They meant to say that he had not studied at their Schools. Jesus answered that it was from God himself, whose Envoy he was, that he had received his

<column-break/>

knowledge and science: *My doctrine*, namely that profound and weighty manner of teaching, *is not mine, but his, namely my Father's, who sent me*. He complained to the Jews about the contempt they showed for his word, and about the intention they had to take his life. They took great offense at this and told him that he was a slanderer: *You have a devil; who seeks to kill you?* They did not know that Jesus read their hearts. It was held against him as a crime that he had made a paralytic <note>Original: *beroerden*, referring to the infirm man healed at the Pool of Bethesda on a previous Sabbath.</note> walk on the Sabbath. He defended himself against the injustice of this complaint by the example of Circumcision, which they had no difficulty performing on that day when it happened to be the eighth after the child's birth, so as not to transgress the Law which commanded that children be circumcised on the eighth day. At this, a great murmur arose among the people; some said that Jesus was not the Messiah because he was from Galilee, and that the Messiah must come from Bethlehem; and the others, without exposing the error of that prejudice, appealed to the great number of his miracles: *When the Christ comes, they said, will he do more signs than these which this man has done?* Two or three days later, on the last and great day of the Feast, Jesus went again to the Temple and began to cry out before all the people: *If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink: he who believes in me, as the Scripture says, streams of living water shall flow from his belly;* that is, from his innermost being and from the depths of his heart. And this he said, as the Evangelist notes, *of the Spirit which those who believe in him would receive*. He expressed himself in such figurative terms because on that day the Jews went with great solemnity to draw water from the pool of Siloam, and they called that ceremony *drawing the Holy Spirit*, referring back to the words from the twelfth...

The entire Sanhedrin <term>Sanhedrin: the supreme council and tribunal of the Jews in Jerusalem, acting as both a court and a religious leadership body.</term> was highly amazed to see that there was one of their Councilmen who gave such foolish advice regarding someone whom they all regarded as a false Messiah, and they expressed their astonishment to him in words that were somewhat veiled, yet fundamentally very sharp: *Are you also from Galilee?* they said to him. Nicodemus could indeed have been from that land; but whether he was or not, it was a silent reproach made to him, that he had little understanding, for the Galileans passed among the other Jews for unrefined people. *Search the Scriptures*, they added further, *and see, that no Prophet has arisen out of Galilee.* One is greatly deceived if one believes that they spoke broadly of all Prophets, whoever they might have been; they could not be ignorant that Jonah and Nahum had been Galileans: and besides that, what did it matter to them whether or not there had formerly been a Prophet from Galilee? Their intent was then only to convince Nicodemus that Jesus could be nothing but a false Messiah, because he was from Nazareth in Galilee, and that it appeared clearly through the Scriptures that the Messiah was to come not from Galilee, but from Bethlehem. Meanwhile, the Sanhedrin dismissed that time without deciding anything against Christ: the time of his death had not yet come; and God never allowed anything in the world to happen against His decrees.

While these things took place in the Sanhedrin, Jesus Christ left Jerusalem and went to the Mount of Olives. The next day, early in the morning, he came again into the city and went to the Temple. Immediately a great many people gathered there, and as Jesus was busy teaching them the truths of salvation, the Scribes and Pharisees brought to him a woman who had been caught in adultery, so that he might pronounce his judgment upon her. *Master*, they said to him, *this woman was caught in the very act, committing adultery; and Moses commanded us in the Law that such shall be stoned; what then do you say to it?* This was a snare deliberately set

<column-break/>

to plunge him into his ruin: for if he had answered that the woman must be stoned, then he would first have contradicted himself, because he had already declared on several occasions that he had not come to judge anyone: And secondly, he would have shown therein a great ignorance of the Law, which, commanding the punishment of stoning against adulterous women, speaks only of those who were as yet only betrothed, and of the others, whose marriage was already consummated, simply commands in general to kill them. <note>The author highlights a legal distinction: under Mosaic law, stoning was the specific penalty for a betrothed woman caught in adultery, whereas "death" (by other means) was the general penalty for a married woman. The Pharisees' question was designed to test Jesus's specific legal expertise.</note> On the other hand, if Christ gave no judgment in a matter so shameful and wicked as that of adultery, they would have accused him of not being a Prophet, much less the Messiah, since he refused to uphold the holiness of their laws by his judgment. Christ immediately noticed the cunning of this whole affair, which is why instead of answering the question put to him, he bent down to the floor of the Temple and wrote with his finger in the dust or sand. They asked him the same question once more, and having raised himself a little, he answered the Scribes and Pharisees who urged him for a judgment: *He among you who is without sin, let him first cast the stone at her.* After which, bending down, he continued to write in the dust. There is great probability that the Lord Jesus silently reproached the Pharisees and Scribes with the same crime, or other sins of impurity, for which they wanted this sinner condemned. Their conscience awakened at these words, and gnawed by remorse, they all went out ashamed, one after the other, and left the woman they had brought standing in the Temple. Jesus then raising himself, and seeing none of the accusers around him, turned to this woman and said to her: *Where are these accusers of yours? Has no one condemned you?* No one, Lord, she answered. *Neither do I condemn you*, said Christ, *go your way, and sin no more.* Thus our Savior wisely evaded the snare that had been set for him, and the woman obtained, along with her freedom, the forgiveness of her crime.

It is well known that their knowledge was by no means *pure* and without flaws until after the descent of the fire of the **Pentecost** <term>Pentecost: A Christian festival celebrating the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles, fifty days after Easter.</term>; and it may well have been a prejudice of their Schools, where it was taught that the souls of children before their birth were capable of certain passions and inclinations that were sins. <note>This refers to contemporary theological debates about the pre-existence of souls or the possibility of "fetal sin" in some Jewish traditions of the time.</note> However that may have been, our Savior did not pass judgment on that supposition, the settlement of which was of no great importance; but wishing only to combat with his reasoning that other prejudice, which so easily creeps into our minds—that the extraordinary disasters that befall someone are proof that he is uncommonly wicked—he answered them thus: *Neither has this man sinned, nor his parents, that he should be born blind; but this happened so that the works of God might be revealed in him.* He then made a sort of clay with his spittle and the dust of the earth, with which he anointed the eyes of the blind man; and then he commanded him to go and wash himself in the pool of **Siloam**. <note>The Pool of Siloam was a rock-cut ritual reservoir in Jerusalem.</note> The blind man went away and returned with good eyes. This miracle caused a great stir in Jerusalem; but the Scribes and **Pharisees** <term>Pharisees: A strict Jewish sect known for their rigorous adherence to traditional and written law.</term>, envious to the highest degree of the fame of Jesus Christ, attempted by all means to rob him of the honor of such a great miracle. They had the blind man brought before them to learn from him whether it was true that he had been born blind and to find out by what means he had recovered his sight. This investigation was fair and necessary for people who sat at the head of the Government, had they acted in good faith and solely to be assured of the truth: but this was not what they wanted to know; on the contrary, they sought nothing other than to obscure the truth and to pass it off as a fable and a deception among the

<column-break/>

people. The man born blind gave them a straightforward account of the manner in which Jesus had given him his sight; *He laid, he said, clay upon my eyes, and said to me, Go away to the pool of Siloam, and wash: and I washed myself, and I see.* At such a clear declaration there was nothing to say, and the deed could not be contradicted. But because that healing had occurred on the day of the **Sabbath**, the Pharisees emphasized that circumstance and accused Christ of having violated the holiness of that day by making clay and anointing the eyes of the blind man with it. *This man is not from God, they said, for he does not keep the Sabbath: we know that this man is a sinner.* The man born blind, on the other hand, said that he was a Prophet. They then summoned his parents to draw something from their declaration with which they might counter that of the son. They asked them if he was their son, if he was born blind, and by what means he had obtained his sight. These people answered that it was true that he was their son and that he had been blind all his life, but that they did not know how he came by his sight; yet that they might ask him himself, since he had come of age to be able to answer that question. Fear prevented these poor people from saying more: for it had already been decided in the **Sanhedrin** <term>Sanhedrin: The supreme judicial and religious council of the Jewish people in Jerusalem.</term> to banish <note>This refers to "the ban" or excommunication from the synagogue, which carried heavy social and religious penalties.</note> those who declared themselves too openly for Jesus. The man born blind was bolder than his parents, as he was more sensitive to the grace he had received than they were. The Pharisees then took him to task regarding the declaration in which he persisted, that Jesus had given him his sight; and whatever they might say to make him afraid, he nevertheless declared to them that he could not believe that Jesus was an evil man and a deceiver, because God is too zealous for his honor to give to a deceiver and a false Messiah the power to give—

THE miraculous healing of the man born blind ought to have opened the eyes of the entire Synagogue, to make them confess that Jesus was the Messiah; but there is no sign that penetrates into the darkness of a mind that God has surrendered to its own prejudices. *I have come into this world for a judgment*, said Christ on that subject, *so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.* By the former he understood the common folk, those lowly and simple ones whom the Scribes and Pharisees looked upon with the greatest contempt from the height of their knowledge; and by the others whom he represents as enlightened men, he meant those same Scribes and Pharisees, who made a vain boast of their knowledge, and believed themselves alone to be wise and alone to be learned in the world. Meanwhile, it was those simple and unlettered people to whom God gave to know that Jesus was his Son and the Savior of the world

<column-break/>

was; while the others, with all their cleverness and great knowledge, did not recognize him, and presented themselves with a thousand delusions so as not to see the most visible thing in the world. Some of them hearing Christ speak thus, asked him whether he then also included them among the number of those whom he called blind. He answered them, that they were only the more unfortunate for having eyes, as they said, and keeping them closed, as they indeed did. *If you were blind you would have no sin*, that is, they would have been less criminal if they had rejected him for lack of knowledge and science; *but now you say, We see; so your sin remains*, which you commit by rejecting me as a false Messiah, always upon you, and it shall never be forgiven you. Our Savior subsequently said that he was the Good Shepherd, and that all the others who had come before him (meaning by those words the Priests and Teachers of the Law) were intruders and hirelings, who only aimed for their own interest and not the welfare of the flock. Their mission was nonetheless according to the usual way, antiquity, and the orderly succession; nothing was lacking for them: but since they no longer preached the truth, and that they deviated from the most essential ground of Religion, from the sense of the Law and the Prophets, so Christ spoke of them as false Shepherds, who did not enter through the door into the

Shortly after Christ had spoken all these words, the day of the <term>Feast of Dedication: Known today as Hanukkah, this festival commemorates the rededication of the Second Temple in Jerusalem.</term> of the Temple arrived, which was celebrated in Jerusalem in the <note>original: "Wintermaand," referring to December</note>. Because this High Feast drew many people to Jerusalem, Christ took that opportunity to instruct the people, who came there from various places in Judea. The Jews cried this out as a blasphemy, and wanted to punish him for it immediately and stone him; but he showed them that since he was the Messiah, he could call himself God without blasphemy, because there is no more than one divine Person, one <term>God-man: The theological concept of the Hypostatic Union, where Christ is both fully God and fully human.</term>, who is able to bear the entire weight of that dignity which the Savior of the world, and King of the Church, comprises within himself. They wanted to seize him again, but he escaped, as he had done once before, because the hour of his death had not yet come.

The Scribes and Pharisees, meanwhile, cared so little for the salvation of persons whose conduct did not seem very regular to them, such as the <term>Tax Collectors: In the biblical context, these were locals hired by Romans who were often despised as traitors or cheats.</term> and other such people, that they could not understand why Jesus would sometimes let himself be found among that sort of men. He finally finds it when he had already begun to despair, and it seemed to be lost forever. He immediately takes it up, and for fear that it might remain lying on the road for lack of strength to be able to walk to the flock from which it had wandered so far, he lays it on his shoulders and carries it with a wonderful tenderness and joy to his flock. Upon his return, he makes his joy known to his neighbors and friends.

The <term>Tax Collectors: In the biblical context, these were locals who collected taxes for the Roman Empire, often viewed by their community as traitors or dishonest.</term> and other persons of an evil life were this sheep that had strayed from the flock and was clearly heading toward eternal ruin. Jesus Christ was that tender-hearted and charitable Shepherd who, out of a powerful affection for the conversion of those sinners, went to seek them out where they were lost. The outcome answered his intention and effort: the Tax Collectors and sinners allowed themselves to be moved by his representation, and he had the comfort of bringing them back from their disorders. Because the joy he had on this account was great, he made it known to all who took an interest in the return of those souls, whose loss had been considered certain; and he said that the Angels themselves rejoiced in Heaven over such remarkable conversions, through which great sinners often become the greatest Saints.

> *I say unto you*, said he, *that there shall be more joy in Heaven over one sinner who repents, than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance.*

Christ alluded by these last words to the pride of the Pharisees and Scribes, who let themselves be known as great Saints, and, taken with a high opinion of themselves, miserably neglected their own conversion and thus were lost in a proud carelessness. For, otherwise, there is not a man on earth who ought not to sigh for his sins and have need to bear a long repentance for them, according to this sincere confession of David:

> *If thou, Lord, shouldest mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand?* <note>original: "Zo gy, Heere, de ongerechtigheden gade slaat, wie zal bestaan?" (Psalm 130:3)</note>

the Shepherd who sought the lost sheep also extends to the Gentiles. One cannot imagine anything more fickle than the wandering of their thoughts in the matter of Religion, alongside the irregularities of their lives. Christ took pity on them and sent his Apostles, who went to seek them out over the entire face of the earth; he had it proclaimed to all men in all places that they only needed to repent, and that God would then receive them in mercy. The word of the Gospel had its effect; the Gentiles returned from their errors and vices and came into the Church to make up no more than one flock with the converted Jews. The earth has never seen anything greater than their conversion, nor the Angels anything which afforded them more joy, than when they saw that entire nations converted from dead Idols to the living and true God who made heaven and earth.

Christ presented the same truths also under another parable, which he spoke immediately after that of the Shepherd. He said that with all these matters, it was the same as with a Woman who had lost a <term>piece of money: The text mentions a "drachma" or a "six-stuiver piece" (zestuyvers-stukje), a common Dutch coin of the period used here to help the reader visualize the value.</term>. She sought it in all the corners of her house, and she allowed herself no rest until she had found it. This was a very great joy for this woman, and she made it known to her friends and neighbors so that they might share in it. The loss of the least of men is great to God, and as His love is infinitely concerned with their ruin, so His joy can be nothing but great when, through their conversion, they are in a proper state to receive eternal life from Him.

## The Parable of the Prodigal Son.

### Luke, Chapter XV. verses 11—32.

<margin>
This parable was spoken at the same time as the previous one.
</margin>

The parable of the prodigal son is one of the passages in the entire Gospel where God’s tender love toward mankind is portrayed for us in the most vivid and heart-moving colors. Our Savior introduces in this parable a Father who had two sons, the younger of whom, driven by a spirit of wild excess, distanced himself from his father's house, while the other—who was more sensible and wise—remained with him always and looked after his affairs. The son depicted here obtained, through persistent urging, the portion of the goods that was to fall to him in the family estate at some future time; and after he had received it, he set out on his way and traveled to a far-distant land. Finding himself thus master of his own conduct and under no one's supervision, he opened his heart to every pleasure and gave himself over entirely to licentiousness. The squandering of his money soon brought him to poverty, so that no longer knowing how to make a living, he entered into service in a certain house of that country. Because he had neither the skill nor the knowledge to be employed in matters that could bring him any honor, he was forced to take up the most despised work; and his master, not wishing to keep him in his house where he might have had his basic needs and comforts met, sent him out to the country to one of his farms to tend the swine. Someone born as a Jew could not descend any lower, nor do anything that more strongly contradicted the character of his nation, which held an insurmountable loathing for pigs; indeed, even the name itself was so hateful that, to avoid speaking it, they referred to it with these words, *an abominable thing*, or through some other circumlocution <note>original: "een verfoeielyk ding." In Jewish law, pigs were ritually unclean, making this the ultimate symbol of degradation for the son.</note>. The scarcity of provisions <note>original: "dierte van leeftógt," referring to a period of high prices or famine.</note> that had

<column-break/>

come to that land when this young spendthrift began to find himself without money continued, and his earnings were so small that he could not subsist on them. The pigs ate nothing but grass, and the lack of fruit was so great that the people of the land diligently sought out all the wild fruits which are otherwise left to fall from the trees to be eaten by the pigs. This wretched youth, finding none of these in the field, begged everyone to give him some; but the scarcity was too great, and love too small, to give such gifts, however meager they were, to a stranger and a foreigner. After he had suffered these hardships for some time, he began to come to a deep reflection; he accused himself as the sole cause of all his misfortunes; and after saying many times, through a repentance that pierced his heart:

> "How many <term>hired servants: Laborers who worked for a daily wage, unlike household slaves who were part of the domestic structure.</term> are there in my father's house who live in abundance, while I, to earn my bread, must tend the swine, and yet still die of hunger!

he finally made a resolution to return again to his country, to throw himself at his father's feet, and to say to him with tears:

> "Father, I have sinned against Heaven and against you; I am not worthy to be called your son; treat me only as one of your hired servants.

With these thoughts, and full of confidence in his fatherly affection, he sets out on his way and arrives back in his country. When he drew near, his father saw him from afar and recognized him. His heart was moved at this first sight, and even this emotion, which was the secret voice of Nature, confirmed in him the belief that it was his son. He did not wait until he arrived, but he ran toward him, fell upon his neck, and kissed him. The son, moved by his misdeeds and feeling this unexpected kindness which his father showed him, confessed his failings, and falling at his feet, he requested of him

The father was moved even more by his son, seeing him so humbled, and in a state so little suited to his birth. He immediately had his servants bring the best clothes he had in his house, and to better show that he wanted to receive him as his son, and not as a <term>hireling<note>A person employed to do menial work for wages, rather than a member of the family.</note></term>, he had shoes put on his feet and a golden ring on his finger—which at that time was the sign of a free person—and he had a great feast prepared, so that the whole house would be in joy over the return of his dear child.

His oldest brother, who as a wise and obedient son had always remained with his father, was in the field when the other arrived; but coming home, he heard that they were singing and playing on musical instruments, and he saw that everyone was in uncommon joy. He asked for the cause thereof, and they told him that his brother had returned. Instead of rejoicing at that news and going to embrace his brother, he stayed outside, sad and resentful over the good reception that his father gave that spendthrift. The

<column-break/>

father, informed of this bad mood of his eldest son, went out of the house and pleaded with him to come in and take part in his joy. But this hardhearted and proud son had the audacity to reproach his father, saying that he had had no regard at all for his steady diligence and service, although he spared nothing for that unworthy son, who had spent all his goods with <term>revelers<note>Dutch: 'flampampers' – those who live a life of gluttony and wasteful excess.</note></term> like himself, and with harlots. "It is true, child," said that good father, who sought to calm this hotheaded son, "you are always with me, and all mine is yours: but should one not be merry and glad? For this your brother was dead, and has become alive again; he was lost and is found again."

This parable was a clever depiction of the jealousy of the Scribes and Pharisees against the Tax Collectors and other sinners, whom Christ received in grace; and it showed in general the conceited and envious nature of the Jews toward the <term>Gentiles<note>Non-Jewish people; the text suggests the older brother represents the established Jewish faith while the younger represents the returning pagans.</note></term>, when God received them into his Church, as one will see more broadly in the parable of the Father of the household who sent laborers into his vineyard from the morning hour.

People generally make such a bad use of their wealth that our Savior could not refrain from crying out against that abuse. He once said, while presenting the parable of a clever and <term>shrewd<note>Dutch: 'doorptrapten' – meaning cunning or experienced in worldly ways.</note></term> Steward, who, seeing his disfavor approaching, entered into an agreement with his Lord’s debtors for his own advantage: *Make for yourselves friends out of the unrighteous Mammon* (which words, according to the Hebrew meaning,

<column-break/>

signify fleeting wealth,) *so that when you fail, they may receive you into the eternal tabernacles.* Jesus Christ wanted to make known through those metaphorical expressions the reward which one is to expect for works of charity. But because most people, always busy with the present and little occupied with the future, measure their happiness by the abundance of the goods which they possess, our Savior presented a parable on that subject, worthy to be often read and always meditated upon.

There was, he said, a certain rich man, who, dressed in purple and fine linen, lived joyfully and magnificently every day. At the same time, there was a very poor man, named Lazarus, who was full of sores, and often <insert>lay</insert> at the door of the rich—
