...[Lazarus] lay begging, requesting only that he might be satisfied with the crumbs, so to speak, that fell from his table, while the dogs, meanwhile—more compassionate than the rich miser—licked his sores. Thereupon Death came to put an end to the misery and sorrow of that poor man; and since he had housed a heavenly soul, full of faith and godliness, within this perishable body of clay, she was carried by the Angels into <term>Abraham’s bosom<note>A traditional expression referring to the place of comfort in the afterlife where the righteous await resurrection.</note></term>. There Lazarus, as a worthy son of that Patriarch through the imitation of his faith, went to taste the eternal rest and delight which Abraham enjoyed with God. The rich man died likewise, for Death spares no one; but beneath the gold and purple wherewith the Great of this world paraded—becoming so formidable through them that one sometimes hardly dares approach them—Death brings his sting into their hearts. This rich man was buried as a man of state, but while his corpse was being shown all the honor and pomp of a funeral, his criminal soul in Hell suffered the pains she had deserved, primarily for that hard-heartedness toward the poor. This man, being thus in torments, perceived from afar Lazarus in Abraham’s bosom; it was his remorse, and not actually his eyes, that beheld Lazarus in rest and glory. And our Savior presents it to us thus, in order to express in the most vivid way the remorse by which that miserable soul was tormented, speaking thus within herself, as if she truly saw Abraham and could speak to him from the abyss of Hell: “Have mercy on me, Father Abraham, and send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water, and just...

<column-break/>

“...as if with a single drop, cool my tongue, for I suffer terrible pains in these flames.” But the pains of the damned are without remedy. Abraham answered that such a thing was impossible, and that one did not pass thus from Heaven into Hell, or from Hell into Heaven; and he gave that miserable one to understand that he suffered nothing but what he had well deserved. For since he had misused his wealth all his life to bathe himself in luxury and pleasure, without having compassion for the poor, it was just that he should thus remain in pains for all eternity, deprived of all help, even if it were but a drop of water. For what is a drop of water in the midst of burning flames—indeed, flames that cannot be extinguished by all the water of the sea, and which shall burn eternally? This man then begged Abraham that he would at least send someone into the world to warn his five brothers, whom he had left there, of the miserable state to which his attachment and passion for wealth had brought him. The damned in Hell are incapable of having charitable inclinations toward men; Hell is nothing but a place of rage and despair. However, Christ wished to add this last part to this parable to teach all people, through the answer he puts into Abraham’s mouth, that someone who is insensitive to what God presents to all in His Word will not change their opinions or inclinations through anything that the damned in Hell might relate of their pains, even if God gave them permission to come out of it and tell their tale upon the earth.

to guard against <note>original: "fen te hoeden", likely referring to "offenses" or "stumbling blocks" from the previous page</note>, in order to prevent the deadly impression they naturally make on the mind. He added to that very necessary warning also this: that we must not have too favorable an opinion of even our best deeds. Most religious people suffer harm because of this; they generally place too high a value on the good they do, and they deem themselves to be holier than they actually are. *When you then, he said, have done all that has been commanded of you (and who is there who ever gets so far!), then say: "We are unprofitable servants, people who have earned nothing by our services, for we have only done what we were duty-bound to do"; and someone who does nothing but discharge his duty deserves nothing.*

Jesus Christ then departed from Galilee to go to Jerusalem; and having arrived at a certain village through which he had to pass, he met a company of ten lepers, who kept themselves there on the road, and having perceived him, cried out loudly, *Master, have mercy on us!* He beheld them with an eye of compassion and said, as if he had healed them at that very moment, that they should go and show themselves to the Priests, since they were appointed to inspect leprosy, to judge whether it was entirely healed or whether some of it still remained. Jesus did not say to them, as he was accustomed to say to the lepers whom he healed, *I will that you be cleansed.* But these men took no particular notice of that, and they believed themselves to be healed as soon as Christ commanded them to show themselves to the Priests, even though they still had all their leprosy. While they were going, the hand of God began to work upon them, and they were all cleansed. One of these lepers was so moved by this miracle that he could not resolve to continue his way with the others; he then turned back to thank Christ, who, appearing surprised that he saw him return so soon, and alone, said, *Were there not ten cleansed; and where are the nine others? Were there none found who return to give God glory, except this stranger?* The Evangelist Luke says that he was a Samaritan, a man who was far from being a Jew like the nine others; for the Samaritans of that time were descended from those old colonies of Assyrians whom <term>Shalmaneser<note>The King of Assyria who conquered the Northern Kingdom of Israel and deported its inhabitants.</note></term> had sent into the land of Samaria with some families of the Israelites, and they were held in the utmost contempt by the Jews. But our Savior generally found more faith among the strangers than among the Jews; because God, weary of enduring the ungratefulness of this people any longer, gradually withdrew his grace from them and began to pour it out upon the strangers. This Samaritan, feeling

<column-break/>

the favor which he had received, fell on his face at Jesus' feet; but Jesus commanded him to stand up and go his way, saying that *his faith had saved him.* He did not merely mean to say that his faith had healed him; that was common to him and the nine others who had not come to offer their thanksgiving; but he wanted to give him to understand that with the healing of his body he had also received that of his soul, and that his sins were forgiven him. This observation applies to all to whom the Lord made that declaration, that their faith had saved them; and one must view the deliverance from the evils with which their bodies were plagued as a tangible representation of the spiritual and salutary graces of the soul; since the Holy Spirit has included both under one and the same wording when he said, speaking of Christ through the mouth of a certain Prophet and through that of an Evangelist, *He has taken our infirmities upon himself, and borne our diseases.*

When Jesus then arrived in Jerusalem, the Pharisees asked him when the Kingdom of God would come. To which he answered that it did not come with any outward pomp, as they imagined, but that it was within them, and had already come into their midst. They did not understand his meaning, for prejudice robs the mind of its knowledge. The Jews were preoccupied with the hope of seeing the Messiah appear with all the pomp and splendor of the greatest Monarchs. This prejudice alone caused them to be lost, and still causes them to run into their ruin: it is of such great importance in Religion to always adhere to the simplicity of the Scriptures.

Because the Pharisees were now constantly pregnant with a great opinion of themselves and relied on their own righteousness, Christ presented the hatefulness of this in the XVIII Chapter of the Evangelist Luke under the following parable. Two persons, he said, went into the Temple to pray; one was a Pharisee, and the other a <term>Tax Collector<note>original: "Tollenaar", often translated as "Publican" in older English bibles; these men were often hated for collaborating with the Roman occupiers.</note></term>. The Pharisee, puffed up because of his supposed virtue, thanked God that he was not like other unjust people, indeed, not even like that Tax Collector; but that he fasted twice a week and gave away a tenth part of his goods. But the Tax Collector, dejected and oppressed under the weight of his transgressions, dared not lift his eyes to heaven, but beating upon his chest, said with a deep sigh, as someone who placed his salvation only in the mercy of the Lord, *O God, be merciful to me, a sinner!* And he went, as Christ said, home more justified than the other. It is of such great importance to walk in humility before God.

He compared the Kingdom of Heaven, that is the Christian Church, to a **Master of a house**, who had gone out in the early morning to hire laborers and send them into his vineyard, entering into an agreement with them that he would give them a penny <note>original: *penning*; referring to the Roman denarius</note> for their day’s work, being the value of about six stuyvers <term>stuyver: a Dutch coin used in the author's time to provide a familiar reference for value</term>, which was likely the common daily wage for such laborers. Three hours later he came again to the marketplace, where, finding some people waiting for work, he told them that they should go into his vineyard, and that he would give them what was fair. He did the same at noon, three hours after noon, and at the eleventh hour, that is when the sun was only one hour from setting; for the Jews, as is known, reckoned no more than twelve hours in a day. When evening had come, this man, who had sent all these laborers into his vineyard at such different hours, gave an order to his **Steward** <term>steward: a manager of an estate or household</term> that he should pay them all and give to each a penny. The Steward had them all come before him and gave each a penny; so that the last-comers received as much as the first. These were completely astonished by this, and unable to understand that people who had been at work for such a little time should have the same wage as those who had worked in the vineyard from morning until evening; they viewed this inequality as a kind of injustice done to them. They murmured about it among themselves and, moreover, had the impertinence to complain to the Master of the house as follows:

> *These last have worked only one hour, and you have made them equal to us, who have borne the burden of the day and the heat.*

But the House-father answered

<column-break/>

them, speaking to one who had spoken for the others:

> *Friend, I do you no wrong: did you not agree with me for a penny? Take then what is yours, and go your way. If I wish to give to this last as much as to you, is it not lawful for me to do with my own what I will? Or is your eye evil because I am good?*

The four callings, from six o'clock in the morning to three o'clock in the afternoon, referred to the Jews and could signify the various dispensations <note>God's various plans or systems of order throughout history</note> which God had maintained with that people from Abraham until the time of Christ. The last, which occurred at the eleventh hour or at the end of the day, was that of the **Gentiles** <note>original: *Heydenen*; non-Jewish nations</note>, whom God has called into his Church, his spiritual vineyard, in the final period of the world, when the Jewish Church came to an end. This is why the laborers, who complained that they had worked the whole day, said nothing regarding the others who were called at nine o'clock in the morning, at noon, and at three o'clock, for all those callings concerned the Jews. They directed their grievance only toward the laborers who were sent last, at the eleventh hour; because these being Gentiles, they provoked only envy and resentment in the others. This equality, then, regarding the payment to all the laborers, signified the equality of the Jews and Gentiles in the Kingdom of the Messiah, in which, as Christ said, the first shall be last and the last shall be first, to make known that in him there is neither first nor last, and that as the Apostle Paul later said in that same sense,
,, in Jesus Christ there is
,, neither Jew nor Greek, neither circumcision nor
,, uncircumcision, neither Barbarian, nor Scythian,
,, slave nor free; but that we are all in
,, him, who is equally the Savior of all,
,, and the fulfillment of that which fulfills all in
,, all.

### *Jesus Christ makes his entry into Jerusalem seated on the colt of a donkey, and people spread clothes and branches of trees before him on the road.*

#### Matthew, Chapter XXI. verses 1—9.

<margin>
The 33rd year of Jesus Christ, at the end of the 4th and last year of his ministry.
</margin>

A few days before the final Passover, Jesus Christ went to Jericho. Everyone was stirred by his arrival in the city, and the crowd was so great that there was a chief tax collector <term>tollenaar: a tax collector, often despised in this era for collaborating with the Roman occupiers</term> named Zacchaeus. Desiring to see Jesus, and fearing that he would be prevented by the multitude of people because he was small of stature, he climbed a wild fig tree <note>original: *wilden vygeboom*; likely referring to the sycamore-fig common to the area</note> at a place where Jesus had to pass. When Christ arrived at that spot, he saw this man, and calling him by name, he told him that he must hurry to climb down, because he wished to stay and take lodging at his house. Zacchaeus’s wonder was no less than his joy: faith was already in his heart; it was much more through an impulse of his faith than a movement of curiosity that he had such a great desire to see Christ. Curiosity alone seldom produces such effects in persons of such status and wealth as Zacchaeus, who was the Chief of the Tax Collectors in Jericho. Upon entering his home, the Lord said that salvation had entered there at that very hour. Zacchaeus, struck by gratitude for the honor Christ did him, and believing he could show it no better than by giving great alms, declared that he gave half of his goods to the poor, and that if he had defrauded anyone of anything, he would repay it fourfold. Such a ready and unconcerned renunciation of such great wealth could be nothing other than the effect of a divine grace in the mind of this tax collector, which at that moment made him see goods infinitely more precious with which he was about to be enriched. Afterward, departing from Jericho, Christ left his peace and salvation with Zacchaeus and took the road to Jerusalem.

<column-break/>

When he had arrived at Bethphage by the Mount of Olives, he commanded two of his disciples to go to a certain nearby village, which he pointed out to them, saying that they would find a donkey and a colt tied there; and that they should untie them both and bring them to him; adding that if anyone asked why they did so, they should answer that the Lord had need of them. In giving that command, Christ guaranteed the outcome, but to that end, he had to be master of hearts; for people do not let the animals that belong to them and serve for their daily use be taken by unknown persons, who seize them as if they were their own property, without even asking permission from the owner. The matter happened in the same manner as Jesus had told his disciples: they found at the entrance of the village a donkey and a young donkey’s colt tied up, and as they went to take them away, those to whom the animals belonged called out, asking why they were untying them. They answered just as Christ had commanded them, and they were allowed to proceed. When they had brought the animals to their Master, they laid some of their clothes on the colt, and Jesus sat upon it. The fact that the Evangelists <note>The writers of the Gospels: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John</note> relate that the colt was tied indicates that it was not so young that it still followed its mother to suckle; for if it had been of such a tender age, no person could have...

The Prophet Zechariah had predicted this unusual event, and what is even more remarkable in his prophecy was that he had foretold that the people of Zion would rejoice, seeing their King thus seated upon a young donkey. *Rejoice greatly, he said, daughter of Zion; shout, daughter of Jerusalem; behold, your King shall come to you, righteous, and he is a Savior, poor, and riding upon a donkey, and upon a colt, a foal of the donkeys.* <note>original: *Verheug u zeer...*; this refers to Zechariah 9:9, a key Messianic prophecy</note> Let a Jew, reading this oracle in one of his Prophets, not say that it was easy for Christ to apply this to himself, because nothing was easier than to go and sit upon a donkey, and thus ride into Jerusalem. Hosanna in the highest heavens!* Amidst this shouting and this rustic triumph, Christ rode into Jerusalem. The entire city was in motion at his arrival. Some joined their cheers with those of the people who accompanied him; others, astonished by such an unusual spectacle, asked what was happening: and they were told only that it was *Jesus, the Prophet of Nazareth in Galilee*. This answer itself, as well as the triumph of Christ, had something great and at the same time something lowly in it; on one hand it was illustrious, and on the other despised; "Jesus the Prophet" was an expression of greatness from which a light and radiance shone forth; but that which was added—that he was from Nazareth in Galilee <note>In the first century, Galilee was often looked down upon by the Judean elite as a provincial backwater</note>—served as a counterweight which was always added to his luster, and as a curtain to cover it from the eyes of the nation.

The Priests and Scribes found themselves so accurately described by this parable that, in order to turn that disaster away from themselves, they cried out unanimously, *Far be it that such a thing should happen!* But Christ, looking at them—to make them better notice that it was they alone whom he had in mind—said, *The stone which the builders rejected, has become the head of the corner. Whosoever falls on this stone shall be broken; and on whomsoever it falls, it will crush him.* <note>original: "De steen dien de bouwlieden verworpen hebben..." This quote from Psalm 118:22 refers to the "Cornerstone," a Messianic title.</note> These words were taken from the 118th Psalm, which primarily concerned the Messiah, and how he would one day be rejected by the Masters of the Synagogue. This was a new arrow, shot with force, that pierced their hearts, and because they could not pull it out, they became the more enraged against Christ. They would have liked to seize him, but the high esteem in which he was held by the people restrained them and made them wait for another opportunity to satisfy their lust for revenge, without exposing themselves too much and putting their authority in danger.

### Matthew, Chapter XXII. verses 2—13.

<margin>The same day.</margin>
THE Parable of the wedding, which our Savior spoke on the same day as the previous one, or the day after, is one of the most remarkable in the Gospel. One finds in it the same purpose as in the parable of the tenants <note>Referring to the previous Parable of the Wicked Tenants</note>, but there are also several other aspects that are entirely unique and of a wonderful beauty and sublimity. *There was*, he said, *a certain King who had prepared a wedding for his son. He himself was that son; the King was God the Father; and the wedding, the spiritual marriage of Christ with his Church <term>Church: translated from 'Gemeynte', here referring to the collective body of Christian believers</term>, concerning which the Apostle Paul said to the Ephesians that it was a great mystery.* The King sent out his servants to call the invited guests to the wedding, but they would not come.

> "other to his business. Indeed, some
> "extended their contempt and defiance so far
> "that they mistreated the servants whom the King
> "had sent with insults and blows,
> "and even took their lives."

These invited guests were the Jews, who for a long time had been invited to the grace of the Gospel: firstly, by God himself in the promises he had made to Abraham; thereafter by the Prophets; subsequently by John the Baptist; and finally by Jesus Christ and his Disciples, whom he sent out through all Judea and Galilee

<column-break/>

to preach. But the Jews made nothing of all those invitations, and they rejected the Gospel. In the meantime, the time for the wedding arrived; Jesus died, and through the price of his blood, he obtained the Church, which he made his Bride. In that time, the Apostles preached the Gospel in Jerusalem and throughout all Judea: they brought about some conversions there, but then also, just as during the first journey, the bulk of the nation <note>original: "grós der landaard," referring to the majority of the Jewish people at that time</note> despised the invitation of Grace, and the Synagogue remained stubborn in rejecting Christ. The Apostles might well cry out that all was ready, and that nothing more was lacking for the spiritual wedding that Supreme Wisdom had prepared: the invited guests were only embittered by the powerful requests that the Ministers of grace made to them to come to that wedding feast; they mistreated, scourged, and killed them. *When the King heard this, he became angry, and sending his soldiers, he destroyed those ungrateful ones and murderers, and set their city on fire.* God became weary of having the Jews urged in vain to acknowledge Jesus Christ as the Son of God and their Savior. He sent against them the army of the Romans, his military bands, and his chosen men; for all men, even Kings and Emperors, are—without their knowing it and without their thinking it—instruments in God’s hand for the execution of his purposes. Titus <note>Titus Flavianus, the Roman General who later became Emperor; he oversaw the Siege of Jerusalem in 70 AD</note> came with his brave legions and brought war to all Judea: a fearful resistance was offered to him behind some poorly secured ramparts: he captured the cities that put up any resistance, and the others opened their gates. He was primarily aiming for Jerusalem; that was the seat of the rebellion, and God was no longer in her midst. The Roman encamped before that place, and while he attacked it from without with his siege engines <term>siege engines: mechanical devices such as battering rams and catapults used to breach city walls</term>, God fought for him, or rather for himself, from within, through divisions that turned one Jew against the

THE Scribes and Pharisees, being unable to behold without grief the wonder with which the people heard the words of Christ, and not daring to oppose him openly or through any act of authority, sought to ensnare him with crafty questions. Having then gone out from the Temple, they consulted together, and it was decided that they would send some of their disciples, accompanied by the Herodians, to set a trap for him. It is not well known who these Herodians were

<column-break/>

of whom mention is made here. Is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar, or not?* The cunning that lay hidden under this question consisted in this: that if Jesus had answered that one must pay tribute to Caesar, he would have made himself hated by the people, who, bearing the yoke of the Romans with impatience, would have been displeased to see that someone who said he was sent by God declared himself so frankly in favor of a Prince who had usurped the supreme authority over Judea through violence; and it would also have been a means to instill in the people the idea that Jesus was not the Messiah, since the Messiah, according to their common belief, was supposed to come and deliver their nation from that foreign power. On the contrary, if he had answered plainly that one should not pay tribute to Caesar, then he would have made himself a criminal of the State, and they would have delivered him over to the secular arm. But Christ understood the full depth of that question, and he wanted—

<column-break/>

—to make this noticed immediately by those who asked him, saying to them before all the people: *You hypocrites, why do you test me? Show me the tribute-money.* In Judea, two kinds of currency were current then; the old, being those which the Jews had used at all times, such as the shekel <term>shekel: the traditional silver coin used for Temple taxes and Jewish commerce</term>, and some others; and the new, which had been introduced by the Romans, with which the tributes to Caesar were paid, because that currency was current throughout the whole Empire. They then showed him a penny or *Denarius* <term>Denarius: a Roman silver coin worth about a day's wage for a laborer</term>, which was a Roman coin, worth about six stuyvers <note>The author uses "stuyvers," a Dutch currency of the 1700s, to help his readers understand the relative value of the coin.</note>, on which the Emperor’s image, with an inscription, was stamped, as is customary on money. Christ asked whose image and inscription it was. *They answered him that it was Caesar’s. Give then to Caesar, he said, what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.* This wise and concise answer agreed with a fundamental rule of their ancient Teachers, which held that one must recognize as the Sovereign in a land the Prince who had his image struck upon the money there. The Herodians <note>A political faction that supported the dynasty of Herod and cooperation with the Roman Empire.</note>, who had joined the disciples of the Pharisees to catch him in his speech, could not complain that he had given too much to Caesar; nor could the people, who heard this answer, find fault that as long as Roman currency was current in Judea, one recognized Caesar’s authority. Thus Christ wisely avoided this new snare which the Pharisees had laid for him, and they left ashamed.

<meta>This page continues the narrative of Jesus’ final week in Jerusalem. Having just silenced the Herodians and Pharisees regarding taxes to Caesar, Jesus now faces a theological challenge from the Sadducees regarding the nature of the afterlife.</meta>

publicly taught the resurrection, they would corner him by telling him that there was a woman among them who had married seven brothers, one after the other, according to the Law of Moses. This law dictates that when a man dies without children and leaves behind a brother who is unmarried, that brother must then marry the widow of the deceased, so that the children he might father from that marriage may be considered to have come from his deceased brother. <note>This practice is known as Levirate marriage, intended to preserve a man's lineage and property within his family.</note> Thereupon the Sadducees asked Christ which of the seven brothers would have her as his wife on the day of the resurrection. Our Savior answered that question—which was brought forth from a spirit of flippancy and godlessness—that it was a matter of the highest ignorance to imagine that people in the future life also married. Coming then to the doctrine of the resurrection itself, he proved it against these heretics (who had built their objection upon a Law of Moses from which they drew false conclusions) by using another passage from that same Prophet. *Have you not read*, he said, *what was spoken by God, I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. God now, who spoke thus to Moses long after the death of those Patriarchs, is not a God of the dead, but of the living:* for what blessedness could the dead receive who no longer exist? Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob therefore still lived after their death; and if their souls lived in Heaven, then their bodies must also one day live again, because the soul of Abraham is not Abraham, but only a part of Abraham; and God called himself the God of Abraham, and not merely the God of his soul. Added to this, since the Sadducees said that there were no spirits, as one reads in the 23rd chapter of the Acts of the Apostles, they consequently denied the immortality of the soul as well as the resurrection of the body: and therefore Christ proved the one as well as the other through one and the same passage of Scripture.

When the Pharisees learned that he had shamed the Sadducees and stopped their mouths, they came to him again with a renowned lawyer, who came to ask him a question regarding the difference and distinction among God’s commandments. This man intended, according to the common custom of debaters, to involve Christ in certain points of dispute regarding matters that were heavily contested in their schools. But the Lord Jesus avoided that snare by answering that the first and great commandment was to love God with all one’s heart; and the second, to love our neighbor as ourselves. Thereupon Christ wished to ask them a question of the utmost importance. He asked them what they believed regarding the Messiah, and whose son he ought to be. They found this question easy and answered without thinking long that he must be David’s son.

</margin>
After Jesus Christ had finished speaking to the people about the matters that make up the subject of two large chapters in the Gospel

<column-break/>

of Matthew, he departed from Jerusalem to Bethany, where he went every evening during the last week. When he had come to the Mount of Olives, which lay on his path and at the exit of Jerusalem, his disciples turned around toward that great and proud city, casting their gaze primarily upon the Temple, which was built on that side, and whose elevated position made it almost entirely

->...<-

visible. There was no difficulty in this; but whether he ought to be the son of no one else but David was the point at issue. Why, said Christ, does David then call him—speaking through the Spirit of God—his Lord, in those words of the 110th Psalm: *The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I have made your enemies a footstool for your feet?* How is it that David, who was a King, a Sovereign who has no one but God above him, called his own Son his Lord? He proved to them thereby that the Messiah was God’s Son, and the true God. This conviction, which was perceived in all the reasoning of Jesus Christ, made his enviers despair of ever being able to catch him through their sophistry; and therefore they asked him no more questions after that day. They took another path, and the time approached when Jesus must fall into their hands and feel the final effects of their hatred.

While Christ was in the Temple, he saw a certain poor widow throw two small coins into the treasury, from which he took the opportunity to praise her above the rich who, out of their abundance, had given much greater gifts. As soon as the Pharisees had withdrawn and left him alone with the assembly of the people, who could not grow weary of listening to him, he commanded all those people that they should strictly follow everything their teachers told them, provided that it agreed with the Laws of Moses, on whose seat they were placed. But since the sincerity of his zeal did not allow him to hide the faults of their teachers, he pointed them out somewhat at length so that they might take heed. He told them, among other things, that the Scribes and Pharisees were hypocrites who heaped observation upon observation but excused themselves quite easily, which he called in figurative language *binding burdens that are heavy and difficult to carry and laying them on the shoulders of men, but not touching them themselves with their finger.* He said that all the piety of the Scribes, who had enchanted the minds of the people through a great appearance of holiness, was nothing but whims and a vain affectation—such as the wearing of broad phylacteries <note>Original: *gedenkcédelen*. These are small leather boxes containing scripture scrolls worn during prayer.</note> and of fringes on the hems of their garments longer than others; making themselves esteemed by the world as people who held the key of knowledge, while they left the people in great ignorance and closed the entrance of the Kingdom of Heaven to them. Through all these rebukes, which are recounted at length in the 23rd chapter of the Evangelist Matthew, Christ taught the people that they should not place too great a trust in their lawyers, but that they should see through their own eyes, and each live by his own faith.

It was not out of a simple impulse of curiosity or wonder that they turned their gaze toward that building, which was one of the most beautiful in the world; rather, it was the sorrow they felt that such a magnificent Temple would one day—and indeed soon—be destroyed, according to what the Lord had foretold. This caused them to turn around to behold it, and they pleaded with Christ that he himself might cast his eyes upon it, as if to soften his heart by the sight of such a beautiful object and move him to spare it. But the decree had been made in God’s counsel to cast the Temple down. The reasons for vengeance against the Jews, who profaned this edifice daily and had made it *into a den of murderers* <note>original: "moordenaars kuyl"; a reference to Jesus' cleansing of the temple where he accused the people of making it a "den of thieves."</note>; and even more, the deep insights of divine wisdom to no longer allow a Temple to stand that was only made to serve the Law of ceremonies, did not allow Jesus to take any interest in its preservation. Instead of answering them according to their wish, he said to the contrary: *Do you not see all these things? Truly, I say to you, of this building over which you so wonder, not one stone shall be left upon another that shall not be broken down.* But to instruct his disciples at length regarding these great events, he wished to stay with them for some time on the Mount of Olives, from where they could behold the city and the Temple; and after they were all seated, he began to set before them at length all the misfortunes that were to befall their nation. He told them that false Messiahs would come, who would lead many people astray; that there would be disturbances, movements, and wars, of nation against nation and of kingdom against kingdom, everywhere: that the persecutions against the Church would be great; that they themselves would be the first to suffer; that they would be delivered to the authorities,

He brought to their minds that prophecy of Daniel in which the Prophet had spoken of that *abominable wing* <note>original: "grouwelyken vleugel"; usually translated as the "abomination of desolation," a prophetic term for a sacrilegious object or event that desecrates the Temple.</note> that was to descend upon Judea and bring a terrible destruction to the Holy Land. He gave them a short description of all those calamities, and because common words were not powerful enough to give a right idea of them, he borrowed from infinite ways of speaking and from the most high-flown metaphorical expressions—which had been the language of the Prophets regarding certain extraordinary events—the power and loftiness that human language lacked. He said that the Sun would be darkened, that the Moon would lose its light, that the Stars would fall from Heaven; and that then the sign of the Son of Man in its full brightness would appear in Heaven, and that it would come with great power and glory in the clouds. This sign of the Son of Man was the coming of Jesus Christ himself on that terrible day of his vengeance; and that

### *The parable of the wise and foolish Virgins who go to meet the Bridegroom.*

#### Matthew, Chapter XXV. vers. 1—12

<margin>
The same day.
</margin>
IN the prophecies which our Savior <note>original: "Zaligmaaker"</note> had made concerning the calamities that were to come upon the Jews, he had said that that unbelieving nation would let themselves be overtaken by God's judgments; and he had then compared the destructive carelessness of the Jews to that in which the general flood found the whole world in the time of Noah. This gave him occasion to signify that one would see the same carelessness once again at the end of the world. And to place such a subject of importance in such clarity where it stood out most, and could make the greatest impression on the minds of men, he presented it in a parable, of which all the parts have a wonderful living power. He said that the Kingdom of Heaven, or the people who lived in his Church, would then be like ten Virgins, who, having lit their lamps, went out to meet the Bridegroom. One sees well that this is a 

<column-break/>

parable borrowed from certain customs which were observed among the Jews on the day of the solemnization of marriage: but since it matters little to us to climb so far back to know what that ancient usage consisted of, we shall here assume it with Jesus Christ and follow the thread of his parable. Of these ten Virgins, who all had burning lamps in their hands, five were wise, but the other five lacked foresight <note>original: "voorzigtigheyd"</note>. These had satisfied themselves with having lit their lamps, but they had taken no oil with them to be able to keep them burning until the coming of the Bridegroom, of which the exact time was not known. The other Virgins, on the contrary, had taken vessels <note>original: "vaten"</note> with oil with them to keep their lamps in order and to prevent them from going out, in case the Bridegroom delayed long. And it indeed happened so, that he stayed away much longer than had been thought; so much so that they, all together awaiting him, became drowsy and fell asleep. At midnight, the usual time of the deepest sleep, there suddenly arose a great noise, and it was cried out that the Bridegroom was coming. At this cry, the Virgins awoke and each took her lamp, but they found them going out. The wise Virgins used

In this inability in which they found themselves to give oil to these imprudent <note>original: "onvoorzigtige"</note> virgins, they told them that they must quickly go to the sellers to buy from them. They took this advice, not knowing what to do, or where to turn. But this turned out poorly for them, for while they went to the seller, the Bridegroom arrived, and entered the wedding hall, followed by the five wise Virgins, whereupon the door was immediately shut. The foolish virgins, who had run off to buy oil, came back shortly after and presented themselves at the door, but the command had been given not to open. They cry and wail; but they are left standing outside, for although they cried, *Lord, Lord, open to us!* the Bridegroom answered, *Verily I say to you, I know you not:* so that the door remained closed to them forever. The Virgins represent the good and bad Christians, who all make profes-

<column-break/>

-sion of the Gospel, and this profession is symbolized by the burning lamps with which the ten Virgins went to meet the Bridegroom. The wise Virgins are a symbol <note>original: "zinnebeeld"</note> of true Christians, who besides the outward profession of the Gospel, have faith and godliness in the heart, which is represented by the oil which they carry with them in their vessels. The others satisfy themselves with a bare profession of Christian doctrine, and have neither godliness nor faith. The Bridegroom delays long in coming, and in that expectation the true believers sometimes slumber with the others; their zeal weakens; and faith is not always equally awake and powerful. But awakening from that slumber, they find within themselves the sincerity of their faith and their love, and with that spiritual oil they light the lamp which they have in their hand, and are ready to receive the Bridegroom. He shall finally come, that divine Bridegroom, and then the true Believers shall enter with him into Heaven, the place of pleasure and of the spiritual wedding feast; while the false Christians, overtaken by the coming of the Last Judgment, without faith, without love, without Christian virtues, shall be left in the outer darkness, where there shall be nothing but weeping and despair.

Long after that, the Lord came home again, and settled accounts with his servants. The one to whom he had given five talents came first, and offering those, he brought him five others besides. The master praised the faithfulness of that servant, and promised him a great reward. *In a few things*, he said, *you have been faithful, over many I will set you: Enter into the joy of your Lord.* After him came the servant who had received two talents, which he likewise handed over with the two others, which he had gained through his diligence and industry. The Lord gave him the same praise as the first, and let him enter into his joy. After him came the third with his talent, which was neither increased nor diminished: and to excuse himself to his Lord for not having gained anything with his money, he said upon handing it over: *Lord, I knew you, that you are a hard man, reaping where you have not sown, and gathering from where you have not scattered.* He did not mean to say that the Lord was an unjust man—that would have been spoken all too willfully, and it would have been as much as exposing himself to a rough reception out of a mere whim—his meaning was only to say that his Lord was a self-interested <note>original: "eygenbaatig". This refers to someone solely focused on their own profit or advantage, often implies being exacting or stingy.</note> man, who would not have suffered with any patience if his talent had been in any way diminished, as could easily have happened if he had done any trade with it, because in that way one often loses more than one wins; and therefore he had preferred to hide it in the earth, to give it all back to him again, rather than put himself in danger of having brought it back with

<column-break/>

loss. "See there," said he, "is all your money; it is true that nothing has been gained with it, but nothing has been lost from it either: take back what is yours." The Lord was not satisfied with this excuse: *You wicked and lazy servant*, he said, *you knew that I reap where I have not sown, and gather from where I have not scattered: to then receive something above my principal sum, you should have given my money to the money-changers, and upon my coming I would have taken back what is mine with usury <note>original: "woecker". In this historical context, this simply means interest earned on capital, rather than the modern negative connotation of illegal rates.</note>.* After this first complaint against the neglect of this servant, the Lord commanded that they should take his talent from him, and give it to the one who had ten; and subsequently he pronounced his sentence thus: *Cast that useless servant out into the outer darkness, where there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.* This parable teaches us that among the great variety of gifts which God has entrusted to men during this life, those who have the least ought to employ them for the promotion of God's honor just as well as those who have the most. For if the useless servant of this parable was cast into the horror of eternal darkness, only because he had made no profit with the talent of his Lord, although he had neither squandered nor lost it; how will it then go with those who let the natural gifts, which they have received from the goodness of their Creator, be extinguished through a luxurious idleness, or a constant distraction of their thoughts? But the damnation of those who, giving themselves over to their passions, turn the goods which they have received from God, such as wealth and knowledge, against Him, shall one day be even more terrible.

determined to judge them all. This day, the terror of the wicked and the joy of the Believers, is postponed until the end of the world, after the number of people whom God has decreed to be born on earth shall be full: and it is a triumph that the Heavenly Father reserves for his Son, whom he will cause to sit on that day of glory upon the Judgment Seat, to judge all the nations of the entire world. Christ gave his Disciples a short description of it, which nevertheless lacks nothing for the faith and hope of the Church that can serve to comfort her over the miseries of this life, and to assure her of the possession of the blessedness that is reserved for her in eternity. He says that the Son of Man—which is, as everyone knows, Jesus Christ—shall come in his glory, accompanied by all the Angels of Heaven, and that he shall sit upon the throne; and then all the nations shall be gathered to present themselves before him. His Apostles explain this to us more broadly, saying that living and dead, all must appear before that awesome judgment seat to hear their sentence; that the sea and the earth shall give up their dead, whom they hide; that they shall all be raised; and that the bodies which for many centuries have been nothing but scattered dust—matter that has passed through a thousand different forms, and which after so many changes, diminishings, and revolutions, exists no longer except under the hand of the Creator—that those bodies, the same as they formerly were, shall be reunited with their souls; so that each soul, finding its body again, they shall be the same people who once lived and died, but whom a power, for whom nothing is impossible, shall bring there to be judged. They shall not appear before the throne of the Supreme Judge of the world in a confused mixture of good and evil together. This Judge, infinitely wise to make a distinction therein without fear that he will mistake or err in it, shall separate them from one another, just as the Shepherd, according to what he himself says, separates the sheep from the goats; and he shall set the sheep on his right hand, and the goats on his left. The Believers are the sheep; the goats are the unbelievers and the wicked. Then, turning to those who stand at his right hand, with a countenance

Whether [he began] with one or with another, is not clearly stated in the Gospel. St. John seems, however, to suggest that he had already performed this washing of feet for someone else among the Disciples; for he says that when Jesus came to Peter, that Apostle did not want to allow him to wash his feet. Our Savior said to him, *What I am doing you do not know now, but you will understand it hereafter.* Peter, however, did not yield to that vague statement, and fearing that it would be an indiscretion and irreverence in him if he allowed the Lord to perform such a lowly service for him, he said in a firm and bold language: *Lord, You shall never wash my feet.* <note>original: "in der eeuwigheyd" — literally "into eternity," a strong Hebraic way of saying "never."</note> But Jesus answered him, speaking of the cleansing of the soul under the symbol of that of the body: *If I do not wash you, you have no part with me.* The Apostle trembled at hearing those words, and was so distraught that he hardly knew what he said, because his thoughts dwelled too much on this earthly object <note>The physical act of washing</note> floating before his eyes: *Lord,* he said, *not only my feet, but also my hands and my head.* Jesus replied that those whom he wished to wash needed only to have their feet washed, because they were all clean, except for one among them who was not. He meant to say that they all had a pure heart, a mind separated from the vices of their age, sanctified by Grace, and washed by the Holy Spirit; so that there were only those remnants of impurity or weaknesses in them, by which even the greatest Saints still touch the earth, and from which they always need to be washed. But he let them know that they were not all equally clean, and that there was one in their company whose heart was evil and corrupt. They knew nothing of this: Judas had always hidden himself under such a deceptive hypocrisy that he had never shown them the corruption of his heart,

<column-break/>

and up until that day Christ had not wanted to pull away the veil of that hypocrite. This was the first time that he set his hand to it, and it was still but very little, and as if only lifting it at one corner. The Disciples did not even pay attention to it, and love—the nature of which is not to easily indulge in evil suspicions of others, and which on the contrary seeks to cover their mistakes rather than to put them on public display—turned the minds of the Disciples away from the observation they should have made regarding the words of Christ, and they did not understand his meaning. After our Savior had washed the feet of all his Disciples (for Judas himself also shared in that solemn service), he returned to the table, and overcome by an extraordinary inspiration of the Holy Spirit, he spoke more openly of what he had previously only faintly touched upon regarding the godlessness of that Disciple: *Truly, I say to you, that one of you shall betray me.* These people looked at one another with a bewilderment that their faces and their silence expressed better than speech could have done. John, the beloved Disciple, was placed at the table close to Jesus, and at his right hand, so that as they lay to eat, according to the custom of that time, on small couches <note>original: "rustbeddetjes" — referring to the Roman-style reclining couches used at formal meals</note> arranged around the table, with the body bent a little to the left side, the head of that Disciple thereby leaned somewhat upon the breast of Jesus. Since now no one dared to open his mouth to request the Lord to explain himself clearly in that regard, Peter gave John a sign <note>original: "wenk" — a nod or gesture</note> that he should ask him which of them he had in mind with those words. Jesus answered that it was the one to whom he would give a dipped morsel. Then he took a piece of bread, which he dipped into the dish, and gave to Judas, saying to him: *What you do, do it*

## *Judas bargains with the Chief Priests and Scribes to deliver Christ to them for thirty pieces of silver.*

### Matthew, Chapter XXVI. verses 14, 15.

---

<margin>
On Thursday before the last Passover which followed the next day.
</margin>

It appears clearly from all the Evangelists that the dipped morsel, which the Lord Jesus gave to Judas after the meal when he washed the feet of his Disciples, was not the same as that which Judas ate during the last supper <note>The author is distinguishing between a meal in Bethany where the foot-washing occurred and the final Passover meal in Jerusalem.</note>. For speaking of that last one, they do not say that Jesus Christ gave it to him, but only that Jesus said, *He who dips his hand with me in the dish, he shall betray me*; which applied no more to Judas than to the other Disciples, who had this in common with him: that they dipped the Passover bread into the dish containing the sauce of bitter herbs. Besides that, Judas ate this last morsel in Jerusalem after he had entered into an agreement with the Priests to deliver Jesus to them; whereas he had eaten the other the day before in Bethany, from where he had then set out for Jerusalem. The Priests and Scribes, who could not decide to let Christ live any longer, were gathered Thursday morning to consult together on how they could most conveniently make their plot succeed. They did not doubt that Jesus, who had been in Jerusalem and in the Temple every day

<column-break/>

in that week, and whom they knew to be in Bethany, would come to the Passover feast. He was far too meticulous in appearing at all the High Festivals of their religion to have failed to be found at this one: especially being so close to Jerusalem as he was. But they did not dare to have him seized openly, for fear of inciting a riot in the city, especially at a time when people from all the cities of Judea and Galilee were arriving. Their decision was then to take him into custody without a stir or any noise; but for that end, there had to be someone who could point out a secluded area where they could find him, and at such hours that he would not have many people with him. Judas comes to present himself just at the right time; he offers to do what they desired and to surely deliver Jesus to them. It now only comes down to paying for his treachery; they give him what he demands; and however greedy he was, he is satisfied with thirty silver pieces, being thirty <term>shekels<note>original: "sikelen"</note></term>, a sum at which the law of Moses had estimated the value of a slave, and the shekel was not above thirty <term>stuivers<note>A Dutch coin of the period; thirty stuivers was a modest amount, emphasizing the low price for which Judas sold his Master.</note></term>. The Prophet Zechariah had, six or seven centuries before, seen from afar this base and dishonorable agreement, this terrible sale of the King of Heaven and Earth for thirty innocent shekels, and he had introduced him in his prophecy speaking thus: *They weighed my wages, thirty*

Our Savior remained that whole night, and a large part of the following day, in Bethany; and it was there, or on the way to Jerusalem, that he held all those divine discourses with his eleven disciples, which are recounted by Saint John in the 14th, 15th, and 16th chapters of his Gospel, and that he especially offered that excellent prayer which occupies the 17th chapter, and is one of the most weighty and precious conversations of Christ, deserving the highest attention and observation of all believing souls.

### *Matthew, Chapter XXVI. verses 26, 27.*

<margin>
Thursday evening being, according to the custom of the Jews, the beginning of Friday.

After Judas had agreed with the Priests and entered into a treaty, he spent the remainder of that day making preparations for the Passover, according to the command which Jesus had given him the evening before, when he departed from Bethany. He bought the Lamb which had to be slaughtered by the Priests, the unleavened bread, the bitter herbs from which the juice was pressed into a dish, and all the other necessary things for that Feast. That same day, being Thursday, Christ sent two other disciples to Jerusalem, to take a room there, and to prepare the things which Judas had bought, so as to eat the Pass-

<column-break/>

-over. A few hours later, he himself departed with the nine disciples who had remained with him in Bethany, and went to the place he had named to the others so that they would wait for him there. When evening had come, he sat down with the twelve at the table; it was the evening of our Thursday before sunset, but the beginning of Friday according to the ancient custom in the East, of beginning the days from one sunset to the other, instead of us beginning them at midnight; and it was the 14th of the month, the day instituted for the Passover; for Christ could not have advanced it to eat it on the 13th without being regarded as an enemy of Moses's laws. Furthermore, the lamb had to be slaughtered by the Priests, who would not have done so a single day earlier. He then certainly ate it on the same day as the Jews, but not at the same hour. # HISTORY of the N. TESTAMENT.

...sunset; and Christ ate his [Passover] with his Disciples an hour or two after the beginning of that same day, exactly at the time that the Israelites had eaten the first Passover in Egypt. This had to be so, in order that Christ, represented by the Passover lamb, could be crucified on the day of Passover; and specifically at that time of day when almost the entire nation had the lambs sacrificed. For if Christ had waited until the usual hours to eat the Passover, it would have been impossible for him to have been taken captive, condemned, and put to death on that same day. He therefore moved forward his Passover, not regarding the day—for that would have gone against the Law—but regarding the hour, against which neither the Law nor custom struggled. And even the fact that he did so without any opposition, and without it being made one of the points of accusation in the legal proceedings by which he was condemned by the Sanhedrin <note>The Sanhedrin was the supreme judicial and religious council of the Jews in Jerusalem.</note>, is a certain proof that the Jews at that time regarded it as a matter of freedom to eat the Passover at the same hour that their ancestors had eaten it in Egypt, or at some other hour before the sun set, which was however the most common; and that everything held to be essential in it was to eat it on the 14th day of the month. While Jesus Christ ate the Passover with his Disciples, he renewed for them the prediction which he had made to them the evening before at Bethany, that there was one among them who would betray him; "it is one of the twelve," he said, "one who dips into the dish with me." It was to make the horror of this deed stand out all the more that he brought these thoughts and circumstances together. They were very saddened by it, but as the Lord named or pointed out no one in particular, and the traitor did not even show himself moved by the sting which these words should have thrown into his conscience, they did not know whom they should suspect.

### *Christ being knelt in the garden Gethsemane, an Angel appears to him from Heaven.*

#### Luke, Chapter XXII. verses 42, 43.

<margin>Between Thursday and Friday the 14th of the Month of Spring <note>original: "Lentemaand" — The Jewish month of Nisan, which falls in March/April.</note> at the onset of night.</margin>
**T**he Jews were accustomed at the end of the Passover to sing a hymn of praise, which their Rabbis say was composed of several Psalms from the 113th to the 118th included therein, for which reason they also call it the Great Hymn of Praise <note>This sequence of Psalms is known as the *Hallel*.</note>. Christ sang it with his Disciples; and he went out from Jerusalem afterward to betake himself to the Mount of Olives. Along the way, he renewed for them the discourse which he had delivered to them regarding his approaching death. He also told them that they would all be offended by him that night, and that they would see fulfilled in his and their regard that prophecy of a certain Prophet, *I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered*: but that he would rise again, as he had often told them, and would subsequently show himself to them in Galilee. Peter allowed himself to be carried away this time by his usual passion, and he assured Jesus that he would not leave him, even if...

<column-break/>

At the end of the meal, just as they were about to rise from the table, Jesus took the bread with which they had eaten the Passover—namely the unleavened and unfermented bread, as no other was available in Judea at that time; and having blessed it, as if he were beginning the meal, he broke it with his hands; for these were all small loaves, like cakes, for which one did not use a knife to cut them; subsequently he gave these pieces which he had broken to his Disciples, saying, *Take, eat; this is my body which is broken for you.* Each of these words referred to the act he was performing, and together they provided the explanation: The body was relative to the bread, just as the truth is to the image: the breaking of the bread found its essence in that of the Savior's body, which presented itself under this mystery as broken, and broken for them, just as it was for them that he had broken the bread. And what he told them about taking and eating it was the symbol of the spiritual eating of the Savior's body, which he had so powerfully recommended a year before in the same chapter of John <note>Referring to the "Bread of Life" discourse in John chapter 6.</note>, and which happens in the Sacrament, under the sign of the bread, in a more tangible way than in the preaching of the word. He then took the chalice <note>original: "drinkbeker"</note>, and having blessed it, gave it to the one of the Apostles who was closest to him, and commanded them that they should all drink from it, and pass it to one another, from the first to the very last: and he told them that it was his blood, the blood of the New Testament <note>Often translated as the "New Covenant" in modern English Bibles.</note>, which was shed for many. The faith of the Disciples sought the truth of the mystery in the shadows, and saw in advance the precious blood flowing from the Savior's veins, which he was soon to shed for the forgiveness of our sins, and which was poured out figuratively in the wine of the cup, just as the body was broken in the image under the sign of the bread.

<image-desc>A rectangular engraving depicting Jesus kneeling in prayer in the Garden of Gethsemane. A radiant angel appears in the clouds at the upper left, while in the background, the disciples are shown asleep under trees. A rocky landscape surrounds the scene.</image-desc>

->Luke XXII. v. 42.<-

*...pass from me.* <note>original: "van my voorbygaan." Referring to the 'cup' of suffering and death.</note> Thus he named his death, but full of submission to the will of God, for the execution of which he had come into the world, he added at the same time: *But not as I will, but as You will.* After that first kneeling, he came again to his three Disciples and found them sleeping, although as he left them he had commanded them *to watch with him*, that is, to think of him and to concern themselves with the state in which they saw him. He rebuked them gently for this, and speaking in particular to Peter, who had boasted that he would surpass the others, *Peter*, he said, *can you then not watch one hour with me!* He left them a second time, and returning to the same place where he had already been, and kneeling just as the first time, he made the same prayer to God. He then stood up again, and coming to his Disciples, he found them still sleeping; for because they perhaps had not been able to rest for a long time, and their minds were filled with sorrow, they could not keep themselves from sleep. The Lord rebuked them once more, and they did not know what they should answer him. He then left them for the third time, and having fallen down as before, he found himself so struck by all the terrifying objects that presented themselves to his mind at that moment, that a sweat broke out over his whole body, of which there has possibly never been an example, and for which one must not seek the reasons in natural causes. It was a sweat of blood which ran down his face in large drops and fell upon the earth. Nothing can more powerfully represent the great internal agitation of Christ, and the struggle he felt in the innermost part of his soul. This may surprise those who, through a philosophical vanity, see death approaching with cold blood; or those who, from a greater and more exalted insight than philosophy and all human wisdom can give, present and show themselves to death, and seek it in corporal punishments.

<column-break/>

But leaving aside the presumption of the Philosopher and the worldly-wise as unworthy to find a place in this Discourse, it is the case that the Martyrs, who died so cheerfully, see death beforehand disarmed of its terrors which are most to be feared—namely, those of a provoked God; they behold it as the way through which God, reconciled toward them and like a Father full of mercy, calls them to himself, to make them enter into his glory; they also know that his Spirit of comfort and strength accompanies them even onto the wheels and funeral pyres <note>The 'wheel' and 'pyre' (stake) were common methods of execution and torture for early Christian martyrs.</note>. But Jesus Christ, on the contrary, saw at that moment nothing but the fearsome glow of divine Justice; while that tender affection which the Father had borne for him from all eternity kept itself hidden, to let his Justice—which demanded his death for the reconciliation of the sins of the world—work alone. It was then this sight that troubled him, and which caused him such agitation. While he was in that sorrowful state, which placed him almost lower than the Angels—who, being pure and holy Spirits, are entirely beyond the reach of what Jesus suffered—an Angel suddenly descends from Heaven, and in a visible form, glinting like the light of a lightning bolt, he approaches him to comfort him. The Evangelist Luke, who tells us of this appearance of the Angel to Christ in his fearful struggle, tells us only in a word, *that an Angel from Heaven was seen by him, who strengthened him*. Our curiosity would be reckless if it were to attempt to guess what that Angel of light said to Christ. He performed for his Lord and his God the service which he owed to a God become man; and we ought to learn, from seeing this deep sorrow of a God-man (solely because he had loaded our sins upon himself), how terrible our fears and anxieties would be if God looked upon us for but one moment in his justice.

<margin>The same night.</margin>
After the Angel had again departed to Heaven, and Christ had received new strength through his meditations and prayer, he returned once more to his Disciples. Finding them all weighed down by sleep, he said to them that from now on they would have time to sleep and to take their rest. *It is enough*, he said, *the hour has come. See, the Son of Man is delivered into the hands of sinners.* Rise, let us go; see, he who betrays me is near. Judas had left them after the Passover meal <note>original: "maaltyd van 't Paafche"</note>, and some have believed, though without much basis, that he had gone out before the institution of the Lord’s Supper. This traitor had gone to inform the Jews of the place where Jesus had gone—a place as suitable as the hour for their plot to capture Jesus without clamor or riot. It was night, and Jesus was outside the city, alone with his eleven Disciples, in a garden and under the trees. A band of armed people <note>The original Dutch uses "geweer," which in this period referred generally to arms or weapons like swords and clubs, rather than firearms.</note>, led by the traitor, suddenly entered the garden; they feared that Jesus might hide himself among the trees and escape without them seeing him. It is true the Moon, which was then full, caused a great brightness in the sky, but they distrusted that clarity, which could be taken from them by a cloud, and which, even when clear, always leaves a shadow under the trees and never penetrates so through the thick branches that some darkness does not remain in that

<column-break/>

place. To prevent all such inconvenience, the servants took lanterns and torches, and came armed with fire and steel to capture Christ, who, seeing them arrive, stepped forward to meet them. The faithless traitor, who went at the front, had told them that the one whom he should greet with a kiss was Jesus. He then went straight to him, and coming to him, he said to him, *Greetings, Master.* "How, Judas," said Christ, "do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?" After that, turning to those who accompanied the traitor, he said to them, *Who do you seek?* They answered him, *Jesus the Nazarene.* Thereupon he said, *I am he.* This word took away their courage and strength, and they fell to the ground just as if they had been struck by lightning. The Lord Jesus gave them time to stand up, and asked them once more that same question: *Who do you seek?* He let them recover their strength, or rather he himself gave it back to them, so that they could carry out the purpose for which they had come by the secret decrees of divine justice. With this new strength and new courage, the servants laid hands on Jesus and seized him, after he had made them realize that he allowed himself to be captured voluntarily, and that neither the arm of the flesh nor the weapons forged against him could have done anything if he had not delivered himself into their hands. This was what he had said to his Disciples some time before: *I lay down my life; no one takes it from me; but I lay it down of myself, that I may take it again, according to the command of my Father.* And the ancient Church had also understood this, saying in the same disposition of spirit and heart to her Father in a prophetic Psalm: *Sacrifice and offering you did not desire; but you have prepared a body for me. See, I come to do your will, O God.* <note>original: "Slagtóffer en ófferande hebt gy niet gewild..." This refers to Psalm 40 and Hebrews 10:5-7.</note>

### John, Chapter XVIII. verse 10.

<margin>The same night.</margin>
Among the Disciples of Jesus, there were some who had their swords with them. If their number had been large, it might have been criticized, as if they were people traveling with an armed troop. However, prudence required that, since they were constantly on the road, they should not go entirely unarmed because of the danger of being attacked by vagabonds and robbers, who committed great mischief in Judea at that time, as one reads in history. It is true that Jesus Christ, who held all creatures in his power and who made the winds and the sea obey him, could have prevented all those dangers by a single act of his will; but it seems he did not find it advisable to use his power for that exact purpose. This was because, living as a man—indeed, as a weak and forsaken man—he wanted his safety, and that of his Disciples, to depend on human means. Those among them who carried weapons <note>original: "geweer"</note>, seeing that he was being seized, wanted to defend themselves; but because they did not dare to do so without his permission—knowing that if he had not wanted to let hands be laid upon him, he could never have been captured—they said to him, *Lord, shall we strike with the sword?* But Peter, less cautious and of a more fiery nature, did not wait for

<column-break/>

Jesus’s answer: he drew his sword, and striking at the head of one of those men, he cut off his right ear. This man was named Malchus, being one of the servants of the High Priest. The Lord Jesus rebuked <note>original: "wraakte," implying disapproval or condemnation of the act</note> this deed of Peter and commanded him to put his sword back into its sheath, saying *that all who took the sword would perish by the sword.* It was not specifically against that Disciple that Christ spoke these words, but he had in mind the Jews who had taken up the sword against him; and he foretold to them that for this deed they would all perish by the sword of the Romans, who would one day avenge the violence they committed against his person. He had also foretold the same in the parable of the Wedding: *The King, he said, sending his armies, destroyed those murderers and set their city on fire:* which the outcome has proven true in the most terrible way in the world. The true cause was hidden in the eternal decrees of divine Justice, which through the sword of the Romans intended to avenge the crime that the sword of the Jews had committed in putting the Messiah to death. If I wanted to have help, Christ said to his Apostle, *do you think that I could not now pray to my Father, and he will provide me with more than twelve legions of Angels? ->Jesus Christ placed before Caiaphas and the Sanhedrin, or Jewish Council.<-

->Matthew, Chapter XXVI. verses 57-59.<-

<margin>The same night.</margin>
From the entire Gospel, it appears that no people in Judea were more embittered against Christ, from the beginning of his ministry until the end, than the Priests, the Pharisees, and the Teachers of the Law. This might surprise someone who does not know that the passions are never more lively nor more powerful than in persons who have the opportunity to indulge them. The Priests, Scribes <note>Teachers of the Law</note>, and Pharisees were the heads of the people, and the rank which they held in the Church provided them with ever-plausible pretenses to cover their own interests with the name of religion. After Jesus had begun to appear, they perceived that their respect and prestige were gradually disappearing; and they saw that their luster was being extinguished by his. This is the last thing that men can bring themselves to witness, and few can tolerate it if they find themselves in a position to prevent it. The High Priest, who ought to have used his authority

<column-break/>

to restrain the suspicion of the Priests and Teachers against Christ, was possessed by that same spirit as all the others. Also, one could expect nothing good from such a High Priesthood as that of that time, which was divided between two persons, who served it by turns—one one year and the other the next—against the express institution of that most excellent office, which ought to rest upon one man alone during his entire life, at least if some extraordinary accident did not prevent him from serving it. Annas and Caiaphas were then the two High Priests who at that time shared this dignity between them, being father-in-law and son-in-law, and both endowed with it by the authority of the Emperor, who had usurped this right over the laws of Religion. For the rest, the Romans left them a free exercise of the same in most things; and satisfied that they had all matters concerning the State and the Empire served by their governors in their name, they allowed the Jews to have their private courts <term>Vierfchaar</term> <note>A term for a tribunal or court of justice</note> regarding matters of lesser importance, and especially those of Religion. That Tribunal which was called the Great Sanhedrin <term>Sanhedrin</term>, or Great Council, upon which all the others depended, consisted of seventy Councilors, and one President, who was usually the High Priest. They were gathered, contrary to custom, at the house of **Caiaphas** <note>The Jewish High Priest who presided over the trial of Jesus.</note>, when their servants, accompanied by **Judas**, had gone to take his person into custody in the garden of **Gethsemane** <note>The garden at the foot of the Mount of Olives where Jesus was arrested.</note>, and this was the reason he was led to the High Priest and before the Council. One had to have great primary charges of accusation against someone to proceed against him with such violence; meanwhile, they did not know, when Jesus had come before them, of what they should accuse him. Everything finally came down to this: that two witnesses were brought forward who maintained they had heard him say, *that he would destroy the Temple of God, and rebuild the same in three days.* If Christ had said such a thing, one would have had to look upon him with pity, as someone whose mind was impaired, or one would have been forced to honor him as one who had the power and might of a God; but to make a crime of those

<column-break/>

words is something that could never have entered the mind of any sensible person. However, these two witnesses did not declare exactly one and the same thing; there was some difference in the wording with which they made Christ speak, and they even twisted his words into a completely different sense than that in which he had spoken them; and that is why the Evangelists call them *false witnesses*. Jesus answered nothing to these accusations which collapsed on their own, and whose powerlessness he could show no better than by his silence. The High Priest, seeing that he despised the accusation, asked him a question that ended the entire proceeding. *I adjure you by the living God, he said, that you tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of God.* This was a question of great importance to answer: Christ therefore did so: *Yes, he said, I am He, and I say unto you, that from now on you shall see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the power of God; and coming on the clouds of Heaven.* They did not well understand in that answer the ruin and destruction which the Lord Jesus foretold to them of their people, and of Jerusalem and the Temple; but they looked only generally at the majesty and glory of a God, and regarding the same as a blasphemy, the High Priest tore his clothes, and they said, *What further need have we of witnesses?* concluding that after such an answer no other witnesses needed to be brought, since Jesus was sufficiently condemned by his own mouth; and they all cried out unanimously, *He is guilty of death.*
