mischief. To all this malice they added a kind of game that one often sees children play, which was to blindfold his eyes, and to strike him from one side and the other, and repeatedly say, *Prophesy to us, O Christ, or guess who it is that struck you.* <note>The guards were mocking the Jewish belief that the Messiah would possess supernatural knowledge.</note> Meanwhile, this was not a simple game merely to mock Christ, but they intended something else by it. There was a tradition among them that the Messiah would not know persons and things through his eyes, by beholding them as we do; but immediately through himself, and through the depth of his internal knowledge. This view was based on a certain passage from Isaiah, who, speaking of the Messiah, says, *that he would not judge according to the sight of his eyes.* <note>A reference to Isaiah 11:3: "And shall make him of quick understanding in the fear of the Lord: and he shall not judge after the sight of his eyes."</note> This tradition was so well known in Judea that not only did Nathanael have his eye on it when, upon what Christ said of him—that he had seen him under the fig tree—he answered, as if with wonder, that he had seen him from so far, and in a place where the sight of the eyes could not reach: *Master, you are the Son of God, you are the King of Israel.* But also the Samaritan woman, a person of little knowledge in matters of religion, had that same tradition in mind when, having gone to the city to recount what had happened to her, she said, *Come, see a man who told me everything I have done: is this not the Christ?* It was then likely with the same intent, but with an evil purpose, that they thus jested with Jesus in the presence of the Sanhedrin; so that if he did not guess who had struck him, they could even thereby accuse his answer to the High Priest—that he was the Messiah—of being false; and if he did guess it, they would hold it for nothing but a game and a jest.

While all this occurred in the hall of the High Priest, many persons had gathered in the outer chamber, or the portal, who longed for the outcome of this great matter; and since it was cold that night, although such is not common in that season in Judea, a fire had been lit, while they waited for the day to be able to leave again. Peter

<column-break/>

had followed Christ from afar, from the garden of Gethsemane even into the house of Caiaphas: the other disciples had fled, and he alone with John <note>original: "Joannes"</note> had followed the troop that led Jesus away. John was known to some of the household of the High Priest, who asked him no particular questions regarding Christ because they did not know that he was his disciple. But Peter had never had any dealings with those people. While they stood there warming themselves, a certain servant girl looked at him rather intently and recognized him as one of those whom she had previously seen with Jesus on another occasion: but Peter denied it strongly, saying, *Woman, I do not know him.* A few moments later, one of the servants of the High Priest, who was a kinsman of the one whose ear Peter had cut off, said, *Are you not also one of those? Did I not see you in the garden with him?* I do not know, answered the Apostle, what you are saying; I am not the man you mean. Some time later a third person came, who, having heard Peter speak and noticing by his pronunciation that he was a Galilean <note>People from Galilee were often identified by their distinct regional accent.</note>, firmly suspected from this that he must be one of Jesus's disciples. But Peter denied this for the third time, saying, *I do not know that man.* Christ, who from the place where he was could see what was going on in the vestibule, turned around and looked at his disciple; and Peter's eyes falling upon those of his Master, he felt an extraordinary agitation in his heart, and at the same time heard the cock crow, according to what Jesus had spoken to him a few hours before. Repentance found entry into his soul, and his faith, his zeal, and even more the Spirit of grace and conversion, placing the horror of his crime before his eyes at that moment, he could no longer contain and swallow his remorse and sorrow; he then went out from that wretched place where he had the weakness to deny his Lord, and his heart immediately giving itself over to his sorrow, he let a stream of tears flow from his eyes and wept for his misdeed bitterly.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the aftermath of Jesus's trial, focusing on the fate of Judas Iscariot. # HISTORY OF THE N. TESTAMENT.

<image-desc>A detailed engraving showing Judas Iscariot returning the thirty pieces of silver to the Jewish authorities. In the foreground, Judas is depicted in a state of distress, kneeling and casting the coins onto the stone floor. Behind a long table, several bearded men in ornate robes and headcoverings (priests and elders) look on with expressions of indifference or dismissal. The scene is set within a grand architectural hall featuring columns and a large archway in the background. A caption beneath the image reads "Matthew 27:3-5."</image-desc>

The Evangelist who tells this story, and Luke, who also spoke of it in the beginning of the Acts of the Apostles, seem to recount the death of this traitor differently; for Matthew says that he hanged himself <note>The Dutch *verworgde* can mean strangled or hanged.</note>, and Luke says that, having fallen headlong, he burst open in the middle, *and all his entrails gushed out;* and he adds that this matter was known to all who lived in Jerusalem. This contradiction surprises those who read Matthew in the translations that have been made of it, or those who do not investigate the Greek word he used any further than the meaning it has in its proper language, and among the ancient authors who wrote in that tongue. But those who know that the wording of the New Testament should not always be interpreted by a meaning that is entirely Greek—such as was customary in Athens and other cities of Greece—are not so troubled by the difference found between Matthew and Luke. One must first establish as an indisputable fact that Judas threw himself down from above, and that his belly, bursting from that fall, caused his entrails to be cast out. Such a precise and detailed account as Luke gives of it does not allow one to seek any other explanation for his words. Furthermore, it is certain that Luke and Matthew were both well-informed of this fact, which was known throughout the entire city of Jerusalem; and moreover, having been led by the guidance of the Holy Spirit in everything they wrote, there can be no essential conflict between them. It must then necessarily be that, since the contradiction which seems to exist is not truly in what they said, it is in what people have made them say, by giving the wording of Matthew, who mentions this all in but

<column-break/>

a single word, another sense than that in which he used it. Now it is certain that in the book of this Evangelist, as also in all the others of the New Testament, there are words which, though entirely Greek in their form and syllables, are nevertheless placed in a sense that is purely Hebrew, and which they do not have in the Greek language. On this point all scholars are agreed, and no one can deny it if he has compared the style of the New Testament with that of the Septuagint <note>The "Seventy Translators" (LXX), the ancient Greek version of the Old Testament.</note>, and the translation of the LXX with the Hebrew text. Now it appears from what several famous authors of Hebrew dictionaries give us to understand, that one and the same word in that language means *to strangle oneself* and *to cast oneself down from above*. Matthew then, giving to the Greek word—which [is claimed] <unclear>is claimed</unclear> to mean this—the same broad meaning that the word *to strangle* has in common Hebrew, used it in the sense of *casting oneself down from above;* just as he also did regarding other wordings in Chapter 5, verse 17, and Chapter 22, verse 24, and elsewhere; as did Luke in Acts Chapter 2, verse 20; Paul in the Epistle to the Ephesians Chapter 6, verse 25; and in many other places. Judas then threw himself down from above. The Priests gathered up the thirty silver coins which he had thrown down in the Council Chamber; but not daring—through a misplaced tenderness of conscience in men such as they—to mix this money with the coins of the Temple in the offering chest, because it was, as they said, the price of blood that had been sold, they bought a potter’s field with it to bury strangers in. Thus God fulfilled that other part of the prophecy of Zechariah, who had foretold the sale of Christ for thirty pieces of silver: *I threw them into the house of the Lord for the potter.*

# Christ brought bound before Pilate.

## Matthew, Chapter XXVII. verse 2.

<margin>Friday morning around six o'clock.</margin>
The Sanhedrin <note>The supreme judicial and ecclesiastical council of the Jews</note> gathered at the High Priest's house, adjourned around two or three hours after midnight, intending to reconvene soon to fully settle the legal proceedings begun against Christ. They had already confusedly pre-judged in that first meeting that he was worthy of death, but they had not yet passed the final sentence, as they would have acted against all forms of justice if they had judged such a matter by night, and elsewhere than in the palace of the Sanhedrin. Their laws and customs stood against it, and they wished to maintain the appearance of legality and at least observe the most important customary practices. When morning had come, or as Luke says, when day had broken—that is, at the rising of the sun, which the Jews in their common language understood by the name of "day"—the Sanhedrin gathered again, not as the first time in the house of the High Priest, but in the usual assembly hall, which was in one of those beautiful buildings of large, hewn, white, and polished stones built onto the Temple, which the Disciples had viewed with wonder from the Mount of Olives two days earlier. It is true, one finds among some Rabbis <note>Jewish scholars and teachers of religious law</note> that the Jews did not meet on Feast Days to pass judgment. But besides the fact that it would have been no great surprise for judges as impetuous as these to have bypassed that custom for reasons that seemed important to them—such as putting Jesus to death on the day of Passover <note>Dutch: *Paasche*</note>, in the sight, so to speak, of the entire nation—that day was not strictly a feast day,

<column-break/>

until toward evening, around the time of the preparation or the readying of the Passover lamb. The Sanhedrin, having then arranged their meeting as orderly as possible, both regarding the hour and the place, had Jesus Christ brought before them once more to ask him the questions that had already been put to him during the night at the house of Caiaphas, and then to judge him according to legal custom based on his answers. We do not see from the account the Evangelists give of this history that the Council members asked Jesus anything regarding the accusation of the two witnesses, who claimed he said he would break down the Temple and rebuild it in three days. Likely, they let that complaint drop as being of no weight at all, and they held only to the question already asked: whether he was the Christ. Our Savior <term>Zaligmaaker: A traditional Dutch title for Jesus, literally meaning "Bringer of Salvation"</term> did not attempt to revoke this, nor to remain silent on a question that so powerfully concerned his glory and the purpose for which he had come into the world. He then gave them the same answer as before, and upon his answer, the Council gave its verdict and condemned him as a deceiver and false Messiah. Now nothing more seemed left but to carry out the sentence; no one spoke for Christ, and the voice of innocence could not reach the judges, who had completely abandoned themselves to injustice. But one thing held them back: they wanted Pilate, who was the Governor <note>Dutch: *Stadhouder*</note> of Judea on behalf of the Romans, to also condemn Jesus. One might think it was because they themselves dared not put him to death for fear of being punished by the Governor for an act committed against the Emperor's authority. But that was not their intention, and here one must marvel at the depth of God's ways. He had foretold through his Prophets that the Messiah would be nailed to the cross.

### Luke, Chapter XXIII. verses 7 — 11.

Among the accusations which the Jewish Councilors had brought against Jesus Christ to Pilate, they had also made mention of Galilee. *He stirs up the people*, they said, *teaching throughout all Judea, having begun from Galilee*. Because Galilee was not under his jurisdiction, but under that of Herod, who was its Tetrarch <note>A title for a governor of a fourth part of a province</note>, he believed that he might thereby fall into trouble with that Prince, with whom he was already at odds; thus his political strategy did not allow him to step deeper into the matter, in which he had no personal interest anyway. But meanwhile, God’s aim was that Jesus should die on the day of Passover, and that he should die in Jerusalem, just as the Lord himself had foretold to his Disciples several times. <meta>The following text precedes the translation provided for continuity. It describes the Sanhedrin's decision to move the trial of Jesus from a private residence to their official hall at daybreak and their eventual decision to hand him over to the Roman Governor, Pontius Pilate, to ensure his execution followed the prophecy of crucifixion.</meta>

HISTORY of the N. TESTAMENT.

# Christ Brought Bound Before Pilate.
## Matthew, Chapter 27, verse 2.

The Sanhedrin <note>The supreme religious and legal council of the Jewish people.</note>, having gathered at the house of the High Priest, adjourned around two or three hours after midnight, intending to reconvene quickly to fully conclude the legal proceedings begun against Christ. They had already prejudged him in that first meeting, deciding he was worthy of death, but they had not yet pronounced the formal sentence. This was because they would have acted against all forms of legal procedure if they had sentenced such a case at night or anywhere other than the official palace of the Sanhedrin. Their laws and customs opposed this, and they wished to maintain the appearance of legality, observing at least the most important traditional requirements. <margin>Friday morning around six o’clock.</margin> *When the morning had come*, or as Luke says, *when it became day*—that is, with the rising of the sun, which the Jews in their common language included under the name "day"—the Sanhedrin met again. This time, they did not meet in the house of the High Priest as they did the first time, but in the usual hearing hall <note>Known as the Hall of Hewn Stone (Lishkat HaGazit), located on the Temple Mount.</note>. This hall was in one of those beautiful structures built onto the Temple, made of large, hewn, white, and polished stones, which the disciples had looked upon with wonder from the Mount of Olives two days prior. It is true that one finds among some Rabbis the claim that the Jews did not meet on Feast days to judge cases. However, not only would it be no great wonder if judges as hot-headed as these had stepped over that custom for reasons that seemed weighty to them—such as the desire to have Jesus die on the day of Passover in the sight, so to speak, of the entire nation—but that day was not actually a feast

<column-break/>

until toward evening, around the time of the "Preparation" or the making ready of the Paschal lamb. The Sanhedrin, having then arranged their meeting as orderly as possible regarding both the hour and the place, had Jesus Christ brought before them once more. They intended to ask him the same questions they had already put to him during the night at the house of Caiaphas <note>The High Priest during the trial of Jesus.</note>, and then to judge him according to legal custom based on his answers. We do not see from the account given by the Evangelists that the Councilors asked Jesus anything regarding the accusation of the two witnesses, who claimed he said he would destroy the Temple and rebuild it in three days. Likely, that complaint was dropped as being of no weight whatsoever, and they held only to the question already asked of him: whether he was the *Christ* <note>The Messiah.</note>. Our Savior did not seek to retract this, nor to remain silent on a question that so powerfully concerned his glory and the purpose for which he had come into the world. He then gave them the same answer as before, and upon his answer, the Council gave judgment and condemned him as a deceiver and a false Messiah. There seemed to be nothing left now but to carry out the sentence; no one spoke for Christ, and the voice of innocence could not reach the judges, who had entirely surrendered themselves to injustice. But one thing held them back: they wanted Pilate, who was the Governor <note>The original Dutch uses "Stadhouder," a title for a provincial ruler or governor.</note> of Judea on behalf of the Romans, to also condemn Jesus. One might think it was because they themselves did not dare to put him to death for fear of being punished by the Governor for an act committed against the authority of the Emperor. But that was not their intention, and one must wonder here at the depth of God's ways. He had foretold through his Prophets that the Messiah would be attached to the cross,

->HISTORY of the N. TESTAMENT.<-
O 2

The 22nd Psalm <note>A Psalm of David which Christians historically interpret as a detailed prophecy of the crucifixion, describing hands and feet being pierced.</note> makes this clearly understood. The cross was a foreign punishment that was unknown in Judea, and one to which the Sanhedrin <note>The supreme religious and legal council of the Jewish people.</note> never sentenced anyone; yet it was the Sanhedrin that had declared Jesus guilty of death. If he had been punished by the authority of that verdict alone, he would not have been crucified; and how then would it have fared with the truth of the Prophecy? The Romans were therefore necessary for this purpose; among them, the cross was a punishment for rebels and those guilty of crimes against the State. The Sanhedrin accused Jesus of that crime and had him led to Pilate. They told him that this Jesus was a rebel who caused the people to riot, and who was capable—if he were allowed to live—of stirring up great disturbances in the State because he claimed to be the Messiah, the King of Israel. The accusation was serious, had it been true in the sense that the Jews wanted the Governor to believe; he dared not do otherwise than take notice of it, for fear of otherwise falling into disfavor with the Court of Rome. He then held Jesus in the Judgment Hall <note>original: "Rechthuys"; referring to the Praetorium, the Roman governor’s official residence and court</note>, the place where he pronounced his sentences and which was also his Palace. He asked him whether it was true that he was the King of the Jews. Jesus answered that he had said so and that it was indeed so. Pilate continued to question him regarding other complaints which the Jewish Councils had brought against him; but having understood that he was from Galilee, he did not wish to concern himself further with the matter, but sent Jesus to Herod.

## Jesus appears before Herod.

### Luke, Chapter XXIII. verses 7–11.

Among the accusations which the Jewish Councilors had brought against Jesus Christ to Pilate, they had also made mention of Galilee. "He stirs up the people," they said, "teaching throughout all Judea, and having begun from Galilee." These words made Pilate ask whether that man was a Galilean; upon being answered that he was, that Roman did not wish to proceed with questioning him. Because Galilee was not under his jurisdiction, but under that of Herod, who was the Tetrarch <note>term: Tetrarch; a ruler of a fourth part of a region, in this case, a provincial governor under Roman authority</note> of it, he believed that he might thereby come into trouble with that Prince, with whom he was already in a state of unrest; thus his political strategy did not allow him to enter more deeply into the matter, in which he had no personal interest. Pilate was then quite ready to show his respect for Herod by leaving to him the judgment of someone who was his natural-born subject and a citizen in one of the cities under his domain; for, as

<column-break/>

we have seen elsewhere, Jesus was an inhabitant of Capernaum. Divine Providence had brought Herod to Jerusalem at that time. If he had been in Galilee, the condemnation of Christ would have been greatly delayed, and in all likelihood he would have been sentenced to death there: for since Herod had to conduct himself cautiously regarding his interests in view of the Emperor, he would undoubtedly not have failed to sacrifice the life of Jesus Christ to them, just as Pilate did. But meanwhile, God’s aim was that Jesus should die on the day of Passover <note>original: "Paasfche"</note>, and that he should die in Jerusalem, as the Lord himself had foretold several times to his disciples. All these difficulties were then removed by the care which wise Providence had taken to ensure that Herod was in Jerusalem on that very day. Christ was led to him, and as soon as Herod saw him, he testified to being very happy about it, because he had frequently heard him spoken of, and he had long desired to see him, hoping that he would see him perform some miracle. He asked him several—

The Chief Priests and Scribes appeared at the same time before the Tetrarch <term>Tetrarch; a ruler of a fourth part of a province, in this case, Herod Antipas of Galilee</term>, to weigh Jesus down with the same accusations they had brought against him before Pilate; and because Herod was somewhat of their own nation (for he was the son of Herod the Great, whose father had been a proselyte <term>Proselyte; a convert to Judaism</term>, so that he consequently made profession of their religion), they spoke even more vehemently of these things to him than they had done to the Roman. But Christ despised all those accusations, the falsehood of which was clearly evident, and he judged it not advisable to answer anything to Herod, because he did not wish to be tried there. Herod and his courtiers, displeased with the behavior of Jesus, and looking upon him as a miserable wretch who had been cast out by the Synagogue, despised and mocked him.

<column-break/>

And because they told them that this man, just as they saw him there, boasted of being the Messiah, the King of Israel, Herod ordered—to mock and ridicule him—that they should clothe him in a white robe, which color, next to purple, was the most respected and valued among the Great. One does not know for certain whether it was not indeed a garment of purple, which was a royal clothing, for the Greek word used by Luke, who relates this history, means *shining*: and that can just as well be applied to purple or scarlet as to a white color. <note>original: "blinkend"; referring to the Greek *lampros*, which suggests radiance or splendor rather than a specific pigment.</note> With this garment Jesus was sent back to the Governor of Judea; such that Pilate and Herod, showing each other mutual courtesies on this occasion, forgot their mutual grudge and became good friends.

->Pilate has Jesus scourged.<-

### Matthew, Chapter XXVII. verse 26.

**P**ilate, seeing Jesus come back to him without having been sentenced by Herod, to whom he had sent him, called for the Chief Priests and Rulers of the people, to tell them that he had questioned that man regarding the complaints of sedition which they had brought against him, but had found them all to be without merit. He also told them that Herod, in sending him back, had sent word that he had found nothing in that man that deserved death. The falsehood of the accusations arranged against Christ must have been very apparent, since all the cunning and dexterity used to give them some appearance of truth—bolstered by the great prestige in which his accusers were held—drew such an explicit 

<column-break/>

declaration of his innocence from the mouths of two Judges who were as swayed as Herod and Pontius Pilate. But God willed that Christ should thus find advocates in the persons of his Judges, who completely justified him from the false charges with which his enemies sought to blacken him, while no one appeared who dared to speak in his defense. The Jews therefore persisted anew with Pilate; they told him that Jesus had everywhere created gatherings of the people, and had boasted of being the King of the Jews. The Governor questioned him privately regarding this; Jesus answered that his Kingdom was not of the world, but that it was of a spiritual and heavenly nature. But are you then a King? Pilate resumed. Yes, Christ gave as an answer, *For this I was born and for this I have come into the world, that I should bear witness to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth, who knows it and is taken with it, hears my voice and knows what this saying means.* Pilate, who understood nothing but very confusedly of all these matters, asked Christ *what truth was*: but without [waiting for] an answer

expected, he immediately went out to the Jews to tell them that he found no crime nor guilt in him. The Jews, however, did not stop saying that he was guilty, and demanding that he be condemned. But the conscience of the Judge resisted this, so that, caught between his duty and the consideration he had for the persons speaking to him, he could not decide to set the innocent man free, nor to condemn him. While he sat on his judgment seat in that state of indecision, his wife sent someone to tell him that he should have nothing to do with the case of that Righteous man (for thus she called Christ), because she had been greatly troubled in a dream on his account. This was a dream which God had sent her to show her Jesus' innocence, and likely to place before her eyes the deadly consequences that this case would have for her husband and household, if Pilate allowed himself to be carried away by the request and persistence of the Synagogue. This advice made some impression on his mind, but not enough to make him take a decision in favor of persecuted innocence; he therefore sought means to satisfy the Priests and the <term>Sanhedrin; the supreme council and court of justice among the Jews</term> by proposing to them a sort of exchange of Jesus for a prominent capital criminal named <term>Barabbas; a prisoner whose name means "son of the father," held for insurrection and murder</term>, who was in custody for a riot he had started in Jerusalem, which had not ended without bloodshed. The Jews accused Jesus of insurrection without showing any proof of it, and Providence, in a stroke of justice, brought forward a man who was convicted of that very same crime, and was moreover a murderer. Pilate thought that people who seemed so zealous for the public peace and for the interests of the Emperor would be glad for him to put that villain to death, and that he offered to grant them the life of Jesus without going deeper into the investigation of a case which, being as devoid of proof as this one was, could easily result in the shame of the Sanhedrin, who

<column-break/>

had initiated it. And to better win over the Councilors to his opinion, and to leave them all the honor of a trial in which they had involved themselves with so little reason, he wished to make them masters of Christ's life, putting it into their mouths that they should request it from him, and assuring them that he would grant their request. The opportunity for this was entirely favorable. The Roman Governors were accustomed to show this favor to the Jews: that, in honor of their Festival <note>The Passover</note>, they granted them the freedom and life of such a prisoner as they desired. Pilate then presented Jesus on one side and Barabbas on the other, and he commanded them to choose which of the two they wanted him to release. They had the impertinence to demand Barabbas, though against their honor, against their conscience, and against the holiness of the laws. "But what then shall I do with <term>Jesus; the name means 'Saviour'</term>?" cried the Roman, stunned by such an unseemly choice. "You may have him crucified," they answered. "What evil then has he done," Pilate replied, "for which he deserves to be attached to the cross?" They answered once more with a new shout, "Crucify him, crucify him." He came to them a third time to tell them that he did not find that this man deserved death; and thinking to satisfy them if he made him suffer a lesser punishment, though undeserved, he said he would have him scourged and then let him go. But he found them consistently unyielding in giving up any part of their demand. Meanwhile, he condemned Jesus to scourging, and this cruel sentence was immediately carried out. Christ was stripped like a villain, and he offered his back to the merciless scourges of those who struck him, just as <term>Isaiah; an Old Testament prophet</term> had foretold in one of his oracles; and the hand of the soldier, who on this occasion performed the executioner's office, came down heavily on the back of the righteous man, and under the doubled blows, caused the purest blood to flow that has ever been in the world.

*Jesus is draped with a purple cloak, and a crown of thorns is placed on his head, with a reed in his hand, after which they fall on their knees before him to honor him in mockery.*

### Matthew, Chapter XXVII. verse 29.

One does not find in the Gospel that Pilate added any insults to this mistreatment. It was not the custom to increase the shame and pain of a wretched man through mockery, whose body, having been carved by the scourges, was in that state an object of pity, even if he had deserved the punishment he suffered. But everything in the sufferings of Jesus Christ had to have an extraordinary mark of cruelty and injustice. The Roman soldiers, seeing themselves in control of him after they had cruelly scourged him, decided to make a game and mockery of his person, and to amuse themselves with the most malicious jesting that could ever come into anyone's mind.

<column-break/>

They knew that Jesus was called the King of the Jews, and they saw that he was a man of no standing, of a low estate, and scorned and despised by the Synagogue. To turn this into a humorous game, they made a sort of King of him. They took a shabby purple cloak, which they hung around his shoulders; they made him a crown of thorns woven together, which they set upon his head; and they gave him a reed for a scepter in his right hand. After they had dressed him thus, they all fell down before him on their knees to greet him as a King, amidst constant laughter and a multitude of biting jests with which they accompanied all these theatrical acts. To this they added blows with the reed upon his head, such that Jesus was thus led around for some time by a band of Roman soldiers in the courtyard of the <note>Judgment Hall or Praetorium</note>, as if he were the most contemptible of all men, and a boor and a madman. He had foreseen this himself, and more than a thousand years before had foretold that it would happen, expressing himself through the mouth of the Prophet David in the 22nd Psalm:
> I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised by the people: all they that see me laugh me to scorn.

This is a reference to Psalm 22:7, traditionally seen as a prophecy of Christ's suffering.</note> And in the 69th Psalm: *Reproach has broken my heart, and shame has covered my face. ... Those who sit in the gate talk about me, and I am the song of those who drink strong drink.* It is highly surprising that Pilate, in whose Palace all these things took place, allowed the soldiers to extend the sentence he had passed over Jesus beyond what he had commanded; or that, if they had requested his permission for it, as is likely, he granted it to them, since he was perfectly convinced of Christ's innocence. He had imagined that he would have satisfied the Councilors of the great <term>Sanhedrin; the supreme judicial body of the Jews</term> with this, and to extend his compliance as far as possible in a matter he did not view as a capital punishment, he wished furthermore to allow the soldiers, who were ordered to carry out his commands, to add all those mocking insults to it in order to please the Jews even more. But Pilate did not know that the rage which incited them against Christ was like the thirst of a <term>dropsical man; someone suffering from edema or "water-sickness," whose thirst was historically believed to increase the more they drank</term>, which is provoked and inflamed by those small refreshments with which one first intends to quench it. Jesus was put on display before them, being awash in his own blood and draped in all the trappings of contempt and shame; but that sight did nothing but further ignite the desire they had to rid themselves of him, and it served only to make them desire his death with even stronger passion.

But so cunning and wicked is the heart of man; it seeks to cloak the most heinous plot with the veil of religion and to delude the eyes of the people, to master the judgment of men by covering itself with an outward appearance of godliness that is powerful enough to mislead them. to show him to the Chief Priests and all the people, he said to them, pointing at him, *Behold, the man.* <note>original: "Zie, de mensch" - the Dutch translation of the famous Latin "Ecce Homo."</note> These two words conveyed much, if those to whom they were spoken had been willing to pay proper attention to them. They told them that this Jesus, against whom they had risen up as against a dangerous man who could cause great disturbances in the State by aspiring to the status of King, was but a wretched one, more suited to move one to pity or a general laugh than to arouse jealousy in the Romans and to gain a great following in the world. They told them that there stood the *man* who had been brought to him as one who deserved the extreme punishment; and that he, after having questioned him thoroughly, had found that all those accusations were of no value; but that nonetheless, out of the regard he had for them, he had wanted to inflict this shameful punishment upon him, and that they ought to be satisfied with that. He then gave him back to them, saying, *Behold there the man*, and he testified to them through those words that he could go no further to condemn him to a heavier punishment. It could also be that God, who through his providence governed even the slightest circumstances in this trial against Christ, caused Pilate to say much more than he intended to say in speaking those two words: *Behold the man*; and that it went for this Roman Governor somewhat as it had gone some time before for Caiaphas, <note>The High Priest who presided over the Jewish trial of Jesus.</note> when he said in the full Council concerning this same Jesus, *You do not consider that it is useful for us that one man die for the people.* For these two words of Pilate could have been, in God’s intent, though not in that of the Roman, a pointing out of the person in whom all the shadows, and all the Oracles, the law and the Prophets, ended, who after they had all pointed from afar and confusedly to Christ, now showed him as if with the

But this meaning, which Pilate's words could have had in the secret intentions of God, was far too deep to be understood by a Heathen; and the Jews who heard him pronounce them were too much preoccupied with their own thoughts to be able to lift them up to God. Embittered then by their suspicion against Jesus Christ, and ignited by a false zeal, they cannot be satisfied with what Pilate had done, unless he extended his severity further against the supposed criminal. They desire his death, and they want it, moreover, to be the death of the cross. All other punishment seemed too mild to them; it must be such a one in which there is the most pain and the most shame. They cry out therefore once more, as they had done before, *Crucify him, crucify him:* The Roman had refused this the first time, before he had Jesus scourged, and he refused it once again: *Take him yourselves*, he said, *and crucify him, for as for me; I find no guilt in him.* He had told them before that they themselves should take him and judge him according to their law; but they had answered him that it was not permitted for them to put anyone to death. At that time he had spoken to them earnestly and in cold blood, because he regarded everything properly as a matter of religion, and that in such a case their <term>Sanhedrin|The supreme judicial and religious council of the Jews in ancient Jerusalem.</term> might condemn someone to death, as appears from the history of Stephen <note>The first Christian martyr, whose death is recorded in Acts 7.</note> and many others. Those who sit in the gate gossip about me, and I am the song of those who drink strong drink.* <note>original: "snaarenspel der gener die sterken drank drinken" — a reference to Psalm 69:12, describing the mockery of drunkards.</note> It is most highly surprising that Pilate, in whose Palace all these things happened, allowed the soldiers thus to extend the sentence that he had passed over Jesus beyond what he had commanded; or that if they had requested his permission for it, as is probable, he granted it to them, since he was completely convinced of Christ's innocence. But it is usually only the first steps one takes into a crime that cost the human heart anything. Pilate initially had difficulty coming to a decision to command anything against Jesus Christ, and he would have liked to have saved him: but human considerations swayed him, and he allowed himself to be led—by the regard he had for the principal Heads of the Synagogue—to condemn Jesus to scourging.

<column-break/>

He had imagined that he would have given satisfaction to the Councilors of the great Sanhedrin <term>Sanhedrin: the supreme judicial and religious council of the Jews in Jerusalem</term> by doing so, and to extend his compliance as far as possible in a matter that he did not regard as a capital offense, he furthermore wanted to allow the soldiers, who were ordered to carry out his commands, to add all those scornful mockeries to it to please the Jews all the more. But Pilate did not know that the rage which incited them against Christ was like the thirst of a dropsical man <note>A person suffering from "waterzucht" (dropsy or edema). Historically, it was believed that drinking water made the thirst of a dropsical patient even more intense, serving here as a metaphor for insatiable cruelty.</note>, which is aroused and inflamed by those small refreshments with which one first intends to quench it. Jesus was put on display before them, being drenched in his blood, and hung with all the apparatus of contempt and shame; but that sight did nothing other than further ignite the desire they had to rid themselves of him, and it served only to make them desire his death with even stronger passion.

to show [him] to the Chief Priests <term>Chief Priests: High-ranking members of the Jewish clergy who oversaw Temple sacrifices and held significant political influence.</term> and all the people, [he] said to them, pointing at him, *Behold the man.* <note>original: "Zie, de mensch" — in Latin, "Ecce Homo."</note> These few words suggested much, if those to whom they were spoken had been willing to pay attention. They told them that this Jesus, against whom they had risen up as if against a dangerous man who could cause great disturbances in the State by striving for the rank of King, was but a miserable wretch, more fit to move one to pity or general laughter than to provoke the Romans to jealousy or to gain a great following in the world. They told them that there stood the *man* who had been brought to him as one who deserved the ultimate punishment; and that he, after having questioned him thoroughly, had found that all those accusations were of no value; but that nonetheless, out of the regard he had for them, he had wanted to inflict this shameful punishment upon him, and that they ought to be satisfied with that. He then returned him to them, saying, *Behold the man*, and he testified to them by those words that he could go no further in sentencing him to a heavier punishment. It could also be that God, who through His providence directed even the slightest circumstances in this trial against Christ, made Pilate say much more than he intended to say in speaking those words: *Behold the man*, and that it went for this Roman Governor somewhat as it had gone some time before for Caiaphas, when he said in the full Council regarding this same Jesus, *You do not consider that it is useful for us that one man should die for the people.* For these words of Pilate could have been, in God's intent though not in that of the Roman, like a pointing out of the person in whom all the shadows and all the Oracles, the Law and the Prophets, ended; who, after they had all pointed from afar and unclearly to Christ, now pointed to him as if with their

But this meaning, which Pilate's words could have had in God's secret intentions, was far too deep to be understood by a Heathen; and the Jews who heard him pronounce them were too preoccupied with their own thoughts to be able to lift them toward God. Embittered then by their suspicion against Jesus Christ, and ignited by a false zeal, they could not be satisfied with what Pilate had done, unless he extended his severity further against the supposed criminal. They desire his death, and they want it, moreover, to be the death of the cross. All other punishment seemed too mild to them; it must be a punishment in which there is the most pain and the most shame. They therefore cry out once more, as they had done before, *Crucify him, crucify him:* The Roman had refused the first time, before he had Jesus scourged, and he refused it once again: *Take him yourselves,* he says, *and crucify him, for as for me; I find no guilt in him.* He had told them before that they themselves should take him and judge him according to their law; but they had answered him that it was not permitted for them to put anyone to death. He took those words in a Heathen sense, and indeed he could not take them otherwise, being a Heathen as he was, and having no knowledge of the divine Books, nor the teaching of the Church. The Heathens now had in ancient times certain uncommon men among them, whom they called Heroes, and whom they said were born, the one of a God and a woman; and the other of a man and a Goddess. <note>Pilate, as a Roman, likely interpreted "Son of God" through the lens of Roman mythology, where demigods like Hercules were the physical offspring of gods.</note> Their books are full of those fables, and however absurd those stories may be, they nevertheless found belief in the minds of the people, who made it an article of their Religion. Pilate, ignorant like the others, and full of prejudice, wanted to question Christ concerning that matter, which caused him more difficulty than all the others: *From where are you?* he says to him. But Jesus gave him no answer. What he would have had to say there would have been too weighty for an ignorant Heathen, whom he did not intend to convert, and to

## Christ led to Calvary, carrying his own cross to which he was about to be attached.
### John, Chapter XIX. verse 17.

Finally the Jews obtained the condemnation of Jesus Christ, and they saw that long-desired hour, in which he was led out to Calvary <term>Calvary: Also known as Golgotha, the site outside Jerusalem's walls used for executions.</term>, to end his life there on a cross. It was at that time the custom that the criminal who was doomed to that punishment, carried his own cross to the place of justice. This was to make the shame the greater, and to make the heart suffer in advance the punishment which the body was soon to feel, by filling the mind, at the sight of that object, with all the cruel ideas which a cross that one touches, and which one carries to be attached to an hour later, is capable of discharging. Christ, who previously had his eye on that custom, when he had said in a metaphorical sense, that whoever wanted to be his Disciple, must decide to carry his cross, (*Let him

<column-break/>

take up his cross, he says, and follow me:*) is himself brought to that state, that he must carry it according to the letter; and one sees him step out of the Courthouse, and go through the streets of Jerusalem, with that ghastly burden, like another Isaac who carried the wood, on which he was about to be sacrificed as a burnt offering, to the mountain destined for the sacrifice. It is true that Isaac did not know that he himself was the victim who had to be offered on the wood he carried; *My Father*, he said to Abraham, *see the fire, and the wood, but where is the lamb for the burnt offering?* But Christ knew that he was about to be nailed to the cross with which he was burdened, and that nothing could protect him from it. God alone could do such a thing, but his decrees lay against it, and it was God himself who called him to die on a cursed wood. This object did not startle him nonetheless: he was at peace with it as far back as when his imagination presented it to him a few hours before in the garden of Gethsemane; but he had submitted himself to it, because it was his Father's will; and that was why he had no sooner said, *Father, save me from this hour*, or he added to that—

## Christ led to Calvary, himself carrying his cross to which he was about to be fastened.

### John, Chapter XIX. verse 17.

---

Finally, the Jews obtained the condemnation of Jesus Christ, and they saw that long-desired hour in which he was led out to Calvary, to end his life there on a cross. In those times, it was the custom that the criminal who was doomed to that punishment carried his cross himself to the place of justice. This was to make the shame greater, and to make the heart suffer beforehand the punishment which the body was soon to feel, by filling the mind, at the sight of that object, with all the cruel thoughts that a Cross which one touches, and which one carries to be fastened to an hour later, is capable of producing. Christ, who had previously had his eye on that custom, when he had said in a metaphorical sense that whoever wanted to be his disciple must resolve to carry his cross, (*He takes up his cross, he says, and follows me:*), is himself brought to that state, that he had to carry it according to the letter; and one sees him stepping out of the Courthouse, and going through the streets of Jerusalem, with that terrible burden, like another Isaac <note>In Christian tradition, Isaac carrying the wood for his own sacrifice is seen as a prophetic parallel (a "type") to Jesus carrying the cross.</note> who carried the wood, upon which he was to be sacrificed as a burnt offering, to the mountain destined for the sacrifice.

<column-break/>

It is true that Isaac did not know that he himself was the victim which had to be sacrificed on the wood that he carried; *My Father*, he said to Abraham, *see the fire and the wood, but where is the lamb for the burnt offering?* But Christ knew that he was about to be nailed to the cross with which he was burdened, and that nothing could preserve him from it. God alone could do such a thing, but His decrees were against it, and it was God Himself who called him to die on a cursed wood. This object did not amaze him, nonetheless: he had been afraid of it when his imagination presented it to him a few hours before in the garden of Gethsemane; but he had submitted to it, because it was His Father’s will; and for that reason it was that no sooner had he said, *Father, deliver me from this hour*, but he added to—

...stood by, as if to correct his words: but for this cause I have come to this hour. <note>A reference to John 12:27, where Jesus acknowledges his purpose in facing death.</note> He then left the city of Jerusalem in that state, where he had made his entry not more than six days prior amid the cheers of a great multitude of people, who had shouted in his honor throughout the entire city and even into the Temple: *Hosanna to the Son of David: blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest heavens!* But his strength began to fail him, and his shoulders, torn by the scourges, were unable to support such a heavy and crude burden as the cross was any longer, when wise Providence brought him to meet a stranger just at the right time—a man from the city of Cyrene in Libya named Simon, who lived in Jerusalem and was coming from the fields to the city at that moment. He was addressed and forced to take up the cross of Jesus and carry it to Calvary. This service held something shameful in itself, and that was why they took a stranger rather than someone from Judea to use for the bearing of this ignominious wood. Then they shall begin to say to the mountains, Fall on us; and to the hills, Cover us.* And if they do this to the green wood, what shall happen to the dry? <note>Jesus compares himself to "green wood" (living/innocent) and warns that if the Romans/authorities treat an innocent man this way, the fate of the "dry wood" (the guilty or the city of Jerusalem) during the coming judgment will be much worse.</note> These disasters were to come upon Judea some time later, especially during that famous siege of Jerusalem <note>Referring to the Roman Siege of Jerusalem in 70 AD, which resulted in horrific famine and destruction.</note>, during which fathers and mothers would wish that they had not brought those unhappy children into the world, who were destroyed before their eyes by famine, the sword, and all the scourges of God united, without being able to give them any other assistance than that of wailing and tears.

## Matthew, Chapter XXVII. verses 33—37.

Near Jerusalem, and among that range of mountains which surrounded it on many sides, was a mountain that was designated as the place of execution for criminals condemned to death. The Hebrews called it *Golgotha*, which in their language signifies something that is round and easy to roll, like the head of a man. <note>original: "Golgotha"</note> This is why the Evangelists explain it by the word *Skull*, from which the Latins made *Calvaria* <note>original: "Hoofdschedel... <column-break/>

has the same meaning. When Jesus had arrived there, they wanted to make him drink a certain mixed potion, which they kept there intentionally, but he refused it. It was customary on such occasions to compose a drink of wine, frankincense, and myrrh, to give it out of a kind of compassion to those being crucified, so that this mixture, which was very strong, might somewhat soften the sharp pain of the cross by heating the brain and filling it with a vapor that numbs it. But the Jews, full of hatred against Christ, had added to that drink, in order to... <note>The text likely continues to explain that they added gall or vinegar to further mock or embitter him.</note>

to make it even more unpleasant, they added gall and vinegar, as Matthew relates; whereas Mark calls it *myrrhed wine*; because that drink was a mixture of all those things. The Royal Prophet <note>King David, traditionally regarded as the author of the Psalms.</note>, or rather Christ himself, had foretold this remarkable circumstance of his death in the *69th Psalm* with these words: *They gave me gall for my food; and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.* Jesus refused to drink of that beverage, less because of its bitterness than because he wished to retain the freedom of his mind until the end, and because, dying for the sins of Mankind—which could only be outweighed by very raw and fierce sufferings—he did not seek to dull his pain by numbing his senses. All his refuge was in his submission to the will of God, and in the assurance he had that he would strive through those great difficulties unto victory. The Roman soldiers, who carried out the punishment (for at that time there were no regular executioners to put criminals to death), began to undress Jesus: they divided the outer garment or cloak into four parts; and concerning the tunic, which was woven entirely without a seam from top to bottom, since they could not divide it without making it useless, they cast lots for it to see who should have it. This was another circumstance of his crucifixion foretold in the *22nd Psalm* with these words: *They divide my garments among them, and cast lots for my clothing.* Subsequently, Jesus was stretched out on the cross and nailed to it with large spikes through his hands and feet, according to the prophecy contained in that same Psalm: *They have pierced my hands and my feet. I could count all my bones.* For these words clearly referred to the posture of someone stretched out on a cross, which is such that one can easily perceive all the ribs because of the great tension of the entire body. ### Christ crucified between two murderers
### Mark, Chapter XV. verse 27.

THE ignominy of the cross of Jesus was increased by the punishment of the two criminals who were led to Calvary at the same time. The crosses were erected close to one another, and that of Jesus stood in the middle, so that he was crucified between these two villains and, as it were, mingled among them. This circumstance, like the others, was indicated in the prophecies of the Old Testament, for Isaiah, writing of the sufferings of the Messiah, had said that he *would be numbered among the transgressors.* It does not appear that the Jews had requested Pilate to order these three executions to take place at once, but such came from a higher hand. Christ was burdened with all our sins, and it was for that reason alone that he died; his death could therefore be neither too painful nor too dishonorable. All this is found in his cross; and this last circumstance, that he was crucified between two wicked crimi-

<column-break/>

-staff taken away when they led him to Calvary. Since it was customary to place a writing at the top of the cross which made known the crime for which someone was being crucified, one was placed on the cross above Jesus's head, in which one read these four words <note>The "four words" refers to the four components of the title: Jesus, Nazarene, King, Jews.</note> in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin: JESUS THE NAZARENE, KING OF THE JEWS. The first of these words signified his person; the second from what country he was; and the other two the cause for which he was crucified, which was that he had given himself out to be the *King of the Jews*. His enemies wanted this writing, which had been made by order of Pilate, to have contained that Jesus had said, *that he was the King of the Jews*: and not *Jesus the Nazarene King of the Jews*, because those words seemed to have too favorable a sense and to signify that he was indeed the King of the Jews. They therefore ran to Pilate, who, troubled by their quibbling, answered them harshly: *What I have written, I have written.* <note>original Latin: "Quod scripsi, scripsi."</note> Jesus was on the cross from about noon until three o'clock, being until that time the object of the mockery and insults of the prominent men of the people and of the frenzied and blind rabble, which did not believe it sinned in anything it did because it had its Priests and Teachers as leaders. Meanwhile, the Lord Jesus prayed to his Father for those who put him to death, without knowing what they did; and at that moment when divine justice impressed the deepest feeling of its vengeance upon his soul, seeing him as the surety <note>original: "búrg" - a legal guarantor or one who stands in for another's debt.</note> of the human race, he cried out with a loud voice, *My God, my God, why have you forsaken me!* After that mournful moment, his soul was filled with divine comforts. Justice was disarmed by the sufferings of the Savior, who immediately called him Father, whom he had just before called only his God; and saying to him, *Father, into your hands I commend my spirit*, his victorious soul left his body on the cross and went to take possession of the glory in Heaven which was destined for him after his sufferings.

But that same Providence, always wise and always good, which had added this new degree of ignominy to the cross of the Savior, willed that it should happily end in the glory of His Son. One of these two Murderers, who were crucified at his sides, could not endure the blasphemies which his companion uttered against Jesus. It concerned His wisdom to thus highlight the amazing state in which His Justice had placed His Son through such extraordinary events, in order to remove the great offense of the cross from the eyes of the Believers. We leave it here to the Theologians <note>original: "Gódgeleerden"</note> to make deep observations on this confluence of height and depth, of glory and contempt, of honor and dishonor, which God has always shown in the person of Jesus Christ: namely in his birth, in his ministry, and especially in his death, where the glory was as much greater as the shame had been exceptional. This reflection is worthy of the contemplation of searching souls, as they practice the attentive observation of those mysteries; and each of the miracles that occurred at the Savior's death deserves special notice. This darkening of the Sun, which covered all of Judea with darkness, was as if to foretell the darkness of unbelief which covers Judaism even to this day. The earthquake that threatened a total upheaval, and the rocks that split apart, served to reproach the Jews for their unyielding hardheartedness. The graves that opened to let the dead they contained go out alive were like a foreshadowing of that spiritual and mystical resurrection which was soon to happen on earth through the preaching of the Gospel, accompanied by God’s Spirit, concerning which the Lord had said: that the time was coming when the dead would hear *the voice of the Son of God, and those who heard it would live;* and as a glorious prelude to the general resurrection of the dead on the day of Judgment, of which our Savior had said in the same conversation, *that the hour was coming, in*

<column-break/>

*which all who were in the graves would hear his voice; and that those who had done good would come out to the resurrection of life; and those who had done evil to the resurrection of damnation,* and of eternal death for all eternity. Finally, that veil of purple and embroidered work—which the Jews say was several fingers thick—which formed a partition for the Holy of Holies <note>The most sacred inner chamber of the Temple, where God was said to dwell.</note>, and which tore by itself, was a sign that the death of Christ made public the hidden mysteries of the ancient Dispensation <note>original: "Bedcelinge" (Covenant/Era). Refers to the Old Testament religious system.</note> and opened the way to Heaven, which had been closed to mankind because of sin. The Centurion who, with his band of soldiers, kept watch at this crucifixion, was so struck by the words of Jesus Christ and by all the wonders that accompanied his death, that he, seized with wonder, cried out: *Truly, this man was righteous, this was truly God’s Son!* Meanwhile, the day had already passed, and the Jews had to hurry to eat the Passover, for which purpose the Priests were busy in the Temple at that time slaughtering the lambs; for it was three o'clock in the afternoon, the time which the Jews called *between the two evenings.* This obliged the Council of the Sanhedrin to request permission from Pilate to quickly take the bodies down from the crosses, so that the Sabbath, which was very near, would not find them still attached to the wood of punishment. Nicodemus, a Councilor and Pharisee well known in the Gospel History for the conversation <note>referring to the meeting in John 3</note> he had from that time on, had been one of his secret disciples. But he still held to his office and status, which elevated him to a rank from which he could not decide to descend to be the disciple of a poor, despised, and persecuted Messiah. One could therefore say that he was but halfway a Christian, since he did not dare to let the good opinion he had of Christ be seen, nor had he dared, during the period of three whole years, to make that costly sacrifice—so powerfully recommended by Christ—of forsaking himself and all human considerations to follow him. they did not even let their thoughts go to the resurrection of Jesus Christ, and it could be that they were still ignorant of that mystery, of which he had indeed given knowledge on several occasions to his Apostles, but they had, in that time of sorrow and distress, paid so little heed to it. Christ could have, by his divine power, prevented his body—which was like a cast-off garment of death—from being subject to any corruption; and God the Father himself was concerned to preserve it from such, for the honor of the offering of a *sweet-smelling savor*, and of the reconciliation which his beloved Son had offered him in that body as an atonement for the sins of the world. Thus Christ, looking toward his resurrection, had said to his Father with that assurance: *My flesh shall certainly dwell, or rest in hope; for thou wilt not leave my soul in Hell;* <note>original: "Helle." The author notes this was a Hebrew idiom meaning the grave or the place of the dead.</note> *Thou wilt not allow thy Holy One to see corruption.* But God did not judge it advisable to use his power immediately to protect the body of his Son from the approach of corruption, since human and natural means could sufficiently prevent it. It was also an honor he wished to bestow upon the body of Jesus: to provide an excellent embalming for it, out of regard for the satisfaction that had been given to his Justice in that sanctified body. When Jesus Christ bore our sins in his body on the wood <note>A common term for the cross.</note>, he was in the eyes of God as an object of the curse, according to the saying of the Apostle Paul to the Galatians, and therefore it was only impure and sinful hands that touched him from the garden of Gethsemane until Calvary. But after he had shown to God that deep obedience to which he had dedicated himself in the taking up of his body—for which reason he had also said to him,
> *Behold, I come to do thy will, O God!*

<column-break/>

so was that body in the eyes of the Heavenly Father nothing but an object of delight and love, and God did not allow any decay to happen to it, nor that any other hands than those sanctified by faith and love should touch it. It was then laid in a new and pure linen cloth, purchased for that purpose; and while the two others who were crucified were thrown into a common pit or onto a dungheap, wise Providence ensured that an infinite distinction was made between those corpses and that of Jesus. Two Councilors of the great Sanhedrin <note>Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus.</note> come to take it down and embalm it, and thus show it the greatest honor that can be shown to persons of the highest rank on such an occasion. After they had wound it in large linen cloths with a mixture of Myrrh and Aloe, they went to bury it in a tomb that was hewn out of a rock, and in which no one had ever yet been laid. This was a tomb that Joseph of Arimathea had caused to be hewn in a garden which was close to Mount Calvary, to be buried there after his death. Thus the body of Jesus received the greatest honor of burial; and through the wonderful care of Providence, that prophecy from the 53rd chapter of Isaiah was seen to be fulfilled:
> *His grave was appointed with the wicked;* <note>Because it was natural that Jesus, being crucified between two criminals, would have his body thrown with theirs into the usual place for those executed by death.</note> *but he was with the rich in his death;* <note>Meaning he would be buried in the tomb of a rich man, for the Scripture gives that title to Joseph.</note> *because,* adds the Prophet, *he had done no wrong, nor was any deceit in his mouth;*

to give it to be understood that Jesus Christ had not unjustly claimed the names of *Son of God* and *King of Israel*, for which the Jews had caused him to be crucified.

-> ## The resurrection of Jesus Christ. <-

-> ### Matthew, Chapter XXVIII. vs. 2, 3, 4. <-

<margin>
Sunday
morning
</margin>

The permission that Joseph of Arimathea had obtained from Pilate to take the body of Jesus from the cross and bury it prevented the Jews from opposing it; but seeing that Joseph and Nicodemus themselves had buried him, they feared that the Disciples of Christ, under the protection of such respectable men, would take the body out of the grave to then spread a rumor through the world that he had risen again. This fear, if one looks closely, arose only from a great malice that was in the hearts of the Jews, who judged what the Disciples might do by what they themselves would have done if they had been in the same circumstances. They had, it is true, some pretext for their fear, and that was enough to oblige them to be on their guard. To that end, they went to the Governor and told him they still remembered that Jesus—or as they called him, that *Deceiver* <note>original: "Verleyder"</note>—had said while he was still alive that he would rise on the third day; and that since it might happen that his followers

<column-break/>

might go to lift him from the grave by night to make it believed that he had risen—which would be capable of causing more unrest than everything he had done in his life—they therefore begged Pilate that he would send some soldiers to guard the grave. Pilate laughed to himself at all that strange suspicion, but to carry his sinful compliance for the sake of the Councilors as far as possible, he answered them: *You have a guard;* <note>These were certain companies of troops which the Jews, with the permission of the Romans, kept in service as a special guard for the Temple.</note> *Go your way, make it as secure as you know how.* They then went immediately (for the hour of the Passover necessitated their haste), taking their own soldiers whom they led to the grave, and they sealed the stone that closed it. All these precautions were useless to the Jews, but they have been of infinite usefulness for us and for the whole Church; for the more the enemies of Christ were busy preventing anyone from approaching the grave during those three days, the less the faith in Jesus's resurrection finds any suspicion to combat, and the greater the evidence and certainty there is in the truth of this miracle. The guard was set on Friday evening, and it remained there the whole night, the following day being Saturday...

->*Matt. XXVIII. v. 2, 4.*<-

day, and the night thereafter upon which the first day of the week, called by us *Sunday*, followed. During all that time, the body of our Savior rested undisturbed in his grave, but as we have seen in the oracle of the 16th Psalm, he rested in hope that he would soon come out from there. The time appointed for that great wonder in the <term>Council of Peace</term> <note>A theological term referring to the eternal covenant between God the Father and the Son regarding the salvation of mankind.</note> between the Father and the Son, of which Zechariah had spoken, arrived; and at that moment when the sun appeared above the horizon, Christ, the *Sun of Righteousness*, stepped out from the darkness of death and took up again the life that he had left on Calvary. There occurred, just as at his death, a great earthquake, and an Angel of the Lord descended from Heaven like lightning to roll away the stone that covered the grave. Jesus stepped out and disappeared from the guards: terror had seized them, and they thought the earth was about to swallow them alive, just as formerly happened to Dathan and Abiram in the rebellion they started against Moses and Aaron. <note>A reference to Numbers 16, where the earth opened to swallow those who rebelled against God's appointed leaders.</note> The sight of the Angel, who appeared before their eyes at that moment like lightning, increased their consternation; and even more than all that, the greatness of the crime they committed by using their vigilance and their weapons against Jesus Christ. They fell to the earth as if dead, and would possibly never have risen from it, if

<column-break/>

God had not wished to make use of them to bring the astonishing news of Jesus’ resurrection to their masters. These wicked men, after having resisted all the miracles he had performed during his life—instead of finally opening their eyes to that of his resurrection and having paid careful attention to the prophecies Jesus Christ had made concerning it—fully shut their eyes and seek only for means to prevent such a glorious event from finding any belief in people's minds. They give money to the guards, so that they might tell everywhere that the Disciples of Jesus had come by night and had taken him away at a time when they were sleeping. The guards, thus bribed by money and by the promises of the Priests, spread this false rumor among their nation. But the truth triumphed over the false testimony and deceit, and this last vanguard of the Jews against the resurrection of the Savior served only to make the truth of this resurrection more certain to all wise minds who were not occupied by prejudice, and even by the very declaration made of what had happened; for according to their own confession, the body of Jesus was no longer to be found in the grave before they left it; and since there was absolutely no appearance that it had been taken away, one could conclude nothing else from all this than that he had risen.

Perhaps these holy women feared that something was still lacking in the embalming performed by persons of such rank and status <note>Refers to Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus, who were members of the high council and might have lacked practical experience in the manual labor of preparing a body.</note>, which prevented them from having all the necessary experience in such matters; and possibly they thought that their own hands, which were more accustomed to such work than those of these two gentlemen, could improve what was still lacking. Because it was at the very end of Friday that Jesus was laid in the grave, they remained in Jerusalem the following day, being that of the Sabbath, either because they thought it would be a violation of the holy day to occupy themselves with that work, or because they feared it would have provoked the Jews, and that those to whom the garden belonged, or who lived there, would have hindered them.

Meanwhile, they prepared everything for the following day, undoubtedly unaware that the Priests and Pharisees had placed a guard by the grave; for it is inconceivable that they would have intended to go there if they had known it was guarded by soldiers. Then, the day after the Sabbath, they rose very early in the morning and left the house while it was still dark. But before they had reached the grave, the sun was already above the horizon, and since no man was with them, and the stone that sealed the grave was very large and heavy—as the stones of burial vaults usually are (for it was a grave hewn out of a rock, and not a kind of cave at the foot of a rock)—they said to one another: *Who shall roll away the stone from the door of the tomb for us?* Thus talking together, they came to the garden, but having come close to the grave, they saw it open, and an Angel, in a human form, sitting on the stone at the side of the entrance. One can easily imagine that they stood very amazed

<column-break/>

over this; but the Angel, turning to them, encouraged them, saying:

> *Do not be amazed, do not fear; I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified. He is not here, for he is risen: as he said; come hither, see the place where the Lord lay.*

They then approached and went into the tomb, which being a kind of spacious and large grotto, they could easily enter. But they were not a little astonished when, having entered, they saw another Angel in the form of a young man, clothed in a long white garment, and sitting on the right side of the entrance, at the place where the niche was hewn in which the body of the Lord had lain: for the ancients did not bury their dead in coffins <note>The author notes that Judean burial involved placing the body on a stone bench or in a niche within a rock-cut chamber, rather than in a wooden casket.</note>, as we have noted in the history of the resurrection of the young man at Nain, and in that of Lazarus; but they made in the burial vaults, which were their honorable graves, various niches in which they laid the corpses, just as if they had placed them in uncovered chests. Therefore it is that John, speaking of the linens which the women found in the grave, makes no mention of a coffin, because there actually was none.

Upon leaving, the Angels said to them that they should go and bring the news of the Lord’s resurrection to the Disciples, to pull them out of that dejection in which they all were because of his death. And the Angel who spoke to the women charged them in particular that they should inform Peter of it: for that Apostle being even more sorrowful than the others, because of the great misfortune he had in denying Christ, the Lord wanted to testify to him that he forgave him that sin, however gruesome it might be; such that the Disciple was one of the first to whom he had his resurrection announced, and the only one who was named in the command that he gave to these holy women.

### *Christ appears to Mary Magdalene, who mistakes him for the Gardener.*

#### John, Chapter XX. verses 14—16.

The Disciples' minds and hearts were still so full of the death of Jesus that when Mary and the other women who had gone to the tomb came to tell them he had risen, it seemed like a dream to them, and they could not believe it. Such is the natural weakness of the human spirit in the mysteries of salvation: there needs only a powerful prejudice, or sometimes just a lack of attention, which, placing itself between our mind and faith, makes us doubt everything. Peter and John were the first to recover from that sort of spiritual lethargy <note>original: "geestelyke doodslaap," literally a spiritual death-sleep or stupor</note> in which the news of the Lord's resurrection found them all; and leaving the other Disciples behind, they immediately ran to the tomb to assure themselves with their own eyes of the truth of the matters the women who had come from there had told them. They both went very quickly, but John ran ahead faster than Peter and arrived first. He found the tomb open, and leaning down at the entrance, he saw the linens lying there in which the body of the Lord had been wrapped. Peter, arriving a moment later and having entered the tomb, saw the linens on one side and the sweat-cloth <term>sudarium|A cloth used to wipe sweat from the face, specifically the burial cloth placed over Jesus' head.</term>, which had been on his head, rolled up in another place. John then also stepped inside, and the assurance which Christ had often given them before his death—that he would rise again on the third day—then coming to their minds, they were completely convinced that he had truly risen. The senses aided in this instance

<column-break/>

through their testimony to faith, and faith, elevating the testimony of the senses to the revelation of the Scripture, created from this convergence of knowledge in the minds of the Apostles such a deep impression of the resurrection of Jesus Christ that they later sealed the truth of this miracle with their blood. They left the sweat-cloth and the other linen they had found there in the tomb and returned in haste to confirm to the other Disciples the news of the Lord’s resurrection that had already been brought to them. While they were returning to Jerusalem, Mary Magdalene—whom Christ had previously delivered from seven devils with which she had been possessed, and what she valued far more than all that, from the damnation of sin and the dominion of passions (which are far more deadly to the soul than all the devils together)—had gone out of the city for a second time to return to the tomb. As she bent down to look inside, with no other purpose than to satisfy her eyes and heart by the sight of a place where, for two nights and one day, the body of the holy Sacrifice <note>A reference to Jesus as the "Sacrificial Lamb."</note> offered on the cross had lain, she saw two Angels dressed in white. One was sitting at the head and the other at the foot of the grave where the body of Jesus had been placed. They asked her the cause of her sorrow and tears, and why she wept. She answered, *Because they have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him.* It is a wondrous thing that Mary, having already been to the tomb early in the morning and having found an Angel there who told her Jesus had risen, now gave such an answer to these two Angels. It is a sign that she had not yet entirely recovered from the distress into which the death of Jesus had brought her, and that the faith of his resurrection

The two Disciples with whom the Lord had joined himself on the road to Emmaus felt a joy far too great because of that appearance to be able to stay any longer in that hamlet <note>original: "vlek," meaning a small town or village</note>, where they had likely intended to spend the night. They returned then, immediately after the Lord Jesus had disappeared from before their eyes, back to Jerusalem, and arrived there still that same evening. They found the Apostles gathered with some others in a house of which they had closed the doors, for fear of being overtaken by the Jews. All these holy persons were in mutual conversation about the resurrection of the Lord, and said that he had appeared to Peter. Thereupon the two Disciples entered, and gave a precise account of everything that had occurred between the Lord and them on the road to Emmaus, and how he had become known to them in the breaking of the bread. But hardly had they finished their story when Jesus appeared in the room, and found himself in the midst of them. The wood of the doors had been as a flowing air for the body of Christ, and had immediately resumed its first form and natural solidity, just as some renowned interpreters of ancient times have explained it.
