...a physical life, <note>original: "dierlyk leeven," referring to a biological existence sustained by food, proving he was not merely a phantom or spirit</note> which is maintained by nourishment; but this was necessary to strengthen the faith of his disciples; and by his divine power, he caused the food—which his hand took and his mouth truly and indeed ate—to vanish. The senses were thus appointed by Christ himself as the judges of the truth and reality of his body, since the body is their proper and natural object; and it was upon their testimony that the very witness which the apostles gave of his resurrection throughout the whole world was subsequently founded.

Thomas was not with the other disciples when Jesus appeared to them; as soon as they saw him, they gave him an account of the happiness they had had in seeing the Lord: but what they told him had so little plausibility that he could not believe it. *If I,* he said, *do not see the mark of the nails in his hands and put my finger into them;* (he still feared that his eyes would deceive him, so he wanted his hands to touch everything his eyes saw, to be completely assured of it;) *and if I,* he continued, *do not put my hand into his side, I will by no means believe.* The power of prejudices <note>The author uses "vooroordeelen" (prejudices) to describe the mental barriers and preconceived notions the disciples had about the impossibility of a physical resurrection.</note> holds the understanding captive and extinguishes the light of faith. Thomas lacked everything in this instance: faith as well as reason. Eight days later, the disciples being again gathered in the same room, while the doors were closed as before, Jesus entered in the same way and suddenly appeared in their midst, saying as the first time, *Peace be unto you!* He himself brought them that precious peace by wishing it upon them. Then, turning to Thomas, he reproached him

<column-break/>

for his unbelief, and said, in order to convince him in such a manner as the disciple had desired: *Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing.* Thomas was ashamed of his unbelief, and he cried out in wonder at the grace which the Lord showed him, after having made himself unworthy of it: *My Lord and my God!* These few words in the mouth of this apostle said a great deal, and were, among other things, a profound adoration of Jesus Christ as his Savior and his God, in that same sense as John later said of him: <note>original: "Joannes," referring to the Apostle John in 1 John 5:20</note> *This is the true God and eternal life.* Thomas undoubtedly deserved a sharp rebuke for his unbelief, but Christ contented himself with giving it to him as if in passing: *Thomas, because thou hast seen me, thou hast believed: blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed.* The great difficulties which the resurrection of Jesus met in being believed, even among the apostles and especially by Thomas, have removed from future centuries all those doubts which a weak mind, held captive by prejudice, might have had regarding this great miracle, which is the foundation of our faith; for *if Christ be not risen, then is our faith in vain,* as the Apostle Paul said to the Corinthians, *and we are yet in our sins.* But he who also believes in the resurrection of the Lord Jesus believes everything; and in that one act of faith, the Law and the Gospel unite as in a common center.
</columns>

### *The appearance of Christ to his Disciples on the shore of Lake Gennesaret, where they had gone fishing.*

### John, Chapter 21, verses 1–9.

THE Disciples of Jesus Christ had returned to Galilee a few days after his resurrection, the region where they were all born and where they had been told they must go, because they would see him there. It appears from what Luke tells us at the beginning of the book of Acts concerning the appearances of Jesus to his Apostles, that he appeared to them several times; and the Apostle Paul indicates the same thing in the fifteenth chapter of his first Epistle to the Corinthians. The appearance of which John speaks at the end of his Gospel was one of the most remarkable: it occurred on the shore of Lake Gennesaret, or the Sea of Tiberias. <note>Lake Gennesaret and the Sea of Tiberias are different names for the Sea of Galilee, where many of the disciples previously worked as fishermen.</note> The Disciples were not all there, as they had been in the room where he had shown the wound-marks of his hands and side to Thomas. Here there was no one but Peter, Thomas, James and John (the sons of Zebedee), Nathanael, and two others whom John does not name. Peter, who was a fisherman like most of the other Apostles, having told them that he was going fishing, they wanted to go with him; and they then boarded his small boat, where they spent the whole night without catching anything. The next morning, when they had come back to the shore, Jesus stood there, like someone walking by to watch the fishing. He asked them if they had any fish to eat; and they answered him, No. Jesus commanded them to cast the net on the right side of their vessel, and as if he, from the shore

<column-break/>

where he stood, had seen fish at that spot, he told them they would find some there. It cost these men nothing to put this to the test, and to do this favor for the one who gave them this advice: they then cast out the net at the place he had pointed out to them, and it became so full of large fish that they could not pull it into their boat. They needed their companions, who had stepped out onto the shore, to come help them drag the net to land, and when they had pulled it up, they found one hundred and fifty-three large fish in it. As soon as the Disciple whom Jesus loved (this is how John refers to himself in this narrative) saw that they had such a large catch in their net, he said to Peter, *It is the Lord.* At those words, Peter allowed himself to be carried away by his zeal, and without waiting until they had brought their boat to land, he girded on his outer garment or tunic and jumped into the sea to swim to land and come to Jesus, who stood on the beach. The others soon arrived with their vessel and net as well, and saw a glow from a fire of coals, with fish lying on it and bread beside it. It was Christ who caused all this to be found there through that same power by which he had multiplied the loaves on several occasions. After he had the Disciples eat their midday meal, without any of them daring to ask who he was—because they clearly saw that it was he himself, although he spoke nothing special to them by which they could recognize him—he began to enter into conversation with Peter in the presence of all the others. He asked that Apostle, who had had the weakness of denying him in the house of Caiaphas, whether he loved him: *Simon, son of Jonah,* he said, *do you love me more than these?* This question, posed in this way, served to bring to this Disciple's memory the zealous, yet indeed somewhat too hasty declaration, in which he had said to Jesus a few hours before his death: *Even if they*

<column-break/>

# HISTORY of the N. TESTAMENT.

Virgin, joined with the Apostles to hold religious gatherings together; for it is only solitary spirits, or free-thinkers <note>The author uses 'vrygeeften' (free-thinkers) to criticize those who avoid communal worship in favor of private prayer.</note>, who despise such gatherings and have fallen into a vain singularity of performing their devotions and prayers alone and by themselves. On a certain day, then, when the assembly of the Apostles consisted of about one hundred and twenty persons, Peter took the floor and proposed that they should choose someone to take the place of the wretched Judas, who had given himself up to despair. This person was to be chosen from those who had been in the company of Christ with the twelve during the time of his ministry and had seen him after his resurrection. This advice was approved by the entire company; but because the choice of men was not enough for such a great Minister as that of the Apostleship, they took from the number of the Believers two men in whom all the required qualities to make an Apostle were found. To leave the choice to Jesus Christ, they cast lots over them both, saying to him: *You Lord, you knower of the hearts of all, show which of these two you have chosen to receive the lot of this ministry and Apostleship.* The lot fell upon Matthias, who was immediately accepted into the number of the eleven Apostles. Then came the feast of Pentecost, famous because it was the day on which God gave his Law on Mount Sinai, and the day on which the Holy Spirit began the establishment of the new Law, bringing his fire and enlightenment upon those who were to be used to proclaim the same in the world. The Apostles were still gathered with those same persons who, with them, made up the holiest company that had ever been on earth since the Lord had departed to Heaven. They were all there with the same spirit of faith and love, busy with godly thoughts, in humiliation and in prayer. Suddenly a violent wind arose, which came rushing down with an extraordinary noise upon the house where the Apostles were gathered; and

<column-break/>

at the same time, flames of fire were seen in the form of tongues that were divided at the ends or tips, appearing and seating themselves on the heads of the Apostles alone, or on those of the entire assembly; for the Interpreters <note>Theologians and biblical commentators of the era.</note> do not agree on the meaning that should be given to the wording of the sacred Text, though they tend to favor the latter opinion more than the former. This fire was the symbol of the Holy Spirit, of whom Christ had said to his Disciples a few days before, *that they would be baptized with the Holy Spirit and with fire.* And this form of tongues, namely tongues that were divided in the middle, signified that the Apostles, for whose sake this miracle primarily occurred, would have the gift of languages, to proclaim the mysteries of redemption to all nations, and to each in his own language. The report of this spread immediately through the whole city, and people came running in crowds from all sides to see this spectacle. There were at that time in Jerusalem Jews who had come there from all places of the world to celebrate Pentecost, and each heard the Apostles speaking in his own language: Hebrew, Persian, Greek, Latin—as many languages as there were nations. And the things they said were so great and so weighty that people could not recover from the amazement in which they found themselves. Some frivolous people (for where are there none ready to mock holy things?) said that these people were drunk, as if drunkenness, which leaves the tongue nothing but broken words without any orderly arrangement, could teach unlettered and unlearned men to speak all foreign languages and to deliver speeches that exceed the understanding of the most clever and profound spirits. The Apostle Peter took the floor for himself and for all the others, and full of that divine power which the Holy Spirit added to his speech, he brought about a conviction in the minds of his listeners, and through that sermon alone he converted three thousand of them.

### The lame man healed by Peter at the door of the Temple.
->Acts, Chapter III. verse 7.<-

Since those first conversions wrought by the Apostles were pure products of the Holy Spirit, in which no human insights had a part, such a living faith was seen in all those persons that they had no greater joy than to come together for their religious exercises. The number of them increased daily under the power and enlightenment of that same Spirit, and the Apostles on their part neglected nothing to imprint the truths of grace in their minds. They sought, as Jesus Christ had often done, for opportunities to do this in the Temple, where their devotion drew them and where they found the people gathered for that purpose. Regular prayer services were held there twice a day, in the morning and in the evening; and it happened once that Peter and John had gone there in the afternoon, at the 

<column-break/>

usual hour, which was three o'clock <note>The 'ninth hour' in the biblical text, corresponding to 3 PM.</note>, passing through one of the doors of the Temple, which because of the magnificence of the building was commonly called the *Beautiful* gate. They found there a man, lame from his birth, who had himself brought there daily to beg for alms from those who entered the Temple. This lame man, seeing Peter and John approaching, requested an alms from them as well as from all others. Peter said to him: *Look at us.* Usually, one sees that those beggars who have settled in places where many people pass by, such as at Church doors, pray to everyone but do not look directly at anyone. This man, hearing what these two men said, kept his eyes fixed on them, hoping to receive something significant. Whereupon Peter said to him: *Silver and gold I have not, but what I have that I give to you: In the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene, rise up and walk.* Saying this, he took him by the right hand, and this man stood up; his feet and anklebones became firm, and he jumped and walked with them. Since this beggar was known by very many people, because he had long been at that door of the Temple—

Having thereafter returned to the other disciples, they gave them an account of everything that had occurred, and they praised God together, having resolved to continue preaching Christ, whatever opposition they might encounter. The Lord blessed their zeal and their preaching; the number of believers increased significantly every day, and the love was so great among them that they were of but one heart and one soul. The wealthy shared their goods with the poor, and the poor, satisfied only with their necessities, did not abuse the generosity of the rich. Yet God did not allow the greed and the deceit of **Ananias** and **Sapphira** to remain hidden, but revealed it to Peter, to whom **Ananias** went to bring his money, intending to make him believe that it was the full price he had received for the land. Peter, seeing him approach, said to him accusingly that he had been free to keep his money or to give it; but that since he, through a loathsome vanity and hypocrisy, wanted to make it believe that he gave everything he had received for his land, while it was no more than a portion that he brought, it was Satan who had filled his heart and moved him thus to lie to the Holy Spirit. **Ananias** fell down dead upon hearing these words, by a special judgment of God, who in the very beginning of the Gospel wished to give this great example of His rightful severity against hypocrites; just as He had given many such examples in the first institution of the Covenant of the Law. The corpse of this miserable **Ananias** was immediately carried out to be buried: and about three hours later his wife **Sapphira** came, who did not know of the wretched death of her husband, to the Apostles. Peter asked her for how much money they had sold the piece of land: this godless woman, who in all this had agreed upon the matter with her husband, named the same price which **Ananias** had told Peter: whereupon this Apostle, full, as Jeremiah says, of the Lord's fury, said to **Sapphira**, *Why have you agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord? See, the feet of those who have buried your husband are at the door, and they shall carry you out.* At that moment she fell dead at his feet; and those same young men who were returning from the burial of **Ananias**, took up the body of **Sapphira**, and went likewise to commit it to the earth.

THE death of Ananias and Sapphira <note>A couple in the early church who, according to Acts 5, were struck dead after lying to the Apostles about the proceeds from a property sale.</note> impressed a great reverence upon the minds of all the Believers, and caused everyone to fear such a punishment in similar circumstances. The Apostles meanwhile remained in Jerusalem, teaching the people the truths of salvation, and accompanying their preaching with very many miracles, which daily increased the number of converts. They generally met together in the Temple, in Solomon’s Porch <note>A grand, roofed colonnade on the eastern side of the Temple's outer court, a traditional place for public gathering and teaching.</note>, where many people gathered; but Luke <note>The traditional author of the Acts of the Apostles.</note> suggests that they were mostly common folk, since persons of some standing did not dare to approach the Apostles. Such power have human considerations always had to prevent people from following the truth when they see there is some danger in declaring themselves for it. The entire Synagogue was embittered against the Christians, and the High Priest with the other priests, along with the Sanhedrin <note>The supreme religious and legal assembly of the Jewish people in Jerusalem.</note>, condemned their teaching. Such a complete and detailed judgment, pronounced by the highest tribunal of the Jewish Church, was for the great and powerful of the world—who never take a step in religion without consulting their own interests—a plausible reason to prevent them from accepting the doctrine of the Apostles. It is true, the doctrine was found to be in agreement with God’s Word, and had moreover this divine mark: that it was confirmed by miracles. This is a quality which the truth has not had since that time, or at least

<column-break/>

not except in a very low degree, in comparison to the first centuries of the Church. But there were almost no persons except from the common people who, not allowing themselves to be blinded by prejudice, accepted a doctrine which was condemned by the High Priest and all his followers. If one does not perceive therein the work of Grace, as well as the divine principle from which conversion arises, then one is without eyes and without understanding. The heart, solely through corruption, resists all the power of evidence, and it defends itself even against miracles until it is changed into another heart by a miracle that is even greater. God did not show that grace to those who seemed to have no light or knowledge except to blind themselves by it, and who with closed eyes gave themselves over to unfaithful leaders, who only served to lead them onto a path of error. But that which comforted the Apostles over the mockery through which they saw the most prominent persons of their nation perish, was to see that they did not preach the Gospel in vain, and that the Lord, before whom all that distinction of greatness, wealth, authority, and human wisdom vanished, *daily added to the Church those who were being saved.* The power which God had given them to heal all kinds of ailments was so great that they sometimes only needed to show themselves to the sick to make them healthy, without speaking a word; their shadow was enough to bring about all those great effects. Luke relates that whenever Peter had to go through a street, people brought the sick out on mats <note>original: "beddekens", small portable beds or pallets.</note>, so that his shadow, or the air that had touched that Apostle, might touch them, whereby they were then healed. They then had the two Apostles come back in, sentenced them to be scourged, and commanded them under heavy penalties not to continue proclaiming the Gospel. But neither those mistreatments nor threats were powerful enough to make them hesitate: they viewed it as a great honor that they had suffered that shame for the name of Jesus Christ, and they did not cease to preach him in the Temple and in the houses.

The Apostles smothered this grumbling in its birth by commanding that seven men of known piety and godliness be chosen to take all those cares upon themselves. Among those who were chosen, Stephen was one of the most remarkable, both for the great enlightenment with which the Holy Spirit had gifted him, and for the miracles which he performed. Persecution soon attacked him; he was accused of having spoken ill of God and the Temple in a certain debate that had been held with him. The Sanhedrin <note>The supreme judicial and ecclesiastical council of the Jews in Jerusalem.</note> having assembled, Stephen was made to appear there to be judged according to the severity of the laws. The High Priest, who presided over that assembly, asked him if those things of which he was accused were so. Stephen was in no way terrified to see himself placed before such a Council, as powerful as this one was, whose members were all collectively prejudiced against the Believers; his innocence, and even more the grace of God, supported him and encouraged him. Before he had even opened his mouth to defend himself, a bright radiance was suddenly seen upon his face, such that one would have said it was the face of an angel. This miracle spoke in advance in favor of Stephen's innocence, and a moment later he himself began to make his defense through a speech full of dignity and power, but which the malice and rage of his enemies did not allow him to finish. He gave a brief account of the most prominent events from the History of the Patriarchs, and especially of Abraham, who was the most remarkable of all. His aim therein was, firstly, to show that he was far from having contemptuous feelings toward the Religion of his Fathers, as he was charged; and secondly, to make his Judges understand, through such a retelling of the history of their nation, that the Religion of their forefathers had existed independently of the Temple, and that God's covenant with them had not been attached to a Tabernacle <note>The portable sanctuary used by the Israelites in the desert.</note> or any other material and earthly building. He pointed out to them from the Prophets that the Most High did not dwell in Temples made by human hands, and to that end, he cited the words of God Himself, which He had spoken through Isaiah:
> Heaven is my Throne, and the earth is a footstool for my feet. What kind of house will you build for me; or what is the place of my rest? <note>original: "De Hemel is my een Troon, en de aarde een voetbank myner voeten. Hoedaanig een buys zult gy my bouwen; óf welk is de plaats myner ruſte?" — quoting Isaiah 66:1.</note>

The gravest point of the accusation against Stephen was that he had said: that Jesus the Nazarene would destroy the Temple and change the institutions of Moses. But he had said nothing regarding this other than what God Himself had given to be understood in that oracle

<column-break/>

of Isaiah; which, having been spoken long after Solomon had built the Temple, could refer to nothing else but the rejection which God would one day make of that material and figurative Temple, and to the abolition of the ceremonial Laws of Moses, which had an essential connection with the Temple of Jerusalem. Subsequently, in his excellent discourse, Stephen depicted the pride with which their fathers had treated the Prophets; and having come down to his own time, he reproached his countrymen for their contempt of the Messiah, and the fury with which they had demanded His death from Pilate. This reproach, which was only too well-founded, ought to have struck their hearts with sorrow and repentance; but instead, it did nothing but embitter them all the more against Stephen. They could not endure that he should set them before their own eyes as they truly were; they then interrupted him in his speech, and gnashing their teeth, mockery and rage showed upon their faces, and a general murmur arose in their assembly. Stephen was at that moment filled with the Holy Spirit, and lifting his eyes to Heaven, he saw the glory of God, and Jesus in His majesty and glory. At the sight of such a great and sublime object, he cried out, enraptured with wonder and joy: *Behold, I see the Heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God*. These words drove the Jews to the utmost fury; they stopped their ears, they fell upon him boisterously, and dragging him out of the Council chamber, they hauled him outside the city to stone him. The witnesses who had testified against him before the Sanhedrin were the first to stone him, and to be able to do so, they took off their coats and gave them to be kept by a young man named Saul, who was then completing his studies in Jerusalem, and who, a few years later, was converted by Jesus Christ and made into one of His Apostles. Stephen saw, with a wonderful strength of spirit and with a heart permeated by the comforts of grace, that moment in which he stood to be stoned; and when the stones began to fall upon him, he holily commended his soul into the hands of the Lord Jesus, and kneeling down, he cried with a loud voice: *Lord, do not charge this sin against them*. As soon as he had said this, the stones, which came flying at him from all sides, made him sink down dead to the earth; and leaving his body of dust and clay to his enemies as the prey of their wild cruelty, his soul went into Heaven to Christ his Savior, to take possession of the glory in which he had already beheld Him.

The death of Stephen was the beginning of a great persecution against the Congregation of Jerusalem. The Believers of that city were scattered throughout all Judea, and Galilee, and the land of Samaria, and went to hide themselves from the eyes of the

God, who destined them for a longer ministry, protected them from the sword of the Sanhedrin <note>The supreme judicial and ecclesiastical council of the Jews in Jerusalem.</note>, which daily shed the blood of the Believers. At the same time, Philip—one of the seven Deacons <note>Elected officials chosen to assist the Apostles in practical matters, such as distributing food and aid.</note> who had been chosen alongside Stephen—departed from Jerusalem for Samaria, both to secure his life there and to use the knowledge with which the Holy Spirit had enriched him for the glory of the Lord Jesus. He preached the Gospel to the Samaritans, who listened to it very attentively and received it with great teachability and zeal. They watched with wonder as the possessed were set free, the lame were healed, and many other miracles were performed by Philip. These miraculous signs, which for many years had been so common in all the cities of the Jews, were entirely new to the Samaritans, who had never seen such things done in their land, neither by Jesus Christ nor by his Apostles; and the city of Samaria, the capital of that land which in former times had been a mighty Kingdom, had been left until that day in its ignorance and errors. Philip was the first who went there to proclaim the Gospel and perform miracles; and once he had made himself very famous there, the people were helped out of the delusion in which they lived regarding the great esteem for a certain man named Simon, who had bewitched them with his deceptions and fine words, and said of himself that he was the *great power of God*; that is, he boasted of having divine authority and a power to do whatever he wished. This vain and ambitious man, seeing himself suddenly fallen from his status, accepted the Gospel, let himself be baptized, and was so overcome with wonder at Philip that he wished to be with him constantly. The news of the success which the preaching of the Gospel had had in Samaria having been brought to Jerusalem, the Apo-

<column-break/>

stles saw fit that Peter and John should go there, to add the laying on of hands—through which the Holy Spirit descended upon the believers—to the Baptism which Philip gave to the Samaritans. When Simon had seen this new miracle, he went to the Apostles, begging them that they would grant him the same power to make the Holy Spirit come upon those on whom he laid his hands, and for that purpose, he offered them a sum of money. But Peter, angered against that ambitious hireling, who sought nothing else than to make a great name for himself and to acquire wealth through such a rare gift, answered him:

## The Conversion of Paul.
### Acts, Chapter IX. verses 4, 5.

<margin>
* Year of J.C. 37 or according to others 35.
</margin>

THE persecution continued in Judea, and the Sanhedrin <note>The supreme religious and legal council of the Jews in Jerusalem.</note> did not cease from punishing all the Believers who were brought before them, and giving strict orders to take them into custody in all places within their jurisdiction. It went even further; they went to seek them out even in neighboring lands where the Jews had Synagogues, and with the permission of the rulers of those places, they had them seized before their very eyes and brought to Jerusalem. Nothing can escape the rage of a false zeal, and there is no hiding place where superstition does not find a means to persecute the truth. Among those who had received orders from the Sanhedrin for those cruel executions was a Pharisee named Saul, born in Tarsus in Cilicia, who, having completed his studies in Jerusalem in the school of the renowned Gamaliel, excelled both through his dili-

<column-break/>

gence in following the will of his Masters and through the fiery passion with which he carried out such orders against the Christians. He was like a raging lion that constantly seeks prey, destroying everything that came before his eyes, and seeking out the fearful sheep of the Lord even in their darkest hiding places. Driven by this spirit of persecution, he took letters from the High Priest to the Synagogues of Damascus to conduct a narrow search there for persons of both sexes who had embraced the Christian religion, and to lead them imprisoned to Jerusalem. When he was on his way to carry out this cruel task and had already come close to Damascus, he suddenly saw a light from Heaven appear, which shone around him like lightning. He was so terrified by that sight that he fell to the earth and heard a voice calling to him from Heaven, *Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?* He answered that voice, which he did not yet know, *Who are you, Lord?* and the

The Lord saw this resistance from a heart that hardened itself at the mere approach of grace, like a Raging horse that rears up, or an untamed bull that kicks back at the mere touch of the iron that goads him: *It is hard for you, He said, to kick your heels against the pricks: You resist your conversion and will not surrender, but you shall not succeed; God shall be stronger than man.* <note>The phrase "kick against the pricks" (original: *de verfenen tegen de prikkels te slaan*) refers to an ox kicking against a sharp goad used by its driver; the more the animal kicks, the more it hurts itself.</note> Saul felt the power of these words, and it increased within him. He then offered no more resistance; he yielded, and all trembling and astonished, he sought to do nothing other than what Jesus might command him: *Lord, he cried out, what will you have me do?* Christ answered him: *Arise, and go into the city, and there you shall be told what you must do.* The men who traveled with him to Damascus to carry out the orders with which he was charged stood completely amazed by this great light which had shone around Saul and by the voice which they had heard; but they had not, as he had, seen the Lord Jesus who had appeared to him, nor

They took the gates of Damascus into their keeping and kept people on watch there day and night to take Saul into custody whenever he should come there. But he received word of everything his enemies were plotting against him, and he escaped their hands through the foresight of some Believers, who let him down over the city walls in a basket at night. From there he went to Jerusalem, where Barnabas first introduced him to the Apostles and thereafter to the Congregation. Since he was a Greek by birth, and therefore had a great knowledge of the Greek language, he went into the Synagogue of the Jews of that nationality who lived in Jerusalem, to proclaim the Gospel there and to prove that Jesus was the Christ. These arguments, which always turned out to the shame of the opponents and were followed by the conversion of many people, brought upon him a persecution similar to that which he had experienced in Damascus. But to avoid falling into the hands of his enemies, it was found best that he should depart from Jerusalem, and they escorted him to Caesarea, where he took a ship to Tarsus, the city of his birth in Cilicia, where the authority of the Sanhedrin was not so much to be feared as in the places closer to Jerusalem and situated in Judea.

### Peter, imprisoned by order of King Herod, is delivered by an Angel, who makes the chains fall from his hands and opens the prison doors for him.

#### Acts, Chapter XII. verses 4-10.

<columns>

<margin>The Year of J.C. 42.</margin> When it was understood in Jerusalem what had occurred in Caesarea regarding the conversion of Cornelius, the converted Jews who made up the Church of Jerusalem were in such great consternation over it that they could not refrain from testifying to Peter that they were highly amazed and somewhat offended <note>The early Jewish Christians initially believed the Gospel was only for the Jewish people; Peter entering a Gentile home was a major breach of tradition.</note> that he had entered the house of Gentiles and had eaten and drunk with them. The Apostle justified his entire conduct, giving an account of the vision he had had, of the commands he had received, and of the manner in which God had poured out His Spirit upon the household of Cornelius and his friends, even before they had received Baptism. No one then found the conduct of that Apostle strange; on the contrary, all glorified God for the grace He showed to the Gentiles, saying: *So then God has also granted to the Gentiles repentance unto eternal life.* Barnabas thereafter departed from Jerusalem to Tarsus to seek Saul, who had gone there some time before;

It was also in that city, and at that time, that the name of *Christians* had its beginning, and since then it has always remained with those who make confession of the Gospel; for previously they had been called, in general, Believers or Disciples. Around that same time, Herod Agrippa, grandson of Herod the Great and father of that King Agrippa mentioned later in the same book of Acts, raised a new persecution against the Congregation, and had James, the brother of John, beheaded. God could not tolerate that a Prince, born in the bosom of the Synagogue <note>Meaning Herod, though an appointee of Rome, was raised in the Jewish faith and should have known that accepting divine honors was blasphemy.</note>, should be susceptible to a vanity which His patience could hardly have endured even in a Pagan—who, making gods of mortal men as weak and wicked as others, and sometimes worse, might have had greater qualities and a purer knowledge than they. An Angel struck him then on the spot, because he had not given the glory to God; thereupon he was gnawed by worms and gave up the ghost.

# The Apostle Paul strikes the Sorcerer Bar-jesus with blindness.
## Acts, Chapter XIII. verse 11.

The martyrdom of James, whom King Herod Agrippa had caused to be beheaded, had saddened the Church more than it had terrified it. The Christians experienced in many ways the protection with which God covered them, and therefore, instead of becoming discouraged regarding the Gospel due to the persecutions of the Jews, they were all the more strengthened by them. They had the joy of seeing that the Congregation increased daily, and that God’s word was preached not only in Jerusalem and in all the surrounding provinces, but also in many others far from there. It is also the language of a person, and not of an attribute or a single quality of the divine nature, such as power, wisdom, goodness, and others. From all this, it then appears that the Holy Spirit is God, and that He is a distinct person from the Father and the Son, just as they are also distinguished in Baptism, which is administered in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and in that famous text of the Apostle John: *There are three that bear witness in Heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one.* <note>original: "Drie zyn 'er die getuygen in den Hemel..." ## Paul heals a cripple at Lystra who was powerless in his feet.
### Acts, Chapter XIV. verses 8—10.

Paul and Barnabas, having departed from the island of Cyprus after the conversion of the Governor Sergius Paulus, came to Perga

<column-break/>

and despising what he spoke against the Gospel, because there was nothing in his words that deserved any refutation, he said to him with the greatness and the authority of the Holy Spirit by which he was inspired:
> O you child of the Devil, full of all deceit and of all malice, enemy of all righteousness, will you not cease to pervert the straight ways of the Lord? But behold, the hand of the Lord is against you; you shall be blind, and not see the Sun for a time. 
Immediately the eyes of this wretched man were darkened and covered with a thick gloom. He wanted to go away quickly, ashamed of the punishment which he had brought upon himself through his defiance; but he did not know where to go, and he turned and groped to one side and the other, until someone took him by the hand and led him out. This miracle fully convinced the Governor and made him decide to accept the Gospel. He believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, and the Apostles thus had the comfort of seeing that a man—holding a dignity which in following centuries has been signified by the title of King of Cyprus <note>A reference to later medieval traditions or perhaps the high status of the Proconsular office being equated to royalty in historical hindsight.</note>—did not let himself be restrained by any human consideration from entering into the Congregation of a crucified Jesus. Furthermore, it should be noted here that Luke, in the telling of this history, for the first time gives the Apostle the name of *Paul* instead of *Saul*, by which he always spoke of him until this chapter. The similarity of this name with that of Sergius Paulus has led some ancient Interpreters to believe (which is also accepted by many modern ones) that the Congregation on that occasion gave the Apostle that name to show him some honor for such a glorious conversion as that of the Governor. But the spirit of the world, which always seeks honor from extraordinary things, has too much a part in that opinion to believe that such a thing came into the thoughts of the first Christians, and that the Apostle, who uses the name *Paul* in all his Epistles, would have assumed that name for himself on such an ambitious ground. He had, then, the two names of *Saul* and *Paul*, of which the first was a Hebrew and the other a Latin name; just as very many Jews had, some a Greek with a Hebrew name, and others a Hebrew with a Latin name, since their nation had been mixed, first with the Greeks from the time of Alexander onwards, and thereafter with the Romans when their imperial domain extended over all of Asia. And that it was without any particular intention that Luke mentions the name of *Paul* in that place is evident from his manner of speaking; for he says only, and as if in passing, that Saul was also called *Paul*; which clearly gives it to be understood that the Apostle already had those two names beforehand.

that the Jews were scattered throughout all the lands of the known world, and [God] had for that same purpose preserved in the heart of Assyria the remnant of those ten tribes who were led captive there under the reign of Shalmaneser <note>Shalmaneser V was the King of Assyria who initiated the siege of Samaria, leading to the exile of the Northern Kingdom of Israel.</note>. After several chapters of the Holy Scripture had been read in the Synagogue of Antioch, according to the praiseworthy custom of the Jews—which was wisely followed by the Christians in the first centuries of the Church, but has since fallen out of use through the neglect of later centuries—the Leaders of the Synagogues, having seen these two strangers there, spoke to them. Following the custom of that time, and likely not knowing who they were, they said that if they had come to speak any word of godliness to the people, they were free and permitted to do so. Thereupon Paul stood up, and having beckoned with his hand to signal that he had something to say, he delivered a great speech, full of pith and power, as can be read in the 13th chapter of the Acts of the Apostles. He briefly recounted the history of his nation, just as Stephen had previously done before the Sanhedrin <note>The supreme judicial and religious council of the Jews in Jerusalem.</note> in Jerusalem, which indicates that such a retelling was quite customary among those people. He then transitioned to the history of Jesus Christ, whose resurrection he recounted as a truth confirmed by a great multitude of witnesses. He cited various prophecies of the Prophets that had looked forward to that miraculous event. To this he applied those words of the second Psalm: *Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee:* and that prophecy from the 16th Psalm: *Thou shalt not suffer thine Holy One to see corruption.* He showed that those words could not have referred to David, whose body had decayed to dust in his grave, which could still be seen at that time. He preached the forgiveness of sins in the name of the crucified and resurrected Jesus, and he rebuked the stubbornness of the unbelieving Jews, who rejected him as a false Messiah—

<column-break/>

The assembly, having heard him, was divided; some were hardened in their unbelief, and others, moved by Paul’s discourse, begged him to stay with Barnabas in their city for some time and to preach to them again on the following Sabbath. Paul and Barnabas granted their request, and subsequently, having proclaimed the Gospel to them and to the Gentiles, Luke records that *as many of their listeners as were ordained to eternal life believed.* This shows that faith comes from election, and that election infallibly leads to faith <note>This commentary reflects the Reformed or Calvinist theological perspective prevalent in the Netherlands during the 18th century, emphasizing God's "election" or choosing of believers.</note>. The others became only more embittered against these Servants of Jesus, who found themselves forced to depart from Antioch. From there they went to Iconium, where they had to suffer the same persecution from the unbelieving Jews, who stirred up the Gentiles against them. They were therefore forced to leave that city sooner than they would have otherwise done, in order to comply with that word of the Son of God: *When they persecute you in one city, flee to another.* For having learned that there was a plan in Iconium to stone them, they went to Lystra and Derbe, two cities situated on the borders of Lycaonia, and proclaimed the Gospel there. In Lystra, they found a man who was lame in his feet and had never walked in his life. This lame man, hearing Paul preach, was touched by his discourse; and whether it was that he had already heard of the miracles the Apostle performed, or, as is more likely, that a spiritual light illuminated him at that moment to make him understand what this Minister of the Lord Jesus was capable of through a special grace of Heaven, he believed that Paul could heal him of his heavy malady and weakness. Paul then looked at him intently, and noticing that the man believed he could be healed, he said to him with a loud voice: *Stand upright on your feet.* Immediately the lame man pulled himself up with a leap and walked.

### *The Lystrians bring garlanded oxen to offer them to Paul and Barnabas.*

->Acts, Chapter XIV. verses 11—13.<-

<margin>The same year.</margin>
AS soon as Paul had healed the lame man at Lystra in the presence of a great multitude of people, he drew to himself the wonder and applause of the Lystrians through this miracle. Having never seen anything like it, and knowing that such a healing surpassed human power, they cried out together: *The Gods have become like men and have descended to us.* It is well known how many foolish opinions the Pagans <note>original: "Heydenen"</note> held regarding their Gods. Once the mind has lost the idea of the true God, it wanders into a thousand vain imaginings, which cause man to look upon those as gods who never were, and which prevent him from recognizing the true God, who has always been and shall be eternally. These wretched Lystrians took Barnabas for Jupiter, the greatest and most esteemed of their Gods, and Paul for Mercury <note>The Greeks called these gods Zeus and Hermes; the author uses the Roman names common in 18th-century literature.</note>, who, according to the theology of the Idolaters, was the God of eloquence and the one whom the other Gods used to convey their commands to men. Barnabas had not spoken, and perhaps he had a dignified and distinguished appearance. Paul had nothing grand in his face or stature; he himself tells us in one of his Epistles that his enemies claimed against him that *the presence of his body was weak* <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 10:10.</note>; but he had been the one speaking, just as that supposed God of eloquence, whom the Pagan Poets called the Interpreter of the Gods, did for Jupiter. The prejudice was so powerful in this instance that even the Priest of Jupiter, or of a

<column-break/>

Temple in the suburb dedicated to Jupiter, swept away by the ignorant commoners and being as unknowing as they, ran hastily to fetch oxen. These were crowned—according to the custom of the Idolaters—with wreaths of flowers of various colors and tied with ribbons, in order to sacrifice them to Paul and Barnabas. But when these Holy men saw this extreme blindness of the Lystrians, and that they themselves, though quite innocently and against their intention, had given cause to those Idolaters to commit such a gruesome crime, they tore their clothes and, running with haste into the press of the people, cried out: *Men, why do you do these things? We also are men of like passions and subject to the same weaknesses as you. Therefore we preach to you that you should turn from these vain and superstitious things to the living God, who made Heaven, the earth, the sea, and all that is in them; who in times past allowed all the Pagans to walk in their own ways; although He nevertheless did not leave Himself without witness, doing good from Heaven, giving us rain and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness.* But these miserable idolaters were so taken with the foolish imagination that Barnabas and Paul were their Jupiter and Mercury, that with all the trouble in the world they could hardly be brought to other thoughts by the explicit declaration which Paul made to them to the contrary, and they wanted to proceed with force to sacrifice to them. Yet they soon changed their opinion regarding these two Ministers after they had allowed themselves to be persuaded that they were but men: for some Jews having arrived from Antioch and Iconium, they stirred up the people of Lystra against them to such an extent that Paul was stoned, so that he was left for dead. -tions of Moses. This was a reproach against Paul and Barnabas, who had been satisfied with baptizing the Gentiles who had received the faith. Peter and James, surnamed the Less <note>James "the Less" is often identified as the "brother of the Lord" and a leader in the Jerusalem church</note>, being the brother of Jude, were then in Jerusalem, and although their authority was not greater than that of Paul—who himself had said against those who wished to diminish his respectability that he was *in no way* less than the most excellent Apostles—he nevertheless desired that the Congregation of Antioch should consult with them on that dispute. To that end, an Assembly was then appointed in Jerusalem, in which Peter was of the opinion that one should not impose such a heavy and rough yoke as that of the ceremonial Law upon the converted Gentiles. James pronounced the decision of the Assembly on this matter, which was: that the converted Gentiles should not eat of foods offered to Idols; that they should abstain from blood, from any beast that is strangled and whose blood was not so cleanly drained that some of it remained in the flesh; and that they should guard themselves against fornication, a matter which the Gentiles generally did not regard as a crime, thinking they did enough by condemning adultery.

Barnabas wanted John, surnamed Mark, who had also been with them on their first journey as far as Pamphylia, to accompany them on this second one as well: but Paul was of a different mind, and he gave his reasons for it. The matter was indeed of little importance, but God allowed this disagreement to rise so high that it caused a separation between Paul and Barnabas, in order to humble them in the sight of such a great weakness, and thereby to keep the most perfect believers in a constant distrust of themselves. Meanwhile, God, who draws good out of evil, ensured that His Church drew more benefit from the separation of these two Apostles than if they had always remained together, because each on his own side preached Christ in different lands. Barnabas, having taken Mark with him, went by ship to the island of Cyprus; and Paul, having chosen Silas as a companion, traveled through Syria and Cilicia, and resumed the route he had previously traveled with Barnabas. He found at Lystra a young Disciple (for that is what Christians were still called then), named Timothy, the son of a Jewish woman who had been converted to the Christian faith; but of a Greek father, namely a Gentile <note>original: "Heyden"</note>, merely a member of the household, who consequently was not circumcised; for it was only full Jewish proselytes, or members of the Covenant, who allowed themselves to be circumcised. Timothy was not circumcised because his father, not being so himself, had not wanted his son to be. Paul, having a particular knowledge of the good qualities of this young man, wanted to take him with him on his journey; and for the sake of the converted Jews of Lystra, who were there in great numbers, he circumcised Timothy, since the profession in those early times of the Gospel was an almost indifferent ceremony <note>Paul viewed circumcision as a secondary matter of tradition rather than a requirement for salvation</note>, so there could be occasions where, through a concession that could only provide some edification to the Believers who had newly departed from Judaism and were still very strongly possessed by the great idea of that ceremony, one acted prudently and wisely so that its use was not discarded entirely. On the other hand, there were encounters where it would have been a cowardice and treachery to have a convert circumcised, when one found oneself among stubborn people who maintained that circumcision was as absolutely necessary through the Gospel as under the Law. Paul therefore used that wise prudence on all occasions that came before him. Here he permitted Timothy to be circumcised, and elsewhere he opposed the circumcision of Titus, *and that, he says, because of false brothers who had crept in, who had come in privately to spy out our liberty which we have in Christ Jesus, who has freed us from the yoke of the Law.* Paul then, having taken Timothy—who later became so famous in the Church—with him, traveled through various lands of Asia Minor, or Asiatic Greece, and went to Philippi, a city of Macedonia, which had the privilege of a Roman Colony. Since this was a very prominent city, Paul judged that he should stay there for some time, to attempt to establish a numerous Congregation there. Outside the

<column-break/>

city, by the side of a river, there was a kind of Synagogue, which we might call a House of Prayer <note>original: "Gebedehuys"</note>, because the Jews of Philippi went there to perform their public prayers. Since in these types of buildings the women were not in a place separated from where the men gathered, as was the custom in the Synagogues, Paul, accompanied by Silas and Timothy, could easily speak of the doctrine of salvation to the pious women whom he found in that House of Prayer. Among others, there was one named Lydia, a native of the city of Thyatira, and a seller of purple in Philippi, who listened to the preaching of Paul with particular attention, and Luke, speaking of her conversion, expresses it with these words; *The Lord opened the heart of Lydia, that she attended unto the things which were spoken of Paul:* to give us to understand that it is the immediate Grace of God that works conversion, and not the ministry of men, of whatever kind they may be. This holy woman, through her powerful request, obliged Paul and the men who accompanied him to come and lodge at her house in Philippi: her entire household availed themselves of that benefit, and they were all baptized. It happened once while Paul, with Silas and the others, went to that place of prayer, that a servant girl, who had a spirit of Python <note>original: "geest van Python." This refers to a spirit of divination or fortunetelling associated with the Greek god Apollo</note>, ran after them in the streets, crying; *These men are the servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to us the way of salvation.* One calls a *Spirit of Python* that which we would call a divining spirit; for this word *Python* is derived from another, which in the Greek language means to consult. Therefore it was that the Heathens called *Apollo*, who was one of their false Gods, by the name of *Pythian*, because they went to him to ask advice, as one of their most famous Oracles, to discover the darkest matters through him, and to know the future. The devil, with whom that woman was possessed, used her to deceive the credulity of the idol-worshippers through crafty and complicated answers; and since she sold her answers dearly to those who had the folly to come to her for advice, the people under whom she served drew much profit from it. Since this continued for many days, it finally annoyed Paul that this possessed woman thus followed him and the other Ministers of Jesus Christ; and although the testimony she gave them seemed very advantageous for them, and was perfectly true, yet he did not wish to accept it from such an unholy person, who spoke through the Devil, since even because it was the devil who inspired it, this testimony in a mouth so accustomed to lying could not but draw an air of falsehood and deceit after it. Jesus Christ, for that same reason, had refused the declarations which the demoniacs made that he was the Son of God, and commanded the devils who inspired them to be silent, and to go out of the bodies of those possessed. His Apostle did the same here: He turned to the fortuneteller, and speaking to the spirit by whom she was driven, *I command you,* he said, *in the name of Jesus Christ, that you come out of her.* And he came out at that same hour.

### *Paul and Silas being placed in the prison at Philippi, the doors of the dungeon are opened by an earthquake, and the jailer wishes to kill himself with his sword.*

### Acts, Chapter XVI. verses 26, 27.

<margin>The same year.</margin>
Self-interest is always the mainspring and the motive of scoundrels and deceivers, and even more so in the deceptions of false religions than in all others; because out of a desire for profit, various other pretenses, which superstition provides to greed, mingle therein. The people who drew a great profit from the city of Philippi through the fortune-telling with which their servant girl occupied herself, seized Paul and Silas and led them with violence to the public square where the Authorities gathered. They accused them of causing great disturbances in the city by a new teaching that went against the laws of the State. The people also rose up against them, and arrogantly demanded of their Magistrates that they should condemn these men, whom they accused of teaching matters that were not lawful for Romans, like themselves, to accept or to practice. The Rulers, without further investigating the nature of these complaints or what it was that had given rise to this riot, condemned Paul and Silas to be flogged. Immediately their clothes were torn from their bodies, as they did not have the patience to pull them off, and they were publicly scourged. They were then brought into the prison, and the jailer <note>original: "stókwaarder," literally the warden of the stocks.</note> was ordered to put them in the deepest dungeon <note>original: "hól," meaning a hole or pit.</note>, with their legs in the stocks. Around midnight, Paul and Silas, comforting themselves in God over their sufferings, lifted their voices with a loud voice

<column-break/>

to sing hymns of praise in His honor, such that the other prisoners, who were in various rooms of the prison house, heard them and listened to them. The earth moved at the song which echoed the praise of its Creator, and it trembled so violently that the foundations of the dungeon wavered and seemed about to collapse. All the doors of the prison were opened, and the stocks and shackles fell from the hands and feet of all the prisoners. The jailer awoke at this earthquake, and running to the doors of the dungeon to see if anything extraordinary was happening, he found them all open. He thought that all the prisoners had escaped, and considering himself a lost man—since he would not be able to deliver them back to his Superiors—he seized his sword like a desperate man to take his own life. Such despair was a common thing among the Heathens. Paul and Silas heard the terrible cry of that man, and struck by compassion upon realizing that this miserable soul was about to give himself over to despair and his soul to the Devil, called to him from their dungeon:
> Do yourself no harm, for we are all here.
The jailer stopped at that word and called to his people to bring him light in haste. As soon as he had received it, he sprang into the dungeon where the two servants of Jesus were and threw himself trembling at their feet. He subsequently brought them out of the dungeon and, convinced by what had happened—of which he perceived through the light of Grace that they were the cause—he listened attentively to what they told him of the Lord Jesus. He asked them what he must do to be saved, and they answered him that if he believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, he would be saved with his entire household. This man believed, and his whole house with him. He washed the stripes <note>original: "straamen," the welts or wounds from the flogging.</note> which

# Paul preaches to the Athenians in the Areopagus.
## Acts, Chapter XVII. verses 22, 23.

<columns>
<margin>The year of J. C. 52</margin>
Paul departed from Philippi, and took his way through Amphipolis and Apollonia, to Thessalonica, likewise a city in Macedonia, built on the seashore. There were many Jews in Thessalonica, because its situation was favorable for trade; and Paul, according to his custom, having gone into their Synagogue for several Sabbath days in a row, entered into extensive discourse with them regarding the doctrine he proclaimed. His way of reasoning was, as that of Christ had also been, to prove the truth of the Christian Religion from the Holy Scriptures, and it was upon that holy authority that he established against the stubborn Jews these three great truths, which are the foundation of the entire Gospel: 1. that the Christ must suffer death: 2. that he must rise from the dead: 3. that Jesus was the Christ. The fruit of all these reasonings was, on the one hand, the conversion of many persons,

<column-break/>

and on the other hand, the shaming of the obstinate <note>original: "halfterrige", a likely variant or misspelling of "halsterrige" (stiff-necked)</note> Jews, who became so angry about it that they brought Paul and Silas before the Authorities as rioters and disturbers of the public peace. For that reason, they were forced to leave Thessalonica and went to Berea, which was not far from there. The Jews of that city were more teachable and noble-minded than those of the aforementioned: they heard Paul’s preaching with attention, and since that Apostle proved everything he said from the Scriptures, they were so diligent that, upon returning home, they searched the Scriptural passages cited by the Apostle. Luke speaks with great praise of this conduct of the Believers of Berea, which ought to serve for the encouragement of all Christians to read and reflect upon the Holy Scriptures; just as the example of St. Paul should serve as a model for all Preachers, to apply sayings from the Holy Books in their sermons, instead of larding <note>original: "doorspekken"</note> them with sought-after ornaments of worldly eloquence, or a multitude of useless quotations and clever remarks, which can neither nourish godliness nor strengthen faith. The unbelieving Jews of Thessalonica, having heard of the excellent success of the Gospel in Berea...

### Acts, Chapter XVI. verses 26, 27.

<margin>The Same Year.</margin> Self-interest is always the mainspring and the motive of rogues and deceivers, and even more so in the deceptions of false religions than in any others; because, from the perspective of profit, various other pretenses—which superstition provides to greed—mingle therein. The people who drew a great advantage from the city of Philippi through the fortune-telling <note>The biblical text specifies this was a servant girl possessed by a "spirit of Python" or divination</note> with which their servant girl occupied herself, seized Paul and Silas and led them by force to the public square where the Authorities gathered. They accused them of causing great disturbances in the city by a new doctrine that went against the laws of the State. The people also rose up against them, and demandingly urged their Magistrates to condemn these men, who were accused of teaching things that were not permitted for Romans, such as themselves, to accept or to practice. The Rulers, without further investigating the nature of these complaints or what it was that had given rise to this riot, condemned Paul and Silas to be scourged <note>A brutal form of Roman punishment using rods or whips</note>. Immediately, their clothes were torn from their bodies, as the crowd did not have the patience to pull them off, and they were scourged in public. They were thereafter brought into the prison, and the jailer was ordered to put them in the deepest cell <note>original: "diepste hól," referring to the inner dungeon</note>, with their legs in the stocks <note>A wooden frame used to restrain a prisoner's feet, often in a painful position</note>. Around midnight, Paul and Silas, comforting themselves in God over their sufferings, began with a loud voice

<column-break/>

to sing hymns of praise in His honor, so that the other prisoners, who were in various rooms of the prison house, heard them and listened to them. The earth moved at the song which echoed the praise of its Creator, and it trembled so violently that the foundations of the dungeon shook and seemed as if they would collapse. All the doors of the prison were opened, and the stocks and shackles fell from the hands and feet of all the prisoners. The jailer awoke at this earthquake, and running to the doors of the dungeon to see if anything unusual had happened, he found them all open. He thought that all the prisoners had escaped, and considering himself a lost man—since he would not be able to deliver them back to his Superiors—he seized his sword like a desperate man to take his own life. Such despair was a common thing among the Heathens <note>Referring to the Roman/Pagan stoic tradition where suicide was seen as an honorable alternative to shame or execution</note>. Paul and Silas heard the terrible cry of this man; struck by compassion upon realizing that this wretched soul was about to surrender himself to despair and his soul to the Devil, they called out to him from their cell: *Do thyself no harm, for we are all here.* The jailer stopped at that word and called to his people to bring him a light in haste. As soon as he had received it, he sprang into the cell where the two servants of Jesus were and threw himself trembling at their feet. He subsequently brought them out of the cell, and convinced by what had happened—which he recognized through the light of Grace that they were the cause of—he listened attentively to what they told him of the Lord Jesus. He asked them what he must do to be saved, and they answered him that if he believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, he would be saved with his entire household. This man believed, and his whole house with him. He washed the welts <note>original: "straamen," the bloody marks left by the scourging</note> which

## Paul preaches to the Athenians in the Areopagus.

### Acts, Chapter XVII. verses 22, 23.

<margin>The Year of J. C. 52</margin>
Paul departed from Philippi and took his way through Amphipolis and Apollonia to Thessalonica, likewise a city in Macedonia, built on the shore of the sea. There were many Jews in Thessalonica because its location was suitable for commerce; and Paul, according to his custom, having gone into their Synagogue for several successive Sabbaths, entered into extensive reasoning with them regarding the doctrine he proclaimed. His manner of reasoning was, as that of Christ had also been, to prove the truth of the Christian Religion from the Holy Scripture; and it was upon that holy authority that he established against the stubborn Jews these three great truths, which are the foundation of the entire Gospel: 1. that the Christ had to suffer death; 2. that he had to rise from the dead; 3. that Jesus was the Christ. The fruit of all these reasonings was, on the one hand, the conversion of many persons,

<column-break/>

and on the other hand, the shaming of the stiff-necked Jews, who became so angry about it that they brought Paul and Silas before the Authorities as rioters and disturbers of the public peace. For this reason, they were forced to leave Thessalonica and went to Berea, which lay not far from there. The Jews of that city were more teachable and noble-minded than those of the aforementioned: they listened with attention to the preaching of Paul, and since that Apostle proved everything he said from the Scripture, they were so diligent that, upon coming home, they searched the scriptural passages cited by the Apostle. Luke <note>The traditional author of the Acts of the Apostles.</note> speaks with great praise of this conduct of the Believers of Berea, which ought to serve as an encouragement to all Christians to read and reflect upon the Holy Scripture well; just as the example of St. Paul <note>original: "H. Paulus"</note> ought to serve as a model for all Preachers, to bring passages from the Holy Books into their sermons as appropriate, instead of larding them with sought-after ornaments of worldly eloquence, or a multitude of useless citations and clever remarks, which can neither nourish godliness nor strengthen faith. He was guided from there to Athens, where he was to wait for Silas and Timothy, who had remained in Berea. When Paul had come to Athens, which was the capital of all Greece and the most famous in the world for the refinement of its inhabitants and for all kinds of sciences and arts, which for a long time had flourished there more than in any other region of the earth, he had the sorrow of seeing that superstition and idolatry held the upper hand in that city. Greece in general was like the center of idolatry, and it had given the greater part of their Gods to other lands, especially Italy. But Athens surpassed all other cities of Greece in superstition; to be certain of this, one only needs to read what the Greek Writers have written about it; there were nothing but Temples, chapels, altars, and statues, which one saw in the squares and in the streets of that proud city. Paul could not behold such utter lawlessness without a very great heartache; Luke says that *his spirit was stirred within him*. Then he went sometimes into the Synagogue to dispute with the unbelieving Jews, and then he would stand in the market to try to bring the Athenians from idols to the living God, the Creator of the world. Some Philosophers, both Epicureans and Stoics (for Athens was full of that sort of people), having stopped out of curiosity to hear what a man was saying who stood speaking on the streets before a multitude of people, and understanding nothing of what he said, nor wishing to take the effort to observe closely, asked mockingly, *What does this babbler, this chatterer, wish to say*, who presumes to speak concerning matters of Religion without knowing what he says? Others said, *He seems to be a proclaimer of foreign Gods*; because he spoke to them of Jesus,

<column-break/>

and of the Resurrection, which they believed Paul was proclaiming to them as a new Goddess; <note>The Greek word for Resurrection is *Anastasis*, which the Athenians mistook for the name of a female deity.</note> for this was the madness of the Heathens, that they made gods and goddesses of everything, indeed, often of a single word. They did not want to let him speak to the people with such freedom for long, for fear that he might instill in them sentiments contrary to their religion: they therefore brought him to the Areopagus, or the Council House, to hear there what he proclaimed. Paul began his speech by reproaching the Athenians for that abominable devotion to all kinds of superstitions; but so as not to go on at length about a matter that might have bored them and embittered them against him, he said that while walking through their city and beholding their Sanctuaries, he had seen in passing in a certain place an altar with this inscription, **TO THE UNKNOWN GOD**. This was an altar that the Athenians had long ago erected on the advice of the Philosopher Epimenides, to deliver their city from the plague, which was then raging violently. Paul took the opportunity from this to proclaim to them that God who had sent that scourge upon their city, the God of Heaven and earth, whom they worshipped under the name of the Unknown God, without knowing that it was He whom they honored. But when he came to speak to them of the resurrection of the dead, it bored them to listen to it; some openly mocked him; and others, somewhat more modest, said, *We shall hear you again about this at another time*. Thus they parted, and Paul had the heartache of seeing that those Athenians, so renowned for their cleverness and for their sciences, plunged themselves deeper and deeper into the darkness of Heathenism. Meanwhile, his preaching was not entirely without fruit, for some Athenians were converted, and among others a woman of distinction named *Damaris*, and one of the Councilors of the Areopagus, called *Dionysius*, whose name has since become famous in the Church.

->The books of the idle arts are burned at Ephesus.<-

### Acts, Chapter XIX. verse 19

**THE** Apostle, departing from Athens, went to Corinth, which was also a city in Greece, and one of the mightiest and wealthiest. Because people from all parts of the world arrived there constantly, due to the convenience of the harbor which made the place a fine merchant city, Paul judged that he could stay in no more suitable place to spread the doctrine of the Gospel to some extent over the entire world. He remained there for a year and a half, preaching first to the Jews, and thereafter to the Heathens, after he had found in the Synagogue a fierce stubbornness in rejecting the truths of the Gospel. Finally, persecution drove him out of Corinth, and he took ship for Syria, from where he took the way to Jerusalem, to be there for the feast of Pentecost. After having been there for some days, he departed again for Greece. He traveled through Antioch and Syria, where he had already been several
<meta>catchword: journeys</meta>

<column-break/>

journeys, and now stayed for some time again. Subsequently, he traveled through Galatia and Phrygia, and went from there to Ephesus, in which place he was expected by the entire Congregation. He found there upon his arrival about twelve Disciples, who had come there long before from Judea, where they had received the first principles of the Gospel through the preaching of John the Baptist. He asked them whether they, when they had made the first confession of their faith in Jesus Christ, had received the Holy Spirit. They seemed surprised by that question and answered *that they had not even heard whether there was a Holy Spirit*. They used those words in the same sense as one reads in the seventh chapter of John, where it is said that the Holy Spirit was not yet, because Jesus was not yet glorified. These two scripture passages are entirely alike, and neither of them refers to the person of the Holy Spirit, but to the miraculous gifts of that Spirit, which in the early times were communicated through the Baptism of the Apostles, or by the laying on of hands. Paul did not yet know that those persons had received only the baptism of John the Baptist.

Agrippa was shaken by Paul's discourse, and answered him like one whose mind hangs in doubt between the truth he sees and the disdain held for those who declare themselves for it: "*Paul, you almost move me to become a Christian.*" God did not grant that Prince the grace to go further; and he was no more deeply moved by the truth of the Gospel than to show by his answer the innocence of the Minister who preached it, and his own guilt in not daring to stand up for it.

The riot was great and rose very high; Aristarchus and Gaius, two renowned ministers of the Word, were in danger for their lives, but some of the chief authorities of the province <note>These were the "Asiarchs," officials in the Roman province of Asia who oversaw religious and civic festivities.</note>, both regarding matters of religion and of the State, favoring the Gospel, protected them from the fury of the people, and by their authority found a means to skillfully disperse that riotous assembly without ordering anything against Paul—whom Providence had prevented from falling into their hands—nor against the others. When this disturbance was entirely over, Paul took ship for Philippi in Macedonia, where, after five days of sailing, he arrived in a city named Troas. There he found Aristarchus, Timothy, Gaius, and several others who had come there from Ephesus to wait for him. They stayed there seven days, and on the first day of the week, when the congregation was gathered together in the evening to perform their customary religious duties—of which the holding of the Lord's Supper <note>Original: "Avondmaalhouding."</note> was one of the most common in those first times of zeal and faith—Paul delivered a great sermon. And as he extended his speech until midnight, it happened that a certain youth named Eutychus, sitting in a window, fell asleep and fell down from that window, which was on the third story of the house, and was taken up dead. Paul, going downstairs, embraced him and gave him life again. Afterward, he went back up to the room where the meeting was held and shared the Lord's Supper there, after which he departed at dawn and set out to sea. Having come to Miletus, he summoned the elders of Ephesus, to whom he said that he was about to go to Jerusalem, quite ready to suffer for the sake of the Gospel, according to what the Holy Spirit made known to him in all the cities through which he passed:

A God to whom the Church belongs can be none other than a true God; and the God who obtained her through his blood can be none other than a God-man, a God manifest in the flesh, as Paul calls him in the first Epistle to Timothy. The Apostle finally arrived with those of his company at Jerusalem, and a few days later, certain Jews from Ephesus, having recognized him in the Temple, cried out against him as a profaner of that sacred place. The Commander of the Temple <note>This refers to the Roman Tribune, or Chiliarch, who commanded the garrison at the Antonia Fortress overlooking the Temple.</note> then came with his soldiers and seized Paul, ordering that he be bound with two chains. When he had reached the steps of the barracks or fortress, he received permission from the Commander, who had had him captured, to speak to the people. He gave a brief account of the course of his life, which was a concise defense, and they listened to him peacefully until he came to say that the Lord, appearing to him, had said that he would send him far away to the Gentiles. These words again turned this wild people, who bore an irreconcilable hatred toward the Gentiles, against him. The next day he was brought before the Great Council <term>Sanhedrin: the supreme judicial and religious body of the Jews in Jerusalem</term>, and at the first word he spoke to testify to his good conscience, the High Priest commanded those standing by him to strike him on the mouth.
