Thereupon the Sanhedrin <term>Sanhedrin: the supreme judicial and religious council of the Jews in Jerusalem</term> was divided on his account, because some among his judges were Pharisees, and others were Sadducees, these being two very contrary sects. The Pharisees then took his side, and the Council having been unable to reach a decision regarding him, the Centurion had him transported with a strong guard to Caesarea to the Governor Felix. Five days later, the High Priest, accompanied by many counselors of the Sanhedrin, went to Felix to promote his condemnation, although they had already begun to sit as judges over him in Jerusalem. The Governor, having heard them collectively, postponed the verdict on the matter until another time. Two years later, Festus came in Felix's place, and having still found Paul in the prison of Caesarea, he wished to send him back to the Sanhedrin of Jerusalem at the strong insistence of the Jews; but Paul appealed his sentence to the Emperor <note>As a Roman citizen, Paul exercised his right to have his case heard by Caesar in Rome.</note>; which was the reason that they proceeded no further in law against him in that country. A few days later, King Agrippa and Queen Berenice, his consort, went to Caesarea to congratulate Festus on his new governorship. Festus came to speak to them regarding the case of Paul, and they showed themselves

<column-break/>

desirous to see and hear him. He was brought before them in the hall of the Palace, and Agrippa having given him permission to speak, Paul did so with such power and great elevation of spirit that Festus—who, being a pagan, understood nothing of these matters of religion—interrupted the Apostle and told him that his great learning was making him mad. Paul modestly excused himself from the Governor's reproach, and turning to Agrippa, he urged it upon his conscience to give testimony to all that he had heard him speak, which was nothing other than the teaching of the Prophets, "of which you, O King," he said, "are not ignorant, and I know that you believe them." Agrippa was moved to waver by Paul’s discourse, and answered him like someone whose mind hangs in doubt between the truth which he sees and the contempt in which those who declare themselves for it are held: "Paul, you almost move me to become a Christian." God did not grant that Prince the grace to go further; and he was no more deeply sensible of the truth of the Gospel than to show by his answer the innocence of the Minister who preached it, and his own guilt for not daring to champion it.

...the island of **Patmos**, which was one of the islands of the Aegean Sea; and tradition says that it was the same **Domitian** who banished him there. The exile of **John** is certain, because he himself indicates it at the beginning of this book; but there is reason to doubt whether it occurred under **Domitian**, because it appears from various places in the book of **Revelation**, and especially from the 7th verse of the first chapter, that these prophecies were written before the destruction of Jerusalem, which nonetheless occurred several years before **Domitian** ascended the imperial throne.

<margin>Year roughly 67.</margin>
**John** was sent to the island of **Patmos** for the sake of the Gospel; and as he himself says, for the word of God, and for the testimony of **Jesus Christ**. It happened to him that he had several glorious visions there in an ecstasy of spirit on a Lord's day; which is the day that the Church from its very beginning has dedicated to the usual exercises of religion in place of the **Sabbath**, which she left to the **Synagogue**.

The first vision was of **seven golden lampstands**; in the midst of which a man appeared, clothed in a long robe reaching down to the feet; and girded about the chest with a golden sash. His hair was white like snow, and his eyes glistened like a flame of fire. His feet were like shining brass, and glowed as in a furnace, and his voice was like the sound of great waters. In his right hand he held **seven stars**. A sharp two-edged sword went out of his mouth: and his face shone with radiance like the sun at midday. This man was **Jesus Christ**, who appeared to his Apostle in the form of a **High Priest**, who was thus clothed in a long <term>tabard</term> <note>A heavy outer garment or robe, here referring to the priestly vestments.</note> of fine linen, and girded with a golden sash a little below the armpits. The extraordinary whiteness of his hair, which is naturally the sign of great age, represented in a more mysterious way—just as in the vision of the seventh chapter of **Daniel**—the eternity

<column-break/>

of **Jesus Christ**, according to which he was, as he himself said to the Jews, *before Abraham*, and as **John** says in his Gospel, *before the world was*. His eyes, flickering like the purest flame, signified the alertness of his knowledge, which penetrates even into the hearts of men, and into the darkest depths of that which is yet to come. The brass glowing like a furnace, which the feet of **Jesus Christ** resembled, was the symbol of his power and the radiance of his virtues. That strong voice, sounding and echoing like the noise of a brook that rolls its great waters with a heavy roar into the valleys and flat fields, was a representation of the resounding resonance of the **Gospel**, which within a short time allowed itself to be heard throughout the entire world.

The **stars** which he had in his right hand represented the **Preachers**, who through the light of their preaching are like spiritual stars, whom **Christ** holds in his hand to direct their course and movement, and to make them shine where it pleases him. These stars were seven in number, because this number, being <term>mystical</term> <note>The original Dutch 'geheimduydend' suggests a symbolic or prophetic meaning hidden within the number.</note> in the Scripture, and especially in the Book of **Revelation** where it occurs many times, generally represented the ecclesiastical service, which cannot be better depicted than by stars in the hand of **Jesus Christ**; and besides that, it had a special relation to the **seven Churches of Asia**, which were depicted by the **seven golden lampstands**, in the midst of which **John** saw the Lord **Jesus** walking. This sharp two-edged sword finally, which went out of the mouth of the **Son of God**, was a wonderful representation of the preaching of the **Gospel**, through which **Christ** has fought and conquered the whole world, and which for the same reason in the 110th **Psalm** is also called the *scepter of his strength*: for thus says the **Prophet**, *The Lord shall send the scepter of your strength out of Zion, saying, rule in the midst of your enemies.*

The first vision was of seven golden candlesticks, in the midst of which appeared a man, clothed in a long robe reaching to the feet, and girded across the chest with a golden belt. His hair was white like snow, and his eyes glistened like a flame of fire. His feet were like shining copper, and glowed as in a furnace, and his voice was like the roaring of great waters.

In his right hand he held seven stars. A sharp double-edged sword came out of his mouth: and his face shone with brilliance like the sun at full day.

This man was Jesus Christ, who appeared to his Apostle in the form of a High Priest, who was thus clothed in a long robe of fine linen, and girded with a golden belt a little below the armpits. The extraordinary whiteness of his hair, which is naturally the sign of great age, represented in a mystical way—just as in the vision of the seventh chapter of Daniel—the eternity

<column-break/>

of Jesus Christ, according to which he was, as he himself said to the Jews, *before Abraham was*, and as John says in his Gospel, *before the world was.*

His eyes, flickering like the purest flame, signified the alertness of his knowledge, which penetrates even into the hearts of men, and into the darkest depths of that which is yet to come.

The copper, glowing like a furnace, which the feet of Jesus Christ resembled, was the symbol of his power and the radiance of his virtues.

That strong voice, sounding and echoing like the noise of a stream that rolls its great waters into the valleys and flat fields with a heavy roar, was a representation of the resounding sound of the Gospel, which in a short time let itself be heard throughout the entire world.

The stars which he had in his right hand represented the Preachers, who through the light of their preaching are like spiritual stars, whom Christ holds in his hand to direct their course and movement, and to make them shine where it pleases him. These stars were seven in number because this number, being mystical in the Scriptures, and especially in the Book of Revelation, where it occurs many times, generally represented the ecclesiastical service, which cannot be better depicted than by stars in the hand of Jesus Christ; and besides that, it had a special relation to the seven Churches of Asia, which were represented by the seven golden candlesticks, in the midst of which John saw the Lord Jesus walking.

This sharp double-edged sword, finally, which came out of the mouth of God's Son, was a wonderful representation of the preaching of the Gospel, through which Christ fought and conquered the whole world, and which for the same reason is also called in the 110th Psalm, *the scepter of his strength:* for thus says the Prophet, *The Lord shall send the scepter of your strength out of Zion, saying, rule in the midst of your enemies.*

# HISTORY of the N. TESTAMENT.

...for lost, and expected nothing other than the moment in which they, along with the ship and everything else, would sink into the raging waves. But God revealed to Paul by night through an angel that He would preserve him to be brought before the Emperor in Rome, and that for his sake, not one of all those who were in the ship would perish. Paul made known to them the revelation he had received, so that they might take heart. Meanwhile, the ship was tossed about violently and was much damaged by the storm, which had already lasted fourteen days. The sailors feared that it would strike a reef during the night, because, having cast the sounding lead <note>a weight used to measure water depth</note>, they believed they were close to land; so that, to avoid that disaster, they cast four anchors from the stern, waiting for daylight to eventually come. They wanted to deceive the Captain <note>original: "Hoofdman," referring to the centurion Julius</note> and the passengers, for their intention was to skillfully slip into the boat and abandon the ship. Paul noticed their plot and said to the Captain and the soldiers that if they did not prevent the crew from fleeing, they would all perish with the ship. Nevertheless, God had assured them that no one would perish; but God's decrees, however certain and unshakeable they may be, do not exclude for men the means that are naturally intended to carry out those decrees. In such a way that it would be reasoned like someone ignorant and reckless to say: "If I am destined for it, I shall be saved, whatever I do." The means for salvation are included in the providence for salvation; and God makes no one happy <note>meaning blessed or successful</note> who does not work toward it. The people on the ship had eaten almost nothing during the fourteen days the storm had lasted. Paul therefore urged them to take some food; this was also necessary so that they might have strength to save themselves in the shipwreck. This shipwreck, which their imagination had so often placed before their eyes, was not far off. When day came, they saw an inlet from afar, and having hauled up the anchors, they intended to run their ship aground on the shore; but

<column-break/>

they encountered a place in the sea where two currents met, which gave the ship such a shock that the bow stuck in the sand and the stern was broken by the violence of the waves. The ship could not withstand these heavy blows; it opened up on all sides, the water came rushing in, and everyone saved himself—some on planks, others by swimming. In an instant, the ship was no longer to be seen, and it sank beneath the waves. It was the island of Melite, or Malta, where they suffered shipwreck. And while all who had escaped were standing by a fire to warm themselves and dry their clothes, Paul grabbed a handful of brushwood to throw on the fire, and an adder crawled out of it and coiled itself around his hand. It was immediately believed that he was a villain whom the vengeance of Heaven pursued, and who, having escaped the shipwreck, would have to lose his life by the venom. But when it was seen that he suffered no harm from it, and that neither his hand nor his arm swelled, they began to regard him as a god. The father of the Chief of the island lay sick with a fever and dysentery <note>original: "roode loop," an old term for bloody flux</note>; therefore Paul went to visit him and healed him. The other sick people on the island were brought to him, and he healed them all. Three months later, he went back to sea with the other prisoners and finally arrived in Rome, where he remained in custody for two years. Meanwhile, he preached the Gospel, because he had permission to go where he wanted, accompanied by a soldier and laden with a chain.

<margin>The year 60.</margin>
It was from this first imprisonment in Rome that he wrote the Epistles <note>original: "Zendbrieven," letters sent to the churches</note> to the Ephesians, the Philippians, the Colossians, and to Philemon; most of the others had been written previously. His bonds had become manifest, as he himself says, in the whole Palace <note>original: "Rechtbuys," likely referring to the Praetorian Guard or the imperial court</note>. After he was set at liberty at the end of two years, he continued preaching to the Jews and Gentiles in the principal provinces of Asia and Europe;

<margin>The year 66.</margin>
until, being imprisoned in Rome for the second time, he suffered martyrdom under the reign of Nero.

### Appearance of Jesus Christ to John in the Midst of the Seven Golden Candlesticks.

->Revelation, Chapter I. verses 13–16<-

John lived the longest of all the Apostles: indeed, some believed that he would not die, because the Lord, speaking of him to Peter, said: *If I will that he remain until I come, what is that to you?* It was not immediately understood what those words meant: it was believed that the Son of God was speaking there of the Last Judgment, and as one error drags another after it, people imagined that it could happen that John might live until that time. And yet the meaning of those words was not overly difficult, because they were the same expressions which the Lord Jesus had often used when speaking of His coming in judgment against Judea. Examples of this are found everywhere in the Gospel. The last verse of the sixteenth chapter of Matthew shows this so clearly that one must do great violence to oneself to

<column-break/>

understand it otherwise. The 24th chapter runs almost entirely along the same lines <note>original: "over dezelfde ſchyven," an idiom for following the same pattern</note>: and in the 26th, Christ declared before the Sanhedrin <note>the supreme Jewish council and court</note> that *hereafter you shall see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of God, and coming on the clouds of Heaven.* If this did not signify, through lofty and metaphorical expressions, the particular judgment of God's Son against Judea—foretold in the parable of the Wedding, in that of the Vinedressers, and elsewhere—then it is difficult to say what those parables might have meant. John did indeed live until that time, and he was also the only one of the Apostles who saw the destruction of Jerusalem and the entire Jewish state. He preached the Gospel mainly in Asia Minor, where Paul had already founded several famous congregations, as we see in the book of the Acts of the Apostles. Church History reports that he was condemned by the Emperor Domitian to be thrown into a cauldron of boiling oil, and that God caused him to come out of it alive without being harmed in any way, like the three Hebrew youths in the furnace of Babylon in former times. ## John sees Heaven opened.
### Revelation, Chapter IV, verses 1, 2. etc.

These seven Churches of Asia, represented by the seven golden Lampstands in the previous vision, were those of Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea. John received a command to write down everything he had seen and heard in those visions, and Jesus Christ dictated to him a special letter for each of the Churches, or for their Pastors. He gives them in those Epistles the glorious name of *Angels*, for the sake of their service, just as for the same reason in the 24th chapter of Matthew, he calls the Ministers of his Gospel *his angels*, who like so many trumpets were to make the proclamation thereof resound over the entire earth. Christ praised in each Pastor of these seven Churches their zeal and faithfulness, but he also reproached them for even their slightest slackness, and he complained of some that they lacked the alertness and courage to strike with the ban <note>The "ban" refers to excommunication or formal spiritual censure</note> certain rising sects that emerged within their Churches. He commands all those Pastors to watch carefully over their conduct, and to persevere in the faith and the exercise of their office and duty until the end of their lives; and he promises to all, under various symbols, the blessedness and glory of the coming world, as a merciful reward which he prepares for their faithfulness and perseverance. He promises to one the hidden *Manna*, and the *white Choice-stone* <note>The "white stone" likely refers to a custom of using white pebbles for acquittal in trials or as a token of admission to special events</note>; to another the fruits of the tree of life; to these white clothes, to those thrones and crowns, and in general the eternal blessedness of Heaven, under figurative expressions, of which even all the most magnificent together could not form a right and perfect concept.

<column-break/>

When Jesus Christ had given John to understand everything he should write on his behalf to the Angels of the seven Churches, he showed him Heaven opened, and at the same time that Apostle heard a resounding voice like a trumpet, calling to him to come up, and see the things that were to happen in the course of time. John was then taken up in an ecstasy by the Spirit of God, and he saw a Throne in Heaven, and he who was seated upon it gave off a radiance like that of a Sardius, or the Jasper stone. Above the Throne appeared a rainbow, of a green color, flickering like an Emerald; and around the Throne were twenty-four seats, on which twenty-four Elders <note>These "Ouderlingen" or Elders represent the heads of the people of God, often interpreted as the twelve patriarchs of Israel and the twelve apostles</note> were seated, clothed in white garments, and having golden crowns upon their heads. From that most magnificent Throne came forth lightnings and claps of thunder, seven fiery lamps were burning before it, and directly opposite it was a sea, like glass or crystal. Four living creatures full of eyes in front and behind appeared above and around the Throne. The first had the form of a lion, the second that of an ox, the third resembled a man, and the fourth was like a flying eagle. Each of these creatures had six wings, like the Cherubim which Isaiah saw in the vision he relates in the sixth chapter of his Prophecy, and they were full of eyes within. They gave glory to him who sat on the Throne, and they cried out without ceasing: *Holy, Holy, Holy is the Lord God, the Almighty, who was, and who is, and who is to come*. When these mysterious creatures spoke their songs of praise, the twenty-four Elders fell down before him who sat on the Throne, to show him the deepest reverence, and casting their crowns before the Throne, they said in the rapture of their joy and gratitude: *You Lord*

### The Lamb opens the book sealed with seven seals.

->Revelation, Chapter V. verses 5, 6, 7.<-

In the right hand of him who appeared upon the Throne like the brilliance of a Jasper stone, was a book written within and without, which was sealed with seven seals. At the same time, an Angel appeared calling with a loud voice: *Who is worthy to open the book, and to break its seals?* No one offered themselves to perform this opening, because there was no creature in the whole world who had understanding enough to explain the matters contained in that Scripture. It was the book of God's decrees, in which the principal events that were to happen to the Church during the course of the centuries were recorded. Such is indeed the depth of the divine decrees, that there is no created understanding that can fathom them, nor any knowledge powerful enough to penetrate into the darkness of the future. John grieved to see that no one in Heaven, where the knowledge of the Angels is so vivid and extensive, was found who dared to offer himself to open the book. ## *The opening of the first four Seals.*

### Revelation, Chapter VI. 1, 3, 5, 7, 8.

Each of the seven seals with which the Book—which he who sat on the Throne held in his hand—was sealed, concealed profound and mysterious outcomes. John makes these known in the same chapter at the opening of each seal; but he does so almost everywhere in such an involved manner, that this holy Book, which none of the Angels and blessed ones had dared to approach to open, is no less closed to us after the opening of its seals than before. At least there remains so much obscurity and such great difficulties, that the most learned theologians are forced to acknowledge it. However, the reading thereof is not useless. One perceives through all those obscurities clear truths, full of instruction for humble souls, who attentively observe the ways of God in the governing of the world and his Church; his judgments over men; the plagues with which he punishes the earth; the oppressions and trials through which he makes his children pass; and in general that absolute authority with which he arranges everything as it seems good to him, and governs the world according to his pleasure. All these ideas present themselves at the opening of the seven seals; and they cannot but

<column-break/>

foot of the Throne, a triumphant Church would fall down before a Jesus, who was but a creature, and in a song mix the same praise to the honor of the Lamb, which she gives to the living and eternal God who is seated on the Throne. Jesus is then truly the Son of God, worthy of the worship of all creatures, God above all to be praised for eternity, just as Paul said to the Romans <note>A reference to Romans 9:5, often used as a proof text for the divinity of Christ.</note>.

altogether give a very great idea of God, and keep us in a deep humility at the sight of that supreme Majesty. He then saw a white horse, and one seated upon it who had a bow in his hands; furthermore, a crown was given to him because of the victories which he had already achieved, and he went out and set off on his way to achieve yet other victories. The second seal was then opened, and thereupon there appeared a red horse, ridden by someone who had a large sword, and to whom power was given to take peace from the earth, and to leave men the liberty to kill one another like madmen. ### The opening of the fifth seal.
### Revelation, Chapter VI. verse 9.

The Lamb proceeded with the opening of the seals of the book sealed with seven seals; and when it had come to the fifth seal, John saw under the Altar the souls of those who were killed for the word of God, who cried with a loud voice: *How long, O Holy and true Ruler, do you not judge and avenge our blood from those who dwell on the earth?* To each of them were given long white robes, and they were told that they should wait for a little while longer, until their fellow servants who were still on the earth, should also, like them, be put to death for the testimony of Jesus.
Part II.

<column-break/>

lity, according to the History which the ancient Writers have left us of the life and deeds of those Emperors; for one finds much similarity there with the description given to us here of the four horses and the armed men seated upon them. Others believe that these are enigmatic descriptions of Jesus Christ, and that they only differ because of the variety of outcomes which they represent. Yet, however it may be, this seems certain, that all these visions referred to the Empire and the Church, through the connection which the Church had in its first centuries with the Roman Empire, within whose scope it was at that time almost entirely enclosed, because the scope of that Empire covered the greatest part of the known world. For the rest, one should always be very hesitant in the interpretation of all these mysteries, and approach the same only with trembling, lest we attribute our own thoughts to the Holy Spirit, instead of ourselves receiving His.

This <note>The fifth seal</note> does not have as much obscurity as the four preceding ones. The basis for it was taken from the Temple of Jerusalem, where the altar of offerings was, under which the Priests poured out the blood of the sacrifices. In Heaven there is indeed nothing of the kind, but the Holy Spirit wished to borrow the sketch of this vision from that symbol. That which he calls the souls of those who were killed for the word of God, was the blood of the Martyrs, for in the Hebrew language these two words *blood* and *soul* often have the same meaning. This blood, the purest that is in the world, was shown to the Apostle as being under the altar, to indicate that God had accepted it as an offering which those faithful Martyrs had made to him. The white robes given to those blessed Martyrs signified that God had washed and cleansed them from all their sins; and that their souls, sanctified by the Holy Spirit and justified in the blood of Jesus, enjoyed the glory of which Christ himself had taken the white garment as a symbol, when he said in the same Book <note>The author refers here to earlier chapters in Revelation, such as Revelation 3:5.</note> that he would give white robes to him who overcame. The answer given to those Martyrs, that God would wait with the avenging of their blood until the blood of their brothers, the faithful companions of their godliness and zeal, should likewise be shed, and that this would happen shortly, could in a general sense have referred to the persecutions

<column-break/>

since the reign of Nero began in the Roman Empire; but even more to those which the Jews did to the Christians in the beginning of the Gospel; for God's wrath against the Synagogue <note>In this context, "the Synagogue" refers to the Jewish religious and political establishment that opposed the early Christian movement.</note> seems particularly signified in this vision, just as it is depicted somewhat more broadly in what follows. These are then not the actual prayers which the Martyrs make to God in Heaven against those who persecuted them on earth: for in Heaven, which is the dwelling place of perfect love, one does not perceive in the blessed souls that resentment and vengefulness which so easily creeps into our hearts of flesh and blood. It is the Justice of God himself who is mindful of vengeance against the persecutors; the more they hasten to shed the blood of the Martyrs, the more they hasten their punishment, and force, so to speak, Divine Justice not to delay in avenging the sufferings of the Believers upon them.

"There occurred an earthquake; the Sun was darkened and black, the Moon appeared to be of a blood-red color; the Stars fell from Heaven upon the earth, as figs fall from a fig tree when it is shaken by a great wind: the Heaven departed as a scroll that is rolled up; and the mountains and islands were moved out of their places. Also, this was the day called in the book of the Acts of the Apostles <note>original: "Handelingen der Apoſtelen"</note> the great and illustrious day of the Lord, and in the Gospel, the days of vengeance, the like of which had never been. It was, in a word, the judgment of God against Judea, the destruction of Jerusalem, and the end of the Jewish nation, over which God had gathered all the heat of his wrath, to break the covenant that he had held with the Jews for more than two thousand years, and to cast them entirely away from before his face. ## The Opening of the seventh seal.

### Revelation, Chapter VIII. verse 1. etc.

After the opening of the sixth seal, and the vision that followed it, the Angel paused for some time before opening the seventh, in order to show John a vision which is recounted to us in the seventh chapter. He saw four Angels standing at the four corners of the earth, holding the four winds, so that no wind should blow on the earth, nor on the sea. He saw thereafter another Angel coming from the East, who, holding the seal of the living God in his hand, called to the four Angels, to whom power was given to strike the earth and the sea with plagues, that they should damage nothing until he had marked the servants of God on their

<column-break/>

foreheads. Thereupon the seal of God was pressed upon them, according to the order of their lineages and tribes, and there were in total one hundred and forty-four thousand who were marked, to be excepted when the judgments of God should come upon the earth to wreak havoc. The purpose of this vision and symbol is not difficult to understand: God thereby first gave to understand that his Church would enjoy a certain respite, and that during that time he would prevent the winds and storms of persecution from rushing down upon her. The Church indeed enjoyed that happy calm under the reign of the Emperor Titus <note>Titus Flavius Vespasianus, Roman Emperor from 79–81 AD, known for his relative moderation toward Christians following the Jewish War.</note>, who was a very gentle Prince, and ascended the Imperial throne after he himself in Judea, in the capacity of Commander over the army of his father Vespasian, had executed the secret commands of divine justice against the Jews, in the vengeance [at...]

While everything was thus in silence, John saw seven Angels before God’s throne, to whom seven trumpets were given; and at the same time, he saw another Angel before the altar of incense with a golden censer full of incense, to offer the same with the prayers of all the saints upon the golden altar which was before the Throne. It clearly appears that this has an allusion to the golden altar of the Sanctuary, placed close by the Holy of Holies, and as if opposite the Ark, which in that ancient dispensation was the most glorious throne of God. The Angel who offered this incense with the prayers of the Saints, or Believers, was Jesus Christ, the Angel of the Covenant and the High Priest, who constantly makes the incense of his prayers smoke in Heaven for his Church, and who offers all prayers which the Believers present to him on earth to God his Father, as though mixed with his own, and infused with the good scent of his sacrifice and intercession.

### Revelation, Chapter IX. verses 1---11.

WHEN the Angel had finished the offering of incense, he filled his censer with fire from the Altar, and threw all that fire thereafter upon the earth. At the same time, there occurred peals of thunder and lightnings, and the entire earth was shaken. Then the seven Angels who had received trumpets prepared themselves to sound them; and at the sound of each trumpet, a new wonder-sign appeared. Upon the sound of the first followed hail and fire mixed with blood, all of which was thrown upon the earth. The second Angel then blew upon his trumpet, and there fell something like a great mountain, burning with fire, into the sea, and created there a horrible destruction among the ships and fish. At the sound of the third, a great star fell from Heaven, burning like a torch, upon the third part of the rivers and fountains. This star was named *Wormwood* <note>original: "Alsem"</note>, because it made all the waters which it touched so bitter that the greatest part of the men who drank of those waters died from it. After this had happened, the fourth Angel trumpeted, and the third part of the Sun, the Moon, and the Stars lost their radiance. All these wonder-signs foretold

<column-break/>

to the earth very great calamities: it is impossible to examine them all here at length: but God prepared yet greater ones after the three trumpets upon which had not yet been blown. An Angel came beforehand to give a warning of it, flying with all his might in the midst of Heaven, and crying with a loud voice: *Woe, woe, woe, to those who dwell on the earth, because of the remaining voices of the trumpets of the three Angels who are yet to trumpet.* Then the fifth Angel trumpeted, and a star fell from Heaven onto the earth, and to it was given the key to the pit of the abyss. It thereupon opens the abyss, and there came a black smoke out of it, just like that of a furnace. The sun and the air were darkened by it, and at the same time there came out of the pit of the abyss an innumerable multitude of Locusts of a terrifying appearance: they were like horses prepared for war, and had on their heads crowns that looked like gold: their faces were like human faces: they had hair like the hair of women, and their teeth were like lions' teeth: They had breastplates on as if of iron, and they had wings which while flying made a noise like that of chariots drawn by many horses rushing to battle: their tails were like those of scorpions, with stinging points; and they had power for five months to plague mankind. The Angel of the Abyss, called in Hebrew *Abaddon*, was their King; this name signifies a *destroying King*, and the Apostle Paul calls him with the same intent as John, *the son of perdition*. it could not be otherwise than that the Locusts, being of such a fearsome appearance as these were, must do great evil upon the earth. But it is noteworthy that these Locusts did not ruin any of the fruits or crops of the earth; they touched neither the herbs nor the trees; which is, however, contrary to the nature of ordinary locusts, which devastate the fields, eat the branches of the trees bare, and leave no flowers, nor greenery, nor any sign of life in all the places where they come. They were only permitted to harm men; and even then a great number were exempted, whom these Locusts, however mighty they were, nor their King Abaddon <note>original: "Abaddon" — a Hebrew name meaning "Destroyer." In the Greek text, he is called Apollyon.</note>, had no power to torment like the others. These were they who had received the seal of God upon their foreheads, those whom God, through His election, has set apart from the rest of the world. *The foundation of God stands sure,* says the Apostle Paul, *having this seal: The Lord knows,* or distinguishes among all men, *those who are His,* <note>This is a reference to 2 Timothy 2:19, used here to explain how the faithful are recognized and protected during divine judgments.</note> to preserve them on the day of redemption. Concerning the other men whom God gave over to the teeth of the Locusts (for they had teeth as well as stings), it is explicitly made known that they should not kill them, but that they should inflict heavy

<column-break/>

torments upon them, which went so far as to stifle the origin of life in the heart through a piercing venom, like that of a scorpion. This entire description, composed with a singular selection from a great number of very different things, generally amounts to this: that the persons signified by these Locusts would not cause such a devastation on the earth as armies do, which destroy forests, orchards, gardens, meadows, harvests, and everything they find; and that they would not kill the people who fell under their power in such a manner as an army that covers the earth with corpses, causing blood to flow like streams by the sword and other weapons of war. Thus, the Locusts had to go to work in a different way, and through a cunning poison that penetrated into the soul, injure the life. But that they had the teeth of Lions, besides the sting of a scorpion, shows that they would make use of violence where craftiness and cunning were too weak. When one reflects on all this with a little attention, one can well recognize these Locusts and their King; and one must guard oneself against their teeth and stings.

...fire, smoke, and sulfur from their mouths, and a third of humanity was killed by these three things—the fire, the smoke, and the sulfur that issued from the mouths of the horses. For their power was in their mouth and in their tails, which resembled snakes, having heads by which they caused wounds and great ailments. The people who were not killed by these plagues did not take advantage of that mercy as they ought; they did not repent of their idolatries; they worshipped, as before, the Devils, and the idols of gold, silver, copper, stone, and wood. They also did not repent of their murders, their poisonings <note>original: "venyngevingen" — likely referring to the Greek *pharmakeia*, often translated as sorceries or magic arts involving potions.</note>, their fornications, and their thefts.

One generally perceives in this prophetic vision a terrible revolution that was to come to the Empire <note>The author likely refers to the Byzantine or Holy Roman Empire.</note>, taking its beginning from the Euphrates and the East, from whence God released these ministers of His vengeance to carry out unheard-of destructions and to bring devastation and terror over the entire East. If this does not refer to the wars of the Saracens and the Turks, who with nearly innumerable armies brought the East and South under subjection, one must nonetheless admit that it bears a striking resemblance to it. The pagan religion had long been banished from the world

<column-break/>

when the Turks made themselves masters of the Empire; but those who know what the Greeks understood by the name of Devils or Demons <note>original: "Duyvelen of Daimons"</note>, and who have considered with some attention that famous passage in the fourth chapter of the first Epistle to Timothy—where, just as in this vision, the "doctrines of demons" are spoken of—will have no great difficulty in finding the trail of this old superstition, as well as that of a religious veneration given to idols of gold, silver, stone, and wood.

Furthermore, what one sees very clearly, and at the same time is exceedingly sad in this prophecy, is that the peoples who had escaped the deadly wounds from the mouths and tails of the horses described by John <note>original: "Joannes"</note> did not repent of their superstition nor of their vices, which had brought such great calamities upon them and their lands. To such a peak of corruption has the human heart ascended that it pays no heed to the judgments with which God strikes entire nations and kingdoms; and nothing is sadder than to see that irreligion and godlessness still dare to raise their heads under the scourges of an angry God, who fills an entire land with mourning and tears.

He cried out with a loud voice like the roaring of a lion; and when he had cried out, one heard the voices of seven thunders that spoke, or speaking voices which crashed like thunderclaps. As soon as John had heard what the seven thunders had spoken, he set himself to write; but he heard a voice saying to him that he should seal up what the seven thunders had spoken and not write it. It would almost seem that it was not necessary to seal those things if he was not permitted to write them; but this double prohibition of one and the same matter under different concepts served to give John to understand that what the thunders had said must remain unknown to the Church until the outcome—the great interpreter of prophecies—made the same known. The Angel, who stood with his one foot on the sea and the other on the land, then lifted his hand toward Heaven and swore by Him who lives forever and ever, who created Heaven and what is therein, and the earth and what is therein, and the sea and what is therein, that there should be no more time <note>The phrase "no more time" is often interpreted in this context as "no more delay" regarding the fulfillment of God's plan.</note>: but that in the days of the voice of the seventh Angel, when he should sound his trumpet, the mystery of God should be fulfilled, as He had revealed to His servants the Prophets. One can understand without difficulty that the Angel who appeared in this vision was Jesus Christ, who elsewhere is shown with a rainbow above his head and with the other features seen here. This posture of having one foot on the sea and the other on the land has something so great and stately that one perceives therein the majesty of a God who rules over the sea and the earth, having them as if under His feet. The open little book that He holds in His hand signifies that nothing is hidden from Christ, and that the deepest mysteries are, so to speak, opened in His hands in the understanding that He 

<column-break/>

gives to His Church. The seven thunders that uttered their oracles after the Angel had cried with a loud voice may have been the symbol of the Holy Spirit, whom the Apostle at the beginning of this book calls the *seven Spirits of God*, and who gives His instructions to the Faithful only in the name of Jesus Christ: *He shall take of mine, and shall declare it unto you* <note>original: "Hy zal 't uyt het myne neemen, en u verkondigen" — a reference to John 16:14.</note>. The command that the Lord Jesus gave to John to seal the matters which the seven thunders had spoken indicated that they would be very obscure to the entire Church until the time they should be fulfilled. The Angel lifts His hand to Heaven and swears by the living God; yet He is not for that reason any less God Himself; but because He is the *Angel of the Covenant*, the Mediator, God and man, and in that respect less than His Father—*for my Father*, He says, *is greater than I* <note>John 14:28.</note>—so it is by no means surprising that He swears by His name, just as He is likewise shown swearing and lifting His hands to heaven in the twelfth chapter of Daniel. The thing which He swears is *that there shall be no more time*; that is, that after the various periods of time He had appointed for the duration of the Antichrist—which He signifies in the twelfth chapter by *one thousand two hundred and sixty days*, or, *a time, and times, and half a time*—there should be no more time, nor any longer delay of the fall of his reign; but that then certainly the mystery of the downfall of that Kingdom, which for so many centuries had waged war against the Saints, would be revealed; and that the Kingdoms of the earth would then unite themselves with Christ, who shall rule over all nations forever. John says thereafter that he approached the Angel to demand the open little book from him, and that the Angel, giving it to him, commanded that he should eat it up: which John having done, he found it in his mouth sweet as honey, but his belly became

## The Two Witnesses Slain by the Beast.

->Revelation, Chapter XI verses 3—27.<-

After John had taken the little book from the hand of the Angel and had eaten it, he was told that he must prophesy before many peoples and kings. He was given a reed <note>The "reed" here refers to a measuring rod made from a stalk of a tall water plant.</note> like a measuring rod, with a command to measure the Temple of God, and the inner court, where the altar of burnt offerings stood, and where the assembly of the people took place: But concerning the outer court, which was nearly twice as large, in which the Jews and the Gentiles who were proselytes <note>Proselytes were non-Jewish people who had converted to the faith or followed Jewish customs.</note> entered without distinction—and which was the same area that in the time of Jesus Christ was desecrated by the selling of sheep and doves—John was commanded that he should not measure it. The cause of this prohibition was pointed out to him with these words: *For it is given unto the Gentiles; and the holy city shall they tread under foot forty and two months.* This outer court, which made up a part of the Temple, represented in this vision a certain society of people who would belong to the Church, just as that court belonged to the Temple of God, and who, being united by many signs in the outward profession of the Gospel, would cover themselves with the glorious name of the Christian Church, but in which various superstitions, taken and borrowed from the Pagans, would have such a great influence that they would be
<column-break/>
desecrated by them. The command which God gave not to measure that court, which was thus filled with Gentiles, shows that he no longer regarded it as a place which he held for his own, or which was a part of his Temple. The holy city, which was to be trodden underfoot or desecrated by the Gentiles during forty-two months—which are one thousand two hundred and sixty days, and according to the <term>Prophetic style</term> <note>The "day-year principle" is a method of interpretation where a "day" in prophecy represents a literal calendar "year."</note> where a day is taken for a year, are twelve hundred and sixty years—was also that same Church, represented under the name of Jerusalem, which even at the time of her greatest corruption, when she was still red and smoking with Jesus' blood, is called the *Holy City* by the Evangelist Matthew. But the Angel who spoke to John, and who, as we have said, was Jesus himself, added to this, *that he would give it, namely the holy city, she who alone deserved to bear that name, to his two Witnesses*, and these two Witnesses would prophesy—that is, preserve the true doctrine of the Prophets and Apostles—during those one thousand two hundred and sixty days that the Church would be trodden down by the Gentiles. He represents them as *clothed in sackcloth*, because it would be a time of oppression. These Witnesses were the true Christians, zealous for the maintenance of the truth, and they were signified by the number *two*, to give John to understand that the number of those who would preserve the pure doctrine of the Gospel in those times of corruption would be very small,

This showed John that the truth had not died with the Martyrs, but that it *would lift itself up and hold its ground more than ever before,* to the amazement of those who had so cruelly persecuted them. After all this, the seventh Angel blew his trumpet, and there were *great voices in Heaven, which said,*

> The Kingdoms of the world have become our Lord’s, and His Christ’s, and He shall reign as king for all eternity:

This was a prophecy of the fall of the reign of the Beast, and the general conversion of the Jews and Gentiles, which will one day constitute the glory of Jesus Christ and the happiness of the entire earth.

### Revelation, Chapter XIV. verse 1.

God consistently maintained this order in the visions of the Revelation: that alongside those which foretold harsh sufferings for the Church, He added a vision that provided great matter for comfort. This can easily be perceived throughout this entire book, and it ought to be noted by us as an effect of the wisdom and goodness of God, who thus tempers all the oppressions of His Church through various

<column-break/>

and over all peoples of various languages; so that all who dwelt upon the earth, and whose names were not written in the book of the Lamb, worshipped it. John breaks off the thread of his narrative of visions here for a moment to give the Christian reader this weighty advice: *If anyone has ears, let him hear; If anyone leads into captivity, he shall go into captivity; If anyone kills with the sword, he must be killed with the sword. Here is the patience and the faith of the saints.* After these words he resumes his story, and says that he saw yet another Beast coming up out of the earth; it had two horns like those of a lamb, but it spoke like the Dragon: furthermore, it exercised all the power of the first Beast in its presence; and it caused the inhabitants of the earth to worship the first Beast, whose deadly wound was healed. It performed great signs, even making fire come down from Heaven; and it deceived the inhabitants of the earth by those signs, commanding them to make an image for the Beast which had received that great blow of the sword to its head without dying from it. Furthermore, it received power to work through its deceptions in such a way that it gave life to the image of the Beast and made it speak, thereby to draw a greater number of worshippers to it. It also had power to kill all who refused to worship the image of the Beast; and it forced all the world, great and small, rich and poor, free and slave, to carry a mark on their right hand or on their foreheads, by which it appeared that they were worshippers of the Beast, without which they dared not show themselves in public or undertake any business. Here, says John, ends the account of this vision; here is wisdom: *Let him who has understanding calculate the number of the Beast, for it is the number of a man: and his number is six hundred sixty-six.* People have at all times been very busy searching for this hidden and profound number; and almost everyone has thought that they had found it in the calculation they made of it. Modern scholars have likely come closer than the ancients, because time has shown them many outcomes which had not yet been seen in the first centuries of the Church, and which have shed much light on the depths of the Revelation: but it is not appropriate to recount those explanations here.

Since the seal, which God presses upon the foreheads of his redeemed, is the Holy Spirit, with which he seals them *until the day of deliverance*, so this seal brings its impression into the innermost part of the heart, where it imprints the features of the light and the flame of righteousness and holiness. He adds to it: *These are they who follow the Lamb wherever he goes: these were bought from among men, as firstfruits <term>firstfruits: the first portion of a harvest, dedicated to God as an offering</term> unto God and the Lamb*: that is, to be dedicated to God and Jesus Christ, just as under the Old Law the firstfruits belonged to God, and were sanctified to him in his Temple. *In their mouth no guile was found, that is*, they have never disguised nor forsaken the truth; for they are blameless before the throne of God. Strictly speaking, there is no one who is blameless before God except Christ; but those whom he cleanses through his Spirit, and washes in his blood, he makes holy and blameless before his Father. This Angel cried with a loud voice: *Fear God, and give him glory, for the hour of his judgment against the great City, and against the Beast, has come: And worship him who made the Heaven, the earth, the sea, and the fountains of waters*. It is not that those who worship the Beast had not also worshipped God, the Creator of the world; but it is that God has never counted such as his worshippers, who, while showing him some reverence, at the same time fall down before images of wood or stone. These words deserve that all Christians keep them always before their eyes, and never let them be erased from their hearts.

# The Seven Vials of God's Wrath Poured Out.

## Revelation, Chapter XVI. 1, 2. etc.

The visions did not cease, and God seemed to want to open all the future before the eyes of John. He showed him the Son of Man seated upon a cloud, with a golden crown upon his head, and a sickle in his hand; whereupon an Angel, who also had a sickle, cut the grapes from the vineyard of the earth, and threw them into the winepress of God’s wrath. I saw, the Apostle says next, another great and wonderful sign in Heaven, namely seven Angels who had the command to strike the earth with the seven last plagues, with which the wrath of God was to end his vengeance. I also saw a sea of glass, mixed with fire; and after that the Temple or Throne of God was opened in Heaven, and the seven Angels, who were charged to pour out the seven plagues, went out of the Temple, clothed in pure and shining linen, and girded with golden belts around the chest. These Angels had the command to pour out the vials <term>vials: from the Dutch "fioolen," these are shallow bowls used in ancient times for offerings or pouring liquids</term> of God's wrath upon the earth, and they all did so one after the other. The second Angel poured out his vial upon the sea, which became like blood, and all the animals that were in it died therefrom. The third poured out his bowl upon the rivers and the fountains, and their waters were changed into blood. After that, that Angel cried out: *You are righteous, O Lord, who is, and who was, and who shall be, because you have judged this; since they have shed the blood of the Saints and the Prophets, so you have also given them blood to drink—*

The fifth Angel then poured out his bowl upon the throne of the Beast, and his Kingdom became darkened, and the men who had given themselves over to his service gnawed their tongues because of the intensity of their pains; they blasphemed the God of Heaven, and they did not repent of their works. But because the paths which these unclean spirits were to take back and forth to deceive men were much to be feared, our Savior cried out at this place, to recommend watchfulness to the Believers: *Behold, I come as a thief. ### *The Fall of Babylon.*
## Revelation, Chapter XVIII. verse 2.

After the seven Angels had poured out the vials <note>original: "fioolen"</note> of God's wrath, one of them came to John and said: "Come here, I will show you the judgment of the great Whore, with whom the Kings of the earth have committed fornication, and who has made the inhabitants of the earth drunk with the wine of her fornication, and who sits upon many waters," that is, who rules over many peoples, as the Angel himself explains. At the same time, the Apostle was carried away in the spirit into a wilderness, where he saw a woman sitting on a scarlet-red Beast, which was full of names of blasphemy: it had seven heads and ten horns; and she was clothed in purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold, precious stones, and pearls; having a golden drinking cup, full of abominations and uncleanness, in her hand. On her forehead was written: *Mystery; Babylon the Great, the mother of fornications, and of the abominations of the earth:* and she was drunk with the blood of the Saints, and with the blood of the witnesses of Jesus. # The Seven Vials of God’s Wrath Poured Out.

## Revelation, Chapter XVI. 1, 2. etc.

I saw, says the Apostle thereafter, another great and wonderful sign in Heaven, namely seven Angels who had the command to strike the earth with the seven last plagues, with which the wrath of God was to end His vengeance. I also saw a sea of glass, mixed with fire; and thereafter the Temple or Throne of God was opened in Heaven, and the seven Angels, who were charged to pour out the seven plagues, went out of the Temple, clothed in pure and shining linen, and girded about the chest with golden girdles. one immediately loses sight of Eden. One notices another vision that is even more remarkable, found in the 47th chapter of Ezekiel. That Prophet saw such a great multitude of waters flowing from under the threshold of the gate of God's Temple, that a deep and wide river was formed from them; and on the bank of that river grew fruit-bearing trees of all kinds, which brought forth new fruits every month of the year, and their leaves served for healing. This description is, in truth, much more similar to the one given to us by John than the first; because Grace is much more like the Glory of which it is the beginning and, so to speak, the design, than Nature—which appeared almost entirely alone in the earthly Paradise. However, the Holy Spirit has still left a distinction great enough between the description of John and that of Ezekiel to make it understood that the purposes in both were not entirely one and the same. The river which the Prophet saw was formed gradually from the waters coming from the Temple. This one seen by the Apostle was great and wide at its very origin. The first came from under the threshold of the gate, and the latter proceeded from the throne of God and of the Lamb. All these differences had their mysteries. On the two banks of the river shown to Ezekiel, there were fishers who made great catches of fish; here one finds nothing of the kind. The trees which stood on either side of Ezekiel’s river were fruit-bearing trees of various kinds; John speaks of only one tree. Those of Ezekiel are simply called *food-trees*; that of John bears the glorious name of the Tree of Life. This distinction is not made in vain; it has its profound depth and mys-

<column-break/>

tery. It is true, however, that those mystical trees, which the Prophet saw in a vision, and these of which the Apostle gives us the image, greatly resemble one another. All these similarities well deserve to be noted: but one must not, because of two or three similarities, take these two visions to be one and the same thing. ### H I S T O R I Y of the N. T E S T A M E N T.

<columns>
The Law and the Church under the Gospel have been signified in a mystical manner under this number of twelve, being that of the Patriarchs, the Tribes, and the Apostles, represented by the twelve <term>showbreads|Twelve consecrated loaves of bread placed weekly on a golden table in the Sanctuary as an offering, symbolizing the twelve tribes of Israel</term>, arranged six and six on the golden table of the Sanctuary, of which we have spoken elsewhere, and which is one of the sacred numbers of the book of Revelation. That which is said of the Tree of Life—that it brought forth its fruit from month to month—signifies the perpetual nature of the life-giving virtue of Christ for his entire Church; for this is the testimony of the Father, says John elsewhere, that eternal life is in his Son. Finally, the power which the leaves of the Tree of Life possessed to grant healing to the <note>original: "Heydenen" - refers here to the "nations" or "Gentiles" mentioned in Revelation 22:2</note> nations signifies that Christ is at once both the healing and the life of sinners. John ends the description of the Holy City by saying that the servants of God and of the Lamb would see his face, and carry his name upon their foreheads; that there would be no night, that God himself would be their light, and that they would reign as kings forever. Upon seeing such 

<column-break/>

great happiness, John leaves those—whom the desire to possess the infinite goods of the coming age cannot bring to a life of righteousness—to their passions and disorders; and he exhorts the Believers to sanctify themselves more and more, because nothing that is unclean can enter into the holy city, or be received into the possession of the glories of Heaven. Our Savior ends all those great visions which he showed to his Apostle by saying that he would not delay in coming to give his Church the reward for all her labor:
> *Behold*, he says, *I come quickly, and my reward is with me, to give every man according as his work shall be.*
At those words, John cries out:
> *Blessed are they that do his commandments, that they may have right to the tree of life, and may enter in through the gates into the city.*
And the Church, hearing from the mouth of her divine Bridegroom that he is ready to come, answers—inspired by his Spirit and enraptured by a divine passion:
> *Come, even so, come Lord Jesus. Amen.*

</columns>

# NOTICE
## CONCERNING THE
### GENEALOGY of JESUS CHRIST.

->Related in Matthew Chapter 1 and Luke Chapter 3.<-

The genealogies which the Evangelists Matthew and Luke have given us of Jesus Christ show that he was descended from David, according to the prophecies of the Prophets. The Holy Virgin his mother was descended from David through Solomon, because Salathiel, son of Jeconiah and father of Zerubbabel, at the time of the Babylonian captivity was married to a Princess descended from Nathan, in whose person that branch of the royal house likely ended; through that marriage, it was incorporated into the branch of the Kings of Judah, which was that of Solomon. This can be observed if one pays careful attention to the 27th verse of the third chapter of the Evangelist Luke, where it is said that Salathiel was a son of Neri, which Neri was descended from Nathan. For Salathiel was actually the son of Jeconiah, King of Judah, as appears from 1 Chronicles 4:17 <note>The author likely means 1 Chronicles 3:17, which lists Salathiel as the son of Jeconiah.</note>; thus Neri is called his father in Luke only because he was his father-in-law; just as Joseph is called the son of Heli in the same chapter, verse 23, although he was only his son-in-law. That which now strongly supports this view is that the prophecies indicating that the Messiah would come from the line of Solomon never mention his brother Nathan on that occasion; from which it must follow that the Holy Virgin sprang from the household of Solomon, and that what Luke relates of the lineage of Nathan is only because it had come to end and incorporate itself into that of Solomon, in the person of Zerubbabel, son of Salathiel.

Regarding Joseph, the betrothed husband of Mary, he was also descended from Solomon through Salathiel and through Zerubbabel; and since he was consequently descended from the same lineage as Mary, the genealogy which Matthew made of Joseph—who was held to be the father of Jesus Christ—could also serve as a genealogical account for the Holy Virgin; for since the Jews did not derive their genealogies from the side of the women, that of the Husband was sufficient when the husband and the wife both sprang from one house, as has been shown in the third History of this volume.

Jesus comes to the house of Martha and Mary, sisters of Lazarus. Both are sensitive to this honor, and their hearts are struck with joy because of it. <image-desc>An oval etching framed by a laurel wreath. It depicts a man on a stone platform gesturing towards a group of people and cattle in a pastoral landscape. People never know the true value of God’s favors: if they knew them, they would value them like Paul, and with him count all other things as smoke and dung <note>original: "rook en drek" — This is a reference to Philippians 3:8. The author uses vivid language to describe earthly things as worthless compared to spiritual knowledge.</note>, for the excellence of the knowledge of our Savior Christ Jesus. The heart never lacks pretexts to excuse itself from the works of godliness, yet the most plausible <note>original: "glimpigſte" — meaning those excuses that seem most fair or shining on the surface.</note> are often the worst; at least they are most to be feared, just like poison, which the finer it is, the more deadly it is. A heart that truly seeks God lets nothing hold it back. My soul cries out to you, O God; My soul thirsts for God, for the living God. When shall I enter and appear before God’s face! Psalm 42:2, 3.

Where sin has increased, there grace has been much more abundant. Romans 5:20.

<image-desc>An oval etching framed by two crossed palm branches. The scene depicts the interior of the Temple in Jerusalem. **The** value of a gift which one person gives to another is in the gift itself: but the value of an offering made to God is always less in the object itself than in the heart of the one who offers. Men weigh gold and silver in a scale; *but the Lord weighs the hearts,* Proverbs 21:2. <note>original: "penninkjes" — small copper coins of very little value, often referred to in English Bibles as "mites."</note>

<image-desc>An oval etching framed by two crossed palm branches. The scene depicts an outdoor meal being served beneath a large palm tree. **To** give alms to a poor person through a simple impulse of pity is to give something to humanity, and in a sense to oneself; because one and the same humanity is shared by both the giver of the alms and the receiver. But to give alms solely for the sake of Jesus Christ, and to a believer, is to give to Christ. *Whoever is kind to the poor lends to the Lord:* Proverbs 19:17.

# HISTORY of the N. TESTAMENT.

<image-desc>An oval etching framed by a laurel wreath tied with a ribbon at the bottom. It depicts the biblical act of mercy: giving drink to the thirsty. Other figures are seen in the background, including one drawing water from a well near a classical archway.</image-desc>

<margin>See page 93</margin>
*I was thirsty, and you gave me something to drink. Matthew 25 verse 35.*

**The** greatest services in the world are not always rewarded <note>original: "vergolden" — meaning to repay, compensate, or requite</note>; because those who receive them cannot always do everything they wish; or they do not always wish to do what they ought. It is quite different with the services we render to God; for even the very least of them never go without reward. He actually receives no benefit from us; for if He could receive such a thing, then He would not be God: but what we do for His children for His sake, He regards as if it were done to Himself, and takes it upon Himself to reward it. *Whoever gives one of these little ones even a cup of cold water to drink, in the name of a disciple, truly I say to you, he shall by no means lose his reward. Matthew 10:42.*

**There** were formerly Saints who, through charitable hospitality <note>original: "herbergzaamheyd"</note>, received Angels into their homes when they thought they were hosting men. Hebrews 13:2. Nowadays, one can extend that holy virtue even further, and give shelter to Christ Himself in the person of a stranger. *He who receives you, receives me. Matthew 10:40.*

# HISTORY of the N. TESTAMENT.

<image-desc>An engraving within an oval frame made of a laurel wreath. It depicts a scene inside a stone building, likely a prison. Several figures are shown: one man sits on a bench, another rests on the floor, and a central figure stands as if visiting them. In the background, other figures are visible through a doorway.</image-desc>

->*I was in prison and you came to me. Matthew 25 verse 36. See page 93.*<-

A Christian who suffers imprisonment for Christ's sake always finds in the cause of his dishonor a rich source of consolation: but nevertheless, he needs to be helped in the pious reflections <note>original: "aanmerkingen"—observations or meditations</note> which faith leads him to make; for since the Christian is not without the human nature <note>original: "den mensch"—referring to the "old man" or fallen human nature that remains alongside the spiritual self</note>, the human often does the Christian an injustice. The flesh fights against the Spirit, and Nature against Grace. *Remember those in prison, as if you were imprisoned with them. Hebrews 13:3.*

---

<image-desc>An engraving within an oval frame made of a laurel wreath. The scene depicts Jesus Christ standing in the Garden of Gethsemane. Three disciples are shown sleeping on the ground around him. In the distant background, a group of figures carrying torches is approaching.</image-desc>

->*Christ finds his Disciples sleeping. Luke 22 verse 45. See page 99.*<-

While Jesus Christ prepared himself through prayer for the great sacrifice of his own person to divine justice, for the reconciliation of the sins of mankind, which he was about to perform, and while his spirit was full of the image of God’s terrors, set in battle array <note>original: "slagórde"—a military term for a line of battle, suggesting the psychological weight of the coming ordeal</note> before him, so that he sweated great drops of blood from it, his three Disciples—Peter, James, and John—whom he had chosen from among all the others to take with him, allowed themselves to be overcome by sleep: every time he came to them, he found them sleeping. How small is our zeal! Even the most lively and alert is subject to weakness and wretched faintness. As soon as God withdraws from us, and we stand on our own, the frailty of the flesh causes us to fail. *Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall shine upon you. Ephesians 5:14.*

# HISTORY of the N. TESTAMENT.
<meta>catchword: Judas</meta>

<image-desc>An oval etching framed by a laurel wreath depicting Jesus being blindfolded and mocked. A soldier is seen tying a cloth around Jesus's head while others strike him or watch. The hardest thing for us to endure patiently is contempt. It places a sting <note>original: "angel"—a thorn or stinger, referencing the pain of wounded pride</note> in the heart of even the humblest, which causes it to swell and awakens a vanity within that has never entirely died. Peter exposes himself to temptation without necessity and succumbs to it: three times he denies his Master in the house of Caiaphas. But it was then primarily that what the Lord had said to him two days before was fulfilled in that Apostle: *If I do not wash you, you have no part with me.* John 13:8. <note>The author connects Christ's earlier act of washing the disciples' feet to the spiritual washing of Peter's soul through repentance.</note>

# HISTORY of the NEW TESTAMENT.

<image-desc>An oval etching framed by a leafy wreath. In the foreground, a man (Judas) is depicted falling headfirst from a high, rocky cliff. In the background, an ancient city with towers and arches is visible under a cloudy sky.</image-desc>

->Judas’s despair. Acts 1:18. See page 103.<-

Judas was at first greedy and self-serving; then he became a traitor and sold Jesus for money. A passion <note>original: "drift"—referring to an uncontrolled impulse or driving emotion</note> leads a person far when it is allowed to run its course: in the beginning, one flatters it and takes pleasure in it, as with a young lion that does not yet have teeth or claws: but imperceptibly it grows claws and teeth, and one is devoured by it. *Then, when desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is full-grown, brings forth death. James 1:15.*

---

<image-desc>An oval etching framed by a leafy wreath. It shows a scene inside a room where a young man (Eutychus) lies on the ground, surrounded by a crowd of people in ancient robes. Eutychus fell asleep during the sermon of the Apostle Paul, and it cost him his life. He sat in a window of the hall where Paul was preaching, which was on the third floor. Sleep overcame him, he fell from above, and died from the impact <note>original: "besturf het"—literally "died of it," implying a sudden death resulting from the fall</note>. The Apostle immediately ran to him with the multitude of his listeners and restored his life to him. *This fall was not unto death, but for the glory of God. John 11:4.* <note>The Dutch text cites John 2:4, but the quote and context refer to the sentiment of John 11:4 regarding Lazarus.</note>

# HISTORY of the N. TESTAMENT.

<image-desc>An oval engraving enclosed in a leaf wreath border. It illustrates the biblical story of the prophet Agabus and the Apostle Paul. In an interior setting with various onlookers, Agabus is bent over in the center, binding his own legs with a long belt or girdle. Paul and others observe the scene with grave expressions.</image-desc>

->Agabus binds himself with the girdle of the Apostle Paul. Acts 21 verse 11.<-

Everywhere the Apostle Paul passed through while traveling to Jerusalem, he found people, inspired by the Spirit <note>original: "door den Geest aan-geblaazen"—literally "blown into by the Spirit," describing divine inspiration</note>, who foretold that the Jews in Jerusalem would seize and bind him. A certain prophet from Judea named Agabus, having met him at Caesarea, took a girdle <note>a "girdle" in this context is a long sash or belt used to fasten a tunic</note> that he happened to see in a room and bound himself with it, saying, *The man to whom this girdle belongs, the Jews shall so bind in Jerusalem.* And it was indeed Paul's girdle. All these prophecies were fulfilled. Paul finally arrived in Jerusalem; the Jews seized him in the Temple and took him to prison, from where he was led to Caesarea, and from Caesarea to Rome. His bonds became manifest throughout the whole <term>Judgment Hall</term> <note>original: "Rechthuys"—referring to the Praetorium or the governor’s palace where legal proceedings occurred</note>, through the conversions of which those bonds were instruments in God's hand. *I suffer trouble, even unto bonds, as an evil-doer; but the word of God is not bound. 2 Tim 2. 9.*

<image-desc>An oval engraving enclosed in a leaf wreath border depicting a scene from the Book of Revelation. A woman, representing the Church, stands in the sky "clothed with the sun" (surrounded by a radiant aureole) and with a crescent moon under her feet. She wears a crown of twelve stars. To the left, a multi-headed dragon emerges from the clouds, poised to devour her child.</image-desc>

->The Woman and the Dragon. Rev. 12 verse 4. See page 169.<-

The Woman whom the Apostle John saw in Heaven was surrounded by the Sun, had the Moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars. This was the Christian Church, which shines all around with the light of Jesus Christ, the Sun of Righteousness: The moon which she had under her feet was the image of the <term>Synagogue</term> <note>in this symbolic context, the "Synagogue" represents the Old Covenant or the Jewish religious system, which the Church is seen as standing upon or superseding</note>; and the twelve stars represented the twelve Apostles. Beside her there appeared a terrible Dragon, who only waited for a fit opportunity to devour the woman and the child she was about to bear. This dragon is the Devil, who always stands ready to tear apart the Church and her children. *Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour. 1 Pet. 5. 8.*

# HISTORY of the N. TESTAMENT.

<image-desc>An engraving within an oval wreath frame depicting the Woman of the Apocalypse. A winged female figure flies through the air towards a forest on the right. In the bottom left, a multi-headed dragon breathes fire or smoke up toward her as she escapes.</image-desc>

->The Woman persecuted by the Dragon. Rev. XII. verse 13. See page 170.<-

Here the first oracle <note>In this context, "oracle" refers to a divine prophecy or revelation from God.</note> of the world presents itself, in which God foretold the eternal war that would exist between the Devil and the Church, and especially between the Devil and Jesus Christ, the Head and the Savior of the Church. *I will put enmity between you and the woman,* said God to the Serpent, *between your seed and her seed: the same shall crush your head, and you shall bruise its heel.* Never has any prophecy been better verified. Jesus Christ triumphed over the Devil at the very moment when the Devil thought to triumph over Christ, by dealing Him the blow that brought Him to death on the cross. And the Church, though always persecuted by the Devil, has never been conquered or destroyed by him.
